Well, here we are again, friends. Another Assassins Creed and another trip back into history. Now that I've had a chance to really pump some hours into it, it's time to update this review and give it some more depth.
In short, this is the best Assassin's Creed since Black Flag. Really, it's the best ever. Period. But we'll get into that.
This time around it's in ancient Egypt, but not like super-ancient Egypt or anything because it takes place in like 50 BCE as opposed to the era of like the New Kingdom in 1500 BCE (it really is crazy to think just how long Egypt had been a great, civilized nation before the likes of Rome and Greece in Europe).
The game starts a couple centuries after Alexander conquered the world and one of his best pals, Ptolemy, established a rather successful dynasty in Egypt. Cleopatra and her rotten brother-husband Ptolemy XIII are feuding over the throne, and now Caesar and the Romans are about to get involved.
I mean, finally some ancient Romans in an AC game. But that's that for context.
What we have here is a game that completely puts on display just how much Ubisoft has finally learned from its own past mistakes and from the successes of other games. Everything from the setting and story to the combat and exploration is vastly improved.
Hell, Ubisoft has even surprised me on the subject of micro-transactions. It has shown enormous restraint, and the game is totally enjoyable and playable without any need to purchase items from the store. I am 62 hours in and I think I've looked at the store all of two times. And yeah, I get that not having micro-transactions in a single-player game is like the barest minimum standard a game should have. But the fact that this ranks as a positive for the game just shows the grim reality of the modern gaming industry.
A good parallel is Middle Earth: Shadow of War, a good game published by a bad company that has pushed headlong into making micro-transactions a fundamental part of single-player gameplay - an effort to improve the company's bottom line obviously.
Shadow of War is a game with pay-to-win multiplayer and a single-player experience where loot boxes and war chests are constantly shoved in your face, asking you to drop $9.99 on tokens each time you want a chance at some new Legendary followers (with good traits for once maybe). AC: Origins is NOT that game.
Just to be clear, if you see any reviewers on here bashing AC: Origins for having micro-transactions, remember that it's nonsense. Steam reviews for AAA titles are ALWAYS full of such nonsense.
Moving on.
Unlike some of the other more recent installments, this game gives you a full world to discover. In many ways, it is akin to The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt.
Remember how we all ended up spending hundreds of hours in Wild Hunt and saying to ourselves, "Wow, that was a game truly worth the $60 price tag." Yeah, AC:Origins is another one of those. Not kidding. It's worth it.
The scope and magnitude of the game is enormous. I don't have specifics but I would dare to say it's as big or bigger than Wild Hunt. I'm 60 hours in and I am on like my 6th region. I haven't counted them all but there are certainly more than 20 different regions. I'm actually still fairly early on in the main quest line, too. There is just a lot to do and it's easy to get lost in this world.
I mean, you can hop on your horse and ride from Alexandria, to the Great Pyramids at Giza, to the sacred city of Memphis and on into the vast desert.
One of the things I really love about the game is it's attention to detail. Like The Witcher 3, which had a dynamic world full of war crimes, racism and other real-world parallels, AC: Origins really seems to have a feel for the time period.
You really can tell a huge difference moving between different parts of the world. For instance, in Memphis you get a more traditional view of ancient Egypt, while in Alexandria you are presented with the Hellenic world (the merge of East and West and the dominance of Greek culture).
There is great attention to detail here, with the game portraying the prejudice and contempt that many of the Greeks in Egypt must have had for their native counterparts - remember, at this point Egypt is essentially under the control of a foreign, Greek dynasty. Ptolemy was a Macedonian general who took over Egypt after Alexander's death and the fracturing of his empire.
This AC game really makes you feel like you have an entire era to explore. Not just a couple big cities or something. The entire freaking Nile Delta and much of the Upper Kingdom of Cleopatra's Egypt.
With Witcher 3, CDPR achieved gaming perfection. And Assassin's Creed Origins is the first single-player game I've encountered that has learned from it. Maybe you think it's a con that AC: Origins emulates Wild Hunt, but I really, really don't. I think more games should do exactly what AC has done.
So in addition to this huge world comprising Cleopatra's Egypt, you have some pretty incredible gameplay. The combat is my favorite of any AC game. It's like a combination of Witcher 3 and Dark Souls. It's also much more difficult than previous installments of the series.
I love the RPG mechanics of the game. The skill tree is pretty neat and gearing out your character is far more intricate and intuitive than I expected.
Plus you get to hunt hippos and crocodiles, so yeah. It's cool.
I've only encountered a few fairly minor bugs. Nothing big. Thus far, the game runs just fine.
TLDR: Assassins Creed meets Witcher 3. And it works beautifully.

Of all the Assassin's Creed games, this arguably has the most negative press aside from Unity (but that's another story).
Connor is a bit of a neutral character, but he isn't likeable from a player perspective.  There could be so many good story arcs in Connor knowing only a native lifestyle and transitioning into a colonial life and being recruited by an Assassin.  Instead there wasn't even a transition, he just instantly fit in with the colonists like he lived with them since birth, and in 6 months he was an assassin, believing everything they believed, and hunting templars.  There was a bit of a revege story, but the way it was portrayed made connor look more petty than anything, and that was reinforced by constant childish outbursts.  By comparison, Ezio's revenge story drove his initial actions, but he developed from that, and realized there were bigger, more important things.  That doesn't happen with Connor.  Finally, the facial profile Ubisoft used made Connor look like he aged 40 years between 1769, and 1773, then toward 1780 he looked younger again which was distracting.  In short Connor was a terrible protagonist with little redeemable character development.
The main story missions are standard Assassin's Creed with more open combat, and less assassination compared to AC 2, and Brotherhood.  Sort of makes sense considering it's a war, but I think the best part of the AC2 series of games was that you actually used your Assassin's blades.  The first 5 sequences (at least) seem like an extended training sequence to me, so that's at least 5 hours learning to play the game.  The reason I think this game is so disliked is because you don't care what happens next for the first 6 sequences, it's only in the last half of the game that the story becomes intriguing.
The Side missions are the most redeeming part of this game.  The Naval battles were heralded, and likely gave rise to AC4 (Probably as good as AC2 in terms of story, play it).  Definitely play through all of those missions, they're a blast.  Secondly, the Homestead missions in this game are the best of any of the series.  You get to the point to which you care what happens to those settlers.  At the end of the game, I would have much rather had a synopsis of what happened to those settlers than what happened to Connor.  The Captain Kidd missions also were fun to play.  The rest to me didn't really seem worth the effort.  Most of them don't even have dialogue, you walk up to them, and they say "Thank You", and that's it apparently.
So long as you are getting this game during an Ubisoft sale, which happens every 6 months or less, pick it up.  It's not a bad play once you get through the first half of the game.  Other than that, there are better AC games out there, so play those over again first.

So, by now it's fairly clear that Artifex Mundi is the king of HOGs, or hidden object games, on Steam. Well, how does their most recent title fare? Let's find out!
Tibetan Quest is the newest title from Artifex Mundi, the Polish developers (and publishers) of dozens of HOGs, many of which are on Steam. From my personal experience, I've really enjoyed most of the games I've played from them (Time Mysteries 1 was an exception, but it was also one of their first games so that's a bit excusable), so I was looking forward to trying out this new one. Thankfully, it delivered!
The gameplay of Tibetan Quest consists of what you'd expect from a HOG: visit a bunch of areas, solve puzzles using items to progress, complete some minigames, and most importantly, play some hidden object scenes! Now, you may or may not know what those consist of; if you don't, they're essentially the "I Spy" books in video game form. You're given a list of objects to find in a picture/scene, and all you need to do is find, or rather, click on them. The hidden object scenes generally looked great in Tibetan Quest, and the objects were quite hard to find sometimes. However, one small complaint that I do have with these scenes is that many of the objects are reused multiple times, like "stars", "hearts", etc.
The story of the game consists of you, a middle-aged woman, traveling to Tibet to rescue your niece after she mysteriously disappears during a trip there. As the game progresses, you slowly discover what the villain's motive is through some of the minigames, which I thought was pretty clever. The game doesn't dump exposition on you either; the focus is definitely on the gameplay, which is quite nice. Sure, the story may not be anything particularly special, but it gets the job done. There was also an extra bonus chapter that I didn't really check out much, though I believe it explains what happens after the game's initial ending, so that's pretty neat to see as most games don't expand upon their endings.
Visually, it's an Artifex Mundi game for sure, even if this one isn't developed by them. By it being an Artifex Mundi game, I mean that it looks great! They somehow never cease to impress me with the high quality, polish, and general attention to detail given to both areas and hidden object scenes in their games. On top of that, Tibetan Quest even features some fairly action-packed cutscenes involving a dragon trying to stop our heroine from rescuing her daughter. Sure, some of the effects (like the explosions) are a little silly and perhaps not the best quality, but overall it was still quite nice to see that the game tried to add some variety to its visuals.
Though, that does lead me to another minor complaint I have with the game - the facial animations. There's only a few times when talking to characters is necessary to progress, but whenever I had to talk to someone I couldn't help but laugh when I watched their faces move. The faces look fairly realistic, so when the only thing that moves is their mouths it looks a bit silly. I kind of found it charming though, so it wasn't too big of a deal for me, and thus, only a minor complaint.
By this point, you may have realized that I'm not criticizing the game much, and that's because it's simply hard to criticize! If you're not a fan of HOGs, this may not be the game for you, though if you enjoy adventure games, puzzle games, or just casual games in general I think you may really enjoy Tibetan Quest. It's not perfect, but it's certainly a great game!
If you're an Artifex Mundi fan, Tibetan Quest is another excellent game from them that is definitely worth picking up. If you're not yet a fan, what are you waiting for?

is a hidden object game style game with nice visuals and an enjoyable storyline to adventure through.  You journey to Tibet to find out what has happened to your niece when she travelled there several weeks beforehand.  You will then begin collecting items and using them to unlock and continue forward through frigid and snowy landscapes of Tibet, and along with intricately designed and stylized Buddhist temples that align the high mountainous in the area.
I like the art work of the people as well as the graphic style of the landscapes.  The animations are nice, and I think they add a lot to the overall game experience.
The sequence of events doesn't feel broken, and I like the continuity in the overall gameplay experience.
There was a large variety of puzzles throughout the game, and I enjoyed solving them.  This has been a pleasure for me to play through.
The voices in the game are well done for the most part, which is a nice thing.  The mouth movements are right on par with the voices.  Nice to see this, but I cannot say how this may be if there are other languages to possibly try, since I did not mess with this to see.  Nothing interfered with my overall concentration or mood while playing.  Everything felt in place with the story.
I thought all of the sound effects were very enjoyable and how they should be, and it all fit well with what was going on.
Collecting the extra items is fun for bonus achievements.  I like having the side things to look for in almost every room that creates a sort of side collection as you are going.  Like a mini-game within the game.
Extras menu has some neat stuff, and I guess you can unlock other things in it as you go.
Steam cloud functionality often goes unnoticed by me, but this would be nice carrying saves over if I played small bits on my laptop before going to sleep or something.
This is sort of a gripe for most all of these I have played, and it's that things you have in your inventory will not work when they should in theory, and the solution is too linear.  You could use your one scepter item to solve many of the things you end up going out of your way for to get an item similar that works instead.  I do enjoy the extra stuff, but it's just something inside me that is a realist, so I kind of get frustrated about some of these kinds of things.  No reflection on the particular game.  Just thinking how I would be in the same situation...  Also the fact that many items that would be of use later are simply dropped and never used again.  If you kept the item the whole time, or simply went back for it over and over, it could come in handy for several other areas where you need an item to get another item, for example.
Other than the above, which is more of a universal thought about hidden object games and many point and clicks in general, I don't have anything to say here really.  There isn't much I can complain about for a hidden object game.  This one is very well done.  If I could nitpick, I suppose some of the facial animations look funny when they are speaking to you, in some cases, but I kind of like this, honestly.
I found one strange glitch near the end near a certain statue you have to alter.  Going two rooms back, then moving into that room makes duplicate scepters.  I think this might only trigger after a conversation in the mausoleum, and the need to grab a gem in that room to charge the scepter, but it was strange to hear the noise and see the number continue to increase.  The noise and increase stopped once I picked up the appropriate item to continue on.
I completely broke my first playthrough by using the teleport feature after going through the portal near the end.  I couldn't use the portal anymore, and I just got a white screen when I entered the room to teleport, so there is no way back.  Maybe there will be an eventual fix for this, so I can finish the game on my original playthrough, but at the current time, there is no real fix for this at the time of writing, and the only solution is starting a new game!
This is a terrific game, and for anyone who likes hidden object games, I highly recommend this.  It's a lot of fun and everything about it exemplifies the genre, from the art to the music to the overall continuity in story.  The puzzles and the finding of objects is great and they do a nice job changing it up a bit with the puzzles, as well as the situational use of objects to find other ones.  This makes me want to play more of the games I already have by Artifex Mundi, since I'm so impressed with this title.  I will not hesitate to grab more of these in the future!  Completely all around great hidden object game.

I don't know about other people but back in the 80's I was a huge fan of those puzzle books, where's waldo, turning page after page, trying to find that red and white striped maniac among a sea of strange and interesting situations.  Was Waldo at a political rally, a circus, a camping ground, sea world or heck even just lounging outside his house, cooking some hot dogs and hamburgers, Ms. Waldo and little Waldo nearby with their own red and white striped shirts.  I can't remember, I just remember spending hours at a time pouring over the books, gritting my teeth and mapping out a grid of the page, searching each sector just waiting for him to pop out before my eyes..
Fast forward 20 - 30 years later and I'm still enamored with hidden objects, while I've outgrown my Where's waldo book reading days, I can and very much do enjoy playing hidden object games.  Finding various items scattered about a trunk, a chest, a crashed airplane, a Tibetan temple, it's all good...   Thanks to the publisher Artifex Mundi I have no shortage of hidden object games to choose from, whether it's clowns, carnivals, murder mysteries, I know seeing the name Artifex Mundi next to publisher I can be certain I'll be in for a real treat.
When you were seeing off your beloved niece three weeks ago as she embarked on an archaeological trip to Tibet, nothing could have foreshadowed the dramatic events that were about to unfold. Only yesterday you received a mysterious letter from which you learned that Larisa and her crew had gotten lost in a snow storm.  When you arrive in Tibet you quickly discover your Niece has set out about 2 weeks ago and has yet to return.  Will you find Larisa, will you discover what happened at Shangri-La or will you become another missing person.
Gameplay is your typical hidden object fare, hidden object, puzzles, collectibles.  The hidden object comes in two forms, either words or shapes, they aren't overly complicated, and if you do find yourself trapped you can use a hint.  If that isn't enough you can choose to play a game of Mojong instead of solving the puzzle.   You also have a mix up puzzle to solve occasionally, a picture is broken up into numerous shapes, you need to twist and move the shapes until the picture is clear.   As you progress along in the story more areas unlock for you to search through.  The game also has several sets of collectibles, swords, coins, stars and apples.
If you're a fan of HOG's, you'll love this game, it's got everything a HOG game lover would want and need...  An interesting well told story, casual hidden object puzzles and crisp graphics and sound, I really don't see any reason for people to avoid buying this game, you should buy it now and start searching, start finding and enjoy this amazingly fun casual game.  Artifex Mundi has yet again brought HOG game lovers another masterpiece..  I certainly can't wait to see what game these guys release next, if it's as good as Tibetan Quest then i'll be a really happy camper.

First, thanks much again Artifex Mundi, for the 'very special key' awarded in one of their contests. :))
Now to the review:
There's a map and fast travel. :) (There are also a few different regions, the previous one(s) becoming inaccessible once you advanced to the next one.)
The scenery is amazing, the shiny colours hit just the right spot in me.
The Hidden Object scenes are fair to easy, and pleasant, with words, silhouettes, and morphing objects as well as some needing a task to be completed first inside the HO scene.
The minigames are interesting, and new compared to what I've seen in Artifex Mundi games before. There's even a kind of Sokoban puzzle. :)
The collectibles would be fun to collect if the map would indicate scenes that had any still. As it is, I'd need a guide to not miss any, and that would just distract from the game (and thus ruin my enjoyment).
Concerning the story, this time it's an aunt looking for a missing niece. I like that for being different. :)
Overall, a really nice experience.

i was _soooo_ looking forward to this one (even posted about it in advance on G+), and it slapped me down in the very first few scenes...
a) the very first set of puzzles insults the user's intelligence. Three blocks of ice, one pickaxe. Only one of those blocks can be broken with the pickaxe. One cannot, for reasons it explains, and the third cannot... simply because. i.e. arbitrary. You've got to get a near-identical tool to break _that_ ice. WTF?
b) it won't let me melt ice using non-boiling water (whereas physics allows me to just fine - try pouring cold water over ice and see what happens). WTF?
c) one of the early-on HO scenes wants you to find a ring. The ring is placed almost directly next to a glove. The ring is big enough to fit around at least 3 fingers of that glove. i.e. it's the size of a bracelet, not a ring (except that that HO calls it a ring). WTF?
i far prefer a mediocre but internally consistent HOPA, like the Queen's Quest or Demon Hunter, to a HOPA with any notable amount of arbitrariness (which this one is full of).
Maybe someday i'll get over these offense to my sensibilities and give this another try, but i can only assume that i'll be faced with more "WTF!?!?!?" moments than i care to encounter.
Next, please...

Your niece Larissa embarked on a journey to the mythical Shangri-La, however, her party goes missing during a snowstorm. Not caring at all for your life, you follow her footsteps to rescue her...
That's the plot of the game: as usual, Artifex Mundi knows to choose the games with interesting stories. I really liked the beginning, though the ending was a little less well-written: it cuts abruptly and it's clear that it needs at least some more explanations or a sequel. Also, I'm wondering how the heroin, which must middle-aged and with a lot of money, ended up with nothing to advance a little more faster and fly a plane. It means that she was at least an adventurer in her youth.
The gameplay is pretty standard: find items, solve puzzles, clear hidden objects scenes (list or shaped). There is a little minor problem: the balance between the list of words and the list of shapes isn't great as you have more of the former than the latter. The puzzles are as usual easy to finish. You even have some passages (like the repair of the plane) where you're guided step-by-step and where you'll need to use objects you found earlier (or that you will find after when you can't advance anymore). You have also a game of mahjong (not really developped as there are only 2 or 3 different patterns and you can't be stuck, as it's shuffling automatically) if you don't want to play the hidden object scenes.
However, some actions aren't making sense: I've a staff that can melt ice and I need a magnifying glass at one moment for that specific act. Or also, a giant lizard is blocking the way and you have a sleeping potion in your inventory. My first move was to give it to it. Well, no. I needed to give it first a rake, so that I can get a pole, then use it as an harpoon to get a fish and to give it to the animal. And the sleeping potion. Well, apparently, it's better to use it on a spider than on the lizard...
While I loved the graphics and the beauty of the temples or of the mountain, there are two problems: I didn't like how the characters were animated. It's not fitting really well with the rest of the game and besides, I don't know why the faces were weird. The second little minor problem is probably how the developers are seeing Tibet as I was more under the impression to be in another province of China than Tibet itself. Besides, given the era where the story is set, I don't think that Tibet was already ruled by China at that moment. I suppose that they let their imagination (and their own view/stereotypes) instead of using a little more documentation and to avoid some clichés.
I liked the soundtrack, that's a real strong point here. It was very enjoyable all along and fitting to the ambiance.
Tibetan Quest isn't perhaps the best in terms of gameplay but I've been hooked into that magical world (even if it's not really Tibetan in itself). I liked it a lot. As usual, Artifex Mundi chose well. However, the next time, if they can at least choose a game with a better ending or publish the first The Secret Order and the others Vampire Legends if they managed to get the rights for Steam, I would be very happy.

I have quit playing Tera and most MMO's but since my experience with this game and its developers/support was quite interesting, I feel that many others may want to hear about it. I just can't do MMO's, my self esteem demands I take my suck elsewhere, I only quit because I can't tank as a warrior.
It's definitely a fun game with a big RolePlay and raid community, but it has very standard (grinding, RNGesus, quests) aspects that do not make it shine.
Like I stated before it has excellent RP and dedicated player groups, but I am here to tell you what makes it different.
Tera has a business model revolving around optional purchases, where nothing is 100% unobtainable through f2p. I approve of this (games cost money guys) and am glad that nothing is game breaking (mainly cosmetics and consumables).
Wait every MMO does that? OMGE WTF maaan
Of course, but I have a tale to tell. One that might set this developer ahead of others who make similar products in this cash money MMO world.
For reasons I will decline to share, I faced the daunting task of needing a refund for 3rd party purchases made through Steam. If you do not know how Steam handles 3rd party payments made with steam wallet funds it can be summed up as "Not my problem". However error occured and I contacted the developer (through a ticket on their support site) about needing a reversal of funds. There was (possibly still) a banner above the "create a support ticked" stating basically that there was a major backlog and support may take a month to reach. After filing all of that information through the dev I chose to get into contact with Steam support (as the purchase was made with their apps wallet) because if the support team at Tera actually took a month I would most likely never get the cash back. And since it was Steam unless I wanted to lose my account and all my games, chargeback (purchase was in error, and I don't use this as a first resort, only after getting in contact and exhausting all my options with a seller) is not an option.
This is the good part, when Steams mighty centurions of mechanically destructive auto support decided what needed to be done was the locking of all my most recent (even months old!) game purchases, the locking of trading and market, topped with the fact that they didn't even answer my tickets questions and addressed everything OTHER than my problem with nuclear force.
After ~4 days of waiting eventually I got a real boy (assuming blame for such a stupid combination of actions only could be placed on automation) and after 3 messages (over a few hours on the final day) Steam saves the day and unlocks my games, that were seperated by over 30 days of time from the addition and error in wallet funds. All in all Steam made my days a lot harder and solved absolutely nothing. Effectively wasting 4 days, Steam had maximized my saltiness.
But wait! There's good news! I soon received a response from the Tera Support team apologizing for the error/troubles I had, accompanied with a confirmation of all my funds being returned directly to my Steam wallet! After thanking them and writing a ****in' awesome review through the "How did I do" standard linky, I proceeded to review what I had learned.
Steam likes to put out fires with earthquakes, and call it 'gud'
(Addressing my very plain and well made ticket with completely unreasonable big brother seizure/locking of seperately purchased games)
Steam managed to confuse me so much I actually had to seek help
(I understand a 'naw bruh, no can do' but locking my games and not even reading my ticket??)
Tera's support not only exceeded expectations, but managed to return all funds without having their day(s) ****ed by Steam.
(I am in the same TZ as Steam's main HQ and they were harder to reach than the edge of the universe riding a snail)
The big picture? This game is cool as heck, nice people and fun gameplay (controller support?!?!?!?!) coupled with reasonable devs and functioning support.
Since I can still manage to use Steam today even with my clinical salt poisoning and permanent dumbfounded expression, I will share this tale and hope someone will see this and decide to try it. It's ****in' free and the developers and support really deserve the cash from those cosmetics. If you ever want to try a game with fun combat mechanics and a good group of people try Tera. The devs work really hard and provide better support than a 1.5 billion dollar corporation (who managed to forget the word 'no' and immediately go WW3 on my ***).
TL;DR Life is pain, Tera is fun and the devs are more than amazing, even when you forget the terribly low bar some games set for developers.

Mini Ninjas is quite a good game. I love the characters, enemies and combat system, (usually) and the game's voice actors do a pretty good job as well. It has quite an "open world" feel, whereas, it's not an open world, but you don't feel limited to a single path. The story is simple, you're a ninja and the evil samurai warlord is threatening to take over the world. You go out on a quest to defeat this warlord and save the ninjas who failed to do so before you. The game looks very nice in my opinion, and the music, while not anything amazing, does compliment it nicely. Combat system works good, you get a couple ninjas you can switch between, To be honest I only used like 3-4 of them, and that's because sometimes you must use a specific character. The bosses are basically: Run from boss until you're able to do a quicktime event. They're all quicktime events, so don't expect a whole lot of difficulty with them.
But for me, I found this game to have some broken aspects/parts. On the "avalanche escape" sequence, It's incredibly hard to see, which is understandable, but I kept falling through cracks, or holes, and instead of dying, I'd be rolling/sliding until the avalanche eventually caught up with me. This was a VERY monotonous part of the game, and it really put a downer on the overall game. When you are in your hat on the water, it's quite soothing. but when you have to use your hat/boat to go through small waterways, it's incredibly slow and can be irritating.  This game is indeed a kids game, don't expect a big story, deep characters or a long playthrough, but I have to admit, the cutscenes between the Warlord and his captains are hilarious.
This is a very good game for 10 euros, and I got it in a sale for 4, so I really recommend this game for players looking to burn off a couple hours without much challenge. I give it a fair 7/10, it's a cute game and it's worth the money.

A corrupt mayor, an underground resistance, and a slew of crazy characters. I’m Weise, aka Thomas, and I’d like to welcome you, to the Streets of Rogue, a new game developed by Matt Dabrowski and published by Tiny Build Games. Available on Steam for $14.99, together, we can join the resistance and take down the mayor in this action-packed, co-op, rogue-like experience like no-other.
You are a member of the resistance, a semi-organized group of rebels trying to take down the corrupt mayor and take back the city. After running a campaign full of deceit, the crime rate in the city has skyrocketed and the resistance wants to bring back order, by any means necessary. You cannot let anyone get in the way of your cause as you travel through the Streets of Rogue.
The typical flow of the game has you progress floor by floor through the city, in a procedurally generated world. Each floor will assign you a random set of missions to complete that could include murdering someone, acquiring a specific item, rescuing a prisoner, or more all in order to help the resistance with their cause. You must use any means necessary to complete the mission, making use of whatever special skills your character has.
You start each round by picking a class that you’ll use until you die. These classes include both typical and VERY, untypical characters. For example, you can play as the soldier, a class that starts with various weapons and armor if that’s your play style. Or maybe you prefer to take a stealth approach with the Hacker, tampering with computers and using your hacker skills to benefit you. Perhaps you’d rather be a gorilla and just smash everything with heavy melee attacks. Truly, this game lets you play however you like as you approach each scenario you’re given, assessing the situation, and determining the best route you want to try to take to accomplish the goal.
As you complete certain achievements, you’ll unlock additional characters too. For example, if you bribe a certain number of cops, you can unlock the police officer as a playable character. I found this to be a fun way to get me back into the game for replay ability, trying to tackle one or two character unlocks each run. You earn a currency that looks like a potato based on the progression you made in each run as well that can be used at the home base or HUB area to unlock more skills, weapons, and mission rewards to use in the future. Truly, it’s a fun gameplay mechanic that just doesn’t get old.
Finally, to wrap this section up, the game allows you to play with up to 3 other people in a co-op medley. Combine your skills to form the ultimate team and be able to handle any situation that comes at you.
Visually, this game isn’t too much to look at. It’s very much a pixel-art game and though its done decently, there’s nothing that set it apart too much for me. Some of the character customization is fun to play with, and the character classes themselves have some extra detail, but in the current version of the world the environments felt a tad more lacking for me. Due to the nature of the procedurally generated levels, it’s very easy to see the various textures and patterns being reused to form the buildings. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing, and really is quite expected, but it is something to note.
I will say that I found the procedural generation to be great however, in that rooms of all different kinds, sizes, etc were found in each playthrough and every floor which really added to the environment of this scummy city you are trying to free.
The soundtrack for Streets of Rogue is pretty fantastic, and you can actually purchase it as DLC in the Steam store for $2.99. It fits the feel of the gameplay perfectly. All the dialog in the game is text-based, but the sound effects for the various weapons, doors, glass breaking and more really are great. Voice acting in a game like this isn’t really needed, but the script writing they did for the different interactions is actually quite good. The tutorial at the start of the game sets the tone, full of humor and jokes that continue to come up throughout the game. Overall, my expectations in the audio department weren’t too high and I was pleased with what I found.
There are a lot of unlockables in this game, and its still in early-access. I’ve mentioned the unlockable characters, but you can also unlock weapons and gadgets for rewards from missions, various traits for when you level up, and much more. Additionally, there is a plan to allow for seeds to be entered, daily-runs for leaderboards, various mutators which will change the way the game is played, and a create a character feature to allow you to create your own custom class.
The mutators alone change the gameplay drastically. You can handicap yourself with things like “melee only” or just change the game up by having all the citizens riot in the streets. Combine this with the procedural generation and multiplayer and you have a game you can come back to over and over.
Overall, I really like Streets of Rogue. At the time of this review, I have eight hours into it and have unlocked almost all the characters. I have plenty of traits and mission rewards to unlock still and have only scratched the surface of testing myself on daily runs or with various mutators turned on. For $15, the Tiny Build name behind the publishing, and the ability to play with up to three of my friends for even more mayhem, I cannot recommend this game enough if you are even the slightest bit a fan of rogue-like RPG action games. Let me know what you think in the comments below, and check out my other reviews from my playlist. If you want to see me play this game, I’ll be streaming it from time to time at
. That said, thanks for watching. I’ve been Weise, aka Thomas, and I’ll see you in the next video.

After finishing the main storyline of this game and playing it for ~29 hours, I am incredibly torn on this game. I love it, and yet, there's some parts of it that really bother me. Ahead may be some spoilers, but I will try to put those in between tags.
Let's talk core gameplay loop first. There are so many cases you will send officers to and many you will get through through simple math which the game explains to you very early on. This is the basis, but the game offers many distractions. The community will come calling, as will city hall and eventually, bad guys in multiple different shapes. This will eventually get incredibly hectic, which I experienced as fun. There's a detective (and one other) minigame where you try to piece together the cases frame by frame and I simply loved it to pieces.
Secondly, let's talk sound design. This game stuck to a lot of basic simple sounds, which are used very efficiently. Whenever I would finish a case, I would hear the clicking of the handcuffs, which would give me the visceral enjoyment of a job well done. Alternatively, I would hear the padding footsteps of a criminal getting away, or the shots of police or innocents dying and I would feel with it. Simple, yet effective. You may also elect to play jazz or blues style music. As a fan of this genre of music, that added a lot. At one point, I was finishing up 3 detective cases in one day and hearing the tones of classical music as my police cars sped away to pick up crims was just an amazing experience.

This is a very challenging match 3 game.  Well, it starts off easy enough. At the higher levels, it can be very challenging.  Basically, you match the spooky symbols in threes or more to collect gold and complete goals.  Pretty standard, really.  However, this game is not about points.  There is gold in the game which can be used to buy special perks.  This game is not about gold, either.  These special perks are very much needed in timed mode to reach the goals in time.  Usually, goals are match X of this symbol or clear all gold background tiles or drop Y skulls to the bottom of the board..  It tells you how many are left, which is nice.  This game is about meeting all goals to move on to the next level.  This is where the puzzle part of the matching comes into play.
TIles can be stone (need one or two matches right next to it which breaks the stone), or it can a web (match the tile under the web in a match or more to remove the web), have a gold background (match it once to collect the gold), or it can have a metal plate (requires two matches - one turns it into gold, the next collects the gold).  The gold buys powerups which can have special effects (exploding an area, exploding in a cross pattern, damaging a whole row, clearing webs in a pattern, breaking stone tiles in a pattern, etc).  These powerups are critically important.  They take time to charge up, so they are used sparingly.  However, they are necessary to use in timed mode to complete the board in time.  It's a little bit of mental planning and a lot bit of keeping track of the board.  Matching four or more can generate special items, and this is also dependant on the special perks you buy.  The game is paced so pretty much you can buy every special perk when it becomes available (some require building up gold for a couple of levels).
I played this for quite some time when I sit down to play it.  It is very addicting.  The dev has two other "bonus" games that are not on Steam, so feel free to express interest in getting those here if you like this game.  Getting the word out is always good :)

"This is Spooky Bonus; a PC puzzle game with 100 levels by Grey Alien Games, a division of Jake Birkett Computer Solutions Ltd.  The game was developed with Blitz Max."
1. Does not run on the Unity Engine! YES!
2. Playstyle is like the Puzzle Quest (MPQ) or Bejeweled match-3 style.

5. The special power tiles that appear on the board you only have to click or drag them to activate. (Doesn't have to be part of a 'matching' movement).

Usually each level will involve either collecting enough tiles of a certain type, or clearing a specific set of tiles on the board. The 'specific set of tiles' clearing is similar in playstyle to the "7 Wonders: Treasures of Seven" match-3 game (without the rotating board though).
Overall this game is an enjoyable experience for beginner or veteran match-3 players and is an excellent starting point for anyone that wants to get into the genre.

I've been sitting a while on this one, not knowing if I want to review it or not, I just couldn't settle for a good enough reason or reasons to give this game a proper 'yes' or a strong 'no'. I don't hate it, but I don't love it either, it has it's issues, some things feel good but others don't. This game is like a gray puddle, if you will.
It has a lot of decent content, it definitely isn't a great game, it has some flaws, but I don't dislike it, I think I like it.
The game has a HUGE world map, and it is as diverse as it is beautiful. I found myself wondering around for many hours at the beggining of the game, and I still do it, now and then, I just call my trusted steed, and ride slowly into the sunset.
Taking on the gorgeous surroundings, the deserts, cities, villages, of the ancient Egypt.
Ubisoft did an excellent job making the map, the world, the feel of it is just as good as one could expect. I for one, who loves history, I couldn't but almost find myself with tears in my eyes at the first sight of Alexandria, Memphis and the Pyramids. It shows that extra year of development the game had. It really does.
THE STORY, it is decent, not something that has not been told before in an Assassin's Creed game, it is one of revenge, but stands out from the others, it has a unique feel to it, as it is empowered by Bayek, who is alomst a force of nature, relentless, ruthless, and his anger towards the ones that wronged him may seem madness, yet one could only agree with it, as we all have a bit of madness in there. He is a husband, to a woman as driven and strong willed as he is. Both taking on the same quest to find the one responsible for their loss. Both sharing the same path, as a wife and husband should. Both Bayek and Aya, are in my eyes probably the best main characters in a Assassin's Creed game since Ezio's trilogy.
I'd like to add that I haven't finished the main story yet. I'm close to doing it though, but I take my time with it.
Along with the main quests, I found some of the side quest really well written, some not so much, but they weren't bad.
There are plenty of them, and if that is not enough there are a bunch of question marks on the map that will reveal forts, camps, bandit camps, treasure, tombs and hunting grounds. There are a lot of things to do.
THE COMBAT AND STEALTH, well I feel both good and bad about those two, as they both have good moments and bad ones.
The combat it is If I dare say, like in the Dark Souls games, also taking inspiration from the Witcher. To me it feels more Dark Souls than Witcher, but it is nothing near as good or polished, But you get used to it pretty quick. It may feel like a bad thing for some and that the way it has been till now was perfect, it wasn't. It felt so damn stupid before, as you could clear a whole city of guards just by waiting for one to attack so that you counter and kill all that was there to be killed. This feels much better, even with all the issues it has.
Stealh, is to easy, I play the game on Hard, and it just doesn't feel good enough, I mean, you simply just whistle from a bush and wait for the enemy to approach then you go in for the kill, similar to Black Flag, in many ways it just doesn't have the same think before you act, Syndicate had to a somewhat degree. In Origins, it just feels way to easy.
I got the achivement which required to kill 10 enemies on a row without being detected, in a camp in an area above my level without even breaking a sweet, early in the game. That just felt...wrong, I'm not that good, am I ?
PERFORMANCE, I did not encounter any big FPS drops or STUTTERS in the game, I have around 55-60 outside the big cities, and 30-45 in them, Alexandria just takes a giant crap on my 1070, literally. :).
Though Ubisoft says it's not because of the anti-crack thing the game has, which makes the CPU go nuts, I don't think a great deal about it, I could say I don't care...but I probably do, as I hate MY FPS BEING STUCK  AT 30. I just look at that FPS counter and...Ah ! You don't want to know...
I almost didn't address this issue in my review because it didn't make the game unplayble, I expected it to have a bad optimisation...
Overall, Assassin's Creed Origins, It's a good game, I enjoyed playing and I think I will keep on enjoing it.
I recommend it to some people, mostly those that love the Assassin's Creed games, that played since Altair and didn't stop at the mess that was Unity and kept hoping for a good game, this is a decent one.
But to the rest, those that are 'fresh' to it or those that played the most recent ones, if you like the game from watching youtube gameplays or want to try it just because you heard it to be good from friends, buy it, but you would also like to consider buying during a sale.
I have to say the same for those wondering about the DLCs, It is not gonna be The Witcher 3 kinda ones, don't expect any 30hrs content, it's not going to happen, if you don't dream of that, good, I don't either. If it does happen. well, f*** me, I was wrong.

This game is basic, even for one of Artifex Mundi's offerings. It's also buggy towards the end, not dubbed very well, and a terrible cultural mish-mash. I got through it, and might even play it again, but there's certainly better in the rest of the HOG genre on Steam, so save your money for those.

Why doesn't Steam have a 'neutral' voting option? This game has points going for it and then it has also quite a few against it. Overall I really can't say that I disliked it, but that's about as positive as I feel about it.
The presentation is good. The graphics are colourful and well done, the animations are awkward as in most hidden object games, the music is nice and the voice acting isn't awful. Some locations feel 'shoehorned' into the Tibetian setting though, but overall it doesn't break the immersion.
There are quite a few hidden object scenes, so if you like those this game is definately for you. The inventory puzzles are rather weak with quite a few feeling really forced. A few examples: You have a magical staff that can shoot fire, but in order to melt some block of ice you have to use a magnifying glass. There is a huge lizard blocking your way and you have a bucket full of sleeping potion, but you rather use the bucket of sleeping potion on the ground under a spider in order to make the spider fall asleep. You need to put a lantern next to a rock and use a flint to light it up even if there are lit candles very near. The list goes on and it really gets on your nerves after a while. The minigames aren't bad, but they are either really easy (match the shape/colour) or quite difficult.
Overall the game offers a couple of hours of hidden object game play, but if you are more into casual adventures that make at least some sense then this game might disappoint you. Certainly one of the weaker Artifex Mundi games and I can only recommend it in a sale or a bundle.

There are alot of hidden object scenes which I don't mind at all but I would prefer there to be not so many in the game. That said, they fitted in perfectly with the puzzles and this balanced it all out for me. The only drawback I have with the game is the lack of people and voice acting. I love games where I am put into something and have to work my way out of it so although there was a map and hints, I found it quite challenging at times to know what to do next.
The game is a good length and it kept my attention and I would recommend it to any HOG fans out there or for people who enjoy doing puzzles. Artifex Mundi always have a variety of interesting puzzles in their games and although they can't take all the credit as only being publishers of this game, you could see that they put their stamp on it.
A very enjoyable game which is very good value for the price with it being a collector's edition. A huge success for me.

An OK hidden-object game all in all, but suffers from sloppy game design, and so I can't recommend it to fans of the genre.
The graphics and design are impressive. The hidden-object scenes are easy but plentiful.
The big disappointment, however, is the point-and-click adventuring: it's illogical and even idiotic. At one point I had to melt ice and was carrying a magical staff that could melt it ... but, no, I was not allowed to use this staff and had to find a magnifying glass instead. At another point, I tried to take one item, and got a message telling me that I shouldn't take it before finding out if it belongs to someone. Uhm, taking stuff is exactly what what I've been doing the whole game until then! A hermit asks me for a “rare plant” that I immediately see growing right outside his house. Early on I think I found 5 axes in a row, and kept using them only to find new ones to use again. Can't our protagonist just keep the axe? Or how about thinking of a puzzle that requires a new kind of item? Too many puzzles involve an item being stuck and you have to pry it out. One of the hidden objects -- I kid you not -- is a “reset icon.” Etc. etc. It's just insulting.
Finally, the story: the Tibetan flavor seems to be window dressing only. The legend of Shangri-La seems quite Westernized, the main and even most side characters are all Western, and in any case nothing of the history and religion of Tibet gets involved. I even think one of the puzzles involved Meso-American runes!
So, though the gameplay is generally OK, I'm going to have to give it a thumbs down. You hired excellent graphic artists, why not hire some capable writers, too? Or at least insist that they don't smoke up while on the job?
Still, thank you, devs, for supporting Linux!

A heartwarming adventure, beautiful graphics, clean looking, cute (and deadly) enemies, and tons of fun wrapped into one epic journey..... Mini Ninjas! Probably the cleanest and smoothest looking game I've seen in a long time. Each friendly character that one finds during the quest has their own unique and special moves. With tons of items, and sub weapons to use on those evil, cute little Mini Samurais and other creative enemies, this game defiantly deserves the "Gore_Torn's Seal of Approval"!  It's worth a play and the wonderfully crafted worlds will immerse you in the ways of the Ninja!
NINJA NINJA NINJA!!

I initially wrote Mini Ninjas off as a kid's game. Along with that assumption came the idea that the gameplay mechanics would be simplistic, the levels would be basic and really guided, and that the game would be small, easy, and not worth bothering with.
Along comes the Steam Winter Sale, and I figure that for a few dollars, I might as well check it out.
This game completely blew me away!
The first layer of gameplay complexity comes when you start rescuing your friends. You're enabled to switch between different characters with vastly different movement speed, attacks, and weaponry at the click of a button, even in the middle of combat. This opens up a whole new world of strategy as you can change your whole attack set in an instant.
To further the depth, the game features a rudimentary crafting system. By finding various plants, you're able to craft potions which help you in your quest. They range from the basic health potion to the very useful Flame Oil (which makes your sword on fire).
On top of the various potions, there are also purchaseable/scavengeable Ninja tools. These range from Shuriken and caltrops to various types of bombs. You even have a fishing rod you can use to fish for food/health.
Finally, you have various Kuji Magic spells you can employ. These are very powerful and will come in handy constantly.
You also have a hat, which acts as a basic shield to block incoming arrows. You also use it as a boat on water, and a sled on snow.
There are a good amount of levels to explore, and exploration is encouraged as you need to explore to find all the Kuji magic spells and plants you need to craft your potions.
The music and sound design is stellar. The world is very alive feeling, and is populated with believable sounds which form a detailed soundscape.
Graphics are also wonderful, mixing careful detail with a very abstract painterly/paper style of art.
The only issue I had was instability. That is easily fixed by finding and installing the OpenAL 2.1.0.0 runtimes. All of the earlier ones caused constant crashing on my computer.
TLDR: Great game, way more depth than one would assume.

I'll do another review after more features have been released. However, with disregard to the unreleased features considering this is Alpha, here is what I have to say:
Pros:
- Every level is randomly generated so you'll never feel like you're playing the same level over and over again
- It's not a pay-to-play game. Thank Bruce Almighty
- You have good amount of options in character choice that you get to unlock and play. (Compared to "race" in other RPG's that determines player skillsets)
- Humor. Great reason to play a game. Type? Not a professional of literature, comedy, or entertainment in general; but I'd say satire, juvenile(child-like humor), morbid, and other uncanny things. Ex. You taking a giant pill, walking through a wall, and everybody exploding when you punch them. Satisfying and hilarious lol
- Mutations keep the game interesting after you've defeated much of everything. Similar to Bungie's Halo skulls in campaign where you can turn a feature on like "Cowbell", giving "more bang for your buck", or in other words bigger explosions.
- There's so much randomly unconceived and unperceived wackiness. I wish there was more commentary to the game besides the tutorial and pixel-bubble story line.
Cons:
- Because it's still in alpha, many features aren't released, but I don't know if you would or wouldn't include this as a con or a side note.
- If you're playing by yourself, it isn't much fun once you've unlocked everything
- Character customization is moderately limited in cosmetic features( i.e. hair, hair color, facial hair )
- Unlocked all the characters, except one, in under 2 hours. Should be irritatingly difficult to get ALL characters unlocked. Also, you can't customize all of the characters.
- The skills you have to unlock with "nuggets", or what I'd like to call expendable skill points, are limited. There's the cool idea of unlocking 2 abilities which reveals a locked ability, but right now there's less than a double digit number;
IMO
- Sadly, once you die you must restart from level 1-1. I don't know how far the levels go up to because I've only reached 2-x, but I wish there was an option or feature to begin where you've died or started off last in the base. If there is this feature. WHERE?!
- Girlfriend didn't want to buy the game because it was too expensive. I don't want to buy another game because it's too expensive (for what it is)
- fun game overall. I'd buy it if the price was lowered, on sale, or a dozen or so more features were added making it playable for long periods of time alone.

For starters, have to say I'm glad this is the final game. Not only was the lore growing harder to solve with each new instalment, but we'd reached a point where not much else could be done with the story. The murdered children, their killer AND his family had all been touched upon. Second, and I can't really blame Scott for this, but having new gameplay ideas at this point in the series when there are countless fangames was next to impossible. But on that note, I have to hand it to Scott - this finale did the franchise proud.
This game finally embraces the true ridiculousness of the story (underground facilities, LITERAL purple guys, you name it) and actually converts it into a new game-mode to run parallel with the five nights. The tycoon aspect is surprisingly fun, especially with the new animatronics and lore bits hidden in what you can buy, and is a nice bit of leeway from the horror side of things. Speaking of which, I've grown to appreciate how this game basically combines the mechanics of the others  (save for the cameras sadly) the best it can while trying to sprinkle new ideas here and there. The idea of having to stare at a vent to ward off an animatronic, knowing full-well it could come crashing through anytime, is terrifying.
Overall, the reason I'm recommending this finale is because at the end of the day (for the most part) its actually a pretty fun game that does something COMPLETELY different from the rest. Balancing horror and relaxation with five nights and pizza place management, getting to essentially choose the difficulty with the salvage sections. It all wraps up nicely in the  end. Though I will warn you about the difficulty curve even with few animatronics, by the time you overcome it I think you'll be able to find a truly enjoyable conclusion to these games :)

Roguelands is a RogueLite with a lot to offer if you enjoy grinding. Progression is [mostly] achieved through death, though partially through crafting and learning mob mechanics.
The game is now officially released, but this doesn't mean its development cycle has concluded. There remains to be assets for the game that have yet to be implemented; namely more bosses, allegiances and storylines, additional weapons, armour and undoubtedly levels.
Visuals and sound are a huge selling point, with fantastic showings on both. Combat is entertaining and has a skill curve, with enough unique weapons, NPCs and bosses to keep you entertained with hundreds of hours already sunk into the title.
If you enjoy a Rogue-like experience, and don't mind the convenient storage based system to assist in progression, this game is something you should *not* miss out on, and I would recommend it to anyone.

This is the Police is a management simulation game revolving around Chief of Police Jack Boyd of the city of Freeburg. You’re tasked with most of the aspects of running a police department, such as hiring/firing new officers, solving homicides with your detective division, maintaining positive relations with city hall and the local Sands Mafia along with a range of other ragtag characters and assignments all within the span of 180 days. Your goal is to survive the next six months and make out with enough money ($500,000) to retire comfortably.
The majority of your time is hovering over a functioning, isometric scale model of Freeburg. Here you’ll spend the day sending out your patrol force to various crimes and often be given different choices on which action to take in an effort to de-escalate and arrest the perpetrator(s). Successful missions earn the responding officers “professionalism” points, making them more qualified and proficient at their job. As the game progresses you’ll be given the ability to send S.W.A.T. teams, paddy wagons and other tools as backup. Throughout your playtime in this mode, you may be called upon to homicides that require detective work as well.
When a detective is called out to a scene, you’ll initially be given various witness statements that will give you a vague idea of what transpired. As the day(s) go on, your detective(s) may reveal new information. In doing so, you’re given a folder with several still photos that you’ll have to piece together the photos in chronological order to solve the crime. Once you do that, you can send your units to pick up the perp. As you advance in the game, the homicides will become increasingly more difficult to solve.
Aside from the main gameplay, you’ll be tasked with appeasing often illicit and otherwise questionable requests by the mayor and other city officials during the day. You may be “asked” to recover some vinyl records from a jilted lover, provide mafia protection or even fire officers because of their skin color. It’s up to you to decide what you’ll agree to and how high up the corruption ladder you’re willing to go and who you’re willing to bury to get there.
Now, I know what you’re saying,
and I’d be tempted to agree with you, but This is the Police drops the ball on what could have been a wonderful simulation experience. To the contrary, it’s hampered by a lackluster story, forced choices and unfair restrictions. Where did it all go wrong and how could it have been prevented?
The first misstep is right in the opening scene at a press conference. No, I’m not talking about the glaring dialogue error, but that doesn’t help my already dwindling outlook on the game. What glaring error you say? This one:
I’m talking about the press conference as a whole. You’re asked a couple questions by the press about your retirement, police corruption, and your general opinions on personnel changes and suspected mafia involvement. You can choose neutral answers or literally tell the press in an off-the-cuff manner that the police totally, unequivocally, help the Sands mafia. Either way, it changes
, which really sets the tone for the whole game; your choices don’t matter. Let me explain…
In one playthrough I tried to be a “by the books” chief and the other as corrupt as possible. In the above mentioned scene I first admitted nothing and then started over, admitting the mafia had the Freeburg (FPD) in their pockets. Nothing changed. The game starts out all the same.
In my corruption-free playthrough I refused all mafia inquiries, made my arrests, solved my homicides and was doing the right thing; I was dead by day 11. I tried it again and by day 11 I was, again, shot dead. In fact, you
progress paste day 11 if you don’t at least dabble in a few mafia favors. The game literally makes it impossible to be righteous and try to run a quality police department.
Coupling the above handicap with bi-polar scenario results and unpredictable personnel left me frustrated and disappointed. Each morning you have what the game’s equivalent of a morning briefing is, in which some of your employees will ask to take the day off, often times for ludicrous reasons. I had three separate offers ask to take the day for reasons ranging from wanting to read a book to being completely intoxicated. Apparently the latest romance novel and a 5th of bourbon is more enticing than keeping their job.
Once my officers were out on patrol, there were still inconsistencies that the game failed to properly define or explain. Example, I sent two officers to a botched jewelry store robbery where a single suspect was chased out by the shop owner as he [the shop owner] tried to hit him with a baseball bat. The suspect climbed up a tree to avoid injury and was there when my two well-trained officers arrived. Somehow the suspect escaped unidentified and both officers lost ten points in their respective professionalism scoring. In times where detail is crucial, the game fails to provide it, leaving you wondering how that cornered suspect escaped or how an armed robbery left two officers dead. Sure, you can choose how to handle certain scenarios, but when things go south, you’re left scratching your head as to why everything went so horribly wrong.
In my corruption playthrough I did everything the mafia asked and found that while I obviously lived longer, the game never seemed to break free from the norm – send the cops to calls for service, try to solve homicides, do a few side jobs, sell drugs, smuggle guns…etc. It sounds fun on paper but the game never really captured the tense feeling of being a crooked cop. In fact, they practically normalize it with the sheer amount of criminal activity they expect you to do.
This is where the game loses me because you’re forced down this path. You can’t refuse too many mafia requests without running the risk of being snuffed out, so you’re handcuffed into them which will either be something you tolerate for the sake of the game, or something that will ruin the experience altogether, which was my case. I really wanted to like this game, but it was a terrible letdown.

Overall, This is the Police had amazing potential and a great creative approach to simulation and police management. However, it was handicapped by terrible game mechanics and an utterly forgettable story and cast of characters.

The Good:
Initially entertaining and involved sim mechanics that rapidly reveal more depth over the first couple of hours of gameplay. The music is excellent, and I was happily buying new music from the catalog the moment it was available. The voice-acting is top-notch (with the notable exceptions of a few characters). The story dumps you into a seedy and intriguing world of police-work that legitimately makes you want to see what's going to happen each day (for a few hours).
The Bad:
The game's main mechanics just do not hold up to the amount of time you have to spend to complete the game. By halfway through the game, it had become a grind and I just wanted the days to be over as quickly as possible so I could get to the next cutscene. The story starts to become a bit predictable as well, and the depth of characters becomes noticably worse somewhere near a 1/3 of the way through the game.
As many others have already pointed out, the game's inclusion of real social issues holds a lot of promise for deeper narrative and difficult choices, but the the issues are presented at such a shallow (and sometimes farsical) level and with so little consequence that it borders on being insulting to one's intelligence. It's a bad sign when the game's primary motivator for serious social encounters, City Hall, is something you start to laugh at and ignore routinely because you know nothing will really come from it.
Recommend?
If you're the kind of person who really enjoys routine, you might find joy past the first few hours of this game. I have trouble sticking with games that don't stay "fresh" throughout, and if you're the same, I'd say give it a pass.

100 minutes in and the game looks very promising. The immersion is rich, with endless NPCs wondering about carrying out actions which are purposeful and convincing. The controls are a bit fiddly, so it's going to take time to learn them and there are some very acute sweet spots where certain actions will or will not work, despite the encouraging HUD tip, so the learning curve is a bit of a hurdle, but can also be perceived as a challenge too, to acquire the necessary reflexes and spatial timing. The graphics are very stunning with plenty of tweaking options to satisfy a broad range of technologies. Crashes have occurred during startup, but thankfully not yet during gameplay. This is a common issue with Ubisoft, so you just have to persevere, and this game is worth the occasional hiccup.
I was concerned about CPU thrashing, and this game does indeed max out all 8 cores at 100%, keeping my i7-6700K at around 67C overclocked to 4.5Ghz. My system can cope with this load though, as other games also thrash CPUs. GTA V for instance, pushes all my cores to between 93% and 98%, with a slightly lower temp.
I have two GTX 1080Ti OC STRIX GPUs in SLI, so graphics performance is a non-issue. I haven't even bothered checking if in fact SLI is operating, as the game looked great and didn't need any further tweaking when maxed out. Perhaps some of the post-processing is a little over the top, but not enough to motivate me to tweak yet. I haven't tested 4K yet, but I expect it will look epic on my big screen OLED TV. If you have a high end card, you will be fine. Lower end cards will cope with the range of in-game settings available to dial things towards the preferred FPS, so I recommend purchasing and checking it out, as you can get your money back if the game doesn't work for you.

To preface: I can't really give a full recommendation, nor outright not recommend this game. The game had a lot of potential to be great, but was held back by a considerable amount of bugs and lousy design choices. The result was a fairly mediocre game and a sloppy console port to PC.
+ Nice visuals and soundtrack. The North American colonial setting is new and fresh for the series.
+ Some interesting characters. Connor was a nice change of pace for a protagonist (unless you consider Desmond as the real main protagonist). The dynamics between the AC characters was good, especially the father and son relationship between Haytham and Connor and the tension that brang.
+ The colonial story arc was neat for the most part. Even though it was kind of revisionist history, I can see history buffs getting somewhat of a treat with all the tid bits of history given (as well as calling out all the places the game got it wrong).
+ The Desmond arc was the more interesting aspect of the story. Unfortunately, it has a weak ending.
+ Desmond finally sees some action, although not a whole lot.
+ Some of the new combat features were cool and aesthetically pleasing. A dual wielding assassin just seems right.
+ The ability to choose between 4 different counters made combat feel more powerful as an assassin. Some people complain it was too easy, but it didn't seem like it to me. More guns in the environment made it more dangerous. Also, there was a lot more variety to the enimies than in past games that required more tactics to defeat. Definitely not a game where you can just mash the buttons and win.
+ Naval combat was a new and fun feature.
+ The Homestead stuff was also new and was actually worthwhile due to the ability to get the best gear in the game.
+ Animus menu is vastly improved from past games. No more hypersensitive controls that make you skip where you want to go and generally frustrate the hell out of you.
+ A lot more interesting recruit abilities. Unfortantely, a lot of them are pretty useless, but some are still cool and gives some variety.
- This game was sloppily put together and lacks polish. There are a lot of bugs and glitches in this game. Problems with colision, randomly falling through the ground and under the world, getting stuck in objects, graphical glitch (like a good deal of rubberbanding), etc. The developers should be ashamed of themselves for releasing this game in the state it is in. Totally unacceptible.
- Some very assinine design decisions that sometimes feel like they were developed by a group of r-e-t-a-r-d-e-d monkies (described in more detail below)
- AC series has some of the worst controls in the industry. They tried to improves things in AC3, but failed miserably. The controls are still clunky and frustrating as hell. You'll still get those annoying instances where the character will stick to walls when running around corners or jump in totally random directions you didn't intend. In fact, I'm still debating whether they made the controls worse than past AC games or not. It's definitely still bad.
- They attempted to hide the optional full sync objectives so failing wasn't so in you face (as complained about in Brotherhood and Revelations). The results was the it much easier to miss what the optional full sync objectives were, yet it was still in your face when you failed them. This just created an even more annoying experience with them.
- Some of the full sync objectives were unreasonable and frustrating. One example is a naval mission that plops you in the middle of a horde of gun ships and frigates and expects you to complete it while taking less than 25% of damage. Another example is an objective to not take more then 30% damage to a pack of wolves, while only being given a fraction of a second to react to the QTE where any failure would make you take too much damage, and ranged weapons were not allowed (essentially impossible without emploiting and cheesing your way through it). It didn't seem like game balance was tested very well.
- Desmond's story arc had a confusing ending that somewhat disconnected it from past games. It was a dissappointment after the build up through 5 games.
- Connor's story had its issues as well with things that didn't fit all that well. The story is definitely weaker in AC3 than in other games in the series. It could've been better.
- The majority of the game is filled with fluff and fillers that served more as novelties than anything fun and worthwhile.
- Crafting has potential (mainly due to the ability to get the best gear in the game), but was held back by atrocous UI and controls. Needs a lot more refinement.
- Convoys replace shop investments as the main source of income. Unfortanately, it's a very cumbersome and time consuming way to make income and more tedious than fun. Another poor design.
- Even though the best gear is crafted, gear is mostly not worth much in this game. The vast majority of opponents are easily dispatched just by counters as one shot kills, which doesn't really account for gear. A better sword would essentially just allow you to kill disarmed enemies a little faster. Gear progression is totally wonky. Most weapons will start off as instantly obsolete. 2h weapons are pretty much worthless. The only weapon that really makes a difference is the kind of gun you have, and that only because some guns let you fire extra shots before needing to reload. Other than that, gear is nearly entirely inconsequential.
- Due to the above, it feels like gear and currency just don't have a place in this game. This series is probably better with it taken out entirely. They're just unfun distractions.
- Recruits feel a lot weaker in this game despite the fact that they can't die (but get injured instead). The guild menu is also clumsier to navigate.
- Stealth in this game sucks. Imprecise controls makes it very frustrating. Also, inconsistent detection machanics also make for a very frustrating experience. To compound this problem, some missions require stealth and there is no options to complete certain missions (not all that open ended).
- This game gives the illusion of open world, but it's not really all that open, especially during missions (this is a series issue).
- And if you needed further proof that this game development was lead by idiots: the credits are atleast 15 minutes long AND CAN'T BE SKIPPED. The game inputs literally shut down during the credits, you can't do anything but watch them. You can't even exit the game without a hard shut down (which means nothing gets saved). This is by far the most assinine design decision in the history of video games!
As I said before, I can't give a full recommendation, but I can't say this game is outright bad either. It's a mediocre game that had potential to be great but was held back by bad design decisions and lack of polish. I can say that after playing this game I've lost motivation to continue with this series as it seems pointless (for what it's worth). Get this game if you are following the story or are just a fan of this kind of gameplay. Stick with the main mission. You can do the naval battle, and perhaps, the homestead missions which are fairly fun, but the rest is a waste of time and not all that fun at all.
Also, this game is a prime example of Ubisoft giving the PC community the finger by giving sloppy ports. Only get this when it's on sale. Ubisoft doesn't deserve full price for this game. It's not worth it.

An enjoyable and satisfying end to a trilogy I have followed since the very beginning. Exceptional story telling, gameplay and combat, but was it memorable for all the right reasons? I give it 3 out of 5. Here is why:
PROs-
- Updated combat, streamlined, epic and fast. Brand new weapons and takedowns, a whole different style of fighting.
