- Story conclusion and 'Desmond' storyline. Excellent and very thought provoking. Not to mention, extremely moving and emotional.
- Graphical fidelity, AI and general NPC activity being the best it could be, really immersive and well mapped.
- PC porting. The game has been really well ported to PC. The controls are intuitive and well mapped, any needed changes are easy to do.
-
CONs-
- Conner, main protagonist, doesn't feel suited to be an assassin, more to the point doesn't make the player feel cool or outright a bada*s. Regardless of pangs and pains that we miss Ezio, giving this new kid half a chance and I just can't warm to him. He feels like a kid. Things pick up near the end and where he -does- feel more like a leader, but this is within 30 minutes of his story ending :(
- Bugs! It's sad and alot of people have said it, but AC3 was the dawn of the downhill for Ubisoft. This game represents a bridge from their legendary game production into a EA-wannabe, mass producing, low content single button mashers. Falling through floors, walls. glitching into trees and cutscene cameras getting caught on objects. Tsk tsk, not good.
- Lack of side-objective drive. In the previous games my 'must-complete' side was ferocious and I turned into a perfectionist. However, without spoiling anything, the need to hire 'assassins', build up the homestead or complete any of the side missions felt trivial and proved little profit. In the end, it was much easier to hunt bear and wolf pelt, selling it yourself for coin.
- Little Progression. Nicely leading on to the fact that, really, you didn't need to buy anything at all. I completed the game with nothing but the tools and weapons on my back. There felt like little need to buy upgrades or even use bombs, darts and ropes, again, all so trivial. Hidden blade and arrows, that is all you needed.
- Poorly timed cutscenes: Whether in a sea mission or coming out of a cutscene on land, too many times have I outright failed the mission because an AI dynamically appeared or moved into my cutscene as it was finishing or the cutscene steered my ship straight into rocks.
- Lastly, stealth missions and optional objectives, the only bane of the game and the reason it's not 5 full stars. You see, 99% of all missions have some mindblowingly foolish side objective. For example - Optional: Whilst killing this enemy do not be seen, use no weapons, never set foot on the ground and do it all in 25 seconds. It's absolutely pointless and only helps to drive you far away from wanting to see a nice shiny 100% completetion at the end of the game. If that doesn't ruin it for you, the amount of 'detection fails the mission' stealth quests is more than I like. AC1 and AC2 allowed you, the player, to decide how you did things. In AC3 you may find yourself at the whim of rage as you repeat the same scenes over and over because of a simple mistake or missed step and 'game over'.
These points aside, if you're like me and want to see a satisfying end to the trilogy, get it! The game is very good, just make sure to take a few breaks to not let the downsides get to you.

This game is creepy, not the "jump-in-your-face-and-go-bloogie-woogie-woo" creepy, it's the kind of creepy that you get with the minimalistic graphic design and atmospheric ambience that makes you think something is going to happen, but nothing does. Home is a fairly short game that you can complete in one playthrough and probably never touch ever again, but the one time you do play it the experience sticks with you. The story is whatever you want it to be, so in a way it could be as creepy as your imagination can make it.
I give Home a 8/10 for terrible replay value, but superb storytelling and sound design.

is a psychological platformer with Metroidvania-style exploration. As you explore ambient dreams you will find power-ups and solve obscure puzzles in a non-linear fashion.  Zzzz is not as focused on gameplay as it is on emotional experience and aesthetic feelings. For comparison, this game reminds me a lot of Dreaming Sarah do to web-like navigation. There are very few games that capture the feeling of playing a video game for the first time and I think Zzzz does that. I would encourage to look past its "simple platformer paint job" because there is something special here.
so it is kind of annoying playing in a tiny window. It hurts immersion of this game which is definitely a downside for me. Developer implied that Fullscreen and a lot more content will be added to the game at some point. I feel like this should have been added sooner since there was a free version of this game. Despite that, it was one of the most enjoyable experiences I had in years so for $2 I am willing to ride this train.
I was not sure what to think of this game at first (it can be a bit confusing) but it won me over with genuinely hilarious events and creativity. This is one of the games that play around with player's habits and expectations. These days it is hard to surprise but I still got those discovery moments in Zzzz. It is worth noting that Zzzz often changes game mechanics and the way you interact with the world.
Puzzles are not very easy so don't expect things to be handed to you. However, finding solutions was a very rewarding experience. For a 26MB it packs a significant amount of content and took me like 10+ hours without using a guide (not even sure if there is one) I had a really annoying glitch which prevented me from getting the ending and reset my progress right at the end.Not happy about that but I will let it slide because I enjoyed 99% of the game up to that point. At least 2 people had that glitch *
Many games use pixel art but Zzzz does it almost like Atari which is very nostalgic. I really like overall design and variety in stages. There are several soundtracks and overall good use of sounds and music. The only little thing that bothers me is the Stage Select area which has no map and takes awhile to navigate.
I think this is a fantastic game if you like ambient exploration genre. Zzzz really made me feel like I was 15 years younger and still discovering what video games were. It looks very simple but has lots of cool visual effects, good music, humor, creative puzzles and some platforming elements. As long as you do not mind spider-web navigation and intentionally weird puzzles you might just enjoy it.

Great game, but not for $14.99.
I'll do another review after more features have been released. However, with disregard to the unreleased features considering this is Alpha, here is what I have to say:
Pros:
- Every level is randomly generated so you'll never feel like you're playing the same level over and over again
- It's not a pay-to-play game. Thank Bruce Almighty
- You have good amount of options in character choice that you get to unlock and play. (Compared to "race" in other RPG's that determines player skillsets)
- Humor. Great reason to play a game. Type? Not a professional of literature, comedy, or entertainment in general; but I'd say satire, juvenile(child-like humor), morbid, and other uncanny things. Ex. You taking a giant pill, walking through a wall, and everybody exploding when you punch them. Satisfying and hilarious lol
- Mutations keep the game interesting after you've defeated much of everything. Similar to Bungie's Halo skulls in campaign where you can turn a feature on like "Cowbell", giving "more bang for your buck", or in other words bigger explosions.
- There's so much randomly unconceived and unperceived wackiness. I wish there was more commentary to the game besides the tutorial and pixel-bubble story line.
Cons:
- Because it's still in alpha, many features aren't released, but I don't know if you would or wouldn't include this as a con or a side note.
- If you're playing by yourself, it isn't much fun once you've unlocked everything
- Character customization is moderately limited in cosmetic features( i.e. hair, hair color, facial hair )
- Unlocked all the characters, except one, in under 2 hours. Should be irritatingly difficult to get ALL characters unlocked. Also, you can't customize all of the characters.
- The skills you have to unlock with "nuggets", or what I'd like to call expendable skill points, are limited. There's the cool idea of unlocking 2 abilities which reveals a locked ability, but right now there's less than a double digit number;
IMO
- Sadly, once you die you must restart from level 1-1. I don't know how far the levels go up to because I've only reached 2-x, but I wish there was an option or feature to begin where you've died or started off last in the base. If there is this feature. WHERE?!
- Girlfriend didn't want to buy the game because it was too expensive. I don't want to buy another game because it's too expensive (for what it is)
- fun game overall. I'd buy it if the price was lowered, on sale, or a dozen or so more features were added making it playable for long periods of time alone.

Taking on the gorgeous surroundings, the deserts, cities, villages, of the ancient Egypt.
Ubisoft did an excellent job making the map, the world, the feel of it is just as good as one could expect. I for one, who loves history, I couldn't but almost find myself with tears in my eyes at the first sight of Alexandria, Memphis and the Pyramids. It shows that extra year of development the game had. It really does.
THE STORY, it is decent, not something that has not been told before in an Assassin's Creed game, it is one of revenge, but stands out from the others, it has a unique feel to it, as it is empowered by Bayek, who is alomst a force of nature, relentless, ruthless, and his anger towards the ones that wronged him may seem madness, yet one could only agree with it, as we all have a bit of madness in there. He is a husband, to a woman as driven and strong willed as he is. Both taking on the same quest to find the one responsible for their loss. Both sharing the same path, as a wife and husband should. Both Bayek and Aya, are in my eyes probably the best main characters in a Assassin's Creed game since Ezio's trilogy.
I'd like to add that I haven't finished the main story yet. I'm close to doing it though, but I take my time with it.
Along with the main quests, I found some of the side quest really well written, some not so much, but they weren't bad.
There are plenty of them, and if that is not enough there are a bunch of question marks on the map that will reveal forts, camps, bandit camps, treasure, tombs and hunting grounds. There are a lot of things to do.
THE COMBAT AND STEALTH, well I feel both good and bad about those two, as they both have good moments and bad ones.
The combat it is If I dare say, like in the Dark Souls games, also taking inspiration from the Witcher. To me it feels more Dark Souls than Witcher, but it is nothing near as good or polished, But you get used to it pretty quick. It may feel like a bad thing for some and that the way it has been till now was perfect, it wasn't. It felt so damn stupid before, as you could clear a whole city of guards just by waiting for one to attack so that you counter and kill all that was there to be killed. This feels much better, even with all the issues it has.
Stealh, is to easy, I play the game on Hard, and it just doesn't feel good enough, I mean, you simply just whistle from a bush and wait for the enemy to approach then you go in for the kill, similar to Black Flag, in many ways it just doesn't have the same think before you act, Syndicate had to a somewhat degree. In Origins, it just feels way to easy.
I got the achivement which required to kill 10 enemies on a row without being detected, in a camp in an area above my level without even breaking a sweet, early in the game. That just felt...wrong, I'm not that good, am I ?
PERFORMANCE, I did not encounter any big FPS drops or STUTTERS in the game, I have around 55-60 outside the big cities, and 30-45 in them, Alexandria just takes a giant crap on my 1070, literally. :).
Though Ubisoft says it's not because of the anti-crack thing the game has, which makes the CPU go nuts, I don't think a great deal about it, I could say I don't care...but I probably do, as I hate MY FPS BEING STUCK  AT 30. I just look at that FPS counter and...Ah ! You don't want to know...
I almost didn't address this issue in my review because it didn't make the game unplayble, I expected it to have a bad optimisation...
Overall, Assassin's Creed Origins, It's a good game, I enjoyed playing and I think I will keep on enjoing it.
I recommend it to some people, mostly those that love the Assassin's Creed games, that played since Altair and didn't stop at the mess that was Unity and kept hoping for a good game, this is a decent one.
But to the rest, those that are 'fresh' to it or those that played the most recent ones, if you like the game from watching youtube gameplays or want to try it just because you heard it to be good from friends, buy it, but you would also like to consider buying during a sale.
I have to say the same for those wondering about the DLCs, It is not gonna be The Witcher 3 kinda ones, don't expect any 30hrs content, it's not going to happen, if you don't dream of that, good, I don't either. If it does happen. well, f*** me, I was wrong.

TL;DR AT THE END
This Is The Police is an....interesting game. It starts out with an amazing premise, interesting gameplay, unique characters and then just doesn't do anything beyond that.
Let's get this out of the way first: TitP is NOT a Visual Novel. It is not a "Choose Your Own Adventure" game that many people seem to think it is. TitP is a simple management sim game and that's all it is. The choices presented to you throughout the 20~ hour story have little to no effect on the story. They may help you get to the end of it but they will never change the outcome. In this way it's essentially nothing more than a management sim with an on-rails story.
Story wise, you "play" as Jack Boyd, a retiring police commissioner who wants to earn $500,000 before he retires in 180 days. The game takes place over those 180 days (gameplay wise it's around 150 days). You'll be introduced to the corrupt Major Rogers  who holds your job by the balls, the Sands Mafia who controls the city from the underground as well as a bunch of other interesting characters as you try to survive for 180 and earn all that money.
As far as gameplay goes it's not overly complicated. You spend 99% of the game overlooking a map of Freeburg (the city the game takes place in). Crimes will pop up around the city and it's your job to send officers to solve them. Your offierces have "Professionalism" points. Each officer will earn +10 every time they arrest the purp and officers with over 500 points are almost entirely self sufficent, being able to solve crimes on their own. There are some unique dispatches as well.  City Hall will sometimes ask you to do certain things (like fire all black officers) and it's up to you wheteher you wish to do things like that. Very early on in the game you get to choose a mafia side to team up with (you can't say no) and they'll sometimes ask you not to send officers to crimes in return for some money.
There are more options that open up as the game goes on, such as bringing back contraband to the police station or the mafia, sending officers to protests and forging evidence to pin any violence caused their on a certain faction. There also detective cases which are really quite fun. Sometimes a murder or robbery will happen and you'll have to send detective(s) to try and work out the crime. Every day a detective is assigned to it there's a chance you'll obtain photos of the scene. Once you have enough photos you can use witness accounts to piece together the crime and arrest the criminal. It's an interesting idea and stays strong throughout the entire game.
So where does it go wrong? The first and i'd say the biggest problem is that the game is just simply way too long. Story elements are few and far between and the game overstays it's welcome even before the halfwway mark. 150 days is a LONG time. The early game is absolutely the most fun as you're struggling to level up your ragtag officers, teaming them up with other awful officers to try and create a strong police force all the while trying to juggle tasks between the mafia and city hall. As the game goes on, it more or less just becomes "send your best dudes and a few smaller dudes to the crime". Once you get an officer past 500 points the game essentially becomes unloseable. If somehow a low point officer dies you just recruit a new one. Even the heavy crimes such as massacres and armed robberies become nothing to a high point officer leading some rookies. You can also choose to send a swwat team and paddy wagon to some crimes but with enough high point officers this isn't at all needed.
Apart from the game being too long, the gameplay remains stagnant. After learning what everything does and how to control your squad, the game does nothing with your experience. You will spend all your time sending officers to crimes. Mid game an interesting side quest pops up, but it can be solved fairly quickly and doesn't deviate from normal play. Choices you make have no impact on gameplay, officers dying means little, not sending officers to crimes doesn't seem to have much repercussion (sometimes you simply just don't have enough officers). Essentially, as long as you don't screw over the mafia you can coast to end game with a few strong officers.
Really, there isn't much else to say. The gameplay is repetitive and never changes and the game goes for far too long. It could have ended after 60~ days and it would have been amazing. You unlock a sandbox mode after beating the game but by that time you'll never want to touch it again.
PRO'S:
- An interesting story with unique and interesting characters
- An amazing concept with (inital) amazing mechanics
- Each crime (and there's well over 500) has unique text that is almost always worth reading
- The detective cases add a nice distraction from the gameplay
- A great art style
- Simple and easy to grasp gameplay
- Great soundtrack
CON'S:
- Story elements are few and far between
- Your choices made in game have little to no impact on anything
- Game ends up becoming repetitive and goes for FAR too long
- After a certain point the game requires no thought and is unloseable
- No way to speed up each day
TL;DR A interesting and unique concept that falls flat on it's face. The game lasts far too long with no incentive to go forward apart from the scattered story elements. If the game lasted for half as long it would have been an absolute reccomend.

I got this as part of a Humble Bundle. From the trailer, it looked somewhat like Terraria (although I haven't actually played Terreria either).
This is one of the least noob friendly games I've played. There is no in game tutorial, and it really needs one since being able to engage in combat requires you to right-click to toggle between combat and gathering mode, and you start in gathering mode. You can't look up controls for this in game, either, so it took me several deaths and an attempt at troubleshooting controller issues to figure that out (the game also has no controller support at the moment, despite what the launchers control selection might implies).
Discovering how to actually fight didn't even help all that much, as the only starting class/gear available on first play means you have 2 hp and deal 3 damage per hit. It also doesn't help that the sword is a rather slow weapon. It also doesn't help that there's not an indication that killing 5 of the eyeball/rock worm monsters summons a massive boss that will kill you while you're still trying to figure out how to get back to the ship to save the handful of credits and supplies you've picked up before you're inevitable demise.
Once I did manage to figure out the basics, and realized how not to summon the boss to kill me (and also unlocked a slightly better starting race that gave more health), the frustration switched from being constantly killed before banking any progress, to the frustration of grinding for materials to make all of the equipment, because you can't actually buy equipment, and can't regularly buy healing potions.
The game does look like the developer is continuing to update it, so maybe the initial learning curve flaws will be worked out, but even though I haven't made it very far in, there doesn't feel like there's a lot of variety even once you do get further in.

Full review on the Indie Detective Reviews series:
Disclosure: Still haven't made my way through the main campaign, so this review is based on 20 hours of gameplay.
Recommending this game because the good definitely outweighs the bad. It has a crazy amount of creative writing, the voice casting is top notch (Duke Nukem himself, Jon St. John is the main character) and the storyline is a compelling one, with mob and vigilante violence, the most corrupt and vile of politicans, and a veteran cop on the edge of sanity. The campaign plays out by making you the dispatcher for your squad, requiring you to make choices on who to send to what crime scenes. Mess it up and your police will die. You can also send them to suppress strikes and protests for the mayor, act as mob muscle for cash, or just suck up to night club owners by providing security. All of this to a soundtrack of smooth jazz.
The downside to the campaign is that after a while it feels artificially inflated. If you take the time to read the hundreds of individual crime reports, you'll be treated to crazy creativity. After 20 hours of the same dispatch mechanic over and over, I stopped reading just to make it go faster. I know I'm cheating myself out of enjoyment, but I'm tired of sameness.
I am eventually going to get to the end of this campaign after I take a break. It's worth the fairly cheap price for the quality of the writing and acting alone, but pace yourself; you will burn out if you try to binge like I did.

My first post will be about the game “Mini Ninjas”. In my review I will not for a long time desctibe the game, because it represents itself, evaluates the items and so on. I do not even put it in front of the goal. I just want to talk about the games that I liked and that I would like to add.
«Mini Ninjas» is not an ordinary game. Even the creators have never had experience in this genre, but still took up the matter, apparently decided to try their hand at a new role. Before IO Interactive engaged in cold-blooded, serious projects, such as “Hitman” (all love bald Agent’a 47) and “Kane & Lynch: Dead Men”(a story of two characters with complicated fate), and now have created a pretty good game.
When I first looked through the trailer even before the game, I liked a stylized (not photorealistic) schedule and the fact that the main character is a ninja. The word calls to mind many ninja games (series «Tenchu», «Ninja Gaiden», «Ninja Blade»), and I was glad to see this “cute” project about the soldiers of the night.
So about the game. Immediately I was strucked by the individual style of the opening video (which tells us that an evil wizard has turned all the animals into Samurai and only protagonist – a ninja named Hiro, and his friends (also a ninja) can save the world), the basic idea painfully banal but for this game fits all. Also other render video (video of each character) are cool.
I was very touched to the depths of the soul by the graphics and landscapes. They are beautiful, they look nice, sometimes I even want to stop and to spend a couple of minutes of playing.
The characters are animated very high quality (the main ninja acrobatics, including somersaults, jumps, and the samurai and funny animals), the interaction with the game world is great (hiding, running along the walls, collecting the fruit of the bushes, and trees).
I was pleased also by the Gameplay.
There is a very interesting system of mixing the ingredients. There first is to buy a recipe, find herbs, then mix them to get what you want (such as health potions).
There is a hat wearing it on the head one hides from the arrows, and the water – one uses it like a boat. On the water it is possible to catch a fish and make “sushi” of it, it helps restore a life. At one level, there was an interesting script time: the flow in the passage was very strong and one can not swim, we had to catch a big fish on a hook, but it was struggling swim through this passage thereby taking with him his tormentor.
The role-playing game system is also presented, but on a very primitive level and one has more than the stronger character’s skills but one choose what he wants that can not be improved.
The game also has different spells, for example one can produce a fire, cause the meteor rain, thunder, wind and more. But the most amusing, in my opinion, is imploring the astral body, you will turn in different animals (many of them).
And at the ending of the game and within the samurai it gives some advantages: when you come out of a samurai he is neutralized, one has more life than the animals. You are not attacked (only when held side by side and are at what you do). To learn a new spell one must first find a special flower, put it on the altar, pray a couple of seconds and the news spells are known.
There is also an opportunity to concentrate while a magic power appears and an arrow indicates the correct path.
In my humble opinion one could add a few things:
By the end of the game it becomes monotonous, and one does not have enough interest, the game could be decorated with the story line, added with some unexpected little twists and turns.
There are no additional, optional tasks (quests), alternative endings that would be complementary and would like to go again.
It is also interesting to see the main characters in the other suits, such as winter, to change the skin to the white suit.
There is no such thing that would force players to return and find all the items to open additional levels, skills (a good example of this series “Spyro”). Also, the maximum development is achieved little in advance in order to better themselves before the final Bos (or after). This will give the player a chance to enjoy the new skills passing game levels once again!

100 minutes in and the game looks very promising. The immersion is rich, with endless NPCs wondering about carrying out actions which are purposeful and convincing. The controls are a bit fiddly, so it's going to take time to learn them and there are some very acute sweet spots where certain actions will or will not work, despite the encouraging HUD tip, so the learning curve is a bit of a hurdle, but can also be perceived as a challenge too, to acquire the necessary reflexes and spatial timing. The graphics are very stunning with plenty of tweaking options to satisfy a broad range of technologies. Crashes have occurred during startup, but thankfully not yet during gameplay. This is a common issue with Ubisoft, so you just have to persevere, and this game is worth the occasional hiccup.
I was concerned about CPU thrashing, and this game does indeed max out all 8 cores at 100%, keeping my i7-6700K at around 67C overclocked to 4.5Ghz. My system can cope with this load though, as other games also thrash CPUs. GTA V for instance, pushes all my cores to between 93% and 98%, with a slightly lower temp.
I have two GTX 1080Ti OC STRIX GPUs in SLI, so graphics performance is a non-issue. I haven't even bothered checking if in fact SLI is operating, as the game looked great and didn't need any further tweaking when maxed out. Perhaps some of the post-processing is a little over the top, but not enough to motivate me to tweak yet. I haven't tested 4K yet, but I expect it will look epic on my big screen OLED TV. If you have a high end card, you will be fine. Lower end cards will cope with the range of in-game settings available to dial things towards the preferred FPS, so I recommend purchasing and checking it out, as you can get your money back if the game doesn't work for you.

WHAT THE HECK?! How is this game fair in the slightest?! I write this review after a rather cruel and unfair death at the hands of this game. I was running a character that was pretty well buffed out and invested into, and then suddenly they were cut down in two hits. That's absurd and insane.
But salt aside, in its current state this game seems more like an early access affair than a finished product. I got this on humble bundle and was rather pleased to see a spiritual successor to Magicite, a dead early access game that had potential and a style I really liked but couldn't carry the concept further than the most basic essentials. I jumped into the world with the first few characters and, naturally, died a lot.
With rogue-likes, you should expect death to be a very common thing. Until you get your character buffed out and supplied, it's best to stick to the first planet. It was there that I immediately discovered the first fatal flaw of this game: the monsters are terribly imbalanced. Most boss-type monsters (the ones you summon by interacting with the level) are far too easy to summon and go down very easily, while the randomly generated elite monsters are tremendously stronger than them! you would think that a monster you summon would be stronger than a random mob who can just so happen to appear right next to spawn and one-shot your very first character, but not by this game's inhuman logic. Before I go on, let me warn you not to take on the elite monster in the caverns because it has TWO THOUSAND FIVE HUNDRED HEALTH!!! half the bosses don't have 1000 health. Plus its attacks are hard to avoid and it takes off half the health of a decent character. There is no reasoning behind this!
But anyway, storyline is another fatal flaw. First of all I didn't even realize there was a story until I checked the wiki. I recommend not trying to do the quest lines until you're level 100 if you do decide to get this game. You will throw your computer at a wall out of frustration of the second galactic fleet quest (but more on that later). You're given quests to fulfill in order to complete the story, but tell me how this makes sense: the rebel storyline starts off by getting 10 tier two resources that are fairly easy to come by even on the first planet, while the galactic fleet storyline starts you off finding and killing an elite monster. I think there was a few problems in the balancing again, people.
But finally, the enemy encounters are what made me finally quit this game after only 5.8 hours of playtime. Some of the weapons are frustrating to use - and before I go on, let me say that the weapon crafting system is needlessly obtuse. Would not recommend. I discovered on my final run that a properly geared sword character is ultimately the best path. That's how it is with a lot of these games, I suppose - the fact that you have to be up close is excuse to totally overpower the melee class. It's a shame because I actually like the combat system. Right click to go into combat mode. Combat is very skillful with the insane number of jumps you can pull off - almost infinite jumping. Stamina is laughably overpowered, by the way, but I wouldn't mind if everything else was well balanced. The first two or three worlds are alright when enemies are only doing 2 or 3 damage to you (in each run I had I wasn't above 25 health), but from world four onwards even the most basic enemies can do 10 or so damage to you in one hit. And because this is a rogue-like and every world is randomly generated it's very easy to unintentionally walk into an onslaught of mobs and get overwhelmed, each one dealing 10-15 damage as you try to get away and heal. One ♥♥♥♥-up can destroy this house of cards, and most of them won't land in your hat! I wouldn't mind if there was a way to save-scum (yes I am a cry-baby sucky loser like that, SHUT UP!) but a character you grow and get attached to will leave no trace if random-number-jesus decides to give you the middle finger like I described a few sentences ago.
I was dealing with these problems from the first run, but what finally broke me was the second galactic quest which I'm just going to spoil because ♥♥♥♥ you: the final boss appears for a random encounter and you have to get to the end of the level without being toasted because, for the encounter, he is invincible. But, like we observed earlier, enemies from world 4 onward can take off half your health in one hit. It wouldn't be much of an issue if the destroyer wasn't as fast as your character. Guess what? He's almsot twice as fast as you! Meaning he'll easily catch you and kill you. And because he is a long, worm-like character he can very easily get you stuck inside him and take that second lethal hit.
This is a game with potential that is horrendously downgraded by its abundant problems. This level of obnoxious difficulty is so obtuse that i don't think anybody could really enjoy it. It's not even the Dark Souls form of difficulty, where the difficulty is the whole point of the game. A difficult game should challenge you to keep getting up and trying again, hacking at an obstacle until it breaks. But the rogue-like nature of this game means every failure starts you back at square one, which absolutely kills this sort of difficulty. Magicite was a better rogue-like game than this and I wouldn't recommend Magicite, so anybody reading now has the excuse to safely write this game off.
Its like a future science fiction magicite some terraria in it too. Difficult yet extreamly addicting. I strongly recomend.

The cursor is very distracting the way it was designed and the combat is overall very unsatisfying.
Many similar type games I have played for hundreds of hours like Terraria, Starbound, and Rogue Legacy (this one isn't same genre as the others) had very fluid exploration and combat systems.
I will gladly revisit this game and even change my review once this issue is sorted out. If you can get past the bad combat system, I believe a rich game lies beneath.
On a side note the game has a bad habit of spamming help boxes that try to explain something when you are in the middle of life or death combat. This is bad game design as when trying to fight your FOV is only about 40% of your total screen due to the size of the text boxes.
I hope this review helps both the developer and the interested players.

Roguelands is a sidescroller game with RPG-elements. You spend your time by grinding for levels in a variety of different planets sporting a few unique enemies with unique behaviors. While exploring these levels, you collect resources in order to craft different kinds of consumables, weapons, armors, robots, and more. Rarer resources can be found on different planets which house tougher enemies and introduce different hazards for you to avoid such as having to deal with different debuffs inflicted by enemies or stage hazards.
Quests are a thing in the game, which usually just consist of collecting a certain amount of items or killing a certain number of enemies. There are main quests. Currently, there's two different main quests in the game which ask the player to do certain things such as collect an item then give it to a certain NPC. There are also events which affect certain planets related to main quests.
Pros:
-Lots of weapons which have different appearences.
-Six different stats, with your character specializing in two of them.
-Cooperative play! Play with your friends online.
-Increase the game's difficulty through the use of Challenge Levels
-Lots of different items to collect.
-When you die, any items in your storage isn't lost, meaning future characters can make use of those items.
-Lots of different Augmentations and Uniforms to unlock which provide bonuses to your character.
-Lots of different races which have different stats and sometimes have different starting items. You are not told which items they start out with unfortunately.
Cons:
-Levels have the same identical layout, but randomly place resources and enemies
-No autosave
-Co-op is buggy. Having a bad WiFi results in the game being very difficult to play
-Players who die during co-op must be revived or the level can't be left. Alt-F4ing results in the character being deleted and items being reversed to the previous save due to the lack of a proper autosave.
-Every weapon belonging to a certain class function identically, even shooting the same projectile. The only difference is stats. Only a handful of weapons will actually have unique functions, such as a battleaxe which fires a projectile.
-Going into combat mode shrinks your screen by adding black bars to the top and bottom. I can tell it's going for some sort of "cinematic" look, but it just makes the screen smaller which is a pain.
-The dialogue boxes randomly appearing during play covers up quite a bit of the screen which is annoying. While being in combat mode this issue is amplified x100.
Overall, there's several issues that affect the game, but it's still an enjoyable experience regardless.

The only match three game I've ever played is Bejeweled. Then I saw Spooky Bonus and I knew I had to get it, since I am a fan of Spooky/Halloween themed games.
It shows inspiration from Bejeweled, but it does not out-right copy it, like other Match three games I've seen being sold on Steam and elsewhere.
Spooky Bonus brings in different mechanics and puzzle pieces that keep the gameplay fresh and interesting, it increases the challenge as your progress. It also brings to you a fantastic art-style and a great soundtrack. You even have a button to change your current desktop wallpaper to the background art of each region of Old Town.
The puzzle boards drop for you,  many gold coins and bags of coins that you can pick up and use the coins to purchase things for the house that you own in Old town. The things you can purchase are decoration and will reward you special abilities or bonuses to existing ones. There is also pieces such as silver bullets, crosses, pumpkin bombs, flashlights, and many more that you can use to help you solve each puzzle. It gives you abilities that once used go on a cool-down, and you must earn points to refresh them.
I have nothing negative to say about this game. It's runs perfect, I have encountered zero bugs or glitches, controls and clicking with the mouse are perfect as well.
I did see that there doesn't appear to be any other game modes besides relax or timed, but there is a possibilty that they can be added in the future. This doesn't stop it being a great game for me. Especially, with the amount of levels they give. Well over 50.
Currently you can choose between a nice relax mode, or a more harrowing timed mode, that makes the more challenging puzzles interesting.
It's a perfect game for quick play sessions, or spending a few hours playing it. I highly recommend this!

This is a wonderful match-3 game. I have owned it for quite some time (purchased from another site), but this one has Steam achievements!
It starts off simple enough. You match a few tokens and finish the level. Soon it becomes more difficult, as you must make matches over golden tiles to remove them, and then over grey tiles that are over golden tiles (so you have to make two matches over that space to get rid of both). Then they add impediments like spiderwebs that must be removed by matching the token on that tile, and rocks you have to break by making matches near them, etc. The game gets harder and harder!
However, you are also given powerups in the form of Halloween decorations on your front lawn. You buy these with money you earn from completing levels. Many of the decorations also level up your powerups so they're more powerful or more efficient. You can also earn certain powerups by making matches of four or more tokens.
All in all, it's a very fun game and gets you in the Halloween spirit.

I had bought this game in a bundle awhile back, and have finally gotten around to playing it.
This game isn't entirely deserving of all the negative reviews that it has received, although this game does have its downfalls.
Judging from the in-game instructions, this was made for the XBOX controller, and does work well with it, except during dialogue. The dialogue advancement is broken. It requires you to press down, and sometimes it will advance right away, while other times there is a long pause before it will recognize the down key. This can be bypassed by pressing the down key on the keyboard, but jumping back and forth from controller to keyboard breaks the immersion a good bit.
This game is also fairly linear with simple puzzles - if you can call them puzzles - that consist of no more than "flip all switches in building to open locked door." Or in one case you flip all valves to drain some water in order to advance. The game instead focuses more on finding objects that tell more of an implied story, as the character tries to piece together what's happened and why he's where he is in the situation that he is in. It actually has a very Silent Hill feel to it, although, aside from a few dead bodies, you'll never encounter another person to talk to. And with its linearity, it only took me exactly an hour to have explored every single room in one play through.
The story gives no definitive answers either, and at the end encourages you to visit the developer's website where you can write about your own theory of "what happened" - or rather, "who dunnit." This is a murder mystery, and it is a nice touch that the developer tried to include the player in the storytelling process, but if you're a seasoned horror fan like myself, you'll probably figure out "exactly" what's going on half way through - and on the website, it seems almost all the other players came to the same conclusions.
Graphically and aurally, I really enjoyed this game. Kind of reminded me of an amalgamation of some old Commodore games I used to play, if they'd had a much wider color pallete. The use of the low contrast black with the digital grain was nice too; it gives the game that "camcorder" look. I was amazed to see how many people worked on this game, as nowadays games of this caliber tend to be made by much smaller teams, however it is apparent that  a lot of work went in to the backgrounds and sound production, so it's not too hard to see where all that manpower went.
Overall, aside from the dialogue box problems, this game can be an enjoyable hour long diversion. However, $2.99 may be too steep for most wallets, considering other games available at this price point, so I'd recommend waiting for a sale. But $2.99 isn't an outrageous price though, although it does seem a little high ( .99 to $1.99 would be more like it!)

A small horror game with engaging and non-linear storytelling.
You wake up having no recollection of what happened. As you stumble across items and traces of past events, you need to construct a story behind them to figure out what happened. This shapes your reality and ultimate fate.
The graphics and sound are minimal, but I was easily immersed (and scared as hell).

Good atmosphere and a decent play, possibly even worth a couple of plays for people that might have missed something and want a different ending.  However, there is no real ending, just a recollection of your experiences and what you previously selected as being the truth, everything is interpretable - for better or worse - and while never being able to know everything does leave the game to linger in your mind a while, perhaps prompting a replay, ultimately feels a little lacking.
This is a very short game, which can be done in 45 mins even when exploring everything.  The intro of the game recommends 1 1/2 hours, but with the limited areas to explore and even accounting for getting lost a little, I really fail to see how so much time could be spent on one playthrough.
Home has the feel of point and click adventure games (without the point and click), but is too shallow to really fit in this category, and as it can be finished quite quickly, can be consumed quite adequately via a Let's Play on youtube.  I ended up both watching a Let's Play and buying and playing the game myself, just to see if I can change the ending, and while choosing different options and exploring a bit more thoroughly, ended up with an extra couple of sentences in my ending.   I bought Home on a 99p sale, and feel this was a fair price for feeling like I'd done my best to get a different ending, and also to contribute to supporting the developer a little.
The best thing about Home is the nostalgia that comes with playing it, reminding me of the games that first introduced the gameplay elements that Home uses, such as the slow opening of doors, and descending stairs like Resident Evil.  Home doesn't rely on Jump Scares or Gore in the same way as modern horror games tend to now.
I just hope that Home inspires more classical suspense horror games.  To me no game comes close to capturing the depth and suspense from the first few Resident Evil games, and even in the 8 bit style of Home, I'd be happy if someone put in the time to give a really rich and deep suspense/survival horror game.
Sadly, all the deep puzzle games of old, like Resident Evil, and Tomb Raider, have evolved into action games rather than puzzle games, and while I enjoyed the Tomb Raider reboot a lot, really miss the games that require some planning, and problem solving.  So here's hoping Home maybe inspires some in the future.

Starting this review off to say I do enjoy this game, but  the problems it has make me not able to recommend it to anyone.
First off if you do go through the process to play with friends, and the net drops on either end when you die. You're hosed, you don't get to be revived, you don't get to get your death unlock crates, and you don't get your character back. I've had it happen to me recently, as I was about to die game just boop. Gone so I start it back up and that 142 level character I've had sense started playing this game, with a number of deaths under his belt is now gone. I'm far from having all the unlocks so to lose a lvl 142 char without getting any chests... Kinda sucks, same happend when played with friends, I have bad net so if it drops when I go down. Bye character, you get deleted. But the biggest complaint about the game I have is this.
The Creator heavily favors ranged combat over melee, you'd logically think that sense melee has more risks and damage output. Incorrect, I've gone through with my friends who had lower level gear then me and had just remade his character after intentionally dieing to get deathchests. He stored all his gear then did solo death run, but him at lvl 1 was doing more dmg then me at lvl 120 with atleast 5+ levels on his basic gear, while I had ultimate armor and we both had lvl 10 ulti weapons... And the only Combat chip that can boost melee's ability, Trickster. It boosts your Movement Speed, Dash Speed, and gives you a 25% chance to negate all dmg. Seems like an amazing melee ability right? Wrong, to use this ultimate chip, you need to have a gun or cannon equiped.
Noticing a pattern here? The Dev heavily and deliberately plays favorites with ranged combat capability over melee, even though you'd not be wrong to assue the more riskier combat would have the better payoff. And the armor modding system even more favors ranged over melee, there's a mod that increases projectile range. Are there any melee boosting mods? Nope. The only mods for melee are the universal mods that everyone can and should get, from stat boosts, to regen, to elemental resistance mods, drop mods, movement(Dash, Run, Jump Height) mods, and xp/credit gain.
And some of the ultimate ranged weapons use the melee stats, strength and vitality... I love this game but hate how byist the dev is towards ranged in this game.
There is literally no reason to make or play a melee character. Its easier to play ranged, you can do more, and you're safer. And neither of my ranged combat friends will take the support combat chips so I have to take the shield and heal, mostly for myself but often times they need it to. So...
Despite Roguelands being a fun game, I cant recommend it to anyone until the character death is fixed, and the heavy favoritism towards ranged combat are fixed. The first one is easy, when a character dies, if you don't get to click retry or main menu, keep the caracter saved until you load it up again where from main menu it gives you option again, so you get your death unlock chests. The second is more about heavy balance to the game, and that's harder to do.

Plot: This Is The Police is about you playing as a soon to be retired police chief of the corrupt city Freenurg set approximately in the 1980s and you having to survive not only the criminals on the street but the elements of city hall, the mob and your own police force. All while tangling with your personal problems and cynicism.
Gameplay: The game is pretty much a strategy game. You send your officers to 911 calls and when theres a crime, you send your detectives to investigate a case. Each time your officers and detectives are successful, they gain "professionalism". The more professional, the more likely they are to succeed and not get killed in action (ie catching the suspect, arresting the suspect, and no civilians being harmed). For cases involving your detectives, over time the detectives will create "frames" and you must put toghether the order of operations in which the crime was commited. Then you must send them and any officers you can spare to the location the suspect may be. Sometimes City Hall, the Mob, or people who own bussinesses in general in the city will call in favors to you that require you to send the minimum amount of officers to help them out. Sometimes these favors end with you getting paid money for the services. And yes, you will need money to do certain favors for yourself, like bribe an official or call a hit on one of your own guys. And yes, your own officers, if dissatisfied enough, can file a formal complaint against you to the Labor Union. The cutscnes in the game are scarce but worth the wait as the acting is very well done. Occasionally you will need to make a big decision in some of the cutscenes.
Pros: The game does well in displaying just how corrupt the city is and theres really no way to be squeaky clean yourself. You either have to get dirty or you're not gonna make it far in the game. And thats dependant on how your relationship is with certain organizations in the city. If your reputation is bad with city hall, they'll deny your request for more officers, detectives, a pay raise, or SWAT upgrades which increases their effectiveness and how many times they can deploy in a single day.  Or if your officers are dissatisfied with how they're being treated, they can report you to the Labor Union and may have to face trial for a lawsuit unless you can convince the reporting officers to drop their suit (usually via bribes).Its really all about keeping everyone happy. This can be frustrating but to me this is how politics is in the real world. Its all about who you know. Its crappy but thats reality. The character of Jack Boyd is great as well. His cynicism is the highlight of the game and it shows in the comic panel cutscenes.
Cons: My first major gripe is the case system with the detectives. As mentioned the detectives will present to you frames showing different stages of the crime and its up to you arrange them in the way the crime happened. Unfortunately this can be frustrating in part due to the game's own smudgy artwork making deciphering whats happening in each frame difficult or trying to connect them to each other. On top of that, you're given a few different choices as to where the criminal may be hiding and the game does little in providing hints as to where the crimianl may be. So its essentially a guessing game in sending your detectives to make the arrest. There were several times I had to look up how some frames were arranged on Youtube because I just couldnt figure it out.
Conclusion: The game is definitely worth a buy, but if you can, get it on a sale. To me the game reminded me of Gotham City and you're playing as Commissioner Gordon in a pre-Batman city. There's no caped vigilante saving the day so you constantly have to make moral compromises just to get things donw. Most of the negative reviews will tell you that the ending is depressing no matter your decisions. This is definitely a Captain Ahab/Moby♥♥♥♥♥♥story and it lets you know that through the Steam achievements. The only downfal of the main character is really from the main character himself.

Universe Sandbox is exactly what its namesake implies. You have the ability to play around with heavenly bodies and change parameters that make them move in strange or unique ways. A word of warning, though: Even the beefiest of gaming rigs can become taxed if the simulation is complex, because this game is making many physical calculations simultaneously.
My only complaint about the game is that it only follows classical Newtonian mechanics. It doesn't account for relativistic effects. For example, I have been able to eject a planet from a solar system at 10c, or ten times the speed of light, but in real life that's physically impossible.

I love this space simulator as i can play around with my own create universe or a pre made one. Rearrange orbital patterns, launch meteors, create planets and moons, change the mass of planets Or even turn the sun into a black hole. I had great fun playing this game, still am.

Got the starter edition from friends, and they also bought packs and operatives, but I wanted to see if I could grind it...
No.
I'm not willing to spend money with this predatory buisness model of in-game currency. At some point, if Ubisoft M decides to make the basic year 0 operatives free I'd reconsider playing outside of my once-a-week friend time.
There is no meaningful teamwork in the game aside from communication, one person can easily carry.
The game crashes without warning and often. There have also been odd gameplay bugs such as the terrorist AI staring at walls, creating an endless game if they're in the killzone.
The mobile-game philosophy doesn't work: I'm not willing to spend more money just to play new Operatives.
Everything about this game makes me think a game like Overwatch is better, even if Overwatch's community is more toxic. It allows me to play every character on any map, I don't have this incentive to grind for content or pay for content that intrinsically changes the gameplay like this does. I don't like having to just pick from 3 attackers or 3 defenders out of a pool of 32, and its appalling that my envy of other players having access to Operatives I don't have can be solved by throwing money at it. Daily and Weekly Qus- 'challenges' don't fix this: what if I don't have an Operative needed to complete them? I guess I'll have to delete it and come back another day/week. The rewards are not worth it anyway, the Operatives are too expensive to justify the meager amount of Renown Currency the game gives. Boosters are a scam to encourage buying more in-game currency. I don't fault a Ubisoft M's development: I'm sure they'd really like it if all players could enjoy all Operatives at any time... like Overwatch.
It's a shame because the community is often lighthearted (outside of my friends that play) and the gameplay is very good, with each Operative feeling balanced in their own way. It's a shame the cell-phone game currency system turns this into League of Legends or Hearthstone... other games I've abandoned because of this greedy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
EDIT:
I didn't buy the game, I got it as a gift from well-meaning friends who thought they were getting a good deal at the time not realizing the grind issue. That could lie in their fault for not reading reviews before giving it to me; we all didn't know when we first started playing. I guess that goes to prove this quote from an article featured on the game's Steam Store page: "I must constantly be skeptical of games, their developers' [publishers] intentions, and my motivations for why I keep playing." So is it wrong to critizise a publishing house to encourage this thinking?
I may have phrased my issue with communication poorly. I may have meant that it was actually frustrating to actively adapt to enemy team strategy (like you can in Overwatch.. that's a common bias running through the review). Sure it's all well and good once a team knows the enemy, but by then it's too late unless they're lucky and picked a team comp. that can effectively counter. Good communication can help overrule this in some instances.
The issue of challenge and skill discrepancy is besides the point of my review, I tacked it on out of frustration. Too many first person shooters that are supposed to be Team-Based end up relying on one or two exceptional players to carry rather than everyone working as a unit. R6 comes so close to this but falls short like many, many others including Overwatch. Yeah, I've been wrecked by other, higher-skilled players, but I've also completely destroyed others. I don't think it's fun on either end. A steam-roll doesn't feel rewarding for either side, honestly. Feeling like you're carrying/being carried shouldn't be seen as a positive in any instance, its just more par for the grind course. It's also why I try to play with friends: we work together well often and have roughly similar skill playing games. It's more fun to play like that for me. I can't speak for others on that issue, but I hope this explanation clarifies it more.

before heading on to why this is an excellent RTS:
Lambda Wars is like your old school assymetrical RTS games - with a twist.
First of all: A lot of RTS games suffer from the "slippery slope" problem. Once you start losing it is very hard to get back on track.
Lambda wars effectively solves this problem by allowing the action (Ability) of a single unit to sway the battle or even a match. For example: efficient RPG microing, a tactical grenade throw or a well manouvered Hunter dodge and charge. Even a last resort headcrab canister or dog leap can turn the game around. Most units and certain buildings come with these special (unlockable) abilities.
Most RTS games also follow a stale "Rock, Paper, Scissor" recipe. Lambda Wars negates this. The effectiveness of a unit depends on its position, how it is micro'd and the composition of the force you are using as a whole. Not the hard counters many RTS games implement. (Swords beating bows, tanks beating infantry, etc.)
Combine Elites can be used against Striders, and Veterans (Crossbow rebels) can wipe the floor with dogs. Yet it is also possible for the latter to beat the previous, even if the size of the force remains the same. Even resource starved teams and players can beat those that nearly control every flag. Late game units and structures aren't "insta win" buttons like in many strategy games.
Barring a few abilities (like the explosive crossbow bolt) the game also tends to stick to the canon.
The music captures the atmosphere of the game and the HL2 universe as a whole, while the sound effects are a mix between those imported from the base HL2 game and newly creates ones. While sometimes they don't seem to play when you select a unit or building, they are characteristic and not overwhelming. Though some of the effects are a bit too loud in my opinion.
Besides that there are several gamemodes ranging from traditional "Annihilation" (destroying all enemy units and production buildings) to "Overrun", where you attempt to stave off increasingly large and more powerful hordes of zombies.
Maps range from 8 player FFA zombie overrun frozen wastelands to smaller 1vs1 canyon style maps. There is enough variety to allow for continuous replayability. A sandbox mode is also included.
Also note that both Rebels and Combine differ a bit in their resource gathering. While both require "Requisition" gained by captured (and upgraded - which increases earnings) flags, the Combine gather - generator generated - Energy as their secondary resource (which they need to store using batteries) while the Rebels gather scrap from (a limited amount of) scrap heaps.

If there is one thing that Home knows how to create, its mystery. With its simple presentation and gameplay, that is really all it has going for it. The game gives itself the horror tag, including a suggestion to wear headphones and turn off the lights like many recent games have done. However, the game isn't intensly scary at all. If there is one lesson to be learned from Slender, it is that sound design can make for very terrifying and suspenseful situations. Home didn't apply this lesson (though it could have been due to fiscal restraints. They credit
as where they got some of their samples). THe atmospheric noise isn't all that tense, and only twice does a loud noise occur that gives me a small jump. More like a bounce actually. Sounds also abruptly stop like when the door animation finishes, or if you suddenly stop your character moving. Its sorta nitpicky, but it took me out of the game. As well as the audio, the aesthetics are just nothing to write home about. It has very plain looking pixel art, and nothing truly looks grimy or dusy or anything that the character narrates. One doesn't need immense graphical fidelity to make an image foreboding or creepy, but rare spatters of pixel blood just don't do the job.
The actual gameplay is simple point and click adventure fare. You interact with objects, and the player character has text describing what it is, or if it can be used to proceed through the game. There aren't any puzzles, just you traversing through these semi-familiar locations.
Whether or not you choose to do certain things in the game (e.g. pick up a gun, go to certain places that may contain extra information) will lead to a different ending. Home plays with the idea of player choice, and makes the mystery turn out however you feel it is going while you make decisions. I can't elaborate too much for fear of spoiling anything, so I have to leave this part thin. There are multiple endings from reading the forums for the game, but I am content with taking the one I ended with.
In the end, the game is very underwhelming. This is clearly an early attempt by a new designer, so it is flawed. I think I just wanted this to be something more. As a horror game, it fails. As a story, it is just interesting enough to recommend, but nothing so thought provoking as a new insight on narrative through play, or even as a mind bending thriller.
Heart-racing thrilling adventure. Definitely recommend as the developer does to play with headphones and in the dark. Gave me the creebies-creepies. Make choices that effect your outcome.

"Each level of the city consists of a diverse variety of buildings and locations. There are shops, bars, prisons, gang hideouts, arcades, homes, slave shops, and more. It is more akin to something found in an RPG or open-world sandbox game than your average roguelike.
That similarity to open-world games extends beyond the environments, and into the gameplay as well. When you enter a given level of the city, you are assigned a few tasks, which can vary greatly. How you accomplish that task is entirely up to you. Like an open-world game, you have complete freedom to do as you wish, and there are numerous ways to accomplish any given task. Each level is basically a small sandbox in which to play. If you have to free a prisoner, for example, you have a variety of options at your disposal. You could go in guns blazing and kill the abductors, or hack into their security system to unlock the cells, or bribe them with money or alcohol, or pretty much anything else you can think of.
Of course, your best course of action will probably depend largely upon your character/class. There is a pretty large cast of diverse characters to choose from, some of which must be unlocked by meeting certain criteria during your playthroughs. Each class has unique attributes, skills, starting equipment, and strengths and weaknesses.  The soldier, with his health regeneration and arsenal of weapons, lends himself to an aggressive playstyle. The doctor, on the other hand, is better served by avoiding combat due to his inability to use weapons, although he can sneak up on people to knock them out with chloroform. The investment banker starts with a large sum of money and has the ability to borrow more from any merchant or shop owner, but also has a drug addiction that constantly drains his health until he gets his fix."
...
(S)treets of Rogue is a fresh and inventive take on roguelikes. It shares as much in common with the likes of Deus Ex as it does with, say, Binding of Isaac, combining elements of roguelikes, RPG's, and even open-world games. The distinctive setting and environments, the diverse inhabitants of the city and the fact that they aren't hostile by default, and the open-ended nature of how to approach any given situation, combine to make it feel like something new and completely unique. I've enjoyed every single foray that I've made to The City, and i plan on making many more."

The storyline is somewhat cheesy, with many uses of hippy terminology such as "maaaaaaan" (feel free to add or subtract any number of a's), but it adds to the atmosphere, or "vibes", of the game. Then there's the overly corny theme that everything can be resloved through, and I quote, "THE POWER OF MUSIC!!!!". It's a fun and creative game, not intended for hardcore music producers, or people into deep, serious storylines. If you're into creating/listening to music and corny shenanigans, you might want to check this out.

Have you played Magicite?
If so, this is a game you will probably like. Made by the same people, and with as much if not more variety than its predecessor, this game is perfect for people that liked the movement mechanics in magicite, as well as its weapons and armor.
Pros:
Faster Action, less downtime between fighting gigantic space demons and dragons
More Weapon Variety (Wooden Sword --> Diamonite Sword? How about Aetherblade --> Magical Blade that shoots lightning? and that's only one upgrade. Also Spears.)
Storyline that isn't just: Travel through all these levels and get to a boss that is a giant moving wall. With more than one story to play through!
Want to gather resources? Don't worry, your drone has that covered.
Multiplayer isn't as buggy (Skipping every world? Looking at you Magicite.)
Combat Mode vs. Travel/Gather mode, Just so you can have your abilities and your items in the same slots, but only a button press away.
Weapon and armor experience. Your gear levels up with you. (Kinda.)
Challenge mode. (Thought you were tough? Oh, oops, that boss now one shots you, as do the weird bugs.)
Customizeable ship. (3x3? got it. The most awesome thing ever? Done. A dinosaur? Sure thing. You want it to look like a meteor hit it and it flew into bits that you have to hop between to get stuff done? Sure, have fun with your new "ship", but yes, it is completely customizeable if you have the scrap metal for it.)
Wanna buy mystery gifts? 1/100 chance you'll get an amazing item! And the currency for buying the gifts regenerates infinitely!
Cons:
Combat Mode vs. Travel/Gather mode. Shoot, my health potion is in my other satchel. And I don't have enough mana to summon a healing field.
Crafting System is different, but this is only a con if you're used to Magicite's crafting. Or if you can't get through the first level, as all crafting is done on the ship.
How to get to Mech city is confusing at first, but you just need to buy a ticket from the guy that thinks you look tasty.
Having a teammate ressurect you, only for you to be taking 238 damage a second and die again due to monsters still being able to inflict status conditions to downed players (798% frost? good luck moving buddy.)
You start with 3-5 health usually. Not the best on melee characters.
Gauntlets. (Sure, they're powerful, but it's not the best when you shoot at the guy right in front of you and the projectile goes beneath your feet and then misses the monster. Right after it hits you. And you die. and get 800% frost.)
There are three types of currency. (More like two, but... Scrap Metal is kinda currency for building your awesome ship.)
Sometimes the random spawned minibosses are harder to kill than the summonable area bosses.
Enemies track dead bodies. (Good luck getting your buddy out from under three rock scarabs.)
Mystery Gifts don't have a chance to give you nothing. (and spawn a box that plays pop goes the weasel.)
Teammates can pick up your stuff that you bought. Only really matters when you're lagging though.
Overall: 9/10
At least you don't have to manually smack rocks to get ore.

If there’s one image that encapsulates the Assassin’s Creed series, it’s that of a hooded figure balancing atop some skyscraping parapet, looking down into the city below. It’s a snapshot that shows off a lot of what makes these games special – their incredible attention to detail, breath-taking verticality, fascinating architecture, unique historical settings - but it also represents their limitations. Assassin’s Creed games are easy to admire, but you often feel a bit distanced from them, too, held back from inhabiting these worlds as fully as you’d like to. You’ve always been on the outside looking in.
Not so with Assassin’s Creed III, which hauls the series across the ocean into a new setting that’s absolutely bursting with things to do. It turns a fascinating section of history into a vast open-world playground, letting you conquer the rooftops, stalk the forests and sail the seas of revolutionary America and authoring a main storyline that puts you in the middle of some of the most important events of the period, like a fly on the wall of history. It’s all about enjoying the freedom of movement the game affords you and immersing yourself in its world, as well as setting up the set-piece assassinations that form the climax of each chapter.
Where the storyline missions usually follow a pattern of gathering information, stalking and eventually killing a high-profile target (with the odd naval mission or large-scale battle thrown in for variety), outside of that you're free to do whatever you want: hunt for trinkets, clamber over the rooftops of New York in search of almanac pages, or pick fights with the Redcoats on behalf of the populace. There is a vast amount of content in this game, from liberating Boston and New York to building up a homestead on the frontier to sailing the high seas to just enjoying the outdoors and hunting wildlife. But perhaps because Assassin's Creed III is so huge, it can be pretty inconsistent. It attempts an astonishing amount, and doesn’t always succeed.
Assassin's Creed III follows hot-tempered Native American assassin Connor for almost his entire life, starting as a tree-climbing kid and growing from troubled young man to vengeful adult – but without wanting to spoil anything, he's not the only character you'll play. Connor's path often intersects with key moments in the American Revolution, putting him in the middle of the Battle of Bunker Hill for one spectacular mission. He finds himself fighting on the side of the Patriots for most of the game, but because he has enemies on both sides, his motivations for doing so has little to do with their battle for independence from the British crown.
Connor isn't as straightforwardly charming as Assassin's Creed II's Ezio, and although writing is excellent for the most part, you never warm to Assassin’s Creed III’s heroes nor grow to resent its villains in quite the same way. It’s impossible to discuss exactly why this is without spoiling something of the game’s plot - which you definitely don’t want, as there are some great moments here. There will doubtless be a lot of discussion around this after the game makes its way into players’ hands, but what it really comes down to is that Connor often feels more like an errand boy than a freedom fighter; within the missions, Assassin’s Creed III can feel very scripted and dictatorial, fettering you with rigid objectives and punishing you harshly when you step outside their boundaries – chase sequences are particularly infuriating on this front. The game is often at its best outside of the story, when it leaves you to enjoy and inhabit its world.
Assassin's Creed III is very enjoyable overall, but it’s not consistently brilliant. Not everything about the game gels together convincingly and the missions’ unnecessary prescriptiveness sometimes undermines the sense of freedom that the rest of the game works so hard to create. But it achieves so much that you can’t help but respect it; no other open-world game has ever given us a setting that's as impressive to observe or as full of things to do as this. Connor’s story has its lulls but it still tells a tale much richer and more compelling than most other games manage, set in a fascinating period of history. Assassin’s Creed III isn’t as huge an improvement upon its predecessors’ achievements as many players will be hoping for, but it’s still up there with the best that the series has achieved - even if it isn't quite the best.

"Each level of the city consists of a diverse variety of buildings and locations. There are shops, bars, prisons, gang hideouts, arcades, homes, slave shops, and more. It is more akin to something found in an RPG or open-world sandbox game than your average roguelike.
That similarity to open-world games extends beyond the environments, and into the gameplay as well. When you enter a given level of the city, you are assigned a few tasks, which can vary greatly. How you accomplish that task is entirely up to you. Like an open-world game, you have complete freedom to do as you wish, and there are numerous ways to accomplish any given task. Each level is basically a small sandbox in which to play. If you have to free a prisoner, for example, you have a variety of options at your disposal. You could go in guns blazing and kill the abductors, or hack into their security system to unlock the cells, or bribe them with money or alcohol, or pretty much anything else you can think of.
Of course, your best course of action will probably depend largely upon your character/class. There is a pretty large cast of diverse characters to choose from, some of which must be unlocked by meeting certain criteria during your playthroughs. Each class has unique attributes, skills, starting equipment, and strengths and weaknesses.  The soldier, with his health regeneration and arsenal of weapons, lends himself to an aggressive playstyle. The doctor, on the other hand, is better served by avoiding combat due to his inability to use weapons, although he can sneak up on people to knock them out with chloroform. The investment banker starts with a large sum of money and has the ability to borrow more from any merchant or shop owner, but also has a drug addiction that constantly drains his health until he gets his fix."

I just finished the game, and it is far and away the best Assassin's Creed Game I have played.  As a few of the major review outlets have already pointed out, there is much greater depth to the gameplay than in previous entries, and I'm fairly certain that a significant chunk of that extra year of development time was spent by the devs playing The Witcher 3 to see how an action RPG is done.  I'm not saying that ACO is an RPG, but it certainly feels more like one than any of the previous games.
Egypt is gorgeous, Bayek is relatable, and the world is full of lore-enriching secrets that made me excited every time I saw a question mark on the map with a distinct golden tint.  The side quests were typically well-designed multi-stage endeavors that made playing the role of Egypt's Medjay feel meaningful, as well as making the world feel very much alive.  The main campaign is good, even great at times.  Without giving anything away, the ending didn't have the positively hollow feeling that Syndicate's did, and more importantly, it felt earned.
The new gear system was appreciated in that it was fun and balanced, as opposed to the needlessly convoluted system of Unity and the overly-streamlined (but by no means bad) gear system of Syndicate.  I actually liked that outfits were purely cosmetic with outfit upgrades existing as a separate crafting system applied to Bayek rather than to individual outfits.  My only real gripe about the leveling system is that given the sheer amount of content in the game, the cap should have been higher.  That said, you can keep unlocking ability points even after reaching the max level, and based on the number of abilities I never wound up unlocking, it seems like the ability tree was meant to be crafted based on preferred play style instead of being maxed out to the point where Bayek just becomes OP.
Performance-wise, the game runs just fine at high settings on a GTX 1060 with an i7 6700HQ and 16GB of DDR4.  By "just fine," I mean that it never quite gets to a stable 60 fps, so I just locked it to 45 and enjoyed the game.  I'll note that while 60 is always preferred, I'll take 45 FPS on a 4K screen at 60% resolution scaling.  It still looked great, and all frame rates above 30 fps are above the "floor" of remotely enjoyable frame rates in video games as far as I'm concerned.  But that's just me.
Might as well just add that this game did not murder my CPU.  Optimization could have been a bit better, but I'll wait and see how things are several patches from now before giving a final verdict on that front.
Overall, this was an incredibly ambitious and thoroughly refreshing instance of an Assassin's Creed game, and I hope future entries in the series are more like Origins.
