This visual novel is a conversation with your dog. She's optimistic, stubbornly so, and she wants to play with you and get you in a good mood no matter what. She doesnt have a clue about the world outside nor inside, and views everything through the eyes of a curious child. Even at the end of your dog's life, she'll be thinking of games, you, and the happy moments she spent with you. She will waggle her tail. She wont know why she'll fall asleep. You will keep talking to her, wether she is right in front of you, or above your head, in the clouds.

Before I start, let me note that since the game is in early access I'm giving it a bit more leeway than usual, but my recommendation is already for the game in its current state.

I'd bought the game through an external website without realising it was in early access, so I was a little anxious to discover it later. I don't have many good experiences with unfinished games. But I'm glad to report that, despite not being able to finish the full story and the game having some issues, I already got enough fun out of it to be worth the price.

Let me start with the good: The visual and sound design are great in style with an excellent soundtrack. The game is insanely customizable; skills, parts, mission difficulty modifiers... Your ship can be freely constructed from parts you receive in any combination and lay-out and with every level you gain you can use more items at once, until you're controlling a massive warship brimming with cannons, missiles and lasers. I've seen people complain about getting weapons they can't use, something I can understand, but I switched from nodes to relays half-way through the game and with the right build you can easily try and combine the two. The more ship classes are added to the game, the more you'll be able to customize in weapons and skills. (There's currently 2 and if I understand correctly there'll be 3 on release with a fourth one planned for the future)

I also enjoyed the oddly surreal setting which fits well with the style. Somehow it also makes just about any ship build feel like it's visually befitting for the world, which isn't easy.

Now, I do have my niggles. The stylized graphics can become a bit cluttered the more weapons you have and the more enemies there are. My main problem with mines was that there was no way to differentiate between my own bounced mines and an enemy's mines. (Part of the reason I switched to cannons instead.) And too many projectiles and explosions can make it harder to see things like, for example, the jamming station's targeting line. It's not too much of a problem, yet, but if the game grows it might become more of an issue.

And I'd want it to; the game gets more fun once there's more enemies on the screen to tear through. Enemy variety is decent, but I’d love to see more, both big enemies with multiple kinds of attacks and more cannon fodder to tear through. (Though they’d need to be balanced for, obviously. Right now weak enemies are a blessing since you still get all your on-kill bonuses for one.)

I also have to agree that there are some balancing issues, but not in the way I see in most negative reviews. I never had difficulty taking enemies down unless I cranked up their armour rating. Just put a lot of big guns on your ship and you're golden.

No, my main issue is more about the risk and reward balance. Missions can be modified to be harder for extra reward. Enemy damage and armour, mission length, ability cost and special modifiers are all available.

However, in it's current form, it's a case of 'go big or go home'. You'll definitely want to activate the appearance of more special enemies since that means more drops and that'll already net you some base extras. Increased ability costs is a good modifier since at higher levels you can generate more ether, so you can slowly crank that up. But increasing the enemy armour or damage starts at doubling it. That's step one. The extra reward for that is minimal, so it doesn't feel worth it and since enemies scale with your level already (Though they feel like the scale up more slowly, which I feel is a good choice since you still feel stronger as you level up) I rarely found myself touching these options. The only time they feel like they might be worth it is if you go all-out to get the rarest parts; every step up adds 100% and the difference between 900% and 1000% is obviously not as big as that first step. But for anything less than mythical, it feels better to rely on drops and purchases.

However, aiming for the best items means cranking up the mission length, which starts at tripling mission objective counts. At the highest settings, this makes missions drag on forever. I really only turned it up to grind in a mission with extra XP bonus while listening to podcasts. (Sadly having to turn down the great music)

I feel the system would be improved if the scaling was more logarithmic, with every step adding 25% on the previous one. Worth dipping into for small extra rewards, but every step up is worthy of consideration. I'm not sure if higher difficulty results in better drops, to be honest. If it does, it'd need to be made clearer. If it does, then that's good; the extra rewards are just the cherry on top. And really, the real rewards are the modifiers that you can install on all the parts you get.

Have I mentioned this game is very customizable? Because it's very customizable.

Lastly, I do have to admit that some tweaking can be done to the skills. Without cranking up ability costs, most of them are too cheap past the start of the game, meaning that only the fairly long cooldowns limit them. If you do crank up the costs, however, the more costly abilities are just not worth it anymore and I'd usually just use my 10-cost one exclusively. I also think it'd be great if the mechanics changed slightly as you levelled up the skills, such as generating more projectiles or even unlocking special upgrades like becoming target seeking at the 5 and 10 level mark. This is perhaps more about the feel of the skill than the mechanics, I'll admit, to make them more satisfying to use. Unless, of course, you could upgrade different elements of skills separately like duration, cost, etc. It'd be a major overhaul, but perhaps could be a replacement for the unleashing system.

...I think I'm more talking to the developer now than reviewing, because I know they read the reviews and listen to feedback. Hello developer! You are a good person for reading all these ramblings. Thank you. As for potential customers: Point is, it could use some tweaking, but it's not broken. You'll probably find yourself picking your favourites for your playstyle, I'm mostly wondering if there's a way to make a larger variety fit for more playstyles. For me it quickly became a game of shield, shield breaker and laser with variety coming more from enemy attacks than my own.

In the end, if you're the type to dip into early access games, this one's worth your consideration. The developer is very active, listens to the community, does active research to see what problems people encounter and has a realistic approach. A game with this much freedom is not an easy thing to balance or keep functional and I only encountered a handful of bugs so far. (Which I'd mentioned here, after which the developer fixed them within a day.) The game doesn't just have promise; it's already fun. There's even a demo available if you're still in doubt, a practice that really needs to make a good return. So thumbs up from me.

I don't have that much play time on this yet, but I see a lot of good stuff, so I wanted to post this now, rather than later. I won this game as part of a promotion from the developer ~7 months ago, but the game sat in my library collecting dust. By the time I actually tried it, I had very few expectations, but I was still very surprised by how much I enjoyed playing. Up front, here are the pros and cons as I see them, but more detail below.

I got this game for free, so I can't really speak to it's value at the current price point ($10). However, I can see myself sinking a lot of hours into this, so I'd say it's probably worth it, definitely if on sale!
This is more than a simple shoot 'em up. There's an interesting story in the background. There are RPG/customization elements and easily customizable controls to suit your style.
You start off with one of a few types of ships, each having different abilities/pros/cons. During missions, you can collect parts which can be used to upgrade your ship, supplying more armor, dealing more damage, improving resource collection, etc. You also have a base set of skills, which the tutorial/intro levels do a good job of explaining, with more abilities you can unlock as you progress.
Better than just upgrading your ship's stats, you actually change the look/arrangement of parts for the ship. I really like this feature, and while it doesn't really affect the game overall the much, it is one of my soft spots. There are no color customizations (at this point that I'm aware of), but the parts all have different sizes and shapes. Even placing them on a build grid, I still came up with a number of interesting looking designs.
Gameplay is relatively slow paced, but that doesn't mean it's easy. Weapon timing is very important and the point is not just to hold down the fire button constantly. The levels are randomized to a point, so that beating a level is not muscle memory, which is great for replayability for me. Apart from the core story missions, you can grind your level up by doing side missions. The levels are randomized (but you get to pick what you want to run), with objectives and rewards changing every time you move to another stage.
There are also challenge bonuses which can greatly increase your rewards (though at this point I have yet to successfully complete any). Each level can be customized with a number of different additional obstacles, such as enemy damage up 100%, 200%, 300%, 400%, enemy shielding up 100%, 200%, 300%, 400%, number of enemies to kill up 100%, 200%, 300%, 400%.... you get the idea. For each of these challenges, you can pick and choose the combination and the severity of the handicap, with more and higher level options leading to even more and more bonuses.
Enemies are randomized within the levels as well, so that - even when the levels all look pretty much the same, unfortunately - the experience each time is different.
Personally, I hated the default controls (all keyboard) and quickly reconfigured them to work with my MMO mouse. Quick access to the abilities this way, plus left-handed movement control proved a much better arrangement for me than what was presented at first. Thankfully, the game's controls are easy to adjust and customize.
The music is pretty darn good, and there's a lot of variety from one level to the next, or even playing the same stage over and over again to grind. The art style is ok. It's certainly not bad, but it does get a little boring after a while.
On top of that, it's very challenging, but not to the point of rage-quitting. It took me forever to complete my first mission/challenge after the first introductory level, but the whole time I was able to work to build up my level, collect better parts, and upgrade my abilities to the point where I could progress further.

Sector Six brings many interesting features to the table, but doesn't seem to understand how to execute any of them correctly.  The experience I had with it was mixed and laced with confusion.  Albiet a polished game with no bugs present, the problem with it exists in the game design itself and I hope the developers will take this in account for their future games.
I will be using my standard format/style for reviewing indie games in this review, so expect a shorter text box with more generalised comments on all the aspects of the game.
Sector Six draws elements from RPG, shoot-em-up and dungeon crawling style games.  Sector Six is a fully singleplayer experience.  The player is allowed to build their ship from scratch in the game's 'shipyard', piecing different modules onto their ship, with each module having its own stats and benefits to the ship.  As the player levels up, the number of modules they can fit on their ship increases.  The issue with this is that the game's simplistic artstyle, while being unique, makes this effort at ship customisation seem extremely lazy, and the ship will obviously always be better off as streamlined as possible to reduce the size of its hitbox.  Also, the all-black, silhoutte style of the game is a double-edged sword.  It gives Sector Six a dark, gritty tone (which sadly fails due to the game's incomptent writing), while over-simplifying it, discrediting the parts of the game which would otherwise have benefitted from a more complex artstyle, so all the pieces won't look more or less the same.
Aside from aesthetics, the game has a few fundamental issues.  Sector Six has an atrocious interface.  None of the ambiguous terms used to coin any of the tabs is descriptive enough, and each tab seems to lead to a network of other ambiguous options.  The map, for example, is one of the game's biggest shortcomings.  The map (AKA 'missions') is displayed in a lattice of differently-shaded boxes, each with a roman numerical on it.  I still have no idea what some of the icons on the map mean, nor do I know which levels I've completed.  Sector Six seems to refuse to tell the player what it is they're doing, and it just makes it even harder to keep track of the game's trainwreck of a story.
Finally, Sector Six puts the nail in the coffin when the player reaches the gameplay.  Enemies take far too long to kill it's far less satisfying than being able to plough through a bunch of enemies.  Animations in the game aren't made interesting enough for me to actually care about what's happening on the screen, which for some reason is still necessary to play the game.  Enemies will shoot the player with equally pea-shooter-style missiles, which sadly put a bit more of a dent on a player than on them.  Skills also seem to have an indeterminant use.  The mortar skill, which launches missiles into the air in a fixed trajectory, will always miss, and seem to do either equal or less damage compared to the basic missile attack.  None of these skills have their uses justified and none of them seem to have any use apart from the shield and shield countermeasure skills.  The gameplay will need some serious work before this game will be remotely fun to play.
I expected far more from such an interesting looking game.  The developers have put a lot of effort into the game, but it appears as if they lack any focus at all.  Each and every element inspired from a different genre seems to miss a mark somehow, which makes the game feel incomplete, empty, and hollow.  There's no satisfaction from destroying enemies, especially when it takes more than a minute to kill one of them.
The game's quite cheap, so I'd still try it out, but it's a completely wasted opportunity for what could have been a proper bullet-hell/dungeon crawler hybrid with a dystopian future setting.

Before I start, I want to say that I got this game off of the Dev's twitch stream.
Now onto the review. (TL;DR at the bottom)
Game Summary: You play as a pilot for a customizable ship of four different classes and pretty much shoot up enemy ships. Also, you can upgrade your ship with parts that you earn from combat, creating the ultimate weapon of 2D destruction.
The concept is good however but...
The bad: The game needs some
balancing. Like no joke, the stats, the enemies, the difficulty modifiers... A LOT needs to be rebalanced. I'll give some examples that I can remember off the top of my head.
-Ship Mod Stats: Say you're level... 10 or so. You find some parts after combat that you decide to sift through. Now, looking at your spoils, you have this shiny little ship mod that gives you... more damage! For the wrong ship type. Disappointed, you move on to the next mod, a crap-tier item. This item gives you only 5% exp. Ok, fair enough, let's go for another run.
This time, you level up and find some higher level mods that happen to give you... a fixed modifier for 5% exp bonus and damage... for yet again the wrong ship type. To be honest, I feel that If you're going to give players a "level" for ship mods... you should probably add some sort of scaling mechanic to make it feel like the mods are actually... working. It feels annoying to see that enemies don't go down as fast as they should when you give your new mods a spin.
Now, I understand that there are shops that you can trade in all of this crap to get new ones, but if I find loot out there that I could possibly use... I don't want to have to sell them.
-Enemies and Modifiers: I'm not sure if I just suck, or I need better gear at level 11. But when I crank up some of the difficulty modifiers for higher damage and "Apparations/Special" enemies, along with bombardment... It's ridiculous. I've only turned up the damage modifier up once (which boosts enemy damage by 200%, boosting twice would be an extra 400% and so on) and I immediately get one-shot by the first claw/missile from the Apparation/bombardment. It... It's not balanced, I tell ya.
Honestly, this is how bad the damage difference is. I tested out the damage modifer up once (200% damage boost for enemies) and got immediately destroyed by debris during one of the forced boss stages where you pick up the last key. I had ~15k full health.
The good: I absolutely loved the music, the skills, and some of the combat. (when all modifiers were set to normal).
-Music: Oh man, I'd buy the soundtrack. It was a nice fit with the game's atmosphere.
-Ship Skills: This is somewhat of a good/bad critique on my part, and I'm pretty sure someone could easily smother my argument with their experience. The first ship (Destroyer, I think?) is a whole lot of fun to play around with. All of the skills easily decimate everything in your path, should you know how to chain skills properly for each enemy.
The second ship, the... Defend... The Mine Ship, (The mine ship, screw it, i'll call it that since I forgot the name) is so god damn awful for some enemies. You shoot mines, you detonate them, repeat. Then you run into a Tank ship + Repair Ship combo and want to off yourself. When I'd got to a certain part of the mission where I had to destroy a stationary target, I was repeatedly and tediously pushing the two buttons to shoot mines and detonate them almost 30 times  just to destroy it. It was NOT fun. I pretty much just texted while I was doing that mission until the damn thing was destroyed. Then I had to do that 4 more times.
Honestly, I would rate this game a... 4/10. I really, REALLY wanted to rate this as a 6/10, but when I thought of all of those missions where I'd have to just grind through enemies... not fun. Especially when things are unbalanced. (shudder)
TL;DR: Intriguing game concept that needs EXTREME balancing around the ship's stats, enemies, and modifiers.

A side scrolling shooter with RPG elements and an interesting storyline. Now that’s a hybrid of multiple genres that shows the versatility of the Steam indie game scene. The developer’s first project as well, so you can bet I’m impressed. If you followed this game since it’s Alpha stage, you’d know that it has progressed quite a lot and from another dreary laser-shooting  game featuring spaceships, Sector Six has opted for missiles and mines, in the end. A more tactical approach than the hectic action of most shoot 'em ups.
And indeed a welcome change from monotony regardless and for once, a 2D shooting game that seems to be story-driven. You control a brave pilot, in his quest to save his homeworld from a mysterious race of flying machines. You will be battling multiple foes at a time or some which are far greater than you in terms of sheer size and firepower. You must overcome them with a mix of hit-and-run tactics since the two ship classes you can choose from and customize, feature either homing missiles or remote detonated mines. So Sector Six employs a non-direct firing mechanism which forces players to think before shooting, unlike most games within this genre that seem to focus on the fire-and-forget doctrine. Apocalypse-class uses missiles and Carrier-class, mines. They are both interchangeable between missions (themselves structured in a non-liniar manner) along with a rich plethora of power-up and customization upgrades.
While altering the ships’ aspect and structure, doesn’t seem to affect in any way their speed & maneuverability, the fact that you can create your own vision of the figher ship, does offer the freedom and personal touches which matter to me. Any game that allows me to create my own version of the character I control, is a title worthy of mentioning. I don’t have to tell you how many of Sector Six’s genre counterparts feature that kind of gameplay liberty. It’s a shame that despite its custom ships and even foe diversity, the objectives and maps don’t seem to vary a lot from one another. Along with the severe lack of a diversified soundtrack, the repetitive mission roster really drags the game’s rating down by a bit. I understand that it’s still in Early Access stage, but Sector Six has got to show more diversity for its current price tag. At least it already features Achievements and Cards for any collector to be swayed into buying it. I’m still recommending you purchase it at a Seasonal Sale discount or when found bundled.
+ Interesting visual concept relating to ship upgrades.
+ RPG elements and story progression.
+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements.
- Limited sound selection.
- Inherent repetitiveness because of the same visual style.
- Slightly overpriced for an Early Access.

This is a relatively minor VN in Key's library, due to its small volume, yet still gets a lot of love for good reason. While not as "heavy" as its siblings, Planetarian features everything that makes a Key work, a quirky girl, who, while potentially annoying at first, ends up being very lovable, a cynical protagonist who plays a foil to her and a story that builds up their relationship until it ends in a bittersweet conclusion. And that all presented with a very good soundtrack, that enhances nearly every scene.
Planetarian is a bit different, however, in that it has a rather dark mood right from the beginning and is much less humorous, due to its post-apocalyptic setting. But Yumemi is not much different from similar heroines, making her really stand out in this setting (which is obviously intentional).
Due to its short length, low price and lack of potentially frustrating choices, Planetarian is very well-suited for people who never read a Visual Novel before. Or just never experienced a Key VN, are interested, but the gigantic, pricey and obtuse Clannad scares them off for now. That doesn't mean that it's just a "beginner's VN", though.
I was skeptical if such a short VN could really be anything great, but it really uses its length very well to tell an interesting an engrossing story that really pays off at the end.

Long story short:  if you play it long enough, you'll see through the illusion.
Whether games, movies, or books --if it's done well-- the gamer, viewer, or reader will suspend disbelief and buy into the world in order to become immersed.
I played this for around ten hours straight the first time around.  It had me truely hooked as I tried to balance the city, the mob and the day-to-day, all whilst trying to fill my coffers and looking after my crew.  I even used a real pen and lined-pad as if it were a real chief's notebook!
This game is (was?!) challenging and at times unforgiving.  But I liked that.  It's not complicated, either, so it fords well for a bit of casual but stimulating fun.  Learn to manage is the key here.
So, I went to bed thinking, 'this is the damn best game I've played in a long while!'  I mean, the recent games I've bought include Hitman, Tomb Raider (meh), Prey - none of which kept me hooked that much.  That much that I was aware of the time, but I thought, 'Just one more shift!' -- oh look, it's 2am...
The game does get a lot right.  And yes there are rough edges.  Some pacing issues.  But nothing is perfect and boy, that becomes very evident after around ten hours plus.
It was like walking into what you didn't realise is a two-way mirror, the glass shattering and crashing to the floor, small shards glitter through the air getting into your eyes and mouth, and -- *screams*
Suspension of disbelief and any immersion is distroyed as through bloodied eyes you see this game for what it is:  it's all meaningless.  And it's not the fault of the game itself, but of the way it was developed.
It's basically a drawn-out grinding mess of inconsequence only driven forward by the occasional narrative.  Sure, there are a few points over hours and hours that you have to make a decision.
Let me explain the point where it all came to light:
After a few disastrious days, or a few missed crimes too many, and the major reducing the force.. repeat.  Oh wait, the major no longer complains, no longer reduces your force.  No recruits to replace my dwindling forece.  Okay, I'm suspicious.  Let's feck this city.  Running it into the ground has no consequnce.  No-one reports it, no newspapers, nothing.  And really, it's the same if you're doing good.  No reward, really.
You suddenly realise that the shift aspect of the game is almost entirely a filler for the next story event.  Which  means, what is the game?!
I really enjoyed this game initially, loved it.  How disappointing.  The elements are good, they're just poorly implemented into a package, so much so that it's all rather pointless.
An anology:
It's like baking a pie, you load up the pie in the cooker, turn it on and set the temperature.  But no matter how you play around with the temperature the pie will eventually cook.  So you remove the pie and it smells great.  It all seems great.  Then you plate it, slice it and realise there's no damn filling.
This Is The Pie and it's a Lie.
Thankfully I got it 50% off.  Thankfully it took about 50% playthrough to get to this damning reveal.  So I guess that's something.

I bought this during the Steam summer sale, played it for an hour, and returned it. I never return games. This was the first. Here's why:
- The events feel random and punishing. Too often, you send your mediocre police to investigate something simple, and the perp gets away, which decreases the effectiveness of your police. Hell, even sending one with a really high level of professionalism didn't seem to really have any affect in a win/loss ratio for a mission. The perp got away. The perp got away again. And again. Oh, this time he got away, and my cops were shot dead. Great.
- The voice acting is really lacking. I can tell that the game wants me to feel something about the character I'm playing by going on about his personal and professional life details, and how he's in a mess; but the delivery is entirely lacking in depth and emotion, that I simply don't care. Can I just tell cops to do things?
- The interface. As a whole, I actually like the interface, but there are a few elements that just don't fit well and are lacking in design choice. In every game I've played, it seems like a standard that the OK (YES) prompt is on the right in cooler colored text, while the Negative (CANCEL/NO) option is on the left and in a bright color to draw your eye. Usually red. This game does the opposite. Your yes prompts are on the left in red.
This doesn't seem like a big deal until you find yourself always leaning your cursor to the right, cooler, blue NO and stopping yourself each time.
Also, before the mission screen, you can pick noir-like music to play for the day. While cute, the sound balance is lacking. Any voice overs were completely drowned out, and the music was lively enough that I couldn't focus on what I was reading whenever I received a call at the station about something suspicious that required me to send police to investigate. There was likely a music volume option that I missed, but that doesn't excuse the music they offer you, which is very upbeat and quick, rather than moody, slow, and subtley in the background so the player is drawn into the game, rather than taken out.
For these reasons, I simply can't recommend this game, and that sucks. I really wanted this game to be awesome.

The only reason to buy this game is its cheap price. However, just because it's cheap doesn't mean it's good.
First things first, this game is not scary. At first Home feels eerie, but you'll soon come to realize that there is absolutely no threat in this game. Like, at all. There is absolutely nothing out there that can hurt you. The only time I ever got scared while playing Home was because one of the sound effects was way too loud. Other than that, there is nothing that should even remotely scare you in the game.
Home is basically a game where you walk around, pick up stuff, and read in-game text. To mix things up, there are also a couple of puzzles that are fairly easy to solve. Home ends in various ways depending on what you do and what items you pick up throughout the game. So if you pick up weapons thinking that you might encounter some threat, you're going to get an ending that you probably don't want.
And speaking of endings, they're dumb. I'm not going to reveal my ending, but mine just didn't even make sense. I literally facepalmed and shook my head after only "playing" the game for an hour, beating it, and then getting that ending. After this  happened, I decided to go out and read other people's endings to see if they were as bad as mine. They too, are dumb. Every ending I read either didn't make sense or was just straight up ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Or both.
Just doing one simple thing can get you a dramatically different ending. This is usually a good thing for games with different endings, but the differences in Home are WAY too huge. They're night and day type differences for some choices. Usually for an ending to be so different you have to do a lot different from your previous playthrough. In Home, however, one change in the right spot completely alters the ending. Some people might play through the game a few times just to see what endings you get, but I usually don't do that. Reading suffices.
Personally, I was fine with paying a few bucks for something so dumb. I'll play anything, and I would actually recommend getting this if you're bored as crap and want something dumb to play for an hour. But if you're a serious gamer that wants something good for the money, don't get it.

I think I can finally write a review on this game. Hopefully someone who is thinking of buying it for the Holidays will take something from my review.
I'm going to start with my Pros and Cons.
PROS+
-Gunplay is nice and rewards the player who takes the time to work on their accuracy. There are times where you will get into CQC with an opponent and holding down left click (or spamming right click for DMRs) will be useful. However, when engaging in long-range combat, tap firing, burst firing, and good precise shots will get you a kill 9-10.
-Headshots always give a kill, no matter the weapon (unless using Cav's Sidearm), no matter the distance.
-Strategy and tactics are needed in order to get better, rise in rank (if you are into playing ranked), and win more games. I don't want to compare this game to CoD, because they're different in so many ways, but the CoD strategy of rushing for frags isn't as effective. It can be useful, but not all the time.
-The endless ways of playing this game give Siege so much replay value. You can anchor as a Rook or Doc and wait for Attackers to push. Maybe you like being sneaky? Roamers like Cav, or Ela are great for flanking attackers. Attackers have plenty of ways to punish these play styles too. Droning into rooms is a great way of reducing the risk of being surprised by defenders sitting in weird spots. Using the Ops Thermite and Hibana are for breaking through Reinforced walls and creating more lines of sight into the Obj. Those examples are only a drop in the bucket.
-Cosmetic only drops from Alpha Packs (supply crates) that give the player more room for customization. Now while the game does have TONS of cosmetic items to unlock with in game currency, they seem to be at a reasonable price for those who can pour many hours in the game a day. For those who can't play too often, but want a cool Skin on their gun can pay in real money to buy currency packs and unlock them without grinding in game.
-Ubisoft has kept up with this game though the couple of years it has been out and it looks like they will continue that practice. New content every 3 months that is free to everyone (maps are completely free, ops take a bit of grinding for in game currency) or you can buy the year passes and get the new ops a week early and for free as well.
CONS-
-The community (from my experience) tends to be really aggresive and toxic towards those who are just looking to have fun, especially in Ranked. While I understand people play Ranked to get a gauge for their skill level, some of them don't seem to understand it's a game and won't kill you if you lose a game or two. Is only a game. Why you have to be so mad?
-Some Cosmetic items are locked behind a real money pay wall and you can only access them through real money.
CONCLUSION:
If you're looking for a game that is different from the run and gun style and is really about strategy and tactics, this is a great choice. I would playing the Situations when first starting out to get a feel for the game (there are a lot of important mechanics to learn). Terrorist Hunt if good for warming up.
[TLDR]
PROS+
-Good gunplay
-HEADSHOTS
-Tons of Customizations
-Replay Value
-Cosmetic only drops
-Developer Support
CONS-
-Toxic Community (from my experience)
-SOME content locked behind a real money paywall
9/10

as the name suggest aims to show the beginning of the Assassin's Brotherhood, over a thousand years prior to Altaïr.
In this game you play as Bayek, an Egyptian Medjay who is on a personal quest for revenge. As a Medjay (a protector of the people) he also encounters a lot of people in need whom he feels is his duty to protect and aid.
During the game you'll visit famous landmarks in the BCE Egypt such as the Sphinx, the great pyramids of Giza, Alexandria, Memphis and etc, you'll also meet important historical characters such as Cleopatra, Julius Caesar and others, as is custom in the AC series.
The game was beautifully designed and the Egypt was amazingly well recreated by Ubisoft using many resources, even NASA satellite images.
The game is demanding, my computer doesn't max it, but that was expected, I can still play decently on high settings.
A lot of people and websites are claiming the game to be having performance issues because of Ubisoft's decision to include up to 4 layers of DRM protection in the game. Unfortunately due to my computer not meeting the requirements to max the game graphics I cannot test that by myself, but there's a lot of evidence online suggesting that the claims may be true.
Now I'll list some pros and cons, keep in mind these are my personal opinions and they may and certainly will differ from other players.
- Beautiful graphics
- Ancient Egypt (I've been crazy for the mysterious land of Egypt since I was a little kid, so playing one of my favorite series on Egypt is a huge plus for me)
- Great characters (especially Bayek, he's a fantastic character)
- Historical locations and characters wonderfully added to Ubisoft's fictional setting
- A lot of stuff to do beside the main content
- Free DLC to be added by Ubisoft next year
- 4 layers of DRM protection (3 if you do not purchase on Steam)
- Bugs (they're slowly being worked on though)
- Extremely high CPU usage even on 8+cores CPUS
- Not very well optimized (but still playable)
- While the game and map feels huge, a good part of it is actually empty desert (that was expected really)
As you can probably see I had to stretch on the cons a bit so people can't say I only listed positive things, that is because for me the game is fantastic and I am loving every minute I am expending on it.
I completely recommend buying it if you the like series or the historical elements it has to offer.

Rating: 8/10 ("Very good")
Recommended for: People who enjoy VNs, people who enjoy post-apocalyptic futures, people who enjoy crying with their novels. I would recommend this to a first time VN reader.
Planetarian ~the reverie of a little planet~ is a visual novel that is about 4 hours long. It has no choices to make and, for that matter, a small number of CGs. Most of the backgrounds themselves are well-drawn. A lot of them have a perpetual rain filter overlayed upon them, given the setting. There are also times, however, where the background is either pitch black, dark grey, or white. One one occasion, this is used to good effect -- the main character is closing his eyes and sees nothing -- however, other times, it feels a little bit cheap.
The soundtrack is adequate. The voice actors really carry the novel -- both the heroine, Hoshino Yumemi, and the unnamed narrator, are voiced. Yumemi is a very pleasant and joyful character, though she can get a bit annoying at times. The narrator is actually fairly enjoyable to read about as well and feels realistic given his situation.
Planetarian's plot is rather simple. Many years into the future, humankind has basically destroyed itself through war. The main character stumbles upon a derelict planetarium that is semi-functionable. This planetarium contains none other than Yumemi. Thus begins the two's interactions as they grow closer together.
It is ultimately a tragedy, and I certainly cried toward the end. That is its main shtick -- the novel wants you to cry for the fate of its characters, for their potential futures. It succeeded with me, but your mileage may vary. The novel also has some philophical themes regarding the existence of robots and humans living among one another.
Overall, I would recommend picking up Planetarian on sale, as othewise you may feel disappointed given the lack of multiple endings and overall short length. For its length, it is a very good visual novel.

I absolutely want to love this game.  The game has massive potential to be fun and its premise is unique as heck, as well as its mechanics, but it’s just so horribly mismanaged.
But in the middle of a two hour game, where it just decides, "nope we're going to kill you full-to-zero right now before you can make any reaction because random events lol" you feel like you're playing in futility, not against a hostile universe.
*The game isn't paced for its own gameplay.
It'll take you more than two hours into the game to realise "Holy crap this is broken as ♥♥♥♥."  It's extremely fun as you start and figure out the mechanics, but then you realise that even at the easiest difficulty, the game piles on negative random events like absolute madness.  Every turn, from a cycle of four (four characters/players) there's a pretty good chance of a negative event happening.  As the game gets later in its play and decks get larger than the original 10 or 12 cards, it becomes impossible to manage all these events with the at-maximum-five cards you're allowed to draw a turn.  You'll have no resource and every one of your job cards and none of your job cards and every one of your resources. That's pretty much game over if that happens for the engineer twice, since that's easily four turn cycles and the ship is either half into hull damage or set up for destruction by events ticking down where all the doors are broken, preventing the events from being resolved (doing damage).  Even with all three other players contributing to the goal of staying alive at the very least, a single bad draw spells death and destruction. It wants you to speed through the universe, but doing so brings you to a quick wall of 0HP.  So does not speeding.  Or sitting in one place.
*Developers cannot identify a release candidate.
Recently, the developers of Space Food Truck released an asynchronous gameplay mode: Great for your friends who can't sit through a two hour long game because of life.  Or wanting to start a game and not finish it and pick it up tomorrow, since the game at default, and up to this point, has not allowed save-and-quit from a multiplayer game (seriously?).  This candidate did not receive even the most basic of cursory playtesting, from our experience playing.  It’s a hot mess of desync issues which require one or more players to leave the whole asynchronous game and rejoin it (annoying more than progress blocking, or it breaks something). A developer who knows what they’re doing would use steam betas to punch through “ay yo this is in testing, so it might (will) break all the time.”
*Hard reliance on RNG to bring challenge
Normally you can build a game off hard RNG in order to build challenge into a game, especially to provide variety, but Space Food Truck relies on it entirely.  There can be two of the same event on a playfield, ticking down individually, the game is allowed to end without reaction from the one player who can stop it, and random events are, quite frankly, overused, though this is previously mentioned, they pile up and pile up fast.  Games that use hard RNG chip away at a player or team until they’re weak enough to be finished off by a small bump in difficulty or a regular threat that they now no longer outclass.  Space Food Truck just decides to linearly (as far as I can tell) ramp the random threats, with no feedback to the player on how that’s done.
*Developer Difficulty
The easy difficulty overuses random events to the point where the game can decide, randomly, about one or two recipes in, it’s time for you to restart your game.  I’m genuinely afraid of the other three difficulties, as they seem to pre-♥♥♥♥ the playing team while throwing them into a universe managed by Cthulhu’s Dice of Dismay.
This game’s flaws, listed above (non exhaustive), creates a deceptive lack of agency.  You feel like you’re in control while you’re playing, but you’re straight down to a dice roll right from the beginning.

This is the first, and hopefully last, time I've had to go back and change a review. SFT started out fun, but every game I've played since has been a bug-riddled, RNG-filled mess in which I was barely able to make any decisions and lost largely because the game deemed it so.
SFT is, at its core, a decent idea. A deckbuilding FTL about delivering food to the galaxy. Where it fails is in forcing players to buy a card every turn, making the only card guaranteed to be available completely useless, and in making is
easy for that card to be all there is. Which would be one thing if you at least had time to work with, but the game dumps a RNG event on you every single turn and every time you visit a new system. These events are overwhelmingly bad and either present a false choice of "damage or no fun this turn" or just deal unavoidable damage right off the bat. Others simply immediately damage systems, which compound rapidly and further reduce your options for doing anything.
As if that's not enough, the netcode is truly abysmal. If you play with friends, expect them to be kicked every ten or so turns and the rejoin button to never work. It does at least autosave games so you can reload from where they were kicked, but its nonetheless completely inexcusable so long after release and in such a simple game.
tl;dr: RNG hell starves the game of any agency and the netcode is determined to make you play alone.

Space Food Truck is a game about traveling the universe cooking food and staying alive. This is as is usual with games something that involves a lot of risks and dangers. That said, it is doable on a first try if you're somewhat experienced with risk-management games.
You play as a crew of four, each with their own job on the ship. The engineer to repair and upgrade the ship, the chef to cook the ingredients, the scientist to research, and the captain to pilot the ship. You can be one of these in multiplayer, or all four in singleplayer. Either way, you're going to have to work together to get through things safely. With that said, it's not actually that hard, at least on normal difficulty. It's very forgiving and you can handle most things just fine unless you've messed up your card deck building.
Speaking of which, you handle your options through a card based system, with cards being your available actions and the fuel to use on these actions. In some cases litterally, with the captain's card to move the ship taking cards with power points to fill up the FTL engine. At the end of your turn, you have to buy a new card to add to your deck. As such, it is important to find ways to trim your deck, or you will be left with useless or lesser quality cards. Several ways to do this exist, and as such you can usually keep your deck under control.
Then there is the actual cooking. Gather ingredients, have the chef cook them up and then deliver the dish to its destination. It seems easy, but it can get a bit more complex. Some ingredients are much more rare, some need to be unlocked by the scientist. And then you have to actually get them cooking too, which again costs you time to find the right cards.
After some time though, it begins to feel like everything is the same. Very few things will ever change and in one or two playthroughs you will have likely seen everything it has to offer. You can stabilise safely and last almost endlessly as long as you have the right cards and did your deck work right. Science becomes mostly useless after they finish researching, and engineering turns into 'play all your cards to fix everything, end turn'. Especially if you play multiplayer, it may begin to feel like your turn is automated where the rest of the crew actually does things.
With a fitting graphical style, simple but functional animations, and what I would definitely say is above average humour with simple but not unthinking or boring gameplay, Space Food Truck rounds out to be a decent game with some replayability troubles. While I would certainly recommend it if it were half price, 20 euro is pretty steep for what you get out of it.

Space Food Truck is a brutal deck building game. On my first play through, the game felt absurdly random and frustratingly difficult. Slowly I started developing a strategy and noticing tricks that enabled me to build up to hard mode and counteract the randomness. The game functions quite well as a challenging optimization problem and it's fun to get better, although on the harder modes it can still be frustratingly random.
Unfortunately, I bought the game with co-op in mind and here I think it falls down badly. If you try playing with someone who doesn't yet know the strategy of the game, you're just going to lose badly. Once you know the strategy, there's not much left to do other than crank up the difficulty and try to fine tune things. The game lacks the depth for trying out various playstyles compared to something like Civilization.
I'd recommend this game for solo play to people who like developing a strategy in a brutal environment. It fails as a co-op game and it has limited depth for replayability once you know what to do.

Pros:
- Excellent deckbuilding and risk-reward mechanics. Every choice feels meaningful and consequential.
- Presentation is very pleasing. SFX, aesthetic, character design and writing are top-notch.
- Each of the characters is very distinct, from their appearance to their dialogue to their playstyle.
Cons:
- Hardest difficulty is practically impossible without save-scumming, due to random event pairs that inflict irreversible damage even with perfect play.
- Music, while great, is limited. You will listen to the same track for 90% of your play time.

Being an Archeage player who converted into a TERA player, I can say that I would definitely rather recommend TERA instead of Archeage to anyone any day.
Yeah, sure, TERA's graphics and several game mechanics cannot be compared to Archeage's breathtaking high spec graphics, and its much larger variety of social interactions between players, and between players and the environment.
Not to say TERA's graphics are not pretty. They are, just not that high spec. The character and their equipment's appearance, wardrobe designs, environment details are very beautiful.
However, TERA is STRICTLY F2P with a unique "true action combat" gameplay style which makes it really fun for both PVE and PVP. The main quests are very story-based, but they're easy to just breeze through, compared to Archeage. So if you're not an MMORPG player who's up for a sh*tload of grinding and just want to have fun along the way, TERA is a better choice.
Waiting on an increase of social interactions in TERA too, for example, in Archeage, you could sit on MOVING trains, carts, boats, ships, tables, chairs, with multiple and high number of players. Horses can carry 2 players while in TERA, you ride solo. (Lol.) Just a suggestion that could make it more fun, since it's an MMORPG.
But all in all, all of these improvements, I can be patient for, because TERA really is beautiful game that would really do well in the future.

No one wrote a review on this classic, well I suppose if ones go too far in depth it's likely to ruin the game. I've had this game for awhile now, somehow I forgot to add a review on it. I only write reviews rarely, but I do feel many are missing out on this classic adventure game. Partly because it does a great job of keeping up the suspense, it really does, often while I was playing this I kept thinking I could see this as a potential movie, for the fact that the story is actually very in-depth. I've played some of Still Life 1, though it's far easier to get stuck on that game in my opinion based on the fact that you can't progress if you haven't completed gathered all evidence. The same is somewhat true in this, but it'll be far more obvious what you should be doing, except there are two really difficult parts (one is in fact a bug that I'll tell you about in a moment). But, with a little observation and diligence (and maybe you have to reload a save every now and then). I mostly played without the need for any walkthroughs, however one of the game's bugs it is very specific what you need to do there, otherwise you have to start your game all over again (but fortunately this happens at the beginning of the game anyway, so it's not a big deal if you screw up).
This bug of speak of is the notorious matress bug. Basically, in one scene, in order to get out the window to the outside of the house, it wants you to pick up a matress, but let me warn you, if you don't know what it's for you can pick up anything else (and it won't let you drop it until you use it). Honestly, I have no idea why the game would kind of trick you like this. I think it was just a bug they didn't fix but it's pretty annoying. It dawned on me I had to use the matress against the window, but not until I had sort of screwed my game up by trying to pick up another item (I forgot how the bug worked exactly but it's pretty game breaking once you have it in your inventory). You need to find and explore everything in that room first before you attempt to use the mattress, just fair warning. Once you have it on you, go to the window and use it on the window. I know it may seem straight forward, but it's pretty tricky. I think I spent like 30 min. or more trying to figure that out, and if you're a person pressed for time, it might be annoying.
But maybe you're asking if there's one or two bugs that could possibly be game breaking, why should I bother? Well, partly because most of them aren't that bad and it really is worth it to finish the story. I honestly think this game is in a way better than the first, but that's just my opinion. I guess I like the fact that you were working together with a fellow prisoner to escape from a lunatic (only the lunatic isn't quite what he appears to be, & if I say more than that it would be spoiling the game. I know at times when I write reviews I perhaps get so excited by the game's concept that I might ruin a surprise, so I've made it a point not to do so with this game. Yes, it has some years on it now, & it may not be as flashy as some of the current GCI's you're used to, so if GCI quality is all you care for, you might want to skip it. But if you love the good old detective games that can unsettle you and keep you guessing (and some excellently designed puzzles that make you think while still being on a moderate level of difficult, not super easy but not super hard...save for mattress part, then yes, this is probably your type of game.
The opening CGI though was very scary, that's why I thought I could have seen it being used as a movie action sequence, it was just that well thought-out. You have some masked criminal who tracks this reporter down who's name is Paloma (it's weird but many of the previous victims name all sounded rather well Mexican or older fashioned names), in fact Paloma seems like she might be Mexican herself though she speaks good English (but after all she's a reporter), she was looking to trace down Victoria Mcpherson and find out more about the killer from the first game (who is never identified, but this game pulls all that together so you aren't left wondering. But the journey of how you get there is really the key). But while, you're staying at a hotel, you get an unsettling phone call where someone tells you he's coming for you & I think you hear some banging on the door (though it's been a few years since I played it, but it was just that memorable of an opening sequence). You're hiding in the bathroom, and next thing you know freakin' gunshots go off and shoot in the door, good thing you were on another side, but no...you soon learn the masked man wasn't actually trying to kill you just then (instead gas comes pouring through the door, and then you realize the reason for the mask). Well sucks to be Paloma, on that day.
You are then carted out of there, and you wake up in a bed no less, and you get this neat little camera view of the killer walking up the stairs with a cam-recorder in his hand and his filming himself coming up the stairs--honestly, from film and story-telling perspective that's very detailed. I've got to give props to the director of this game. Then the camera pans to him looking at you through the camera (even though you're fully clothed it does feel a bit pervy, but hey, great story step up. He's telling you vaguely why you are there but is ♥♥♥♥ing cyptic. You think God I hate this D-head already. But hey, I guess that means game has done of good job of character creating & as the game progresses you feel more & more sorry for all the crap Paloma & Vic have to go through, the game switches between the two only Paloma never gets a true weapon (she's only a reporter), but she does make use of clever ways to put 'cogs'into things. Vic does get a weapon at some point, but this isn't a shooter, you mostly are solving puzzles, gathering forensic evidence so when you get go to investigate what happened to Paloma...you're in essence trying to piece together how to find her in time to save her, eventually you get caught too (and you both have to save each other, so that's the part that appealled to me, two smart chicks fighting back, and make no mistake either one of these ladies would probably punch a criminal in the nads, so they don't make them super meek. It's just unfortunate, that the person involved is just that mentally unstable, that it's hard to fight true crazy sometimes. It might sound weird, but even seeing them in helpless sitation but knowing there was always a way out if you did the right thing (though sometimes you only have limited time to figure things out, so you might have to reload a save a time or two, just fair warning on that game mechanic. Some people really hated that, but I found it challenging, because it does give you enough time if you can calm down and think. If you are stuck, there are several guides that can help at least on the internet, there's not too many on steam. One word of caution, this is not a game meant for children & I'd recommend it being for only older teens, would not recommend anyone under 14 or perhaps 16 to play this game (there is some possibly disturbing content, at least the ideas contained). And remember Victoria is technically a forensic specialist, so you know she might be seeing remnants of crime scenes. It's not as shocking as the first (I remember how shocking I thought the bath tub thing was in the first, & I was 30 plus playing it. Mostly the scenes she revists relates to the kidnapping & you know Paloma isn't murdered yet (sadly it was on his agenda). You learn a rather interesting tidbit, the game is very clever about referencing the golden age of Hollywood movies and actresses, I would actually say it's a very key role in th game, without giving away too much (pay attention to some of the female victim's names & the co-relation to the movies/actresses. Very good use of deductive reasoning there.

It's hard to explain why I am still so in love with this little game/toybox, because it doesn't sound like much. Basically, imagine a tiny music sequencer, simplify it until a three year old can use it, populate it with a weird and weirdly entertaining collection of samples (dog-bark syntesizers anyone?), add some fascinatingly odd visuals and a trippy story, mix it all up with acid and make the head of an utterly crazy yet completely adorable corgi drive it into space. Get the idea? No? I don't blame you, I wouldn't have believed that this could possibly work as a game either.
The campaign is admittedly very short but makes up for it by offering you one of the most ridiculously awesome stories you could have never imagined. And after you've recovered from that experience, you're still left with the quick play, a super simplified but surprisingly fun little sequencer that is there for you every time you need a 15-minute boost of joy in your day. If you like the idea of fiddling with music and beats, even if you've never tried anything like this before, you need to give this little marvel a go. Fear not your musical incompetence, I am persuaded that the game is rigged to make whatever odd things you create sound brilliant despite your worse efforts.
Cosmic DJ is not a game, it is the perfect cheer-me-up machine, the cheapest happy pill on the market. For some strange reason I have a stupid smile plastered on my face every time I fire it up, and every time without exception I feel like hugging the devs afterwards. If it also gave me the munchies I'd be surprised it was legal. ;)

What could, and really should be an intriguning and atmospheric adventure through the tatters of a poor, confused man's life is marred by technical issues, poor execution, and a tired, cliche story that never fully resolves itself.
Defaulting to controller with no options menu, the questionable decision to use down on the analog stick to advance dialog makes it painfully easy to skip important text. Given the way that the text slowly and agonising reveals mundane details about uninmportant objects, this may have been a blessing in disguise.
"Atmosphere" in this sense pretty much comes down to two things: It's dark so you have to use a flashlight, and there's a noise filter. Occaisionally music or ambient sound will help a little and it is usually to signify something that should be important and horrifying. Partially due to the presentation and your character's narration, events fail to have significant impact beyond "oh, okay then". I spent the whole game waiting for it to start in earnest.
The story itself, and its "big reveal" is pretty obvious from the offset. I missed a few clues here and there due to the previously mentioned text issues, or one way doors that inform you that you have missed something and yet prevent you from returning. At the end, you are basically given the option to let things play out in the way you expect, or to have the horrible reveal simply not be there. This might have been a good element if it weren't for the fact that when choosing this option the plot simply does not resolve itself; the character is content simply to say "there are still unanswered questions" Maybe picking different options will give a more satsifying conclusion, but I have no desire to replay it.
Home is very short, which is not something I consider to be a negative, especially when telling a short story with replayable elements. Even at its advertised playtime of 1.5 hours, Home outstayed its welcome. Puzzles that involved using things over and over until they click, mazes, and "hunt the progression ball" made the entire thing a dull slog to an underwhelming end.
If you want a short, atmospheric horror game, play Serena, or Justine, the free story for Amnesia: the Dark Decent. If you want a 2d pixel horror, play Lone Survivor. As it stands, I cannot reccomend Home. It is a dissapointing waste of potential.

On the one hand, I like the concept.
On the other hand, I dislike the execution.
Let me explain:
Game seems really interesting. The base of the game comes from managing a police force. Keep your team staffed and trained and happy so that they are effective police men. Send them out on calls to respond to criminal actions around the city. At the same time you have to provide a public perception of being a lawful police cheif. However, the mayor is inherently corrupt. Various criminal organizations, in league with the mayor, may ask for your allegience and usually demand you to do things that stress the resources you are provided.
Sounds like a interestin time, but heres where I run into problems. Almost every minor decision you make compounds into something that either effects your ability to police, or causes the public or some other entity to percieve you as a threat. It's a matter of juggling political face, with a viratey or organizations and individuals. Boils down to DO X, make Y happy,♥♥♥♥♥♥Z off.
Ultimately you can't just do your own thing because the narrative forces you to make choices. Those choices are usually do horrible thing one or do horrible thing to. And while you might be able to come up with a better third alternative in your mind, the game simple makes you pick choices that give you bad results. It stacks penalty upon penalty upon penalty upon you, with no real relief. Any relief you can hope for, comes from the corrup mayor in the form of upgrades to your police force that are provided on a seemingly random % chance of occurance.
The game also takes a very European tone regarding employment law. For instance, it's "illegal" to fire your employees, in spite of the fact that the narrative is supposively taking place in a fictional American city. Apparently employment at will is not a concept widely practiced in Europe, as you can google all kinds of information on employment practice and illegality of firing. Police in the US get fired all the time, even under contract. There is usually a severance clause that allows for firing of an individual with not penalty other than a financial payout.
I want to like the game, but at the same time, but I feel like the random nature and penalties make it such a grind or simply a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ I have not been able to get past the 30 day mark without either being arrested by the mayor (whom instructed me to do something illegal) or murdered by the mafia (because I didnt have resource to commit to them).
The game is good, quite met my expectations, but expected more to it, like more endings, the style is great, and it's quite worth it if you're into management games. 7/10

Overall Rating - 8/10
+ Fantastic art and music which matches the tone of the game perfectly
+ Story is grity and for the most part keeps the player interested in the outcomes of their actions
+ Investigations are interesting and in some cases challenging
+ Properly managing your officers and responding to calls takes skill and planning
+ Game is worth the price
- Gameplay can get repetitive after the first 90 days or so
- Without giving any spoilers, your actions have limited impacts on the story
- LOTS of RNG
Tips
1. Keep city hall happy. One of the most important aspects of keeping your stats high is by having enough officers. Make sure you choose officers/detectives/SWAT over salary increases.
2. Train your officers. What I did was if a call required 4 officers for example, I would send 1 veteran with 1-2 stripes and 3 of my worst. Works out well 90% of the time.
3. READ THE CALL LOGS. No point in wasting officers when they will be needed later. Basically, most elderly calls are BS.
4. Don't be soft on the officers. I only allowed them to go home if they came drunk (in which case I fired them), if they had a super low happiness rating, or if there seemed to be a genuine issue that they needed off for.
5. Don't be afraid to fire people. I see other reviews of people complaining about how their officers keep calling out and it makes the game unenjoyable. Just replace them, it's super easy...

Took me 19 hours to beat. It's my least favorite game in the series, so far.
I'm guilty of just trying to rush through the main story so I could check off this game as beaten and move on to a more consistently fun game. I think that, if you approach this game with the mindset that you just want to play around in the open world sandbox this game presents, you may have more fun with it. I just couldn't get into that mindset, for some reason. Partly, this was due to me feeling that there was not much reason to pursue the side content, since I was perfectly able to complete the main story while doing absolutely nothing else.
The main things I didn't like about this game were the bugs, the writing (and, in particular, the protagonist), and its failure to deliver consistent fun at the same rate the previous games were able to achieve. I just felt that I spent a large percentage of the game not having fun and actively having a bad time. This was due to frustratingly stupid mission design, bugs, and having a hard time getting the character to do what I wanted them to do. As far as missions go, the stealth missions are some of the worst offenders. The game does not offer precise enough controls to support the stealth gameplay. Coupled with the sparse checkpoints, you'll find yourself getting very frustrated at these missions. It all just adds up to a frustrating experience, especially if you're not feeling motivated to actually play around and have fun with the open-world aspect of the game.
If you come at this game with the right mindset - that you just want to run around and do all the various side missions and activities, I think you may enjoy it, but just know that you're not really giving yourself much of an advantage for completing the main story. And know that there's plenty of other open-world games that are going to give you a MUCH more consistently fun experience. This game tries to do too much, without sufficient polish, and without carefully considering how the design impacts the moment-to-moment fun of playing it. It has lots of ideas for side activities and mechanics that may sound fun on paper but, when implemented, don't provide a consistently entertaining experience.
I feel like this game could've been improved by having people play it and periodically asking them if they were having fun. They would very quickly discover that a large majority of the play is just boring or anti-fun. Maybe they tried that but didn't have enough time to do this thoroughly because there's just too much content.

Sector Six is a spectacular mash-up of light rpg and strategy elements fused with a side scrolling shoot 'em up. Upgrading your ship's modules and weapons has enough depth to serve the greater purpose of the game without being overwrought or limiting. In fact, major credit to the developers for allowing the player to downgrade a previously upgraded weapon and assign the upgrade points to a different weapon at no penalty. This flexibility really encourages the player to try various play styles and strategies mission to mission, which really keeps things fresh.
As for the main course, the shooting is satisfying, the controls are sublime, and the enemies are nicely varied in both attack and defense. Visually, the user interface and menus are well done and easy to navigate. While the in-game graphics may lack a lot of flash, the minimalist kind of look works well here in spite of the abundance of brown. Overall, I have really enjoyed my early play time with Sector Six and I envision spending quite a bit more with it, especially if the replay value is as good as I think it will be.

Sector 6 is a nice horizontal shoot-em-up.  With decent controls and lots of ship customization options, this is a great game to have.  I recommend this game to those that are interested.
The game plays like a standard shoot-em-up, move around and shoot.  What differs is that this game has skill slots where you get to use different abilities at the cost of cooldowns.  There are 9 slots as of now and as you play the game you may unlock more and equip them.
There is a campaign, which has missions you need to complete.  It is not all linear though, you are free to complete as many side missions as you want which consists of "defeat X number of enemies" and at the end you can earn money, ship parts, or xp.

The other differences are the enemy encounters, you don't fight hordes of enemies, there will be  a much smaller amount like 1-5 depending on the enemy ship type.  Battles feel more "tactical", as in you have to dodge enemy attacks, counter attack, and defend.  This gives a feeling of accomplishment and that you earned your victory.
There is also ship customization which I feel is the bread and butter of this game, it is fantastic.  As you play the game you find ship parts that you can use to build and customize your own ship.  You can make it look like anything you want to.  Ship parts also have randomized stats on them that can either boost your damage, defense, or others, this gives the game a lot of replayablity.
A gripe I have is the current movement system.  It is a bit "Jerky" and doesn't feel to smooth.  But this is minor and is subject to change in future updates.
From a hours to price ratio, you will definietly get your money's worth, or at least break even.  Enjoyable game with loot and ship customizing, can't really go wrong.  I hope this review was helpful.

SUMMARY: A challenging and deep deckbuilder roguelike game that is made for (but does not require) cooperative play - where you run a food truck in space.  Charming visuals, interesting gameplay, and replayability make this a must-buy for fans of deckbuilders - but the difficulty level means its not for people who aren't fans of this kind of game.
Space Food Truck's title is perhaps one of the most honest you'll see - you run a Space Food Truck.  Every game your goal is to complete three recipies and deliver them before the hazards of space send you to another line of work.  Truth in advertising.
Game play involves four different members of the crew - Captain, Scientist, Chef, and Engineer - having to work together to keep the ship running, cook meals, navigate to other worlds, and find new technologies.  The game can be played cooperatively online, offline, or solo depending on your inclinations.  Each person can take one or more of the roles and work to deliver meals to the stars - or one person can play them all.
The core gameplay is deckbuilding.  Each character's turn starts with some random occurence (mostly hideously painful), and then they play their cards to have various effects.  At the end of the turn they purchase more cards from a resupply (chosen by the captain, who also acts as quartermaster) - and if they can't buy anything they'll have to take the dreaded Lefrovers to be added to their deck.  As player's hands run out, their cards are reshuffled and sent back to them.
Obviously the goal is to get new and better cards, get rid of bad cards, and keep moving from world to world to find new supplies and unltimately craft dishes you deliver.
As characters travel, various crises occur that may require expending cards, moving around the ship to solve problems, and so on.  Very careful planning ahead is necessary to avoid being overwhelmed with crises - this is where the roguelike nature comes in - the game is perfectly happy to smash your cosmic cullinary dreams.  Cooperation is paramount.
The roles of each character are also unique - and they have unique "job" cards they have - and can be granted - to do certain tasks.
Captain - Moves the ship around, choses resupply options, and gets special command abilities to move the crew and get information.  If the captain has a bad hand you can't move, and if the captain is locked out of the bridge you're really in trouble.
Scientist - Unlocks new cards for the crew.  Not only are these powerful, they also prevent their hands from becoming overloaded with bad cards.  If your scientist is incapacitated, no new cards.
Chef - Not only cooks the meals, but has card-manipulation abilities.  He can take cards, use cards in discard piles, and even destroy unwanted cards.  The chef is required not just to fulfill missions but keep everyone's decks in order.
Engineer - Repairs and enhances the ship.  He makes sure the ship gets better and fixes what's broken on the gastronomic POS the crew is stuck on.  If the Engineer can't do his (its?) duty the ship will fall apart.
The game is tight, well-planned, challenging - and when you fail (and you will) you can usually see why - which makes you want to try again.
The music and visuals are excellent, with a fun, colorful, cartoony look and appropriate music.  The presentation really brings the entire experience to life, making a deep and challenging game even more fun and enjoyable.  Space Food Truck delivers the complete package.
Who's this game for?
* If you like Deckbuilders, it's one you'll definitely want to try.  There's a lot to explore in this game, and some clever mechanics.
* If you want a team play game (each game is probably 45-90 minutes depending on how well you do) and have friends into Deckbuilders, it's a great purchase.  This would be an incredibly fun party game.
The only warning I can add is that if you don't enjoy deckbuilders, this is not for you - because it *is* a deckbuilder that just happens to have team-play and some roguelike elements.  If you're not ready to ask which cards you want in your deck and calculate odds, you probably won't enjoy it.
On the other hand if you read this review and went "Yeah!" it's probably worth your money.

This game is a deckbuilder game in which you (in singleplayer) manage nog 1 but 4 different decks, each with their own function. The game is fun and you can spend more then enough hours in it to get your moneys worth. Specially if you decide to play multiplayer (which imo is more fun then the singleplayer).
Pros:
-Slick animation and style. It doesn't have much animations but the game feels smooth and polished. The style fits the theme and the humour is great in a game like this.
-Decks are unique and fit their own unique purpose. This means you need to get to know every deck before you can play this game well and end it on the higher difficulties.
-Card and deck balance are well thought out.
-Game mechanics like keeping your shop stocked + mandatory buys are a great challenge.
-The events are meaningfull and impactfull.
-It's alot of fun.
- trying to figure out what to do with others in multiplayer makes for a great multiplayer puzzle and great multiplayer interaction. (although i've only played this with friends and not with random others online, so my experience might be different)
Con:
This game has one major flaw that might keep you from buying this. I've read several reviews and I keep reading that people find this a very hard game, meaning even more playtime to master. This may be the case for those who are not used to deckbuilder games. However if you are experienced in deckbuilding games then there is a very likely chance you figure out how this game works fairly quickly. You will most likely have seen all the events and cards when you do your first playthrough so the only thing that you can then change is the difficulty level. And that's where the problem lies. The highest difficulty is not achieved by adding new or harder challenges, it simply gives you a maximum time and an bad starting setup (-1 card per character). Once you figured out how to optimize your plays/decks, there is not much new for you to do. Simply rince and repeat untill you find a playthrough that gives you the right events, cards and draws. This means that instead of increasing the challenge it simply becomes a factor of luck whether or not you can actualy finish the hardest setting.
note that i'm still recommending this game despite the flaw, simply because the fun i've had playing it was worth the money imo. I just lost my motivation to keep trying to play the hardest difficulty setting, which is a shame.
