Post Mortem was a bitter disappointment, with bad game design and an uninteresting plot, so I wasn't sure I'd continue with the Still Life series. However, the first Still Life was actually alright, showing marked improvement in puzzle design and plot development, so I figured I ought to give the sequel a try. Unfortunately, the third installment in the series reversed much of the progress made by its predecessor.
+ The only reason this game is worth playing is because it wraps up the loose strings left hanging by the first Still Life.
- For most of the game, the protagonists are trapped, waiting for a psychopath to come and torture them to death.
- The protagonists are not particularly endearing, making it difficult to care what happens to them.
- The same environment is used over and over for nearly the whole game.
- Limited inventory space is used to artificially increase the difficulty of puzzles by inflicting upon the player the tedious task of carting large items back and forth.
- The puzzles are rarely difficult, and usually only because of bad design.
- Solutions are often either illogical or puzzles offer multiple logical solutions, only one of which is correct for no discernable reason.
- Timed puzzles with impending death are often used to artificially create drama, but they are triggered somewhat at random, often leaving you doomed because didn't collect all needed items/clues first.
- The rotten trick of items only becoming interactable after certain plot triggers is often used, especially with timed puzzles.
- When all logical solutions failed, I often had to run to a walkthrough, only to find the first solution I attempted was correct, but either the clunky interface or dependence on plot triggers was preventing it from working.
- The last puzzle actually discourages the player from attempting to solve it by making running to a walkthrough the only tolerable option. Encouraging players to cheat in an adventure game...
- Lastly, the ending was not at all satisfying.

Still Life 2 is a good enough game. Its main problem is that it comes after Still Life 1, an exceptional game, and as such it pales in comparison.
Whereas Still Life 1 and many other Microid games, like Syberia and Sinking Island, have a fixed camera angle in each scene, Still Life 2 decides to make the switch to a fully fledged 3D experience, where the camera follows the movement of the character. The implementation is not exactly perfect and seems quite immature. At the same time, the 3D models of the characters are rendered differently and their movement seems occasionally a bit more jittery. Alas, if you want to backtrack and the camera angle is from the opposite side! There was even a point
where my character got stuck in a corner and I had to reload a previous save. Fortunately, this was the only occurence through the whole game.
The story starts strong, with Victoria in Los Angeles, right where the previous game ended. She's in the midst of the investigation into the Ackermans and the (new) Chicago killer. I was wondering if we would again go back and forth, maybe to Gus McPherson during the Chicago killings, or to the L.A. killings in the 50s. This time, we go forward to an altogether different serial killer in Maine. This is not something bad, but as the story progresses it gets clearer that we're not going to spend too much time on the past.
The "new" storyline is quite good, at least in the beginning. It mostly unfolds in one location. The fact that you start as Paloma and afterwards you re-examine the same scenes as Victoria is quite amusing. The CSIA kit is fun to play with, although its usefulness is debatable; you collect evidence but many times the analyses don't even elicit a single comment from Victoria. Why bother then? :P Halfway through though, the interest kind of dissipates. The game feels dragged out, both story-wise and puzzle-wise. You expect the story to wrap up, but it keeps going and going, all the while collecting and analyzing even more evidence. At some point it seems nonsensical to wander through the same locations over and over again
The colour palette was fitting to the theme, with the earthly browns and greens
and the more dark and cold greys
. It's generally just as beautiful as the previous game, with one exception: Still Life 1 had similar, drab colours to set the mood, but the paintings were, oddly, full of life! They were a major part of the story and conveyed an artistic quality, which is, sadly, totally absent here.
All in all, Still Life 2 is not a bad game. The comparison with its predecessor is a bit unflattering and there may have been some missteps in the pacing or the direction, but it is a solid title, that provides hours of gameplay. It only needed that little bit of oomph to make it great!

Cosmic DJ is a musical game, much like Audiosurf and Symphony, but this time, you make your OWN music using a sequencer or what I like to call the "tap cymbals". You can switch and use them interchangably at any time. Unlike Audiosurf and Symphony, however, you cannot USE your own music for gameplay, as this is a creation game.
There's a tiny bit of storyline to this game. Basically, some cosmic cube is in charge of jamming out the cosmos and he decided to teach you how to jam out with him and make your own music. But, while you're hosting this rad party, some other dude comes in and starts to rudely broadcast his music instead. The controls are easy as well as the difficulty, as even my dog could probably make good music by stepping all over my keyboard. As for the audio, it's basically the entire game and it's awesome. The graphics are pretty stellar, too.
My experience with Cosmic DJ was awesome. Shortlived, but awesome. At first, it seemed like a stupid game that should just be on the mobile store and that's all there was to it. But, as I played, it turned out to be easy to control with the mouse and ZXCV keys. I personally thought it was very cute. The sequencer was used--as I found out--for more accurate tunes whereas the Tap Cymbals were more for "Press random keys and hope for the best" kind of deal. I actually really wanted to see how far the story went, so I decided to finish it in one runthrough. It took me exactly 58 minutes to finish, which was disappointing, but then I remembered seeing the "Quick Play" Option in the menu and
tried that out for a while, which was not disappointing.
From the realistic puppet bros to the assembling of a jetpack corgi, Cosmic DJ was a great game. Although early access, it still was complete with no bugs that I saw my entire runthrough and the game is basically finished. Though there's music programs out there that can do the same thing Cosmic DJ can do, if you can't sequence or even put together a great track with something like Fruity Loops Studio, Cosmic DJ will take the random input you put in the Sequencer or the Tap Cymbals and make it sound like magic.
What I would've liked to have seen, however, was a bit more storyline gameplay. But, for $6 and running on Unity, this game is amazing. The only trouble I potentially had with it was if I was running something in the background, the dialogue audio by that Cosmic Cube would skip a little bit. It wasn't really much of a pain as you'd think, so don't let that stop you from checking this game out.
I would reccommend this to just about anyone. It's a great game and definitely is worth the $6 I paid for it. If you were on the fence about buying this game previously, just do it and don't look back. It's not as bad as you'd expect. Plus, with that hilarious trailer, why wouldn't you?

The story is elaborate, but the gameplay is pretty underwhelming. Maybe I lack imagination, but what really bugged me about the game is that it felt like a boring text-based adventure with fancy pictures. I tried and I couldn't get myself to care or to get immersed. Animation is seen mostly in the cutscenes and the rest of the time while playing we get to see stylized drawings and text popups. There's no complexity to the gameplay - you just go to work every day, dispatch your officers to various locations and do some light management, such as off-days and things of the sort. In between you get to make some choices which affect the main storyline and solve puzzles for ten-year-olds.
If you like playing games just for the story, you might like it. If you're looking for strategic challenges or an immersive world, this is not it.

This is a game where your choices matter in an organic way. As well as being given overt choices to make between A and B, every micro-managerial decision you make on which staff to hire, train and deploy and which shady deals to accept have a significant impact on the outcome of each of the 180 game days you have left in office. There is no RNG here. If your junior staff die in the line of duty, or your best officer accepts a job elsewhere, this is a result of a poor decision you made somewhere, sometime, possibly game weeks earlier or on the spot. Learn from your failures and make better decisions the next time around.

Story/Plot/Setting:
The game gives you a quick intro of what happened in the previous installments to those who may be new to the series. While it does a decent job, I would still highly encourage you to start from Assassin's Creed II at least and work your way up, as you'll be robbing yourself of the thrilling experience that is the Ezio Trilogy. However, if your interest is in the past setting or storyline, you at least will not be lost for the most part.
The Desmond plot and present setting in this game is definitely the most involved and fleshed out of the series, to the point where there are actual gameplay sections, which I'll talk about in the next section. We find Desmond out of his animus coma, going to different parts of the world to find different keys to help Juno, a precursor to life before humanity. It's certainly an interesting new take on the modern sections in terms of story, and how the modern plotline wraps up will certainly surprise you... if you haven't played Assassin's Creed 4: Black Flag yet (PLEASE DON'T! I encourage you to find out yourself by playing the games in order if you still have yet to play the series).
The past storyline is interesting and certainly a treat to those who have a vested interest in American History. You interact with key icons that helped shape the American Revolution and the United States, although not in the same capacity as say Ezio had with Da Vinci in the earlier titles. You begin the story as Haythem Kenway, an experienced assassin with intriguing motives. His section was quite long and involved taking me about three or four hours to finish, and helped to shape the rest of the game when you later take control of his son, Connor, whose mother was Native American. Dare I say I found Haythem a much more compelling character than his son. Connor, however, I feel gets too much of a bad rap for... well... not being Ezio. Connor is not nearly as charismatic or charming as Ezio or even as much as his father. I do feel, however, this was necessary to the story, as english is a secondary language to Connor, and his culture is exceedingly different from pretty much any character in the series even to date. His personality is more in his body language and facial expressions than in his speech, which I should give much credit to the animators and graphical artists who certainly helped with this achievement. Connor is still a well written character who grows in his experiences as the game progresses and the people he interacts with helps shape him into the man that he is.
Gameplay/Content/Controls:
The core gameplay remains and is refined upon in this installment. Combat is more fluid than it ever was, and new takedowns have been added when attacked by several assailants. This time around, the AI is a little smarter and therefore more of a challenge than in the Ezio trilogy. Enemies will often surround you and back up their buddies, and now set up a firing line while you're in the midst of fighting, with which you can counter by taking a human shield. There is no additional armor this time around, so the health you start with is what you'll have through the whole game. You can get different outfits, but the store bought clothes don't appear in cut scenes. The new crafting and trading system is a nice feature that you have the choice of getting involved with, though having to attack or defend convoys can sometimes be a nuisance and in all honesty added nothing to the experience. Ship gameplay is introduced in this game. I actually cannot understand why this part of the game was ill-recieved, as my only complaint with it is that it wasn't featured ENOUGH into the game. Having played Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag before the third game, the ship gameplay, though improved in later installments, is still solid, albeit treated almost like a side quest.
Speaking of the Naval gameplay, the ship content is absolutely stellar! I did every Naval mission regardless if it was integral to the story because it was just so damn fun! Additionally, collecting the peg leg trinkets unlocks additional naval and ground missions that in and of itself is a thrilling experience in both presentation and story, but also gives you a bonus when you find all of the peg leg trinkets throughout the world of the game and do all of its missions. In addition to this, there is PLENTY more to do. While the main missions are the usual "tail this person, eavesdrop on these people, kill this target," new missions are introduced and some side missions return. The Assassination target missions that were absent in Revelations return. You can also do courier and mail delivery missions. No race missions, though. Collectibles such as almanac pages, trinkets, chests that you have to lockpick, and feathers are there for completionists. Hunting is also introduced in this game, though unnecessary for progression and often too easy, especially when wolves are easy to take down and skin, as they'll seek you out if you draw near.
The controls in this game, though no different from previous installments, feel a little sluggish this time around. It seems like combat was slowed down somewhat from the previous installments and it messed with the fluidity of the gameplay. I did get used to it, but the UI certainly didn't help. Where in Brotherhood and Revelations your action buttons were clearly identified, in Assassin's Creed III only two of them were clearly identified with the appropriate button. The other two weren't and I'm wondering who thought this was a good idea.
An additional detail I mean to mention is that the Parkour in this game is the weakest in the series up to this point. I don't think this could be helped as the location in this point in history is a developing nation, so tall buildings are hard to come by. Forest exploration and parkour didn't alleviate this problem, either. As forest trees tended not to vary much, and the forest environment looks too dull and would often get confusing. Climbing mountains and cliffs proved to be a chore as it was hard to predict at times where to jump and climb.
Graphics and Sound:
Graphics are the best in the series to this point. We saw where they were headed in Revelations, but thankfully in this installment they made sure to give NPCs some added life... well mostly. The children in this game look butt ugly. As I mentioned before, animations are top notch and this is helped by the fact that everything is very detailed. The changes in seasons were really well done graphically, and the details with the snow in the winter are very impressive.
Sound is very well done in this game as well. Guns are loud and impactful. Ambient noises in the city and the forests help with immersion. The naval segments are also very well done with the cannon blasts. Voice acting is really well done, even with Connor, who I initially didn't like until I realized why he spoke so on point and slow in English. So kudos to Connor's voice actor for making it feel real. It was also a pleasure to hear Kevin McNally voice a character in this game, whom you may know as the actor who played Joshamee Gibbs in the Pirates of the Caribbean movies.
Additional Notes:
This game has the most amount of glitches I've seen in an Assassin's Creed game that I've played, though I have yet to play Assassin's Creed: Unity. I not only glitched into a rock, a carriage hauling hay had lost track of where it was headed while I was in it and glitched into a building, in which I got stuck in. Sometimes Connor would get caught on the environment at weird times, and although this is familiar to the series, I had seen it occur the most in this game. In a cut scene near the end of the game, Connor's animations had glitched out and his arms were stuck at his sides. While all of these were humorous, the first two required me to restart from a checkpoint.

You would think this is a mod for Supreme Commander 2.
That is not the case.
Lambda Wars is an RTS set in times of the combine, you choose either Combine or Rebels and you must lead your team to success by training troops, building bases and taking other capture points. You win the game when you destroy the Rebel's Headquarters or the Combine's Citadel. There are 4 players on each team (4 is max) and the opposing teams must destroy each of the other teams Citadel/HQ. Once your main base is destroyed, you are basically defeated because you cannot build engineers without your main base, you become unable to play when the opposing team destroys all of your structures. This game requires patience and it can get very laggy at some times xD. In my opinion, combine is the better team, although rebels get very strong ground troops, combine can build striders and hunters, they can even build............. scanners :o
The best part in this game is when you wait 10 minutes for your troops to train and send in 100 combine soldiers to utterly destroy the other base. It is even better when you are on Teamspeak and you each train 100 soldiers.
Now for the negatives :(   ( not much)
The AI is very .... dumb and will often get trapped in buildings or will be stuck in a wall.
The Combine's Sniper is a very powerful unit which takes 5 seconds to charge a bullet then shoots an enemy target, instantly killing them, the only problem is, the range is very small and you will often get shot before you can even shoot 1 bullet.
The Turret in this game is no doubt the best thing in this game ( apart from striders), it can destroy any groups of enemies within seconds and is near impossible to kill. Without a strider of course. All i'm saying is to probably nerf this thing :P .
This game needs more AoEs ( area of effect) like more mines you can plant, maybe even predator missiles xD . The only thing powerful that can probably take out a whole base with is Headcrab Canisters, if you put 3 of them in the middle of their base it will no doubt overrun it with zombies, instantly killing your troops and turning them into mindless undead, attacking whatever they see.
Okay thats it for negatives and I must say I rate this mod 9.5/10.

A few years ago, when I first played Still Life, I was blown away by the mature nature of it. My point-and-click experiences had been games that could be geared for the whole family. I had recently played Syberia and when I saw that Still LIfe was done by the same publisher I jumped at the opportunity to take on the Still Life saga. Still Life was a great and gritty game and the story continues in Still Life 2.
At the end of Still Life, it appears that Agent Vic McPherson has stopped the main antagonist of the game, but we the players never felt the strong resolution of knowing the identity of the killer, or if he was dead for that matter. In this game, we receive closure, and a whole lot more. There are many twists and turns in the plot that make playing SL1 absolutely necessary. However, the story is solid, and the plight of the two heroines of this game is very believable.
Our two heroines are of course Agent McPherson as she tries to bring another serial killer to justice, while trying to resolve issues that deal with the first game. The other protagonist is a reporter named Paloma Hernandez. She gets kidnapped by said serial killer and must try to survive his games. This makes the game have two different tones, and helps with the pacing. As Mcpherson, you have a field kit, and you are acting like an agent would: sweeping a crime scene for clues, conducting forensics tests, putting together the facts. Very little point-and-click puzzles, but actual detective work. It really gave the game a sense of realism. Then you switch to the hell that Hernandez is facing and the game changes. This particular serial killer likes to play games with his victims to see if their lives are worth living. This is where the puzzles come in. They are not horribly difficult since they are constrained to certain areas, but the pressure is on and the tension is high. It feels like a serious accomplishment each time you beat the killer at his own game. He is also impressed by the way.
Now I would like to address some game mechanics that seem to get some slack from other reviewers. In this game, you have an inventory limit, and I love that. It's realistic! You can only hide so much in a short skirt and tank top! There are various areas in which you can store items for later use, and there are a fair number of them, so backtracking shouldn't be a huge problem. It wasn't for me anyway. Also, there are timed puzzles/scenarios. Sometimes you only have so much time to react or bad things will happen. This is not like in other games where you stand still and the game will wait for you to make it to the next checkpoint. No, this game really tries to be realistic as far as letting you know that in some life and death situations, you don't have a lot of time!
The graphics for this game do not have the same quality as the first game. But then again, the game takes place mostly in a serial killer's lair and house, so how pretty would you want that to look? The graphics are gritty, not pretty and glossy, and to me it works. The cut scenes are great, and once you watch them you can rewatch them in the main menu. Yeah, I've rewatched a few... The voice acting for the most part is great. Some of the animations, especially during conversations can look a little awkward since the characters keep repeating the same gestures, but the voice acting carries. There have been some complaints of bugs, and while I did encounter a bug near the end of the game, I found a way around it. If you are concerned about bugs, wait for a sale.
Overall, this was a great game that reminded me more of a real detective investigation than a point-and-click adventure game. The game wrapped up all the loose ends of the first game and came to a fitting conclusion for both heroines...if you do everything right of course :) .

Like the first game it had an excellent story switching between two characters’ perspectives. The plot has its twists, some of which are predictable but others took me by surprise. The puzzles again avoid feeling arbitrary. I like how the game switches between you feeling like you are outsmarting the killer to feeling that he has everything planned and you are playing right into his hands. I think the puzzles are a bit more difficult than the first game and I found myself looking at a walkthrough more frequently.
The music is excellent but sometimes is played at incongruous times. When something dramatic happens and you have a time limit to solve something then the tense music really adds to the atmosphere. However sometime you would find a clue that would trigger the suspenseful music as you just carry on casually dusting for fingerprints.
The key steps backward from the first game are as follows. Firstly the inventory system. You now have a limit to what you can carry so you have to second guess which objects you are going to need in the future, stash the rest randomly in bins and cupboards, then back track to get and object when you find you need it again. This is just a completely unnecessary feature which only serves to cause frustration. I’m sure I spent half the game carrying round a large pipe that I never found a use for. The game is noticeably more buggy, it crashed a fair few times and I got stuck in the basement simply because I did things a different order to what the game expected. The camera angles were a bit annoying too. Rather than having a single fixed angle in each location moving around can cause the camera to change which makes finding thing just that little bit more difficult.
Where the previous game had various locations across the city this has just a few, so it feels smaller.  The main location is rather extensive, so it is quite difficult to gauge how much smaller the overall map is.
The game adds timed sections which are sometimes really great at raising the drama but at other points it can be annoying when you haven’t collected all the relevant objects prior to starting the timer.
I’ve listed some issues with the game but don’t let that put you off it is still a creditable follow-up to Still Life.

Read through some of the negative reviews and realized that 99% of them are people looking for an easy, "please hold my hand", "I don't know how to deck build" kids. This game is insanely fun and exciting while also being surprisingly relaxing.
There are 4 roles, The Captain, The Chef, The Scientist and The Engineer. Contrary to really any of the negative reviews, all the classes work very well with each other and the game is not overwhelming.
The Captain's main job is to move the ship and refill the ZapMart. You should expect to move the ship each turn you can, as keeping the ZapMart full and stocked is important to getting utility cards and food cards. Use your investigation cards to plot a safe route and save some events for emergancies i.e. don't travel to Handy Man planets if you have full shields!!! Another thing to remember is that while that's your main job you have a secondary "ghost" job which is to oversee the ship. Consider putting 3-4 Diplobots on the Captian to keep the "Crisis" events in check and not get out of hand.
The Chef is reasonable for cooking the meals! You need to collect whatever ingredients are needed for the 3 meals. You have to cook each meal in order but you don't have to turn in any of them to continue, in fact you can cook all three and then drop them off. In the beginning, you should grab all the ingredients on the Chef, later after you get your Free Samples and Discard Dives you can afford to have others grab food that you can take later. There is a second job that is probably almost as important as the cooking and thats burning cards. Consider having the Scientist research Flambe's earlier and grab Gamma Toasters and Burnilizers whenever you can. It makes it easy to have the Chef burn all trash and grab more trash from others. THIS IS LITERALLY THE WAY YOU KEEP DECKS SMALL. Anyone who complains about the decks getting to "big" obviously doesn't know how to play the Chef.
The Scientist on top of being one of my favorite roles, is important to unlocking more cards for other roles. It seems simple and for all reasoning it is, but its also sort of a guessing game. You start off with one "node" unlocked in each role and for every node unlocked the cost goes up. In the beginning you should be pumping AS MUCH power as possible in to the uncovering skill card so you can see all the nodes (this is important since they are in a random order each time). You should try to get the Chef's Flambes, Engineer's Wrenches and Duct Tapes and The Scientist's Breakthroughs and Mimic Cubes. On that point... The Mimic Cubes are AWESOME! They allow you to make a temporary copy of any card in anyone elses hand non-job related. This as allowed me to Mimic a Powerr Glove to draw two, to get a Claw to grab A Claw Of Duty from discard, to get another Mimic Cube to Mimic an Exchangetron and push him over 20 power and 15 worth in one turn... It's just crazy. It reminds a whole helluva lot of playing a simple Blue Mage from MTG. In fact, I'd surprised if the guy that worked on The Scientist wasn't a Blue Mage player :P
The Engineer is one of the most crucial jobs and yet kinda boring. It's not a bad boring, just wish he had something else to do. He really only has one job and thats to repair stuff... which breaks, a lot. You have Wrenches, Duct Tapes, Upgrade Ship and Exterminator cards. The first two give you repair points to fix shields, broken lab equipment and busted doors. The Upgrade ship allows you to iincrease the max shields and FTL drive by one point in one or the other. This becomes a relatively useless card late game when they are both maxed out and you can even burn them at that point to save space. The exterminator card allows you destroy Vexels, which are cards that get added to players decks (through a random turn event) and while they are in your hand they only give -1 Worth. 2-4 of them isn't a huge deal, but anymore then that and your average worth starts to decline and they just become annoying. The Exterminator card (theres only one) can only be gotten from the Scientist, so grab it fairly early to mid game to keep ahead of the Vexels. Other then that, make sure you put AT LEAST 4 Claws Of Duty on the engineer, as not having a Wrench or Duct Tape on a round that had a lot of damage or breakage can be quite bad and possibly make you lose.
All in all, this game is super fun, can be relaxing and forces you to work AROUND the RNGesus not against him! This game can be hard and yeah, sometimes you're going to get Life Support breakage, Xanus attacking, Shields deplete or pay 4 power (which you probably won't have on that guy) and Cyber Punk all in the same round. It will♥♥♥♥♥♥you off and you may lose, but just try again! I love what's in the game so far and can't wait to see what DLC they add! More cards? More Roles? Maybe Themed Galaxies with corresponding events? All that and more please!
Either way, this is worth $20 and if you still are "sold" then wait till a sale. If this game goes to $10 and you don't get it then you never wanted it in the first place!

I'm probably not the best a writing reviews but here it goes.
Space Food Truck has a lovely sense of humor, as well as an enraging trick of making sure that you know your hated by it and it will do everything in its power to make your match as haphazard as possible by knowingly removing the cards that you need to use on your turn, damaging the ship when your team knows in their hearts its the worst possible time for it, and breaking draw pods on the most important characters to make sure your drowning in only the worst cards.
But you will love it. You will laugh and cry at the same time, and that will bind you and your friends (Or strangers if you play online) into a closer knit group than you may experience in many other games. (My friends list has grown by 5 already)
The things that i think you the reader should know.
-You can play this game locally at home, i plug the PC into the tv in the living room and we pass the mouse around like any other game we would play on the table.
-You have to talk to people in online and use actual teamwork. If you don't, you will miss out on opportunities that will most likely explode your ship and chalk up another win to the PC.
-On medium a normal match for me runs about 1h30m to 2h30m. Depends on the team, your luck, and just how angry the game is at you.
-For me local play is perfectly stable, *****online is less than perfect at the moment. This game is pretty new out there so i'm giving it the benefit of the doubt that the hiccups of online play will be ironed out (Adding a server for posting games to join would be great so people who crash or leave can return to the same group instead of hoping that the host will rehost at the same time you rejoin and land in the same server.) *****
**** Online play has been improved, bugs have been cleared out more, and a lobby system has been implemented.  Still not quite perfect as there is some crashing, but worlds better. :D
Purchasing on steam gives people the opportunity to use the chat channels outside of the game to match up again.
Overall i give this game my deepest approval because it delivers an experience that ive been wanting and i hope that you are willing to give it a chance with your friends and be patient with the online!

Here's the short version: Interesting premise but let down by the slog of hours you have to put in to complete and the final game option I chose left me unfulfilled. Ultimately I wouldn't recommend as I don't think it's worth the hours.
ALSO look at the positive reviews and see how many hours they've put in then look at the negative ones. Look at the ones who have completed the game (18-20 hours) and then make your decision.
Fuller version (SPOILERS):
The game was fun for the first few hours but then it became such a chore to push forward. I felt like I was only pushing myself to try to get to the end game.
The start of the game you're put in with an interesting art style and it's all new so it's fun and enjoyable to play. There's subtle hints towards pop culture and it's all rainbows figuring out how to do the best job you can. Problem is that you're corrupt right from the very get go, like there is no option to be not corrupt. It's either try to be less corrupt or go full on corrupt.
I think the middle part of the game is just the slog of having to do day after day where no story element is involved so you're just going through the motions to get to the next checkpoint where you get a cutscene of what the next story arc is.
The end game got a little more interesting, the part where the political views under each officer actually comes into play and you know what they're for. Kind of annoying since the beginning of the game, these had no meaning whatsoever and could of been left out. But the ending I chose which was to go with Chaffe was ♥♥♥♥ing boring. I felt like I got nothing from it. I'll obviously look online to see what the other option would be later.
And I think the real kicker was the fuel option towards end game which ♥♥♥♥ed me over and forced me to write a negative review. You get the option of choosing to swap fuel for a bit of money. Okay, fair enough, I'll take the damages as I want the money. One of my officer's dies from a car accident and apparently it's unknown why. I know exactly ♥♥♥♥ing why. But the game doesn't give me any option to reconcile this. No option to investigate why the murder happened and take a penalty for it or pay money from my own funds to replace the fuel.
But no, I keep losing officers every single day where I was left with 3/4 on each shift cause the game ♥♥♥♥ed me over. I had an idea it may have been a bad idea to switch the fuel but I didn't know the reprocussions of what would happen until after I had chosen the option. And this lead me to not care about the game. As I was losing officers everyday and I wasn't able to fill their positions, city hall doesn't like how I'm handling things so they take an officer slot from me which reduces my numbers still. Then the new officers either turn up drunk ot not at all. Again dwindling my numbers.
So the cycle repeats and I feel like there's no point in trying anymore. And I wait for the finale to come so I can be done with the game.
Some other criticisms of the game include:
- Sloppy typo errors. I saw regular occurances of "he" when referring to female officers and vice versa
- The sound design for certain things is lacking. For example, the sound for a civilian dying is a gun shot. But in the mission, the person has been stabbed. Last time I checked knives don't go "bang bang"
- I'm sick at opening the game when the main protagonist goes "before I go shaking my♥♥♥♥♥♥for the press" in his deep elderly voice every single ♥♥♥♥ing time. I get it but I don't want to think about this old man's♥♥♥♥♥♥every time I open the game. Once was enough.
Overall, the negatives outweight the positives and I don't think it's worth your time.

FNAF 4 is... interesting... to say the least.  I will say that it certainly isn't the worst game in the series.  I still think nothing holds up as well as the first FNAF, but this one is the most diverse and different from the others.  The major difference most people pick up on right away is the lack of a phone guy.  Funnily enough, he might have been why the other games were easier to get the hang of so quickly.  Even though this game DOES have explenation text, you can only read it on the first night, plus this game forces you to take your time listening (and I mean REALLY be careful) while rushing you to micro-manage other parts of the room.
There are no spoilers here, but if you can get the hang of nights 1 & 2, the game becomes highly skill-based with very little luck involved, so if you get good, then this game should be a breeze.
I give this game 3 stars out of 5, and it is my 2nd favorite FNAF game.  Be warned though, the story of this game makes no sense at the moment.  Also, there will be DLC released eventually (the release date is Halloween, but you never know with Scott), so I actually recommend waiting to buy this game until the DLC comes out.  I believe it's supposed to be free DLC, but you can never be too careful, and if the DLC ends up being paid, then maybe people who waited on buying FNAF4 might get a deal. I am a Chinese and my English is not very well, so I played the Chinese version. I am glad to share my feelings in English. There may be some mistakes in my essay because of my poor English level.
Planetarian is not like most of the visual novels. Most of them have many characters and take place in city where there are many people. Planetarian has only two characters and it takes place in an abandoned city. So it seems that there are only hero and heroine in the world, which makes players have strange feelings. The time needed for playing is also short, only 2 hours. It tells a short but beautiful story. A scavenger entered a planetarium and encountered its custodian robot, Yumemi, and the story starts there.
The story of Planetarian is very impressive. I, being like the hero, first thought Yumemi was chatty and annoying and thought the story was boring. But as the story went on, I gradually immersed into it. Finally I only felt sad and took pity on Yumemi. Her wish is only to serve human and bring the starry sky to the people, but the world is too cruel to let it come true. Her awkward behaviors only add to the sadness of the story.
I think there are at least three themes of Planetarian. First, it tells us that we should pay some attention to spiritual wealth. We are always busy in the temporal work and forget the beauty of the starry sky, so this game lets us recall it. Second, it tells us that we humans should not begin a war, for it has showed the terrible world after a war. Finally, it eulogizes ”the people who tells stars” like Yumemi. The world in the game symbolizes the world we are living in now, for our world also has many problems and dark sides. In the bad environment some people corrupt themselves, like the robot weapon. But others still strive to spread beautiful things and thoughts, like Yumemi. It is the existence of them that gives us courage to strive in bad environment, and see the light in the darkness.
To end up, I think the most important value of Planetarian is to purify our heart. We may be impressed by the goodness and perseverance of Yumemi, and live a better life in the following days. “When you are caught in the darkness and are not able to see the real starry sky, please recall the scene you see now. It is my little wish.” It is a beautiful wish of Yumemi, isn’t it? Nothing else is important then.
“Why don’t you come to the planetarian?
The beautiful twinkling of eternity that will never fade, no matter what.
All the stars in the sky are waiting for you.”

takes place in a dystopian future years after a devastating war ruined the environment and caused civilization to collapse. In this world, almost all of humanity has perished. The story is told from the perspective of an anonymous "Junker," a man going around scavenging for supplies and trying to survive. He comes across an abandoned building in a dead city and encounters something that he does not expect. It is a young woman, who turns out to be a robot, named Yumemi Hoshino, the cheery guide for a department store's planetarium. He is at first annoyed by her, but ends up spending time in the planetarium recuperating while trying to repair the main projector so Yumemi can show him the stars.
This game is a kinetic novel, a type of visual novel with no branching storylines and only one ending. If you listen to all of the dialogue, I would estimate it would take around four hours for the average person to complete the game.
Considering that the game was originally released in 2004, some aspects of it may seem a little dated. However, this is not an issue as this is a story-driven game. The art overall is pretty good, even if it is rather limited. The backgrounds are all very well done and really evoke the post-apocalyptic setting. Only one character really appears in the game, that of Yumemi, which is a little disappointing, but it is not really a problem as this game has a very minimalist cast.
The audio in the game works well, too. The music all around is good and really help sets the mood, even if the mood in many of the scenes is more on the dark or sad side. The game's dialogue is also fully voice in the original Japanese which is enjoyable to listen to.
As with most visual novel games, the main thing is the story. I found the story here to be a well-written science fiction story about a robot lost in a world that she cannot possibly comprehend and her human companion. As this game is on the shorter side, I want to avoid spoilers.
In conclusion, this is an interesting kinetic novel. Considering the length, it is up to you to decide if it is worth the full asking price of $9.99. I purchased it on sale. Either way, this emotional game is definitely worth the play for fans of visual novels.

TL;DR: If you're looking for a fun, quick, casual music "game" it's worth it.  If you're looking for a more serious music game or sequencer, move along for now.
Basically, you're given the option of a Story Mode or Quickplay.
Story Mode: You're taken on a short journey in a futuristic cyberworld thats sweet jams have been taken over by a buzzkill.  Your quest is to repair 5 "Jamtennas" in order to bring bands and groups of people (and one puppy) back together, then take the city back.  Each Jamtenna consists of 4 or 5 segments that tell a story, and each segment forms a different part of the song.  Each part of the song gives you 4 or 5 different instruments, a background track, and a 2-bar loop to program in.  Each instrument gives you 4 different pitches (or sounds depending on the instrument).  Once the Jamtenna has been repaired, the game then crafts your segments into one sweet song and gives you the option to export to MP3.
Quick Play: You're randomly given 4 or 5 different instruments and a shuffle button to swap all of the instruments (there is currently no way to manually select the instruments, or the hold onto the ones you don't want to shuffle in).  You're then given a background track selected at random, and are allowed to go to town on it.  I haven't spent much time with this feature yet.
All in all, it's currently a super basic music sequencer with a cute story attached to it.  If you only do one playthrough, you could probably beat it in about 1 or 2 hours, and other than the patterns you throw down, you can't really deviate from what you're given (in terms of notes and instruments).
As far as I can tell from reading the discussion, there's a lot more coming with this game as the developer works on it.  MTCS is a pretty solid guy - he's very active in the discussion boards and listening to what we all have to say.
As stated in the tl;dr: If you're looking for a fun, quick, casual music "game" it's worth it.  If you're looking for a more serious music game or sequencer, move along for now.

There is a certain charm from simulation games which allows anyone, even the ones who haven’t attended any music classes, to easily create their own content. You bring home a sense of accomplishment you don’t often find in other games. Cosmic DJ is one good example of this type of game.
You are the cosmic DJ
You, a floating no face protagonist, are deemed the cosmic DJ by STEVE3, the cosmic conductor of the universe. After learning how to create your own beats and making everyone in the party rock to your groove, STEVE4 crashes the city with bad vibes. It is now up to you to fix the jamtennas with some sweet tracks.
Gameplay
Calling Cosmic DJ a game may not be entirely appropriate. This isn’t like dance revolution or guitar hero where you need to correctly follow a certain QTE like sequence in order to play the tracks correctly. There are also no game overs or consequence to be had here (except for some ear damaging music).
In Cosmic DJ, you play out a scene which is separated into four parts. You select which instruments to play during these parts. You are then presented with a sequencer to input the notes of the instruments. Once you filled in enough notes (regardless of sequence), you are given the option of adding a new instrument to play during a part of the scene. In order to advance to the next part of the scene, you need to fill the “joy” bar by adding enough notes to play the instruments.
Once you finish a scene, you can save the track you created as an MP3 file. While the game encodes the track, you can create the cover art which will be attached to the file you are creating. The game allows you to save your MP3 in any folder in your hard drive.
Presentation
The art style of the game is something straight out of the 80s. From the neon colours to the 3D pixel characters, everything fits the theme of Cosmic DJ. When an instrument plays, you get a visual cue of it playing at the top part of the screen.
My thoughts
One major flaw of Cosmic DJ is its limitation of options in creating your own music track. You create about 60% of the music track where the notes you inserted plays along with the main sequence of the track. There aren’t any other options to help you customise your music to your liking such as controlling the tempo. Since this is just an early access game, gl33k might add more options and sequences for the full retail version.

. It's not just a run in and shoot people game, and I think if you want to get it, that's something important to know before going all in (like with the season's passes or the full blown version). It's about intelligence, about strategic play, about knowing relative positioning through all three dimensions.  And the more you play, the more your learn, and the more you know the better you'll play. The maps have amazing verticality mobility and shoot-through access to enemies. Which also means that the timing on what you do and when you do it can be a very lucky or unlucky thing, so situational luck is a real thing in this game.
And when you die, you're out of the game until the next round. You can sulk or you can help your team win by being intelligent about both callouts and cams.
The community can be amazing or super toxic.  Though pay for play was good, with the newer low-cost edition, there's more and more people on that don't really care so much about the game.  Most of the players are amazing, respecting the game and each other, but a small percentage are far more toxic than I've seen anywhere other than CS:GO. The ability to team kill each other is real, and being a girl, I've been headshot simply 'cause I opened my mouth and someone recognized I was female.  There are times when someone will go into the casual game just to a) kill the hostage, b) kill their own team, or c) sling racial slurs around and take potshots at their own team.
Ubisoft has tried to put something into place to report toxicity; but looking closely at the rules, it's only against racial slurs. We'll see if that pans out, and they have also said that they're going to so something about some of the rampant team killing on console.  It's better on PC... but it still happens.
On the other side, I've also run into a lot of amazing players who are considerate, kind, and respectful of everyone on their team no matter their level or ability. And the game has been designed to reward coordinated and skillful team play. When people play well together in this, this game is better than anything else I've ever played. It's a lot like the TF2 competitive 6's that I played, but with all the tools to make callouts and coordination easy and fun, and maps designed for 5v5 instead of maps that were designed for 12v12.  In a way, the game assumes that people are going to be trying to do their best to play the objective and try and be good teammates; but that does leave room for those who want to just make everyone's day a bad one to do that without restraint.  A hard thing to balance.
The releases of new content are regular and spectacularly fun. They are so good at that, and it's obvious that the developers love the game.  That's all to the good.  So, yes, I'll recommend this for people who want a steep, hard learning curve, and for skill to matter as much as great reflexes.

I will start with the aspects of this game that I enjoyed:

Things I was not keen on:

I would really like to recommend this game, being a huge fan of coop board and card games in general. The asymmetric roles and decks keep everything interesting, game after game. The game mechanics are pretty intuitive and very thematic. The digitization helps with all of the countdowns that would be so difficult to keep track of in tabletop form. The RNG doesn't bother me and its use actually makes sense to me in this context - this is a card game at heart, and events should resemble pulling a random card off the top of the deck. I have played physical games with mechanics similar to this (Pandemic, Eldritch Horror) and know that Bad Stuff happens on a regular basis. This type of game is NOT supposed to be easy, and it's not for everyone. This is for the type of person who can enjoy a game without beating it, but who can also get a great sense of accomplisment on that rare, skin-of-your-teeth win.
All that being said, I can't recommend this game in its current form. Not because of the game rules or any balance issues (all roles are critical to your game's success), but because of the Vexyls in the programming. Hall passes randomly cannot be cancelled, the game stops responding entirely after the Chef plays any of their role cards every once in a while, the Next Phase button sometimes decides to shift a little to the left to sit right under the trash pod and become unclickable... the list goes on. While playing online with 3 friends, we had to leave our session and be reinvited by our host no less than 20 times in a single game, so the current player could try to get their deck to work properly. It is nice that we didn't lose much progress, but this shouldn't be happening in a game that we as a group spent $80 for.

This game is way more fun that I expected it to be. Its a unique deck-building game with some innovative systems layered on and some FTL-like randomization and thematics. I highly recommend it to any fans of deck-building style games.
The game is played like a cooperative team card game, where you must tailor the deck of 1 of 4 unique characters in order to complete various goals and eventually win the game. You can play it completely single-player (controlling all 4 characters on your own) or play online multiplayer where you control only 1 role and make the decisions for only that character's deck. The various added systems and other elements keep it interesting and are actually very fun to engage with.
Rarely do I post reviews on Steam, but this game just gave me such a unique and fun experience that I felt compelled to share my positive feedback. I wish there were more creative strategy games like this being developed.  2 thumbs up from me!
EDIT: I've noticed many other reviews for this game that claim the game's balance is out-of-whack and that the gameplay is simply too hard (or even impossible.) I'd like to comment on those feelings from my personal perspective.
My only criticism of the game's difficulty is that there does not feel like much of a difference between the easiest and hardest settings. On the hardest setting, your ship's starting stats are worse, researching new cards costs more, and the ingredients become harder to track down... however, everything else is seemingly the same. The random aspects of the game are identical on all modes. This means that once you overcome a bit of discomfort at the start, and get your decks properly tuned, the overall difficulty feels very much the same. I could see some adjustments being made so that the easiest setting had more 'postive' random events each turn (or on discovery of a new planet) and the harder settings more negative outcomes, but it's a pretty minor gripe for an otherwise excellent game.
As far as the game being 'impossible' to beat -- I have played through the game 3 times thus far, once on each difficulty setting, and I have not yet even come close to losing my ship. I think that success or failure will often come down to whether or not you really understand the game's core mechanics (or the general principles and strategies of deck-building games).
Since not everyone is as familiar with the genre, I'll try to share some important tips here: First, it is important to have a goal in mind when you are buying new cards. Don't just add a card to a deck because it sounds cool, think about how it will affect the other cards you already have in that deck and what you want to accomplish with that character/role. Second, you should constantly be destroying the weakest cards in each deck whenever possible, so that each turn you draw as powerful a hand as possible. The game will force you to add new cards each turn, so try to utilize card destruction effects to keep your deck as small and focused as possible. Lastly, you want to be exploring a new planet on every turn, so that you can restock the available cards in the shop. Because the Captain role goes first, they can easily buy up the best available cards, allowing them to continously travel to new planets without much issue.
That's all I can say about that. Once you understand the strategy and the systems, getting the most out of all your cards is actually a lot of fun. :)

Space Food Truck is a cleverly designed deck building game. That is the first thing you need to understand. It is not like FTL (Faster Than Light). It is more like a card game called Dominion. I will therefore explain what that means so you do not get the wrong idea.
Dominion and similar card games have deck mechanics designed for four players. Space Food Truck has four characters that take turns in sequence. You are not allowed to check your main deck unless you play cards that allow you to. You may check your discard pile, though. Your decks will grow in size, and there are cards that allow you to attempt to thin your deck of unwanted cards.
Most of the challenge comes from trying to keep your decks from getting too congested. The other challenge is to try and keep a mental note of what may be in your current deck, or what may be in the other decks.
It is not like Magic the Gathering that allows you to build your deck the way you want.
Dominion has certain deck mechanics that must be followed, or it changes the game. Space Food Trucks card mechanics are very similar.
Perhaps the best example of this is Blackjack in casinos. We all know that digging in the dealer's cards is not permitted there. Card games operate in a different way.
If there were no deck mechanics, this game would simply be a board game with assorted pieces. Keep that in mind before you decide the mechanics aren't to your liking.
Random events also keep you on your toes. You must always decide whether to stay or keep moving. Sometimes parking in a spot can lead to your downfall real fast.
Keep playing, and you will get better. Space Food Truck is quite fun and a very welcome addition to my library. It is way better than the same ole copy cat games out there.
A special thanks to the developers for not sticking me with another crumby zombie game. I am personally sick of zombies.

I really, really want to like this game. But as others have pointed out, the RNG engine is tiresome and near impossible to feel satisfaction from. As soon as you clear first meal, you will get what feels like a 60% chance of the RNG events to be negative. After you finish the second, it feels more like 90%. I went through 4 rounds (a round being each character playing) and got a negative RNG event EACH ROUND. The only positives I found were from planets that are pre-determined at the start of the game.
Another thing is card-draw. The aspect of forcing a player to buy a card that's useless makes it extremely hard to make a clean deck. I had multiple hands of just leftovers, solely because everything else in the shop was 7+. I have only a handful of times got enough money for a 7 item, and the last ingredient I needed was /10/. I couldn't even reach 6 most of the time, let alone 10. This combined with the idea of forced leftovers makes it feel like the game is designed to go against you, even in the lowest of difficulties.
Lastly, this game is labeled as a deck-builder when it only takes the very small aspect of a DC- the deck- and everything else is just chaotic. I have never seen a deck builder that didn't have structure, something this game lacks. The starter cards give no value whatsoever, so you have to rely on your job cards for the first part of the game. Which wouldn't be too bad if the value cards you get were in an easier range, instead of pulling 5-7 cards constantly.
TLDR; The game is extremely unbalanced, and is not worth the 18$ tag. It's fun for a half hour with friends, but without buffs to the player's chances of winning, there is no real value in this game.

This game is very forgiving compared to the other games in the series from what I see. In this game, you can choose to completely abandon 1 or all but
1 animatonic, but as a side effect you can't get the best ending. This is a trait similar to FNAF World, one of the few games in the series that I've played(Which I would love to be put back on steam and improved upon) where if you simply took the easiest path to the end you couldn't beat the game. However, despite this games great gameplay, voice acting and story telling, this game does have some flaws.
FLAW 1: Which Timeline is this? The books or the the games?
Scott has made it clear that the books and the games are 2 seperate universes. In the books William Afton is the killer. In the games he supposedly handles the business side of the company. Well, in the end of Sister Location's Custom Night, we find out that Michel Afton is the one trapped inside springtrap, as he says that "I Should Be Dead... But I'm Not", because the spring locks should have killed him, as they did, however, he now posseses springtrap. Then in this game, not ONLY does Springtrap have an ENTIRELY different voice, but he acts more like a killer. Then at the end Henry, who is supposedly the murderer of the games, turns out to be the one who ends it all. He says the person inside Springtrap(who identifies himself as Michel Afton in Sister Location) is treated as a murderer by Henry. Now, he could just be unaware of the fact that it's Michel, or Michel could be the killer, but there is no evidence supporting either of these claims. In fact, there is some evidence to suggest that the animatonics know the player character. Springtrap says "You may not recognize me at first, but I assure you, it's still me", implying that he has some sort of relationship with the player. Baby says something similar, which has made youtubers like Dawko think we play as Michel Afton, which would make sense if we were in the books timeline. But we're not. Either that cutscene in sister location has been retconned or I'm missing something. Or, this takes place in the books. Which means that none of this game would be cannon. Which, considering how ennard is all the animatonics combined, is apparently in the destroyed casing of Fun time Freddy, and yet baby is seperate also raises some red flags. Maybe this takes place in the book's timeline. If so, a lot of this would make sense, and it would make the possibility for another game possible. On to flaw 2.
FLAW 2: We see springtrap, Baby, Ennard and Lefty(AKA the puppet), but where is Golden Freddy or Toy Chica/Normal Chica?
Ok, I get the golden Freddy/Fred bear thing has been done a lot, and that toy Chica is scrapped, and that normal Chica was destroyed by purple guy, but the only things Chica related in this game are Rockstar Chica and Fun time Chica, who never showed up in Sister Location. Springtrap is here as well. He's from the same establishment as Golden Freddy/ Fredbear. We see only 2 refrences to Fred bear in the entire game and those refrences are VERY small. 1st: A crappy drawing of them in the office. 2:A death screen where Lefty is in the pose Golden Freddy has in FNAF 1, with the puppet inside of him. This game and sister location are the only 2 games in the entire series to have no traces of Golden Freddy/Fred bear. Which is kinda sad. He used to have a lot of mystery around him, but now with fnaf 4 the mysterys are solved, and he has yet to make another cannon apearance. Plus Chica has now been absent for 2 whole games. I get that there was a lore reason for sister location as explained by Mat Pat but for this game there is no reason for there not being a version of Chica. In fact, Scott had an artist put a piece of art depicting a withered classic Chica into the latest book. It's like how No Man's Sky promised all these things and then it turned out that it was all false promises. But that's all the flaws really. Now to cover other things.
Gameplay:The game is a pizzeria simulator by day, and also a FNAF 6 during the day as well. While people eat their pizza, you are in a confined space with no exit, ordering cups, plates, utensils, pizza kits and more. These are some of the ones that make sense. But then there are ones like how your supposed to print new menus, posters and flyers for each day. Why does every day need a new menu? The only food they serve is pizza, and even if there was a new special every day, restaurants will often just stick a piece of tape over the old special and write what the new one is. The pizzerias are a budget type establishment, so I don't see why they wouldn't do this. Printer ink is expensive, so this just doesn't make a lot of sense. Also, how the ♥♥♥♥ do you escape the confined area you are trapped in during the day to tend to your pizzeria? The place litteraly has no exit. Actually, that brings up a bigger question, how the ♥♥♥♥ do the animatonics get in the place? It's not like their all there on night 1, no, you salvage them and then they come in as they please. THERE IS NO WAY IN OR OUT. SO HOW DOES THIS MAKE ANY SENSE?!? Also, why do the adverts put advertising on your work computer? THEY PUT UP ♥♥♥♥ING SIGNS AND POSTERS ALL OVER THE ♥♥♥♥ING PLACE AS IT IS. SO WHY THEN HAVE THEY BEEN GRANTED ACCESS TO MY PC THAT HOLDS MY ONLY KEY TO SURVIVAL? It's not even like the customers would even SEE that, only the manager who accepted the offer in the first place! Also, why is it that I can't see♥♥♥♥♥♥in the vents? I get the sense of hopelessness is part of the game, but could I not at least see some part of the animatonics through the vents? It's like if you are trapped in a dark room and you keep hearing the SAME DAMN NOISE and wondering what the ♥♥♥♥ it is and where it is. Oh yeah, that reminds me, THE SOUNDS FOR MOVING AROUND THE ESTABLISHMENT AND GOING IN THE VENTS ARE THE SAME ♥♥♥♥ING SOUND EFFECT! You'd think it'd echo or something in the vents but NOPE! Also, the motion scanner apparently can't tell where an animatronic is unless they haul their♥♥♥♥♥to another room. Either this is budget or its something that wasn't thought all the way through.
In short, this game is a mixed bag for me. I plan to buy the other games in the series, but this game just doesn't seem to be able to make sense.

Good Stuff:
Combat, If you enjoy Action Combat MMORPGs you have a good chance of liking the combat in TERA because the skills are very fluent and make you look awesome!
Customization, The Customization (in my opinion) is pretty good! It allows you to be pretty creative, though with a race, there is a chance you will see a person that looks very similar to you. (I believe the only race like this are Elins but I could be wrong).
Classes, In TERA, I believe that there is always a certain class that is for your own play style which means that if you don't enjoy this game, it is very unlikely it is because of the class you chose (if you chose the right one).
Story, I believe the story (after the start) is very well done! If you enjoy the starting quest always depends on you (though I always thought it was too rushed) I like the Story because it actually feels like your improving while the game goes on.
Just The Things You Love, This seems like a weird one but there is only one word for it. BAM's (Big♥♥♥♥♥Monsters). TERA makes you challenge tons of BAM's just for the story! The battle's always feel difficult and things could turn south at any minute during them.

Bad Things:
Reused Skins, This is about NPC's being reused but this isn't a major problem because you need to understand that they may have had some financial issues so you need to look past these problems, but it becomes a little more common in the higher level areas. This is understandable with the armor and weapons though because of this game being free to play.
Starting Quest, As I mentioned before, I felt that the starting quest and story just felt too rushed. Basically, 5 children that you just meet go into something similar to a coma. If you follow exactly what the story and the quest want, you only talk to 3 out of these 5 children.
UI, Or User Interface can get a bit crowded at times. This is because of when you kill something needed for a quest, it comes up with the story quest your up to, but these quests can be gotten rid of easily.
Mail, You get alot of mail in this game. Not a big problem when your not doing anything, though annoying in things like dungeons or boss fights.
Gender Locked Classes, Something I really dislike about this games classes are all the new ones are always Gender Locked, which leads men that are very interested in the new classes get forced to make girls and get some hate for it.

It is a nice game, with nice graphics, great gameplay and huge possibilities. Give it a try, be your style hardcore, role-play or casual gaming.

Gameplay wise, it is competly different then past games. It seems to be a mixture of breath of the wild and Dark Souls. Dodge attacks, charge up attacks, do a few light attacks, rense and repeat. While playing I noticed a few issues with the combat. When dodging attacks its not always reliable and sometimes it felt like Bayeak wanted to dodge foward instead of away and this caused me to get hit multiple times as he would dodge in the direction i didnt want him to. Combat also is at its best in 1v1 situations. When it does become a sceneario where you have to fight off multiple people it can get annoying as enemies keep spawing in waves and at times this can cause being hit from attacks you couldnt see coming because of the camera, or because Bayeak decided to attack the wrong person.
The Story is also nothing to write home about, and the games greatest weakness. For a game that is advertised as the origins of the Assassins, there is very little about them, until end of the game. Really its just a journey of Bayeak getting revenge and hunting down members of the pre-templar group, order of Ancients. The targets in this game are by far the weakest element. There really is no getting to know these characters, or why they are apart of the order. They are simpley bad guys who want power. In previous games, there were sequences dedicated for each target and proper build up for the assassination. With this game, it just becomes a matter of finding out their identity, then immediatly finding and killing them in the next mission. It is rather simple and dissapointing.
But the real reason to get this game is the exploration that is similar to the Witcher series. The game map is wide and vast and will easily take days to explore every nook and cranny in the game. Hell, i have over 30 hours in the game while writing this review and I only explored about 3/4 of the map and still have plenty of things to do.
Microtransactions and loot boxes also exist in the game. Though I have a gripe with the lootboxes, the real issue i have is with the "Time Savers" that Ubisoft so promplty displays. With the Helix credits that are purchased with real money the plaer can purchase a wide vareity of things such as, upgrade materials, weapons, upgrade points and gold. This is appaling as it gives the impression that ubisoft doesnt feel as though their game is worth playing if they are giving the player the ability to skip content. While playing though i never felt as though I needed to buy helix credits, even when hunting for upgrade material (By hunting the wild life) began to feel tedious.
All in all, Assassins Creed Origins has its issues but I have had a fun time playing the game and do not regret my purchase.

Not really a game so much as it is a musical experience, I can see this working as an entry-level music composition tool meant less for creating personal, quality tunes and more for simply becoming familiar with the act of creating music.
Cosmic DJ functions as something of a simple music sequencer, with separate options for each "course" you choose. "Course," in this case, being a series of scenarios that the game's "story" lays out. The narrative of the game consists of you, the Cosmic DJ, repairing "Jamtennas" so that the galaxy can be filled with good vibes again. It's actually pretty great to see the game almost lampoon its own culture--the visuals are psychadelic, the audio consists of the EDM music you help construct (much of the base track has already been laid out for you), and it generally feels like a fun, at times silly process to create these songs.
My favorite part of Cosmic DJ is the way it mixes the song portions you create into an MP3 track that is ready to play instantly. While these tracks aren't really all that long, it's still fun to go over your creations and try to outdo yourself. And who knows, maybe this game will get you into buying more expensive but more robust software with which to create and mix your own songs. I kind of wish this game would allow for something on that level, but if that were the case then it probably wouldn't be selling for $6.

Cosmic DJ is a game that musical novices and experts alike can fall in love with.
With a variety of upbeat instruments and themes to work with, you are able to compose your own ravey music and watch amazing backgrounds come alive to the beats of them. The track production is parallel to many free music production softwares you can find online, so it truly is a "pick up and play" game.  Overall, it makes for a fantastic experience for those who like sound waves that cause ♥♥♥♥♥♥s.

Currently, this game doesn't have the content to back up it's asking price but I'll definetly be following it as it continues to be developed. Note that I reccomend this game as promising, if the developer continues to add content, this game is gonna be great as the groundwork is already solid.
The game is a top down, 2d, move with WASD/aim with the mouse shooter. Very similar to Enter the Gungeon but rather than a level that has to be completed one room at a time, you are presented with a 'level' of the 'city'. There are randomly generated NPCs and buildings. Each level you are given a handful of missions before you can move to the elevator and proceed to the next level. The focus being on the Rogue like elements, survival is the number one priority. You don't need to succeed at the missions in order to unlock the elevator to the next level, you just have to complete them. If you succeed, you get money/equipment/food.
You have an inventory and gain xp and unlock passive traits. There are lots of different classes, all with unique passives and special abilities. For example, you can play as a Gorilla! You get extra health and a super cool punch ability! But you're a Gorilla so you can't speak, so you can't interact with NPCs in the city and they usually attack you on site if you walk into their buildings. The differences between the classes are fun and meaningful. For every bonus a class has, that class also has a negative passive, this makes the unlockable classes fun and engageging rather than just 'better'.
The game encourages experimentation and usually presents several paths to a goal. Hack a buildings security system and turn the turrets on the guards? Sure! Put a bunch of unknown drugs in the ventalation system so everybody inside will OD and you can collect the loot? Oh wait that unknown drug made them invulnurable for 15 seconds? RUN!
Game's buggy right now and realistically only has like 2-3 hours of content at this point, but I really like what I see and can't wait for more content to be added to this game. Multiplayer would be amazing.

Still Life 2 is a detective point & click adventure sequel to the very dense and dark first Still Life. We're taking control of Victoria McPherson once again in this really requested second chapter, as the story in the first one ended in an ambiguous and ominous way (which is great for a dark game like that, in my opinion). Years after the first chapter Microids decided to work again on the brand preparing this sequel. There are few innovations in the game mechanics like the inventory slots, or the CSI portable Kit. Another thing remains: the dual character. You will control both Victoria McPherson with her investigations and Paloma Hernandez a kidnapped journalist trying to escape or at the very least survive her kidnapper.
Unfortunately even though the story has some good ideas vith few great plot twists really unexpected, really looks like a game badly or quickly developed, as this chapter is supposed to close the story of the first Still Life. And it does, but in a very brief and unsatisfactory way. And while in the first chapter we saw a wide variety of beautiful and different locations, this time we are stuck in a house... Definitely not worth the first chapter.

Still Life 2 is a decent sequel to the original game. It picks up some time after the first one left off. Most of the action happens in the large house in the middle of nowhere. And I have to say, that after a few hours it gets really boring running around the relatively large building, trying to fix stuff for the game to progress. The story itself is decent and playable but the level design and slow progression really set me off with the game. If there was more variety in scenes and progression, this would be a great game. Now, it really doesn't quite get there.
