To me, this game is simply awesome.
I played a lot of these stealth games, but always on Flash websites and with different graphics.
Of course, this game hasn't awesome graphics - it runs perfectly and fast, but has a top down camera and everything is pretty minimalistic.
I think this is the maximum I can take - every other game since the '90s, the stealth things, I hate them all XD
Back to this, you're a ninja who looks like the turtles of the old cartoons (ok this is to me at least ahah) and you've got to find keys computers and other things in every single level and get to the end.
You can be spotted by cameras, by lasers, by noise alarms and such so you need to understand every single menace and know what to do to keep them from harming you.
So, there's some strategy involved. You'll need cards to freeze the lasers, you'll need to move boxes, you'll need to watch your steps in order not to be spotted by cameras and so on; the game has short levels and lots of automatic checkpoints so everything runs really smoothly.
Considered that the game comes at 0,90€ as full price (not even 1 full € xD) it's really cheap to me!
The concept is not that new of course, but everything seems polished and nothing is left out at random. Everything works in the way the developers wanted it to work and controls and camera angles are always super responsive, so that you can play on keyboard perfectly the whole game.
And as I said, the later levels can get quite challenging with all these things to avoid and to watch to. If you like these kind of games - just watch some screenshots or videos, of course it's minimalistic and 2D so there aren't big graphic changes - I think this title really deserves some playthroughs.
It requires 4 or more hours to complete and you got also lots of achievements :)

It was fun for the short time I played it, but I have no desire to play it any longer.  It's not what I expected or wanted.  I was hoping for what some of the reviews say about it being like a remake of Road Rash, but it's very different.  Road rash was a racing game where you had a sense of progress from track to track.  Road Redemption is like a challenge mode where you have a different objective each time.  There is no sense of progression in the campaign or story, each play section or race is too short, and the upgrades are far more simplistic than one would expect from the game's description.  Each non-race even seems to play the same, you start off using lots of nitro to get ahead faster and then hit enemies to refill it before you complete the objective, it's more like the old arcade game Outrun than Road Rash and more like a mobile game than a full pc game.
It's more like Outrun because in the campaign you play until you die or fail to complete too many objectives which takes away your health.  All the upgrades are done during the loading screen in-between these checkpoint-like times, after which the game starts you off moving.  I played through maybe the first 6 of these and never was there a 3, 2, 1, go race from start to finish.
If you just want to bash heads on motorcycles for an hour at a time or less, maybe you'll like it.  But if you want a game like the Road Rash series, with rpg elements, track progression, and AI bikers you love to hate; Axle, Biff, Belladonna, P.E. No. 1  etc.... Road Redemption has none of these things and will leave you dissapointed.  :(
-  Good music
-  Good graphics
-  No substance

It's just like the old 'Road Rash' games and just as fun. When I want to play something that moves fast, this is the game I keep coming back to. It's worth even full price.
That said though, there's a few things:
1. This game is the God of cheap deaths and lame losses. You're feeling comfortable in a race since you only need to finish 3rd or better, and you're currently 2nd. Then all of a sudden 2 enemy bikes spawn in front of you right next to the finish line. Or you're cruising along and crash into a log that was just over the ridge of a hill and completely invisible. There's so many situations where you say, "OMG that is ***cking bull****".
2. Boss levels don't impress me. It's not so much that the boss is a hard opponent, but that they're on bikes that are so fast that even catching up with them is a challenge (I've got bikes 1-4 in my inventory) and once you get there they're probably about 10 times as strong as regular bikes. You've got a limited amount of track in which to kill them, so your biggest opponent there is the clock. If I haven't started really damaging a boss within a minute or so, I let them get away because using nitro after that is just a waste of resources.
3. The levels get less fun as you go up. At first, you're just bashing it out with people - you and them both using melee weapons. Great fun. Then you get truck enemies that can only be killed with dynamite, and 'ninja' riders that block every single melee attack you throw at them so you need to use guns (BTW switching weapons on the fly, especially when you're up against different types of opponents at the same time that require different weapons, is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Then guys with some sort of energy shield show up, and then you've got NPC riders who use automatic weapons and seem to have unlimited ammo, only shoot at you, and are hard to kill because whenever they hit you, they knock you back. And you've got snowy roads, too. It's more challenging and I know you've got to scale up, but I like the first two levels the most by far.
Those criticisms seem harsh, but the way you can build your character using experience, the fast paced action, and the full out fun of the early game make Road Redemption worthwhile regardless.
****Edit****
I got a response saying that the problem might be that I'm not very good. Usually I'll argue with such responses, but this guy probably has a point. So check out B Dawgs response, too.
Either way, this is an excellent title.

This is more a feedback than a review, but it's also a review. My overall impression though is that it's a pretty solid game, especially for an "alpha" build.
The way the game is presented (the intro video with the genre soup) and trying to shove in talking points like "Nuclear throne (did it change from Isaac?) and Deus Ex with GTA" was pretty offputting, but it was free so I tried it out. Going off of that, the tutorial is also pretty bad. Mechanically it's a fine way to learn the mechanics but the 'narrative' of it was also kind of off.
Despite early misgivings I think the game's actually very good. There's "only" 2 zones currently but as I messed around with a handful of characters for a while, it took me till nearly the end of my play time to realize that (and it was only because I was specifically trying to get to the end). That play time was 6.3 hours, and in that I played through like 5-6 of the characters and got all the current achievements. The 6 that I played (Thief, Assassin, Hacker, Doctor, Jock, Police, and the Scientist to unlock the ghost) seemed pretty fun, though as I saw someone else comment, a lot of the classes are defined mainly by items they have, and those run out relatively quickly.
Thief can still pickpocket but will run out of his other tools, and while that actually won't happen much in the game because of the 2 zones, it'll most likely happen with other classes and more frequently later on. Classes whose quirk is a permanent thing, like the hacker, assassin, and jock feel much better because you don't have to be very stingey with it. I'm not entirely sure how you'd balance around it, (and it might be because of the classes I ended up playing but I didn't actually run into this almost at all) but that seems to be the main balance issue. Assassin is also super overpowered (though fun, through that).
The only other issue I can think of is the relative lack of variety in mission types. There's a small handful, and while they don't seem that bad because of the random generation, I'm sure they'd get very tiring later on. I'm assuming that later on in the development more might be added, as this is an alpha.

Streets Of Rogue. A game that combines many mechanics into one, unique style of gameplay. I've tried it when it was launched and on it's free weekend, and 2 hours into the game convinced me to fork up that 13$ that it was at the time, as I believed its content and enjoyment will go up in price as it's development gets further.
For those who haven't read the description yet, it's a game where you can come up an seeming endless amount of tactics to try and accomplish missions throughout the small town area. (It's actually a huge city, cut off into 3 regions for each sector. There's currently 2 sectors, but as development continues, more sectors will be available to play, making longer runs.)
This game actually has a story as well. In a nutshell, it's simply about a major whos gone curropted with power and greed, and a faction who calls themselves; "The Resistance" has been formed to kill the major and turn the city back to normal. You, the player, has recently joined the resistance was put up with some training. Once your training was complete, you went out into the city doing whatever it takes to complete the tasks given to you. Trading a rare currency called Chicken Nuggets, that lets you be able to gain powerful traits as you level up (which resets every time you die on a character) or unlock new types of rewards to find new ways of completing missions. You could also use a small amount of those nuggets to grab a useful item that might come in handy when you go out next time with your character.
The gameplay itself lets you be able to do an seemingly endless amount of tactics/strategies to complete your missions.
Oh? Need to take out the shopkeeper in that building? Distract it by hacking into its computer, walking out of the building with suspicion, then BOOM! a landmine to the foot. Or, you could silently kill him as an assassin. Hmm.. How about shrinking the fellow and crushing him good under your shoes. That seems satisfying.. I could rant on and on about the strategies you could do to finish the mission, but that would take quite alot of your time.
There's also Classes. Characters that have their own personality, stats, starting items, and even special abilities. You can be able to unlock more classes by doing certain things on your mission. Like taking out many members of a single gang, getting drunk, or even breaking tombstones.
There's also Multiplayer for the game as well, both Local and Global. Have more chaotic fun with your friends. However, I did encounter a few bugs and only one of them broke the game. Didn't have as much problems in singlelayer.
The developer also has plans to release lots of more content as well in the distant future, some of which I have probably mentioned earlier and more of these below:
-Being able to create your own character.
-SEED. Have no idea what it does to be honest.
-More items, buildings, and even sectors.
-Obviously bug fixes.
-Probably more mutations? (Normal runs with a twist in them)
Now for the Pros and Cons of the game:
Pros:
-Amazing gameplay. I already mentioned this several times.
-Gives you the ability to be creative in handling missions.
-Has good stability. Haven't gotten a crash yet for me. People who have slower pcs might run into issues.
-Has decent content that lets you be able to deal with certain situations in many ways.
Cons:
-Lack of Content. It's kind-of both a pro and a con because while it does have some content that can keep you busy for a while, it doesn't seem endless after many hours of playtime.
-Bug issues. It's normal in alpha, and I tend to see them more in multiplayer.
-AI can be idiotic/stupidly smart. This one time, I try to attack a theif in self-defense while a cop is cruising by and it suddenly starts attacking me because I was "breaking the law". Kind-of resembles real life tbh. Not something major, but forces you to make certain decisions you otherwise wouldn't. Probably just my opinion however.
Overall: The game has great gameplay, loads of hours of replayability, started out a decent plot for the game, and is constantly bringing in more content with each month or so. (Whether that be bug fixes or additional content). Though be open-minded about the seemingly lack of content it has at the moment and the multiplayer bugs it has. (they're also in singleplayer but are minor things that don't impact much)
This is a game that you can currently buy for at a small price right now. And it's price will casually rise as it soon gets closer and closer to full release. You'll be paying for the amount of quality it has to offer, and you will be getting more of it in enjoyability profit as the game continues to expand and add more content.

While not the most complicated of games, I rather enjoyed it. It's a fairly easy to play, simple puzzle game where your decisions affect the outcome of the game. It's not very long (takes maybe an hour to play through completely) and has some repeat playability due to the multiple endings.

In this game you guide your character through a very linear environment and occasionally make decisions. Depending on the decisions you make, the text based story changes (sometimes dramatically). Unfortunately you're the only character in the game: you never encounter another living person or any kind of scarey creature. So it's basically a "choose your own adventure" book dressed up in some 8-bit graphics. The graphics are nicely stylized, but since you'll only ever be walking around them they really don't do much for the game. The writing is poor and the plots available are on par with "choose your own" adventure books too.
Skip this one and read a book instead. Even at half the asking price a used book will offer more choices to make and a more satisfying experience since you'll imagine what's happening instead of being dissappointed that it isn't shown in the game. Or skip this one and instead play a game that does horror or mystery well.

Before this, the only AC creed game I had ever played (and finished) was the first game of the franchise, Assassin's Creed. It was the most BORING GAMING EXPERIENCE EVER. It was (along with Far Cry 2) the most repetitive, gameplay-wise, experiences I 've had in my life. It was a torture to find the strength to make it through the end!  All that is changed radically in Assassin's Creed III. (I 've heard it was already much improved in AC 2). The missions have a much bigger variety now. The historical setting is interesting for me because I 've never played a game about the American Revolution before, although I have to admit the Holy Lands setting is much more mysterious. There is also a lot of American history you can learn through the Animus database, which is good for whoever is interested. The graphics are atmospheric and adequate for the game's age, and the game is well optimized, I play on a Core2Duo E6850 non-OC with a GTX 560ti with everything on max except AA @1920x1200 and the game runs perfectly and fluidly, without having crashed once for more than 60 hours that I 've played it (I 've only experienced a few in-game bugs - missions that wouldn't trigger/show on map, that I fixed by quitting the game and restarting). The behaviour of both steam AND Uplay, which gets so much hate, has been perfect so far. I don't understand why people have problems with it. I have basic, run- of- the- mill adsl connection and everything is great, no problems whatsoever with the account I created , or with anything else. The only cons I can think about are that some of the climbing mechanics are still frustrating, and that maybe it will get a bit repetitive if you play it for TOOOO long, and you want to collect everything/complete all the optional stuff (although they put so much content in the game, it's hard to not appreciate the effort! -Naval battles are my favorite!)

A genuine piece of art marred by poor delivery and execution. Still Life 2 remains unpolished over its predecessor continuing its lack of high resolution support. The story is involved and engaging, yet takes twists to the extreme and often ends up being more comedic than dramatic.
There is significantly more user interaction than the original Still Life sometimes to the point of being overwhelming. The inventory system definitely takes a step backwards and the timed events remove the typical casual point-and-click play style.

Game suffers from issues related to high CPU usage along with multiple layers of DRM that cause the game to tank in area's. Cut scenes don't iniaiate, models are low polygon, base models on second, and then the next they pop in to full texture. All of this happens while running at 60+ FPS at 1080p 144Hz. with everything maxed outside of the Resolution mulitplier which is left at 100% (putting to 200% runs at 45 FPS).  The game taxes my i5-6600k at 4.6 ghz liquid cooled cpu at 100%. It will take up the entire CPU load  and if you run anything else at teh same time it will make lag. Example: Any other title out of Mass Effect: Andromeda, when I run it at Max Settings I can play twitch or youtube on my other monitor without any issues. This game will not allow this at all. I can stream any other game to twitch, without a capture card or second PC uploading it, at max settings and have like .05% frame drops.
The game suffers from an extra layer of DRM which tanks the performance. I told myself I would never buy another title from this company but I had brain fart and pulled the trigger.
Now, I am waiting on ANOTHER patch because the one they put out today didn't resolve any of my issues. I have a support ticket open and they have yet to even respond back.
Worst part? I enjoyed what I was able to play and only stopped when I was having quests not start or half way in the middle of one, such as the escort through the Canal's in Alexandria, fail in the middle causing me to close the entire game and relaunch. That doesn't always work either. I was finally able to finish that quest today only to have the next one I tried not even let me talk to the NPC. The NPC is a blank model, with no textures. It finally pop's in and the quest giver won't intiate.  ALL THIS WHILE RUNNING OVER 60 FPS according to Uplays counter. This was a first for me. A game that runs at high FPS but suffers from these issues.
I've been told on the steam forums it is because I am using a potato CPU, but I have heard from others with a lot more powerful CPU's having the same issues. Funny thing is that I don't have this issue on any other title outside of ME:Andromeda, which we all know was a poorly optimized game to start. Also, lowering the settings DOES NOTHING, it doesn't resolve the issue.  I can put it all on the lowest settings and it still eat's 100% of my CPU.
I know the cause: VMProtect.
I am wondering when companies are going to realize that taking these steps to stop piracy is not only futile, but it is causing harm to the customer who actually pay for their games. We have studies that show that people who pirate software are the same people who wouldn't buy the product in the first place, even at lower price.
This is what causes people to pirate a product. I would be very curious to see how much CPU it would eat if they put out a patch that removed all the DRM. We know they won't, but I can bet you dollars to donuts that it wouldn't take up 100% of my CPU.
At this time I can't in good conscience recommend this title to my worst enemy.
EDIT: Good lord the Ubisoft Fanboys are out in force defending this game. I am not the only one facing this issue and people with Newer and FASTER processors have made the same claims I am making.

A incredibly surpising but welcome departure from previous Ubisoft titles, the open-world of Watch Dogs 2 isn't a huge map of question marks to spent tens of monotonous hours on, but an environment populated with rich, well-written story missions. At no point during Watch Dogs 2 did I feel I was doing 'busy work' - every moment was a rich, meaningful experience.
The flow of this content is supported by the incredible hacking mechanics. To simply call this game a 'stealth' or 'action' game is to deny the credit due to all the interesting, varied and useful hacking abilities on offer. The huge variety of approaches you can take to solve a problem feels so liberating, while none of the methods ever feel overpowered nor useless. It may be quite a big call, but I think it may event beat out Deus Ex (2000) on this front.
The choice to make the protagonist anything but silent is fantastic! It may not be for everyone, but I for one felt like I had so much more agency and connection to what was going on, because my character actually expressed those emotions! The only moment the protagonist's vibrant personality backfired was when he told another hacker "I aint no hipster" while he was wearing the red skinny jeans, purple button-up shirt and rainbow beanie I'd dressed him in just prior - a momentary bump in what was otherwise a hugely relatable character performance.
And finally I have to mention the cast of NPC personalities that make up the core of your hacking ring. These characters are (for the most part) well written, and VERY well acted. The game did a great job making me feel invested in these people and this group. That alone is reason enough to recommend this game.
I've been disappointed by Ubisoft games for years now, but Watch Dogs 2 completely flips that on its head. I hope this development team gets to stick around for a while because they do some really great work and I can't wait to see what comes out of this team in future... and I hope they get to retain their creativity they demonstrated on this title.

Roguelands is a RPG Rogue-lite (not to be confused with
) game that was developed and published by SmashGames, the same people who made Magicite. Roguelands is, needless to say, a difficult and fustrating game to say the least, however there is a lot of potiental and good points to make about the game itself.
.
Needless to say, Roguelands is meant to be a difficult game. You will die repeatedly and you will have to learn by your mistakes, with every death you will learn something new that you will carry out through your next playthrough. For me this game really wasn't that great until I played a couple of hours into the game. After about 10 hours in, I felt like I was enjoying myself much more than when I first started the game since I could easily replace my armour and weapons. Let's go over some of the main mechanics of the game, some of which I think should be changed or tweaked with to make a more enjoyable experience for the players.
The main system in the game, which you will have to take into account, is the roguelike element that the game strives to be. You will have to expect permadeath, difficult gameplay and randomly generated levels. There are other mechanics in the game that you will encounter, but for now let's just talk the general gameplay, and then these mechanics.
The gameplay is rather fun and addictive to play through, generally I would have a hour or two session of the game to make sure I don't overplay it and get bored. Unfortunately, there isn't much of a tutorial for the game itself, the bare minimum of the game is explained by talking to people of the ship. This leaves the rest of you to figure out, which isn't much of a bad thing but people will have different opinions on this. I really like the fluency of your movement of your character, really urging you to use your slide in the air move to get around fast. This is definatly a big technique when it comes to avoiding enemies and moving around fast.
Permadeath is a simple yet effective mechanic in a game to make the player take more caution throughout the game, knowing that at any moment could be your last. You will be punished if you die, so keeping your character alive is of the utmost importance. The punishment for your death is your character resetting back to level 1 and you losing all your equipment, weapons and resources that were in your inventory at the time. At first I didn't much enjoy this system, as when I would die I wouldn't be able to craft my armour again, but now I am further into the game I am able to easily replace my armour and weapons.
The difficulty of the game is somewhat understandable as the game is of the rogue-like genre, but it feels too difficult with the repeated deaths and that means your character will reset back to level 1 with the starting equipment you are given. I feel like the difficulty of the game should be toned down a bit to make the game less frequent with player deaths, and overall sometimes ruining the experience of the game for the player.
The reason why players gaming experience may be ruined is because if you have taken a while to create a strong character and then die, the player may feel like they have wasted their time and made no progress with that character. This really feels like the game is too high risk with little reward to offer to you as you play through each run with your character.
So now that we have talked about the difficulty and the permadeath systems of the game, now let's go into the randomly generated levels. The randomly generated levels are alright I guess, they are pretty repetitive as you play through the game. I feel like the game has really focused more upon the weapons, armour and resources that you collect rather than the randomly generated planets you explore.
Something that makes the game fast paced (at times) are these random events that can possibly happen when you enter a planet. No matter what level your character is, you may have a chance of triggering a random event. This event could be pirates attacking you, meteor shower and various others, this will make you rush to exit the world so you take the least amount of damage. This is especially true if you are fairly low level as you could die rather quickly.
The graphics of Roguelands is fairly similar the Magicite style of graphics. Each planet has their own individual style of graphic, all of them being rather colourful and vibrant, depending on the environment of the planet. I really like this, it varies the graphics so you don't get bored of it easily. As well as the main graphics of the game, the weapon and armour design is very good. I really like all of the designs of the different types of weapons, it's obvious that there has been a lot of work put into all of the weapons.
+ Perma-death system makes the player more cautious throughout the game
+ Multiplayer co-op with friends
+ Fluent movement of your character
+ Even though there is no tutorial, exploring the game itself is interesting and fun to figure out what everything does.
+ Random events make the game more fast paced or you will get rare items
+ Colourful and vibrant graphics and varied armour and weapon designs
- Difficulty is too high, needs to be toned down a bit (High Risk, Low Reward)
- Randomly generated planets get repetitive after a short period of time
- No tutorial
- Sometimes feel like you have made no progress
- Crafting system is boring
Roguelands is a addicting yet difficult game. It requires patience, quick thinking and speed to avoid taking the most amount of damage. The game has some great weapon and armour designs, fluint character movement and multplayer co-op. The game however seems to be a bit too difficult, which takes some enjoyment out of it. The crafting system isn't that great and sometimes you may feel like you haven't made a lot of progress through the game.
Would I recommened this to you? Well that really depends how long you can put up with the difficulty of the game and the rogue-like system. If you really enjoy the rogue-like genre then I would definatly recommend buying this game.

Streets Of Rogue. A game that combines many mechanics into one, unique style of gameplay. I've tried it when it was launched and on it's free weekend, and 2 hours into the game convinced me to fork up that 13$ that it was at the time, as I believed its content and enjoyment will go up in price as it's development gets further.
For those who haven't read the description yet, it's a game where you can come up an seeming endless amount of tactics to try and accomplish missions throughout the small town area. (It's actually a huge city, cut off into 3 regions for each sector. There's currently 2 sectors, but as development continues, more sectors will be available to play, making longer runs.)
This game actually has a story as well. In a nutshell, it's simply about a major whos gone curropted with power and greed, and a faction who calls themselves; "The Resistance" has been formed to kill the major and turn the city back to normal. You, the player, has recently joined the resistance was put up with some training. Once your training was complete, you went out into the city doing whatever it takes to complete the tasks given to you. Trading a rare currency called Chicken Nuggets, that lets you be able to gain powerful traits as you level up (which resets every time you die on a character) or unlock new types of rewards to find new ways of completing missions. You could also use a small amount of those nuggets to grab a useful item that might come in handy when you go out next time with your character.
The gameplay itself lets you be able to do an seemingly endless amount of tactics/strategies to complete your missions.
Oh? Need to take out the shopkeeper in that building? Distract it by hacking into its computer, walking out of the building with suspicion, then BOOM! a landmine to the foot. Or, you could silently kill him as an assassin. Hmm.. How about shrinking the fellow and crushing him good under your shoes. That seems satisfying.. I could rant on and on about the strategies you could do to finish the mission, but that would take quite alot of your time.
There's also Classes. Characters that have their own personality, stats, starting items, and even special abilities. You can be able to unlock more classes by doing certain things on your mission. Like taking out many members of a single gang, getting drunk, or even breaking tombstones.
There's also Multiplayer for the game as well, both Local and Global. Have more chaotic fun with your friends. However, I did encounter a few bugs and only one of them broke the game. Didn't have as much problems in singlelayer.
The developer also has plans to release lots of more content as well in the distant future, some of which I have probably mentioned earlier and more of these below:
-Being able to create your own character.
-SEED. Have no idea what it does to be honest.
-More items, buildings, and even sectors.
-Obviously bug fixes.
-Probably more mutations? (Normal runs with a twist in them)
Now for the Pros and Cons of the game:
Pros:
-Amazing gameplay. I already mentioned this several times.
-Gives you the ability to be creative in handling missions.
-Has good stability. Haven't gotten a crash yet for me. People who have slower pcs might run into issues.
-Has decent content that lets you be able to deal with certain situations in many ways.
Cons:
-Lack of Content. It's kind-of both a pro and a con because while it does have some content that can keep you busy for a while, it doesn't seem endless after many hours of playtime.
-Bug issues. It's normal in alpha, and I tend to see them more in multiplayer.
-AI can be idiotic/stupidly smart. This one time, I try to attack a theif in self-defense while a cop is cruising by and it suddenly starts attacking me because I was "breaking the law". Kind-of resembles real life tbh. Not something major, but forces you to make certain decisions you otherwise wouldn't. Probably just my opinion however.
Overall: The game has great gameplay, loads of hours of replayability, started out a decent plot for the game, and is constantly bringing in more content with each month or so. (Whether that be bug fixes or additional content). Though be open-minded about the seemingly lack of content it has at the moment and the multiplayer bugs it has. (they're also in singleplayer but are minor things that don't impact much)

This game has a lot of things going for it which makes it good. Atmospheric, keeps you on edge and the old school graphics are really neat. I loved the idea that only a small part of the screen is lighted, to add to the already creepy mood. I'm an easily spooked person and scared of the dark, so my imagination went haywire.
The problem though is that the game literally hands you a notebook and says "Here, write something down". You walk around, trying to piece the story together and basically depending on what you answer, your character will think that is exactly what happens. But there doesn't really seem to be any consequences or rewards to it. So technically, the game could end in many different ways, but when you've played it once, then you'll already know all the other options.
Once you realize this, the game becomes a huge let down. I played it to find out the story, not just answer Yes or No to a couple of questions and then basically write a story myself. Everything is also thought out in a "That probably happened.." and "I probably did that...", which makes the answers in general seem like nothing really did happen.
I guess the game is supposed to be thought provoking like the movie "The Blair Witch Project", and personally I don't like such stories. I want a solid story which you can follow, not just things that happen and then you have to make up your own mind as to what -really- happened in the end.

Nearly 20 years ago, before PTW & Loot boxes even existed, Electronic Arts were all about the gameplay and were producing absolute classics like Road Rash on Sega.
As a fan of the original my interest was immediately peaked when I heard about Road Redemption, could it really be the spiritual successor to Road Rash?  Will it do the original game the justice it deserves? & Can it improve on a classic or will it get it’s melon cracked open?
EA released six editions of Road Rash on a multitude of platforms the last of which was on the original PlayStation.  Road Rash offered something that had never been seen before; a high tempo, High speed, all action beat’em up on motorbikes.  It was an instant hit and people still speak fondly of this classic today.
Thankfully, and in equal measure unfortunately, Road Redemption (developed by Ian Fisch) does retain a vast majority of the features found in the original.  It looks very similar, the gameplay mechanics are almost identical and the physics are practically indistinguishable, however I want to make you aware early on that there is a considerable amount of swearing in this game, a heck of a lot.
At first this is quite disconcerting, having paid your £15 for this NEW game released in 2017 you almost immediately feel like you are playing a direct port of the original.  The physics are dated, the gameplay is dated, the graphics are poor and the UI is messy.
For the first 20-30 mins I was adamant that I was going to get a refund on this shambles of a game! However, as time passed and I started to find the similarities of the original less offensive and more familiar, I started to warm to it a little.  Let’s be honest the original was a hit for a reason; it offered a huge amount of fun and some noticeably challenging gameplay requiring you utilise your skills and often riding your luck to complete; something which modern EA titles don’t appear to be able to manage today.
There is a host of new stuff too; rooftop tracks, critical hits, Vertical Jet Boosts and genetically enhanced man-robots….I kid you not.  There are ranged attack weapons like rocket launchers, spades and poles.
There are short range weapons like swords, shotguns and baseball bats with nails sticking out.  There are pistols, sub-machine guns, dynamite, timed explosives and much, much more.
Unfortunately this is simply not enough to satisfy modern day gaming expectations.
There is a distinct lack of polish all over, the UI is a mess and the in game physics and collision detection have not been improved one iota since the original; some may argue that this is in-keeping with its heritage but I would have liked to see something a little more GTA.
There are 4 gameplay modes available;
•	Classic Quick play
•	4 player Local Co-Op
•	Online Multiplayer
•	Campaign
Basic Quickplay, as the name suggest is just instant gameplay action.  Pick a track, bike and character and away you go.  Nothing much to report here, it is what it is.
Both the multiplayer and 4 player co-op options will likely leave you feeling somewhat dejected. The 4 player Co-op just looks terrible and I suspect that to be true even if you are playing on an enormous 4K TV.
The online MP is considerably limited.  It comprises of a race between two teams of 4, the objective is to win the race and kill as many of your opponents as possible along the way, first to 3 is the winner.
At the end of each race there is a countdown where each team takes it upon themselves to try and wrack up a few more kills….In MP mode it is very tricky to hit an opponent at all.  Unlike the campaign single player mode there is no speed matching in place, everyone is swinging about and changing speed at will, hitting someone is nearly impossible, even for those who are masters of the game.  The most popular method is deadly and involves a stationary motorbike and a magnum.
Then there is the campaign which is intentionally made lengthier due only to the fact that you are not really meant to complete it on your first attempt but rather through multiple repeated attempts, each of which is made a little easier thanks to some permanent upgrades unlocked through gathered XP.
There are 4 stages, each of which have 4 missions and an end of level boss to defeat within the given track length.  Despite the game telling you it is “randomising track layout, enemies, weapons and vehicles”, I have to say I think it is always the same track, and worse than that some of the later tracks I am almost certain are just the reverse of the earlier ones.
What is overwhelming and undeniable is the level of satisfaction that you do get when you manage to link together some killer moves and takedowns.  Progress is slow but the fun is often, oddly high.
There are quite a few weapons, some of which I still don’t know how to use as there is no tutorial and there are quite a few bikes to choose from; all of which seem to handle the same way and none of which can actually catch the leader bikes no matter how fast and clean you take the corners with boost.
Within the game itself there are a variation of characters, some of which are targets and others which afford you power ups and boosts.  Some are enhanced human beings and others have special powers and abilities whilst the bosses just tend to have a large health bar.
You can find up to 20 characters onscreen at any one time, maybe more and you will on occasion take an absolute battering but on the most part you can easily pick off whomever, whenever you choose.
Fun for the first hour, after that it gets annoying and repetitive.

So I only played this for a good 15 minutes roughly (to the 3rd level), because I just couldn't force myself to play any further. The concept is really good, and I really liked the idea of mixing different people at different tables for different bonuses (and occasional negatives). That was a nice, fresh mechanic that I'd like to see more of. The graphics are great for this kind of game, the music is alright and the sound effects are good.
My problem is how clunky it is. I really dislike that I have to drag patrons over to their chair. Dragging patrons over to their seat is hit or miss - you can be as accurate as possible but it still won't work. At first I thought this was because the previous patron stands next to the chair after paying for a second (which really should not stop you seating anyone), but that doesn't seem to be the case. You can queue up actions, but there's no point in doing that since you're never sure when a patron is going to mess up the table, or ask for a snack. The second they do, consider the rest of the level screwed because you'll be late on everything following.
The tutorial guides you to buy the first upgrade, but it's very very likely that you won't have enough money to do so from the first level if you made a single mistake. It also doesn't even bother explaining the extra snacks they might ask for. Everything goes so so so slowly. The patience indicator obviously goes down bit by bit but there's no way to tell that it's about to happen - and there's no way to recover when it does (say, by being quick on everything else).
There's potential here, for sure, but it's like the developers looked at all the things other games in this genre did right and ignored them. And then added a few unnecessary mechanics to make things worse. Maybe it gets better in later levels, but it really wasn't worth continuing to find out.

Doing perfectly fine for a beta. I've always been a big fan of the Half-Life universe, and seeing it reach out to real-time strategy rather than step back into more of the same FPS element makes me, and countless other fans very happy.
Good soundtrack, decent-looking UI, and acceptable sound quality. I'd also like to say I really like the way the developers engaged and adapted Half-Life's assets from FPS to RTS. For example being given the ability to build Headcrab Canister Launchers when playing as the Combine and then bomb the ♥♥♥♥ out of the Rebels, or giving the Rebels the ability to enable a blitz buff when you send your rebellious, defiant units to rush into Combine territory.
As far as my complaints and requests, I'd say the AI is at times really silly, but I guess AI will always be annoying especially in this sort of game. It would be good to see more maps, and greater map detail as well, albeit I'm certain the developers are already working on it at the moment. Another thing that would be fantastic would be another faction, one for the Antlions. Now that could make things a lot more intense and interesting, giving us a setting sort of like StarCraft's -- two military forces warring against each other, and at the same time holding their ground against the menace of the unrelenting evil icky gross hive-mind controlled insectoid ew-gross aliens.
In any case, I'm as hopeful and expectant in the final product as all the many other fans that are anxious to see a good game come out of this.

A truly unique side-scroller. I'm not a big fan of horror games, so when the opening screen called itself a "unique horror adventure" I was a bit skeptical, but while it is horror, it truly is unique. Instead of using a persistent enemy, your own weakness, or jumpscares to scare you, it messes with your mind more than anything else and leaves you thinking "What if?" throughout the entire game.
This is due to the fact that every playthrough is unique; you could literally play the game a dozen times or more and every plaaythrough could still be unique - and it will always have a different outcome SPOILER:
which gives it incredible replayability.
I beat it while on a road trip and loved it immensely. Soon after, I talked my sister into playing it as well so I could see what choices she would make and how her ending would turn out. She's not a big video game player (she usually hates them), but this is one of few games she really enjoyed.
From the games that I've played, this one is truly unique and I honestly have no complaints at all about it.
I'd rate it a 9.5/10.
You do a lot of walking, waiting for the game to start, and then it ends.  At the end you feel there was about half a story.

I should probably preface this by stating that I'm not really a big fan of horror media in general...
But all the same I don't feel like Home really has all that much to offer. It tries to run solely on atmosphere, with story delivered through pages of text. I actually quite like this approach, allowing the player's imagination to really shape the story, but what plot DOES exist is sparse and ambiguous. It's supposed to be, but even so, that also makes it incredibly unsatisfying. The gameplay is just walking around, finding keys to open doors. With a bit more depth to that, combined with the atmosphere (which is admittedly pretty good) the game could have been really good. It's an interesting diversion for an hour or so if you can get it really cheap, but for the most part there are better games doing similar things.

I rarely write reviews for products of any kind, but I am truly outraged... that this game isn't getting enough buzz. I love this game and I am completely hooked with it's beautiful storyboard-style almost "Art Deco" design, excellent noir voiceovers, and an intoxicating jazz and classical music collection that you can select from as you play. You enter into the world of Chief Boyd, a guy past his prime that is stuck between a rock and a hard place, but not exactly reluctant to enter the world of police corruption either. I love how the main character is pretty scummy, but he feels like such a real person you really get invested in him.
Critiques: -The detective mechanic isn't as intuitive as it seems it should be, and sometimes you're unsure if your detectives are actually working on the case or not. It feels like it should be the coolest part of the game, but sadly it just becomes a game of shuffling around cards, because you're unsure what the images are trying to convey.
- The intro is kind of annoying after a while because it starts immediately before the menu screen. I wish you would go to the menu first and maybe it would play if you idle, but the way it is now is a little frustrating
Despite its minor flaws, this game is WELL worth the money. I got it on sale, but I would have paid full price if I knew how good it was. Get it now.

I read the reviews on dropped framerates and I see it occasionally in game but it has not once messed up a kill or interrupted the game. Syndicate was a mess that had to be manually set to even run. AS Origins has done better job.
Now to the actual review. *Spoilers* I am a huge Assasin's Creed fan. I like the world, the timelines, the interactions. Lately though they have lost their touch. Unity was immediately forgettable and Syndicate was almost as bad. Origins seems to be getting back to their roots. They did away with the dreadful Helix system and moved  back to the Animus and single modern day character which instantly drew me in more than Helix ever did. The main character is complex with relationships that are intwoven into the story. In addition bringing back PreCursor tombs enriches the world in a way that Unity and Origins just failed to. The horse riding system is the best I have seen since since Red Dead, and the amounts of mounts and weapons is impressive.
My main issue is that they did away with the free running aspect. That was a central aspect of the game. Now it is extremely difficult to run up and down buildings. In addition you can kill yourself again by jumping off high places even though you are aiming correctly. I thought this was eliminated in AS 2?
Overall if you like the series and aren't hung up on a few small graphical issues then you should buy it.

Does the world really need yet another story exploring the differences between A.I and humans, wherein the creation, having been having been meticulously designed by humans for one specific purpose, turn out to be all too similar to their creators?  You could probably list pages of examples of this kind of story across the decades, from Asimov, Star Trek TNG to Chobits and so on.  Yet it turns out that this genre entry is by no means unwelcome, as production company Key - possibly the most famous brand in the Visual Novel world – have found a way to inject genuine emotion and pathos into proceedings, giving this old idea a fresh new spin and imbuing the whole with a number of other subtle and intelligent ideas that leave a shellshocked reader eventually both thinking and feeling deeply.  It’s a rare trick to pull off and writer Yuichi Suzumoto deserves the highest praise for doing so.
Our protagonist, a nameless Junker living in a war-torn future, lives a lonely life travelling from place to place, making ends meet on what he can scavenge.  When he chances across an old disused planetarium he also discovers a semblance of life in the form of Yumemi Hoshino, an android (or, gynoid)  abandoned and waiting to greet customers that will never arrive for a period of 30 years .  Initially the junker is simply irritated by her presence and constant stream of verbal diarrhoea, but he can’t convinve himself to move on before fixing up the rundown projection unit and watching the show that Yumemi is so anxious that he enjoy.
One of the most interesting things about the story lies in the development of the relationship between the two.  Yumemi never acts like anything but a programmed android and in terms of empathy she’s sorely lacking.  Would she pass a Turing test?  Probably not, because she can’t really think for herself outside of a strong desire to see customers in the Planetarium and to serve them to the best of her abilities, and she continually points that out or twists everything in the conversation back towards how wonderful the show is.  In some ways, as the Junker’s attachment for her grows it’s more akin to the developing bond between a human and their pet.  However, the meaning behind the growing relationship is perhaps more profound than that; Yumemi, as cute and adorable as a companion she may be, also represents a strong link to a faded, idyllic past; a past which for the Junker symbolises hope and opportunity.  Yumemi’s astral projections therefore paradoxically come to represent for the junker both a nostalgic window back into the past and a glimmer of hope for the future.  She provides a window to a past world where tacky space projections can fill halls full of gullible consumers but also a past where – just as now – people have hopes and dreams of a great human race expanding ever outwards and colonising galaxies.
That whimsical nostalgia is the kind one feels when visiting a popular retro-museum or exhibition to see old relics, scenes or perhaps childhood toys.  Still objects are often presented in cabinets with text explaining their purpose and one imagines, but is never quite able to immerse oneself in the reality of another life.  Yumemi, on the other hand, as a figure of enthusiasm, provides a constant reminder to our protagonist that this past was once very real, and also a constant reminder, as the power continues to fade and the reality of her eventual shutdown kicks in towards the end of the novel, that it’s a past that has tragically slipping out of sight with ever slimmer hopes of a return.  And - just as she did with the nostalgic past- in the present Yumemi manages to provide an image of hope for the future, showing the way to the stars and not allowing others to forget that there’s a potential for a much better life than the one the current world offers.
Planetarium manages to create a situation, then, that’s far more emotionally resonant than simply that of a man meeting an AI and discovering that there’s more to her personality than her programming.  That aspect is certainly present in this story, and executed superbly, as Yumemi ends up being as unable or unwilling to let go of the Junker as much as he can’t let go of her, eventually revealing a side to her programming that looks – if just a little - like a human emotion or desire.  But Key’s Visual Novel is thoughtful enough to use its Planetarium setting to even greater purpose, showing us readers that when it comes to simple stories about AI, robots or love, there’s a lot more on our horizons that we’ve yet to explore.

11 hours in and thus far Roguelands is an excellent game. Progression is very akin to Risk of Rain where you go in with garbage gear, get destroyed, die, unlock some better gear or classes etc, go back in with that better gear and eventually you are the all powerful god smiting the puny bugs. Its a very difficult and unforgiving game, you will be killed and your favourite character with that amazing armour will dissapear, but you will be rewarded with new races and special suits that boost different aspects of your place. Good luck fellas.

is a rather casual stealth game about a ninja breaking into a high-security facility and stealing the chemical weapon that the categorically evil antagonist has been developing in his evil facility.
Your mission in each room is to find the key and get to the next room without being detected. If detected, you start at the last checkpoint, i.e. at the door or the key you found.
Your adversaries include moving lasers, cameras, guards, noise detectors and on-and-off switching lasers. Boxes and walls logically block off their line-of-sight. You can also push boxes and hide inside some of them, probably as a tribute to
.
Since
is a top-down 2D game, there is no hiding in the ceiling, climbing, jumping or even crouching. The so-called ninja cannot even attack the guards. Detection means instant death. All this makes one wonder whether the protagonist is really a ninja at all despite their looks.
Most adversaries are quite predictable: lasers rotate at constant pace, noise detectors (that only detect you if you move) go on and off at constant intervals etc. The basic mechanic is simple and nice: avoid everything that changes or moves, get the key and leave for the next room. However...
The moving lasers sometimes have hit box issues, quite literally. The boxes you push may block the laser but sometimes the laser just finds a way through the boxes if there's a tiniest crack and hits you extremely briefly. Of course that counts as a hit.
Noise detectors work more like motion detectors: when they turn on, you may not move in their area lest be detected. Being a ninja, aren't you supposed to be stealthy (i.e. be
in addition to staying out of sight)?
The guards behave in a weird fashion. While they follow set routes, when changing direction they just
into the new direction instantaneously. This can be unnerving and surprise you in an unexpected way and it feels unfair.
Actually the only feature that I would count as stealth is that some guards are sleeping. Bumping a crate or causing other noise like that will wake them up. However, they won't change their routes based on shuffling crates or similar, so that's kind of a bummer.
There are no stun grenades, poisoned shurikens or similar ninja'esque gadgets to play with. Everything being deterministic, it's not much of a stealth game but more one of smart movement and tactics.
The gameplay starts extremely easy to the point of being boring, and it slowly works up to moderately challenging in the very last few normal levels. I would have liked the challenge get up sooner. Only the last level and the bonus levels (that you unlock by beating the game) were truly challenging, with multiple fast moving lasers and guards and noise detectors in awkward (i.e. challenging) places.
A set of Halloween challenge levels,
(update: now you can play them whenever) were released this October. These ranged from moderately to very challenging and the level design was nicer than in basic levels.
They also introduce a bonus enemy type, a ghost that seemingly randomly bounces around the level. The apparently random behaviour was a cause of many unnecessary deaths so I found them mostly annoying or frustrating.
is presented as a casual stealth game. Thus I find it a good thing that the developer altogether removed the limited lives that were present in the main game.
Also, the new keyboard/gamepad controls are better and more responsive than the mouse controls that were removed. While it has been released from Early Access, there are still content updates planned.
Menus are very basic: you can only change volume of music and sounds (separately and together), and Unity launcher handles the resolution and controls. Default controls (on keyboard) are WASD for movement and E for action. Action is only used for getting into or out of a box.
Graphics are clear, and thus good for this game. Music is pulp style with just two or three tracks (check the trailers for sample).
The DLC for Episode 2 was just released (my review of that is
), and having played it I find it adds about half an hour of playtime of moderately challenging levels.
UPDATE: Episode 2 is now free and has achievements.
It's a really short game. The Episode 1 lasted 25 minutes for me. Add 10-15 minutes for the six bonus levels. Add ten or twenty minutes for the Halloween event. Add half an hour for the DLC (+idling for cards). It's not terribly lot.
Nevertheless, I did enjoy it and the bunch of easy achievements that came with it. I'd say get it on sale though - in my opinion, the content is currently not enough to warrant the full price.

This game is short. And yet, a delectable morsel to behold.
Intelligent Games really outdid themselves with this game. It's simple. It's clean. It's elegant in design, aesthetics, and wonderful in music. And yet they managed to accomplish this with such minimalistic assets. This game truly goes to show just how little material and how a lot of polish can really bring out a wonderful game. That and a brilliant voice actor who narrates the game and really does bring the charm of this little puzzle to life. It isn't "innovative" per se, as the game is an adaption of a long lived game, but its style is something that is not commonly seen in video gaming: stuffy Victorian animals drawn on parchment with clean calligraphic ink strokes on dancing "Fox & Geese" board to the accompaniment of orchestral ballroom music.
The game is simple. There are two parties. The Fox and the Flock. The Fox wishes to eat the Flock. The Flock wishes to not be eaten. The Fox must cleverly snatch and kill the Flock, one by one. The Flock must either herd at the exit or corner the Fox before there are too few to resist the Fox. But the Fox is limited by wanting to remain unidentifiable by the Flock he's hunted, thus he can only attack one nearby Flock at a time provided there is room. And the Flock, with their insufferable arrogance, refuse to be caught "uncivilized" by dancing improperly, thus limiting their own movement to escape the Fox. You will alternate between the two parties, either guiding the Fox to a fat dinner before his quarry escapes or aiding the Flock in their attempt to flee their foe.
It's all very elegantly done: clean and straightforward. No gimmicks. No flash. No distractions.
I do have one complaint about the game, and that it's sometimes difficult to get a fuller view of the board considering how the pieces do take up a lot of space with their art. It isn't a horrible complaint, especially as the game gives you a simplified board view off to the side, but it is something that, at times, did frustrate me.
But for the meager price of 2$? I say it was more than worth it. You can easily finish the "story mode" in an hour at most, but I think the execution of the fable was an experience that definite had me grinning as I played. It's decadent. It's cheeky. And as said before, a delectable morsel.

I didn't think this day would come, but here I find myself, writing a negative review about an Assassin's Creed game. Sometimes, we fangirl/fanboy subjectively over games and we even develop the ability to forgive any mistake the creators could have possibly made because the game becomes sacred to us. This saga was just like that for me, but holy freaking shet. Just when I thought AC Revelations was the most disappointing one.
The game offers a brutal amount of additional content (I know this sounds like a positive thing, but wait until I'm finished). This includes hunting, crafting, homestead missions, assassin recruit missions, courier tasks, treasure hunting, collectibles, etc. This could’ve been amazing, but it turns into a bad attribute the moment it becomes the 70% (probably not the right percentage, but that's how it felt) of the game's content. If you were to take away all of these extras, and you only played the main missions you'd finish the game quicker than Tarzan swinging from vaseline-covered lianas. It's almost like they realized how weak the storyline was once they had finished, and decided to add a bunch of extra activities to make up for it.
Secondly, at this point the story just feels like an excuse to use the Animus and play as a random ancestor, rather than the Animus being a device to know more about what’s really going on with all these freaky gods and the end of the world. The story progresses as slow as a turtle giving head on the moon. I’m sorry, but it does. I could’ve just YouTube’d the cutscenes and saved myself from losing time and money. Maybe it’s just that I’m the only player who cares about the backstory and people just care about jumping from building to building. Could be. But that’s why this is my personal review, right? Right.
The same thing happened to me with Revelations. I ended up playing just for the sake of knowing more about Juno, Altair’s past, the apple and whatnot. I literally forced myself to finish Revelations and the only reason why I played AC3 right away was because the only good thing that Revelations ever did, was the ending. Man, that was good and it instantly encouraged me to play AC3.
I guess what I’m saying is that I wished the game had a stronger connection between the ancestors and Desmond. That we get the same amount of information about the main story as we get about the ancestor we’re playing at that moment. Some sort of balance.
More negative stuff:
- Uplay. Just get rid of it, for the love of Juno.
- The naval missions. Terrible, terrible controls.
- Connor himself. He’s depressing, boring and doesn’t have pro flirting skills like Ezio. Me no like him.
- The crafting system and hunting are simply pointless.
- The way you unlock fast travel locations is interesting, but tedious after a while.
- Stealth. Last time I checked assassins were stealthy.
Congratulations on getting Desmond’s skin colour right this time, though.

Very unrealistic game. AI loves to build huge stacks. There is no trench warfare. Its basically huge stacks chasing other huge stacks. Whether this is an alright game or a very bad one depends mainly on whether you want to play single player or you have someone else to play as the other side. Why? The AI is laughable. It will stack forces in the nation's capital while its armies are losing everywhere else. It will waste resources on units that it would leave to rust far away from the front lines. It will waste all of its resources and still won't field a decent army. From what I've experience in several campaigns, you won't experience trenches, deadlocks and even consistent front lines. The enemy will keep most of its forces far away from you and will never manage to create and keep a coherent line alongside yours, like it would in any other strategy game like Hearts of Iron for example.
If you have someone to play with you or you want to play both sides, keep reading:
1. A lot of mostly historically accurate units. Uniforms and equipment changes over time so that your men are more effective. Formation of sturm units and their Entente equivalents is depicted too.
2. The engine is pretty decent and can simulate very complex battles - units are very detailed, and they have a lot of statistics that are unique for each unit and historically accurate. For example the British will shoot faster than Germans due to their superior training and better rifles.
3. Map is pretty good, with all the cities depicted.
4. Trenches evolve as they did historically and will get almost impossible to get through over time. To counter this, you will need to use a lot of artillery, gas, and specialized stormtroopers. This simulates how the warfare evolved very accurately.
5. Engine was tweaked to support aerial warfare which is done quite well.
6. Diplomacy is pretty well done and tends to evolve realstically.
7. Supply is modeled pretty accurately and is crucial to any military operation, just like in real life. You can't expect to penetrate enemy's lines and get very far before being cut off from your supply lines and defeated easily.
1. The engine is not very good for simulating trench warfare. It was designed with older conflicts in mind - armies march together, fight, and then one of them has to retreat as the loser. WW1 wasn't like that. Armies were close to each other and at least on the Western Front hardly ever retreated to the nearby town/province after being defeated, Also, trenches disappear once the unit has moved - in reality the attacking army simply returned back to its trenches after being defeated.
2. It's really buggy sometimes. They fixed most of it but it can still be quite clunky. Sometimes units may magically move somewhere else for example.
3. Sometimes your units are too stupid. If you want to give an order to your fleet to intercept an enemy's fleet and it just happens to be heading home your fleet will follow it till the end and get blown up on enemy's minefields.
4. AI, as mentioned before. This game is unplayable vs the AI because it makes too many stupid mistakes and won't arrange proper frontlines.
If you have a lot of time to spare and reliable friends to play with, go for it. It's a lot of fun even if the engine can't simulate a static warfare correctly, and technology in the game progresses just as it did in real life, which adds to the accuracy. The main campaign is pretty long and different war plans allow great replayability. I cannot however fully recommend it, as it fails to deliver proper game when you don't have friends around and for its bugs that prevented me from playing it for quite a while.

A short yet touching story about a man who found a planetarium, untouched by time, in a post-apocalyptic world with never ending rain. Made by Key, this is another tear-jerker made to really punch you in the feels.

Simply beautiful. Visual Arts/Key Studios and the Sekai Project did such an amazing job creating this VN and localizing it for English speakers. It only takes 3-4 hours to complete, and there's only one arc--no choices; simply put, this is a kinetic novel.
If you're familiar with Key Studio's games/anime, then you know what's in store--particularly in the feels department.
Voice acting was superb. I'm really glad they included the Japanese vocals, as the Japanese voice actors do a superb job at connecting the viewers with the characters. Soundtrack was amazing (I'm listening to it right now via the Music Mode available once you complete the game). Gentle Jena and Song of the Rotation of the Spheres are simply beautiful and set the mood for the story. All in all, I totally recommend Planetarian ~The Reverie of a Little Planet~ to anyone--especially if you're new the visual novel genre. It was definitely worth the $10.
TL;DR:
Just buy the game and play it through. The story may seem slow and boring at first; however, it really picks up a grows on you as you progress further. It's worthy of the title "Onion Cutting Simulator 2016".

A very touching kinetic novel (meaning there are no choices to be made), with great art, some absolutely gorgeous and emotional music tracks and a powerful climax. Suffice to say I've considerably inflated my in-game hours just by listening to some of its poignant tunes on repeat (roughly 1/3 of my playtime was spent on them at the time of my writing this), and that's a first for me.
It's short lived, granted, lasting 3 hours or so depending on how fast you read, but that takes nothing away from the tale. In fact, I feel it went on for the perfect length for me to sucesfully connect to the characters yet leave the world cloaked in bleakness, solitude and mistery, which ultimately adds to the game's narrative and overall feel. Oh, and definitely expect tears to be shed or at the very least choked up at some point. More than worth it at normal price, a no brainer at a sale.
tl;dr: Short but sweet kinetic VN with a stellar soundtrack and some real feels to be had.

Not sure what everyones saying about DRM, as ive had no problems with the game. My pc gets warm, but thats to be expected. otherwise, this game is amazing. they did everything right, from combat to the world.
The combat is similar to Dark souls combat, though more forgiving, with parrying, and dodging. It is hard at times, though usually only when you do something stupid or make mistakes, especially if you miss that sweet sweet parry window. Most heavy attacks (except for the heavy weapons guys) seem to be parryable as well. The mounted combat is alright, sadly you cannot jump from horse to horse and assassinate the other guy, but it still works. You can block on horseback, and shoot, so thats something. Also watch out for archers.
The world is quite large, much larger than any previous game. It has multiple zones, and quests all over. Which is something else they changed. there are random encounter (sort of anyway) quests, along with small quests dotted around cities for helping people. The nice part about these small quests, is they dont usually branch out into big chains, meaning its something you can do on the way to your actual objective in 20 mins. keeps travelling interesting. Not to mention the main story is actually pretty neat. (no spoilers)
The game doesnt hold your hand much, after the small tutorial it puts you out in the world to figure things out for yourself. I'm not too far into it, and there are still a ton of things ive missed in earlier areas, like that den of super high level dudes next to the starting city (what an odd place for that).
A few cons, more just bugs really but. Sometimes he gets stuck on terrain, like small hedges or weirdly angled edges. He won't move till I go in another direction. Sometimes his weapons get "stuck". I use a power attack with a sword and switch to an axe, his hand remains in the swords charging position, though i can use regular attacks, I cannot use charge attacks with the axe until i switch back and use charge attack again. Also just general movement at times on walls, I know its just an AC thing but it still annoys me a bit. Also combat in the water kinda sucks, usually just you getting staggered over and over till either you die or run to land. I can see why they added it but if it were a bit better...
All in all id say its a solid 7/10, maybe even 8. its really good, I love playing it. its kinda like open world DS. Way better than the previous games (except 4, which was stupidly fun).
still not 100% sure its worth 80$, but if it goes on sale, buy it.

Home is a pixelated horror game that I really enjoyed. The gameplay is rather intutiive and consists of moving your character and selecting items for puzzles. A run-through is a about an hour and a half. Replayability is somewhat limited but making different choices and getting different endings is interesting. The puzzles were enjoyable and kept major back tracking to a minimum. The graphics are pixelated which I really enjoyed due to the dark nature of the game. There is no music in the game only sound effects. The sound effects are great and really build suspense and dread.
The game's plot is not linear and is up to interpretation, especially the ending. The game focuses on the player's choices and psychology. Although the game is labeled as "horror", the game is more about dread and the atmosphere of the unknown. This is not a game about jumpscares or scary monsters, but more about the suspectiability of human memory and how humans can become monsters. The creator of the game is also very engaged, making sure to fix bugs and even adding an additional area after the initial release.
If you like a story that is interpretative, like suspense, or like psychological games, I would highly recommend the game.

Those who complain about the lack of action in this game are doing nothing more than showing the ignorance that they adorn proudly. Home is an interesting indie game about a man who wakes up with no memory of how he got to his current position and makes his way back home, piecing together the events through clues found on his trail. This game has no action, it is simply walking and reading, then making choices. That may not sound fun but it might just surprise you. The best description for this game would be an atmospheric psycological adventure game. Through your actions you shape the ending of the story in a number of ways. BUT, the ending isn't "in your face" it is left open for interpertation by the player. If you are into those mindless zombie shooters with no goal or story, then keep walking because this game is not for you...
An interesting experiment in having a narrative's conclusion be based on what the player found and did. Unforunately it's just too small a game and not terribly exciting to really explore this idea.

I remember a time when Half-Life 2 and its engine were the things of legend and only the finest of computers could run them. Now, it's used to power an RTS. I feel old.
On the other hand, with this aged-ness comes much rejoicing and excitement. The game is pretty fun and seems balanced. I have yet to play more than just the single player and tutorial (I'm living overseas and my connection isn't always reliable.)
PROS:
-balanced. Neither faction seems over-powered ATM, but more play-testing might change my views of this.
-easy to learn. As other have pointed out, it follows the Dawn of War I gameplay pretty closely.
-faithful to core material- Nothing outrageous was done to the storyline of HL2. The soldiers/rebels look and feel like they should. They're fun to play as and their abilities are interesting and fairly true to the original game.
CONS:
-buggy- which is totally fine, since it IS in beta.  Glitchy terrain/units stuck in position.
-limited developmental potential- The original game has only two factions, so getting a variety of approachs will be unlikely. I'm guessing that eventually the best play styles will be perfected and one faction will gain an edge over the other.
-no single player campaign- Now, I know this is tailored as a multiplayer game. BUT I'm a huge fan of story-driven content. Half-Life's universe has huge potential for interesting story-arcs.
My suggestion would be for the developers to get a group of community members to create several campaigns.
For Rebels-
The Rise (Pre-Gordan)
The Turning Point (With Gordon as NPC you need to help)
After the Fall (Gordon  or Alyx or Prof. gives you missions to help deal with contrary human groups and/or remnants of Combine)
For Combine-
Establishment (How the Combine sets up shop on Earth, could feature unique military units)
The Fall- (How the combine dealt with the Rebellion and some sort of internal struggle in the Combine Leadership)
After the Fall- (Combine Forces trying to survive without their former advantages or bolder human forces, etc.)
Unique Campaign ideas-
How Ravenholm (or whatever the zombie town was called) Falls. From the point of view of survivors or people TRYing to be survivors (could end with just the Preacher being your last unit).
A New Enemy (Could be a way to introduce a third faction into the series. Maybe some enemy of the combine that was forced to leave their previous planet and now wants Earth as a homeworld)
For a Beta? 10/10
If this was a full product, I wouldn't be happy with it's rough exterior (like, 7/10). However, I am looking forward to its polished final version. GO DEVELOPERS

So, I just picked up a copy of Road Redemption from the Steam Winter Sale; and let me tell you, it does NOT disappoint!
As a longtime fan of the Road Rash series, I am quite fond of bike racing games. Road Redemption hearkens back to a time when it was okay to get your kicks by beating the snot out of other racers.
Do yourself a favour: use a controller when you're playing this game. I love the mechanics of it; and having the different combat tricks and maneuvers in the buttons, while leaving the throttles in the triggers was a smart move. You can actually separate between what's most important to you as a play style. Whether you want to use your NOS to fly ahead of the competition; or hang back and beat the ever-loving hell out of your opponents; you have that choice with Road Redemption. The different bonuses for kills, such as decapitations and crash bonuses, help to rack up XP for when you eventually do get a Game Over and spend points on skill trees and unlockables. In Road Redemption, it is okay to lose. Because your XP and cash points roll over in the campaign mode. So you can bank as much as you want, and keep playing to unlock more and more fun stuff! The campaign mode of the game really starts to get challenging around the 3rd or 4th level, but I assure you. It is a very fun and replayable experience.
If you have the extra cash in your pocket, do yourself a favour and get Road Redemption. It really is this generation's Road Rash, but to the next level. With an original soundtrack, smooth gameplay, upgradeable stats and weapons, unlockable bikes and riders, and a tonne of extra in-game and in-race bonuses, you will not be disappointed. I fully recommend this game to anyone who's a longtime fan of combat racing games. I WILL be playing it more in my free time.
Cheers!

I had some fun with the previous games and Altair's, Desmond's and Ezio's stories was something I immensely enjoyed. It was well paced and fun, just the right pace to ensure a pleasant playthrough with a nice story.
Also, I learned some interesting stuff about history.
Assassin's creed III, on the other hand, is really boring.
It introduces some new elements - fine. That is something to work with, but the setting is something you see pretty much every year, at least once. I get it that for the Americans their Civil War is super important, but everybody - the whole wide wolrd - has seen it throusands of times and I'm pretty sure a random kid in Amsterdam or Warsaw could easily pass an exam on Civil War due to all the exposure this topic gets in movies and games.
And one of the selling points -"Experience the truth behind the most gruesome war in history: the American Revolution", are you serious? Have you ever been to Africa?
The gameplay is barely different from the previous games, just because there are some new tools doesn't mean it's suddenly so innovative.
The story is another cliched one - the lone survivor, abandoned by his father finds a father figure and takes revenge on father. I don't think I can digest the same story AGAIN.
Naval battles are ok (I was glad they went farther in that direction in Black Flag and made it actually really enjoyable), hunting is also ok (terribly repetitive though).
Crafting was fine too, but the delivery/shopping/running around in circles instead of just handing in a bunch of quests in a more convinient, smaller area was a little too much.
If there was a scale here, I would give this game 40% out of 100%. It was a pretty thing to look at.
