To End All Wars is the digital equivalent of a board war game. You are taking sides on the Great War, the global conflict between vainglorious European nations that happened some 100 years ago. There are three alliances initially: the Central Powers (Germany and Austria-Hungary), the West Entente (France and possibly Great Britain), and the East Entente (Russia and Serbia). I said "possibly" for GBR, because how quickly the United Kingdom can join the Entente may depend on the war plans each and every nation will choose, in case you as a player want to investigate an alternate reality war plan. There are 4 for each side, including the historical ones if you simply want to reenact WWI as the masterminds of the era envisioned it.
The players are in command of their alliance and try to win the Great War the best way they can, using warfare and diplomatic pressure. Aspects such as important historical decisions, R&D, and the armaments war effort are also abstracted. It's up to the player to decide which units (from simple independent brigades up to the General HQ) to engage and when. Logistics, weather, and terrain are parameters that are taken into consideration by the engine. Each turn is two weeks. Being a turn-based game is a virtue, not a vice. It will allow the player to think considerably about the pieces to move and how to achieve his/her overall strategy. Naval and air warfare are also abstracted. Certain important battles led by brilliant Generals will also give the option to select a tactical plan that can change the battle result even when the odds are saying the opposite.
The game is portraying mainly the Great War in Europe, but most colonies and satellite nations that were involved are also there. The engine is smart enough to considerate the historical tactical division between trench war in the West and relatively mobile war in the East. It's up to the involved protagonists to use decisions and diplomacy to influence (historically or not) different nations in their alliance. For example: what would have happened if Italy entered on the side of the Central Powers? What would have happened if USA was convinced to stay out of the war? It's up to the player to investigate these aspects...
Last, some notes about multiplayer. As with all AGEOD games (that I strongly recommend you investigate), there is a very interesting multiplayer option. Playing such a game with human players is the outmost challenge! Albeit I bet the AI will give you a hard time in single-player, the cunning and genuinely unexpected moves of a human player will surprise you every turn.
This is arguably the best title of a WWI strategy game currently available. Once you master its details, it will keep you entertained for many many hours. Hit the AGEOD forums for more specific advices or to read some interesting after-action reports.

AGEod is a great strategy engine and WWI is a forgotten war in videogames. So this is a very good combination. Honestly, it's not easy and not easy to learn. We need much time to understand the mechanism - even if you play with American Civil War for ages - and we need time to set everysmall details in the turns. But it worth the time. Oh, and this is an another 'one more turn' wargame.
With a little bit more polishing this game will be the strategy game of my dreams!

I'm a few hours in, and it seems solid.
Now, I don't know how it holds up with HL2 lore, (I'm not a geek, bite me) but I can definetly say that the engine is stable and functional, which is an accomplishment in its own right. That said it has some minor issues, but given the beta state, they may be overlooked... But may need fixing.
But before we get to that, let me talk about the things I liked. First of all, the engine is still a bit... Gmodish which means stuff's gonna fly all over the place. Building debrees, unit corpses, random junk, all sorts of stuff. Even units - at one point in sp_abandoned a fast zombie lunged at one of my units and went skydiving after it bounced off a pile of garbage. Things like this keep the game _slightly_ unpredictible which makes it a little more fun, as there's a slight chance that 2 setups will have different results. I see it as a merit, even though some may see it as a flaw.
Another thing I like is the fact that in order to do damage, you actually have to hit the enemy units. For example if a Shotgun Rebel will try to turn around and pump a combine full of lead, he may miss. Why? Because he fired before he finished turning around. It may not seem all that afir but honestly, I kinda see where the creators are coming from. This also means that shotguns won't just do fixed damage at a short range, but instead can be used as a strong short distance weapon and a weak mid-range weapon. Kudos.
I also like that you don't have to build your buildings to a grid. Even though I think it should be an option, it'd be best if it was an OPTION. Aka, you can both snap to grid and freeplace them. Rotating buildings would also be a welcome feature, in case I missed it, and it would allow for some creative base construction. At the very least allow the structures to be rotated 90 degrees.
What I don't like is the text-based, minimalistic interface, but again, it's a Beta. Their priority should be making the game functional and balanced before they hone the visuals.
Also while I understand the whole "shortcut corresponds to icon placement" concept, I found it very, very, very, very counter-intuitive, especially after Blizzard's rise to power and their use of contextual naming of the shortcuts - A for Attack, also for Offensive Movement, B for building, S for stopping (oh also, you don't have a "STOP" command. There's only a"HOLD GROUND") I went out of my way to re-bind those just so I can more or less normally play with what I'm used to since childhood. That said, I can see the merits of such control scheme, but it's simply not what I like.
Another gripe I have with this game is a pretty serious issue, especially on maps like sp_abandoned. INTERACTIVE OBJECTS (such as weapon crates, fruit and other) WILL GO INVISIBLE IF THE CAMERA'S FAR OUT ENOUGH. While I admit that it's fair to include this feature, someone should make sure that THE FADING DOESN'T OCCUR WHEN THE CAMERA IS ZOOMED OUT TO THE MAX! Why? Well duh, otherwise how are you gonna see the crates? And in strategy games, the bigger your field of view is, the better. Imagine if you had to play Starcraft or Red Alert using a camera that only allows you to see one tile at a time! Granted, zooming in one step is enough to make the objects visible, but that means you either have to spend the entire game on a reduced screen, or randomly zoom in back and forth like a toddler with a camcorder just to check the objects for being present.
Another thing, again having something to do with sp_abandoned. As you may accidentally find out, the various gas cans and carnisters EXPLODE!!!!!111!!1!!1i1!1oneoneone! That's fine, I'll just order my troops to shoot them so they're not a threa- *soldier wals onto the can, dies* Ooookaaay Maybe I'll blow them up with a grenade. *throws a grenade to get rid of 2 carnisters, aiming somewhere between them* Nothing? Maybe I didn't throw it close enough. *throws another one, aiming bullseye to blow it up, nothing* Well, those grenades are wasted. Greeeeeeeeaaat... I think the devs should make it possible to shoot those damn things, or at least make them grenadable. After all, they cost 10rq, might as well make them worth using, right?
As I said, it's beta and needs polish. I hope that they'll at least include different cursors depending on what you're ordering your units to do. Right-clicking an enemy makes the same animation as telling them to walk on him, and they don't have an alternate response that would vocally differenciate their attacks from their movements.
And I believe they included a custom music option... Which I haven't tried yet, but if it works, SHUT UP AND TAKE MY MONEY!
While not the perfect title, it's pretty good. If you can get past the 3 major problems, which are... bearable, you get a neat little mod that, if given some polishing and a campain editor, is probably gonna be a pretty solid title. In fact, I'm looking forward to seeing this come out as a full title. Perhaps the devs could use what they learned to make their own RTS in the future? [Disclaimer Regarding Hours] I've played this game since ~2012 and have invested hundreds of hours into the game; I just hardly ever use the steam launcher or have steam running while playing (The game wasn't always available on steam).
I'm recommending this game very hesitantly... Here we go
The visuals for this game are absolutely stunning (if your computer can handle the higher presets). The armor, characters, and scenery for this game are beautiful; consult google images if you need evidence. However, the game is relatively CPU and GPU intensive, so many people (especially laptop users) cannot play on decent settings without experiencing a performance drop. Furthermore, the game is designed to run on only 2 logical processors/"cores," so many people notice a huge fps difference between this game and games of a similar graphical standard. There are many forum posts which claim to offer methods for running this game on 4 logical processors, but they don't actually work (Trust me, I've tried them all). But this isn't really that much of a problem if you have a decent computer.
Unlike some MMORPGs, there is no lock-on or auto-attack; so you'll have to aim most of your attacks (there are some exceptions). Some people like this, others do not. However, for those who suffer from constant dips in fps, combat may be more difficult, especially in large battlegrounds. The combat animations are pretty distinct. Each combination of class/race/gender has it's own combat animations (some are better than others), and they're pretty fun to watch IMO.
Leveling your character is one of the more fun parts of this game (depending on which class you choose - some are more fun than others). Leveling used to be more tedious, but EnMasse now has regular double XP leveling events and grants many xp bonuses in-game. Most people can reach max level by just doing the story quests and a few extra dungeons. You used to be able to level-up fairly quickly by doing battlegrounds, but EnMasse now reserves battlegrounds for people who have hit max level.
The dungeons in this game are pretty well-designed. Some of them are a little repetative and obvious clones of eachother, but these instances aren't too common. Because the game has less to render within dungeons, most people will experience great increases in performance.
The end-game is pretty tedious. It mainly consists of grinding dungeons and battlegrounds until you can craft/enchant the best possible gear for your character. The tedium is somewhat relieved if you join a guild and regularly engage in guild events. However, all battlegrounds and many dungeons are reserved for characters with max level; so this is essentially when the game is supposed to "start." They recently added a semi-survival mode for players who reach max level (I forget it's name). Some people find it kind of fun, but it's really short (about 3-10 minutes depending on your class/gear).
Battlegrounds are perhaps the most cancerous element of the game. The most popular battleground, Corshair's Stronghold, is 20vs20 and difficult for many people's computers to process efficiently. However, most people still play it because if has the shortest queue time of all the battlegrounds and the daily rewards chest is an easy way to get essential end-game materials.
Here's a run-down of how this lovely bit of torture usually goes:
1. You enter the arena
2. (a). Leader is afk absent and you have to kick it. (b) the leader doesn't want to lead and is frantically looking for someone else to lead. (c) leader gives first orders
3. [Coin flip] There's a 50/50 chance as to whether or not people will follow the leader's orders. If they do, great. If they don't, they probably don't care or don't speak english (so sorry).
4. By about 4 min into the game, you can usually predict how things are going to go. If things are going smoothly, great! If they aren't, this is usually when people start fighting and barking their own orders in chat... enjoy.
5. If your team does decent in the first round, expect a fairly smooth second round with full leader support and participation. If you don't, expect a second round with some of your team AFK and everyone barking orders, fighting, and finger-pointing in chat. Welcome to CS :)
**Note: Game outcome is determined by the overall expense of your team's computers in addition to skill and team cohesion. If most people can play the game with good fps and rendering (in other words, they can actually kill people), then you win. This is known as "hardware carrying," the true pay to win.
Of course there are other battlegrounds you can join, but their wait times are usually longer (and in some cases, indefinite because nobody is queued for them at the time).
The community is pretty split. There are lots of people with really low IQs and people who get frustrated really easily... In other words, It's a troller's paradise! "Hey trolls, are you looking for a new internet community to prey on? If so, welcome to TERA! This short-tempered community where about half the people have a homologous chromosome count of 47 is perfect for your evil little perversions!" But seriously, trolling people is super easy. Sometimes I like to imagine that I'm shortening the lifespan of some of these people by frustrating them and increasing their stress levels, and in essence, crafting a better and more sophisticated internet community. (You're welcome.)
The other half of the community is fantastic. There are lots of people willing to help new players and make friends. Also, if you like meeting people from different countries, this game is perfect. I now have lots of new friends from Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, Brazil, the US, Croatia, and the UK as a result of playing.
The game is fine as long as you can run it. Like most MMORPGs, it has it's problems, but none of them are too major. Go into the game with thick skin and don't expect everyone you meet to be nice to you. The gameplay gets a little repetative at times, but there's enough content to make it worth a playthrough. Just get a character to max level and stop if you don't like it. That part of the game is free, so there's no risk. (Only recommending game because it's free. Would not recommend paying for anything.)
If you're absolutely horrible at MMOs or games in general and have a crap computer, I recommend gunner for your first character. They are ranged, heavy armor, have lots of combos, can self-heal, can restore their own mana, have a turret and a robot to fight with them, and are really easy to handle at low fps. I fell in love with this game immediately after playing it during the free weekend. It's immensely fun and amusingly violent. There's a wide variety of character classes to choose from and unlock. They provide a lot of different ways to play the game-such as sneaking around breaking into places as the thief, blasting everything to bits and hacking the world as the hacker, or just run around bashing everything and everyone as a giant gorilla.
It's got an interesting interactive world. Most doors can be bashed in, or you can blast apart walls and objects, or you can dump items into air vents to poison enemies. Combined with the many dialogue options (such as bribery with items or cash, or intimidation) and the different items and skills granted by the various classes, there are a lot of ways to approach the decent variety of missions the game has available so far. One of my favorites is to make enough money in a run to bribe the police to ignore my crimes and then purchase a slave or hire a guard to do my bidding. Hiring a homeless person to cause a ruckus in the police station so you can sneak in and bust out your target is just as much fun as tossing a grenade in the room and running in swinging swords and whatever else you can grab.
I can't wait to see what else this game adds in the future and fully intend to keep coming back to play it again and again. As it's a great couch co-op game, i'll probably be playing it a lot with friends.

Gameplay wise, the game is closer to a time-management simulator than anything else, and it's an entertaining one.
The majority of the game is spent on a single city map screen, trying to balance the time of your officers and detectives: sending as many as you can to make sure every incident is resolved while leaving as many people behind as possible to resolve other issues. Spontaneous incidents or requests from City Hall can catch you off guard on a busy day so you always need to be second-guessing your decisions. Officers will die as a result, and some calls will go unanswered.
The game is fun for maybe the first eight(ish) hours, but the pace of the plot really starts to fall off mid-game, and there are several game days where nothing important seems to happen. Things pick up again towards the end and I'm glad I got over the hump, though the ending leaves a lot to be desired.
[Mild plot/theme spoilers follow]
To really enjoy the game, you have to embrace the hardboiled/noir storyline.
The game does itself a disservice early on, suggesting that you might be able to play through the game as a good guy. But you can't, and you'll die trying. There are a few chances to decide on the lesser of the two evils, but there's no place in Freeburg for an honest cop.
A lot of the content feels a little immature and hammed up. False alarms are quickly explained away by someone forgetting to take their anti-psychotics, there's a disproportionate number of callouts for public indecency, and the situations are generally a little ridiculous. But I suppose anything less would be boring to play.

Much as I prefer to let each game stand on its own, certain games demand comparisons. In the case of Cities: Skylines, developer Colossal Order has overtly modeled its game after SimCity – not just the fundamental concept and methods of building and maintaining a simulated city from the ground up, but much of the look and feel as well. And on almost every count, Skylines compares very favorably to the former standard-bearer of the city-building genre. It is, in fact, the best of its kind to come along in a full decade – a powerful, flexible, beautiful, and all-around impressive simulation that lets you build sprawling, single-player metropolises to your heart’s content. Building has to be its own reward, though, because the lack of random events or disasters leaves the job of running these towns feeling sleepy and meditative.

This is the Police is a decent management game which appeals particularly to the niche gamer who enjoys the theme more than the mechanic.  It has a solid style to it - minimilaist but not faux-retro, and a fantastic sound; both music and voice-actors really set this game apart from a typical management sim, and serve to deliver a very satisfying atmosphere of grim moral compromise.
The game itself can be repetitive, but that is understood by the set-up: you're managing the city of Freeburg's police department in your last days of office - beset by administrative beurocracy and mafia pressure to serve the people best and get out alive.  The action is in staffing and dispatching officers and units to emergencies, investigations and events between the narrative cut-scenes that keep the game clipping along.  With such a linear plot, it doesn't offer much replayability, and is a repetitive game over time; but the evocative ambience and short action periods (in-game days) means that it doesn't outstay its welcome.
Definitely recommended, but this is more of an experience than a truly fleshed out strategic game, so would wait for sale-prices or discount before committing.

So, this was supposed to be it. Desmond had "brought us to our end". Pitched as the game that would answer all of those questions and bring the Assassin's Creed trilogy (pentalogy?) to a stunning conclusion. The only problem is that of course it didn't.
It just left us with more questions, and after playing five games in the series it has left me feeling as if I were falling down a hole that actually has no bottom.
There were times though when I found the game enjoyable and fun to play. If you have played, and enjoyed (as I have), the previous instalments of the francise, you will probably get some enjoyment from this episode too. I like the addition of seafaring and the naval battles. There is a feeling of panic, unique to this game, when you see a 100 gun Man of war appear in to view. And it is fun using your more manouvable frigate to send one of these giants to Davey Jones' locker. And of course it never gets old appearing over a rooftop and as an enemy starts to challenge you, leaping on him and burying your hidden blade in his chest.
Having said this, in all honsety the fifth installment of the series still suffers from many of the same problems and bugs previous versions had. The story still has a disjointed feel to it and there were times when there were characters that were refered to and I ended up thinking "who on earth are they?" You could rush through the main story without the need to fulifil any of the optional missions and in honesty I felt that they don't really add much to the narrative. On top of the standard AC plot issues there are the standard game play issues. Connor loves to stand on walls watching as his target disapears off into the distance, leap of a builing in the wrong direction and jump over an assassination target that is on the move. After 5 years development time you would have hoped that Ubisoft would have many of these issues solved, yet they still persist.
All in all I give this game a 7.5/10. I've scored it this high only because I bought it in the sumer sale for £3.75 and at that price it's good value for money. If I see AC4 available for a similar price I will probably give that a whirl too, but not at the £15.99 Steam and Ubisoft are currently asking. And I certainly won't be pre-ordering AC Syndicate ;)

So, I'll start with the good:  The product has a ton of different games to play (though many are different variations of a common casino game).  You can customize your avatar, which is kind of fun to do.  Finally, you can control the music and there's a wide selection to listen to.
Now, the things that bother me:
1) The AI won't shut the heck up!  They're compelled to talk during every bet and there's no way (that I know of) to hurry them along.  It's cute for the first three rounds.  After that, it's just useless chatter that just delays the game.
2) No tool tips / mouse-overs.  How much do I have on that Pass Line?  What's that icon for?  What's the odds on this bet? If that information is there, I can't find it.  No big deal if you're playing blackjack, but, when you've got money all over the craps table, it would be nice to know.
3) The mechanics to raise/lower your bet just stinks.  There's a pencil that you can click - for the life of me I can't figure out what to do when you click it.  The only way I can see to raise / lower a bet is to click and hold the up/down arrows next to the bet amount and slowly watch it tick up and down.  No typing, no chips to click, nothing.
4) No multi-player.  Granted, I knew this going in since the store page states single player.  It just would be nice if that feature were added since it seems that most games have an interactive aspect these days.
5) No real satisfaction from winning / losing.  I haven't played it very long yet; but, I don't see any achievements or other visual rewards for having a good run of luck or managing bets well.  You just have your bank amount under your player icon.  That's a bit....boring.
6) I could be wrong, but, it seems the mechanics of the craps table don't work correctly.  Can't place odds behind the pass line.  Appear to be able to pull down the passline bet after the point is rolled.  No easy way to press bets.
Overall - the game just seems to be tossed together without much regard for the user experience.  Is it fun?  Well, I haven't uninstalled it, but, I could easily see myself moving to a different casino game if one came out.

+++ Fun action that focuses more on hacking and thinking your way around heavily guarded items
+++ Huge and beautiful open world based around the real city of San Fransico is vibrant and feels quite realistic.
+++ The idea of fighting for privacy and against mass surveillance strikes a chord with today's world of Google Home and Amazon Echo's.
++ Characters are fun and interesting which provides a nice contrast to the moody, angsty characters in the first game.
-- Not a lot of variety to the game world.  Most items found while free roaming are guarded, but most of those encounters play out similarly.  Items that aren't guarded typically have the same kind of puzzles to solve.
-- Escaping from the police is almost too easy, especially when you use aquire the special ability to disable helecopters.
- Gun play is good in general, but your character can't take a hit.  This speaks more to the design direction of the game, and I respect that.  However, there are times where you accidentally get caught, and its almost impossible to fight your way out.  I also find that gangs have comically more firepower than the police (gameplay > realism, I guess).
- The drone and RC car can often times make some "challenges" almost ludicrously easy.  A lot of guarded items in the game can be aquired by simply using the drone to find the item, tag the guards, and then send in the RC car to quickly retrieve the item.  Once you have the item, you can instantly call back the RC car, and there you go: too easy.
- The narrative is kind of a miss for me.  Not a lot of focus, and it leans too much on the strength of the characters to make things interesting.
Overall score: 8/10

I have a lot to say about this game. Because to be perfectly honest it's a great game in my opinion. When it comes to mmorpgs, I am very picky about a few things:
The Combat System
The Overall Gameplay
The Graphics for the type of style of the game
And the community
Tera overall has a great score in my book on all these accounts. A new player can level fairly quickly and can follow the decent storyline of the game. Or if you don't like storyline gameplay, you can just do the dungeons and other side quests. And once you get to a fairly decent level and skill in combat you can get some pretty cool gear even if you play for free.
The combat system in particular is one of my favorites I've ever had the pleasure of using. The controls are usually smooth depending on your class. And the servers hardly seem to lag in combat unless there's like a dramatic amount of monsters or other people spamming.
The graphics for this game are lets just say are downright gorgeous. I love pretty much every location in this game for different reasons. And the graphics fit this syle of game splendidly.  And character design is a wonderful experiance with a good amount of choices on each level of the designing.
And the community is overall a very.. interesting one. Depending on the server you can have some hardcore wanting to battle type people, the more helpful friendly types, Casual players, and even sometimes some of the more.. umm.. lets just say more unique kind of people. No matter what each time you log on something new happens. Whether the thing is good or not well.. I'll leave that for you to discover if you try the game out.
But one thing I must warn new players about is the pvp modes in the game. They will make you cry sometimes. The newest classes are bred to destroy the former actually good classes. A really good slayer could be wrecked by a brawler or ninja for instance. But even then, you can always just avoid pvp all together. Or maybe just suicide bomb if you dont care about surviving.
Besides the pvp, I'd say this is one of my favorite games of all time. So do I recommend it? Yes! It's a fun game with fun characters and a fun community. The graphics are good enough to make you enjoy seeing your character wreck everything in their path. New updates happen fairly often so you can always do something new. And if you get bored, join a guild. It adds lots of chances to meet new people and battle together. So basically Tera is a game worth playing. In my opinion, I'd say give it a try.

Planetarian The Reverie of a Little Planet
Hmmm, so coming into this VN I didn't know what to expect, I had heard quiet a lot about it but I was hearing a lot of mixed impressions, however I was pleasantly surprised to find what a great story it had, it was a very interesting read; and suffice to say I have reread this VN many times.
The Story is based long after a great war that left the world in darkness, most if not all life gone, acid rains ever covering the planet in an erosive downpour.
Though a story just centered on what had happened to the planet would be good enough, then the  focus comes to two characters living 30 years after whatever tragedy had overcome the planet, and the journey they must take through this harsh world.
Length wise it is not the longest VN I have come across taking four to five hours depending on how fast you read, however it doesn't need to be any longer; it tells its story well in the period of time needed, any longer and the feel would be completely off, as if to make it worse by drawing it out so though some will be disappointed at its short length it is for the best.
The art style I must say is incredible, it has a certain charm to it; and not just the characters the backgrounds are very good also, the VN has a great use of colour to contrast between various scenes and locations.
The music is well done and adds to the atmosphere and complements the game quiet well, it really helps to immerse yourself in the story.
Overall Planetarian is beautifully written piece of work; It is visually appealing, the characters are interesting; learning about the pasts of the two main characters, seeing them interact, and seeing how the whole thing unfolds what you get is a story that is incredibly touching, anyone who likes Clannad, Air or any other of Key's works, Planetarian will be a welcomed addition to your library.
I'll leave you with this, Planetarian The Reverie of a Little Planet is a great read and will no doubt keep you interested throughout its duration....so why not give it a try.
(Like all my reviews I do not put a score as it is my belief that games like all forms of art are subjective and therefore it is impossible to afix a number to them)

Home is a great little horror/lite adventure game.  A play through only takes roughly 30-45 minutes but it's designed to be played 3-4 times to see how the story plays out each time.  A lot of the plot points are up for you to decide based on how you interperet the evidence you were able to find during the murder mystery.  The game is as much about what you clues you didn't find as to which ones you did.  There are plenty of points in the game where you will make one choice or forget to go back and check on something that you will want to revisit on subsequent play throughs.  The creepy atmosphere the developer was able to achieve was quite well done through sound, text, and pixels.  It is best to do each play through in one sitting, with the lights off and with headphones.  It was a really nice change of pace for an evening and I highly reccommend it for anyone looking for something a little different in between more time consuming games.  Also, it is super cheap so the short length shouldn't be a deterent to anyone.

While I personally enjoy this game to some extent, it is not for everybody. What threw off most people is how slow the game is for the first 3-4 hours. It does pick up after that, but a lot of your time is spent running around from cutscene to cutscene with an action setpiece every now and then. While I personally am a fan of more storydriven cinematic games, don't play this game if you want non-stop action-packed assassin awesomeness. Go play Black Flag if you want that.
As for the story itself, its good. It tells a personal story of Connor, and there is a lot of development in the characters of Achilles and the villains. However, Connor himself is a very boring and uninteresting protagonist. The combat is good, but very easy. All you have to do is counter, break defense, and then kill.
Overall, I would recommend this game if you enjoy a very immersive world, and good story, if a bit slow moving.

This game is a true sleeper.  The graphics don't exactly reel you in right off the bat so you might think that you're about to play just another crappy game with low production values.  But the storyline kind of sounds interesting, so you put it away to play maybe later...
When you finally get to playing the game, you realize that the true gem here is not the storyline (which is pretty good), but the management system.  It's really a one of a kind game.  If ever you have run a police dispatch board or have experience in police administration, this game is very realistic.
The simulator puts you in situations where you have limited manpower.  You have to dispatch your cops wisely and play the political game of having to please City Hall.  Different cops under your command have variant experience levels, personality quirks and specialties.  Some are detectives and some are partolmen and some are SWAT guys.  You may choose to send them for extra training.  You can only imrove your manpower and SWAT capabilities if City Hall likes the job you're doing.  You have to observe the dispatch calls carefully cause you will ulimately pay for it if you send 6 cops and the swat team because some kid wouldn't eat his brocoli and called 911 that he's "being held hostage". haha
Anyway, don't get me wrong I like the subplots and mafia stories, but I would love to see this game develop as an even more detailed police administration simulator.
I usually don't recommend things at full price, but if you're really into the subject of police administration, this one is worth it!

This is one of those games that you're really going to like or dislike based on the game style and whether that style appeals to you. There are few games I know to compare it to, but at a very basic level, it's a story-driven time management game, but so much more detailed to that.
The biggest thing that jumped out at me, and the biggest thing you'll enjoy if you're into this kind of thing is the dialogue. I'm serious, I have played games with 100 times the budget of this game that would still be put to shame by it. The dialogue and conversation options are seriously probably the best I've ever seen--I've played all the big conversation option games--Mass Effect, Skyrim (my personal favorite dialogue game to hate on, LA Noire), etc, and none of them hold a candle to this. This is probably the only game where given my dialogue options, when I pick one, I actually say: "Yes! That is what a smart, crafty person in my character's position would ACTUALLY say."
I will say some of the actual gameplay does feel a bit repetative, and maybe I haven't played far enough to determine if they really deal with the consequences of my choices in game, but honestly I would still give this a huge thumbs up regardless. Buy it just for that, because it's honestly a breath of fresh air when it comes to actually feeling like what you say has an effect on the story and what comes out of your character's mouth.

The combat in the game is pretty RNG based and probably more reliant on luck than any actual skill, that said it appears as your character grows there will be more thought around skills picked to counter other fighters and adapt to different situations. Unfortunalty having got to 5th place in the Rookie league and beaten up a few guys including a teenage mutant ninja crocodile(?! yes) i feel the game play rather repetative and labourious.
I had already put fight speed up to x4 (the maximum) and just waited to lose just to grab those 2 skill points  (needed like 11 more for a skill up... yawn) the game became just too much of a grind to actually remain fun.

I figure the price I paid was the same as a pint of beer, normally a pint of beer (on its own) gives me roughly 5-20 minutes worth of entertainment depending on the situation, punch club gave me around 6 hours. Aid a young girl and her trusty dog companion in a struggle to survive in a flooded world.  Flame in the Flood is a mix of distinct visual style and climatic soundtrack. The main idea behind the game seems to be a notion that a journey is a goal in itself, no lesser than reaching the destination.
There is no telling what exactly happened to the game’s world but one thing is certain – the civilization as we know it, was reduced to ruins, drifting down the river. The only mean of transport is your raft and only stop is an occasional patch of land where you may finally resupply. This is one of core mechanics of the game – navigating the raft through treacherous currents, filled with piles of junk and obstacles, that damage your raft when you hit them. Raft durability is limited and its destruction leads to untimely death. On the other hand, you can both upgrade and repair your vessel, if you can reach right place on time and have necessary resources. Perhaps a big “if”, but survival was never meant to be easy.
Lion’s share of the time though, will be spent on land. Occasional pier allows you to enter into small inland areas, where you can find some much needed supplies. There is quite a few different types of places you can anchor by - such as farms, camps or a gas station. They vary depending on what part of the river you are swimming through at given time – you are more likely to find a camp while strolling through the forest, and a shop when passing ruins of the city. There will be plenty of stops, as only on land you can gather resources – food and building materials. As you progress through the game hazards gradually become greater. Bunnies you snacked on early in the game make place for wolves and bears that will gladly eat you. On the other hand greater challenges grant better rewards and a bear fur coat will keep you warm on the cold nights if you can get one.
The game can be fairly challenging, especially in the beginning, but once you get a bit more used to the world around you and pass certain threshold, you will find yourself possessing far more resources than you can use. Thus, allowing you to simply enjoy the sojourn. You can craft everything, quite a while before the game ends. For those who want a further challenge or simply carry on, after completing the main game, there is a endless mode that is far more difficult from the start, and lasts however long you wish.
Cartoonish visuals of the game might be a virtue or a vice, depending on your taste but they do set the proper tone for the game. Atmosphere is further amplified with pleasant soundtrack, that after some time makes you want to sing along, no matter the rain or an empty stomach. Experience in effect, feels far more like a camping with fireplace, sausages and a tent. Flame in the flood is an oddly soothing journey, for a game that is essentially a struggle to survive in a post-apocalyptic world; given a deeper thought.
Despite many positives, Flame in the Flood has a few problems too. Game is riddled with plenty of minor bugs, such as bugged raft interaction animations, plants randomly generated outside of reachable area.  On one occasion, I had a dead bear casually spring back to life, luckily it just stood where it died, and roared at me. What seemed undercooked the most, were the pieces of narrative, creators tried to smuggle into the game. Pieces of parchment, and few other people you meet during your journey, allow you to take little glimpses at the world of the game. Sadly, those pieces hardly fall into place and the encounters do little to grant you extra insight into the world. Characters are just kind of there, almost none of them having impact on the game, but it’s interesting to see what people made of the dying world, if nothing else.
Flame in the Flood is a climatic indie game I can recommend to any single player enthusiasts who enjoy distinctive atmosphere and unique visuals. Best served with a cup of warm drink after a long day.

You thought this was gonna be a Call Of Duty reject? You were so wrong...
Rainbow Six: Siege is a tactical FPS that is best played with a group of friends, this game took the gaming community by storm as it focused less on fast paced combat and more on strategy, teamwork and knowledge. Their are a multitude of unique operators to play and this results in multiple counters to others, different ways to breach a building or different tactics to engage enemies. The community can be a bit... toxic at times but none the less you will occasionally find some great people who are willing to have fun and play a couple of rounds with you. The damage system is also unique, being more realistic than other shooters (They do this by making headshots an instant kill and body shots will severely wound you). You have to think about how you want to breach, what operator to sue for that situation and all possible ways you can get yourself out of trouble.
So now that the starter Siege pack has come out, it is definetly worth a buy if you want a solid game with a growing community and constant updates.

A short and very sweet visual novel with outstanding localisation.
The way the world is built up around the main character's current situation is orchestrated wonderfully. The dull and grey animated city backgrounds and the descriptions verging on poetic make it easy for the reader to form a strong sense of the world being portrayed -- and that's coming from someone who hardly ever reads books, partly *because* I can't visualise them well.
Watching the main character develop as chapters progress is the other best thing about planetarian. It never felt forced (though a bit rushed at the end), it was always interesting, and it keeps the story moving at the perfect pace.
One more point to emphasise: the brilliant translation/localisation. I remember seeing only one grammar error in total, and it was minor. There's a point where they use the 'when in Rome' saying: I thought to myself, "oh no, they're not using this right at all", but the next line proved me wrong. Seriously, it's a pleasure to read.
Having only played a few VNs before I think I can say reasonably safely that this would be a great starting option for people who haven't played many before. planetarian is 100% non-interactive, so stay away if you prefer choices in your visual novels -- but for anyone else, especially if you enjoy sci-fi, this game is a great pick.
2016-07-25 edit: Yeah it's still an amazing experience. I was constantly impressed with how well the story reads. Good variety of music to fit different scenes. For anyone interested, it takes 4.5 hours to read through in auto mode with a slightly faster than default speed setting.

It's a visual novel consisting entirely of two characters and their conversations.

is an emotional piece of work, and one I didn't know what to expect from.
The story is very basic, a scavenger who the game calls the Junker ends up in an abandoned city destroyed by a huge war that decimated most of the planet to look for supplies. In this city he ends up inside an abandoned Planetarium, where he meets a robot named Yumemi. She offers a projection for him of the night sky, something he has never had the chance to see, and agrees to fix the broken projector in order to get that reward.
That's all the story summary I'll give, but suffice to say, it is quite good. However, I didn't really get very emotional until the last half-hour or so, but by then, I was most certainly bawling my eyes out. The main meat of the story is just the building relationship between the Junker and Yumemi, which is the only reason it works at all.
In terms of graphics and sound, the game is fine. I wouldn't really say the music is anything too special, especially not compared to Key's other Visual Novels, but it gives just the right atmosphere and mood for each scene, so that it's not really that much of a problem. Yumemi and the backgrounds are fairly well drawn and detailed, and the game is fully voiced (Japanese only).
The only big turn-off this game has is in it's length and asking price. As much as I recommend this story, $10 is a
steep price for something that lasts all of 3-5 hours with very little replay value. Granted, I'm the kind of guy who can read stuff like this multiple times, but I can't speak for others. I'd recommend waiting for a sale on this one, but whether you pay full-price or discounted, this experience is well worth it.

Home is alright, but nothing spectacular by any means.  A mystery is afoot, and you have to decide which clues are relevant, and which ones are not.  Choosing which items you pick up (or don't) decides the fate of the story.  There are multiple possibilites of how the conclusion is drawn, and there are no good or bad specific endings.  There is no way to die in the game, which eliminates a lot of tension as far as making mistakes go.  The low quality graphics also encourage one to exercise their imagination a bit.  The sounds do raise the tension quite a bit, so I have to recommend head phones for full effect.  The length of the game (play through) is supposed to be about 90 minutes, but my first run was 75 minutes, even with my need to deeply explore.  All in all, this is a great ghost story for casual gamers, but the hard core crowd won't be very wowed by this one.

This game is decent. But it definitely has it's flaws.
EDIT -- I've played further into the story and have sadly encountered more stuff to list in the cons section.
Pros:
- Open world feels very alive.
- Story so far seems solid and Bayek is a strong character.
- Graphics are ridiculously good. Egypt feels and looks very alive. Running it at 3440x1440 on a 5820K OC'd and a GTX 1080. I run near max settings with a couple things like shadows dropped a bit because they make absolutely zero noticable difference. Additionally I run Reshade to resharpen the image after the temporal AA blurs it(I feel bad for people who don't use these tricks, it makes a HUGE difference), and to pop the colors just a tad more. I usually get 50-60FPS, never dropping below 40, which is just fine for me. I absolutely do not know what the people complaining about optimization are talking about. Update your graphics drivers maybe? It runs very well for a game of such massive scale and detail.
- Combat is fun as♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's actually reasonably challenging now and has a good amount of strategy to it. Enemies no longer wait their turn for you to one hit kill them in a chain. They actively flank you and use special attacks and can block you entirely, and parry you on top of that. It's seriously awesome.
- Impressively small install size for the ridiculous scale and detail of the game. 34GB. Compare that to a lot of other games out there, none of which even compare to this game when it comes to what they fit into that space.
- Side quests are ♥♥♥♥ing awesome. In previous AC games, there was the main questline and then whatever they could tack on. In this, there are all kinds of stories and characters scattered about the map for you to run into. They definitely took a look at Witcher 3, and the result is beautiful and immersive.
- Stealth still isn't perfect, but is far far FAR better than previous AC games.
- Level system adds to progression in the game, and helps keep enemies fresh and interesting. But.. it has some other major flaws that I'll get into.
-Controller support is A+, and the game controls beautifully.
-Difficulty modes FINALLY exist! (How did it take so many games to realize this was needed..)
Cons:
- Level system is often very inhibiting. Boss enemies just a couple levels higher than you can insta-kill you through block, while any enemy lower in level deals quite paltry damage to you and will die in a few hits.
- Side quests are tied to the level system, meaning it's either too hard or too easy if you're not within a couple levels of the side quest's locked level. This is stupid, I really enjoy the more involved side quests and the level system completely gets in the way of them. This should've been caught in play-testing, it's obvious and stupid.
EDIT: Additional Cons ---
- Heavy CPU load! I have a quite powerful CPU so I didn't notice initially. But once I got curious and took at look at the task manager, it's clear that AC:Origins is a very CPU hungry game.
- There's plenty of SJW crap right in the main storyline... Very disappointing. I want HISTORY, and I have zero interest in what the executives at Ubisoft want to say. I didn't think much of the silly gender identity garbage at the beginning of the title sequence.. but now I see those morons also had a say in an otherwise fantastic story.
- Presentation of the story elements... The pacing of the story is often VERY awkward. Cutscenes and dialogue between characters both have plenty of issues. There were a lot of stupid instances such as one cutscene where Cleopatra is in the biggest city in the game with guards on every pillar to give a speech to like 10 people... Additionally dialogue always gets screwed up by characters running and bumping into things.
Minor Cons:
- The FOV slider is way too limited. I might try playing with M+KB, but I can't stand to be that close to the screen because I can't get the FOV high enough.
- Hard difficulty makes combat last a lot longer, but not much more difficult. I've instead aimed at trying to be underlevel for quests and playing on Normal mode, because then combat is more realistic and satisfying, but still challenging.
- Stealth doesn't incorporate sound enough. Footsteps, loud noises and nearby arrow impacts are noticed by enemies, BUT they are often deaf to very close assassinations, enemy combat noises, and a bit blind to stuff that's clearly happening in their peripheral vision where it should be very noticable.
On the off-chance that any dev is reading these reviews, an easy fix for the level system would be to make the enemy strength difference between levels much smaller. For stuff like the gladiator arena activity, just toss in higher level enemies instead.
I splurged and bought the Gold Edition for 100 bucks. Edit: Mild regrets now. I do wish I'd just spent the basic 60. The SJW ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and glitches ruining the flow of the story really take me out of the mood of the game. It's just so disappointing to see people injecting their uninformed political nonsense into an otherwise brilliant experience.

A huge improvement over WD1. WD2 takes the hacking formula, puts a relevant "hacktivist" modern (and sometimes heavy handed hipster) spin on it, and outshines the first game in pretty much every way.
This game is at it's best when you DO NOT play it like GTA. It makes zero sense for a hactivist group to be running around gunning down people in the streets. Use your gadgets, RC car & quadcopter, hacks, stealth, and other hacking related things and you'll have a much better time. I found a good balance of non-lethal/lethal that I think makes sense and fits with the theme of the game.
First off, I don't equip any lethal guns. Only use the stun gun, paintball gun, stun grenade-launcher, etc.
Second, don't just murder everyone every mission. It makes no sense to kill cops, security guards, civilians, or even most main mission targets. The only type of people I do anything lethal to are the gang members. I'll call other gangs in to cause shoot outs (its a hack you can do) and drop mini-explosives from my quadcopter drone and RC car. Aside from gang members, I take out pretty much every other enemy non-lethally (baring some accidents that tend to pop up during intense situations :D) and I think it makes the game feel a ton more real like you're a hacker instead of a murderer or thug. If you just run around murdering every one, the playful light hearted cut-scenes during/after the main missions don't even make sense.
The game has 3 different "styles" of hacker you can be (although if you play long enough, you will eventually unlock all skills). These styles are: Aggressor, Trickster, and Ghost.
Aggressor is the most obvious and brute force one. You basically blast your way through enemy bases/buildings/areas with guns/explosives and physically hack the mission objectives in person as Marcus while fighting enemies and their possible waves of reinforcements.
Trickster is in my opinion the most fun because it utilizes all of the various hacks and gadgets you have the most out of the three styles. You use your RC car and quadcopter drone to complete the missions by distracting and setting booby traps for enemies, remotely hacking objectives with your RC car, calling in cops/gangs to confront the guards in the areas you hack, etc. This style usually consists of parking Marcus at the edge of a mission zone (be it behind a fence or something) and sending your robots to do all the work. Its really cool because Marcus is never actually seen or in danger, and if your RC car or drone are blown up, you're still safe and can start over again. Like I said, IMO this feels like the most "hacker" way to play that fits with the game because you are using your full arsenal of tricks.
Ghost is fun too. It involves using hacks/gadgets that distract, disrupt, or generally just do stealth related things to get the objectives completed. You can jam comms, cause blackouts, then sneak Marcus into the mission area and hack the objectives while darting from cover to cover hidden. While doing this, you'll make enemies cellphones ring to distract them or make their earpieces blare static so they are "stunned" for a few seconds.
Now, the open world. This game's open world might be one of the most detailed, immersive, and convincing one I've ever played in. All of the NPC interaction, and the fact that the NPCs are constantly going about their routines and have detailed behavior really make the world feel alive because they don't just feel like some static placeholders in the background. They really made the playful and sunny San Francisco area come alive. The visuals and atmosphere of the world are top notch. There is always something going on around you, especially in the various tourist locations where a lot of NPCs are around at once. There will be dogs playing with each other, people playing guitar, doing yoga, etc, and they all react to you. Whether you bump into them, start to take selfies with them in the background, flick them off or dance with emotes, every NPC will interact with you, what you do, or other NPCs around them.
The story is fun, quirky, light-hearted most of the time, and full of awesome characters that each have a backstory and personality. You do actually feel like you are apart of a hacktivist group by the way Marcus interacts with these characters before/during/after the main missions throughout the story.
I had about 65 hours into the game by the time I uninstalled it the first time (before DLC came out). I did all of the main story, all of the side missions, a bunch of the repeatable co-op missions, and a ton of collecting research points. After trying each one once, I skipped out on the "mini-game" side missions like drone races, go-kart races, DriveSF (Uber), etc because they didn't really feel "hacker" in any way.
I have reinstalled, and bought both story DLC packs and am playing through them now. So far they are great, and feel like a continuation of the main missions in the base game in terms of quality and content.
Definitely recommend this game!

So after we'll just say 19 hours in-game, I do find this game so much fun to play. The graphics are well done, and yes I would sacrifice graphics for gameplay, the story as I have seen so far is amazing, I can't wait to find out what happens next, and the mechanics are easy enough to get the hang of from early on in the game. I only have two things that I would change about this game, and they are mostly for my own preference, although others seem to share my point of view on this. While the various classes all have their strengths, as well as weaknesses, the ninja and reaper classes are locked to not only one specific race, but one specific gender. I understand enough to know that these two classes are tied to the respective race through lore, but as I am a guy, and I prefer to play in accordance with my gender, I would love to be able to be either of these classes as a male character. I am sure some people will feel the same towards the gunner class, which is also locked to female characters only. Don't let this take away from the game, though, as the game itself, in my opinion is wonderful. I would just like to be able to play a seemingly epic class, and stick to my gender at the same time. I made a character under the ninja class, but it is merely for the purpose of seeing for myself the skills and playstyle this class has to offer, and I plan to do the same with the reaper class. Also, there is the problem of the requirements to play the game, although I don't actually see it as a problem, since the majority of people with a computer of any type, could be able to play the game, but for the few people who can't, they are missing out on a friendly, and deep experience. Still I would rate this game 10/10 regardless of such a tiny speck on an otherwise spotless game.

I backed this game on Kickstarter when it was first drummed up. They said they released the game October 4, 2017 and I didn't get my digital copy. I decided to buy it anyway (for a second time) in order to play it.
Firstly, I love Road Rash. Played it on SEGA Genesis back when and I was wondering why something like it was never made again. This filled portions of that hole.
However, it should be noted that this game very much reflects an arcade style. There are no extravagant physics,
the campaign is rather short, and there's a slight learning curve. What this game does well is MAYHEM. Slaughtering other motorists left, right, and centre with 5 melee weapon types (blunt light, heavy, long, sword, and cattle prod), 3 types of skin flaying guns, 3 types of explosives, and the nearly useless Grappling Hook. Cars fall from the sky. Cop cars barrel at you from the on-coming lane. It can be difficult to keep track of (which is pretty much the point).
The difficulty dries up pretty quickly because of the half-baked skill tree "rogue-lite" motif they decided to try. This is circumvented by playing the game and unlocking quirky riders that out-right increase difficulty, nullify the skill tree, strip you of all guns, or force you to use nitro unless you feel like dying. Beat the normal campaign 3-4 times, then the game lets the replayability shine.
Oh, and there's multiplayer...
Sort of...
We don't really talk about it.
There's nothing like powersliding a motorcycle, perpendicular to the road, slam into a wall, your rider to wiggle like he almost lost his balance.
Physics.

Lots of good changes since it left beta - most notably the addition of the Aussie voiceover and the main narrative frame with road gang affiliation. Rephrasing some of the challenges has also worked out well, and it definitely helps that a lot of the off-road glitches are either non-existent or much smoothed over. The combat aspects have definitely improved over time: gotta love that machine gun at 100+ mph. The spirit of Road Rash is alive and well!

Home is a very simple and fun indie horror game that isn't scary in the usual sense. Its not graphics-intensive, and the gameplay isn't very intricate either. Its strengths, however, lie within its superb narrative and the sense of dread and foreboding that occur as you progress through. The objective of the story is to find your way home, after waking up in a house that isn't yours, while uncovering some disturbing and haunting secrets along the way. Its easily played through in at least a half-hour, but the replayability comes from multiple endings based on how much you explore and what choices you make with key items and events. There's a surprising amount of hate on this game, but to me, this seems likely because people are comparing it to something its not. Its not Slender, its not Amnesia, and its not intended to be. Go play those if you want a more intricate horror game, but Home holds its own as a title that brings something different and unique to the table.

A short but well crafted Visual Novel, from presentation, to the art, to the music. It fires on all cylinders, tells the story it wants to tell, and does so without overstaying its welcome, without ostentatiousness, without leaving you feeling short.
It's a tale about a dying world brought about by our own self destructive tendencies, a man who survives by ekeing out an existence robbing tomb cities guarded by autonomous machines of death, and his encounter with a lone android abandoned in a planetarium, unable to do anything else but what she was created to do, which is simply to show you the stars.
Some may balk at the price of admission for such a short tale (My time shown is pretty much how long it'll take for one to finish the story) but I feel it is well worth it given how well crafted all the features are--It is also voiced too. If it truly is an issue, you can wait for a sale, where it'll truly be worth it if you're into visual novels with a post apocalyptic setting.
It's a melancholy tale that'll make an impression that sticks with you if nothing else.

Out of all the Assassin's Creed games this one was my favorite. This was the first of the series that truly felt like an open world to me. I spent more time working on side missions and exploration than I did the campaign by far. The characters are strong, the plot is thick, and the "feel" is legit. You can really lose yourself in this title.
There is one particular twist in the beginning of the game that really started the story off on a great foot. I wont spoil anything, but impressing a player right off the bat truly sets an awesome tone.
Since this game finally brings the series home to America, I finally took an interest in the historical side of Assassins Creed. For the first time, I actually enjoyed looking in to the finite details and reveling in our nations past. Being able to relate to some of the locations throughout the game and most of the events made every action feel more significant for me.
If you like Assassins Creed this game will not dissapoint. If your new, this one is going to break you in nicely but you really should spend some time with the prior titles to appreciate the story. I would be concerned for new players because the underlying plot involving Desmond Miles is going to feel extremely cheesy without the proper background.

As with other Assassin Creed games, the gameplay was pretty fun but is honestly nothing new compared to older games. Combat still mainly consists of the standard hit and dodge. Perhaps the weakest point of the game is the story, events were just too predictable and boring. There really was a lot of potential here that Ubisoft missed out on unfortunately. However, I really enjoyed playing as Haytham Kenway's character, though I cannot say the same about Connor's two dimensional character. If you're looking to play one of the newer Assassin's Creed games, you should put your money into Black Flag or Syndicate instead.

A calm and relaxing atmosphere makes this game somewhat unique in it's survival genre. The colourful world and artstyle help with that, so even when the game is treating you unfair, won't let you find ressources to tend to your wounds, repair your boat or when you are starving, when you are "fighting" wolves, it still doesn't stressful to do.
The gameplay consists of the main character and her dog, who helps with inventory space and finding ressources, travelling down the river and stopping from time to time to explore the (randomly generated?) places along the shore. You unlock new crafting recipes by finding new items, you level up your boat and repair it and always keep checking your survival stats, so far so standard. You will encounter hostile wildlife and without any means to fight you have to rely on traps, your running/dodging skills or tactics such as luring different predators together. Quests and some NPCs spice things up occasionally but the focus is on the journey.
The charm of The Flame in the Flood is the soothing atmosphere and a relatable main character. She doesn't speak much and without story there is not much of a character there but the nonverbal communication is enough: Seeing her crawl on the boat when wounded and you're back from looking for bandages but found only a wolf, shiver in the cold or duck in the rain, throwing her torch to the dog when departing a camp, it's the little things like that.
Overall this game is (as I said many times before) about the atmosphere and the experience of survival in a rather colorful, almost peaceful world. It's probably not a game to play for hours straight, but something you pick from your library from time to time, when you want to have fun in the evening.

FIVE NIGHTS AT FREDDY'S 4 REVIEW
First off, it has taken me forever to beat this game. Not because it was impossible, but because I've been incredibly busy. I honestly have to say that I really like this game. The obvious camera-checking mechanic is gone, and in turn has yet again changed the game entirely. That's the thing about the FNAF games. No one game is the same. They aren't cheap remakes, they're each innovative and change how the game is played in their own way. The FNAF series in my opinion really picked up around the third installment. In that game, there was less randomly-generated stuff and more skill-required gameplay. THAT is what the game needed. In the first two games, there was frankly too much random-generated BS that would kill you when it's not even your fault. In FNAF4, you have to rely entirely on learning sound cues and knowing where to go at the right time. You have to adapt to a new kind of game. You aren't overwhelmed with keeping up with things, you just have to listen and act adequately. This is a hard game. I mean that when I say it, I died many times on the first night. Granted that's because I still had to learn how it works, but it's no joke. All the way up until the game mixes things up on Night 5. You defend yourself against one animatronic, as opposed to four (hearkening back to FNAF3). You get so used to hearing certain audio cues, then realizing that "Hey, that's not normal,". You check outside your door and see something you've never seen before, and immediately die. Night 5 changes, even while you play. You're constantly learning new things and adapting to them. Not to even get started on Night 6 (which I beat) and Nightmare (which I did not). Scott receives a lot of hate for putting out the games too fast, but that's just how he is. He works exceptionally hard, and he outdoes himself. He makes good games. Overall, it's a good game. The story to be uncovered is intriguing, and the gameplay has nearly been perfected. It's a horror game, but one you can have fun and enjoy yourself with. I recommend giving it a try.

The club can feel like a racing game at times, due to the linear hallways and courtyards you are lead through, and much like a racing game, you will have to re-run each level to perfect your score.
A GFWL download fix is necessary to get this game to load up.

After that, I recommend lowereing the mouse sensitivity, as the aiming feels twitchy at default.  I would also switcing the aspect ratio from 4:3 to 16:9.  Resolution support is surprisingly good.
The Club is one of those off-beat SEGA releases, so it might not be for everyone.  Overall, I would recomend The Club if it is on sale.  It's fun, and will run smooth on a moderate PC. Punch Club is a fairly streamlined time management sim where you control the "Hero" as he tries to avenge his father's death by becoming a boxing champion. Gameplay consists of managing your time between work (which provides money), exercise (which buffs your stats), sleep, social interactions, and boxing matches. In fights you select a set of abilities for your character to use with the option to change tactics after each round, and then the fighters punch each other until one gets knocked out. It's simple enough to understand and fairly hands off, but the game as a whole has more depth (not a ton, but still enough) than the above description would lead one to believe.
There are three primary build paths- strenght, endurance, agility- that affect how your character fights and what stats he wants to buff during workouts. Hybrid builds are possible and pretty much necessary, so there's actually a decent amount of character customization and flexibility. I play through with an agility path/partial stamina hybrid, I've played a strength path who maintained some agility as well as stamina, and both options seemed equally viable.
The plot of the game is a pastiche of classic boxing and action movie cliches- Never Back Down, Rocky, Fight Club, Ninja Turtles, and much much more. The various plotlines and side quests keep the mood of the game light, although it seems a little inconsistent at times. For most of the game your character is on railroads as far as the plot goes, but there's more player agency than you'd expect. There's usually only one way to explore/solve side quests, but there's enough of them that you don't feel pressured to complete every one. There's a major decision about halfway through the game that pretty dramatically changes how the endgame plays out, which is a nice touch for added replayability.
I didn't have any crashes, the visuals and the soundtrack had a nice retro feel to them, although the soundtrack did get a little repetitive at times. The meat of the game (at least in repeated playthroughs) is optimization, but there's enough of a story to explore that even a playthrough on the easiest mode where fights are a breeze can offer something. On the whole Punch Club is a cute little boxing sim that offers a little more than what appears on the surface.

From the creators of Project Gotham Racing. They bring quite an unorthodox video game.
It's a game that your main focus is achieving the highest score rather than progressing through any form of plot. Except the characters' brief backstory, and an ending in the same shortness of earlier fighting games.
8 skilled killers have been taken into an organization called 'The Club'. Whether they wanted to be in it or not. They fight in several tournaments of ultraviolence to reclaim their freedom or what they desire.
Each contestant has unique attributes to them.  How fast they move, how much damage they can take, and how much damage they dish out. It allows for some experimenting to see who can rack the best chains of kills quick as possible in various events regarding survival, moving through the level at a quick pace, or sustain damage better when health is scarce.
If you like score attacking video games, just killing your foes stylishly and quick as possible. This game is for you.
If you want plot or deep storyline. Don't expect it in this game.

In this game, you play as Jack Boyd, a middle-aged Chief of Police that has 180 days till he has to retire, and for reasons which you will tragically come to learn, has to earn $500,000 before the dateline. Due to this time limit, you will be pressured into engaging in the numerous illicit activities that the game offers: from selling the drugs and weapons you confiscate to the mafia for a personal profit, to using your authority as chief to send officers out to perform illegal activities, to even killing your own officers for some reason or another. You will have to toe the line with your own morality to decide what or what not to do, and the game gives you a refreshing opportunity to make your own moral choices as a person with power in the safe space of a video game.
If you enjoyed "Papers, Please", this is a must-try. It's certainly much longer than Papers, Please, and it has a gameplay loop that is well implemented and engaging throughout.
PROS:
+Engaging Story that will keep you engaged and keep on playing to find out what happens next
+Good Gameplay that has you role-play which officers to dispatch and how you resolve crimes in progress
+Excellent Soundtrack with a variety of offerings
+Music Menu is very intiguing. Love the flavor.
+Events are written up very well, where so far every crime that popped up in my 33 hours playthrough was unique and interesting to read.
+Investigations are genuinely intriguing and fun to solve.
Meh:
~Serviceable Graphics Style that might be attractive to some but offer a lack of detail and effort to others. Check Screenshots to see if you are intigued
~Core Gameplay loop is unable to sustain entertainment throughout the 30+ hours of playtime I played. It is excellent at the start and whenever you are introduced to new game mechanics, but after 20 or so hours of the same routine, I got bored, and the only thing that kept me going was the good story.
~Voice Acting was only great in particularly the Player/Protagonist Jack Boyd. Many of the other Voice Actors were complete trash and did not suit the character.
CONS:
