My experience with
at this point, after finishing the campaign, is more then satisfying. I was hooked almost from the get go, and the core gameplay just got me addicted on defending(offending?) law in Freeburg.
You are a chief of police in Freeburg. You are in charge of everything that is going on in your police force, while you have to deal with mafia bosses, mayor office, various other people who not always got best intentions for you.
Basically a solid management game with great story.
Game mechanics are not really hardest to grasp. All you need to do, is click on ongoing crime pop-up pick some adequate cops for the job and roll with it. Or solve cases with your detectives that are these little puzzles, you need to piece together. You are also need to fulfilling tasks from various people, or you don't have to, but be aware of consequences that might come to haunt you later.
It is kinda
, what might fend off some people, but if you dive deeeeeeeep into role playing, you are up for a grandiose ride.
Technically its not something spectacular, but it's fulfilling its purpose.
The comic booky sequences are nice, voice over is great. Choices of music were just soothing to my ears, and make it look like, you are buying a vinyl/cassettes/CDs that you put into a player was really nice touch. Visuals of the town replica you operate in, and the UI are good, nice and clean, easy to orientate in - but to be honest few things could be done differently in terms of UI.
My biggest gripe with gameplay is definitely professionalism points.
I don't think having just +5/+10 and -5/-10 is good enough scale for something like this.
My reasoning behind this is, when you send a cop to do something easy (arrest a kid who broke a window) he will get same amount of points as doing some harder jobs (bank robbery). Also failing jobs isn't fair as well. You go to a crime scene suspect will run away -10 points; you going to a crime scene suspect will run, kill someone in the process -10 points - when you starting thinking about it, it just doesn't make a lot of sense. Or when you send them to a event just to find out, nothing was happening there just a fake out, I still think you should get at least those five points that you even bother to come there and check out the situation.
I think due to the nature of these events being scripted to some extent, it could be done little bit better. I'm not a programmer or anything like that, so I don't know how hard would be implement more fair pointing system, but if it would be done right it could only help the product adding more depth into the gameplay; and also the role playing aspect as well.
With that said I think it would even more helped in sandbox mode.
I was quite excited for sandbox mode, because when I finished story, I just wanted to play more as a chief of police and creating my own stories, and nonsense like this in my head and fantasies.
What kinda bugs me is that, same events are happening couple of times in span of few days, so basically you already encountered this event two days before so you know ho to approach it; and it is shown mostly in "fake" calls. Those should be from time to time more dangerous to not underestimate them to keep me more on the edge, so I wouldn't get to comfortable dismissing those events. But in the grand scheme of things, that sandbox can get pretty rough, it is maybe a good thing .... I don't know ... I'm little bit 50/50 on this one.
But sandbox overall is really fun to play, even with the strong RNG there.
My love interest of this game is for sure and undoubtedly campaign and the story that is told there.
Oh my god, I can't express how much I enjoyed following Jack Boyd and everything that was happening to him.
It was exciting, dramatic, funny, interesting, intense, sometimes just stale ordinary work days, it felt like a TV show - a good one. I wish this would be picked up by a HBO/AMC/ FX and made into three seasons, 10 episode each police drama. I was so invested in it, I couldn't get enough of it.
Yes, I'm aware that some people doesn't share my passion for the story.
Some say that choices doesn't really matter in this game - yeah not really, but I'm fine with it.
Some say the ending is far from being satisfying - no, it is perfect way to end the story.
Some say that we need more explanations to what happened with certain characters - and I'm fully on board with this one.
I think
had done enough to spike interest, and deliver a lot of fun if you are able to connect on certain wave length. This is certainly NOT a truest possible police-sim-management game, because it is mostly black or white type of scenario, with black mostly being the dominant color, where everything is bad, and you should (but you don't have to) play bad if you want to stay alive and well. I don't even think it would be possible to do so - to do perfect sim of being in police.
From what I can see, and what everyone can see (hopefully) there is so many more things in doing police work, then just read a line of text and sending someone to the world based on how many professionalism points they got. There is so many variables in real world that no game ever could fully grasp what is really happening outside our homes.
If you are the type of person who will be ♥♥♥♥♥ing about a game that let you pretend to be a police man in a fictional world with own preset rules and story, then you maybe should go and try be a one in real world, if you have this unyielding need to experience true hard police work.
In the end of the day, This Is Just a Game.

Reviewing as a Early Access : Version 20.
I would recommend this game but not for $15 in it’s current state. I expect significant and rapid changes to take place given the sudden popularity and obvious developer engagement. I would wait until the developer puts a bit more down on what the vision of the end product will be.
After playing through the game once on my own, and once in a 2-person coop, the game definitely has replay value. In its unfinished state I wouldn't pay $15 for it. I also do not see a plan put forth for where the game is going, so I wouldn’t invest on the hope that in the future the game is worth $15. I expect to get about 20 hours of game play per $10 spent, so with this game I think it would begin to feel grindy after the 5th or 6th play through and lose its charm after the 10 hour mark.
The level generation is well done, but lacks the cause/effect mechanics I would expect from a Rogue style game. Case in point, there are really only three tasks: (1) Kill someone, (2) steal something, and (3) rescue someone. Of these the solution to tasks are very straight forward and free form, but lack depth and consequence. Usually a one step approach either succeeds or fails; IE: Go in kill everyone take the safe. The map layout, door mechanic, and ownership are well done to produce a living world.
NPC’s feel alive due to their interaction with the environment and reaction to different character types. The actions of your character causes reactions and ‘problem solving’ logic in the NPC’s that caught me a few times thinking, “How’d they catch me?!” Many of the items to buy or pickup feel like they run off of a simple algorithm and are less useful than initially expected.
The multiple characters’ with differing skills and starting items is an excellent touch. The leveling system is bare bones, with little control over how the level up progresses the character. I would expect more customization in this regard as the game is flushed out.
Notes on Improvement to get me to buy the game:
1)	The levels should get more and more difficult and essentially go on forever. Sub floors, and larger structures that require a combination of hacking, brute force and manipulation to get the job done would make multiplayer significantly better.
2)	The tasks need to have more depth. An example would be;  you had to free a hacker to break into a special computer that would then open a door so you could steel an item that would be used later in the game to save a leader of the resistance force you are working with. Another example would be to free a scientist that gives you a special weapon that is needed to fight a boss.
3)	Bosses.
4)	Added character leveling depth. I would like to see maybe 20 core attributes (speed, strength, hacking skill, language, etc..) that you would get a couple points to allocate per level, plus a general point bonus based on level and type of character. If you were a soldier you may get a weapon upgrade per level, or be able to gain a skill in explosive weapons so you could use grenades more effectively.
5)	Larger map with larger field of view. It would seem reasonable for a game that allows warping in a mini-map that would allow scrolling out then ctrl-clicking on a location to jump. The minimap seems redundant. The map in general seems like it could be larger by maybe 2x.
6)	Use the idea of a greater mission to have long term tasks and short term tasks. Like bribe 20 cops and take over the district, or run a drug trafficking ring to make 1,000 gold. This sub-game then builds to a higher leveling tactic for each type of character. Like the soldier could pick up goon’s by the intimidation skill and level up his rank to general which would allow him to command the cops around later in the game.

This is the problem with roguelikes/"high difficulty" games: you have to make me want to play.
Admittedly the threshhold for the original, rogue, was not easy to surpass, it really did take hours to learn. But that had a lot to do with the way the game was built and the tech available at the time; if it's all you had you might be willing to stick with it. The accomplishments of the past notwithstanding, too many roguelikes abjure that fantastic feeling of starting out and making discoveries in manageable or random ways. I must've been playing offline because I've played longer than two hours and after several starts I never seemed to get much in the way of different resources. I got the schematic for a snare but was never able to create it. The "caches" with the quests seem to dry up right away. The raft got me into at least one pickle where I was trapped between a marina and the current being battered against the rocks with the steering "correcting" me back into the marina and, consequently, the rocks.
All this to say, I was unable to discover any fun. This game felt like a slog, the soundtrack, though peppy, did little to alleviate the boredom. Even though they say boredom can be dangerous in survival situations perhaps realism is best sacrificed for a more enriching experience.

It's just not interesting to play.
The gameplay comes down to, pick things up. Craft things. Consume things. Then try to navigate to the next area and repeat. Which sounds like a typical survival game for the most part, but in this one it just is so bare bones and uninteresting to experience. The above description is directly accurate to the gameplay, just that. In the most empty way.
The inventory and crafting system is poorly balanced. Players have barely any inventory in comparison to the amount of resources they are given even on the harder difficulty which has less resources then the standard. The inventory menu is awkward and time consuming to navigate every single time you need to do any little thing. And trying to craft anything feels like a chore not only because of the menu but because of the tree of stages you need to go through to craft it. Which again, is typical of a survival game but in this one it just feels tedious. What's even worse is because players are constantly moving to different places with different resources, if you craft something like an animal trap you have to wait to use it until you randomly find a new island with animals on it. More things clogging up your inventory, more not-gameplay.
The rafting system is a mess. Besides how arbitrary and random it is for you to just get caught in a bad spot and take mandatory damage, which is very common, the locations you can visit are biased based on where you currently are on the water in comparison to that oncoming location. If it's too far or there is debris in the way, you can't visit that location the game just spawned it in for the sake of nothing. Ignore the part where I got stuck in the geography.
Only took an hour of playing to notice repeated maps in the random generation. Played twice, died to arbitrary stuff twice, all the unique single buildings that can spawn in each of the few unique maps there are; is the same building each time per map. The church is the same church, the farm is the same farm, and after only two attempted playthroughs already noticed distinct map shapes and geography repeating. Where did the development time go in this game, the graphics look weird at best even on maximum settings, the maps have little randomization, the crafting and gameplay system itself is generic and predictable.
You can't even place down a fire wherever you want to, you have to be in specific designated locations to be allowed to do it.
Usually I play games like this for quite awhile before I type up my findings on it since Rogue-like and Survival games are a genre that often requires decent playtime for the gameplay to really come into focus. But that doesn't mean you should feel bored in the opening hours which is exactly what it felt like to play. It's just not interesting at all and I really just don't want to play anymore, the game gives me zero reason to want to.
Literally; literally, a three dimensional Don't Starve minus absolutely everything that made that game fantastic.

" The Club is Fast paced , fun and chaotic 3rd person shooter. Its all about trying to get best possible score in level. Biggest problems this game has are GFWL and Somewhat repetitive gameplay. Could still recommend for people who like old-school games and want to try something new"
General
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Club is very unique and refreshing Third-Person shooter, its not story driven game , but instead its all about the score.
You get points for each enemy you kill, depending on where you shot him, how difficult was the kill etc. You also have combo meter ticking down and each kill refreshes it and adds more combo. There are also other ways of getting combo points (shooting skull signs on the walls). So the whole point of the Game is to do stylish kills and chain them for maximum point gain. The stages also play out always the same way, requiring you to memorize enemy locations for best possible points.
There are different characters and they all have different stats (health, speed etc) , but differences are quite small and you unlock new Characters by playing Campaign.
Campaign
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Main Gamemode is Campaign, where you are taking part on these Club Bloodsport tournaments altough there isn't really much story going on here, you have AI opponents and your goal is to beat their time/score depending on the mode, sometimes you can only stay in chalked are or you will blow up, sometimes you need to reach end of level in time, but they are all essentially the same, all about score and time. This is how the campaign plays out pretty much from start to end, you have different locations where you play, prison, bunker, venezuela , factory .. etc and it brings decent enough variety to the levels. Campaign doesn't seem to be that long ,about 3-4 hrs long, without retries. But you can always try to get better time, or crank up the difficulty, which is the point of the game really.
As said, the campaign mostly plays out the same way, so it does get bit repetitive at the times, but its good in short burts
Other Modes
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
You have also freeplay mode where you can replay all these missions and try getting better time and the game also has versus mode, but atleast i didnt get it to work.
Also worth noting is that the game does still use Games for Windows Live, which means that some players might have problems launching/playing the game. I Didnt have thoes but its been reported that this might cause problems to some.
Gfwl also seems to affect said versus/multiplayer mode and you cant play online anymore
Summary
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ Fast paced, fun and hectic
+ Great level layouts
+ Varying Locations
+ Good in short bursts
- Still bit repetitive gameplay
- GFWL
- Lack of Different gamemodes

An intriguing, slow, minimalist and moody horror game. You wake up in a strange house next to a body, you want to go home.
At only an hour or so long you can play the game in a single sitting, which the game suggests. Whilst the game is linear (to be expected for an 'adventure' game) you actually have some amount of input in the final outcome. The clues you find and the way you choose to interpret them has some bearing on how the story ends.
The interaction is fairly minimal, but it felt effective as I played, choosing whether or not to disturb a body, touch a murder weapon, peek into someones drawer or take a discarded photograph. The art style leaves the environments sketchy, with good use of sound and text building immersion. In fact, sound is a very key part of the game and heightens the experience considerably.
Whilst the game is generally quite slow, the atmosphere is well achieved and there is a feeling of mystery and elements of dread throughout. You feel like you're stumbling over questions and possibly answers as you explore, gaining insight into what has happened.
If you do commit to playing the game, do it one sitting, play it with headphones on, in the dark, as the game suggests. Interact with everything you can, watch for clues in the environment, listen carefully and try to piece the story together. At the end you'll shape the ending to reflect your take on the story.

GAME HIGHLIGHTS :
1. Retro Pixel based Style, exploration mystery solving.

Home is a experimental horror game, and when they say "experimental," they mean it.  The narrative, while still falling into some of the more traditional tropes of the genre, throws the user a very mean curveball toward the end of the game, and I'm about to spoil the heck out of it, so turn away if you don't like spoilers.
Actually, I'm going to do the exact opposite of spoil the ending, because that is  the same thing the developers did.  The spoiler is that the game never spoils anything.  Nothing is ever revealed.  Was there a monster?  Was there a serial killer?  Were YOU the serial killer?  Did you kill your wife?  Did you even HAVE a wife?  Was it all in your head?  The games gimmick is that YOU, the user, get to figure out the story, and there is no wrong answer.  After the game is completed, you are prompted to go to the games website and input your own interpretation.
While a cute idea, it didn't really work for me, and took me out of the "scared" mindset.  That, on top of the fact that the game itself isn't that scary (You cannot actually die) made me really unimpressed with the game.  The gameplay was one-dimensional, and the story played out like a choose-your-own adventure novel.  I'm just not really sure that style of storytelling works in the horror genre.

It’s been a while since I played a gritty game about cops, so This Is the Police really hit the spot. L.A. Noire is still my favorite video game of all time, so I knew pretty much what to expect from the noir subgenre even if This Is the Police is at least partly, a police station simulator. Now that’s something you don’t play daily. Developer Weappy Studio’s first Steam project and I have to appreciate their attempt to simulate a topic that few PC titles approached so far.
To call This Is the Police a story-driven experience seems more like an understatement. Along with the soundtrack which I shall detail further below, the story is the game’s strongest point. Ironically the weak points are also drawn from its narrative thread. I shall do my best to avoid any spoilers since you need to find most of the subplots yourself while playing. Noir subgenre means first and foremost, a story about flawed characters in an equally flawed environment. In our case, city-wide corruption. Freeburg seems like a small-scale carbon copy of Gotham City. With morally questionable city officials, it’s no surprise that the Freeburg Police Department shall have its share of the taint.
Our journey begins on the day Police Chief Jack Boyd finds about “his resignation” during a press conference. Freeburg’s shady Mayor Rogers wishes to install one of his cronies in Boyd’s place and get rid of our seemingly incorruptible protagonist. Boyd may be the perfect stereotype of the aging police officer with his own assortment of vices and dysfunctional family, yet so far he avoided taking bribes or following through on amoral orders from his superiors. This is sadly about to change and you have to accept that This Is the Police won’t let you take the Serpico path of unrelenting justice. To understand how rare an incorruptible cop might have been in the 1970s media, see Al Pacino’s 1973 classic, Serpico. The action in the title I’m reviewing today might be estimated to have taken place in the 1980s, judging by the cars and prevalence of vinyls and turntables.
What’s important to understand in Jack Boyd’s shifting behavior is that he only has 180 days remaining in office before he gets forcibly retired from the police force and curiously, he has so far gathered no amount at all in his pension fund, despite the fact that he’s 60 years old. Jack drives a jalopy, has a modest house and often clashes with his corrupt superiors from City Hall and even some subordinates from his police station. So the chess pieces have been set in motion: six months to amass half a million dollars for Jack’s apparently carefree retirement. If you think that you can earn that much through honest cop work, you missed the point of the game. I guess in the end, This Is the Police wants to see how far will players go in their quest to earn an insame amount of cash (as far as civil servants are concerned, at least) in such a limited time frame. The salary won’t cut it, that’s a certainty.
I mentioned above that you can’t reach far without getting your hands dirty. That is sadly true and I am not particularly fond of being offered just the illusion of gameplay or storyline choices. Being a hardworking and completely honest police chief and refusing to cooperate with the city’s thugs, shall get you whacked by the local mafia in less than two weeks of in-game time. On the other hand being rotten to the core and helping them out all the time, may result in a quick illicit profit, but the State attorney general and Internal Affairs shall put you behind bars in about a month. Getting killed or incarcerated spells “Game Over” in both cases, naturally.
So you have to alternate between the good cop/bad cop routine as if you’re suffering from Multiple Personality Disorder. Boyd musn’t follow the corrupt mayor to the letter,  but he has to assist or turn a blind eye to the criminal activity on some occasions and also keep his staff happy while splitting the loot with them. Not the kind of police chief I was expecting to simulate, to be frank. Don’t give me black & white options if you know grey is the only way to complete the game.
This Is the Police is made with Unity Engine assets and has opted for a mix between the minimalist and comic book visual styles. It’s pure 2D rendering along with skippable cutscences and no graphical elements that might put a strain even on older GPUs. I experienced no bugs or glitches and obviously, no problems running it at a stable frame rate and 4K resolution.

No gritty cop tale is complete without smooth jazz playing in the background. Couple that with some very convincing voice acting and you have a video game that successfully manages to endear or antagonize by case, the title’s rich cast of characters. The OST needs to be included separately on Steam, in my opinion. It reminded me of Boardwalk Empire and its sharply dressed and equally corrupt officials of Atlantic City. Freeburg draws inspiration from many gangster-infested cities. At least the music was great back then.  Here’s a sample of This Is the Police’s soundtrack:

Storyline intertwines perfectly with the gameplay so I’ll try to write over here, what’s been left out on the Story section of the review. You might be tempted to compare This Is the Police with a board game since it offers you the interface of Freeburg’s map and deployable cards for the patrolmen under your direct control. You need to send out either policemen/policewomen to daily cases & emergencies or detectives for the more sensitive operations involving gang warfare and organization. The fact that you have to collaborate with so many corrupt individuals does take a toll on your overall performance and ability to rid the city of offenders and suspects.
Your subordinates work in two shifts, alternating daily. Yet some of those lazy and/or drunkard cops might find even the most outlandish reason to skip work for a day or two. It’s up to you to reign them in and also request from the City Hall more employment slots. The more officers you have at your disposal for various tasks, the better the chances to right at least a few of Freeburg’s many wrongs. In a darkly humorous manner, the prosecution team breathing down your neck (meant to be the incorruptible faction in the game) seems to harm justice as well by always trying to reduce your work force. Fire half my team, guys. That’s gonna do the city a whole lot of good!
The game is fully worth its price tag and offers the Steam Auxiliaries that any collector desires. As for a conclusion, I consider myself to be more pragmatic than cynical yet my version of cynicism doesn’t seek out victory at any and all costs. L.A. Noire’s Detective Cole Phelps may be deeply flawed yet he stays true to his convictions and chosen profession: upholding the law. This Is the Police’s Chief Boyd? He burns as many bridges as he has to, in search for his damned retirement fund. It’s still blood money, Jack.

After playing it for over 500 Hours and reaching level cap in 4 classes I can give a somewhat valid review of this game.
-Story 7/10
The story is not bad IMO, but the questing is somewhat average and kinda ruins it, most quests are "go to X part to recollect X herb or rock" or "go kill X mob X times" which takes off a bit of immersion, but not many follow the main quests because everyone sticks to dungeons because A) They give more Exp B) You get good gear and C) It's more fun.
-Combat 9000/10
PVE:  This is true action combat, if you don't dodge you get obliterated by literally everything, the games puts you in a position where you need to be looking around to see what the boss will do next and what you need to do to avoid it, every hit feels so satisfying.
PVP In this game is actually really nice like PVE it keeps you on your toes to see what your opponent is going to do next, Corsairs is really nice and if you're a sorcerer or a gunner you're going to be an unstopabble killing machine (unless, you know, your team is wank), Corsairs involves actual strategies and formations which are always 2:3:2 or 3:4:3.
-Classes 11/10
You can be a Panda.
-Animation Quality and Sound 9/10
Animation wise the game is gorgeous, but the lack of optimization makes a lot of players lower settings and not many get to enjoy it, but it's really beautiful, the scenary is so crisp and the mob quality and skins are realistic. The textures are consistent through out the game. I didn't give it a 10 because i found some sound glitches along the way Mostly when I Was playing Warrior and Reaper but for most of it the sound quality was really nice.
-Performance 3/10
This is where the game loses it's shine and glory, the game is poorly optimized you can have the most OP 50000$ Computer and it can run 20 FPS, In crowded areas (Velika I'm looking at you) I got as low as 10 FPS, In raids like Akeron's Inferno I would get unstable framerate, sometimes it was around 50-60 and then it would drop to 20 or 10 FPS, This is sad really such a beautifull rendered game but awful performance.
-Enjoyment 8/10
The game never really bored me until i started questing near lvl 58, if you dungeon you'll reach level cap in a few days but it will feel repetitive and grindy which makes it a bit boring, I personally would recommend doing quests, if you go through the main story you'll reach level cap without the need of doing sidequests (Something they changed a while back) , It will be a long tedious process but it's rewarding and you'll get to explore every inch of the world, something that you won't do if you dungeon all the way up.
-Overall 7.5/10
This game is really nice, beautiful graphics and textures, REAL ACTION COMBAT, nice questing (lvl 60-65 questing is enjoyable), it has really nice classes which all work really nice and each have ridiculously overpowered moves, especially Gunners, Reapers, and Slayers. It's really easy to get to level cap if you dungeon which may be good to some people but bad for others, so why did i give it a 7.5? Well, blame Optimization, i would have given it a 9 if it wasn't poorly optimized. But still great game.
Would I recommend it? YES
Would I be a Panda Again? Without a doubt.
Would I rush ladders again? Nah, I'll stick to the tank.

Most of the time, randomly generated instances will provide no solutions besides bruteforcing your way through, making some classes (*ahem* thief *ahem*) completely useless.

A shame, since the classes are fun, seemingly broken, but quite manageable. The vast array of weapons is fun, and the flavor text is fun to read (at times).
Some of the most amusement I got out of this was when I was shooting ghostbuster lasers at ghosts to unlock the werewolf, breaking gravestones to unlock the vampire, dumping myself to 10 health so I can banana suicide to unlock the comedian.
The unique and nonsensical ways to die are what makes this. Unfortunately it loses its charm when you start noticing a method in the madness.
Maybe this flaw will be fixed in future updates, but after almost 8 hours, it's become unplayable.
It is seriously fun, with so many ways to play the game and solve the random objectives. A friend is recommended.

I recieved the first game for free from ubisoft, and was surprised by just how good the story actually was, it was linear, unique, and utterly unpredictable. The second game however was nothing like the first one. The missions basically play like Grand theft Autoand are basically the exact same missions oever and over again, until you eventual reach the ending you were expecting to reach after the first 3-4 missions. No true clear resolution, no sense of accomplishment or wonder, and no reason to feel like it was even worth playing.
The first games missions may have been a bit repedative but the story line itself was interesting enough that that could be easily over looked. The second game however does not benefit from the same advantage, the story is broken into missions which each have around 3 to 5 seperate parts, without giving any spoilers away, each mission is basically the same, just in different places.
Character wise the first game was great, you play as aiden pearce, a hacker out for revenge for the death of his neice, who has attained the repeutation of "The Vigilante" for stopping crime throughtout chicago. Throughout the whole agme you are introduced to unique and interestign characters whos fate seemed meaningful in the end. The second game you play as marcus, who befriends a bunch of hipsters, each unique enough however the game never gives you any reason to like or care about most of them.
Which brings me to the cars. With the cars I do not even know where to begin, I am a ford guy who also favors lamboghini over ferrari, so naturally a game with NOTHING but chevy's and chryslers, fills me with a disgust I cannot quite put into words. There is one lamborghini and there is an astin martin and I think a jaguar, so I have a few cars I can tolerate, but driving over all is pretty dissapointing. the first game was the same way actually so I guess I did not expect any better.
Story wise the game is not worth the light of day, however online play, world exploration, and sandbox activities are undoubtably better. Online play is worth playing for a few hours every now and then, and the map is worth exploring in between missions. I however did not play much of anything other than the story, and am not a very fair judge when it comes to anything else.
In clonclusion, if you are thinking about buying this game, I would highly recomend waiting for it to be on sale. 20-30 dollars seems fair since the world is pretty big, and there is atleast 20-30 hours of gameplay.

Anyone who lives in the San Francisco Bay Area will feel right at home in Watch Dogs 2. The important landmarks are there, even odd intersections that may only stand out to residents. But I don't think you need to be familiar with the real Bay Area to appreciate how Watch Dogs 2's mix of nature and urban sprawl makes for a picturesque, playful open world. Its people and places are colorful and over the top, kind of like the real thing.
Sneaking around guards requires critical thought and precise action, but the more you play, the more you discover ways to work around the heaviest hitters and enemy AI in general.
There's no shortage of wacky quests to break things up and offer light-hearted goals, such as rescuing a Tom Cruise-like celebrity from the clutches of a cult.
Even when playing solo, Watch Dogs 2 remains a fun, energetic game filled with possibilities.
Watch Dogs 2's world is a step up from the first game's dreary rendition of Chicago, and even though Watch Dogs 2 can't go toe-to-toe with genre heavyweights, it's hard to walk away from its fun-loving attitude and exuberant cast.

Scott Cawthon is an expert when it comes to making enough changes to keep a game fresh, while still leaving enough of the ground work that made the original a masterpiece.
Interface and scenario aside, this game feels the most akin to the original Five Nights. It is just you against the four monsters who have the run of the building, and the only way to beat them is to survive. Be sure to be prepared for more than a few deaths, as the rules and mechanics can only be truely understood by trial and error. In between levels, players are treated to small glimpses of the story through 8-bit style minigames. While the game is challenging, the difficulty never reaches that rage-inducing-chaos level that Five Nights 2 was known for (at least through the main plotline).
While still yet to complete night 5, I believe this game diserves a spot amongst its predecessors. Biggest complaint so far is that the creature-sounds are just recycled Springtrap shrieks from FNAF 3.

I'll make this quick.
The Flame in the Flood takes place in a post-apocalyptic American society, where everything's flooded.
You have simple survival mechanics which are easy to fulfill after you've managed to get basic tools. If you're frugal enough, you won't have much of an issue after 2 hours.
You'll be using a raft for around 50% of the game, going down the linear river. It's full of dangers and obstacles and while it can be annoying and difficult at times, careful players will most likely never destroy their raft.
The game can get monotonous after a couple of hours, but there are two main things that should keep you motivated. Those are the soundtrack and the overall artstyle. Going down a river with thematic country music playing with the water sound effects is amazing, but adding the colourful world and beautiful setpieces makes this game an awesome experience.
In conclusion.
If you want a serious survival game, then this isn't for you.
If you want an interesting concept with servicable gameplay and an amazing visual and auditory setpieces, then most definitely get this.
This isn't a survival game, it's a survival experience.
Overall:
8/10

DISCLAIMER: This review is based upon experiences in endless mode. There is a campaign mode with a "Survivor" difficulty mode you can select. I will explain my feelings about this in the negatives section of this review.
I'm gonna be honest I really wanted to love this game and mark it as another gem in my library, but the negatives outway the positives too much. So first lets give this game credit where it's due and start off with the positives.
The good:
The soundtrack. Just about every user review here will tell you the same thing, "This game's soundtrack is amazing, beautiful, gorgeous!" And it is. The wonderful country atmosphere of Flame in the Flood is brought to life with the upbeat fast-paced music as you're traveling down the river through a ruined land or exploring your current stop on your trek of survival.
The graphics and art-style. This game looks gorgeous, props to whoever created this wonderful eye-candy. The lighting makes you the world feel desolate at times and alive at others. Shelters look abandoned and the river looks either calm and floaty or fast and ferocious. Animations are pretty good too, but nothing particularly special.
The bad:
The gameplay. Personally I feel pretty mixed on this, but really it's more about repetitiveness of the survival in this game. Basically your usual game of endless or campaign starts out like this: Pick up all items on starting point, start down the river with your first taste of the rapids and how it feels to control on the river, stop at every possible pit stop you can to gather important resources such as flint, saplings, cattails, etc, spend your first night in a shelter or under the stars, kill rabbits you found, poison meat, supply yourself with food from farms with as much corn as possible for ash cakes, kill wolf with poisoned meat, make more poisoned meat and repeat process. Eventually you will begin to gather enough resources to upgrade your raft, make better tools, craft better clothing, make a bow to ward off predators, kill a bear! But that's when you begin to realize the simplicity of the game. Once you have everything, which doesn't take long, you start to just repeat the process of making spike traps to kill boars, wolves, and bears and navigating through the river without taking damage becomes a breeze with the motor on your raft as if it weren't already easy enough. Bears are the most dangerous enemy in the game... until you realize you can setup three spike traps in front of their cave, shoot them with one arrow and have them run into your traps and instantly die. Pretty much all survival games have a boring late game, but Flame in the Flood's late game happens too fast because of how easily exploitable the mechanics in this game are. I see some of the reviewers here talking about challenge and exciting gameplay, but you can exploit the "safe zone" at the start of an island to be rid of any threats in your way. Progression in this game is too quick and the difficulty is faulty ESPECIALLY when RNG is in your favor at the start. Food is almost never a problem, in fact during my endless run I hunted so many animals that I had entire stacks of cooked meat rotting because of how much you can find. Water isn't hard either as you start out with a safety net in the form of a water filter with 3 uses as if it didn't already rain enough to supply you forever and if you're really unlucky with rain it's extremely easy to craft water filters.
Replayability. A staple of survival games with endless modes this game seriously lacks with it's repetitive nature and quick progression system. There are plenty of locations in this game, though only a few become relavent to you with how easy this game can turn out to be. The characters you meet are not great in number and do little for you, making meeting them in a different playthrough the same as last time.
Difficulty. I pretty much already critiqued this in my "Gameplay" section, but I'm gonna write down the finer details in a list here. The only real "danger" to the player character, known as Scout, are wolves. They are the only animal that attacks you for existing. Boars only attack you for entering their territory of the location you are at and are easy to bait into spike traps by setting them just outside of their aggro bubble and making them chase you only to stupidly run straight into the trap and die. Bears are the exact same as boars the only difference being that they require 2 more spike traps to kill and a bow and arrow to aggro and cause damage. Bears disappointed me, because of what little threat they pose to the player. Afflictions are a joke. The only threat they pose is early on and that's if you get extremely unlucky with loot. Now I did see a "Survivor" difficulty option for campaign mode, which I didn't play through as I only played through endless mode. Now for whatever reason, this difficulty isn't an option for endless, though if you decide to play campaign instead of endless I highly recommend choosing this harder difficulty as the game is just far too easy to overcome it's obstacles in it's current state.
Overall: Now I really wanted this game to be good. I got it when it was in early access, because it did look really good. Well, now that it's out of EA I'm going to criticise it as a completed product and to tell it plainly I was disappointed. This game had so much potential yet fell so short from the finish line. My final verdict for The Flame in the Flood is a 5/10.
It's not amazing, but it's not horrible. I recommend getting this game through Humble Bundle or buying it on sale when you have money to spare. If you want a true survival game with realistic elements and you're looking to spend your money now, I would rather suggest The Long Dark. If you want something more wacky and casual go out and buy Don't Starve with the RoG DLC and SW if it's on sale. Both of these games exemplify what a survival game should strive to be; a true test of your wits and skill with the highest of stakes being your life. Now something I really plead the devs to add to Flame in the Flood are more hazards, difficulty settings for endless, and slowed down progression so you don't complete the game in a day. I thought I was going to run into a form of raiders or bandits at the industrial region, but there were just more boars and wolves, nothing special just usual procedure. I think this game can still be good and fun, but it feels more like a "rainy day" kind of game for when you're bored.
If you have anything to add or criticise about my review, I encourage you to rate and comment so I can improve my critique of games and offer better formed opinions for fellow gamers. I hope this helps you and have a good night.

First off, for people new to the genre, this is a kinetic novel, meaning there are no choices, no paths. It's just text and images and music, and it tells a beautiful and bittersweet story.
It follows two characters from the moment they meet. One, a "junker", a man who braves autonomous military robot infested ruins in search of valuable relics of an earlier age. The other, a servant robot, tasked with running an old planetarium, who's been faithfully waiting for thirty years for the return of co-workers and customers that no longer exist in this post-apocalyptic world.
What's really brilliant is how well the writers conveyed the lonliness of an artificial intelligence that was designed to serve human beings. Her behavior patters clearly indicate a desperate need to interact with people, even as her possible behavior's are limited. Lonliness, even anguish, are portrayed through the juxtaposition of various pre-programmed behaviors. It was as heart-wrencing as it was brilliant.
Won over in spite of himself, the junker attempts to repair the projector so she can run another planetarium show. Does he succeed? What happens after? To go any further would be to spoil the story beyond what is reasonable.
A word on whether or not the ending is happy or sad, since that seems to matter to some people.

For anyone who likes CLANNAD, Air or Angel Beats! they will enjoy this kinetic visual novel.  Put it on autoplay and sit back to read. (Since I read all three of those manga and have watched the anime, plus "know" the types of stories Key puts out, I knew what I was getting into even before I bought this "game".  Let us just say I knew what type of ending this would have before I started, and bought it anyway.)
Storyline: A Junker (a scavenger, really) on a future post apocalytic Earth accidently (and quite possibly by fate) runs across a non-lethal still functioning companion robot named Hoshino Yumeni.  Yumeni is the caretaker of a department store planetarium. (I am sure the word, planetarian, in the title is simply a misspelling.)  Still performing her duties as greeter and narrator, Yumeni greets 'Mr. Customer' formally and politely.  She offers to show him a special presentation of "the starry sky", a sky which in reality is covered with perpetually falling toxic rain.  There in that forgotten planetarium in the middle of a biologically contaminated and abandoned lethal 'Sarcophagus City' patrolled by murderous mechanized war machines these two share a reverie (a daydream) of a once and "future" world.
Excellent story, and have a box of tissue handy.

So I picked this little game on sale, knowing it was from Key. And in case you don't know, this studio likes to literally ♥♥♥♥ with your feels. So I knew what I was going into.
So, what is this game? This is a kinect visual novel, that means it literally is a book with pictures, music and voice acting. In most VN you can choose your own ending by making choices that affect it. Here, it is just like normal book: one plot line from the beggining to the end.
What is the story? It is about man, imply called "Jumker", who once visits planetarium, where lonely robot, called Hoshino Yumemi, wants to show your stars, but unfortunetely, the projector is broken. I believe that is all you need to know about this game. I was certainly suprised how grimm this story is and even more of its setting. I highly recommend you to NOT read the summary and/or tags, I think it kinda ruins the whole suprise thing. But why? Because the story is so touching that you should experience the bad things as you play, not before you even start. At least that is how I look at it.
I can't really say much about the story because I would just spoil it. Let's move on chacters. There are only two. The main protagonist, "Junker" (yeah, we don't get to know his name) and Hoshino Yumemi. Junker is your solitary protagonist, minding his own bussines. Yumemi is the polar opposite. Robots in this world are programmed to serve and obey humans. She cares about our hero only because her software is telling her so. Oh, and she is very, but very talkative. Even though Yumemi is robot and is behaving like one, there is no way you won't think of her as a human for at least one time. And that is truly something. We are constantly reminded that she is indeed robot, both by her actions, dialog and by narrator. And yet, I could not help myself but think of her as a human. It was not her character sprite, it was the writing that has done so. And I did not even notice it. There was a perfect balance between reminding us that she is just a robot and making her feel so human. It was just incredibly well made. The sprite, the voice acting, the dialog, everything worked.
The chemistry bewtween these two is also quite noticible, especially near the end. I did not believe that all was Yumemi was doing for Junker was because her software told her so. I just didn't. And I think that was the point. I think it is amazing that they managed in less the 5 hours make robot feel more human then our main character and everybody else in the world.
And speaking or writing, you could just rip it out of this game, paste it on paper and nobody would really notice that this was at first VN. Unlike some other VNs at Steam, this is a huge achievemnt. That is not to say rest of it is completely unnecessary.
I can say like 10 words in Japanese so I have no right to judge the voice acting. Yes, this novel is fully voice acted, even MC got his own voice actor. But VA of Yumemi was just joy to listen to. Her voice felt robotic and human at the same time. Junker does not really talk much with the exception of the ending. But he gives of that "lone wolf" vibe, if it makes sense. Nonetheless, they were both very entertaining.
The art in this game is great. Yumemi's design is just gorgeous, you can see for yourself in the pics above. The overall art really helps the atmosphere. However, one issue I have with the look of this game is its layout. I don't understand why they thought making the background one small imagine and putting it on the top of the screan and filling the rest with some random gears while putting the text into the box at the bottom was a good idea. It feels odd, especially since Yumemi covers the entire right part of the screen and it does not really add to anything in my opinion. Some images cover almost the entire screen too, that looked great, I don't know why they made almost the entire game like that. *SPOILER FREE REVIEW!*
There's a lot of debate as to whether the price of this visual novel is justified, considering its length, so here's an attempt to set it straight.  Warning: if you have a heart, you will enjoy this adventure regardless of the price!
Key is renowned for producing emotional VNs that tug on the heartstrings, supported by a good soundtrack, striking visuals and memorable characters that will stick with you long after you stop playing.  I can say that Planetarian fulfils all of those criteria in different ways.  There's just one difference: it's very short.  I'm quite an avid reader and can take a lot of narrative without a break, so I completed Planetarian in one 3 hour sitting.  I didn't race through it though; I paused for reflection and to enjoy the story at points.  However, if you're a slower reader or would prefer to enjoy the story in smaller bouts, you'll get more mileage out of it.
Considering the VN itself, I'm not going to lie - my immediate impression was 'oh, this is the VN Key put out as filler between bigger projects'.  The fonts are a little glitchy to read in places.  The visuals were slightly too pixellated on full screen mode - I had to switch to windowed to gain clarity.  And the soundtrack, for the most part, wasn't massively memorable, though it contributed to the atmosphere.  Sounds like a list of faults that make this VN probably not worth it, right?  That's not quite the whole story.
Despite my original doubts about Planetarian, the more I read, I found myself getting sucked into the story at a rapid pace and becoming attached to its characters, of which there are few, but that just makes those who appear all that more compelling.  I won't mention plot points in case of spoilers, but the more your choiceless story moves uncontrollably towards a both heartbreaking and affirming end you knew might come, the more you feel.  There are no choices to make.  There is nothing you can do to affect the story.  You can't stop what's inevitably going to happen...  but when you reach that ending and consider the short journey you took to get there, you really feel things.  The fragility of the human world.  The stupidity power can inspire.  The beauty hidden within the things that are right there in front of your eyes...  yes, it's more like paying for a movie ticket rather than buying an interactive game, but I can promise you that you will feel things that will make you forget that ticket price.
Okay, yes, it's probably a good idea to wait until this VN is on sale to make you feel a bit better about it...  but in all honesty, Planetarian began in my mind as a potential mistake, and turned into something I truly enjoyed and don't regret spending a single penny of that price for.  It was truly touching, like an anime you didn't expect to make you cry at the end...  oh, did I mention you might cry?  Yeah, it's a possibility.  I TOTALLY didn't , of course.  *cough*
Summary:  Begins in a way that doesn't promise much, but within five minutes, sucks you in and delivers a heartfelt, honest and moving little tale you'll be glad to experience.  Nice visuals, with lots of movement in the CGs, which is rare for VNs at times - gives you a break from static sprites on static backgrounds.  Soundtrack appears rather average until you're hit with the beautiful vocal-laden dream of a song at the end.
Only real drawback?  You might start Googling around for the nearest planetarium when you're done.

This is the Police is a game about Jack Boyd, Freeburg Police chief.
He is 60 an 3 months away from a forced retirement.
The game is like a cartoon kinda thing, but way more grim and dark, almost like a film noir.
But first things first: the Soundtrack is amazing and very fitting!
Like something from a♥♥♥♥♥♥Tracy novel or the first Max Payne.
The main part of the game is managing your Police force, taking calls, sending out units, lead investigation.
And this is kinda dull but there is always some condition to it, it has highs and lows but it is a Desk-Job being Police chief.
All this is interrupted by cartoon segments which drives the story forward.
And the story is brilliant, not superb but it really got me.
In the Act 1 you start to understand how everything works, who everybody is, what Jacks motivation is and Jacks goal.
And just when you understand what it take to achieve that goal, everything changes.
Act 2 is filled with some sort of hope. Things start to work out, go the right way and Jack gets some allies.
And all of a sudden, there is a sense of: "this could just end well." and the moment you get comfy with it, all comes crashing down on Jack.
In Act 3, hope is gone, the grim reality of politics and intrigue kicks in. And in all this, you have to figure out a way to achieve Jacks goal.
In the end it is still Jacks Story, not the one the player imagined to play.
Jack knows more than the Player, the player is too naive, because games teach us, that there is some sort of a good ending.
But Jacks story is not like that.

You have 180 days left until your retirement as a chief police, and you have the full power of the police force and you decide everything in the police station.
This game is exactly what you would expect based on the videos you see, you have a variety of options and choices that will lead to different circumstances, which may or may not affect your gameplay until the end.
If you don't like reading a lot, listening and watching to cut scenes a lot, and only care about the gameplay and not the plot, then you shouldn't buy this game, otherwise you would find this game addicting,
The story mode of the game lasts long, and you can play it again if you want to chase down the achievemt and see what happens if you go with different choices, get different endings, perhaps with different results.
Pros:
-This game is a time killer, you may rarely get bored of it and it is addicting
-Freedom of choices
-Entertaining plots
-Long story mode
-The songs are something to look into, there are many songs you can choose from, some of them are decent, some of them are good, but some of them are really good and relaxing, depends on what genres you like, but most of the songs  are jazz.
===
Cons:
-You may get bored if you hate reading, lots of reading, but sometimes there aren't lots of reading
-Perhaps it is something the game needs to change for the best, if a day gets screwed and something bad happens, anyone can restart it and start the day again, this may eliminate the fun, and I myself do it, I can't really control my frustration when it comes to certain situations
-Just like any other game, people can easily cheat online to get the answers to certain mysteries, investigations are perhaps one of the most entertaining part of the game, mainly because it requires you to use your imaginations, but ofcourse if someone gets stuck at something most likely they would seek help online, which also eliminates the fun
-Some people may find this game overpriced
Overall, you can easily cheat in this game but you will still be able to enjoy the most aspects of the game.
I do recommend this game.

Now to tell people why this game doesn't take place in 1987. "Of course, your gonna use the commercial argument!" Actually, no. Even before I discovered that commercial, I knew that there were story elements from other games that prevent this game from taking place in 1987. Here are the facts. (spoilers for all games ahead)
First, it's to note that it never says in-game when the game takes place. People assume 1987 because an animatronic bites a child. As such, don't assume 1987 automatically. Secondly, we need to know the timeline of the restaurants. FNAF4 comes first during Fredbear's Family Diner, second is the first Freddy Fazbear's Pizzaria (which no game has taken place), third is the 2nd Pizzaria in FNAF2, fourth is the 3rd Pizzaria in FNAF1, and lastly Fazbear's Fright in FNAF3. The only game with a confirmed date is FNAF2, which is in 1987. So, if FNAF4 is also in 1987, then there would be three different restaurants existing in one year, which is ridiculous. And remember, the 2nd Pizzaria was only open for 2 weeks. But, we are here for hard evidence, not an argument against something ridiculous.
1. Passage of Time
On Night 5 of FNAF2, Phone Guy says
"Uh, I think the name of the original restaurant was... 'Fredbear's Family Diner' or something like that. It's been closed for years though, I doubt we'll be able to track anyone down."
So, Fredbear's Family Diner had been closed for YEARS before FNAF2, making it impossible for it to be in 1987.
2. Moving Animatronics
The first message we ever get says
"Uh, they used to be allowed to walk around during the day too. But then there was The Bite of '87. Yeah. I-It's amazing that the human body can live without the frontal lobe, you know?"
So, after the Bite, the animatronics weren't allowed to move around. So, if the Bite of 87 was at Fredbear's Diner, then the animatronics shouldn't be able to move around afterwards, right? Well, not according to Phone Guy on Night 1 of FNAF2.
"They've spent a small fortune on these new animatronics, uh, facial recognition, advanced mobility, they even let them walk around during the day. Isn't that neat?"
Even so, in the Foxy minigame (which takes place at the 1st Pizzaria, since Pirate's Cove doesn't look like the one in FNAF1) it shows Foxy being able to move around during shows as he is running on stage. And when you think about it, it's ridiculous to blame the Bite on Fredbear in FNAF4 when it wasn't even his fault. The 4th game shows a bunch of teens putting a little kid inside Fredbear's mouth, making it their fault, not Fredbear's. Plus, Fredbear wasn't even moving around.
3. Position of the Child
Look at the bite in FNAF4. It doesn't look like his frontal lobe is being bitten off. The child's position makes it seem that his head is being crushed, not just his frontal lobe.
4. What Happens To Dreams
The Game Theorist made a point proving that, scientifically, if someone loses their frontal lobe, they wouldn't even have nightmares. They would instead have happy dreams.
There you go. I didn't even have to use the commercial to prove it. The only reason people look to the 1983 in the commercial for the date is because it's the only date ever shown that makes sense, not because it's randomly there. So, hopefully this taught you information you didn't know.
I will also answer any questions you guys have.
Edit:
So, there is confusion on whether or not FNAF4 takes place at Fredbear's or Freddy Fazbear's Pizza.
The FNAF3 minigame (which is confirmed to be the first, thanks to Phone Guy) is NOT the one we see in FNAF4. While similar in design, look at the hat of the bear. The minigame's hat is brown and Fredbear's hat is purple.
Secondly, the main antagonist of FNAF4 is Fredbear, which puts him as the most important.
Lastly, poromotion everywhere for the restaurant refers to Fredbear, NOT Freddy. Why else would the commercial say "FREDBEAR and Friends"?

Streets of Rogue is an engaging roguelike where you traverse different, city-like, generated dungeons and complete objectives for upgrades, new weapons and level progression. The game provides different ways to tackle objeectives, compounds and situations with friends or by yourself. With that in mind, get ready to use the Endless mutagen after completing what little there is in the standard game at the moment.
While I find the game to be fun for the schenanigans that occur when playing with friends and the Mario Party-esque friend loss that will occur depending on a player's choices, the game still has some work to do. So, here are my gripes and feedback for the game:
1. Issues with the gamepad
When playing the game on a gamepad, I experienced issues where action menus sometimes disappeared and the camera locked into place. This is an issue because some actions are outside of your character's inate traits and skills. For instance, the hacker has a ranged hacking move. While others do not have this special move, there are items that allow for remote hacking. This is an issue when you may only have one chance to hack a distant computer and end up losing that chance thanks to the menu disappearing. My guess is that the game has issues with understanding when the mouse is not in use.
2. Bar Blocks
Sometimes when dealing with vendors and retailers in the game, the person you are talking to will ask you drop an item or cancel out your shop menu in other ways. I understand if a building a block away explodes and the seller wants to check it out; however, when they ask me to drop an accuracy mod again and again by canceling out the menu, it becomes annoying.
3. Progression Traits
Please remember, I understand this is in early access and more should be coming down the road. That being said, some of the progression traits for each level may not benefit your character. Cherry picking a scenario and using self-reference criteria here: I did not find the early skill traits when playing as the Doctor to be useful towards my gameplay. Having extra crit hits and the ability to identify syringes does not help me when I am playing as a pacifist character that can already identify syringes. While a trait like increasing followers and the ability to not trip lasers and floor traps seems great alternatives, I hardly found any use in them when playing as this character.
4. Seed Generators (Feature Creep)
It may not be out yet and may even be the greatest thing ever for the game depending on how the community uses it. That being said, this is more of a cautionary: watchout for feature creep. This isn't  a negative, just a reminder that the community is here and some want to work with the developers by helping the game become better through feedback and opportunities. Sometimes those opportunities may not be what the community really wants or needs, but what the loudest group desires.
TL;DR
Streets of Rogue is an engaging rougelike in early development stages. There may be issues with the game, such as minor blocks and progression issues here and there; however, the game does a great job at combining multiple elements into a fun experience for you and your friends. Warning: you may lose friends depending on your playstyle.

What's better than shooting people? Running and shooting them at the same time! Welcome to the Club!
The Club is 3rd person action packed shooter focusing heavily on run and gun gameplay. I have never seen game that would focus on run and gun as much as this game in single player mode. Whole game is designed around combo system. If you kill a guy, you get x points (depends on where you hit him, and which type of enemy you kill, as well as distance from which kill is scored). If you kill another one before your combo ends, you get 2x more points, and then 3x. The higher combo, the faster "downtime" (time before combo ends). So yeah, if you don't like to kill fast and move a lot, this game is probably not for you.
Otherwise game is well optimized from performance point of view. However menus are very sad, they are designed for gamepads, and if you have one you should really use them in menus instead of mouse and keyboard. Also there's no way as far as I'm aware, to change FOV, which is not very high (I think it's around 60).
Another sad thing is, that they designed split screen, but removed it in PC version. There's online multiplayer, but not active anymore. But you can still play it if you get a couple friends in the game, it's a lot of fun in my option.
Game is using Games for Windows Live. Yes dat DRM. 98% of people play this game only for single player, and that's why I think you shouldn't worry about GFWL as you can:
a) create offline account and just play without MS account
b) install xlive which removes GFWL, and lets you enjoy the game without DRM
There's no coop, but there's gunplay. Gunplay is gamemode designed to be played against friends. You basicily select maps, and weapon you want to use in that level, and try to get as many points as possible. Then your friend plays, and his goal is to score more points than you. This mode can be played with up to 4 players, and it's fully compatible with X360 gamepads, so if you have 2 or more, you can each play with your own gamepad.

I enjoyed The Flame in the Flood for around 2 hours and then it was k. The game is not bad the production value is actually quite good. I liked the artstyle, the SFX and the music is top notch. The introduction to the various gameplay elements is well done and the tutorial short and interactive.
What keeps me from playing is the repetitive gameplay and the fact that every single island later in the game has so many enemies on them and so little ways to defend oneself. What starts out as a pretty chill resource management game with some exploration turns out to be another one of these instadeath rogue-lites with clunky combat. And combat is bad, sometimes enemies are hidden behind objects, you can not change the camera. You have exactly two ways to defend yourself, one being placing a trap and the other is shooting arrows.
If you can survive depends a lot on being lucky to find an island with the right objects which is not riddled with tough enemies as well. You can influence your luck by choosing the right island to land on but sometimes RNGesus is cruel. I would have enjoyed the game more if it would have expanded on weather and natural hazards more rather than throwing more and tougher enemies at you. So many games just do combat better and in this game it just feels like a cop-out to cover up the lack of deeper gameplay mechanics. The premise is a post-apocalytic earth. You can do more with that.
Overall the 15€ price tag is a bit much for the content The Flame in the Flood provides. If you are intrigued by the artstyle and the overall feel presented in the trailer I would recommend to buy this game in a sale. If you are looking for a survival game to spend more than a couple of hours on I would recommend to get Don't Starve instead. Both games share a lot of concepts but I think Don't Starve executes them better in the end and offers just more content overall.

I'm not sure if this is a bug, or if the devs for some reason decided to make these deaths random. All it does is cause confusion. Just give me a clear threshold for failure en dont put it behind RNG.
In the case where the death IS consistent though, the game only keeps saves from once every ingame week, so often you'll find yourself being set back by an entire week (over an hour of gameplay), having to redo way too much of the game. I've resorted to manually making backups of the saves after every day to avoid this problem.
This is my main problem with this game, the random confusing deaths (also the ones that happen to your staff, like I send my two best officers to a child stealing another child's candy stick, and somehow one of the officers gets killed???), and the large setback in the case your death isn't random.
There are other issues that disconnect this game from IRL, like "why do I need to send an officer to this unique assignment NOW, and not 1 second from now when my officers get back to the station" or "why can i not go back and pick a different frame for this serial murder investigation, did my investagors really already burn them? :/ " or "These officers on their way back from a crime will drive past another crime, why can't I send them to deal with it/why can't I send officers on patrol". These can be bothersome sometimes, but I can accept these as logical gameplay decisions, whereas saving only once every hour and a half and having death be behind a Random Number Generator are game design decisions I cannot wrap my head around.
Still recommend playing, as the game is very fun regardless, but don't expect an immersive experience.

4/10, will look like 7.5/10 for the first two hours (and then the content drought begins).
STRONG NO on this one, do NOT buy this game. It is dreadfully underwhelming, and the kicker is that till the first two hours you're still being impressed by the flashy animations and new features being added, so you'll expect the game continues to innovate thereafter. It doesn't.
The game becomes extremely boring and grindy as hell, just redo-ing the same dispatches over and over. You basically have to spin three plates - town hall, police force, and mafia - without letting any one of them get too annoyed at you.
Town hall will randomly say - fire all blacks/old people/hire asians/hire women arbitrarily, without any other context and if you try to FIND who's Asian/Old/other variable, there's no way. Heck in a few cases a few of the girls looked like guys and there's no way to find out whether the person you're firing is a girl or a guy because no where does it offer a fact card for your people. It's clumsy as hell.
You can not play good cop either, because the mafia will outright kill you with hardly any warning, so that path's out as well, so much for variety. Mafia missions pop up, saying 'don't interfere with my crime in exchange for money' and that's that.
I don't really know what keeps my police force happy other than sending them on BBQs on my own money and the random event.
The game does a TERRIBLE TERRIBLE job of giving feedback. Each officer visit is resolved as Perp Caught/Escaped, Officers Killed/Alive, Civilians Killed/Alive, Loot Not found/found. This is a pathetic way to explain consequences, and I'll give an example to show why - You're dispatched to talk down a suicidal man who has two kids with him on a bridge. This is an 'involved' event where the game will offer you one of three choices to swing the event's outcome. If you 'empathise with him' and then ask him to 'think of the kids' what's the payoff? Perp escaped, officers Ok. WHAT DOES THAT MEAN? Did the man jump? Did my officers let him walk away so he wouldn't harm his kids? This is infuriating, and expect this same problem to happen in EVERY. SINGLE. EVENT. You just NEVER get any closure.
Investigations are a bit more fun, solving each one is a puzzle, and to its credit there are perhaps one hundred puzzles so there's a slight amount of replayability. The act of getting puzzle pieces is extremely rote - assign detective/s to a case, and at the end of the day they'll gather a few more frames if there are any left. It's another faceless system, and what's worse is that the game never tells you that there are idle detectives lying around, you have to go INTO the menu, choose a case, and then see if any detectives are free. This is just pathetically lazy design.
The game's also slow as hell, every new day you'll be shown the same unskippable car start animation (if I were him, with all the money I'm hoarding the least I would do is repair the car!), and are forced to choose a music record to play, which is lazily mounted on a gramophone. It's very cool the first time, infuriatingly boring the 179th time.  There's no speed up button on the screen proper, so just expect to wait around for 30 seconds or more for something to happen. Painful.
When officers are dispatched and later return, their availability is shown in a MMO Cooldown anim over their face-card. If they'd just added a timer (Returning in 5 seconds), it'd have been so much easier on the brain.
After seeing how rote the game had become by the 4th hour I applied for a refund with most of the above points mentioned, and was denied. Please do not make my mistake, this game is not worth your time or money. Oh, and that sandbox mode? Only available after being a bad cop and completing the game once. They couldn't even put that in from the start.

I do kinda like it. It's got an impressive breadth of content in some areas, but seriously lacks in others. Specifically, there are dozens of consumables, tools, buffs, weapons, and even character classes. There's an insane number of ways you can approach most mission objectives... provided you're actually afforded the opportunity to do so, which, this being a randomly generated roguelike-like, you often aren't.
Example: You need to loot a safe or detonate a generator in the back room of a shop staffed by an armed owner and two hired goons. The back room lacks any access points besides the door from the main room. There are no computers, no vents, nothing in the area you can use to your advantage. You're playing as a thief, which ironically further limits your available options as all shop owners will accost you on sight even if you're behaving yourself. You COULD use a blink tool to phase into the back room through the outer wall, do your thing, and use another blink tool to get back out -- but now you're down TWO of those precious and often irreplaceable tools for one dumb mission. Short of that, your only real recourse is to brute force your way in through the front... through three armed guards, as a thief. Good luck with that one, champ.
It's really nice when through whatever oddball combination of RNG elements you ARE given the opportunity to MacGyver your way through an objective. Unfortunately, all too often you just don't have that sort of opportunity no matter HOW you play your cards with what you're given. Loot from containers is an absolute crapshoot (spend a hack tool and a lockpick getting at a treasure chest and it has $3 inside; examine a trash can outside and find $13 and a sandwich), and utilities cost way too much given how quickly you have to burn through them and how slowly you get money.
I also can't figure out how to access online co-op for the life of me.

Streets of Rogue is an engaging roguelike where you traverse different, city-like, generated dungeons and complete objectives for upgrades, new weapons and level progression. The game provides different ways to tackle objeectives, compounds and situations with friends or by yourself. With that in mind, get ready to use the Endless mutagen after completing what little there is in the standard game at the moment.
While I find the game to be fun for the schenanigans that occur when playing with friends and the Mario Party-esque friend loss that will occur depending on a player's choices, the game still has some work to do. So, here are my gripes and feedback for the game:
1. Issues with the gamepad
When playing the game on a gamepad, I experienced issues where action menus sometimes disappeared and the camera locked into place. This is an issue because some actions are outside of your character's inate traits and skills. For instance, the hacker has a ranged hacking move. While others do not have this special move, there are items that allow for remote hacking. This is an issue when you may only have one chance to hack a distant computer and end up losing that chance thanks to the menu disappearing. My guess is that the game has issues with understanding when the mouse is not in use.
2. Bar Blocks
Sometimes when dealing with vendors and retailers in the game, the person you are talking to will ask you drop an item or cancel out your shop menu in other ways. I understand if a building a block away explodes and the seller wants to check it out; however, when they ask me to drop an accuracy mod again and again by canceling out the menu, it becomes annoying.
3. Progression Traits
Please remember, I understand this is in early access and more should be coming down the road. That being said, some of the progression traits for each level may not benefit your character. Cherry picking a scenario and using self-reference criteria here: I did not find the early skill traits when playing as the Doctor to be useful towards my gameplay. Having extra crit hits and the ability to identify syringes does not help me when I am playing as a pacifist character that can already identify syringes. While a trait like increasing followers and the ability to not trip lasers and floor traps seems great alternatives, I hardly found any use in them when playing as this character.
4. Seed Generators (Feature Creep)
It may not be out yet and may even be the greatest thing ever for the game depending on how the community uses it. That being said, this is more of a cautionary: watchout for feature creep. This isn't  a negative, just a reminder that the community is here and some want to work with the developers by helping the game become better through feedback and opportunities. Sometimes those opportunities may not be what the community really wants or needs, but what the loudest group desires.
TL;DR
Streets of Rogue is an engaging rougelike in early development stages. There may be issues with the game, such as minor blocks and progression issues here and there; however, the game does a great job at combining multiple elements into a fun experience for you and your friends. Warning: you may lose friends depending on your playstyle.

The Club is, in a nutshell, Battle Royale meets the 100 Meter Dash.  It's a third-person shooter where the point is to run from point A to point B as fast as possible while staying alive and killing as many enemies as skillfully as possible along the way.

The Club is one of those games that you'll randomally find in a $5 cheap bin at gamestop, buy it because your bored, then find out it's actually ♥♥♥♥ing awesome. Not even partially looked at its released, this is a hidden gem. Anyone who's played Tony Hawk Pro Skater will enjoy the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this game. Reason why? It shares almost the same exact score system, just instead of doing tricks to get combos, you get kills! Every single round played is around 2, 3, to 5 minutes long, so it feels like an arcade game right inside your home. (It's perfect timing for listening to hardcore pump up music too)
The weapons/shooting are extremely satisfying to use, while the gameplay is your addicting, "Well... JUST ONE MORE ROUND" type. It's a unique combination  put together extremely well. Totally give this game a look. If the $15 price tag is to much for you, check it out on Amazon. I heard it was $2.50 with free shipping from a friend not to long ago.
