Assassin's Creed III involves a new gameplay mechanic different from its predecessors. The new counter system and enemies' reaction are revamped. The combat are somewhat more difficult at first, but is very easy when you already mastered it and know the type of enemies you'd face. The freerun technique also differs slightly and includes new animations. The graphics of the game is great, one of the best in its time. Also, there are lots of new weapons in the game, ranging from muskets, tomahawks, pivot hidden blades, gun stocks, rope darts, flintlocks, etc. The game is by far one of the most brutal in the series; expect to see more blood and combat in the game. Fists also have new combat mechanics and are deadlier than ever. For the story, it is told in a fun way and will put you in twists and expectations.
Pros:
-New Combat System (Counter, Enemy Type, etc.)
-New Animations (Brutal Combat, Freerun, etc.)
-Weapons and Tools (Guns, Rope Darts, etc.)
-Story
-Graphics
-Side Missions and Contents (Lots of Them)
-Pivot Hidden Blades
-Assassinations using ANY TYPE of Weapon
-Present Day Missions
-Crafting (Items, Pouches, Custom Weapons, etc.)
-Map Area (Frontier)
-Naval Combat
Cons:
-Some Bugs (not Game Crashers)
-Uplay Integration (Might be a difficulty on some occasions)
-Plain Present Day Resolution
-Lack of Optimizations in some part of Map (Boston Mostly)
-Some Lags and Frame Rate Issues (not hardware problem)

Tera is a free to play mmorpg with an action packed gameplay style. As a person who loved World of Warcraft and played hours and hours of the game I was pretty stumped to find I could no longer pay the fee that came with playing the game and I soon left before the Warlords expansion came out. I'm a totally huge mmorpg fan so of course I went to see if I could find a game to fill the void that WoW had left in me. I had stumbled upon Tera due to my sister's recommendation. I went ahead and created a Tera account and soon made my own character.
I played through the Fate of Arvun beginning area and I did become frustrated due to the one boss you had to kill for a quest and almost every player stood there waiting. In some servers there was an actual line for the boss which I found quite odd due to the many people I have seen who would rather stir up havoc then order in a mmorpg. Unfortunetly the starter area has been revamped but it has been revamped in a good way. I felt glad that I could create an alt and not have to worry about that one quest. Tera is a free to play game so of course they are going to make items which will drive you to the cash shop. Things like costumes, mounts, and pets. I found it really frustrating and wanted a costume so bad but didn't allow myself to buy one. Tera's gameplay is very fun. It was a refreshing feeling after using the tab targetting system for so long. You could actually dodge abilities which makes both PvE and PvP very fun. Although most of the classes are really fun to play there a few which are more of a "spacebar" class. In which you simply click your mouse then spam the space bar. The classes I found this to be true were the gunner,reaper and ninja. They are suppose to be "combos" but I find that these combos make the class boring and stupidly over powered to the point where playing these cool looking classes just felt boring. I find that the Elin race has attracted a lot of attention from the anime community. Other YouTubers as well attracted the anime community. I do find this to be quite frustrating due to the fact that half of Tera's population is mostly made of Elins. And as far as I see it Elins should mostly be played as support not as a warrior or some kind of tank. Of course Elins can play ninjas and reapers due to the fact they are race locked to the Elins but it is extemely annoying to play with a full party of ninjas. As a player who mains the support class I found it very annoying when the ninja classes came out. There would be four ninjas and then the healer which was me. Don't get me wrong ninjas are a great source of dps but as tanks they are nowhere near that. Ninjas are very squishy and when I had to play with four different ninjas in one dungeon group healing became very difficult for me. Ninjas actually can dodge very well and I thought that healing wouldn't be that bad but I was very wrong. These players were very very unskilled. They could not dodge at all. Even if I remove the debuffs they could not dodge.
I also find that the ninja classes along with the brawler,gunner, and reaper were overpowered. Even though the classes are a bit bad I find the art style of Tera is be absolutely gorgeous. In areas with forests and water it is very beautiful. The character creation is very detailed and allows many players to create an unique look. Overall I would recommend this game to anyone who loves mmorpgs or have used to play WoW

Spoiler Free Review ( In case anyone was worried. )
Overall I really enjoyed this game. The dialogue is great as is the character development ( with some exceptions I'll get to later) and the voice acting is pretty solid. The soundtrack is also a huge plus and the whole noir atmosphere is great. Your character is well put together and relatable, he isn't perfect but at the end of the day he's just trying to do right by everyone even if he can't always manage it. The positions you are put into seem entirely plausible and really draw you into the story. There are some issues I do have with this game though. Such as the detectives finding the right frames for you to put together. This is entirely dumb luck whether or not they find the right ones quickly or take the most time possible and to my knowledge they can only find three per day so this gets particularly frustrating with the larger cases.
On to my biggest issue though. As I said the character development is generally great especially with Jack Boyd as you really start to feel for him and his struggles. The flaws come in as the game is coming to a close. Two fairly important characters who we had seen a decent amount of during the game suddenly drop off and there's no real resolution with them. They simply disappear and that's that. It left the ending feeling a little empty like it could have some more to it. The ending as well to be quite honest is nothing special. As you play through the game you can probably gather that Boyd is in a bad situation and he doesn't have a lot of options but this ending felt very limited. Once again however this game was incredibly enjoyable and the story really drew me in immediately as I had to know more about this universe and I do recommend this game for anyone who enjoys story driven games, but I would also recommend you grab it during a sale.
Thanks for reading and I hope my review helps!

Well.... I got what I paid for. This was thoroughly uninspired and underwhelming.
But, I do have a few praises to sing:
The interface and camera controls are fairly similar to Starcraft, and that makes it at least pleasurable to play. I didn't fight the interface too much.
It's relatively easy to tell what is what. At least it didn't look cluttered and overly complex, and the graphics are actually fine for an RTS. It's source though, so not a huge surprise there.
And... that's about all it has going for it.
The economic design is fairly lackluster. There are resources, but it takes minimal effort to get them, so you really can get a fully saturated economy going quite quickly. This leads to problem 2: Macro is BORING. There's just not much to do, and there's no flood of resources feeling that you get from say, 5 base Zerg in Starcraft Broodwar.
Okay, not every game has to be simcity on steroids, but what about the tactics? Well, they're boring too. Infantry are fairly identical, and so early game play is just boring and 1 dimensional. Units beyond that might be somewhat interesting, but given how limited the economy is, you can't make many of them. And to make matters even worse, there's barely any tech tree at all.
Overall, it feels like I'm not architecting any grand strategies, employing finessed micro, or exploiting the terrain and tactical advantages to win a match. I just feel like I'm doing the most basic routine and pressing attack-move and going to sleep. I don't feel engaged. I don't have fun using the units. I don't like the game.
Bah, what did I expect?
But, maybe if these guys got a real designer to sit down and actually architect a meaningful game flow, it'd be pretty good. I mean, they put all this effort into building a fairly decent RTS client for the source engine. That's kind of awesome.
Until then, I'll be uninstalling.

Road Redemption reminds me of a PS2 era game, and to me, this is a good thing. It might not have the flashiest graphics, or the best overall polish, but what it is manages to be very fun & engaging in short & long bursts. It focuses on one thing & does it well: Driving very very fast, and killing all of your adversaries.
The gameplay takes the Road Rash idea of motorcycle racing with lead pipes & steps it up. Several melee weapons, explosives & guns all work fluidly while speeding along. The combat with these weapons takes just the right amount of skill to pull off, always giving you many options to fight or flee. And being able to shove other riders makes you take the environment into play.
With plenty of unlockables, this game gives you even more reasons to play past the initial thrill of racing-combat. The rogue-lite campaign works very well thematically & gameplay wise. There's multiple goals besides racing, & your skill at the game (With a little bit of luck) determines how far you get towards your characters goal of claiming a $15 million bounty. There's even couch-coop & some online too.
The controls are rebindable, & work very well with mouse & keyboard. Because the game is pretty much built to be going full speed at all times, I've never felt the need to use a controller. There could be more graphical options, but the options it gives you are plenty & work well.
The only big negative is that it isn't as polished as a AAA game, but of course it overcomes this with charm & exhilerating gameplay. Graphics look somewhat dated, some areas of some tracks could be smoothed out so there's less to get stuck on/crash into, and some areas aren't graphically optimised as well as others (Mainly the snow areas). But the sheer amount of fun this game has for such a reasonable price is worth it.
I definitely recommend Road Redemption.

A short visual novel (~4 hours) that is equal parts beautiful and painful. The scenario:
The last remnants of humanity fighting for survival carrying out a decades old war which has wiped out the majority of life leaving nothing but an ever present acid rain to slowly erode the planet.
That is a fantastic backstory by itself, but take that and focus in on two individuals living 30 years after the aftermath, while learning about their pasts, seeing them interact, and seeing how the whole story unfolds you end up with a visual novel that is incredibly touching. Even at planetarian's corniest moments even when you know those moments are going to be there before you start the game you still can't help but smile or tear up when those moments arrive.
Two well written characters, great music, nice art, and a backstory that isn't as far fetched as it should be all come together to make a must play game for fans of VN's who aren't afraid to feel a little something once in a while.

This Is The Police is a really captivating prototype for a police simulation game, combined with an enjoyable film noir atmosphere. For the first few hours you really get into roleplaying as a police chief slowly getting thrown into a world of crime and corruption. It was fine for me, but some people may be put off by the fact that you can't really choose what kind of police chief you want to be and after a couple hours the game forces you into being a dirty cop with a pretty much instant failure if you choose to not comply with the mafia. If you can look past this shortcoming and just accept that you are crooked, you get another few hours of well written cutscenes, cases and crimes.
The game really starts to fall apart with the management aspect of your police station. You get maybe a dozen cops to start out with, all having a skill level assigned that tells you how reliable they are. The game tells you that a skill level of 150 is average, although you really can't tell what that means.
The whole affair of assigning your cops to crimes comes down to trial and error. All the feedback you get is basically wether you managed to solve the crime or not, but any feedback on WHY you may have failed or succeeded is missing. In the beginning this is fine: You get a call, fail a crime and the suspect escapes without any perceivable consequence, so you just assign more cops or a more skilled one the next time. However about 20 days into the 180 days this game spans, you start to get unavoidable and completely untelegraphed deaths among your officers, where some quests can wipe out practically your whole PD, forcing you to restart the day. It's really frustrating when you assign every available officer and even your SWAT, and still half of your level 500 officers die due to a crazed woman fumbling a gun around in her office, but a well armed gang gets arrested by 2 level 200 guys.
This would be less of a problem if you had more officers at your disposal, or maybe even just a generic "cop number" statistic instead of a few permadeath-able officers with irreplacable skilllevels.
The management just leaves me with a lot of questions: Does a single skilled cop perform better than several less skilled cops? How does the presence of SWAT influence the performance of my police officers? When do I need to upgrade the "efficiency" of my SWAT? What actions cause my officers to file a complaint against me?
I could keep going all day, but I am pretty sure the answer to all of these is: "We don't know, the random numbers generator takes care of that."
After catching your attention with an interesting atmosphere, story and game world, the game just keeps breaking your immersion over and over with completely trial and error based gameplay, which breaks my heart, since it is so close to being good. All my criticism could have been offset by a little more information about the inner workings of the game given to you, like a few statistics at the end of a mission, or maybe a small three sentences debriefing text illustrating the solution of the conflict. Were the suspects arrested? Were they killed? How did my officers accomplish that? Were the game to display this information, it would immediatly turn into a playable and enjoyable experience.

You start on a camp/farm or whatever that should be. You get your food and some other stuff and start using the raft. On the water you try to evade some obstacles and look out for symbols, that show you where you can dock to. There are four different docking symbols I have seen so far. A repair dock, wildness, abandoned farm and a fishing point. All of them seem to contain different versions, so it is not exactly the same place over and over again. So you loot most of the stuff there and fight yourself through the terrible UI to craft stuff, that doesn't really help you. Like a stone knife, that you can't use to fight or a raft frame, that isn't really necessary. Stuff like traps, weapons to fight or anything else, that you could build are not possible to build in the beginning, because you don't have the necessary ressources on the dock points. So it happens (even on the easiest difficulty), that you die of starvation or by being attacked by some boar or because you didn't have the luck to find a damn watersource, even while it was raining.
A game has to have stuff in the beginning, which makes the game interesting. The annoying dog barking, that is freaking misleading (dog barks don't mean necessarly, that there is stuff to loot), doesn't help. The music itself was pretty nice in the beginning, but after taking it for about 20 minutes it got pretty annoying. Not being able to kill a rabbit, even while standing exactly next to it and hitting, was a real bummer. The same goes for the boar, but that was okay (it's a boar, right?).
There are no voices in this game. It would be nice to have a little voice coloration. Like the fact, that you are starving or thirsty or dying. That brings me to another point. You can die on your raft thanks to starvation and thirst. The missing feature of eating or drinking, while using the raft, makes it pretty annoying, because you can't know what exactly is in front of you. So you start on the raft, thinking there will be something not far away, and in the end you die, because there was a part of the waterarea, where no docking points were.
So here are the points, that could make this game more interesting for me:
- Complete UI overhaul
- More sounds
- Possibility to fight with the stick (at least against the small animals)
- More life ambiences
- Better dog AI
It just didn't felt complete.

Watch Dogs 2 is a massive improvement in every way over the first game and what the series should have been from the start.
Watch Dogs 1 was a self-serious and gormless games focused on a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that wasn’t even actually a real hacker that the writers thought was a hero even when he was anything but. 2 on the other hand actually has a sense of humor and a real a sense of character. 2’s spirit feels like a cross between a 90’s hacker movie and Jet Set Radio.  It’s much more colorful with a really neat punk aesthetic mixed with a modern Internet meme aesthetic. This could have all easily fallen into “How do you do fellow kids?” territory, but I feel that the game has such a genuine sincerity and charm to it that it never feels cringy, just endearingly and intentionally goofy. It really helps that the characters are fun and are intentionally a bunch of goofy dorks. Marcus is the protagonist the series needed and is the polar opposite to Aiden in every way. The game’s writing is good, as mentioned the cast is likable and the plot is solid, handling topical stuff with some deftness. My only real complaint is one of the cast dies and it feels completely out of place, it’s pretty disconnected from the main plot, doesn’t fit the tone of the rest of the game, and robs the game of the interesting interactions that character had with Marcus.
Gameplaywise the game actually feels like more like the hacker sandbox game it should have been from the get go. Aiden was just a GTA character with a magic phone, but Marcus has more tech in his arsenal such as drones that really add to the stealth elements, as well as non-lethal weapons which seem far more appropriate for him to use. It’s testament to how likable Marcus is that I tried to stay in character when I played story missions for the most part, I tried to keep casualties to a minimum and rarely stole cars. (It really helps that the game lets you spawn cars you own through your phone, because Marcus really doesn’t seem the type of guy to commit grand theft auto on the regular) I just wish melee takedowns weren’t all lethal.
As the PC port goes it’s not the best optimized. I’ve had three crashes and the game freaks out whenever I alt-tabbed. It obviously wasn’t close to being a deal breaker though if you look at how much I played.
Overall Watch Dogs 2 is a real good sandbox game and what the first game should have been to begin with.

It's taken me a while to write this review. Mainly because it's hard for me to put my feelings about this game into words (also I'm lazy). I will admit it, I ♥♥♥♥ing cried at the ending. And let me tell you, I rarely cry at this sort of sentimentality.
Planetarian ~the reverie of a little planet~ is about the Junker and his meeting with Yumeni, an android left behind to care for a planetarian within an abandoned city. Everyday she does the same thing, she heads outside, even when admist acid rain, and tries forlornly to attract customers. Her one companion is Miss Jena, a broken projector. When the Junker visits the Planetarian in the hopes of loot, he encounters Yumeni, who claims he is their 2,500,000th customer. The Junker agrees to fix 'Miss Jena' in the promise of seeing their show. What follows is a tear-jerker of a VN about a robot who's only wish is for heaven to not be split between machines and humans, and a man who learns to dream of stars.
The story is set in a dystopian world, where nuclear war has left humanity in ruin and leaves the ever-present 'Rain', acid rain as a side-effect of the nuclear fallout. The few humans that survived are hunted by automated robots that act as if the world never ended, killing any human they detect. Some people act as scavengers, referred to in-universe as 'Junkers', of which the MC of Planetarian is one.
Get it. Just get it. It's a masterpiece. The soundtrack ranges from the beautiful and dreamy, to the slow and melancholic. The artists did an excellent job capturing the dystopian feel and bringing characters to life (although it is a bit dated in terms of fidelity. Keep in mind however that it was originally released in 2004). It's brilliant and worth every penny. £6.99 is well worth this title.
Congratulations Key on making me cry my eyes out.
And also, ♥♥♥♥ you for making me feel.

If the concept of grinding turns you off you will hate this game.
That being said, I quite enjoyed it. The aesthetic is nice, the complex fighting system is very malleable and customizable,  and the specialization tracks allow enough flexibility to suit any style of player.
The story, as others have noted, is fairly goofy, but provides enough cover to add some depth to the game.
I enjoyed  the soundtrack, although hearing the same track for several hours straight gets a bit grating. I get that they were going for the 80's aesthetic, and the song choice was good, but some more variety would have been a nice touch. See games like Domina, Hotline Miami, etc. for examples of this  being well done.
My main critique, without spoiling the game for anyone, is the ending. Anticlimactic doesn't even begin to describe it. And the most infuriating part is the lack of ability to keep playing after completing the story.  Why can't you continue fighting, improving your character, and winning leveled fights? Nope, it just ends, and you have no chance to go back and reload a save from before the final two 'boss fights'.
I quite liked the game, good way to spend 10 hours or so (personally finished after 8.4hr and 186 in-game days) but damn that ending was disappointing.

You will have fun when it starts and maybe a few hours after that, but once the grind gets real and stat decay gets rough, you will realize the futility in continuing. If you snag it for a buck or two, you'll get some fun out of it I guess. Otherwise, use that money towards something else. Great game, terrible grind.

This one edges into unfavorable territory for me. In Punch Club, you train a fighter to, let's just say...meet his destiny. This is done by working out to improve his endurance, strength, and agility. As you complete fights, you're also given skillpoints. These skillpoints can unlock new attacks, blocks, passive buffs, or stat upgrades. You can build your fighter to be more powerful, more agile, more defensive, or some combination of these. As you advance, you'll meet a wide variety of wacky characters who are often references, to things like Street Fighter II, Rocky, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, and real people like Hulk Hogan, Bruce Lee, and Don King. The game has a slick pixel style that's quite charming.
When I first started I was having a lot of fun - not winning every fight, but trying to create a character that was maybe a little like Anderson Silva, the MMA fighter. Then, things really began to slow...down. If you've read other Punch Club reviews, then you know what I'm about to talk about - stat decay. At the end of each day, you lose a bit of each stat (endurance, strength, and agility). Stats at high levels seem to take a bigger hit. You can mitigate this somewhat by taking certain stat upgrades with your skillpoints. However, there are some complicating factors.
First, your fighter has to eat, and must initially spend money to train in depth as well. Although one of the jobs that you have available can slowly increase a few of your stats, in general, time spent working means time not training. So I felt like I went in this cycle: I ate a bunch of food and trained hard (focusing on key stats of course), ran out of food and money, went to work and my stats decayed, then began the cycle anew. Initially, I was still making decent progress through the fighting ranks, but then I hit a standstill and was no longer progressing through the ranks. My stats were just not increasing enough. I tried to mitigate some of the decay by saving up for a Wing Chun dummy (which appeared to quickly increase agility, my main stat). However (and I can't prove this), I didn't feel as though I was gaining agility any faster than just hitting the speed bag at the gym. I also thought it might be worthwhile to fight in the game's equivalent of a UFC league, in which you can get hurt but will make more money. In the main fighting league, you can't get hurt, but also don't make very much money (at least at first). By fighting in the UFC league, I could gain skillpoints and extra money without wasting time at work. I took out my first few opponents, but then got a concussion in a loss. I'm already feeling quite ineffective in this cycle of futility, and get this: the concussion reduces how effective my training is. *sadface*
So after playacting the myth of Sisyphus, I decided to try the "Super Easy" mode, in which there is no stat decay. Immediately after choosing the mode, you're told that your playthrough is going to be unbalanced, and then you're given an extra comment about how the developer is going to "let you do this" (despite their better judgment, apparently). This tone does not set the stage for a fun time, instead making you feel like Dad's letting you stay up past your bedtime just this once. I had a decent time, this time playing a Mike Tyson-like fighter. The wild thing is that I still lost a couple fights!
I suppose that one of the developers had a lot of emotional investment in the stat decay idea, and was pretty offended when Steam users kept repeatedly trashing the mechanic. In some ways, I think the mechanic can encourage insightfulness. For instance, it is indeed harder to stay on top than it is to intially work your way through the ranks. The most prominent thought that I had during my first attempt was "holy crap I need a sponsor." So, if Punch Club is an accurate representation of what it's like to be a fighter, I now have a new appreciation for fighters who work jobs while trying to start fighting careers.
Despite my negativity, I'm looking forward to Punch Club 2. Apparently, the developer is removing the stat decay mechanic. Although I've played a game in the Fight Night series, I haven't played anything else quite like Punch Club.

Road Redemption reminds me of a PS2 era game, and to me, this is a good thing. It might not have the flashiest graphics, or the best overall polish, but what it is manages to be very fun & engaging in short & long bursts. It focuses on one thing & does it well: Driving very very fast, and killing all of your adversaries.
The gameplay takes the Road Rash idea of motorcycle racing with lead pipes & steps it up. Several melee weapons, explosives & guns all work fluidly while speeding along. The combat with these weapons takes just the right amount of skill to pull off, always giving you many options to fight or flee. And being able to shove other riders makes you take the environment into play.
With plenty of unlockables, this game gives you even more reasons to play past the initial thrill of racing-combat. The rogue-lite campaign works very well thematically & gameplay wise. There's multiple goals besides racing, & your skill at the game (With a little bit of luck) determines how far you get towards your characters goal of claiming a $15 million bounty. There's even couch-coop & some online too.
The controls are rebindable, & work very well with mouse & keyboard. Because the game is pretty much built to be going full speed at all times, I've never felt the need to use a controller. There could be more graphical options, but the options it gives you are plenty & work well.
The only big negative is that it isn't as polished as a AAA game, but of course it overcomes this with charm & exhilerating gameplay. Graphics look somewhat dated, some areas of some tracks could be smoothed out so there's less to get stuck on/crash into, and some areas aren't graphically optimised as well as others (Mainly the snow areas). But the sheer amount of fun this game has for such a reasonable price is worth it.
I definitely recommend Road Redemption.

The roads are lengthy and hilly, as if you were driving in a mountainous part of the west United States, and are somewhat randomly generated, but you will start to notice repated "parts" of a level after multiple runs. Levels tend to have 2-3 shortcuts that can help you get ahead and have powerups. Some stages will have a modifier that will cause vehicles to randomly drop from the sky for you to dodge, and/or drop pipe bombs, but unfortunately there doesn't seem to be any other "Hallucogenic Effects" or modifiers to make the game more interesting. I think the developer definitely needs to make more potential level modifiers that can apply to a level. While there are desert levels, snow levels, rooftops, and ruined city levels, the world overall looks drab and repetitve - which is somewhat fitting for a post-apocalyptic world, but nothing looks memorable and much of it is almost ugly to look at.
That said, I had a ton of fun with this game and even when I lost runs, I still enjoyed my experience. Beating and crashing enemies gave me alot of chuckles, and like most modern roguelites, you can still progress after each run due to an XP based skill tree after you win or lose the run. You also can pick upgrades and restore resources after each race with the money you earned.

Good concept. Really bad execution.
The writing is awful. One obvious example: an early crisis involves racist gangs targeting black people and you are tasked to fire all black officers as a result of their threats and public support for them. If you refuse, this is simply counted as failing the objective. This is absurd. Actual public relations and politics involved in running a police department are a fascinating and nuanced subject, but this game goes full retard in implementation. There are numerous other examples equally unsubtle as this. Also, the character is the chief of police but he regularly goes to a strip club and gets hammered *while in uniform*. I don't mind exploring the dark side of law enforcement, but the game is cartoonishly ridiculous in its depiction while having a pretentiously serious tone.
Another frustrating feature of this game is that you are forced to play as a corrupt cop and it is literally impossible to play it straight (you get a game over immediatley if you attempt this). This is just as stupid as the political dynamic of the game; you should be able to weigh integrity vs expediency, but instead the game presents the illusion of choice and you have to play dirty.
The last major criticism I have of this game is that you allocate resources based on descriptions of crimes and sometimes the outcomes are nonsensical and absurdly trivial descriptions can result in the deaths of several officers and civilians (with no explanation of why this happened whatosever). This majorly undermines the strategic element of the resource management.
EDIT - There is another particularly infuriating major flaw in this game I had not yet encountered at the time of initially writing this review: certain events require you to act within a specific timeframe or while specific officers are on shift, but the story skips certain days (and by extension shifts) without warning. This is a baffling oversight as it completely derails strategies and makes it impossible for the player to plan things out.
EDIT 2 - It also is extremely repetitive and drags on and on to advance in the story and unlock new features...I kept thinking "I am not enjoying myself but there are obviously more features that I have not progressed enough to unlock yet so I'll stick it out" only to realize I had spent a few hours going through a few weeks in game without advancing at all. Length is not necessarily a good thing with extremely dull and repetitive gameplay, but it is frustratingly padded out for no other reason than to prevent criticism about the game being too short.

This game is very unpolished and feels rushed, which is sad because it has a big potential. There's almost no story, the dialogues are something that an alien would write and the entire game is badly designed in terms of user experience (UI is mediocre, there are no descriptions of upgrades so we invest scarce resources blindly, the same can be said about armor, which by the way is not displayed on your character when you equip it). The game is beautiful, but the main character is something straight out of a horror film, she delves deep into uncanny valley with her skewed artsy but not cute at all face. And don't even get me started on endgame, which has literally nothing to offer but bears and the absence of catharsis. After some time you may just as well swim down the river instead of stopping because there's no reason to, you'll be full on items and the encounters will not be a challenge halfway into the game. And near the end the rains will be so long you'll initially find yourself spamming sleep mechanic trying to wait them over multiple times in a row. Overall, the game needs some heavy mechanical polishing, as you'll find yourself alt+f4ing in anger when you accidentally depart and find out it's impossible to re-dock.
If the above points were fixed, you'd end up with a really immersive, addictive and highly replayable game. Sadly, it's the opposite.

Let me start by saying this game at its core, is a pretty good game. I enjoyed the gameplay, visuals and characters so far. My main gripe, like many others is Ubisoft's decision to implement a layer of VMProtect which essentially turns your PC into an emulator.
I've tolerated Denuvo because despite its flaws, it always valued keeping a very low performance cost when implemented correctly, RIME is the only example I can think of that was a poor implementation that hurt performance due to have way to many triggers.
VMProtect on the other hand, is pretty much confirmed to lower performance as your essentially running a virtual machine on top of the games code and Denuvo. We know from what Denuvo has stated, that it only does its "checks" during non critical periods, such as the startup screen or a loading screen. From what has been shown in AC: Origins, VMProtect is constantly running in the game's core at all times.
I've refunded this game, which is a shame. Ubisoft's agenda in anti piracy measures once again causes them to make all the wrong decisions and hurt legit, paying customers. Although, coming from a CEO who says 95% of PC users are pirates, it doesn't surprise me they would prioritize these types of decisions.

I got this during a sale, and I frankly cannot commend this game - for disclosure I did not finish it and it's because I just found the frustration with the mechanics overcome my enjoyment of it, even when playing the optimal path.
Easily the high point of the game, they're crisp, got that feel of a mid-SNES era game and not only everything looks good - you can identify everything that can be interacted with without it sticking out like a sore thumb.
- A subjective point, and while it's clearly meant to be reference factory for fighting and boxing related pop culture from 70s-90s, it actually lets the references speak for themselves rather than think pointing it out and saying the name is enough.
I didn't get severe bugs but I ran into a few very glaring ones - there's one glitch involves two questline actions trying to run at the same time, causing overlapping sprites until you leave the area it's affected.
It's relatively minor, but when sleeping, the hero will not wake up if his rest stat maxed out, so if you're not hovering on the stats or get distracted, he won't wake up until he's starving.
For a game about a boxer climbing up the ranks, it's actually astounding how little control you have over the actual fights. You can only select what skills to bring into the fight, and hope they're a good counter to the enemy and the RNG lets you win - though on that note, the RNG is not so generous as to reward you a win if your stats are just too low - no underdog stories here.
Okay, early game, it can be very easy to get into a state where it's impossible for you to progress. Training beyond doing pushups in the garage requires money, and the trainer will only feed you so many times, and has an extremely high, if not 100% chance of firing an event where you get robbed if you're carrying over $250 in case, which is very likely if you're buying gym equipment - it's as if the game's trying to punish you for trying to optimize your workout.
Also note, if the hero's hunger and sleep stats are too low, he refuses to work or train - so if you're careless with your purchases, or are unlucky to lose the rob event, you can end up in a state where he's too exhausted or hungry to work, and unable to afford training, and thus unable to beat the matches leading - and the training is a killer because:
The Decay factor. Everyday your stat will decay, regardless if you train or not - but this decay ramps up the higher your stats are and you have to watch so it doesn't
. There's no means of slowing down or reducing the rate of decay, and if you're trying to unlock storylines or optional bosses, it makes getting any progress extremely difficult.
They try to answer this by releasing an easy mode that removes decay, but it also locks achievements and the game becomes too easy. What the company should've done is reduced the rate of decay for normal mode to about half it, and reduce the rate the decay scales to your level, so getting high stats is a reward, not a chore.
Overall, the game had a potential to be a really fun love letter to the past, but the game seems intent on punishing players trying to sink their time in. I would honestly say give this game a pass.

Ah... Punch-club. A once in a life time time opportunity to become town's boxing champion with nothing to back you but your fists... and your elbows, feet, magic amulets and Chinese Master Splinter's wise teachings.
The game is a strange mixture between a "point and click" and a fighting management game that works better than it sounds! You start as a young wanna-be martial artist in a retro environment and through training and fighting other people in legal and illegal fights you try to become the number one. Two things obviously make this game unique. First, its wacky story, filled with nostalgia moments and movie/game references that most people will immediately recognize, and its mechanics.
Mechanic wise, the game is somewhat solid. You go through a 24 hour day, managing your health, money, energy and hunger while training yourself in 3 different stats which influence how strong you are in a fight. As expected, you can work in different jobs to earn money, eat different types of food to decrease hunger and so on. Eventually, you get the chance to specialize in a fighting style which is dependent of which stat you train the most. However, these stats decay at the end of each day. The decay is of exponential growth, meaning the higher the stat is the stronger it will decay. You learn different skills from a branching skill tree depending on which fighting style you master, allowing you to create different strategies which can be surprisingly different. You have no control of fights, as they are automated. You do set your skills beforehand allowing you to create a strategy. It is a solid concept which has worked before. However, as many people complained so far, the problem with the mechanic is mainly the exponential decay. Given that the higher your stat is, the longer you need to train to get a level up and also the larger is the decay, grinding becomes very obvious, very tedious and very painful. Since training requires you to watch an animation of your character training, late game it takes too long to get anywhere and I found myself alt-tabbing multiple times in midst of training. This shouldn't ever happen in a game like this. On the very late game, I spent more time waiting than actually playing the game. The game tries to balance this by giving you a skill that makes decaying impossible below a certain level for a certain stat. But even if you have the skill points needed for such skill, you most likely will only be able to do this for 1 stat which unfortunately is not enough. This single mechanic is the sole reason why this game could be not recommended. It is THAT frustrating.
The other main aspect of the game is definitely the story, which I must admit, will not fit everyone. It is wacky and doesn't take itself seriously at all. And, in my opinion, neither should you. Authors clearly were aiming for humor and movie references so don't expect Shakespeare. It still pieces me off that the game strongly suggests you all over that you are a boxer competing in boxing and then the first skill you learn is to throw a low kick, but still. All good fun.
Art style is OK, retro, nothing new. However, music should be more variable. Since you spend too much time grinding, at least you should be able to listen to a different tune every now and then. Otherwise you're stuck with a song for 10 minutes straight. Again, it seems devs truly underestimated how grindfull their game was.
In short, although flawed, the game still deserves a playthrough at least until grinding becomes too tedious. It has an interesting concept with strange yet funny story which will provide you some laughs.

Edit: On a more serious note though, the developer(s) (I'm really not sure whether it's a small team or just one man, so excuse my ignorance please) are constantly bringing more, and more content incredibly frequently via updates to the game.
The game is a fun rogue-like experience, yet the use of being able to store your items in a HUGE chest which stay there even after death (the only things you lose upon death are the items on you at the time) makes this game a lot less frustrating than you may expect it to be, as you keep a lot of your things. A lot of people may be glad about this, while others, who are looking for a more serious rogue-like game, will probably find it too easy for a rogue-like genre of game, but my personal views on the matter are mixed. Without the chest, you would be able to replay the game from the beginning and have a different enjoyable experience every time, while it being more of a classic rogue-like game. Whereas the usage of the chest means that you can 'complete' the game ('complete' meaning get the best gear possible as there is no 'end game' per se) a lot easier than if there were no chests, meaning the game will last a lot shorter amount of time overall. However, dying does delete your character, meaning that you have to make a new one and start from level 1 again and gain all of your stats back.
The last thing I want to touch on is the fact that you are able to build your own ship... well, customise your own ship. It's a very basic, yet fun, addition to the game which allows you to make loads of cool rooms where you can add more machines or hang the badge/poster/photo things that you can receive from killing enemies - even bosses - on the walls of your ship (it's a rare drop but looks like a sort of photo of the creature in a frame which you are able to place on the walls in your ship or sell for a hefty price. Pretty neat).
The developer(s) are going in the right direction with this game and it's updates; they are always adding new weapons, armour, biomes and bosses for the user to battle - making the game a lot more fun and giving the player many more things to aim for with each update.

After finishing MGS1 earlier this week, I was craving more stealth but wanted a break before diving into MGS2. I had recently listened to an episode of Podcast Unlocked from right after the game came out and remembered that I owned it on Steam but never finished it, so I started a new game on Hard and played through it in a few days. It took me about 17 hours and I only did about half of the side quests.
Man, this game was pretty great. It's a shame it shares a name with the first game, because I feel like that really hurt its sales. This world feels much more lived in and including Silicon Valley and Oakland make the game a lot more believable and interesting than just... grey Chicago.
I think that the in-game parodies of other companies is arguably better than the way GTA does it: they aren't over the top "slapstick" ridiculous, but just exaggerated versions of themselves. Look at the Nudle campus (googleplex). It's got the slides and other fun♥♥♥♥♥♥but it's not as much a parody as a homage.
The characters were interesting, which is a nice contrast to Watch_Dogs 1's "gruff white man." I really liked Wrench by the end of the game. A character from WD1 makes an appearance as well. The game's plot does get a bit ridiculous (Why is the government not conducting an all out manhunt for Dedsec after some of these stunts, in which they kill hundreds of police officers and security contractors?) but it's all in good fun and doesn't take itself too seriously. My only real complaint with the storytelling is a questline where a supporting character is killed off in the middle of the game, but because of the way the game assigns Main Questlines to you, it doesn't have a SOLID place in the narrative. Meaning if you have a heart and start looking for him immediately when he goes missing instead of completing the current questline first, the tone gets very dark for a few missions then immediately returns to laughing, smiling and joking as if nothing had ever happened when you return to the questlines you were working on before he disappeared. I don't want to spoil anything so I'm not going to put my idea for how they could've fixed this, but his death should've been worked into a specific part of the ending and it would've made a lot more sense.
The hacking in this game feels a lot more fleshed out and I LOVED the parkour. The parkour and melee combat gave a good amount of depth to the stealth options in gameplay. My only complaint in regards to stealth is that sometimes, the entire enemy force would be alerted to your presence even if the person that saw you was killed before they could radio in. Maybe that expectation of having a realistic amount of time to kill the enemy before he radios in is just born of playing Metal Gear games lately. Still though, the stealth gameplay was very fun and made me feel like a badass.
I really want to see a third game in this franchise and see if they can keep building on this concept.

Wow.  Okay.  So, this game really is something special.  I had never heard of this, it appeared on Steam, and after one look at it, I had to try it, particularly since it was having a free weekend at the time.  2 hours of awesomeness later, and I knew I was hooked for good.
So what is this game?  Well, I can sum it up pretty easily:  A Roguelike, plus GTA, plus Deus Ex, with tons of emergent gameplay and really hilarious moments.  And depth... so much depth. Which I have to say, absolutely stunned me.  This is a game of possibilities and opportunities, and TONS of choices to make.  Perhaps the most defining aspects of the game are two things:   1, the sheer ridiculous number of options you have, in terms of things you can do, items you can use, and ways you can interact with the environment, and 2. The emergent nature of the gameplay, due to AI characters that all act on their own, creating all sorts of situations for you due to their interactions with you and the environment, and often complicating things in ways that are both unexpected and absolutely hilarious.  When you combine these two aspects of the game together, you have the potential for something truly amazing, a game with no end to the possible situations that it can create for you.   And what's more, when dealing with any situation, chances are, there's about 5000 possible ways that you can get through it, all of them fun and challenging.
At it's core, the goals of the game are pretty simple:  On each floor, you are given 2 to 3 missions.  These appear on your map screen, and there are a variety of different objectives that each mission can be comprised of.  Each floor is almost like a small town, with a variety of different buildings filled with all sorts of things, and each individual mission will always be given it's own building.  Once you've completed the required missions, you can then access the elevator that takes you to the next floor.  Each mission also gives you a variety of possible rewards, and some floors will contain a character that can offer you a totally optional mission as well.
Missions can differ wildly in how they work, even among ones of the same objective.  For instance, perhaps you have a mission to neutralize a certain character.  This character could be an important dude housed in a labyrinth of security systems, armed guards, and traps, or it could be the shopkeeper of the local store, sitting behind a desk in a very simple building with nothing but a bunch of customers in there with him, going about their own business.  Both of these situations offer up their own unique complications that you will have to deal with.  The building with all the security presents obvious problems:  cameras, laser tripwires, trap tiles, roaming guards, locked doors, all the stuff that makes a dangerous labyrinth exciting.  But that store seems kinda easy, right?  Not quite.  The question is, how can you take out the shopkeeper without getting yourself destroyed?  Sure, you COULD go in there, guns blazing, and just try to take him out quickly, but not only is he likely to defend himself with something powerful, but you risk attracting the local cops, or perhaps even one of the customers may pull out a shotgun and try to fend you off.  Perhaps stealth is the way to go... but how can you do that, with so many others in the small store?
Figuring out how to go about your goals is the biggest part of the game as a whole.  You have TONS of different items that you can find and buy, all of which are important and useful in different ways, and you can get pretty creative with them.  Here's an example situation:  I had this guy that I needed to take out, but he was housed in a rather nasty spot, with tons of cops roaming around, and generally tons of risk if I approached directly.  So, I had a look at my items, and found a solution in a combination of two of them:  A remote hacking device, and a land mine.  There was a computer in the building that guy was in, and air vents, and hacking into that remotely allowed me to trigger an option to release gas into the building, causing the guy to panic and rush for the door to get out, into the fresh air.... and right into the land mine I'd placed in front of the door.  That was the end of him, and since I'd done my hacking from inside an adjacent building in a secluded room, the cops suspected nothing.   All they knew was that this guy exploded.   Of course, with other items, I could have chosen different solutions... it all depends on what you have, what's in the environment, what different characters are doing, and your own ability to puzzle things out and come up with creative ways of dealing with the situation.
Or, you could just take a Gigantizer pill, grow to mammoth proportions, and crash through the building and step on the guy.  You have that option and more, due to the sheer number of creative, fun items in the game.  The amount of creativity here is outright stunning, with every item being unique and interesting while offering tons of possibilities on just how you can go about using it.  Not that your schemes will always work out, of course.  There are loads of people in this bizarre city, each with their own agenda, and they can often screw up your plans in ways that you never expected, bringing you new troubles and causing chaos, adding to the emergent nature of the gameplay in a very dynamic and fun way.  And you have tons of different ways of interacting with all these characters.  Hire some goons to do your dirty work, or even bribe the cops on the current floor to ignore your crimes for awhile, among tons of other options.
Of course, dealing with items and interacting with stuff isnt all there is.   Sometimes, pure combat is the answer, and I have to say, the game's combat system is fantastic.  I really couldnt be more pleased with this part of the game.  It's challenging, it's interesting, it's deep in it's own unique way, and there are tons of possibilities in any given battle, as the emergent nature of the game pervades even the combat.  You have the option to use melee weapons or guns, each having their advantages.  Melee weapons of course require that you get close, and you have to time your attacks carefully and worry about your positioning, and your enemies can hit just as hard as you can, or even harder depending on what they've got.  Guns of course are obvious in their use, but many tend to be loud, and you have limited ammo.  Or sometimes you have stranger options, such as a shrink ray, making your opponent tiny, causing them to run away in terror... or get squished, if you manage to catch them.  Just like every other aspect of the game, creative use of the environment and your items just adds even more to the excellent combat system.
But there's even more than just that.  You gain experience by doing different things, and all sorts of activities can offer you some.  Even non-lethal things such as using chloroform to quietly take down a guard gives you XP, so you are not restricted by playstyle here.  Get enough XP, and you can choose a new trait, which are all just as interesting as anything else.  And lastly, there is a wide selection of characters, each one being very different from the last.   One run you might choose to be a soldier, bristling with weaponry, but in the next you could choose a doctor, a class that cannot use weapons (though you can always still punch people), but has other unique ways of dealing with things that creates a whole different feel to the gameplay.  All of the classes, from gorilla to comedian to vampire, are like this, and they're all a blast to play.  The same creativity and potential for possibilities exist with them as with everything else.
I could rant on, and on, and on about this game, really, but I think I've given you the basics here.  Games that are this good are incredibly rare, as are games with so many possibilities and fun.  Do I even need to say more here?

Just to get that warning out of the way, the TL;DR is that the starter edition SIGNIFICANTLY increases the grind for the base game operators, from an 500-2000 renown per operator to 12,500 renown per operator, over a tenfold increase. As a point of reference, you earn 200-400 renown per 15-30 minute match. Please just buy the regular edition as your skill level will progress faster than you can unlock operators in the starter edition, and I think at the sale price of ~$24 it's absolutely worth it.
That being said, R6: Siege is a fantastic FPS focused on 5v5 attack/defend in mostly CQB situations. Compared to CS:GO, the focus on pure mechanical aiming skill (speed, accuracy, knowing spray patterns) is not as necessary; expert map knowledge and clever tactics will make you a great player even if you have only decent aim. What sets Siege apart from other competitive FPS games from my personal experience:
I'd also like to comment on
. Ubisoft really did a good job with Siege. Player count is still rising for a 2+ year old game; they went from 20 to 25 million players in a few months recently. Each year has four seasons where they introduce new DLC operators and maps.
. Cosmetics such as player and gun skins are NOT tradable. You can purchase specific cosmetics from Ubisoft for a fixed price, no x% chance lootbox bullsh!t. You can also earn skins for free just by playing the game; after each game you have an increasing chance to get dropped an Alpha Pack, which can be opened for a cosmetic of different rarity; however you CANNOT BUY AN ALPHA PACK WITH REAL MONEY. The cosmetics have zero effect on gameplay. The game is not perfect--there are still bugs and optimizations that Ubisoft is working out--but they are pretty rare to encounter and the game is absolutely in a playable state.
: 9.5/10, great gameplay, high replayability, ever-growing playerbase, fair progression and monetization. I got my friend to stop playing CS:GO altogether to play Siege. Would highly recommend.

Must-Have for every Couchlover. Though half of the modes are barely any fun, the other 3 make up a very fun experience.
You should play this game with some house rules, since the built-in systems do not support some mandatory stuff.
I recommend the game for the following:
Death Race: Extremely fun. Everyone is one of the about 20 characters on screen, the other being NPCs. You can only Press A to walk or Y to run and shoot with a crosshair on screen. First to finish wins, but if you are too obvious someone will shoot you and you are out.
Houserule: sadly, the game does not give you the ability to get an extra shot if you actually killed one of your friends. So just set shots to 4, only have everybody shooting once, except they get a player kill, which gives them another one. WAY better that way.
Thief Party: Fun overall. There are 2 Teams, thiefs and snipers. the thieves are one of the otherwise NPC characters on the field, about 20. There are coins, which give a sound once a thief walks over it and they disappear a random time after that. Snipers have a crosshair and 3 shots to kill the thieves. You should always play 2 rounds, switching teams on each. The thieves which collect more coins win. If the snipers waste all their shots, the thieves win automatically and a new set of round starts.
Assassins: Same as thief Party basically, but the assassins kill the NPCs instead of collecting coins. Same fun though and still quite different to play out.
The other gamemodes are quite awful though.
Nonetheless: MUST-HAVE. Extremely fun to play. Even if you are only playing this for 20 mins on a day with your friends on your couch, it is totally worth it every time.

Despite how much Home markets itself as a horror game, it really isn't. Home is better described as a murder mystery adventure with a psychological thriller bent. Outside of the eery atmosphere and fake shocks sprinkled throughout, there isn't really much in the way of actual horror. Actually there isn't much in the way of actual Adventure gameplay either, most puzzles are easily solved by just looking through the environments for items to pick up while the game takes care of everything else.
However, this isn't the point of Home. Home's selling point is that each playthrough (clocking in around 90 minutes) is different than the last, inviting players to play multiple times to dig into the mysterious narrative. At its best Home is an intriguing experiment in the flexibility of interactive fiction, but it outright denies investing players with actual gameplay.
Home isn't a failed experiment by any means, it's worth a look for those interested in gaming as a means of storytelling, but those looking for skin-crawling horror or puzzling adventures need look elsewhere.

Once again, Key brings us a visual novel that just shoots you with an arrow, straight through the heart. I would strongly reccomend this to both new and experienced VN readers. (Also, the Japanese version is available when you buy the game on steam, if you can read Japanese characters. The language can be changed in the game's prefrences by right clicking it.)
Its about a 4-5 hour read if you like to listen to the dialouge, and maybe about 2 and a half hours if you skip most of it. The music is ok, its nothing amazing, the CG and backgrounds are fairly decent, but what makes this game is the story and the writing. Honestly, I just burst out crying at the end. It is such a powerful and beautiful story that everyone should read. Honestly, this is just incredible. My rating of the title is 9/10. The only reason it doesnt score a perfect 10 is the repetative music and sound effects. Honestly, some more work could have been done there to further justify this otherwise stunning and incredible story.
A little about the story:
This short novel set in a post apocalyptic earth, tells the story of a "junker", who meets a half broken robot in a long abandoned planetarium. There, seeking refuge from the never ending, radioactive "rain" and lethal murderous robots, he happens to enter during the one week of the year which the robot is functunal. Bad luck? Faith? Regardless of the reason, the robot, Hoshino Yumemi, (ほしのゆめみ), tries to do her job and show him the stars. But the big telescope inside the planetarium is broken after 30 years of not being used. In the abandoned and worn down planetarium, in a broken world, he decides to stay and try to fix the telescope...

The range of emotions this VN made me experience was incredible. Like many other players, I cried unabashedly in front of my computer for at least ten minutes. Twice.
An easy 10, made by one of the best visual novel creators in the business. However, due the short run time (it took me about three hours), unless you've got money to burn, you might want to wait for a sale. Either way, it's easily worth it.

Do you like reading? If so, cool, keep reading my review to get a better idea as to whether or not this game is for you. If not, then this game likely isn't for you. This is a Visual Novel; Visual Novels are basically novels with pictures that have voice acting, music, sounds, and in a lot of cases, choices for you to make.
In regards to planetarian ~the reverie of a little planet~, it is a Visual Novel in all of the above ways except that you don't get to make choices, however, if you look at it as a novel with voice acting and music, then you might find it super attractive for its price tag. How many books can you buy that has different voice actors for different roles, sounds and music (audio-books, I guess, but for this price)?
If I am having trouble convincing you, then I have this to say: “Key wrote it”. Key is a company that writes Visual Novels and produces Anime, both are positively received. What makes Key so great, in my humble opinion, is  that  they make fun, beautiful, and heart-breaking stories- particularly the last bit- such as Clannad and Angel Beats! which are Anime and Visual Novels themselves.
So, if a post-apocalyptic setting, robots, and a heartwarming, but tear-jerking story appeals to you, then I recommend picking this up.

Now that the devs consider this game done, it is a very big let down.
It had so much potential, but they didn't polish the game enough to make it enjoyable.
The core gameplay of the game is good, but there's a bunch of little problems that make it more frustrating than fun. You are constantly sucked out of the gameplay as you're experiencing little problems, bugs and moments that lack polish and make you feel like you're playing a proof of concept rather than a fleshed out game.
PROS:
- The only real Road Rash successor out there.
- Solid mechanics for the most part. It feels good to ride fast and use weapons while dodging obstacles.
- Good maps, bikes, weapons. The actual content is very good.
- Progression and unlocks is oldschool and is fun.
- Soundtrack works.
- Multiplayer, while lacking refinement, works fine.
CONS:
- Serviceable graphics but no real polish. Weak effects. Dull colors. Feels too much like a Unity game.
- HORRIBLE sound effects. They sound like something some aspiring indie dev made in his garage with a cheap mic and shared online. The sound effects are probably the worst part of this game. I absolutely hate them. I have never exerpienced sound effects that dampen the fun of a game like they do with this one. Everytime I hear a gunshot, crash or engine rev, I make a face like im smelling a fart because it disgusts me.
- UI is dull looking. Menu and sound effects dont convey that feeling of casual fun. Too unpolished.
- Not smooth. You can get stuck too easy on the side of the road. There are too many little instances that take you out of the speed and mayhem of the game. It needs to wipe you out and reset you quickly and more fluidly. Too many open spaces on the maps where you can drive off road into nothing without being reset.
- Still some horrible bugs. Half of the time when exitting, the game locks up windows, forcing you to hard reset.

This game needs a heavy amount of polish to make it widely enjoyable. If you really want to play a Road Rash successor, then you can get some fun out of this, especially if you can ignore how amateur it looks and feels. I just can't sit down and play this without getting distracted by its problems.

I am really glad these guys set out to make this game, even if it failed in my eyes. I feel if they had more money and/or experience, this game could have been polished and more accessible, and tons of fun. There isn't anything else out there attempting to fill the void of Road Rash. I hope what little success this game leads to more attempts at this type of oldschool gameplay. Not everything needs to be a roguelike, progression based, unlockable, metroidvania, survival, open world, lootbox fest. We need more games that attempt to recapture the simplistic fun of the games of the past.

I've had this game on my wish list for a very long time. I've wanted to pull the trigger, but wasn't fully convinced that it was worth the cash. I don't think I would have tried the game if it wasn't for my friend who gifted it to me. Road Redemption is quite satisfying, but can leave a bit of a sour taste the more you play it. The game is fun, interactive and engaging, but I felt like a little more attention to detail could have taken the game to the next level.
Road Redemption
follows an arcade style game in which your primary goal is to survive. The game follows a rogue-like structure where you start from the beginning and try to make it to the end every time. As you race and gain experience, you will be able to unlock perks to compliment the game play. If you get tired of starting from the beginning all the time there are perks that exist to start you 1/4, 1/2, and almost 3/4 of the way into the game. Other perks include new bikes, stronger attacks, additional stats and even weapons. Some perks can be upgraded multiple times to improve their impact. Some of the really useful upgrade will not be available until you unlock previous perks (thus the "tree" portion). Either way, the upgrades are reasonable and attainable.
I always feel the best racing games (especially ones that involve destruction) are best when they mix in arcade and simulation. Even though the game is engaging it does lack in the
department. The turning feels okay, but relatively simple and not so challenging. I wish there was a little drag or some sort of skips when you are taking turns at a ridiculous speed. There really isn't drifting and the stopping is bland. The feeling of actually being on a bike isn't quite there even when you collide/bump into certain things. Speed is more or less constant and the only time you really accelerate is when you use boost. I wish there were more traction settings to give the player a better feeling of what it is like to be on a bike. I realize with the context of the game it might be difficult as there is a lot of violence, but I feel this would have been a great compliment to the game. It seems as though there is a system in place to keep the players and computers close to one another. From a programmers stand-point it seems that this mechanism is in place to add excitement to the game. It is a catch 22 situation because it does work well when you want to start smashing people, but it fails as no matter how fast you are going - you'll be stuck with this group of riders for some time. Basic controls include swinging weapons (usually 1 blunt weapon, 1 sword like weapon, an explosive weapon and handheld guns), the ability to shove opponents (kicking them) and the ability to grab opponents. Stringing all the attacks together at a high-speed can be quite fun even with the lack of attention to bike controls.
The
are at best okay. I feel a lot more could have been added to the background and to some of the other objects within the game. How the levels change is a cool progression, but it doesn't feel all that different. They did add some random factors (for example in hallucination mode) such as cars dropping in randomly from the sky. This is cool, but unfortunately their only attempt to add more depth in this realm of the game. I feel they could have done a lot more to immerse the player into the game better. The
and music are ok at best (as they are a bit bland). The voice acting isn't too bad, but I think a little more emotion could have been put in. Even though this isn't the meat and bones of the game, it can definitely separate a good game from a great game.
Overall, the game is not bad in its delivery. It is fun and engaging due to its arcade playing style. For myself it bugs me they didn't try to do a little more and give the player a little more control over the bike (or less). I wish some of the features of Moto GP13 would be found in this game while driving. It wouldn't have to follow a simulation format, but add some of that exciting danger that comes with riding a bike! In future Road Redemption games I hope to see the control of the bike reworked, new modes and lots of additions to the maps. The local co-op is definitely a notable (and appreciated) feature!

What impresses me most about This is the Police is how well it all flows together. With a choice-driven story, daily station management, and ongoing requests and investigations, it’d be pretty easy for the game to fall short somewhere, but every single piece feels fully fleshed out. The daily grind is a smoothly-running sim game backed by a fantastic jazz-heavy soundtrack, and the story sequences are compelling, well-written, and fantastically voiced.
- An interesting story
- A lot of moral choices that affect the course of the story
- Variability of operations
- Sensible strategic model
- Excellent voice-acting
- Climate, vector graphics
- Many vivid secondary characters
- Diagrams after a long time the game;
- Sometimes too large accumulation of problems with the police.
All things being equal, I’m hard-pressed to think of a game that more exceeded my expectations than This is the Police. A fully-formed, engaging story that’s tied together underneath a solid and demanding simulator game is certainly something I’ve never seen before, and it’s all handled excellently. The game’s more sensitive content, including references to abuse, homophobia, racism, and more may make it tough for some to enjoy, but even these elements are handled in a way that fits the game and its themes.

Now, I have about 10 friends that have this game so far.
The game itself is very entertaining, and by FAR my most favorite in the series at the moment.
Scott has done a wonderful job with his games (With exception of FNaF 3 in my opinion) so far with such a small amount of time.
I as a person almost live off this game and it's theories that people make in the lore.
Although the game is good, the lore... IS BETTER!
There are so many twists and turns throughout the game
I have a little table here for you with what I rate everything separately.
I loved the mechanics in this 4th installment to the FNaF franchise. The flashlight usage, child in his room, listening at the door. It all fit in so well with it's atmosphere. Only thing was that the camera idea was gone... It was the thing that really set the feeling for the games, and it isn't a bad thing necessarily! It is just something crucial to the past games.
The new "Nightmare" design to these animatronics have me hooked. They are something new and revolution to the feeling of "scary" that Five Nights at Freddy's has introduced so far. The rush of being jump-scared was enough, but this step up from that with a new Hellish look to these already freaky things was the tip of the iceberg to FNaF.
Alright, the sounds of the game were all creepy and atmospheric. There was a few things that made me a little angry... the footsteps of your character were literally re-used sounds from Foxy's run in the first game, the sounds are still a little to quiet for me to be honest, and instead of Scott making a new jump-scare sound affect he just smashed the previous 3 sounds together. Yes, yes, I know it made it seem as if they were Nightmare-like with there voices being mashed together, but I would've preferred a deeper pitched roar compared to a loud scream.
There is still one thing that I haven't fully gotten into...
This game leaves so many new questions unanswered compared to the ones that could've been answered. The Bite of 87 could've been this poor child, or possibly another from a later time or different building. The Purple Guy Easter egg could mean a few different things that I won't get into right now. I love the franchise's lore and I always will, and I will also continue theorizing as much as I can!
My friends tell me that you've made too many mistakes. Mistakes that you can't make up for. Little things that make no sense when compared to things. But I refuse to believe it. Every LITTLE thing that you've done must have some sort of reasoning behind it. I refuse to believe that you make a mistake knowingly or lazily. Show everyone that their wrong your own way, through your brilliant games. You've confirmed FNaF 5 won't be happening anytime soon (Which you NEED to do, just 5NaF5 sounds so cool :P), and a prequel won't be happening either. So DLCs and Spinoffs are bound to happen. I wish the best of luck to all of you out there in the FNaF fandom, and game on!

To all of the people who say this game can get too boring too fast:
From the beginning of the game, you notice there are different types of locations, each with their own loot. That alone gives you a reason to explore and collect different materials to craft very different things. Then, you need to get warmer equipment by hunting animals, while also making sure you don't starve. Searching and collecting everything that you need is not boring, and when you finally get those sweet steel tools it feels nice to be able to craft the best clothes and the bow.
The raft can be very tricky to control, but that's fine, because if it was easy as hell, THEN it could be called boring. But you have to be constantly on the lookout for the nearest camp and boost to it as soon as you see it, or you will just miss it completely because of the strong river current. You also need to pay attention to dodge as much♥♥♥♥♥♥as you can, for repairs can be hard to obtain, especially in the early game.
Also, there is a very nice sense of progression. You start finding more wild life. First some bunnies, then a boar, then a wolf, then multiple wolves at the same time... and apparently there are bears too, which I have yet to find after hours of gameplay. Fighting them is also not boring at all, and it feels rewarding to get the skin off them as a proof of survival.
Some people also say having the game not paused while crafting is unfair, and while it does make the game harder, it is refreshing to see you actually have to find a safe place to derp around with your inventory, and having to quickly interrupt what you are doing if a storm catches you to find shelter makes it more realistic.
In the wild forests, when you least expect it, things can get really chaotic:
-Be exploring around a building.
-Notice 3 wolves.
-Panic and throw all your poisoned meat at them while they claw at you.
-2 of them die.
-Realize you don't have any more traps.
-Pull out your bow and 3 arrows.
-Miss the first shot.
-Land an arrow and watch how the wolf goes out screen.
-Think he is dead, begin healing yourself.
-The wolf comes back, arrow stuck on his body, attacks you while you're healing.
-Panickly get your bow back out and aim carefully. You want to shoot fast, but it's your last arrow.
-Aim carefully and shoot. Land a hit, the wolf falls dead to the ground.
-Heal your multiple wounds with bandages, while the adrenaline on your body expires.
If THAT is not getting more interesting, I don't know what is. Can't wait to find my first bear.

Let me start by saying this game at its core, is a pretty good game. I enjoyed the gameplay, visuals and characters so far. My main gripe, like many others is Ubisoft's decision to implement a layer of VMProtect which essentially turns your PC into an emulator.
I've tolerated Denuvo because despite its flaws, it always valued keeping a very low performance cost when implemented correctly, RIME is the only example I can think of that was a poor implementation that hurt performance due to have way to many triggers.
VMProtect on the other hand, is pretty much confirmed to lower performance as your essentially running a virtual machine on top of the games code and Denuvo. We know from what Denuvo has stated, that it only does its "checks" during non critical periods, such as the startup screen or a loading screen. From what has been shown in AC: Origins, VMProtect is constantly running in the game's core at all times.
I've refunded this game, which is a shame. Ubisoft's agenda in anti piracy measures once again causes them to make all the wrong decisions and hurt legit, paying customers. Although, coming from a CEO who says 95% of PC users are pirates, it doesn't surprise me they would prioritize these types of decisions.

I've only played the game once so far, but I think there is some replay value in making different choices to get different endings and see aspects of the story.
