Picked this up in a bundle because it looked neat but I'm just not enjoying it.
You control a girl with a surprisingly useless dog, whose only abilities are barking at stuff and carrying a few items. The girl has a torch on a stick that momentarily scares animals to give her a small window of opportunity to run away. Running away is all you can do until you acquire materials necessary to craft a bow and arrows which I was unable to do. You can set up traps or throw tainted meat to poison and kill larger animals but you can't move while selecting the meat and if you're moving when you bring up a menu your character gets locked in that direction until you jiggle the movement keys. It happens constantly and has nearly gotten me killed multiple times. Fortunately, the animal AI is dumb as dirt and you can just run circles around them when necessary, and it is necessary. I have to admit that seeing the spear trap spring into action for the first time was pretty neat.
Half the game you're on an uncontrollable raft. You're suppose to be able to steer and row in the direction you choose but it just does whatever it wants. This is by far the most boring part of the entire game and since it's half the gameplay, it wore out its welcome expeditiously. You are able to upgrade the raft to have a motor, stove and shelter from rain but it requires a lot in order to craft these upgrades so again I couldn't be bothered to play that far. The other half of the game you're walking on the tiniest islands imaginable attempting to harvest various vegetables, medicine, meat and animals which you use to craft into useful items or consume to fill your hunger meter or heal different types of injuries. The game could almost be fun if the islands were larger and there was more variety but there's only 5 different island "types" that you can randomly happen upon. When you're on an island you'll be pretty disappointed that every single island of any given type looks exactly the same as every other island of that type. There's minor detail changes but it all becomes a blur really fast. As you float down the procedurally generated river you may only be able to land on the same 1-2 island types repeatedly due to horrible raft steering along with the rivers completely random patterns and direction always taking you the opposite way of where you want to go.
The random nature about this game is my biggest problem with it. Everything is random. It's a roguelike so it's expected but on my 2nd attempt at playing I went an hour and a half without finding a single stitching kit which is needed to craft clothing. As a result the girl became sick due to the temperature consistently dropping as you progress. By the time I finally found the first stitch kit the temperature had dropped so low that there was no way I'd ever be able to keep up and just quit the game. I had already lost, there was no recovering at this point, but it could have taken another half hour before the girl finally died.
The graphics are unappealing and there's so much crap crowding the foreground that a large amount of time you find yourself walking/rafting behind objects and not being able to see at all what is in front of you which is a great way to smash in debri in the river. What the hell is with all those black, 2D, cutout trees just floating off the islands into the water anyway? Sound cues are way off. Sometimes you hear loud, rushing, roaring water when on the rapids and other times you hear nothing at all... while still on the rapids. Some music tracks are much louder than others and none of them really go with the flow of what's happening on screen it seems like it usually just randomly plays at any given time after long periods of silence. I prefer the silence.
Also, character dialogue.. Who the ♥♥♥♥ do they think speaks like that? I barely have a clue as to what the characters are saying whenever you happen upon an NPC. They don't say anything or do anything of value anyway. Sometimes trade an item for something you probably already have or tell you how to craft something that you already knew about because once you get those items the games crafting list tells you what to do with them.
It just feels incomplete and I've no interest in spending anymore time with it.
How is this game fun?

Everything you can experience in TFitF happens in the first hour. But the campaign can easily take 10x that to beat, and there's close to zero story or story advancement.
This game is like a very stripped down Don't Starve. The only reasonable way to play it is to float down the mighty Alt-F4 river, because due to the many design flaws, things will inevitably go horribly sideways, often.
The viewable area is wonky, sometimes giving you a good enough, large enough view, then sometimes it doesn't scroll for no apparent reason, or zooms in for no apparent reason, which can lead to you accidentally running into a snake, a boar, a wolf, or even a bear if you're unlucky enough. Also you spend a significant time running behind buildings and trees, which in this isometric view completely obscure your vision. If a boar or wolf catches up to you while you can't see, you're finished.
There isn't so much "combat" is there is "the same strategy every time" for dealing with enemies. Spear trap or bow-and-arrow boars. Spear trap, bow-and-arrow, or feed wolves tainted meat. Spear trap and bow-and-arrow bears. Wash, rinse, repeat. It's always this with no variation, and it will happen a thousand times. Using items in combat is so unwieldy, and even wielding the bow in combat is so wonky, that without preparation, you can easily die to the loneliest boar, even many hours into the game.
There's a crafting system, that you pretty much max out in the first hour, and offers almost no complexity or variety. Bad shoes, then rabbit pelt shoes, then boar shoes, then wolf shoes, then bear shoes, repeat for other clothing slots. You can't aim to unlock anything and there's no "tree," you just collect everything you can and the recipes unlock. You will spend a ton of wasted time on inventory management.
The game bills itself as roguelike, which means it's procedural, which also means it's incredibly samey. The art for different areas is only very slightly different. 10 minutes in, and you've seen what the world has to offer. Then it's 6-10 more hours to beat the basic campaign.
There's so little *game* here, that I get the feeling TFitF is mostly a vehicle for its bluegrass soundtrack. Which is fine--good even--but you'll be sick to death of it well before the game is done.
In the end, you can either play with the scarcity and the random item placement and awful combat and the same procedural areas, or you can save-scum your way to the end. But because there's zero variegation in what you're doing, and what you're seeing, if you play the tough way, you're simply using up the hours of your life. A storyline might have helped gloss over the punishing repetition, but there really isn't one. Roll down river for some reason, die or get to end. It doesn't really matter either way.
Some of the reviews describe TFitF as riding down a "seemingly endless" river. They have this exactly right, but I can't for the life of me understand why anyone would think this is a good thing.

You're 90% at the mercy of the game's RNG.
In survival games, you typically go look for whatever you need, experiment, etc.
In this one, you're in a little raft and some locations pop-up near you, where you'll find supplies. These, as far as I can see, are completely random (with a different distribution in each area or the game, but still outside of your control). Which means that you don't really plan much, at least in the crafting aspect of the game.
I'm only playing on "Easy" mode (which really is easy, but I also have no wish to play the harder modes, since I don't see how it could get better with the very little that the game has). This was the recommended for new players.
The survival part is almost removed from this game. I died a couple of times at the start, mostly because I had no idea what each item did or where to find it. Once I figured things out, the game got very easy.
That's fine, that's what other modes are there for, and it did teach me the way around the game!
The problem is the crafting. You want to craft the higher level stuff. But for this, you need a bunch of tools, which break, and then require other materials, etc.
And, as I mentioned at the start, there is no way that you can go look for whichever materials you need. If they happen to fall your way, great! If not... well, keep going until you find something.
I don't play many survival games, but this doesn't very a good design decision at all. I'd like to explore a map to figure out where I can find things, and then try to gather the ones I need. Instead, I'm constantly doing some awkward (and sometimes buggy) inventory management because I need to change what I'm looking for based on what I'm given.
The game seemed to have a nice setting, but there's barely no story here. Almost no characters, etc.
Seemed like a cool game, but I don't like it after playing it for a few hours.
There's a very small amount of items, and the only reason they take time to craft is because the game decides not to give you material X for a an area (which takes maybe an hour to complete), and then material Y, and so on. So, in the end, I have an inventory full of "high level" Bear Hides, but I can't do anything because I'm lacking "low level" rabbit hides, or flints, or something else.
There's very little player input in this game. You're spoon fed (whether you like it or not) everything and you're supposed to play with what you're given. Not really my thing.
P.S.(1): The difficulty also seems to grow in a very unnatural game, given the setting.
You see more and more wolves or bears basically everywhere, despite the fact that the areas are the same as the ones you visited before.
The rains also start occurring almost all the time, which is annoying (no rabbits, you get wet, can't light fires, etc.).
I realize this is a game about a flood. That's fine. The problem is that it didn't start with a lot of rain. The rain increased to make the game more difficult later on. But... it doesn't feel right.
The game isn't about overcoming rain. The rain is a generic difficulty barrier.
P.S.(2): The interface has some bugs and many other overlooks that make the overall experience much worse than it should. Scrolling through the menus isn't fluid, sometimes the slected inventory item teleports to something else, etc.
There's also the fact that you can craft either 1 or ALL (all for which you have materials) of a given item. These take exactly the same time. But you can't craft 2 or 3. If you want 4 instead of 6, you have to click, wait for the bar to fill, click, wait for the bar to fill, click, wait for the bar.... you get the point.
All of these interface things pile up in a game that's a looot about inventory management and using the crafting menu.
I could understand in a small game that wanted to pass a message instead of focusing on the user experience.
But this is not that. The game is extremely padded (it's very repetitive with no good reason other than to justify its price), and it seems to say very, very little.
Kind of boring. I didn't realize it was one of those survival games. The crafting and scavenging just didn't click for me.
Cause of Death: Boredom

It feels some Soul game vibes, you get bonus for attacking enemy in the back, attack after breaking their shields and attacking after a parry, but there won't be any any special attack moves being dealt to the, and the attacks feel legit, especially with hammers, or dual blades, but the move set is repetitive, so in the end it is just you are slashing them, and you don't feel really immersive in all the fights, or you can make fun of different moves as you can in previous AC games.
Stealth is not bad in fact, unlike previous AC the assassination moves are pretty fast and easy to execute, this time it is slower and harder to execute. This is forgivable considering how Bayak is bad with this new weapon. (i had quite a laugh when he ♥♥♥♥ed up using hidden blade, no spoilers lol) The result is you need to rely on very, well, old-school stealth techniques, however the new forts and camps are pretty fun to stealth in, and the location objective doesn't make it too boring, like in AC3 i can just rush in and kill the target without triggering the alarm, yes, it shows Connor being one of the most skilled assassin in the history, but it is just not good for climaxes. Move set is repetitive, yes, but endurable.
Now the bad parts
The RPG-like level restriction is dumb, no matter how much you upgrade your stats, like you have golden hidden blade and golden health and golden melee, you can't do much of a damage to enemies approxmately 3 levels above of you, it is not logically realistic, like it just doesn't fit into logics,♥♥♥♥♥♥like that just in no way might happen, even in AC's fictional worlds, and it breaks immersion. It also makes stat upgrades seem useless, why do i even bother to upgrade them if they doesn't take me higher? And you might say "I'm good at Souls, i might kill that son of a ♥♥♥♥♥ with my skills." i thought the same, but ACO's move sets are pretty over-fancy, so unlike Souls the dodge and attack is not clean and immediate-responsive, and the aiming is not accurate, this inaccuracy can also be seen while doing parkour and assassinate other people. Once you get the level, you get super op and you are Connor all over again, so in the end Ubisoft still made a berserker-assassin, with less fancy moves to kill enemies.
So overall, if you are into lore, plots and a mixed side quests, you should definetly try this out, as they did make up the lack of fun in RPG system, it even helps to get over the problems, so that you can level up as you are enjoying all this small stuffs.
I might come back for the Main quest, since it seems good but I need to finish it first.
BTW, the exclusive pyramid mission sucks, and i'm looking forward to the new God trial boss, because Anubis is only good visually, but the fight itself is dull.

Watch_Dogs 2 is one of my favourite games I've played. If you're a fan of GTA-style gameplay, stealth, and modern settings, I'd highly suggest giving it a chance.
In a lot of ways it's essentially the same as the first game - upgrade tree of hacks, hacks work generally the same, and the shooting and driving are similar to the first game (albeit all three have been improved). However, the setting, story, and style of the game is so much better than the first: instead of trying to hit the general audience with the most basic hacking elements and semigeneric characters, they went full in on the hacking aspect and embraced the nerdy, tech-obsessed twenty-something audience. The characters are a lot more interesting, the dialogue is a lot more fun, and it's clear they weren't trying to have some "deep" and "heavy" story in this one.
The animations are expressive and detailed, very similar to the first game but once again improved, the graphics are bright and enticing, and all of the music is fantastic. Whether it's the liscensed music on the radio (music from all the genres in this game is amazing) or the fittingly electronic soundtrack created by Hudson Mohawke that plays during missions, all of the music fits the game's setting and style perfectly.
The big things, like the technocratic setting of Silicon Valley and San Francisco or the electronic soundtrack, and the little things like 3D printing your own guns and controlling quadcopters and driving drones to complete missions all come together to form a cohesively entertaining near-future electronic experience. If Ubisoft can create more solid and unique games like this, they could certainly be on the road to redemption.
All around, a great game for the tech-obsessed.

You are roped by your friend Lucky into the job of preparing pizzas for her friend Gastone's new pizzeria. Officially, you are in charge of rolling out the dough (with just one click), and pouring sauce and sprinkling ingredients onto the flattened dough. This is your main role when the pizzeria's open. After work though, you are also in charge of the kitchen's setup and the type of pizzas on the menu.
After work, you are also unofficially in charge of advertising, setting work hours, and buying furniture and gifts for the shop. (Considering you also get to name the shop and pretty much have the deciding vote on things, how much ownership does Gastone really have over this place? lol)
You basically run the pizza place.
The core of the game is to drag and drop pizza ingredients onto the dough/board and serve it in time to please the customers. This is a bit of a challenge once you're popular enough that most orders have 6 pizzas each; and also if you have complicated pizzas, so make sure to design your pizzas with moderation.
I recommend this game because it's enjoyable and slightly humorous.
My advice to future players:
1. Go to options, set the mouse "Control scheme" to Type B or Type C so you don't accidentally serve an unfinished pizza.
2. Play with moderation. I played this game for 3 days straight (admittedly with tons of pizzas in my menu) and my brain is just exhausted, especially with the 12-hour shifts you're forced to take during an event in story mode. I'm in pizza burnout lol.
Recommendation to the dev: Add more key bindings please so not everyone is forced to use a mouse, and also to speed up the setting dialog (e.g. "Lucky's Place. That evening.") because that takes forever lol.

I'd heard a lot of bad things about ACIII, but after finally getting around to play it I found almost none of them were true. ACIII is a good game. Not a great game and not the best AC game, but still fun to play and worth playing.
It wraps up Desmonds Story, tells a good historical story in the 18th century, explores the whole Templar/Assasin conflict from a different angle and Conner is an interesting Protagonist(Not as cool as Ezio but none of them as as cool as Ezio). Not to mention the Naval Combat is fun, the Treasure hunting/Peg Leg missions are nice extension of the whole Assasin Tomb/Prince of Persia Platforming levels and even the homestead development is interesting.
My biggest issue with the game(other then remapping the controls yet again) is that is doesn't feel much like an AC game. Sure, the bad guys are Templars but a lot of it feels in name only. The homestead is interesting but does feel very removed from everything else(and the crafting system also feels a bit useless when you realize furs sell for a lot more then more of the stuff you can craft).
My other Pet Peeve: Conner occasionally gets Forrest Gumped into things. Why is he there to witness the signing of the Declaration of Independence? Who knows other then Ubisoft wanted him there. Why is Conner picked to command troops during certain battles, despite him not actually being in the Army? Why is he riding Paul Reveres horse? Illusion of Agency? It's a lot of fun, don't get me wrong and it's better then watching from the sidelines but it does break suspension of disblief at times.
That being said, the King Washington DLC takes Suspension of Disbelief and tosses it gleefully aside. In an Alternate History, King Washington has an Apple of Eden and uses it to make the US into a dystopian nightmare that he rules as King, shooting Laser beams at those who oppose him. Conner, meanwhile, drinks drug laced tea from a magic tree and gains magic shapeshifting Native American Superpowers that allow him to turn invisible in plain sight, fly between rooftoops and bear stop American Soldiers. It's Wonderfully Silly, despite being a lot darker then the base game and worth a try. It's to ACIII what Blood Dragon was to Far Cry 3(also by Ubisoft, interestingly enough).

Do not buy this game, if you want a good gritty police game play LA Noire, if you want a good police movie watch the original Bad Lieutenant (1992).
You are a 60 year old cop who has defended his city for the better part of his life, but in 180 days you retire. You need to make 500k. How you do it is up to you.
This game is great for the first 2 hours or so, interesting character with great voice acting (side characters not so much) and a great premise from a rarely explored perspective. Gameplay is a mix of cartoon snippets with voice acting (story) and officer management where you send your cops to crime scenes.
This game is not PC, there will be moments in the game where you have to surpress feminists or meet black officer quotas, these can sometimes be hard to handle but I am glad these elements are covered in a game because it is rare. There are also interviews or press conferences where you have to defend or explain yourself for your actions, if you end up squashing that protest, very cool. These moments are fun in the beginning as they seem to respect the player choice and show that while wanting to be fair, you cannot please everyone, you will have to side with people. However none of this matters as there will be moments in which you pick one option to side with someone but the game forces you to kill off that person.
After the start of the game the cut scenes get less frequent as you slog through to the 180 days, the other elements that were in the start of the game that added depth and strategy degenerate into luck as officers and other resources will be killed off, it would be devastating but it doesn't matter, if you don't anser any calls for a few days you will still reach the end of the game. The biggest letdown of this game is that none of your choices affect you or change the outcome, it would also help if the game was 10 hours shorter, it took me 17 hours to complete this game and I was close to stopping at least twice. I give props to the developer for their interesting concept but the lack of depth and choices make no difference and the player is not rewarded with a great ending either.
PROS:
-art style
-music and voice acting
-gritty and not PC
CONS:
-gameplay gets boring
-choice driven gameplay yet choices do not matter
-way too long
-terrible ending

This is a mediocre novel wrapped around a shallow and incomplete mini-game. Its moderate success is indicative of the low standard of writing in video games that survives in 2016. If the writing in this game were a novel, nobody would read it. It's fine, but it's cliche and uninspired. If the gameplay elements alone were a game, nobody would play it. You simply can't combine these two subpar halves into a worthwhile whole.
I wanted to like this game. The writing, while subpar for novel standards, is passable to link the gameplay elements together. The animations are solid. But the gameplay elements fall completely flat. The daily routine involves dispatching officers to calls and investigating crimes. Cool!?
Except:
No realistic feedback on crimes. You are asked to make decisions, like to resolve a standoff by either storming the building or surrounding the building and holding out. Intrigue! So you pick a choice, and ... no follow up. Simply a generic outcome screen that tells you whether you apprehended the suspect, whether you lost an officer, and whether any civilians were killed. This plays out over and over as the game tries to convince you that you are making nuanced decisions, while it becomes clear that you are just flipping a coin and hoping that you picked the right arbitrary choice.
The investigations? Don't get me started. You assign investigators, then forget about them as you wait for them to complete the investigation. At some point, you tediously move around screenshots into the right order to solve the "puzzle," but you have an infinite number of moves and it's basically just a chore with no drama or tension whatsoever.
Employees are sold as having "personalities," but that just boils down to having employees refuse to show up to work for ostensibly no reason at all, and with no clues to discern those reasons.
The mobster story line, without posting spoilers, is flat. And that's putting it nicely. I kept slogging through this game, hoping it would get better ... and it just never did. It's seriously like it is engineered to have enough slow-moving storyline to drag you out past the refund period before you realize that the game lacks content.
I would buy this game maybe at $2.99 to walk through a few days and check out some of the concepts, but overall it feels like someone assembled a few decent concepts and then completely mailed it in on turning those concepts into any semblance of a robust video game.

This is the Police is a great idea...very poorly executed.
I wanted to like this game.  I really did,   The idea of running a police department is appealing.  But then, comes the problems.  First, the game makes it look like your choices matter.  Trust me, they don't.  Police Chief Jack Boyd is strapped to the engine of a freight train on rails, and there is no way to avoid the end of the line, a very bad end.
The Good.
The elements of a good story are all here.  An estranged spouse.  A spunky, gung ho ingenue who has all the appearances of a love interest if you follow an honest path.  Having to navigate a town torn between a corrupt mayor and an equally corrupt mob.  It has all the potential elements of a great detective story at a more bird's eye view than a point-and-click adventure.
The gameplay, the day to day grind of managing your police force, fighting for your budget, dealing with a crooked mayor and a variety of challenges, was interesting, if repetitive.
The bad:
Lose the repetitive cutscene of Jack starting the engine to his rent-a-wreck every morning.  Oh, dear god, did I want to physically punish a developer after putting up with that over 100 times.  If a cutscene doesn't advance story, or represent a milestone in a story, it shouldn't exist.
As constructed, the game is about 20-25% too long.  More stuff needs to be happening with repetitive gameplay, and frankly, that gameplay needs to be more randomized.
The story.  Dear god, the story.  First, to describe it as a railroad is an insult to railroaded games.  Specifically the ending.  It can be summed up in one sentence.  At the end of the game, do you support the corrupt, long-time mayor, or the equally corrupt, literal murderer of a businessman that is challenging him for control of the city.
The rest of the story?  It's pointless.  The wife?  She begins the game separated from you, and your few interactions with her basically allow her to crap all over you.  The perky young love interest Assistant City Attorney?  She decides she'll make her name by indicting you when, surprise, surprise, in a city with no redeeming features whatsoever, she learns you are aren't 100% clean, and wants nothing to do with you.  The Mayor?  He's a racist, sexist a**hole.  The Opponent?  He's a literal homicidal performance artist who makes the Heath Ledger Joker character look like Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm.  And your fate?  It doesn't matter how honest a cop you are.  It doesn't matter how carefully you walk the tightrope that is this awful town (Freeburg really should be nuked from orbit, just to stop the disease from spreading).  No matter what choices you make in the game, your reward for a job well done is that everything and everyone you care for takes a dump on you.  Or you get killed.  Honestly, getting murdered is better.  At least it gives a sense of closure.
Do yourself a favor (if you haven't already played it).  Wait for the next Steam Seasonal sale, and go grab yourself L A Noire.  It'll be about the same price, it tells a much more satisfying story, and at least you won't be wanting back those two hours you watched an animated hand spend turning the crank on a rent-a-wreck.

This game is a representation of Ubisofts design philosophy. They greenlight great ideas with tons of potential and force them into generic genre tropes like a square peg into a round hole. I finally realized that I buy into that potential and find myself constantly saying "wouldn't it be cool if..." during their games. After the Witcher 3, Breath of the Wild, Dark Souls, and Metal Gear Solid 5 Ubisoft can't rely on that potential anymore. The lack of cohesion in mechanics and a core gameplay loop are completely absent. This used to be excused by the open world structure but too many games have proved that excuse a fraud. Not only is this a bad open world game, bad rpg, and bad action game, the elements used from these genres hurt each other and make for an infuriating experience. It feels like it will come around eventually but it's that hollow Ubisoft promise of potential. Let's break down the elements.
Combat- They changed it! It must be good! Unless you aren't just the right level. I was level 8 and get one-shotted by level 10 enemies. Okay, so pick away at them and then run to isolate the target. Well now enemies can scale three story buildings in a matter of seconds so there's no exciting chases. There's no breaks to build up the tension of the fight. If you listen carefully you can hear guards say, "we have a new combat system! This is what you wanted!" as they chase you across the entire Alexandria skyline. You also didn't like how only one enemy would attack before. Now you get to fight a whole Roman legion over ten scraps of wood for that crafting upgrade.Because that's the only way to get wood in the game. These systems just don't mesh. The loot clashes with the artificially difficult combat, and therefore the combat system, and therefore the leveling system and you get a gameplay loop of frustration.
Leveling- The skill tree in this game is a joke. Remember when in Zelda you could collect arrows out of wooden shields. Cool attention to detail, right? Well you have to level up and spend skill points to get that level of detail in this game. All those slow mo jump attacks looked cool in MGS5, right? Well you have to level up to get cool looking, functional combat. Health regeneration and the counter button are skill tree upgrades. Those are key mechanics that inform how the game plays. The upgrades aren't cool additions, they are core mechanics and small details that elevate the experience. So if you want to good experience with this game, level up. But you have to win combat encounters to get xp to level up. You could grind by fighting grunts or challenge yourself by taking on higher level enemies,,, no wait I'm thinking of the Witcher 3 that they aped the open world leveling system from. You can't fight higher level enemies. They just use their canned unblockable animation to kill you in one hit. So if you want to have a fun polished experience you need to farm weaker enemies with half of a combat system.
Story- Ubisoft's CEO's five year old son watched Ancient Aliens on the History channel so modern day is here to stay. Whoohoo! You know that Sci-fi crap that has crippled the ability for this series to explore relevant themes of some of the most interesting and tulmultuous times in history. It's back! I started checking my phone during the second cutscene at about the fifth time jump. Where the story started halfway through a revenge tale (original for Ubisoft) and expected you to be engaged by what was happening. By the time the Title screen pops up two of the five main targets are dead and you have no idea who they were. Then the game decides to flash back to why you should care, then jump forward thousands of years because ALIENS and isn't that what the hip kids are into these days? People just can't relate to history unless they have a snarky modern day scientist spouting off in order to keep the kids interested. What is even going on in the overarching story in these games. Cliche one- evil corporation, cliche twist- IT WAS ALIENS! The time period this game chooses to trip over is the most ripe time period for a game about assassins. Literally the most high profile assassinations of ancient history happened.This game could have explored the political turmoil which led to it but instead we need a mustache twirling conspiracy cult that name drops historical figures.
Stealth- Nonexistent, moving on... well there is a crouching animation. But if you're not the right level you can't assassinate people, In assassin's creed, during a time full of high profile assassinations all around the mediterranean. If you do manage to grind to the place where you can take out one guard before you see a higher level one, and have to grind some more, the enemies will spot you if they are in a hundred yard radius. Then you get to fight and die in one hit, or run and die in one hit. I first really started disliking this game when I perched on a high tower to plan out my first assassination mission. This was for the nonexistent tutorial which drops you into a complex rpg and doesn't explain anything. Hey, Zelda did it and it worked there! I used my eagle to find my target through his house walls. The reticle said sleeping next to it and I thought, "Oh cool!" I though that meant I could sneak in and assassinate him in his sleep, if I was the right level of course. Then I see that there are two entrances. with guards just standing in the doorway. If I land on the building they hear me. If I approach the building they see me, so that means if I creep along this wall they see me. Maybe I can, nope they see me. What about, nope they see me. I hear a guard call out, "Hey! don't you like our new combat system!" I then proceed through a slapstick fight with the target and twelve guards jumping between as many rooftops as they can before I pepper them full of every arrow in my quiver and the outpost supply. Thus concludes the prologue. I am half done with this long epic of an off-screen journey. Social stealth and thick crowds have completely been removed too. That was what differentiated the barebones stealth system in this series and it's gone.
Setting- I must give praise to the art team. Honestly, the world is stunning and one of the most visually striking recreations of the ancient world. No joke. That is why I bought the game and it delivered. travelling to Alexandria and seeing this game capture that clash of cultures was breathtaking. The video crash requiring a hard reset also took my breath away.
Performance- I don't mind 30 fps. My system was struggling to hit it on absolute max. Understandable. My computer's a little bit older. Then I lowered the resolution. Still under 30. I lower my settings. Still under 30. 1080p no tesselation or anti aliasing. Still under 30. I heard reports of this game always maxing out the processor and only using half of the gpu's power but I haven't seen any concrete evidence so I won't hold it against the team. My toying with settings seems to suggest that may be true. Not sure though. The game looks stunning on max so crank those settings up. Your performance won't change.There are rumors that this game has two background DRMs running and that's what bottlenecks the performance. I hope not because then Ubisoft won't be a misguided punching bag, but flat out disrespectful to their honest customers. We've been down this road before. I would rather pirate the game and be able to adjust my settings to an optimal experience without crashes. It looks like this game can't be played unless you have an i7 that released in the last two years. Something is wrong and as much as I would like to revisit this game to get a more complete picture, I can't. I can't risk frying my cpu and for that reason I cannot recommend this game.
Final thoughts- Hey, games got potential!

All in all - Can i recommend it?  If you like to game with high fps definatly no but if 60ish is good enough (with pretty darn highend hardware) then sure you might like the game.
Personally with 7700k, 1080ti, 64gb ram, game installed on an 1tb 960 pro running @3440x1440 100hz gsync display 65ish fps aint ok due to the games insane cpu loads (and i personally suspect the 4 layers of drm is responcible). I simply expected more FPS with such hardware and AC:O in its current state wont deliver.
So untill that CPU hogging title is patched i cant recommend it if you care about having a high fps.
UPDATE: Ubi have fixed some of the CPU issues in the first patch, all in all its a favourable outcome now.

. Your home (where you need to rest and regain health and energy to train as well some story parts) and an important NPC location (as well as the NPC himself) get removed when you've cleared The Dark Fist DLC storyline. There should've been an option to turn this off or at least have manual saves in place so we could rollback.
In my current save, it is impossible to continue past getting a certain membership card - this is highly frustrating considering how far into the game this happens.
On that note, I cannot recommend this game to anyone.

I've decided to give this game a positive review but it wasn't an easy decision.
The story is very fun - the game parodies all those 80s-90s action movies and does it in a very fun way. You will see a lot of references to famous movies.
Unfortunately, the main gameplay of the game is boring. The game has a mechanism what reduces all your parameters during the playtime. And to maintain your abilitites or to improve them you need to constantly "grind" - execute the same operations again and again.
It is intersting at the beginning, but it becomes boring after several hours of grinding. I dropped this game because of this.
Several months later the game developers introduced "super easy" mode what basically cancel the process of abilities degradation.
The problem is that super easy mode is too easy, while normal mode is too boring. In the end I finished the game in the "Super Easy" mode. It was easy, but at least I enjoyed the story and the humor.

I've always been a big fan of the Cooking Mama series and things like it, and got this game because I figured I'd try something new. Can't remember if I got it on sale or for the full price, but either way, I still think it's worth it if you're into this type of game.
Pros:
-Rather simple to figure out from the start, I feel. I never had any trouble figuring out what to do at the beginning, even if the initial pizza-creation tutorial was slow and boring.
-Easy to remember the controls and how to do things if you've gone a while without playing. I've only got about nine hours on this game, but I still think it's relatively easy to play.
-When there's actual gameplay, it's face-paced and challenging, which is a lot of fun.
-The pizza customization is a major selling point for me. I really enjoy being able to completely custom-make a type of pizza to sell, even to the point of setting my own price on it. It's a really fantastic feature that I think adds a lot.
-Cute pixel art and cute music, and the characters were decent enough even if they were a bit shallow.
-Even if the breaks between gameplay are a bit long and boring sometimes, I still appreciate them. If the activities in-between gameplay were different, I'd appreciate them a whole lot more.
Cons:
-The storyline bored me to death. I typically don't mind stories, but this was pure mundane back-and-forth talking between characters about things I didn't care much about. There was more story than not and it barely held my attention.
-The main menu is kind of confusing to navigate sometimes, but I don't mind too much.
-Tutorials for doing things are another thing that bored me to death, and quite frankly I don't even remember much beyond how to customize pizzas. Absolutely everything was explained all at once, which was frustrating- having the main "how to navigate this screen" tutorial and then having little question marks next to certain parts, so you COULD look at what they are if you WANTED to, would be a lot better in my opinion. A lot of the details are common sense if you already know how games work.
-It would be kind of nice if there was a way to change the size of the text; it's hard for me to read stuff sometimes, especially on the main menu, because of how large the pixel text is. This isn't a major issue though.
-I get being able to advertise your pizzeria and set your hours, as this is, from what I can tell, supposed to be realistic. I don't get why it has to be so complicated and necessary. I don't see the point in setting your hours or doing advertising beyond the basics.
-The entire reason I only have nine hours in the first place is because there's so many complicated features that the true gameplay is swamped in them. I get bored with this game easily because of that.
Despite the amount of cons I've given, I still would recommend this game. It's still a fun game to play, and my mere nine hours were nine hours well spent. If you can get past the complicated bits and the storyline (which I understand might not be a negative for some people, I just personally don't like too much story in a game like this) it's a really well done game for the most part. Devs obviously took their time to smooth out any bugs and make the gameplay part actually playable.
The actual pizza-making is all right... too bad the painfully slow (and tiny) dialogue boxes keep you from doing that very often.

I finished the campaign in one day because I just couldn't stop playing this game. The music was spectacular and learning some of the mechanics and strategies as you go, for me, only added to the content. As you are a survivor in an unforgiving world, you must learn what is an effective strategy of crafting progression and what is not. I look forward to my second playthrough of the game, checking out the director's commentary, and trying endless mode.
If you don't have patience, this could be a frustrating game for you. There don't seem to be manual save points, as far as I could tell, so in the mode I played, if I died or if I had to exit the game, I was reset to the beginning of the region which can be rough if you are struggling and die just before making it to the next region. I also had some issues where the character would auto-run in one direction if I accessed my items and movement in a certain order (fixed by pressing escape and then returning to the game) or at one point, I lost the ability to move my character using my keyboard (mouse clicks still worked but I had to exit and restart the game to fix the issue). I also wish we could change the key bindings (I like "Tab" to be my inventory) hopefully that can come in the future.
So the game is not perfect, but it has become an unexpected favorite of mine. By providing nearly no overt narrative, the beautiful art, environment, and characters, provide a more powerful inferred tale of what this world is and who you are within it. Would recommend.

This game is a representation of Ubisofts design philosophy. They greenlight great ideas with tons of potential and force them into generic genre tropes like a square peg into a round hole. I finally realized that I buy into that potential and find myself constantly saying "wouldn't it be cool if..." during their games. After the Witcher 3, Breath of the Wild, Dark Souls, and Metal Gear Solid 5 Ubisoft can't rely on that potential anymore. The lack of cohesion in mechanics and a core gameplay loop are completely absent. This used to be excused by the open world structure but too many games have proved that excuse a fraud. Not only is this a bad open world game, bad rpg, and bad action game, the elements used from these genres hurt each other and make for an infuriating experience. It feels like it will come around eventually but it's that hollow Ubisoft promise of potential. Let's break down the elements.
Combat- They changed it! It must be good! Unless you aren't just the right level. I was level 8 and get one-shotted by level 10 enemies. Okay, so pick away at them and then run to isolate the target. Well now enemies can scale three story buildings in a matter of seconds so there's no exciting chases. There's no breaks to build up the tension of the fight. If you listen carefully you can hear guards say, "we have a new combat system! This is what you wanted!" as they chase you across the entire Alexandria skyline. You also didn't like how only one enemy would attack before. Now you get to fight a whole Roman legion over ten scraps of wood for that crafting upgrade.Because that's the only way to get wood in the game. These systems just don't mesh. The loot clashes with the artificially difficult combat, and therefore the combat system, and therefore the leveling system and you get a gameplay loop of frustration.
Leveling- The skill tree in this game is a joke. Remember when in Zelda you could collect arrows out of wooden shields. Cool attention to detail, right? Well you have to level up and spend skill points to get that level of detail in this game. All those slow mo jump attacks looked cool in MGS5, right? Well you have to level up to get cool looking, functional combat. Health regeneration and the counter button are skill tree upgrades. Those are key mechanics that inform how the game plays. The upgrades aren't cool additions, they are core mechanics and small details that elevate the experience. So if you want to good experience with this game, level up. But you have to win combat encounters to get xp to level up. You could grind by fighting grunts or challenge yourself by taking on higher level enemies,,, no wait I'm thinking of the Witcher 3 that they aped the open world leveling system from. You can't fight higher level enemies. They just use their canned unblockable animation to kill you in one hit. So if you want to have a fun polished experience you need to farm weaker enemies with half of a combat system.
Story- Ubisoft's CEO's five year old son watched Ancient Aliens on the History channel so modern day is here to stay. Whoohoo! You know that Sci-fi crap that has crippled the ability for this series to explore relevant themes of some of the most interesting and tulmultuous times in history. It's back! I started checking my phone during the second cutscene at about the fifth time jump. Where the story started halfway through a revenge tale (original for Ubisoft) and expected you to be engaged by what was happening. By the time the Title screen pops up two of the five main targets are dead and you have no idea who they were. Then the game decides to flash back to why you should care, then jump forward thousands of years because ALIENS and isn't that what the hip kids are into these days? People just can't relate to history unless they have a snarky modern day scientist spouting off in order to keep the kids interested. What is even going on in the overarching story in these games. Cliche one- evil corporation, cliche twist- IT WAS ALIENS! The time period this game chooses to trip over is the most ripe time period for a game about assassins. Literally the most high profile assassinations of ancient history happened.This game could have explored the political turmoil which led to it but instead we need a mustache twirling conspiracy cult that name drops historical figures.
Stealth- Nonexistent, moving on... well there is a crouching animation. But if you're not the right level you can't assassinate people, In assassin's creed, during a time full of high profile assassinations all around the mediterranean. If you do manage to grind to the place where you can take out one guard before you see a higher level one, and have to grind some more, the enemies will spot you if they are in a hundred yard radius. Then you get to fight and die in one hit, or run and die in one hit. I first really started disliking this game when I perched on a high tower to plan out my first assassination mission. This was for the nonexistent tutorial which drops you into a complex rpg and doesn't explain anything. Hey, Zelda did it and it worked there! I used my eagle to find my target through his house walls. The reticle said sleeping next to it and I thought, "Oh cool!" I though that meant I could sneak in and assassinate him in his sleep, if I was the right level of course. Then I see that there are two entrances. with guards just standing in the doorway. If I land on the building they hear me. If I approach the building they see me, so that means if I creep along this wall they see me. Maybe I can, nope they see me. What about, nope they see me. I hear a guard call out, "Hey! don't you like our new combat system!" I then proceed through a slapstick fight with the target and twelve guards jumping between as many rooftops as they can before I pepper them full of every arrow in my quiver and the outpost supply. Thus concludes the prologue. I am half done with this long epic of an off-screen journey. Social stealth and thick crowds have completely been removed too. That was what differentiated the barebones stealth system in this series and it's gone.
Setting- I must give praise to the art team. Honestly, the world is stunning and one of the most visually striking recreations of the ancient world. No joke. That is why I bought the game and it delivered. travelling to Alexandria and seeing this game capture that clash of cultures was breathtaking. The video crash requiring a hard reset also took my breath away.
Performance- I don't mind 30 fps. My system was struggling to hit it on absolute max. Understandable. My computer's a little bit older. Then I lowered the resolution. Still under 30. I lower my settings. Still under 30. 1080p no tesselation or anti aliasing. Still under 30. I heard reports of this game always maxing out the processor and only using half of the gpu's power but I haven't seen any concrete evidence so I won't hold it against the team. My toying with settings seems to suggest that may be true. Not sure though. The game looks stunning on max so crank those settings up. Your performance won't change.There are rumors that this game has two background DRMs running and that's what bottlenecks the performance. I hope not because then Ubisoft won't be a misguided punching bag, but flat out disrespectful to their honest customers. We've been down this road before. I would rather pirate the game and be able to adjust my settings to an optimal experience without crashes. It looks like this game can't be played unless you have an i7 that released in the last two years. Something is wrong and as much as I would like to revisit this game to get a more complete picture, I can't. I can't risk frying my cpu and for that reason I cannot recommend this game.
Final thoughts- Hey, games got potential!

and
. There is no "choose your on route/story" in this VN, its a direct story with no choices.

Another strong factor here. The music and soundtracks are possibly the most satisfying thing you will love about this VN, considering that it is over 10 years old. Probably the most common question when buying anything is "Is it worth buying it?". If you like light romance and sad stories. This is your best bet. You won't regret your choice, it was made by 'key', so you know it's worth it. TERA TERA TERA
. . . sighhhhh . . .
After nearly 700 hours, I can't recommend this game as an MMO.
It is a fun singleplayer experience up to level 65, which you can get to in a few days.  The environments are freaking gorgeous.  The variety and art direction is truly a wonder.
Running dungeons with friends is fun at first if you're in a guild.  It is the WORST for pugs.
PVP . . . not even going to get into it, some like it, most don't, I'm ambivalent.
THE GEAR GRIND. Uggghghghgh.  So after you max, your true journey begins.  Grinding for each level of gear after max is progressively time consuming.  And after you've run the same dungeon for the 100th time and that drop still hasn't come, you want to punch TERA in the face.
And after you get your RNG drop you have to upgrade it, which is RNG based.  The further you progress, the more everything is based on RNG.  And that's the rub, after a certain point, the game stops rewarding skill and becomes a skinner box slot machine time sink.  Couple that with the fact that there is a certain P2W element (underwear, EMP, loot boxes) and it becomes clear that the game ceases to be about fun, but about time and money invested.
I'm not even going to get into class balance and content updates; it's really a moot point given the above, but it's another detraction.
If you only play for 40 hours, this is a fun singleplayer MMO, and the flaws are completely irrelevant to the casual player.
But getting into this game beyond casually will only lead to inevitble disappointment, as the flaws become obvious, and you realize the game is fundamentally broken and will never be fixed.

This definitely has the fun feeling of the old Road Rash games, but they also added enough to the formula to make it their own game. They took out wheelies (no more ramping off cars to save yourself like in the old games), but they added guns, explosives, blocking, and enemy riders with different resistances (some have a shield that is resistant to blunt weapons, others have armor that is resistant to slicing weapons). They also added "hallucination" mode where cars start raining from the sky for an added challenge, and jump jets for your bikes that can help you hover back onto the road if you're starting to fall to your death. Of course the biggest change is the rogue-light campaign -> you gain money to buy temporary boosts between races, but you also gain xp to unlock permanent upgrades in between campaigns (once you either beat the campaign or die trying).
What I love about the current game: Progression/unlock system. Rogue-light campaign that can be played in co-op (EVERY racing game should have a co-op campaign imo). Solid, energetic soundtrack. A decent selection of bikes and riders that can be unlocked by playing the game. The visceral combat is just as satisfying as the originals.
What I would love to see added to the game: Campaign ++ mode -> currently, campaign+ is very manageable, but it's the most difficult mode available. Furthermore, they need to add some super cool upgrades to the end of the upgrade tree that take an absurd amount of xp to unlock. This would go together well with a campaign ++ mode that could be very challenging, but could reward significantly more xp. As it currently stands, I've unlocked the whole tree and have finished maxing about half of the skills and I've only put 10 hours into the game. If the upgrade system was expanded, it could provide replay value for over a hundred hours, not just 10-15. The last thing I'd like to see added is bomb suit enemies that are resistant to explosives, and ballistic vest/mask enemies that are resistant to firearms. If they were as common as the shield/armor enemies, it would force you to engage in the more dangerous melee combat, instead of just hanging back and mowing down opponents with your automatic rifle or grenade launcher. I think that's a necessary change, as that's by far the easiest way to eliminate the bosses right now. They COULD one-shot you with their melee if you got close, but if you just feather the gas and stay right behind them, they are about 50 bullets away from dead. The last thing is the game could use more tracks.
TL;DR  -  Great combat, cool rogue-light campaign (with co-op up to four people), rockin soundtrack, good variety of bikes/riders to unlock. Could use more tracks, bullet/explosive-resistant opponents, a more difficult campaign mode, and some end-game xp unlocks that will take some effort to unlock. Overall so far 8/10. Could easily be 9-9.5 if they add a bit more content.

As much as I wanted to like AC3, I consider it the low point in the series. Most importantly, I will focus on two things - the game itself and the PC version as such.
First things first, I like things others might not like. I'm easy to get suckered into enjoying management minigames even if they're pretty hollow in this kind of games. They're a casual take on what the Patrician series does, but they're often a non-essential thing. Some people consider these an abomination, though I personally like extra variety in gameplay.
When it's done right. The caravans in AC3 managed to screw it up. They went slightly for a trade game angle and botched it. The rewards are piddly for the effort - while your main source of income in the earlier games was passively buying businesses, you have to manage low-profit crap yourself here. The interface is far from intuitive and it gets to the point where it just adds unnecessary micromanagement. I find trade games rewarding on their own but the minigame is tied into the action part heavily and you can't expand your empire from within while the assistance you get from it essentially makes stabbing some ♥♥♥♥♥es a more optimal way to get money. This is the first deadly sin.
But hey, it's still Assassin's Creed! Free-roaming and combat, right? Well, I found both rather crap. We get a hunting system with atrociously many quick-time events. This is the game's second deadly sin. While I agree that QTEs -might- work in some games, they are a horrible, horrible practice. I'd consider them a last resort because most of them are lazy. The one game I found the QTEs not too obnoxious and paced about right was Shadow of Mordor. AC3? An example of messing up an already flawed mechanic. That's part of the exploration right there, and it's gone wrong.
But hey, at least we have the awesome Assassin's Creed combat, right? Well... no. One word: firearms. I generally loved AC because you can feel like a badass dispatching loads of guards. But AC3 is where the expansion in variety of combat is starting to hurt it. You could argue that it adds difficulty because ez and all games must be hard, and then I could punch you in the face. Difficulty has its place but most people who whine that games are too easy are obnoxious little ♥♥♥♥♥ who want to boost their ego. This is coming from someone who likes Dark Souls. Partly because it's a bit more challenging. Some people call it hard, I could agree with that... and then say that it's not -entirely- that hard, actually and go off on a long rant. Point here is, combat is no longer stompy. While in ACR this point was closer to the end, you have to contend with a lot of firearms from an early point in the game and fights are no longer very fun. You could argue something about subtlety but we're supposed to have a freedom of choice. Of course, it's gotta come with some consequences but that's the problem; it's not strictly -hard-. The problem is that it's somewhere between the golden spots of Brotherhood and Dark Souls - I simply found the combat in the game not fun. For something that puts you in combat a lot, it's a bad thing. The third deadly sin. These two things are somewhat improved in AC4 but we're still talking AC3, where wild animals, hunting and firearms in combat are still♥♥♥♥♥♥  Did I forget about something? Oh yes, naval combat. Do you know why? Because it still feels like it was just tacked on. It's a core and fun part of AC4, in here... well, it feels redundant.
So from the other things to say; Desmond still sucks. The overarching plot only shows the ultimate pointlessness of it, because spoilers. The setting is quite refreshing, as the whole estabilishment of the US of A by these thankless colonials is an interesting point in history, it probably could've been made a little better but the effort wasn't just wasted effort. Well aside from how as a game, AC3 sucks.
I could go on yammering about the typical Assassin's Creed things but, obviously, I'm just gonna stick to where it is in the series. If you're looking at #3 you probably know what the general idea of the series is, and that's parkour, killing poor sods who were unfortunate to get in your way, fighting an ancient conspiracy and/or trying to survive in a hostile world. Virtually every other game in the series is better and AC3 really just feels entirely, completely and absolutely skippable.
Now, let's get to the real dealbreaker - Ubisoft. First of all, they insist on Uplay. That's one thing you should hate them for, by the way, but they put out a few good games so they get away easy. But the real deal is they decided to take the money from their customers, then take a dump on them and run away laughing. What do I mean? Well, technical issues of course. I got the game to run but then -around Boston- I found the game borderline unplayable. Low framerates and stuttering. Even the supposedly more advanced AC4 runs better on my PS3 - which happens to be weaker hardware than my PC. Even on minimum graphics settings. Even without getting to how they deliberately cut down the graphics in their new releases and can't even make a trailer that actually shows you a game. You have the goddamn assets, why do you spend extra time to make them worse? "Not making next-gen buyers feel cheated" is not an option because no one in their right mind would consider a console cutting-edge hardware.
The last few points are not entirely relevant to AC3 but they sort of started with it; it's the point in the series when it was no longer running smooth for me for no apparent reason at all. My distaste with Ubisoft's practices aside, there's a genuine problem with game performance here (and hey, consider Saints Row - 2 was poorly optimized but SRTT works very well even though it has more advanced graphics!) and the fact that we're forced into another download managery thing on top of Steam. I like Steam, thank you. Uplay and Origin are both cancer and downright♥♥♥♥♥♥ We only just got rid of Games for Windows Live, why can't we remove that crap and just agree to use the cutting edge platform instead? I didn't buy it ON STEAM only to have to go through another, inferior service.
In short;
+ It's still got the core AC series stuff
+ Rather pretty, all things considered
- It's still got the core AC series stuff (the modern times Desmond bits breaking the flow, that is)
- Poor side mechanics (caravans - trying to add depth to the minigames and making a monstrosity)
- Screwing up core mechanics (failed experiments with QTE and in combat)
- Bad optimization
- Forces you to go through Uplay

I don't think I can recommend this, but clearly there must have been some reason I kept playing it.
After finishing AC3's main campaign last night, I feel like I basically spent 55~ hours waiting for a payoff that never happened.  There are some really interesting and innovative mechanics here, but I feel like the core mechanics of the series were lost or forgotten.
Arguably the stealth mechanics of Assassin's Creed have been questionable up until this point; you're either hidden or not hidden with nothing in between.  It seems like the game wasn't supposed to be about stealth -- and maybe it wasn't!  But instead of making those mechanics work better, they were all but removed.  Even the scripted stealth missions feel like they're more about finding the road some Loyalist commander decided none of the soldiers are not allowed to look at.
The combat changes seem too cautious to stand out in the series, but notably the animations can be a lot of fun.  The changes to the parkour mechanics, particularly the flow of certain movements (such as ducking and vaulting), were really great.  If there is any one reason to play this game, it's the naval missions.  The conservative innovation of this mechanic is probably the only reason I'll want to play this game's sequel, Black Flag, anytime soon.
I lost interest in the story pretty quickly.  Way back in AC1, I couldn't help but feel for Desmond and I wanted to know more about his side of the story... by the second part of AC2, I was sick of hearing about it.  The main part of the plot following Connor is restricted by actual history and seems to lack ambition.  As for Connor himself, I feel like the writers had more love for pretty much anyone else.  His character has depth and promises growth, but never really delivers it, making him a really interesting icon for the game itself.  The antagonists and supporting cast, on the other hand, continued to surprise me until the end.
By far my least favourite thing is the way the game ends...  Not the story bits, those were all right if perhaps underwhelming, but there was a 20 minute unskippable intermission of credits I didn't really want to read smack in the middle of them...  and there you have it, the perfect symbol for my experience this game.  I enjoyed myself a bit, sat through a lot of things I didn't really care for because I felt like I had to, and then left a little disappointed by the payoff.

Not as mediocre as many user reviews suggested. In my opinion it's one of the better games in the series so far.
There is a great amount of varied content (less than Skyrim, but not far off arguably). The main story is quite decent and of a good length, but it is a bit messy at times. There are also a large amount of sidequests, but as with other games in the series, many are low-key and their sub-plots lack plausibility. Gameplay is standard AssCreed fare - familiar and accessible, but sometimes a bit contrived and poorly balanced. The wide variety of activities prevent things from getting too repetitive. It's almost always too easy, except when the controls and game mechanics are being a pain. Missions have optional objectives for added difficulty, which often works well, but sometimes is more annoying than anything else. Combat looks cool, but usually lacks depth and challenge. The new naval missions may lack plot, and the ships may handle more like motorboats, but these missions are fun, and a great change of scenery. The visuals and sea wave effects are also excellent. The soundtrack is good, even better than in AC-Revelations.
So, as always, realism and historical authenticity leave much to be desired, but the game is still fun. It caters well to the mainstream, but may leave hardcore gamers a bit hungry for more challenge and immersion.
Most environments look decent, and on a technical level the graphics are slightly superior to Skyrim (even with the HD textures DLC), but at the same time, some things still looks a bit dated due to the Xbox360's limits. Like with most console games, the open world still lacks some persistence (bodies vanishing right after you look away, people and even carts spawning or vanishing right in front of you). The detail on the main characters is excellent though. (tip - the low anti-aliasing setting looks better than the high one which makes things blurry).
The checkpoint save system is better than many others, but can still be annoying sometimes. As with past games controls are ok, but a bit temperamental and not optimised for mouse and keyboard, of course. It is a pity you cannot have a standard FPS setup and programmable 1-9 weapon/gear hotkeys. These kind of things are to be expected with this series, and while annoying, they are not too bad, and certainly don't break the game. I have noticed a few minor bugs (the odd missing model or floating object), but otherwise the game runs very stable. Overall, porting to PC has slightly improved since AssCreed2.
Sadly the animus combat training centre has been removed. And one more thing - why can't I gallop(sprint) my horse in town?! In AC-Brotherhood you could gallop only if you had the game installed on an SSD (yes, seriously!). I still have SSD, so WHY U NO GALLOP horsey?!?!
Verdict: It may not be an excellent game, but it is decent, and I can easily recommend it, even if you are new to the series.

The main character was not the brightest, a flaw I could handle, given he was sort of thrust into the larger storyline - but it made for so many stilted conversations, and pauses in the game for exposition in order to make up for the way the arc sort of jumps around.
Visually, I really enjoyed the game. Gameplay-wise, anything's better than the first one. The story was just...bad. I don't expect James Joyce or anything from writers, but if the conceit of this game is that every major conspiracy you'd find on
is really an eternal struggle between Templars and Assassins over alien technology, then the founding of the United States is like a veritable toy chest of rumors and plotlines for everyone from the casual reader of history to the tinfoil hat crowd. Yet the best we get is Oak Island - and that's only if you are willing to explore those sidequests.
But between boring gameplay and a story that was too wrapped up in telling and not showing - making me feel like the game couldn't decide whether it wanted me to play it, or sit through a narrative interrupted with short missions to make sure I was paying attention - is a very unsatisfying experience, overall. Maybe the developers wanted me to feel no real investment in the other characters, so I could better identify with Connor, who was also a fish out of water thrust into doing things for others that he didn't particularly care for. Or perhaps I'm just projecting too much.
Was it worth the $10 I paid? Yes. I got $10 worth of entertainment out of it, and many hours on top of that which I will never be able to reclaim. Then again, I'm easily entertained. Would I recommend it? No. I've played through the story, and I'm feeling zero replay value in this.
Go play AC: Black Flag, instead.

Honestly a fantastic game, from a buggy underwhelming launch has arisen one of the most popular current shooters, with a active and growing community.
The gameplay is fantastic, often deeply punishing yet equally rewarding. Every gun in the game kills with one shot to the head, and you must wait until the mext round to respawn. For people like me, tired of the compressed skill gap enforced by low respawn timers and tiny maps (in games like CoD), Siege offers tactical gameplay favouring team co-ordination and planning. That said, the aforementioned low death times mean it is always possible to salvage a win from drastically unfavourable odds. Nothing in this game is more satisfying than winning a 1v3 with 30s on the clock (at least that's the best I've achieved).
In addition, the one shot potential of every weapon in the game mean that to an extent, every operator is viable. In other team based multiplayer games like Overwatch, I would often feel at a disadvantage due to teammates' decisons (We all know the feeling of seeing Symetra picked on offence), yet in Siege, I never feel disheartened when a certain operator is picked (even Tachanka). However, this isn't to say all the operators in Siege aren't different, they all have distinct roles and playstyles. For defenders favouring a run and gun playstyle, there are charachers like Caveira, Ela and Vigil whose attributes favour a mobile assault. On the other hand, we have 'anchors' like Doc, Mira and Echo who are better suited to guarding the obejective from a stationary standpoint. They are all very fun and have varying degrees of depth, and it is fun to read the bios and watch the intros for the first time. Some of my favourite operators include Zofia, Sledge, Ash, Ela, Smoke and Doc.
To continue, these is a diverse set of maps, all available from the very start of the game. You will spend time learing things like camera locations and obscure flanking routes. Because of every round the objecive spawd in a different location on the map, combined with almost every wall being destroyable, no two rounds play out the same, and Siege has that addictive 'one more game' feeling to it. My favourite maps are the Presidential Plane and Oregon, although I feel they're all great.
I might also mention that the graphics and optimisation for Siege are excellent. Every map features a stunning amount of detail, with an emphasis on authenticity. I never dropped frames even in the most chaotic moments of combat on maxed 1080p (GTX 1060 6GB, i7 6700). The first thing I'd recommend for new players is turning the Field of View (FOV) all the way up to 90 under 'Display' for the best experience.
All this being said, Siege is not a perfect game. Through my 60 hours of playing, I have encountered several minor bugs and connection hiccups. Also, I would strongly recommend against purchasing the starter edition of Siege on Steam. If you were like me, you bought the SE because you were hesitant about whether you'd enjoy the game. I can confidentally say that for most people, the current £13.8 difference is not enough to justify the frankly absurd amount of time taken to unlock the base-game operators. As with any online gaming community, there is a moderate level of toxicity present in Siege, you will encounter many toxic temmates in voice chat and in the text bar thing. I won't try to sugar coat things, my first few matches were frustrating not because of lag or bugs, but teammates taking turns to shoot me before ultimately voting to kick me from the match, simply because I was a new player. Also, I fail to comprehend why Ubisoft decided to allow friendly-fire in the casual playlist, in my experience it leads to toxicity rather than realism.
To conclude, I think Siege is a game everyone should try, even if you thought you were tired of the first person multiplayer genre (like me). Challenging for newcomers, yet very rewarding and ultimately fun, I really do think this is a great game that won't go away anytime soon. Siege has me by the hooks, and I don't see myself letting go anytime soon.

First impression:
This game is beautifully constructed, artful, and at the least the voice actor for the protagonist is to be commended as professional and engaging. Still, I find the gameplay somewhat limited, frustratingly, and the "tell your own story" a slight falsehood.
It is gorgeous and sleek, in its cutscenes and UI. It is simple, but contains about every detail you need short of the probability formulae, and maintains a unique art style that paints the picture while leaving much to be imagined.
Choices you make in the plot do not, unfortunately, influence much about how the story goes, other than within the cutscene to immediately follow, and as a trigger to the game end. As police chief you inherit a crap situation in this game, and while many players might wish to fix the problem uncompromisingly, the game will not permit it. Starting the game, it felt almost like Democracy 3 - make your choices, but stay popular, stay in power, change the city - but such a legacy is not so possible here. In this, playstyles are limited.
Content is wonderfully written and portrayed, but repeated immediately on restart, which you will be doing. Oddly, the game makes a point of telling you when you hit a checkpoint - yet continuing after you've died will just replay the cutscene informing you that you have died. Gamepad support is unexpectedly included, but is buggy as top-level menus or dialogs may not always have focus, or selection continues beyond its reach. You may also seem to be forced into unpleasant choices - sometimes this is the fault of the menus, and may be escaped with some button mashing.
The game's condemnation to corruption or death could be fitting for the gritty reflection of government and policing it may be aiming for, but to me it ends up feeling like being doomed to follow the same one-way street to its end, and I can't bring myself to walk further.

Soundtrack is great. This dev has got 8-bit jamming down pat.

overall, this game is VERY worth it's pricetag. Assuming you aren't anal over having to use a mouse to play it.

This is the First Assassin's Creed since the Ezio Trilogy that truly blew me away.
The world is large and filled with interesting side activities that, for the first time in any AC game that i played, MEAN SOMETHING! They're not just there to fill out the map.
Also, the game looks absolutely fantastic. From the badass outfits to the Pyramids of Giza i haven't found a single thing that i didn't want to look at.
The story starts out a bit slow but gets better and better all the way to the kicker ending.
other pros:
-a skill tree and RPG-like progression system
-absolutely great combat system, far better than any other AC game. You actually have to work for your parry kills for once
-the game rewards exploring, which is great because there's a million things hidden in this game.
-no limits. the world is yours to explore in its full extent from the moment you finish the mandatory intro quest
-you get pulled away from the main quest line a lot , and getting side tracked is not boring at all.
-no BS stipulations for maximum synchronization. In fact, no stipulations on anything. you are truly free to tackle every challenge as you like.
-diverse choice of weaponry
-diverse boss encounters.
-YOU CAN FIGHT BLOODY WAR ELEPHANTS
-game runs smooth. although i read there can be some performance issues, i had none.
-The Bath towel outfit. nothing funnier than slaughtering some Romans in a towel.
-Those Who Came Before give you a lot of food for thought. If you are willing to listen.
-The game's built in Screenshot feature let's you take and look at breathtaking and hilarious pictures from the whole community. Yup this game has its own Instagram. sort of.
some cons:
-farming your upgrade materials can be a bit time consuming
-occasional small bugs here and there, but definitely nothing major or game breaking.
-even though some bosses can be quite the challenge, overall the game is a bit too easy for my taste. I'd like a difficulty setting higher than "hard"
-the AI can be a bit derpy if you have to follow someone or they follow you. Minor annoyance.
-microtransactions. well, it's Ubisoft, what do you expect. but throwing more money at them certainly doesn't give you acess to easy mode.
-Main character tends to have the vegan syndrome. He tells literally everyone who he is and what he does in the first sentence after they met.
Overall verdict:
definitely worth the 60 bucks i spent on this game. i clocked in almost 46 hours now and I'm far from done with this game. Exploring Ancient Egypt at the turning point of human history has been the best gaming experience i had in a while.

This is one of the best stories i've ever had the joy of experiencing.

Now, you might ask: what, exactly, makes Planetarian so great?
