Clocking in at just under 5 hours if you leave auto-read on, planetarian is quite short for a visual novel, but manages to tug quite hard at your heartstrings considering its length. Those of you who have read Key visual novels in the past or watched anime adaptations of them (Clannad, Kanon, Angel Beats, etc.) will know what to expect from planetarian in the emotions department. Those of you that haven't done so, fair warning:
Be prepared to cry.
Key's works are famous for their tear-jerking properties, and planetarian is no exception.
Getting back to the cold, analytical side of things, planetarian was made back in 2004 - 11 years ago, as of this time of writing. Unfortunately, its age shows a little bit. It's restricted to a 4:3 presentation, so you'll get black bars on the sides of your monitor if you try to go fullscreen.
Unless I didn't dig hard enough, you can't manually set the resolution either, which is annoying, but only that; the resolution that's set is just fine - it's probably whatever resolution the original graphics were meant to appear in - and I never had a need to change the resolution for anything during my run. Thankfully, none of the aforementioned graphical issues really detract from the enjoyment of planetarian, as they're all minor annoyances at best, and understandable ones at that.
The soundtrack is good, though I felt a couple tracks early on were too short considering how long they played. The title theme and "Perfectly Human" in particular stuck out to me as memorable tracks. I can't claim to understand Japanese aside from a few common words and phrases, and the voice acting is entirely in Japanese, so I can't comment on the voice acting much.
I notice a lot of people praise the translation. I can't read the original script, but the translated one felt a little bit stilted to me, as if the translation was purely mechanical, paying no attention to how an ordinary English speaker would normally phrase things. Again, nothing major, just a nitpick.
All in all, planetarian was a short, sweet, touching visual novel that I heartily recommend to anyone, regardless of prior visual novel experience.
But bring tissues.
You'll be using them, trust me.

Gameplay is fun at first but after a few hours it gets pretty repetitive. You realize fairly quickly how much it sucks. Overall it does not feel finished. I got this a year ago and it hasn't changed much since it was in Early Access.
It still feels like a beta here and there because of obstacles and level features you can clip through. Namely freeway supports. They aren't that frequent, but they are there.
Weapons are unbalanced. Guns would be the number one weapon you use if it weren't for the fact that aiming is severely crippled. I use a controller and there is no setting that is accurate. Same issue back in early access.
Game punishes you for failure! You can lose 25% of your health for failing to meet objectives, even by a small margin. I mean, really? So if you do poorly you are guaranteed to lose, you just aren't allowed to recover? Stupid idea.
You have to do very very well in order to get powerups since most of your cash will be spent on health recovery. Again with the severe punishment for a lack of skill.
Characters stats are all pretty bland. I have seen two, maybe three characters/bikes actually worth playing as. Basically, just use the standard vanilla setup. Don't bother with anything else.
Handling is bad at high speed, often forcing you into obstacles. I have gotten better but, it's still hard not to crash if you corner fast. Just save the turbo for straight aways.
Level objectives vary from kill targets, to races, to survival. That's pretty much the spectrum of objectives. They are random, but there is only three of them, so not very random. Aside from objectives the game is always the same. Boring fast.
Level design isn't varied at all, despite being randomly generated. Rooftops are always the same, they get boring almost immediately. Every zone has pretty much the same layout just with a different amount of obstacles. Snow level has harder shortcuts but camera issues often turn those into bad detours.
Camera sometimes gets in the way in that you can not see what is coming next. In games like Midnight Club you can see ahead at all times so not knowing where the curve of the road is your own fault. In Road Redemption the camera can hide the road, like in shortcuts, which means shortcuts have to be avoided, except in early levels.
For some reason there are friendly guys, but they are actually your enemies. They get in the way and take targets you need like Mr. Cash or Mr. Healths. Very annoying. I hate the Jackals.
Control is not excellent. Using Nitro is often too easy for me. You double-tap the throttle to activate it, so often enough I will boost away from enemies since lining up an attack often requires you feather the throttle and brake. Brakes when applied hard do not feel powerful. I have mashed brakes before and not come to a quick enough stop, leading to my defeat.
The sound is pretty decent, except for your motorcycle sound, it never varies, is too quiet, and sometimes it isn't there. Seems like another bug that should have been fixed during early access.
Overall a pretty basic and often frustrating game. I find no reason to play it anymore. I find it repetitive now, so it simply can't hold my interest. It would be FANTASTIC as a mobile game for iOS or Android, but on the PC....very lacking in quality. I have played it primarily in single player, and two player a few times back in Early Access. I'll give it another go in multiplayer later, and maybe I will change my review. For now, I can not recommend.

As  it is with almost all Paradox Games at this point,  I have to begin this review with saying that Cities:Skylines is a fun game to play. It is more flexible compared to other (city) building games and revived the old genre somewhat. Now to why this game recived a negativ review: DLC-Policy!!!
To me it is incomprehendable why Paradox keeps going with the way they release DLCs. Either they live in their own bubble, where they keep recieving praise for there DLC or there are enough people falling for there scam..
The game was released in 2015. Since then little chanced in this game. As it is typical for Paradox there were occasional "free" patches acompanied with a somewhat expensive DLC compared to what you acutaly recieve. Mayor free Changes where the Night-Day-Cycle, Weather and upcoming "Green Cities". All of these mechanics where- to put it nicely- a nice addition to your game, above all it increased the immersion.  But then there are the DLCs.
Paradoxs DLC-Policy was always somewhat questionable but with Cities:Skylines it almost feels like your part of a big scam!
There is almost zero subtance to all of the published and to be published DLCs. Don´t get me wrong there are mechanic hidden in the DLCs but it is content that should have been in the game in the first place.
All you get when buying one off the DLCs is a new building here or a new specilization for your districts there (like leisure or tourism in after dark) . Other existing mechanics get more fleshed out. The upcomig DLC "Greener City" will finally feature the possibility to handel the sewage! What a revolutionary feature!

This is an initial review of sorts. I've played 24 hours of the game so far - over about a week and a half.

Now, free vs. paid. Obviously, if you give them money, you get more stuff. Fair enough, they want that. You get 8 char slots up front if you pay. But you only get two if you don't. I had no idea. You can earn in-game gold and purchase another slot. But that's 40,000 gold from what I read.
Anyway, it seems like a good game so far - and while there are benefits for paying & playing, you appear to be able to get everything over time anyway.

I decided to pick up this at full price having seen a brief game play of it. I thought it was going to bring something new to the single player narrative genre, and I wasn’t wrong, it just wasn’t in the way I expected.
Before I drag this game, there were aspects that I did enjoy. Firstly, I loved the direction that the game artist(s) took when making this game. Low poly and crisp lines was an excellent decision allowing the creators to convey a moody feeling through the games muted colour palette. This was one of the things that had me returning to this game. Being one of the few games in the modern era to not have whirling lights, or an overly complicated UI, it was almost relaxing to just look at.
But combine these with the game’s mechanics, and Weappy did an actually good job for the most part. Although I didn’t buy it as a police simulator, that is what I found I was playing. For the first few days I enjoyed sending around my police squad, arresting perps and solving crimes. It was simple enough to navigate and the early dilemma of who to send and how many was challenging. As the game progress I was delighted that the developers continued to add in new mechanics to keep it fresh. From being able to play poker, to the secret account, to even the small things like the update of music players, each one was a nice new addition.
Speaking of music, it was fantastic. Although I stuck mainly to the classical or noir jazz, the range of music was excellent. I was excited when I bought new songs and I had to wait for them. Just the ability to choose your own game music while playing rather than being forced to listen to unwanted songs was a great twist.
But other than that, that is where the good things end, and each one (other than the art) has its own problems. Firstly, the story. I found the narrative to be engrossing when it occurred. However, that is the reason why I didn’t like it. I bought this game as a narrative story, but what I got was mostly a police simulator. Therefore, the story was far and few between the days. As I tried to complete each day as quickly as possible, trying to just get to the story, I was let down more times than I wasn’t, making me actively hate the game as I played it. Don’t get me wrong the story and voice acting was great, but the scarcity of it was disappointing.
The reason why I hated the majority of this game was actually the police simulator. Although I don’t mind playing a few simulators, hell I’ve even enjoyed a few before, this one was tragically flawed. Initially it was alright as you came to grips with the system, but it became repetitive very quickly. Although each case that I sent my police staff on was different (there must have been hundreds of individual cases), each felt like a carbon copy. You just looked at the required number of cops, see if swat or the van is required, send them out, give back up, then they come back. Then you just rinse and repeat for the rest of the game. I’ll have to admit, it wasn’t the most innovating game in the world, not the most complicated.
I know what you’re thinking though, what about the mechanics that got added into the game that I enjoyed so much? Well, although those additions did make the game bearable for at least few in game days, due to the natural pace of the game, these additions soon merged in with the rest of the game. These additions might have been new, but they didn’t add a whole lot to the game, they didn’t actively change the game in anyway. That is why I got bored and hated it, because there was no challenge, it was an easy game with easy mechanics.
Don’t even get me started on the story. That ended up being a total let down. I’m not going to spoil it, but I felt that all my hard work wasn’t even reward. The game wrapped up quite quickly and just dropped me like a fly. With that said, I would not recommend this game to anyone. Unless you like flawed simulation games with a have half written story, then I would save your time and money and buy something else. There are a lot of games out there which are doing a much better job than this.

First things first: If you only watched the trailer, be warned: the game has changed a lot since that trailer. Secondly, this game is an Early Access game. In Rogueland's case, that means things are unbalanced and there isn't as much content as there will be in the future. That being said...
The environments, enemies, everything, is colorful. The music is really good. The gameplay is simple to pick up and easy to improve at. Unlike Magicite, death is no longer entirely permanant. You lose your character, but you can store items in a safe so that your next character can use them. And that makes the gameplay pretty addicting, because you can just keep collecting. Since the game is procedurally generated, it's never identical (even though it's a repeating pattern) which lends itself to how much fun it is to play this game, no matter how much you've already played it.
And the game is being updated every Thursday, with plenty of new content. Just last Thursday, an entire new biome was added, bringing the total up to 5 from the initial 3. A different week, the ability to customize your spaceship was added. The point is, there's always something new to do. Getting a bit bored? Just wait a few days and some other new toy will be added to the game to enjoy.
And the community for this game is really great. The
is pretty active with people giving suggestions, reporting bugs, and answering questions, and the best part is Sean (the developer) is active there too.
"But is it worth the $10 in it's unfinished state?" Oh yeah. For sure. And that's $10 for the whole package, delivered in weekly bundles of goodness. It's pretty loyal to Magicite's playstyle, but different enough that if you didn't like Magicite, you could still like Roguelands.

Also there are unique and different battle styles, items, crafting mechanisms, bosses and lots more. Most of the controls are the same as Magicite's controls so if you played Magicite you should get the hang of this game quicker than others.

One genre that I have always been reluctant to attempt has been sim/management games due to the depth and complexity they seem to project in either previews, lets plays, videos, or reviews. I would give both Yippee Ki yay Mr Falcons quick look video for Pizza Express and the absolute giving it away price of .65 that finally pushed me over to finally give it the ol' college try. Im glad I did because Its totally accessible, addicting, simple, challenging and fun.
Pizza Express is a restaurant simulation game where you are given the reins to your own pizzeria. Here you will manage everything from working hours, advertising, restaurant interior, specials and most importantly the pizza. Their is a story attached to Pizza Express that has multiple ending and choice but its all totally skippable and to briefly summarize in a nut shell you are trying to become the #1 restaurant in town in 30 days. There are also other modes outside the story such as challenge and arcade both of which have online leaderboards. There is a lot of content here and I can't praise the tutorials enough as they are done extremely well to get you started.
The management aspect of Pizza Express is pretty simple as each day begins you will be given the opportunity to upgrade your restaurant with additional tables, change the hours of service or improve the atmosphere with disco lights, music, air conditioning, etc. These upgrades improve the restaurants chic factor which will help you gain customers, improve your restaurant status while also allowing you to increase your profit if you pay attention. You will also manage advertising opportunities with radio, internet, flyers, etc. but on my 2nd playthrough I found advertising to not really be needed and since most choices were expensive I ignored it for the most part. Overall the management opportunities are not overwhelming which makes decision making pretty quick and allows you to get into the real challenge, pizza.
After getting the restaurant ready your next task will be setting up the kitchen with your ingredients, quantity, quality, creating your own pizzas, delivery type, etc and also the menu of what pizzas you will serve and how much you will charge. This component is pretty deep with a lot of variety and important choices to be made and its all customizable to your liking. As a numbers guy I loved everything about this and just the quality of ingredients you choose and the size of your containers can make an impact to the day. After my initial playthrough just moving ingredients around for ease of access, size of the containers for the most popular pizzas, adjusting my hours of service helped increase my profits . There is a slight learning curve but when it all come together its very satisfying.
The action really heats up when you hit the start the day button and you are placed in the kitchen because its Go, Go, Go. Your orders for each table(max 6 customers per/ table 9 max) populate on the left hand side and if you hover over the order it will show the ingredients(thank god). You simply roll(click) out a dough and click and drag each ingredient onto the pizza. That's it. Simple, right? OMG, it is so frantic and there is a timer to serve each order which at first will seem impossible but as you learn recipes and your layout its manageable. It really feels like a dance as you are eyeing the orders and watching your supply because if you run out the wait time to refill an ingredient can be up to 60 sec depending on the service you choose. Once you near the end of day 20(if you don't go bankrupt) with your restaurant close to max capacity and your rep has increased each day can feel like the end of a boss fight and seeing the positive results will provide you with a feeling of victory or in some cases defeat.
As the day ends you are given a score on your service and the restaurant. You will also see your profit or loss for the day which basically is telling you to review what is or isn't working. Are the prices too high, ingredients any good, not enough tables, using the wrong supplier, etc so many factors go into winning. While there are a few graphs provided the one important missing factor I would' like to see is a graph detailing what are the popular pizzas and at what price for each day. If I raise the price of a certain pizza, did I sell less or more on this given day? Its a minor exclusion but you I guarantee you will be asking yourself that question as you continue to grow your menu.
Graphically Pizza Express does not stray to far from most indie games using a very NES coat of paint. Its bright, pixelated and it does the job but I would like to really see this with a more updated look. Sound also takes cues from the NES era and I found them to be a nice mix of beats whether doing upgrades to the restaurant or during the action in the kitchen. Another nice feature I was surprised to find is you can add your own custom playlist. I didn't try it but it looked easy to complete. If Pizza Express is one thing its is driven to provide a lot of player customization which should be applauded.
Pizza Express is a perfect entry for anyone looking to try out a restaurant/ sim management game. It keeps the management aspect simple with enough choices to not overwhelm a player and still provides enough strategic price/ cost depth that will keep even veterans entertained. The strength of Pizza Express still lies in that satisfying, addicting, one more day gameplay. Its fast, frantic and trying to maximize that profit and win the game is really fun.

All you have to do is make pizzas, right?  At first, yes.  Then, in less than a week of in-game time, you're fully managing Gastone's restaurant — stocking new ingredients, creating and serving your own custom pizzas, purchasing ads and decorations...  it goes on and on, but you'll get the hang of it.  And you'll have fun doing it.
One major note, though:  Repetitive motion strain is a thing with this game, especially if you're like me and set long operating hours and a complicated menu.  It'd probably be
gentler on your poor mouse-hand to use a touchscreen, if you have one.  (BTW, hey devs: Any plans to port to mobile or DS?)
A handful of pixels at first feels like an odd aesthetic choice for such colourfully detailed Furries, but the game quickly charms you over.  And I'm guessing that, in general, part of the 8-bit charm is how well it works, in spite of its limitations.
A variety of catchy, upbeat chiptunes.  Excellent motivation to make those pies faster.
Simple, familiar, perhaps even cliche: Dude opens a restaurant, follows in father's footsteps, butts heads with business rivals, etc.  But again, it's charming, and it grows on you.  I haven't gotten very far yet, but already I genuinely care about our little band and want us to succeed.

A nice little wholesome experience for anyone looking for a rough, but fair rouge-lite survival game. Dare I say, despite the rather diminutive size of the game, I found this to be my favorite survival game. 15$ might vary from person to person, but I thought it was worth it.
You play as a lone survivor named Scout who is found by a dog named Aesop. Together, the two try to survive and find their way to a safe haven. The story you get as you play is rather empty and is just mainly "Follow the river until you find civilzation," with a couple major events in between. More adventerous players can find Quilts and even NPCs that spill out hints as to what possibly could have happened, however I still feel like there could be a little more explaination as to what exactly went down.
The actual surviving aspect can be a pretty detailed in some areas and requires a bit of a planning and caution. But (and this is just me personally) if you can get your footing pretty early and know what you need to look for, the game can get a little easy. It stops being survival and becomes more exploration and occasionally fighting off wolves, boars, and if you're unlucky, bears. If hunting is your thing, there are legendary animals you can sometimes come across. Unfortunately the only thing I've heard you can get is their pelt, which is mainly used for crafting warmer clothes.
But surviving on land isn't the only thing you have to worry about, as Scout has her own boat that her and Aesop use as their main source of transportation. It's a simple concept that mixes things up a little, but might get boring for some. You control the boat and try to steer it away from debris, collect loot that can occationaly be found on small chunks of land, and disembark when you find a suitable dock. The boat can be upgraded with little things that definitely make things a lot easier. A stove, a tent, and even an engine just to name a few.
This game is pretty looking. It's got a cartoonish vibe to it with some unique character designs. The houses are old and rickety. Trash is flung everywhere. Roads are cracked. Cars and other metallic objects are rusted and broken. The game has executed that post apocolyptic feel nicely.  A feeling of serenity and solitude is casted from the old and weathered settings Scout can find herself in. After a while, however, you'll probably notice similar elements. Being randomly generated, some sameiness is bound to happen eventually. Landmasses in particular don't have too much depth, so you'll probably notice an island that was shaped just like the one you landed on a few miles back.
The UI is a bit wonky. It can come off as cumbersome and has also been the source of a few bugs and weird quirks I've ran into. It's not unusable though and they do try to make some convienent little comforts for the player. Wrestling with three different inventories (Scout's, Aesop's, and the boat's upgradable storage unit) can lead to overgathering and possibly misplacing some items. Furthermore, I don't see a need for an entire menu for Scout's clothes when you can just as easily use the inventory.
Finally, the music. Let me start by saying the music is mainly folk music. Harmonicas, guitars, violins etc. The music was made by artist Chuck Ragan. If you can appreciate the good ole natural, possibly "hipster" soundtrack, then you are in for a treat. The soundtrack is gorgeous and compliments the setting nicely. It can help keep the spirits up of even the weariest traveler and goes perfectly with scavenging and adventuring the southern backwaters and damning rapids of the river.
Overall, the game is small but provides enough to satisfy that survival itch. Even if you don't get the game, the soundtrack is nice treat for the ears.

The Flame in the Flood is an atmospheric survival game where the player, accompanied by a canine companion, commandeers a raft and travels down a river. Occasionally, the player can stop at a location where they can rest and gather resources. The player then hops back onto their raft and they are back to traveling down river. The raft creates an interesting dynamic as most surival games encourage hunkering down in a single location rich with resources and building towards self sufficiency. TFitF is designed inversely to traditional survival games, forcing the player to keep moving, in a constant state of flux, consistently on their toes. But does it work?
Aesthetically, the game offers an interesting art style with a relatively uncommon color palate packaged into an alluring water color environment. The score is unbelievably engrossing and is easily my favorite aspect of the game. Essentially a compilation of apocalypitc acoustic guitar songs akin to the works of Johnny Cash immerses you deep into the game and couples well with the game's animated climate.
I genuinely enjoyed the short time I spent with this game. The first few hours were enthralling, immersive, and entertaining. The player gathers resources to prevent death or to craft items. There are several types of places the player can visit, and each place will likely provide a certain resource, creating an interesting dynamic in which the player is required to visit a combination of each location. At least it would be, but the loot is mostly randomly generated. Each new visit to a location is gamble, as it will either have seemingly boundless resources that will extend your playthrough substantially, or be met with scarcity, or  even  certain death as you are faced with hordes of wild animals, such as boars or wolves. Despite the random generation, the lack of diversity fails to create interesting encounters and diminishes replayability.
+ Interesting Premise
+ Great & Appropriate Soundtrack
+ Neat Art
- Minimal Diversity
- Little Replay Value
- Finite Gameplay
- Has a fair amount of bugs
The game is definitely worth a play, but I cannot recommend it at its current price and condition. Pick it up on sale if you want to take a break from other games and have a relaxing, melancholic experience.

This here is a prime example of a good kinetic novel.
Both characters interactions and development are fantastic and believable.
Beautiful fitting soundtrack and eye catching illustrations.
While short, the story is amazing, believable and worth your time.
Also you will experience feels, especially by the end.

It is overall difficult to spoil when the game is so short. If you are still text-impatient, there is also an animated OVA that will cover the entire story. As one of Key's first games, it aged well and there was a quite a bit of concepts that will influence their later development. The post-apocalyptic world setting will resound in the Clannad: After Story, Angel Beats!, and especially Akane and Terra Route of Rewrite.
The story is a simple one, a junker found a robot in a planetarium that has been long abandoned. In its core, a typical boy-meets-girl story, hopeful but with a bite. The presentation itself is masterful. World design is distinct but not far-reached, creating a mournful and mysterious mood. The strongest point is probably the character design. Both the visual and audio presentation is superb given the amount of interaction with the player. The weariness and indifference of the main character plays a perfect foil to the enthusiam and curiosity of Hoshino Yumemi, the robotic host.
As short as it is, no words are wasted. Yet there is a slight sense of unsatisfactory:  you would think more robots would be around. Though the desolation was probably crucial to engage the story as a fairy tale of these two. For what it is worth, Planetarian is a bitter-sweet detour. You can quickly become emotionally invested but also quickly become emotionally detached. Compare to key's later work, the build-up is fast and the period of agonizing is rather minmal. Of course the later can leave a deeper mark, but Planetarian will do plenty.

While there were certainly times where I felt the writing was not proceeding down a route that would be considered "good", it always rounded out, and ended up working itself out to be fun and great for character development.  In short, I'm trying to say that, while it may not seem like it at first, the writing works out and is very good throughout the entire 4 hour playthrough.
The 4 hour time that I gave this game is based on reading the game at a normal pace, trying to listen to the voice acting while reading, and possibly spending a few minutes clicking through the CG and Music modes that come with the game.
How does this visual novel score in terms of quality?  Well, writing, characters and story-wise... it's very good.  Heartwarming, even.  I would play it again if I could enjoy stories twice-through, but I'm not that kind of person.
However, visually and technically, this is a very simple, low budget game.  The artwork is very nicely done, but there are VERY few actual scenes within the game, and there is only one character drawn.  There is no animation, and roughly half the game is filled with scenes that are either black or white fills with text.
None of this should deter anyone looking for a good story, though.  The game delivers, and for $5 or less, it's well worth your money.  Just skip the bag of chips next shopping trip and pick of this game (if on sale or otherwise).

Road Rash for me was all about the attitude - sure, the gameplay was fun, but it was ultimately the FMVs, the soundtrack (feat. the likes of Soundgarden), and the menus/shop/general unique art style that immersed me in the badass biker mentality that made me stick around.
This game does an alright job on the gameplay side, with the exception of the wonky sharp turn controls, and the numerous NPCs on the road that don't really serve a purpose, other than to distract you from going after the actual contestants in the races (identified by placement numbers above their heads) or giving you powerups. They got the part where you're on a motorcycle and racing or doing other objectives, giving you a nice arscenal of weapons, but the devs really seemed to miss the point on the art style.
The world is bland and looks like a 360/PS3 or even Xbox/PS2 era game, and the menus/shop/unlockables screens all feel like a spreadsheet thrown together in MS Paint, and just feel a little soulless. A lot of it just feels like placeholder content until they add more polish to it. The campaign is basically just told through text and some below average voice acting done over some non-animated character portraits, and the actual campaign maps are randomly generated, which may add replay value, but doesn't really motivate me to want to play through it for the first time. The online mode didn't really offer any explanation as to what the objective was, and I was pretty much just driving over big gaps in a circle with nobody in sight.
TLDR; for a v1.0 product, it still feels very early access. I'd like to give it another try down the road, but as is, it lacks the substance and overall character of the original Road Rash.

A solid game with an interesting time period and story. The story itself is great, developing more on the ideology of the Templar Order than previous games. The American Revolution was also the ideal event for the rebirth of the Assassin Order. The game delivers one of the most engaging stories of its genre.
The gameplay was really good; the combat became more realistic and entertaining with various weapons to play with, combining ranged with melee. It also added features like the ability to climb not only buildings but cliffs and trees, and also command a ship through fantastic naval battles.
The graphics are amazing to look at, from the american landscapes to its cities. But are some of the most unstable I’ve ever seen in a PC game. The game itself is unstable, crashing randomly and delivering an unstable framerate regardless of your hardware and with some tricky bugs like corrupt save files and bad synchronization. Should these problems like graphical optimization be addressed, this would probably be one of my favorite games and we as consumers shouldn’t be the ones fixing the game after paying for it.
However, if you somehow don’t experience these issues or manage to correct them yourself like me, the game should deliver you with an amazing experience.  The characters are very well written, it really is movie material as well as its music.
I really do recommend this game, but should only be bought on sale due to its poor optimization.

Pizza Express is a fast paced game where you make pizzas on the counter. However, unlike most other games, it boasts a full storyline, in-depth management (you can make your own pizzas on the menu! You can set your opening and closing times! You can add a happy hour!) and a realistic simulation of customers (be prepared for lunch hour).
It also includes Challenge Mode (to test out menus and pizzas, and participate on the world leaderboard) and catchy 8-bit music.

I am unexpectedly delighted with this game!  I grew up during the DOS years, and have seen gaming evolve over several decades.  I never thought that something that nowadays looks so primitive on the surface would entertain me for so many hours!
Pizza Express is a casual game in which you build your pizza restaurant in order to be top in the town.
Gameplay revolves around two phases: planning and business hours.  During Planning, you find out what new ingredients you've earned, create new pizzas to put on your menu, spiff up your restaurant with furniture & special deals for customers, buy advertising, and set work hours.
One of the cool things is that you can create your own pizzas to put on the manu, even customizing the name to make them easier to remember.  They can be as simple or as complicated as you wish.
During Business Hours, notify your carpal tunnel to be on the lookout!  It's a fast-paced build-a-pizza sim where you construct each pizza pie in the orders before the customers lose their patience.  Up to 6 pizzas per order, these come directly from your menu.  You can mouse-over the name to remind yourself of the recipe.  If you make a mistake, just start a new pie.
The game simplifies baking and giving to the customers -- a simple click on the pie will send the pizza on its way!
Pros:

+ Customizable ingredients UI: choose which ingredients you want to use and where they go.
+ Customizable work schedule: make your day longer or shorter.
+ Upgrades for: Ingredients, furniture in the restaurant, tables, etc.
+ Advertising options to fit any budget.
+ Decent and varied soundtrack
Neutral:
~ Controls are a bit wonky during the tutorial.  If in doubt, press Space.  During regular gameplay, things work fine.
~ 160 Achievements -- eek!  Most of them can be gotten by playing through the story, and also making items over time.
Cons:
+ Story segments are often quite long, and usually bring out the negative side in one of the characters.  (Gets a bit tedious over time).
I'm still amazed that I have been entertained for so many hours... Pizza Express has that addictive "one-more-turn" gameplay, and the enticement to see what will happen next in the storyline.  After 6 hours I'm about half-way through the story.
Definitely recommended!

I was looking at this new itteration of the AC series with a skeptical eye. Not because of Ubi being known for performance issues on release but because of the revamped gameplay route they decided to take. I must say I never had this much fun in an AC game. I thought the new combat system had not its place in an AC game, but man, how wrong was I. With my hands on the game, I love the new gameplay, real good surprise here. And the bows, omg the bows I love all of them, thank you Ubi for making them all have a unique and relevent playstyle. And the storytelling, it has gone up by a big margin, I have never been this much eager to play an AC game before for its story.
I have only one complain gameplay wise : stealth kills. I don't know why nobody seems to notice it, but only 1 kill animation feels realy wrong here. Since the last AC games had so many animations for hidden blade kills I'm very sad to see Bayek doing over and over the same single move. You could argue he is the 1st assassin, and there for he doesn't have as much skill as the lastet assassins from th 19th century. But still I'm disapointed by that.
Now about performance, I have a GTX 1080 with a i7 4790k and 24GB of RAM. As you might imagine I get fps dips in the cities and I tried to figure out how I could prevent it from happening, but it seems there is no work arround it. No graphic settings nor resolution can change the poor performance in the cities. Almost constant 100% CPU usage on all cores in the cities. I heard Ubi is gonna adress this issue. But I don't know how they gonna do that since it apparently comes from the anti crack software Denuvo on top of another one (which I don't remember the name) which supposably are using 40% of your CPU power.
So if you are a constant 60 fps lover like me you ganna have a hard time living with the fact you can't change the performance. I spend most of my game time trying to fix this stuttering. But then I gave up and started to realy play the game.
In conclusion, this is by far one of the best AC game ever released and I highly recommend it to any one not concered with performance at all. Just jump on this game its well worth it.
If you have a "beast" CPU, one of the latest to be released, you'll probably have no issue with the game.
That being said, if you have a "good" CPU you have a high chance of experiencing poor performance in the cities.
If you can't play a game if it's not at constant 60 fps, I'd recommend you waiting on new comming patch until people stop complainig about high CPU usage and bad performance in the cities.
I was almost tempted to give this a negative review, but after giving in to trying fixing the preformance problem and just experiencing the game, I must say this is the AC game I had the most fun with in a long time. So I defenetly recommend this game!

Once you've played about 30 minutes you've basically experienced the entire game. You have to travel down a river for no particular reason while stopping to pick up supplies on the way. It's basically like driving down the same boring highway for hours except you don't know where you're actually going and you have to pull over at a rest stop every five minutes so you don't starve and die.

There are very few games containing these elements  (substantial procedural generation and rogue like mechanics) that are able to balance fun AND fairness.  This succeeds at both, in my opinion.  There is a mode available that is great for an introduction to the game, where checkpoints that have been reached can be used as spawn points if you die.  This is great as it allows you to get used to the game without being punished consistently.  Once you're familiar with the game, there is a secondary mode which functions more like a traditional rogue like, where you have to start from the beginning if you die.
The crafting is very realistic and manages to have depth without being overwhelming or redundant.  The pacing is great.  The art style won't appeal to everyone but is consistent and functions well.  The music is great, as well.

The Flame in the Flood is a story of a little girl and her dog travelling down a flooded river on their makeshift raft. The world has been heavily flooded and you have to survive. The Flame in the Flood is basically another survival game, think of games like Don't Starve. The objective of the game is to make it all the way to the last zone alive.
The gameplay shifts between 2 modes, river rafting and location exploration. While river rafting, you steer your makeshift raft down the river looking for special locations to land at to collect resources, sleep or complete quests. While location exploring, you run around a procedurally generated location looking for resources, crafting, sleeping, using a fire, upgrading your rickety raft with engines or topping up gas. How a little girl manages to do all that on her own is never explained logically in game.
There are 4 stats that you must watch out for tiredness, body temperature, hunger and thirst. If any of these hit zero, get ready to die. There are also a whole host of diseases, afflictions, wounds and hazards to deal with. E.g. Broken bones, snake bites, food poisoning, etc
Conclusion, while the game may look interesting at first glance, it is hard to find any fun within. It is mainly about surviving the "pseudo-random" encounters generated for you. The game is designed to give you resources to solve a specific problem or else. So, you are lead down a garden path with specific problems and solutions. The problems also make the game more about taking safe choices rather than taking risks and exploration. You try to avoid any dangerous paths. I would not recommend this game for fun.
Note: This game was funded on Kickstarter.

I thought I was over this VN, only to stumble upon one of its songs months later and feel tears well up in my eyes.
As short as it is, Planetarian presents a thoroughly well-written (albeit not perfectly translated) emotional ride that will not be easy to forget. It never seeks recourse in common anime tropes and stands stoutly on its own writing, as should be the case of any well-executed narrative. This is done to such an extent that the anime art style feels almost inapproriate (but don't take this the wrong way - the anime aesthetic is by no means a failing). Overall, I feel Planetarian is a grossly underappreciated VN that deserves far more success and popularity than it has received. Coming from a scrooge, perhaps the most powerful praise I can give to this game is this: in spite of its short length and lack of any gameplay, I consider paying the full $10 is a perfectly justified purchase.
Should anyone prejudiced against the anime genre somehow find himself reading this review: I urge you to throw away your preconceptions and consider this VN in isolation. If there is ever an exception to be made to the rule, Planetrian is it.

Reminds me of my childhood! And then your friends came around to your house and you were wasting hundreds of hours playing that game.
And now I feel like I am back on the track! Back to the memories, back to that feeling when you was playing games for hours and was not bothering yourself with some creepy adult bs. I loaded the game and I played few hours in a row and didn't even notice how time did past.
So, first of all, to any of you, who don't know a thing about the original game - this is an action motorcycle game, where you are playing as a leader of a bike gang which is obsessed with a justice. Your whole mission is to get past the three different locations to kill anyone who crossed your way and the trick is that this game was designed that you will die. A lot. Like, I mean it. You will die a lot. So the whole idea is that you need to ride as far as possible to gain experience and money to spend it on upgrades and every time you upgrade yourself it becomes a lot easier for you to play this game.

Truth be told, the whole graphic in this game is a bit outdated and driving can be a bit awkward sometimes. But, it doesn't bother me at all, to be honest, cause I still have a lot of fun and I feel really great spending time on this game.
So, to sum everything up! You should buy this game if you:
+ Love fun arcade action games
+ Love driving
+ Played a predecessors game and feel nostalgic
+ Love upgrading your hero
+ Obsessed with a bikes (obviously!)
+ Wanna spend at least 10+ hours full of fun
You should not grab it if you:
- Wanna see something amazing, new and innovational
- Looking for a game with a blat grapgic
- Don't feel like dying a lot of times and then starting a new game again and again after upgrading yourself
- Just not interested in this kinda games but still wanna try it to give a chance.
Enjoy!

In almost all the obstacles in the opening hour I felt like I was guessing half the time, throwing myself at a brick wall. Often solving the puzzles didn't lead me to understanding the game mechanics any better since the 'physics solution' that I came up with in this "physics platformer" was not the right way to solve the puzzle, but I had to do it single right (weird) way.
The music was pretty good, although at the sloww frustrating parts in the beginning hearing loud cheerful gleeful music made it feel really pretentious. It's a similar feeling to when video editors put emotive music behind the video to make you feel a certain way, but it's not how I am feeling; I don't want someone to tell me how to feel about something, especially in a game. That's just a small point - on the music - but I wanted to say.
The graphix did look pretty good, the style of the game was neat. This is the Police presents you with a relentlessly bleak world. The mayor is corrupt. The police department is corrupt. Your wife just left you. And the game starts with you being fired from your job, which will become effective in 180 days.
Very early on, the game presents you with a stark choice: Abandon a life-long friend who made some very poor choices and got himself stuck deep in a hole, or save him and sell your soul to the mafia. I decided that as the police chief, I would sacrifice everything to focus on one thing: do a good job as police chief. I sacrificed my friend.
In between, every day of work started with the same rituals: you turn the ignition in your car, three times, until it gets going and is ready to take you to work; and then you go through your vinyl records collection to choose which song you want playing throughout your work day. It's charming the first two times. It becomes unbearably long thereafter, needlessly wasting your time before you can get to the gameplay.
The gameplay itself is fine, and is the only thing I liked about this game. You can get an idea for what it's like from the game's video trailers.
What's not fine is that the gameplay sells you the illusion of choice. When you had to choose between abandoning your friend or selling your soul? It was not a real choice. You had to give up your soul no matter what. I though I was off the hook with the mafia, and I did everything I could to oppose them. My character was promptly assassinated by the mafia afterwards, which can only be avoided by giving in to their demands. Rather than become a servant of the mafia, I accepted this outcome: I tried to be a good police chief, and my character died in the line of duty, signalling the end of the game for me. It made for a short, disappointing game, but it was preferable to embracing the hopelessness of the setting and have the game keep wasting my time with those eternal car ignition and music selection screens.

This game, despite it's simple drag-and-click gameplay, kept me hooked. Don't feel discouraged when I say drag-and-click though, because it's about how cleverly the developer revolved other features around that drag-and-click gameplay.
You get almost the entire power to choose how you want to play. You can make your own menu super complicated with a large reward, or play casually and put in only a few ingredients per pizza for a modest sum. You can even determine the difficulty at the beginning of the game too, so the entire game almost caters to everything for your own convenience and skill level and allows you to enjoy a smooth gameplay. For the story, don't expect something philosophical or complex really, it's just a simple linear story, but it still has a decent amount of surprises to keep you engaged until the end.
One issue though is the long and boring tutorial. But you can skip that, and you won't miss much if you do. It could deter you a bit, but I promise after that it only goes uphill from there.
Another small issue is the spike in difficulty starting at Day 20, but maybe that's only me. Doesn't really matter though, but I opened a discussion about it in Steam anyway. Surprisingly, the developer commented on it in detail about it, and I noticed he comments a lot on other discussions regarding the game too. So it seems he cares a lot about this game.
I may be slightly biased or I may be overexplaining everything, but I really enjoyed this indie game.

Punch Club is an oldschool arcade fighting manager. I dont call it simulator, because you dont actually fight with your character, you only train it and decide, how it will become stronger.
The story is something from the Kung-Fu 90s movies - you are to avenge your fathers death so you have to train harder and become one of the champions to challenge the bad guy. The gameplay takes a bit getting used to and there are actually quite few tricks you have to find out, before managing to proceed further with story. The gameplay is based around managing your character, deciding when to fight, train, eat, sleep and work for money. The story is really well combined with side quests - you feel like every character in the game has its place and is somehow connected to your main story. Besides that, you will have some decisions in the game, that will change how you will proceed and finish the game. There are two main quest lines of which you can pick only one. The ending is not absolutely satisfying, but the road there was much fun and some side-quests had nice dialogs and the reference to famous fighting movies, games and super-heroes magazines are amazing.
The combat in Punch Club is heavely luck based, especially if you take agility based builds. You can win a fight without taking a single blow and knocking your opponent in the first round, but you can also lose without hitting the enemy once because "RNGesus" is spitting on you. It is nice you can speed up the combat to x4 speed because when farming achievements or replaying the game it gets boring to watch the passive fights. Since you cannot control anything during the fight itself, the only thing to do for you is swapping the skills between rounds if needed or getting the experience which skills to get next to beat the opponent you lost against.
The game is quite challanging because of "stat decay", that means your fighting abilities dwell over time, so you have to carefully plan when to train and when to work for cash to be able to feed yourself. If you play the game on "Hard", it gonna definetely take some time to beat it especially if its your first run.
Retro style graphic absolutely fit the game and there are some nice details here and there to look for. The small details greatly increase the immersion and make the game more fun (for example take a look at who is standing outside Apu's shop, or the pictures hanging in some houses, etc.). The interface is simple and offers not many functions, maybe lacking a bit in flexibility. It would be nice to set-up how many hours you want to train on a bench or to what exhaustion level you want to work. The game is based around decisions made for your character, but the interface does not provide all needed tools for perfection.
The progress depends heavily on the difficulty you picked. On the hardest difficulty the progress becomes quite grindy, since you have to "work, eat, sleep, repeat" a lot. Then you lock yourself for few days in the gym training to be able to take 1-2 fights and you are out of cash again, so the cycle starts again.
On the middle difficulty the progress is much quicker, so it is possible to finish the game in few hours achieving the hidden 100 days achievement. Sadly, on certain phases of the game it does not let you progress quick enough by holding back the fights telling you the opponent gonna be "read in few days". It slows you down unnessesary, but gives you some more time for training.
There are no activities to be considered mini-games in Punch Club, so this point is not taken into rating.
The music and audio in generel absolutely fit the style of the game. Retro sounds to retro graphics make you feel like playing this old coin machines that were standing in clubs in the 90s. The game has nice details for immersion, some side effects like flashing graphics and squicky sounds that increase the immersion effect at the right spots in the game.
Punch Club is so far the best fighting manager in retro look. The game has great feeling and immersion, especially if you loved oldschool Kung-Fu or fighting movies and has tons of references to movies and characters somehow connected to fighting. It offers nice challenge, replayability value and impactful story decisions.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.

Planetarian is a relatively short VN (~4 hours) that has no choices for the player to make, instead preferring to tell a set story of its own choosing. While this might bother some since that means that this "game" is little more than a few hours of reading with voices and artwork to go with it, the creators of Planetarian are none other than Key/VisualArts. If you are at all familiar with Key/VisualArts or their other works (notably Kanon, Clannad, and Little Busters!), then you have a pretty good idea what to expect from this: a well-written story, quality artwork, and a deeply emotional conclusion. While Planetarian is tiny compared to Key/VisualArts other VN's (Clannad is at minimum a 50+ hour game, and Little Busters! is about the same size), the quality of their other works ought not to be ashamed by this. In other words, Planetarian is quite good, despite its length and lack of choice.
If you are familiar with Key/VisualArts other works and enjoyed them, then checking this out should be a no-brainer. If you are not however, consider Planetarian a small teaser for what is to come: Clannad will be released on Steam before the year is out (Fall 2015 most likely), and hopefully Key/VisualArts' other works like Kanon or Little Busters! won't be too far behind. Or you can just watch their anime versions if you can't wait that long (I personally recommend Kanon 2006 and Clannad/Clannad After Story for that). Enjoy! :3

Planetarian: The Reverie of a Little Planet is a short Japanese kinetic visual novel from Key.  Anyone who knows visual novels knows Key.  They are one of the most respected studios out there, known for their amazing characters and touching stories.  Released on Steam just in time for the 10 year anniversary, how does Planetarian hold up?  The short answer?  Quite well.
Planetarian is a simple story, set in a post-apocalyptic landscape.  The nature of the harsh world is hinted at throughout the experience, handing out bits and pieces of information regarding the reason for the fall of humanity and the harm we did to our own planet.  Our protagonist is a middle aged man known only as "The Junker."  He is a scavenger.  He lives by finding things to not only maintain his own survival but also by finding things of value within the ruins of humanity and bring them back to the various outposts and villages.  He even had a partner, at least for a while.
The story takes place in one of the "coffin cities," locations of horrible biological and germ warfare.  While avoiding automated war machines and searching for supplies, our protagonist heads deeper into the city interior, towards a dome shaped building.  Initially thinking it might be some type of military instillation he proceeds further only to discover that it is a department store (based off of the Matsubishi Department Store in Hamamatsu) with a planetarium at the top.  It is here that he meets Yumemi and Miss Jena.  What happens?  Who are these two characters?  Find out for yourself.
But to summarize the tale itself is heart breaking and very well written.  It can be a bit wordy at times but I personally feel that is part of the charm.  At a certain point you'll start to feel this sense of dread creeping up your spine and by the time our story reaches the climax and the scenes following you'll be reaching for something to dry your eyes.
The visuals were beautiful when Planetarian released over ten years ago and they hold up to this date.  The sprites are gorgeous, the backgrounds, while simple, do a fantastic job of painting a bleak picture for a bleak world.  The only major issue I have is the resolution of the resources, which are a result of age, nothing more.  Despite being as old as it is Planetarian still looks great.
The music is great.  Fantastic.  Designed to take a back seat to the visuals and the story, the various tracks fit the changing moods well.  At times whimsical and upbeat while or foreboding and downtrodden, it is honestly shocking how well it holds up.
Planetarian also features full voice acting, in Japanese.  The quality once again shows its age but is still well done.
From a technical standpoint, and remembering the visual novel is more than 10 years old, it is functional but that is about as nice as I can be.  The font is...readable and everything functions the way it should...but it is old and it shows it.  Upon completion you will unlock the CG Gallery and Music Gallery.  They're expected but still nice little treats.
Is Planetarian: The Reverie of a Little Planet worth your time and money?  Absolutely.  It is a classic of the visual novel medium, the perfect length for the story it sets out to tell, and to this day still beautifully haunting.

This is the First Assassin's Creed since the Ezio Trilogy that truly blew me away.
The world is large and filled with interesting side activities that, for the first time in any AC game that i played, MEAN SOMETHING! They're not just there to fill out the map.
Also, the game looks absolutely fantastic. From the badass outfits to the Pyramids of Giza i haven't found a single thing that i didn't want to look at.
The story starts out a bit slow but gets better and better all the way to the kicker ending.
other pros:
-a skill tree and RPG-like progression system
-absolutely great combat system, far better than any other AC game. You actually have to work for your parry kills for once
-the game rewards exploring, which is great because there's a million things hidden in this game.
-no limits. the world is yours to explore in its full extent from the moment you finish the mandatory intro quest
-you get pulled away from the main quest line a lot , and getting side tracked is not boring at all.
-no BS stipulations for maximum synchronization. In fact, no stipulations on anything. you are truly free to tackle every challenge as you like.
-diverse choice of weaponry
-diverse boss encounters.
-YOU CAN FIGHT BLOODY WAR ELEPHANTS
-game runs smooth. although i read there can be some performance issues, i had none.
-The Bath towel outfit. nothing funnier than slaughtering some Romans in a towel.
-Those Who Came Before give you a lot of food for thought. If you are willing to listen.
-The game's built in Screenshot feature let's you take and look at breathtaking and hilarious pictures from the whole community. Yup this game has its own Instagram. sort of.
some cons:
-farming your upgrade materials can be a bit time consuming
-occasional small bugs here and there, but definitely nothing major or game breaking.
-even though some bosses can be quite the challenge, overall the game is a bit too easy for my taste. I'd like a difficulty setting higher than "hard"
-the AI can be a bit derpy if you have to follow someone or they follow you. Minor annoyance.
-microtransactions. well, it's Ubisoft, what do you expect. but throwing more money at them certainly doesn't give you acess to easy mode.
-Main character tends to have the vegan syndrome. He tells literally everyone who he is and what he does in the first sentence after they met.
Overall verdict:
definitely worth the 60 bucks i spent on this game. i clocked in almost 46 hours now and I'm far from done with this game. Exploring Ancient Egypt at the turning point of human history has been the best gaming experience i had in a while.

This game is amazing. Definelty should be on your must get list. Especially if you loved any of the previous games.
Story (8/10): An amazing story filled with lots of dynamic characters. The main character, Bayek, is wonderfully portrayed. He is a very fleshed out character with a relatable story, witty comments, and is someone you will care about as the story progresses. Aya is also really cool and fun to watch/play. Even the villans have diverse stories and characters, each doing the things for their own reasons. The side quests are also varied to some extent and have great wrting and add to the main story in a good way. The only complain I have here is that there tended to be a lot of quests that involved "pick up this person and bring them there", but overall this doesn't ruin the experience at all.
Fighting/Stealth/Ranger Mechanics (9/10): These gameplay mechanics clearly had a lot of time put into them. You can really stick to playing one of the styles or a mix and mash. The abilities in each ability tree give you lots of freedom and anything you pick will be useful to you. Fighting itself has improved greatly from previous games even if it takes getting used to. The previous games' model of fighting is all gone now and is replaced with a witcher 3/dark souls model. Positioning and weapsons/gear are now important and so is the new loot type system they have implemented. Overall fighting is challenging and fun and it even comes with 3 difficulty settings.
Open World (8/10): There wold of ancient Egypt is filled with lots of places to go and see. There are a ton of side quests to the point it can seem overwhelming at times. There are also varrious activities and collectibles to go and do/collect. There are even random missions that can happen while you are traveling such as animal attacks or avenging another player. You will not get bored exploring this world.
Music (9/10): It's phenominal. Really great music at the perfect moments. You will enjoy it and feel it's epic
Crafting/Loot (7/10): This part of the game is important and works well but it feels like it lacks diversity. Crafting materials are easy to obtain, just a bit of a pain to go and find. Loot also works well but feels the same as crafting. Various weapons/bows and shields drop from certain enemies you kill or you can find them in chests you loot but overall most of them are useless. You find yourself selling/dismentaling them all except the rare or legendary ones. I find myself desiring a bit more variety for these systems but overall they work well so don't fix what's not broken.
Senu Mechanics (10/10): Eagle vision has been replaced with an actual eagle buddy, called senu, for you to use. Senu flies up and gives you an arial view. He can mark certian objects/enemies for you. This works significatly better than the old eagle vission. Your view is no longer marked with red/orange/blue highlighted guys. Senu gives you a clear picture of enemies in the area with a small little triangle on screen. Honestly this is a perfect mechanic that i wouldn't change at all. I hope they keep it for future games.
Performance (6/10): The game looks beautiful and on my current build I can max it out no problem. It's very playable and there are barely any bugs that I have noticed. I am however quite desapointed with the resource alocation that this game uses. I quite offen in densely packed areas find it using my cpu to 100% while leaving my gtx 1080ti to around 50%. This really caps frame rates to about 60 and sometimes under at max settings. I wish the developers would look into this for the future and make sure it gets patched later.
Overall score: 8/10

Not the most forgiving game, certainly. On water, your raft is tricky to maneuver until you've had a lot of practice. The controls are a bit of a mess, or at least difficult to figure out, i.e. left and right cause the raft to turn, left plus paddle causes it to shift to its left (not your left, necessarily), and the currents prominently affect which direction it moves, and how fast. Expect to spend some time getting the hang of each aspect of rafting... but then, that's half the reason to buy this game, isn't it? And it's well implemented, overall. Challenging to learn, satisfying to master.
On foot, you'll likely have a similar learning curve. The crafting system gives you access to a variety of tools for survival, including the tragically impractical bow and arrow -flint, a sapling and a feather for one single arrow which, if you don't miss (which, with the aiming mechanics, you are likely to do, especially while learning) will still not kill any of the things that like to charge at you and gradually murder your frail girly form. There's the torch for scaring off animals when it's not raining, which seems to have fairly limited utility. There's the gas bombs that stun things (including you) caught in their temporary cloud of fumes, fairly useful with a little tactical thinking. There are better ways to take down the scary things, though; find them, use them, or just evade the beasties if that's your thing. Probably want to invest in a stove and shelter for your raft in that case, though, to help manage the freezing cold as you progress toward the latter areas of the game... and even if you do become a fearsome monster slayer, the process of creating the best beast hide clothing is convoluted to say the least.
The health system is a little odd. Get hurt, you slow down. The more hurt you are, the slower you get. Makes logical sense; wounds do tend to impair focus and motor function. It makes for a fairly all-or-nothing combat system, though; every time I died to creature attacks, it wasn't a close thing, nor were the times I survived a sticky spot. With three or four wounds, you really stand virtually no chance of escape or fighting back, which is where the game can get highly frustrating... especially if the last checkpoint was a long way back, or your pride compelled you to choose permadeath mode. I don't recommend the latter for your first campaign, incidentally; you can always come back and attempt it on a second run, no? So, returning to the topic of the health system, you have craftable items that cure cuts, herbs to cure stings, and splints to help mend broken bones. You also have antibiotics in case you don't fix a cut or sting in time. Here's the thing: I used an antibiotic /once/ in my entire first successful playthrough. There simply weren't enough wounds to exhaust my stocks of healing supplies -well, early on maybe, but not later- except perhaps those few times when I died of five or six lacerations and time skipped back to the last checkpoint. There doesn't seem to be much point to keeping a substantial stock of medical supplies; either you die in an encounter, or you come out mostly fine. You can't bandage yourself while under attack; it takes time, and enemies attack with frightful speed. So running, evading, stunning, trapping or just fleeing back to a campfire or the dock become your primary means of surviving attack... thematically appropriate, perhaps, but jarring for more action-oriented gamers, and anyone hoping that using the bow to fight off attackers would be... at all viable.
So, we have a harsh, tricky-to-learn game which at this point probably mostly sounds like a major pain in the butt. Right?
Wrong.
The Flame in the Flood is a masterpiece. Maybe not the most engaging
experience, but the thrill of white-water rafting, running around foraging for lumber supplies in a storm, slowly but surely making your way to the journey's end... it's a powerful and remarkable blend of impressions and challenges. That this game was put together by individuals who left the big-budget triple-A quagmire to pursue independent development, and to see them create something with so much soul, so much heart... that truly inspires me.
Also, the soundtrack is frickin' sweet. I'm not even particularly fond of that style of music, but it really, really works here.
In closing: Hard, but also beautiful; well worth the effort. It's not a very long game, but definitely worth experiencing at some point.

This is Minesweeper with more than one life (the player can be granted up to seven lives at a time). As Minesweeper is half-deterministic and can be played as "classic mode" in Fine Sweeper as well, Fine Sweeper can be seen as an extended version of Minesweeper including an editor for random maps created from the following data:
- Height (of the rectangle)
- Width  (of the rectangle)
- Number of bombs to encounter
The standard campaign, where the size of the randomized rectangles rises continuously with the number of bombs, is supposed to be played till level 51 and beyond, which, for friends of Minesweeper, signifies a clear recommendation.

I'll admit that the original minesweeper from the 90's was my favorite way to procrastinate and waste time whenever I had important assignments due or serious finals to study for.  I've spent hours playing it straight into the wee hours of the morning only to realize at 6am that I was completely screwed because I hadn't yet started writing that essay or even cracked open a text book.  Nothing like turning on the computer with the very best of intentions and thinking "hey I'll just play one game to get my brain going before I get started" only to fail miserably every time.  Ah, the nostalgia...
If you were a fan of the original minesweeper, this game is a must have for your steam library.  It plays much like the original and has some added improvements which makes it even more addicting if you can believe it.  Multiple modes are included in the game, my favorite one being the campaign mode which progressively gets harder the more you advance.  I've long since collected every achievement in the game but I keep playing it because the challenge is so enjoyable .
I find this game to be very satisfying and relaxing but I don't think everyone will feel the same way.  If you are on the fence about it, I would suggest playing the free 90's version first to see if you enjoy it at all.  If you don't, you likely won't like this one either.
UPDATE 11/26/17:  I am nominating this game for the "No Apologies" award category in the 2017 Autumn Awards.  As of today I am STILL playing this game, and no one I know in real life can understand why I'm so into it.  I don't really understand it either but the important thing is I'm still having fun and don't care what anyone thinks.  =)
If you are a minesweeper lover, this game is for you! :)

First played Road Rash back in the early 2000s on a Windows XP (I think?), didn't even know how to save the game nor why the menu and gameplay had such disparity in graphical style back then.
Now there's this revamped version of that old pixelated love that accompanied me through my childhood, and I absolutely love it (regardless of how people say this is not a racing game or not a true rogue-like game or whatnot). All I have to say is this game delivers the same (or more) adrenaline I felt from the old Road Rash, and that's all that matters.
I understand there are still imperfections in the game like how it is advertised to work on macOS but still has many bugs, or how the black screen stays for a really long time when the game starts, or how the storyline is really bad compared to the old Road Rash (believe it or not, the characters in Road Rash all have their own backstory that made me emphatised with them), or how the game physics still need improvements.
But this game had been on my wish list for the past 2 years, and given how small the development team is, I think I can no longer wait. For the very first time, I believe my impatience served me well.
Despite all troubles I had at the beginning, I throughly enjoyed the game and I highly recommend it for old fans of Road Rash.

Just finished up the entire series for the first time (not including black flag, unity, liberation and rogue) and I have to say I recommend all of them. It was a lot of fun going through this whole series but this one really stands out for me. Not because it's better than the other ones, which if I'm being honest it isn't, but rather the hate this game has recieved. I feel like this one is extremely underrated. The intro with Haytham is amazing, it was so well done and parts of Connor's intro were also good. However this game does kind of start to fall apart at times, I'd say hold out on this game until you pass that stupid Paul Revere section half way through because past that this game picks up speed big time.
The big problem with this one is that it really does insist on beating you over the head with historical references in a really annoying way. Like the Benjamin Franklin scene is a good example of being very half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and especially the Paul Revere section as I already mentioned, the teaparty event was all the work of an assassin of course and a templar was responsible for the Boston Masacre, wtf. And here's the Decleration of Independence being signed guys!! *wink* *wink* It felt like I was having my intelligence insulted at times, because of how cheesy and uncreative it was, they handled it really poorly. Oh and the bugs, this game has lots of bugs. I got lucky and didn't experience too many but I've seen the reports on bugs, so be careful buying this game, same with revelations, I'd recommend getting them on sale just to be safe. Also, the mission design and the controls in this one are clearly the weakest in the series.
To wrap it up, the first quarter of the game is overall good, the second quarter was when things started falling apart, then third and fourth quarter it completely comes together and turns into an awesome story. I wont spoil any more stuff beyond what I've said. It also finishes off the desmond storyline which was done well overall but I felt it could've been much better if they included an epilogue to his story but I can't blame them seeing as how it's easy to run out of time when your being rushed by ubisoft. Overall I recommend it, just hold out on the story and have some patience is all I ask and if you don't like it I don't blame you, it really is a hit or miss game.

Assassin's Creed III is a game of many flaws, but at the same time, it isn't a bad game in itself.
The plot is about a man known as Ratonhnhaké:ton, a native American, who is on a great important mission in which he searches for a man known as "Charles Lee" to protect his people and take revenge following the burning of his village. However, before this, you play as Haytham Kenway, who goes through a somewhat long and controlled tutorial. Fortunately though, these memories introduce nearly all of the major gameplay mechanics, and feature some of the best developed characters in the game. Other major plot elements include Desmond making a massive choice that he doesn't get to make, involving some end of the world situation, and him building his relationship with his angry father. Some characters, especially the leading Templars in the Animus sections are quite well developed, and all the cast are very well voice acted, with some brilliantly written dialogue, especially between Haytham and Connor in the scenes that they share. However, sometimes the plot sometimes feels wafer thin, most characters are very well developed, with exception to some of the historical figures, such as George Washington, and sometimes Connor's naivety can become annoying, especially to those with proper hindsight to what becomes of his people, and the templars (again, Haytham) come across as more likable, which doesn't help. Despite this, the game tells its story well across the gameplay time, even if it does seem to develop very slowly.
Graphically, the game is extremely appealing, with high detail models and cloth physics, with large expansive environments and areas. However, certain areas in the game will stutter all over the place regardless of settings and setup due to classic Ubisoft PC porting. Although it doesn't make the game unplayable, it is extremely noticeable in some areas within the game.#, and can completely ruin a session, regardless of hardware.
The audio is well designed. As mentioned above, the voice acting is solid all-round, and the OST is well done for the game as well. The music changes based on where you are, how many enemies are nearby, or how many are in open combat, and whether you are fighting or running from them. The OST is brilliantly done, and these little features help build on the gameplay and atmosphere.
However, the parkour within the cities is a letdown, compared to both its predecessors due to less to climb on and fewer landmarks compared to its predecessors. Because of this, the flow is different, and this doesn't work well in this game because outside of the frontier tree jumping, you feel awfully grounded compared to earlier and later assassins. Naval combat is this games big addition, and this is the great contribution of AC3. The naval combat plays well, and was ripe for expansion, which thankfully, Ubisoft did in some of the later games. Outside of assassining (it’s not a word yet); you can build on Davenport Homestead and make loads of money. However, this is pointless as money is practically worthless, due to a lack of things to spend it on.
Overall, this is a weaker game in the series. That isn't to say that it is a bad game though. There is a lot of crap on Steam, and this is not one of those crap games. The length is good and the game plays well, and in many departments, the game still excels far above the average.
