When I first played the game, I was hoping it would be chill, decently difficult, but that I would pick it up over time. I then started to lose quicker and a lot more on certain occasions, spending way too much time on what should have been much easier. I later dropped the game for a while, because it frustrated me. But because it's such a beautiful and heart-warming game, I started to cry because I was so frustrated about the game. Even made a rant about how much I despised the game, but over time grew to appreciate it a bit more like the first time I saw a lets-play of it. I later then played the game with a friend of mine to completion. It was a struggle, we even made the game a little easier to ourselves once we couldn't get through a certain point.
[Concept]
I saw someone criticise the game for only allowing you move with abilities and not being able to move left, right etc. But the thing is that that's the whole point of the game. And it makes it unique. I have yet to see any other game that takes platforming under such a way of playing. More games should do what Element4l has done; being unique, creative and displaying it in a great artistic way.
[Level Design]
The level design is interesting, and great aesthetically for the most part (the acid visuals could do with some work, however), if you can get through a level without any or much losses. But the thing is that you usually will and the level design behind like half or even more of the check points is herendous; the game has a huge focus on momentum, and often you don't have enough momentum to get from a checkpoint back on track. And I'm not talking just about the momentum as the stat, I'm talking about the speed that you get limited to after you get locked to a certain check point. There was one glitch in particular with the first level that contained a cart, level 7 I believe it was, where the cart got somehow stuck where it wasn't supposed to and I got to a point where I had to struggle to get through somewhere without using the it when I was supposed to. That was really irritating, and I don't think it has been fixed either since, as the developer said they couldn't identify the issue. Perhaps someone can see for themselves and make a recording of it, I'm not too bothered since you can still get through the area without the cart.
[Price]
I think that it's good that the game has such a price, though I think it could have been better with more levels and more content in terms of some mechanics. One such example could be that, perhaps the Ice formation could have been moved to the spacebard, while having another element, electricity, which would move Left (as opposed to the Fire that moved to the Right) and could teleport you a few meters in that direction, allowing you to pass through some relatively thin walls.
[Gameplay]
While, again, I couldn't really get things right with the momentum
[Soundtracks]
Music simply elicits emotion. It's beautiful and compliments both the visuals and sometimes also the dynamics of the gameplay. I'd suggest even listening to these soundtracks on their own when you're not playing the game. You could probably fall asleep in comfort to these! Cheerful and sad, if I was to summarise them.
[Visuals]
As you might guess, I adore the visuals. Games like Limbo and some levels in World of Goo have used something like this already, but here, while familiar, it's still uniquely new somehow. I don't know how you would be able to just not look and adore the art put into this sometimes.
[Story]
Quite undeveloped. There were some key points made with some neat animations at the end of some levels, but the gameplay didn't really have anything to do with the subjects presented through it. It was more like there was gameplay and then there was some background story you could follow through. I think integration of the two in some form could have made for a much more immersive experience, otherwise it's just the feeling of awe for no particular reason, if you will.
[Achievements]
I honestly don't know too much about achievements. Some have said that the game has some unbearably ridiculous achievements, and perhaps that is indeed true. I have unlocked, may be half of them and haven't really had a fuss with that. I did miss a lot of the "Lost Elements", I believe, though I wasn't really looking out for a lot of them while playing, so I wouldn't know about how well they were placed and such.
[Bugs]
Aside from anything previously mentioned, there was one bug where melted ice had a texture of unmelted ice appear due to some condition, though it doesn't break the game in any way, just a glitch. There aren't that many glitches, and from playing, I have not encountered any errors either.
[Recommendation]
I recommend this game if you want to try something new, while staying to the idea of platforming. If you're a hardcore platformer and expect every platformer to have all key mechanics established for many platformers like the average jumping, moving left-and-right, this probably won't be something you'll be too fond of. But if you like something new, or even are looking for something new, then this will unlikely be a disappointment. I find that a lot of games nowadays seem to have the same mechanics and aren't too creative, even if their execution is excellent in what the game was trying to achieve, so having more games like this that look for something fresh, new and unique is of my great taste. Be warned that it is extremely difficult. Someone mentioned that they didn't find any ease in gameplay when changing a setting that gives you more momentum to use, but I found that I did get some more momentum. Perhaps not too much, but it still made the game a ton easier, so, if you can't bare with it, I'd suggest going into settings and giving yourself some more momentum.

This game is alright. It definitely nails the atmoshpere, art direction, and sound. (Although the odd white noise in the background seemed strangely out of context, why does my game about elemental platforming have "loud room full of people" noises going on?) The gameplay itself has you changing between an air bubble, and ice block, a rock, and a fireball to traverse the levels, and the way it controls is pretty interesting and leads to some fun interactions with thing in the world. THe controls are responsive, although the way the various element forms control vary from "floaty as ♥♥♥♥" to "a rock", but that's just part of the challenge and wasn't annoying in its own right. But, that brings me to the main reason I wanted to write this review...
The level design, especially in the latter half or so, is kind of lacking. I mean, for sure, it stays interesting and throws new challenges at you at a regular basis, but it's got a more unique problem than that. The levels don't flow. The game description says this is a atmospheric platformer that flows, yeah? Well, unless you're either the help-sprite or someone who's routed the entire thing, the game is going to be about 85% "slow-moving, jankily progressing" and 15% "Actually moving forward in a smooth, natural way". The way the ground/obstacles are laid out seems to just hinder any sense of natural flow, like  the game had a very specific way it wanted you to do things that involved hitting 7 buttons in the span of 7 seconds at exactly the right time, in the right sequence. It's not something you'll figure out quickly, nor is it something you'll probably figure out in your first run. Instead you'll find yourself kinda-doing it, but mostly pathetically limping your way along.
All in all, It's fun enough, for the price, so I'd recommend it. I griped a lot about the level design, but if you can get over the desire to move smoothly through a level then there's plenty of fun to be found. About 2 hours long for my first playthrough, and I'm not gonna bother with the collectibles. But if you go into this expecting something of the caliber of, say, Dust Force? Sorry, not gonna find it here. Go play Dust Force again.

It can also be a painfully slow day if your menu sucks, or your pricing is off, and too many slow days will spell doom for your pizzeria. As a light simulation, it makes me think in a lot of the same ways as I did in real life about pizzeria work. I would enjoy a little more depth, but the game as it stands now is very accessible and fun.

This is a great game. Ok, it looks terrible, and it's full of talking animals. But it's actually really good.
In this game, you run a pizzeria. It's an authentic Italian pizzeria, so that's cool - don't go in expecting all donner / tandoori meat pizzas with garlic bread and fries. Expect Italian ingredients, and choice of about a dozen types of cheese.
You choose the names and what's going to be on the pizzas, the quality and quantity of each of the ingredients (each ingredient has taste ratings, e.g. how salty or sweet etc - so you can really balance a pizza), and the pricing, then each in-game day you'll be taking customer orders and making those pizzas. That bit's all fast-paced dragging and dropping.
You also get to control advertising, furniture, services (e.g. free customer wi-fi) and there's an overall story which is pretty funny.
The overall effect of having complete control over your naming and creation of each pizza is that every creation is your own doing - and in turn, you are in control of the game's difficulty. If you want to give your pizzas weird names where you're going to have to slow yourself down by looking up what's on it each time someone asks for one, it's your own fault. If you want to advertise to get more people through the door before you've bought enough tables to seat them all so they get impatient and leave, it's your own fault. But it's all ok, you will learn by doing.
Also, if all the business management and story is too much, you unlock arcade mode after a while where it's purely the pizza-making portion of the game.
So - to summarise:
Pros:
* lots of detailed customisation in shop management
* fun arcade gameplay, as challenging as you choose to make it
* interesting story and characters
* funny dialogue
* I really like the chiptune music
Cons:
* having all these animals in the kitchen feels kind of unsanitary
* the user interface is a bit dodgy in places
* the graphics are pretty ugly

This is the Police presents you with a relentlessly bleak world. The mayor is corrupt. The police department is corrupt. Your wife just left you. And the game starts with you being fired from your job, which will become effective in 180 days.
Very early on, the game presents you with a stark choice: Abandon a life-long friend who made some very poor choices and got himself stuck deep in a hole, or save him and sell your soul to the mafia. I decided that as the police chief, I would sacrifice everything to focus on one thing: do a good job as police chief. I sacrificed my friend.
In between, every day of work started with the same rituals: you turn the ignition in your car, three times, until it gets going and is ready to take you to work; and then you go through your vinyl records collection to choose which song you want playing throughout your work day. It's charming the first two times. It becomes unbearably long thereafter, needlessly wasting your time before you can get to the gameplay.
The gameplay itself is fine, and is the only thing I liked about this game. You can get an idea for what it's like from the game's video trailers.
What's not fine is that the gameplay sells you the illusion of choice. When you had to choose between abandoning your friend or selling your soul? It was not a real choice. You had to give up your soul no matter what. I though I was off the hook with the mafia, and I did everything I could to oppose them. My character was promptly assassinated by the mafia afterwards, which can only be avoided by giving in to their demands. Rather than become a servant of the mafia, I accepted this outcome: I tried to be a good police chief, and my character died in the line of duty, signalling the end of the game for me. It made for a short, disappointing game, but it was preferable to embracing the hopelessness of the setting and have the game keep wasting my time with those eternal car ignition and music selection screens.

This game isn't horrible but I just cannot recommend it. Ultimately, it was a great idea for a game but poorly executed. The storyline (which makes up a significant % of the game) drags on to the point that I hated when cutscenes popped up. But at the same time the actual gameplay was shallow enough that I got bored with it pretty early in the game. This is the kind of game that really saddens me because I think the devs were really onto something here but ultimately they just missed the mark. 5/10
Pros:
- Concept is really neat
- Art style is well done and goes with the game mechanics nicely
- Music selection and ability to change songs was a nice touch
- Some story elements (like the serial killer) are generally compelling
- The detective missions were well thought out and a fun part of the game
Cons:
- Pacing is horrible. The game is split up into 3 different phases with each being progressively harder through the release of new game mechanics. You have to put in many hours of gameplay before being able to see the more complex portions of the game which makes the entire experience a shallow grind. Introducing these new mechanics at a much quicker (or better yet, immediate) pace would have greatly improved the player experience
- Storyline is boring and uncompelling. I found the main character to be whiny, obnoxious and just plain unlikeable. When bad things happened to him, I really didn't care. I actually started to get a kick out of seeing him fail towards the end.
- The gameplay only mimics RPG elements and character development is extremely shallow. I had a few officers that had been with me through the entire game and with whom I thought I had a bond. But when a few of them died, I realized it hardly affected the gameplay and since there are no actual backstories to the characters, I didn't even feel bad to lose them. Officers dying should have been a seriously compelling part of the game but instead it was just another event to shrug off.
-  Mission success/failure is pretty much arbitrary and only on false alarms did you ever get a background on what happened. These missions are pretty much the meat of the game but the gameplay basically boils down to send as many officers as possible to a mission and see a success or failure pop up as a result. Rinse, repeat.
- I found this game to be far too easy and there was no difficulty setting. The storyline of the game revolves around a beat-down police chief who is struggling to reign in crime in a big city. But the gameplay was a piece of cake. I never really felt like I didn't have enough officers or I was fighting against the odds.
- There was only the illusion of choice. I had seen this complaint in reviews and comment threads before buying the game but I shrugged it off as just being a part of a story driven game. But I can now confirm what other had said and I understand now why it is such a big deal. This isn't like a 1st person shooter where the level design railroads you towards a specific goal to continue the storyline... This type of game revolves entirely on giving the users the ability to play "their way" but This Is The Police doesn't deliver that kind of experience. The story outcome is going to be the same regardless of what you do but more importantly there is really only one way of playing the game successfully. Faction happiness is introduced too late in the game to make a difference  but really it doesn't even matter because being good or bad seems to have little affect on the gameplay.

This game comes loaded with promise. You play Chief of Police Jack Boyd, a hard-boiled old-school cop trying to get enough money to retire and survive a city full of gangs, political corruption, and apathetic citizens. It's very atmospheric, and I was drawn in almost immediately. The voice acting for Jack really helps set the scene, and there are lots of little touches that make the game's world feel real.
At first. *MINOR SPOILERS FOLLOW*
You see, this game gives you 180 days to get Jack to his goal of $500,000. I had met this goal by day 80, and even with some story-related time skips, the game drags and the story gets sparser and sparser until I felt like the developers hadn't had any idea how to wrap things up. Main plot threads are tied up in increasingly contrived manners and the game railroads the player in its final act into a forced binary choice about which corrupt, sleazy individual to support for head of the city. Sure, it lends to the game's dark atmosphere, but by this point the player feels no sense of agency. I was playing like a hustler and a supercop- City Hall loved me, my staff adored me, I made tons of money off the mob only to betray them and break up their operation to the tune of almost half my monetary goal- and then the game says "No, you suck again. Which one of these two characters who cannot succeed without you would you like to have win rather than you?" I badly, desperately wanted an option to tell them both that I didn't care and wouldn't help either, which would have perfectly fit Jack's character. Heck, even an option to run for mayor myself would have varied things up, maybe given me a chance to call in all the friends and connections I had built in gameplay... but nope, pick your flat Pepsi or sour Coke and watch a final disappointing cutscene.
I'm fine with stories where the protagonist doesn't win, but this is diabolus ex machina of the worst kind. Everything in gameplay was going my way, but the story went its own way and decided that heads I won, tails I lost. If this struggle had been reflected in gameplay and tied in with the overall narrative better, fine. As-is, I got a little bit of foreshadowing and then had the game metaphorically beat me up and take my lunch money.
The ending of a game is important. And this one has a complete lack of respect for the player, its world, and the game as a whole. While I had fun in the first half of the game, the latter half of the campaign is a slog and the story unravels and careens in wild directions. Not worth your money.

I'm not generally fond of survival games - to be honest, I'm mostly avoiding them, because most of survivals are sandbox, which means either you end up dying in wilderness, or you get the best gear/provision and the game starts to bore you at the end. Well, this game made me change my mind.
First of all, the graphics is original and cute.
Second, gameplay is smooth and satisfying: you actually feel like walking the ground, picking up resources, and so on. Very nicely provided sound scheme does the trick too.
Then, it takes a lot of time for this game to get old and boring. I've played through the whole campaign, and only at the end of it felt bored just because I've crafted the best gear in game and had plenty of resources to keep me up for many many days without having to step out to wilderness. This boredom lasted for 5 minutes, and then I've made it to the end of game, and that was satisfying too, just in time.
Soundtrack is awesome. I loved the style, loved all songs, they fit really well to game!
Raft mechanics is cool and fresh, and I didn't have any troubles controlling the raft. Though I think there could be more upgrades for your raft.
Finally, I loved the ending. It's really bright and well made, you actually feel happy after reaching the end.
Cons:
- There are bugs, and it's possible you'd run into something unpleasant like your raft getting stuck on autosave. Got such issue once, but managed to get out with a few scratches. Other bugs don't really matter and are easily avoided.
- Endless mode seems senseless, as campaign is more than enough to feel the whole game and receive experience you'd like.
- Animals are quite stupid (like boar running into bear's lair, or wolves letting you put the trap right in front of their nose), but I dunno if it's a con. Probably not. =)
Overall I strongly recommend playing this game, it's not that long and it's a nice experience.

As it stands, this game will damage your computer and/or run extremely poorly.  Until Ubisoft stops the DRM that tanks the game, I advise you avoid this game.

I was looking at this new itteration of the AC series with a skeptical eye. Not because of Ubi being known for performance issues on release but because of the revamped gameplay route they decided to take. I must say I never had this much fun in an AC game. I thought the new combat system had not its place in an AC game, but man, how wrong was I. With my hands on the game, I love the new gameplay, real good surprise here. And the bows, omg the bows I love all of them, thank you Ubi for making them all have a unique and relevent playstyle. And the storytelling, it has gone up by a big margin, I have never been this much eager to play an AC game before for its story.
I have only one complain gameplay wise : stealth kills. I don't know why nobody seems to notice it, but only 1 kill animation feels realy wrong here. Since the last AC games had so many animations for hidden blade kills I'm very sad to see Bayek doing over and over the same single move. You could argue he is the 1st assassin, and there for he doesn't have as much skill as the lastet assassins from th 19th century. But still I'm disapointed by that.
Now about performance, I have a GTX 1080 with a i7 4790k and 24GB of RAM. As you might imagine I get fps dips in the cities and I tried to figure out how I could prevent it from happening, but it seems there is no work arround it. No graphic settings nor resolution can change the poor performance in the cities. Almost constant 100% CPU usage on all cores in the cities. I heard Ubi is gonna adress this issue. But I don't know how they gonna do that since it apparently comes from the anti crack software Denuvo on top of another one (which I don't remember the name) which supposably are using 40% of your CPU power.
So if you are a constant 60 fps lover like me you ganna have a hard time living with the fact you can't change the performance. I spend most of my game time trying to fix this stuttering. But then I gave up and started to realy play the game.
In conclusion, this is by far one of the best AC game ever released and I highly recommend it to any one not concered with performance at all. Just jump on this game its well worth it.
If you have a "beast" CPU, one of the latest to be released, you'll probably have no issue with the game.
That being said, if you have a "good" CPU you have a high chance of experiencing poor performance in the cities.
If you can't play a game if it's not at constant 60 fps, I'd recommend you waiting on new comming patch until people stop complainig about high CPU usage and bad performance in the cities.
I was almost tempted to give this a negative review, but after giving in to trying fixing the preformance problem and just experiencing the game, I must say this is the AC game I had the most fun with in a long time. So I defenetly recommend this game!

Road Redemption is a singleplayer and multiplayer game with 4 different game modes. Up for offer is Campaign, Campaign + (Avaliable after finishing Campaign), Online and Quick Play. Campaign offers a lot of grinding and time consuming effort but also a nice story with boss fights. There are also different missions (i.e Kill the targets, beat the clock, kill a certain amount of marked guys, get 3rd or better etc.) It is hardcore and if you die, you have to start from level 1 unless you unlock checkpoints in the skill tree. As Online offers a chance to play with randoms or randoms and friends on stable multiplayer servers with good connection and quite a few players to play with. It can be extremely fun and it is first team to reach 3 points. It is all dependent on who gets to the finish line first, what team and how others are ranked.
Quick Play is campaign but not hardcore. To unlock other maps, you must get a specific ranking on the previous maps (like 2 gold trophies to unlock other maps etc). It's good for a short space of time with nothing to do. It doesn't add progression to the game, just take it as a mini Mario Kart like race.
The graphics are absolutely beautiful, even at low settings for a PC, it still runs perfect and has a bit of perfection to it. It's stunning to look at, 100%. It is also a well optimised game and that does amazingly well in this day and age with lots of unoptimised games (i.e PLAYERUNKNOWN'S BATTLEGROUNDS). If i had the money, I would buy over 30 copies for ALL my friends.

This game was Awesome!
You are Dutch (or whichever biker you pick that you unlock) a member of the Jackal biker gang in an apocalyptic world, you and 3 other biker gangs are all hunting down one person, an Assassin who has a bouty of 12,000,000$ dead or alive.
and that is basically the story of this game.
In this game you are suppose to drive through 3 different territories, each territory for each gang, but it's suppose to be that you never stop, whenever you beat a mission, the next one will start you with the same weapons, health, nitro and jet fuel that you had in the previus mission, so it really makes you plan on what to buy inbetween missions.
The thing is however! you only have ONE life, if you die, you gotta start over from the first mission, but each time you die you will have picked up EXP from everyone you have killed, which can then be spent in your Skilltree, so dying isn't always a bad thing, but be prepared to die, a lot.
It takes some time getting used to but it has a good balance between being aggresive and defensive.
It annoyingly enough lacks a tutorial, but the buttons are quick to learn.
It is best to play it with a controller in my opinion, it really seems like it was made for it.
The two buttons you Must learn to not spare, is Kicking and Deflecting, if you are playing on an xbox controller (like i was) then Kicking is B and Deflect (it allows you to do a Counter if you strike after the deflect) is A, make sure you work on your timing on A, because you Must use it to kill certain bikers.
Also every time you fail a mission, you will lose 25% of your max health, so losing is not something to just brush off, you Need that health.
Granted the game is short, i beat it in 2 hours (and i only died 4 times, cause i was still learning) but god damn! those were 2 epic hours!
also on a plus side! you can actually play with others! either as enemies or as allies.
So if you like to just kill kill kill kill with tons of Chaos!
This! is the game for you!!
Sidenote: make sure you kill Everyone, doesn't matter if it's just some rando, if you kill them (guns makes it a lot easier) you gain Exp and Cash, but the real thing that makes you want to murder everyone, is that each kill gives you Nitro, without Nitro you will NOT be able to beat it, Nitro is key, so spare No-one!
Have Fun! :D

The initial concept of this game was something that bugged me. I didn't think that this game could be scary, especially after my disappointment with FNAF 3. Boy was I wrong!
Cameras are no longer a thing and your only way of knowing where the animatronics are is by listening out for the audio queues and, to me, this was a brilliant design choice. Having to stand there in the doorway, carefully listening out for breathing to make sure it is safe outside is something that is truly terrifying and puts me on edge. The fear of not knowing what you will see when you flick your flashlight on is amazing.
This game has given me some of the biggest scares I have had in a long time and this is without a doubt the scariest entry in the series yet.

A visually appealing game with responsive and meaningful controls, awesome soundtrack, but a fairly unexpected challenge.
Just as a pre-warning to anyone thinking this game is all cutesy and fun and smooth and an entirely chill time, you're in for a shocker. The game appears to be fairly smooth while you play it, with a couple possible threats, dangers, and/or obstacles every now and then, but whenever you get past roughly the halfway point, the game becomes something else.
~
~
Element4l is a unique platformer where you transform into different elements to make your way through the level. You have air, which makes you rise and is essentially your "jump". You have ice, which is your main element for general travel throughout the level, as you can slide on the floor and mantain momentum that way. There's rock/earth, which makes you turn into a heavy boulder, and forces your momentum downwards, kind of like a Mario-esque ground pound in a sense. And last, but certainly not least, there's fire, which turns you into a fireball and gives you a little jolt of speed towards the right.
Using all four of these elements, you progress through snow, sand, fire, lava, and some toxic waste. The gameplay is very smooth, chill, and relaxed for roughly the first half of the game, but it picks up to eventually be pretty difficult by the end. There's several "puzzles" close to the end that require near-perfect timing to complete, which, personally, I was not much of a fan of.
~
~
The physics are great and I heavily enjoyed them. If you're underwater and transform into your air bubble form, you will quickly rise to the top of the water and pop out at a high speed. The transfer of momentum is also incredibly good. If you're rising in water quickly, and you transform into rock, you'll still be travelling at a decent speed, but you'll decelerate fairly quickly due to the rock form being so heavy.
There's an interesting little feature where there will be orange-ish bits on walls, and you can turn into a fireball to bounce off of these bits. The amount of speed you usually get off those walls can be a bit frustrating at times, since the timing and angles can be fairly cutthroat in the available window that you have.
9/10 for physics.
~
~
The description of the game says, word for word, "with a strong focus on flow and smooth gameplay". I feel like you should take this sentence with a grain of salt, due to the later portions of the game being rather difficult. The first half of the game is chill and flows extremely well from area to area, and it feels great just enjoying the music and solving the fairly simple physics "puzzles". As soon as you get into the more difficult areas, my focus shifted more from the scenery and music to the game, and trying to figure out the timing and such of the levels rather than the flow of things.
I appreciate the effort put into the level design and how the game easily went from place to place, but some sections were just painful to work through.
I give the "flow-ness" a 9/10 for the beginning of the game, and about a 4/10 for the latter half.
~
~
The soundtrack was awesome. It helped me to immerse into the game in the beginning, and actually kinda helped me calm down a bit when frustration hit later in the game. If I was chilling and wanted to relax, I personally would prefer to listen to a soundtrack such as FTL: Faster Than Light. But in the game's context, art style, and gameplay, the soundtrack makes sense.
On its own, the OST is a biiiiit too busy for my taste, but I'm sure there's some people out there that would enjoy it.
I give the soundtrack an 8/10

Element4l is clever little platformer game in which the player switches between "elements". The elements available are air, fire, stone, and ice, with the occasional water.
The game eases you into increasingly difficult challenges that require use of all four elements. The catch is, you have a power meter of sorts, so timing and pre-planning are crucial if you need to switch elements in quick succession. The game never throws you into utterly impossible challenges, and if you feel that it has, just try, try again. Eventually, after enough trying, you'll have the ability to see how the obstacle is meant to be tackled, which is extremely helpful.
Soundtrack: Each song is superb, and fits the level design perfectly
Graphics: Fun graphics, with an interesting style choice. The happy faces and semi-bright colors of the elements contrast perfectly with the dark shadows and sillouette of the terrain.
Controls: Tight controls, with an easy learning curve
Overall, Element4l is an extremely fun game, and is a joy to play for even the most casual of video game players. The controls are tight, and the challenges are never hair-pullingly difficult. The music of every level is unique, and works in harmony with the level design. Although, tii\ming and pre-planning are crucial, the game make is a bit easier with the little walkthroughs provided once the player fails enough times. Element4l is worth every penny, and is a joy to play.

A fun, buggy mess. Takes everything you loved from Assassin's Creed Revalations and expands upon it in this sequel. The story goes from pretty good to a little "meh" as you progress through Connor's story. But the story keeps you engaged enough to make your way through a ~20 hour story plus a ton of side mission content which can be entertaining too.
That being said, Connor as a character is a whiny mess. He'll often shift between hardcore assassin and angsty teenager which can be annoying. But the biggest issue with the game are the numerous bugs. I've had the game crash on multiple occasions. I've teleported seemingly randomly more than once. There are many visual bugs, such as NPCs materializing out of thin air OR magically changing outfit before your eyes. Pathing can be another problem where Connor will go out of his way to parkour off of walls repeatedly during a chase resulting in plenty of frustration. At one point the game locked me in some grey void causing me to have to close and re-open the game.
Going for $5 it is definitely worth the price, despite its many many flaws. I say play it for the gameplay and mechanics, which are both absolutely wonderful and will make up for the glaring problems.

Ah, the days of this game. I've known Fiesta Online since I was 12, and fwoooo has this game's development gone for a ride. Though I still play Fiesta from time to time, and even capped my character when it was 125, I cannot hit the yes on recommend because for new players... There's not much to see. Most of the player base are those of us who have been with the game for years and still love it despite the many flaws, but for new players Fiesta is nothing but a mess. The first 60 levels are far too frickin easy now, and entering the 60+ zone has a huge difficulty inbalance as that room of zombies will eat you up faster than Majin Buu if you don't have a proper team. But as said, this is only a problem for the newbies as old players already know what to expect from this crazy world, and likely have equipment and money around to support themselves. The biggest problem though lies in the fact that the devs... Just can't get everything done. We've had nice updates that made leveling faster and all, but I recently read a post saying they had no model artists on hand to fix an issue. Updates are constantly being announced and cancelled, or just forever delayed (that merge though). I could go on abot pay2win drama, but we've probably all already experienced free online games and know all about that s*bleep*tstorm. Oh yeah, and the community can be close and friendly, but also scary in that sense. If you mess with ANYBODY, you could end up on some player wanted lists and what not. Though personally I've never had issues with this as I'm a lovely perfect angel ^u^ (95% of the time), but I can see it driving some players away with headaches. Gameplay wise, be warned that Fiesta does not hold back with difficult bosses, at all. Though many dungeons became a lot easier with the lvl entry update, don't let the cute slimes and adorable hobo men of the early levels fool you. You'll get your squishy tush torn to shreds by the demons, beasts, and uhhh... bigger slimes of the high levels! And glitches, lots of them, fwoo! But that goes with the development issues. Overall, Fiesta is a game that still holds a place in my heart, and I'll still hop on from time to time when the devs give us those surprisingly decent updates (they exist whether the community admits it or not). But it pains me that I cannot recommend it to new players. This game will likely stay a gem for the old until the server eventually shuts down.

I've finally made myself write this.
Fiesta Online was a bumpy road. Absolutely amazing gameplay that rivaled World of Warcraft: WotLK, and while the "anime" aspect can be annoying if you hate anime, you couldn't deny the community was close-knit and happy, as well as the moderators were fun and would take the time to get to know you one on one. That was when Outspark developed the game. Sales, events, and patches were frequent and the game was at the top MMOs list. Then, Outspark disappeared and "Gamigo" replaced it. Let me tell you now. GAMIGO IS THE WORST COMPANY I HAVE EVER SEEN. They lost my account of $400+ purchased items during their transfer from Outspark to Gamigo servers, and their support was horrendous. Two weeks apart from each response and each was some broken english telling me to "change your email" or "change your password" or "we will allow you to change your username this once" to "fix it", when they never did. Still haven't recovered my account. While I soaked years into this game (At least 5600+ hours), now it's just dead, sad, full of people from other regions so nobody speaks English, and unfun. Not to mention all my accounts are gone and those months of grinding items and filling 5+ pages of my bank with rares and legendaries to give to new or learning players. I miss tutoring new people, giving out free stuff, chatting with mods in game, doing events with mods, and more. This game will always have a place in my heart. Rest in peace Fiesta Online.
EDIT: Contacted support and they finally gave me access back to my "account". I logged in to find that everything I had was missing from every single server. They carried over my "account", sure, but no characters, items, or my inventory. Nothing. Contacted them again and got this:
"If you are currently missing characters, this is probably due to an issue that we currently have with the Migrator Script that is currently not working properly.
Due to that, your characters have not been properly moved to the new servers of Fiesta Online NA.
Our IT team is already working on a solution and once the latter has been applied, you should be able to connect on your characters again.
We kindly ask you to be bit more patient. "
Okay, so, for 4 years now (Gamigo obtained the game in early 2013) the so-called Migrator script has not been working? It's 2017 and you still have accounts that aren't migrated. That's pretty sad, and it's not like I wasn't active before the changes, because you can tell when an account was last online (like most standard games these days). This is pretty unacceptable and infuriating for people that were there from the start and are now getting royally ♥♥♥♥ed.

Planetarian is kinetic visual novel, meaning that it is completely linear and there are no choices involved. I would like to point out that it is also the first VN I have ever completed.
This novel revolves around the main character, a "Junker" who scavanges the wastes of this post-apocalyptic world, and a robot named Yumemi who was created to work at a planetarium that has now been abandoned for nearly 30 years.
It is a fairly short story, however it still manages to go into keen depth on the back-stories of the characters and the world they live in. Moreover, this novel has some very heartwarming moments, as well as some absolutely heartwrenching ones, which is to be expected from the legendary VisualArts/Key, creators of some of the best VNs (and anime) of all time.
This story will make you laugh, it will make you cry, but most importantly of all, it will tell you an excellent story of a man and a robot, in a very well realized "Fallout-esque" world.
I would heartily reccomend it, and as someone who has only ever finished this VN, I can say that it is an excellent entry into the genre, as it left me with the want for more of its kind.

Good:
Absolutely gorgeous - easily one of the best looking games I've ever played.
Historical period and attention to detail - world is amazing to explore, it feels alive, authentic and organic.
Story - full of intrigue and the main character is well written (has actual emotions beyond being angry all the time, well done ubisoft).
UI - minimalistic and has removed the minimap entirely, making you pay attention to what's around you. Helps immerse you in the game world.
Combat - a welcome change of pace, positioning, attack type and sizing up your enemy matters. Gone are the days where you could snooze your way through a fight by just spamming counter-kill. Makes you think before you enter a fight against multiple opponents.
Bad:
Side content - mostly uninspired and largely boring, fetch quests and kill quests done in a copy paste manner. Would have liked to have seen more meaningful interactions with the inhabitants of the world. With the exception of one side mission early on, nothing feels hand crafted or detailed when it comes to these missions. Only exceptions would really be chariot racing and arena fighting.
Hand holding - game gives you hints, tips and tells you what to do waaaaay too often. Challenging puzzles would have been welcome in tombs, the tagging/wall-see-through ability shouldn't be there, so players can use their eyes.
Crafting - I don't mind grinding for better gear, but it doesn't feel good to do it, in black flag hunting down ships for materials felt fun. Looting animals gets old fast. Really fast.
Character facial animations - not "bad" per se but alot of character's mouths don't sync up with their voices correctly, I've been seeing it alot and it detracts from the game a bit.
Recommended:
I would recommend it because despite it's issues this is the most fun I've had in an AC game in ages - it's renewed my interest in history and I want to see the rest of Bayek's tale play out.

Let me explain with all honesty why this game, from a design perspective, is just not good.
Firstly, I have played the first game and quite liked it. Athough the jump scares were effective, I would say its more accurate to call them "jump startles". The reason why the first worked quite well is because right at the start, you are introduced to the basic idea of the game. You know who you are and why you are there. You are hinted at your enemies/what could be lurking out there, you are hinted at how you "win". That is basic game design. The player now has an idea of what to do to win and has an idea of what to do to avoid losing. The vagueness works because you are given just enough information to go on and to compell you to explore. This game has none of that.
It was good that hints are placed to explain how to interact with the game, but I never heard any breathing. I should not have to put the volume so high to hear it, that is an obvious cheap "startle" waiting to happen, and is a cheap way to create "fear". It's never explained what exactly you are doing, why you have to shine the torch, or why the torch goes out or how to stop it. The game entirely relies on trial and error.
I give massive credit for the creator for his hard work creating this series and well done to them for his success, it's not easy to make a game, let alone on your own, but this seems like basic design theory and respect was ignored.
I hope if there is another game, that this is taken into account. If you haven't already, Silent Hill 1, 2, 3, Penumbra: The Black Plague, Amnesia: The Dark Descent and a whole load of free indie horror games are a good place to start to get a good horror game experience, that is just more than a startle simulator.

All I can say is that this game is really a hidden lil gem. Extremely atmospheric, great soundtrack and absolutely beautiful artstyle. This game does a great job in delivering a sense of pure desperation in the survival aspect of the game. Meaning that your choices really DO matter, and you constantly have to re-think and re-plan your next move based on what the game throws at you.
People complain that this game is too difficult, and I can agree with that to a certain extent. The game isn’t very good at explaining important survival tips through the game (game wiki is important if you don’t wanna die figuring some stuff out yourself) and the hot keys option that is available isn’t optimal for fast-paced action which, by the way, will happen A LOT in this game. But once you get into the groove of things, I don’t think the game is too difficult. However, I did cheese the game at times by running to my “safe spot” and set up traps near it to kill wolfs. I also had a torch bug working in my favour for a while where the torch light never ran out lol.
One mayor aspect of the game I felt lacking was the story. The Flame in the Flood is a flawed game that still manages to hit some really great high points. While it seems like the developers wanted people to be able to replay it forever, you will likely get sick of the game after completing the campaign once, and you will probably be rushing through the end of the game. Still, the overall experience that this game gives is really solid, and despite the flaws, it is really worth playing.
The gameplay consists of rafting segments and land segments. During the rafting segments, you essentially float down the river while avoiding obstacles and debris. The controls here are fairly simple, but satisfying enough. There are various upgrades that can let you go upriver or steer a little bit better.  During the land segments, you explore small areas where you search for supplies/food, encounter animals (only Rabbits, Boars, Wolves, and Bears, and occasionally larger variations of the latter 3), and craft. You need to find food to eat, supplies for crafting upgrades (clothing, weapons, and raft), and tools for survival.
There is a LOT to like here. The game's stylized graphics are really well done - everything looks beautiful. Initially the feeling of progression feels awesome as you explore each segment. You feel really pressed to find the items that you need, and getting to finally upgrade your raft feels awesome. The music also really knocks it out of the park too - especially when it kicks in after pushing off into the river. The whole experience gives you this awesome feeling of adventure and mystery.
However, by the last half of the "campaign", things start to drag quite a bit. I had enough food and water for several weeks by the 6th or 7th area. Raft upgrades are severely limited by a specific item (Old Lumber), and it's extremely random how much lumber you can find. There is no proper "combat", you usually have to deploy traps, but there are certain items that make killing wolves absolutely trivial, and the boars are easy to dodge. The only weapon that you can get is a bow, but arrows require flint, which is another extremely limited resource, so you end up not wanting to waste your arrows. Given that I already had enough of everything to survive, I ended up just making a beeline down the river and skipping 20+ landing spots since there wasn't anything that I actually needed. Basically, the game lacks depth.
I have no real need or intention to play the game again, but I do think that it's a game worth playing by anybody who enjoys survival/crafting games.

Bear in mind I've been playing this game since it's Itch.Io days, so the hours shown here are about twice as low as it should show, and that I'm not a guy who enjoys rogue likes at all.
With that said, this game is AMAZING. The amount of things you can do in it is beyond massive, and every session can feel different.
So basically, what is this game about? You play as one of around 6-8 available starting characters and you start climbing through randomly generated floors to (eventually, probably, and not in the alpha...ly) kill the corrupt mayor of your city. During each run, by performing rather easy tasks, you unlock characters, and earn chicken nuggets (a form of currency with which you'll be able to purchase traits that could possibly show up whenever you level up).
Gameplay: It's a top down brawler. You can get access to guns, flamethrowers, machine guns, shotguns and a variety of science weapons and melee weapons. Each character has it's own benefits, Gorillas, for example (and yes, you can play as gorillas), are very powerful and tanky, but can't use computers and speak to humans, Assassins, on the other hand, can become invisible and backstab, but have limited HP. Shapeshifters can steal NPCs bodies and use them against other NPC, however be warned, because if your NPC is killed while you're using it, you'll be thrown out and have a portion of your HP removed as well.
If the characters don't provide enough variety for you (and, like I mentioned, there are more available characters for use I haven't even mentioned), you may get a kick out of trying the random drops of loot and items, syringes, for example, may provide buffs, or debuffs, depending on the syringe  (which will most likely be unidentifiable for you unless you have special traitrs or identify wands). You can either inject them directly to yourself, polute the air ducts of a building with them, or with one of the crazy unlockable consumables (like shrink pellets, or rage bottles).
Even with all the possibilities I mentioned, it's hard to imagine the game is only in alpha, and includes both online and offline co-op, and in the future, more features will be added (Map seeds, Player-made mutators and your own custom character!)
I can't recommend this game enough, it's fantastic in it's current form (Although there are only 6 levels, highly replayable, though) and there are more things to be added on top of it.
Lovers of the roguelike genres will highly enjoy this game, even if it's a bit easier than most roguelikes (Which, in my book, is a benefit).

I just watched a supercut of all the
training montages online. It was awesome. And, when it was over, I rewatched the really good ones (parts I, III, and IV) again, with just a few mouse clicks, thanks to the uploader's handy embedded timestamps. Even more awesome. I could have pulled out my
box set and done more or less the same thing myself, but that wouldn't have been so awesome. For me, at least, all of that disc-swapping and scrubbing through footage wouldn't have been worth the effort. And that's
: too much low-level busywork for too little payoff.
What looks like a colorful retro-style pixel art clicker game---fill the resource bars, and watch your stats inch steadily up as you admire the 80s/90s in-jokes and references---is actually a management sim, with only one challenge: to optimize your routine to fit the constraints of the simulation. Played as designed, it's a grindfest. Stat degradation offsets your efforts to a discouraging degree until you find the right combination of actions. Once you've found what works, you repeat it endlessly until the variables change. Then you adapt your strategy to account for the new data, and resume the cycle. And then, eventually, you win.
If you're the type of person who enjoys debugging the implementation of an algorithm, getting a dopamine hit every time the counter increments, you'll likely enjoy
. If you're the type of person who only feels satisfaction when the counter gets large enough to unlock new content---a new area or mechanic or pixelated pop culture reference---you might struggle. If you're the type of person who takes no pleasure in incrementing counters as such, or is likely to resent time spent reaching blatantly arbitrary goals against artificial difficulty for little narrative payoff, you're unlikely to enjoy
.
What tips
into Not Recommended territory for me has to do with the way the developer has handled post-release support, abandoning multiple platforms and responding to the single greatest complaint of the community with a passive-aggressive "suuuper easy" mode that, by their own description, breaks the game. I played the game for a while on both Normal and Suuuper Easy, and they're right: removing the absurdly high stat decay does remove essentially all of the challenge. But doing so also allowed me to progress far enough to realize that there really
anything to the game other than that grind.
Personally, I find the
of optimizing a loop appealing, but don't find the process of actually doing so through negative feedback inherently interesting. There just aren't enough mechanical, narrative, or aesthetic wrinkles in
to incentivize me to care. If you find the process intrinsically satisfying, then there are certainly worse ways to spend your time than playing the game as it was designed. If you don't mind lobotomizing the core game loop in order to have a clicker game with a fighter-management skin, go for it (on discount). Otherwise, despite really wanting to like this game, I simply can't recommend it.

Curator Review:
This puzzle platformer is an indie gem. Take control of four elements and solve puzzles while moving up, and to the right (sound familiar?). I-Illusions made a great game that is sufficiently challenging, aesthetically pleasing, and perfectly balanced to create a fun gaming experience. In a genre so full, Element4l outperforms many with its' brilliant composition. 9/10

Part clicky-minigame, part management sim. Start up your own pizzeria, unlock ingredients, create new dishes in any combination you want. I advise making a pizza that's just plain dough and a single handful of hotdogs. Call it the "STUPID IDIOT SPECIAL" and watch as your stupid idiot customers gobble them up by the dozens.
Pizza Express is a somewhat less polished and more crunchy/low-fi version of Cook! Serve! Delicious!, with less fluid/fun action gameplay, but much deeper and more interesting management. Making the actual pizzas is an exercise in fast and accurate clicking (and memory, of course), which is a lot less precise and satisfying than CSD's responsive controller-based gameplay.
As I hinted at earlier, the management side of the game is what is truly engrossing. It's paced well, and there are a ton of systems that work together to create a great deal of depth - advertisements, shop upgrades, new ingredients, ingredient upgrades, the incredibly organic and freeform recipe creator...
You'll eventually juggle up to 30 different recipes that you've put together, each one unique and hopefully a good balance of different flavors - while you can technically create any random mishmash of ingredients you want, you'll only get the best scores with dishes that hit all 5 of the target tastes (sweet/salty/etc). It's surprisingly difficult to come up with a balanced menu, and even more difficult to remember all 30 of those recipes in the heat of the fast-paced kitchen segments.
Over all this is a fun, lighthearted story with generic, but inoffensive characters. I got a few smiles out of it, and didn't really cringe during any of the dialogue, which is all I ask out of games.
If you're into management simulation, arcadey-clicking, and decent-to-mediocre pixel art, you've got a great option in Pizza Express. I recommend it to any fans of the genre. Newbies will probably want to start with Cook! Serve! Delicious!, which, as stated, is a lot easier to get into and more immediately fun.

Solitaire has already seen several enjoyable re-workings, but now it's Minesweeper's time to shine with a modern update in the form of Fine Sweeper. And you know what?... It ain't half bad.
Presented with a grid full of square panels that are hiding several mines underneath, you click on a panel and reveal some blank spaces and some numbers. Each number represents how many mines surround that tile, and based on that information, you must deduce the locations of every mine and avoid them as you click and remove all the unoccupied panels on the board. With each cleared grid, you move on to another that's either bigger and/or has more mines hiding from you. Make a mistake and you'll have a fully primed ball explode in your face. Do that several times, and it's game over.
The difference with this update is it's far more lenient than its original granddaddy. You now have hearts that allow you some breathing room where each heart will give you a free pass should you click on a mine, more of which can be found hiding under some random squares that can be used to replenish your stock and give you more room for mistakes. Or, alternatively, instead of using them you can save them in a bank and eventually cash them in for special, one-time use abilities to help you clear the board. And for hardcore score enthusiasts, this version has scoreboards for you, too, along with additional methods of play available to maximise that goal.
A little extra flair is added with some clean, appealing visuals (the grid and its surrounding boarder resembling the top-down dungeons from the original NES Zelda) and some funky bass licks to keep the mood up from stage to stage. It's all perfectly pleasant and functional and serves as a nice, relaxed, modern take on a fun but dated classic. I'm not sure how many stages there are, as I stopped at the 50 required for the achievements, but with multiple stages of increasing difficulty, a custom mode with sliding scales of variables, and a sweet little price to boot, for fans of Minesweeper, whatever your flavour is, this has you covered. Although, even in this updated version, clicking on the wrong mine in a final 50/50 situation and wasting the past 20 minutes of your life never stops hurting.

Planetarian is an amazing visual novels. While it has no choices, and is quite short compared to other Key works, but it still manages to capture one's imagination and give a thrilling emotional experience.
Usually I personally avoid Visual novels without choices, but Planetarian has definitely proven that they can still telle an amazing story and engage you in the world.
This is not a game, but it doesn't need to be one to be fun and engaging.
Visual novels are in many ways like a mix between a book and a movie (And in some cases a game, but not in this case). It is personal like a book, but it is also vivid, engaging and visually stimulating like a movie.
I strongly recommend Planetarian, especially for someone who is curious about Visual novels, as this perfectly captures how wonderful they are, assuming you immerse yourself and take the time to play it.

TL;DR - I think the game is great and I would recommend anyone to buy it. Ubisoft did a great job of taking the serie a step further and while the game can never compete with early AC's in my heart I'm very much enjoying this new fresh start. It feels way more engaging gameplay and story wise which I felt was missing in the couple previous games!
So, I've been considering posting a review for a couple days. I've, so far, loved all of the RPG elements I think it adds to the experience of the player, like you're part of your character's life and that makes the game more engaging. Like anything it has it ups and downs as it makes the game have somewhat of a small grind. There is an alternative way to collecting ressources which is constantly fighting to get loot and just dismantling it which might be a bit more enjoyable for some of us but I personnally don't mind hunting for a while. The game is so beautiful that it doesn't feel as much of a chore, it will never be 100% enjoyable to run all over the place doing the exact same thing but still I don't mind doing it, especially because of how much of a living world Origins is.
The combat system, I'm still getting used to it, I'm not going to say it's great or bad, it's different and I'm enjoying it. Was it better before? I honestly don't know since I liked it very much as well it was simple and elegant, made you almighty! I feel like the new one is again more engaging and adds to the difficulty which I enjoy very much. Before you could just take on 20 enemies without thinking and stand in the middle of them and wait to counter, now you actually have to focus and get rid of archers first and be mindful of trying to dodge arrows and combos consistantly, fighting 20 enemies is still possible but it takes some more skill. The control scheme is were I'm all messed up, by that I don't mean I hate it, it just isn't the same to previous AC's so I'm kind of dying inside when I play. I'm better than when I started the game but I'm not as skilled as I'd want to be. It's something to get used to!
I like the story so far, I'm not too far in because I do a lot of side quests and exploring, the game is so beautiful I just can't help myself in taking it slow. I think Bayek is one of those characters we'll remember for future AC's however I doubt he'll ever reach Ezio's or Altaïr's level for me. I do feel more engaged with this new game than the couple previous AC's we've had and it's due to many things. I've already mentionned the combat and RPG elements, but even the story adds to it, I think Ubisoft had lost track of what I felt was important in the first couple games of AC's and the further along we got the further off it seemed. I liked the fact that we were linked to Desmond for a bit and without the shadow of that lineage I felt underwhelmed by the other AC's. Since we'll never get Desmond back I wasn't sure to ever have the same feeling about the serie and Origins has brought back some hope. I feel like I can relate better to his story and his character than the twins or even our lovely pirate Ed for that matter. We've still got a bit to go I think but it's way better than it was. If my view changes I'll update this review, I mean I'm still not done with the story so it could all go to♥♥♥♥♥♥ though I doubt it.

I don't often review games, however this game is an exception. Firstly just playing through the storyline is incredibly boring, I have absolutely no compassion for the characters, or their goals. Not to mention the ridiculously annoying cutscenes, playing this game is like watching a boring movie, the number of cutscenes quite frankly baffles me, they are simply boring and have no place in the game. Another thing that I must mention is the poor quality of the cities. In Assassin's Creed 1 and 2, I felt as if the cities were actual cities, yet here they are like small towns, the building's do not feel as if they belong in an urban city environment, and for that the cities are awful.
The gameplay pains me even moreso, when I'm not dealing with bugs such as losing control of Connor, falling through the world, or something involving the incredibly buggy NPCs then I'm trying to wrap my head around why Ubisoft made the decisions it did with this game. For some reason unbeknownst to me Ubisoft thought it would be a good idea to combine the sprinting and parkour under one key, which is a real bother when you're running through the streets and find yourself jumping upon carts, up walls and other such places. To me it seems completely unnecessary to make this change. In Assassin's Creed 2 you could purchase health vials, to be used in combat, another feature removed which was beneficial to gameplay.
Another fault which I've found with the game is the poor performance, this is one of the most irritating factors for me. I spent money on a relatively powerful computer, which has higher specs than what is recommended for the game, yet I still find that frame rate dropping, sometimes as low as 30-35. Another port from Ubisoft which little effort has gone into.
There are many more points that I would like to make as to why I don't recommend, I could write to no end about the faults, but unfortunately this review must end.

Punch Club is that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who intially tries really hard to get your approval, only to push you away as soon as you start getting too cozy. There is much that I absolutely adore about this game: the artstyle, the characters, the sound design. Leveling up your character is an absolute nightmare due to stat degradation. You can save up money to buy training equipment to help you in said pursuit, but then you get robbed for half your money if you save up too much. I do hope the developers learn their lesson in Punch Club 2, because despite me bashing both the devs and the game, there is a lot I like about it. It is just incredibly frusterating to see such a potentially good game soiled by such blatantly bad decisions.

This is later combated with perks that allow the player's stats to not fall below a certain level. In all, I'd say this is a half decent game because I personally don't mind the grind, but most people won't be interesting in grinding stats constantly to ensure their character's stats don't degrade into oblivion.

This game was such a surprise package from start to finish! From being colourful and fun to dark and creepy, Scott has made an amazing concluding chapter to the Freddy franchise. By putting the player in full control of the workings of a pizzeria, how scary or challenging the game is relies soley on the savvy business decisions of the player; a formular not included in former Five Nights games. The pursuit of money can get you into some pretty sticky situations! It's actually a welcome and interesting change. I had such a great time with this instalment as well as it's mysteries and revelations. Everything is wrapped up in a satisfying ending and will be enjoyed by all Freddy fans who want answers to some of the most pressing questions we've had lore wise. Although, I predict that some will be left scratching their heads as the most crucial characters seem to be directly crossing over with the novels at this point.
Going by what we see in the good ending, I feel as if we've come to the end of the road with these games. It was an honor (and somtimes a curse with all those jumpscares and hair pulling from writing out theory upon theory!) to play through this crazy world with all of its insane characters. Thanks for the ride, Scott!

Cute music, nonesensical story (if there is one), moderately fun game for some.
BUT, if you can't deal with alternate controls or are not too good with platformers, you will find this frustrating. While some say this doesn't compare to things like Dark Souls in difficulty, I actually disagree. Often times you will see the solution and the solution will even present itself with a ghost, but execution is much, much different. I struggled very much, even though I found the controls quite intuitive and easy to use. I could see what I was supposed to do many times, but often struggled much on levels. I began to question if my reactions were terrible, which at times they were, but even when I'd be on point with reactions, if I didn't do something properly earlier, I'd be completely screwed and would have to start over at a checkpoint. This is both frustating, and given time, very mind numbing. At certain points I found myself struggling to the point of popping blood vessels in my forehead because of a dumb mistake or because of points where there is virtually ZERO margin for error, similar to parrying a select few mobs in Dark Souls.
I may not finish this game, but even if I do not, I will enjoy the music very much. It is easily the very best thing about this game.
Pros/Cons
Pros:
Fairly hard gameplay for some (good for you speedrunner and hardcore types)
Intuitive and instantaneous marginal controls
AMAZING music
Cute graphics and character
Cons:
Frustrating and repetative
No way to skip a part outside of skipping an entire set of levels which makes you miss out on all the witty sayings from the character and quotes of famous people.
For those that are good at this sort of thing, the game is actually amazingly short
For those that are bad at the game, you'll find yourself spending more time than you want on a level. (At one point it took me 20 minutes to beat a single level that would take a speedrunner about 30 ish seconds)
The methods of help (a ghost that moves too fast at times) and a helpful boost barely make the game more playable for derptastic people like myself
Overall, I still found myself coming back, though it might've been the completionist heart I have, though it was probably the music.

Element4l is a pretty neat platformer. The controls are really simple: you use one of the arrow keys to transform into a specific element which gets you through a level. It's a cool idea, and for the most part, it plays out pretty well. Occasionally the movement frustrated me, but I think that was more of a lack of skill, rather than a game fault. I thought about it and I figured the game would be much simpler and possibly too easy if you were given more freedom with the movement. Possibilties could be endless though.
The soundtrack is really good, and it creates a really relaxing atmosphere, even if you are stuck at some point in a level. I found I was never frustrated when I had to repeat an area over and over. It's a cute game too, with little quirky written dialogue that kept a smile on my face while playing. The achievements were also fun to get and add replayability. (100% in just under 10 hours.)
There's definitely some downsides though. While I understand this isn't supposed to be a story heavy game, I wish they put more effort into it; I feel like there are so many cool concepts of life and death that could have been applied. Instead you get these little cutscenes featuring some weird ghost creatures that have creepy eyes. I still don't really get what the point in them was. And towards the end, for some reason i was getting a lot of FPS drops, even though my Macbook surpasses the requirements by a mile. Also, I really wish it supported Retina resolutions on OS X, it would have made this game so much prettier.
I'd give it a final score of 6.8/10. It's a very decent game, but if you're patient, then grab it on a sale. The developer is very nice too. Active on the forum and gives help when people need it.

Extremely detailed and expansive management sim + tense, reflex-testing pizza-making marathons. It manages to feel both very fun and very tiring. Honestly, this game feels like hard work! With the stress comes great relief and a sense of accomplishment from surviving another throng of customers. Best in short bursts but has enough content to keep you playing for a long time.

I'm 7+ hours into this game and still enjoying it immensely. Its pixely graphics may lead the casual browser to perceive that it is a bit of a cheap game and will perhaps not have much that's satisfying to offer, but don't let the appearance fool you: this is one of the best business simulation games on Steam! I am very surprised at its depth.
There are essentially two phases: day (open hours) and night (closed hours).
During open hours, customers will flood into the store, order pizzas off of your menu, and then wait for you to make them. In this part you'll be playing something akin to "cook, serve, delicious" where you actually have to assemble the pizza from your batch of ingredients and then send it out to the customers. You dont' want to keep the customers waiting too long, so you have to build the pizzas quickly and accurately. One thing that potential players may NOT like about this section is that you can't just assemble the pizzas using hotkeys, like you can do in "cook, serve, delicious". In this game, you must click each ingredient and manually drag it to the pizza, and you have to do it accurately. If you don't drag the item directly over the pizza, it doesn't count. This will be a turn off to some people, but if you are okay with this, you are in for a treat.
The real surprise with this game is how robust the business sim elements are during closed hours. The longer you play, the more features start to unlock. You get to order your pizza shop's inventory of ingredients from a large catalogue to give your shop a flavor you like (while taking into consideration the needs of different customers, e.g. vegan, carnivores, lactose-intolerant options, etc). There are more ingredients in the catalogue than you can possibly have in your shop, so there is some choice to consider. The game tells you the "stats" for each ingredient as well, as far as how it will alter the flavor of the pizza and/or what kind of customer taste it will please (e.g. sweet, spicy, salty, bitter, sour, etc).
In addition to stocking your own ingredients, you also have to design, name, and price each specific pizza on your menu. This part actually takes a lot of management, because you actually have to consider the range of options your parlor offers different types of customers while building, and then for pricing you have to add up the total expense of all the pizza's ingredients, then determine how much you want to charge for it. I found that charging about 180% of the pizza's ingredient cost does not make the customers unhappy and still earns you a good profit. For complex pizzas anyway. For simpler pizzas, I may do closer to 160%. You have to perform the math yourself, though, so keep a calculator handy. (For another game, I might not like that, but for a business sim, doing my own math feels great.)
Then, for each individual ingredient, you can upgrade different stats as you go. For example, you can upgrade the quality of that ingredient, the quantity you keep in the shop at one time, or upgrade the delivery so that new shipments arrive faster. BE CAREFUL, THOUGH. Upgrading the quality of an ingredient will increase the COST of that ingredient, which also increases the production cost of every pizza it is on, so you will need to reprice all of those pizzas if you don't want to lose money from the upgrade. You will have to adjust the price of each affected pizza manually, so I find it's better to do quality upgrades for all ingredients at once if possible, so I can get all of the price adjustment done in one fell swoop.
Also, the longer you stay in business, the bigger your pizza menu gets. You start off only being able to have maybe 5 or so pizzas on the menu, but every day you stay open, you can add another pizza. On one hand, it's in your best interest to build really simple pizzas at first (e.g. just crust with sauce counts as a pizza) because you can build them quickly and they don't cost too much. However, more complicated pizzas (e.g. whole wheat dough, marinara, oregano, mozzarella, olives, feta, pineapple, onions, bell peppers, mushrooms, and bacon) can earn you a LOT more money per pizza sold, but they take a LOT more time to build and increase your chances of making a mistake during the building (potentially costing you money from the wasted ingredients and affecting your reviews). You'll want to strike a good balance of super easy pizzas (fast but low profit) and complicated pizzas (slow but more profit). It's also good to try and evenly distribute each individual ingredient across pizzas. For example, if you have 20 pizzas on your menu, and all of them use oregano, you're going to run out of oregano FAST, and running out in the middle of the business day could screw you over. But if you evenly distribute the ingredients, using each ingredient on only a few pizzas, then it lowers your chances of running out of ingredients in the middle of the work day.
And then you get tons of other management options as well. You'll want to upgrade your parlor with decorations and features (arcade? music? disco ball? wifi? high chairs?), which can improve your parlor's reviews (atmosphere) and make customer's willing to wait longer (which you will definitely want). You can also buy a wide variety of advertisement with different prices, different levels of effectiveness, different times of day, and targeted at different demographics. You can set up different discount offers. You get to set your own hours, so you can open longer or stay closed longer as you need. You can purchase more tables, which allows you to accept more orders at once. You can acquire a tip jar and a comment box, and so on. There is really a lot to play with.
A good sim always keeps new upgrade opportunities rolling in so that you are always salivating to make your operations better and better, so there is always something to work toward, and Pizza Express keeps that pace incredibly well. As an added bonus, the game even has a cast of characters and a story that involves corruption/scandal in the food industry that affects your characters AND your business (e.g. if there is a scandal involving the distributor of a particular ingredient, you might have to remove or replace it, etc).

Ingredients
2 large eggs
Salt and pepper
2 to 3 tablespoons shredded cheese (optional)
1/4 to 1/2 cup filling, pre-cooked if necessary (optional)
2 teaspoons unsalted butter
Minced parsley, to garnish (optional)
Equipment
Mixing bowl
Whisk
8-inch nonstick skillet
Spatula
Dinner plate
Instructions
1. Whisk the eggs: Crack both eggs into a mixing bowl. Whisk the eggs until completely combined, and season with salt and pepper. If you\'re adding cheese or other fillings, make sure they are prepped and nearby.
2. Warm the skillet and melt the butter: Place an 8-inch skillet over medium-high heat and melt the butter. Tilt the skillet as the butter melts to evenly coat the bottom. When the butter stops sizzling, the pan is heated and ready.
3. Pour the eggs into the skillet: Pour the whisked eggs into the skillet. Immediately tilt the pan so the eggs coat the entire bottom. The eggs should sizzle on contact; if not, continue cooking, but remember to heat the pan a little longer next time.
4. Drag and push the eggs to form waves: Use a spatula to gently drag and push the cooked eggs from the edges toward the center of the pan, making space for the uncooked eggs and forming waves in the omelette. Tilt the skillet so that the uncooked eggs flow into the open spaces.
5. Cook the omelette for 1 to 2 minutes: The omelette will finish cooking in 1 to 2 minutes. When done, the bottom will be set and the edges will look crisp. The top of the omelette should still look fairly wet and uncooked, but there will no longer be any loose, easily flowing liquid egg — the omelette will continue cooking off the heat, so finish when you think the top still seems a bit underdone.
6. Top with cheese and fillings: If using, sprinkle the cheese and fillings down the center of the omelette.
7. Fold the omelette: Fold the bottom third of the omelette over the center, and then fold the top third down. Alternatively, fold the omelette in half.
8. Slide the omelette onto a plate: Gently slide the omelette onto a plate and garnish with parsley. Eat right away while still hot.
