Well nearly 2k hours into fiesta and still haven't decided to write something about it I figured I'd write one now, anyway, your probably wondering why I'm not recommending this game. Clearly 1.8k hours I SHOULD know something about fiesta and how it works. Well your in luck as I do, bare bones this game is extremely P2W and grindy as **** to the point that it just became to much.
Now in some more detail about this game:
Lets start with the bad parts of the game!
-The cash shop:
Most MMORPGs usually have a cash shop which you buy stuff from and for me personally any cash shop that offers boosts to a player's stats things such as DMG,crit, crit rate, HP or whatever form of boost aren't exactly something I like unless it's from a event or obtainable via in game boss or dungeon run things of that nature that can give F2P players the same opportunities as P2W players and I do understand that companies must be profitable to maintain operations of a game however fiesta I feel just lets you download the game for free just to make a few hundreds or more off of you and make you work your *** off for close to nothing. Not only that but their cast shot is virtually stat boost that only last for 30 days at a time before you have to buy something to replace your old outfit.
What's also kind of funny the cash shop can make a mage into a tank.
-The community:
Now this one is a little hard to put on the bad however there are a lot more bad apples then there is good ones when I first started playing this game I joined a guild abid it was a small guild with a good guild leader and members and they REALLY were the only people that kept me playing for as long as I did, however, a more big guild eventually absorbed our guild into it and I met a much larger community and that's when I realized how bad the community really is most of the level 100+ abid some aren't as bad as others but still it's bad most people I met seemed to be WAYY to power hungry and into PvP (Which is really broken due to the nature of the game) ill admit that being power hungry isn't a bad thing or being into PvP, however, one instance from the guild I was in one of the strongest players (We had 2-3 of the top players in our server) in our guild decided that instead of sharing loot which was distributed by how many runs you do which normally take about 2-3 hours to get done per run to keep the loot they got that did get our guild leader angry but decided to let them keep the loot because of the fear of losing one of our top players rather then keeping his word and promises to the other within our guild.
For as long as I've been with this game I did noticed that newer player areas really don't have any life to it normally you wont see other players in Roumen (Newb town) or they'll be afk or something like that. Most people that are lower levels get power leveled by higher level players normally for free or they'll ask for gold in return for leveling (yes it's not against the TOS at least the power leveling part is not so much the asking for money part).
-Events...
This one is pretty short, Events in this game are practically nothing. Most events are done on forums which I can say just is lame because it gives the game a feel of nothing interesting is happening which is most part nothing IS happening. And when a event is out it's normally just something for Halloween or xmas that's really the only 2 events you are normally guaranteed to have. Most other events happen on blue moons or out of the blue.
-The player market
Another short one I'm getting tired of writing so ill try to keep everything from here on out short. The player market everything is really over priced even after I quit the prices of things only really just gone up and that's about it. It's a real problem.
-Scammers
Not that often you'll find people that would go out of their way to screw you over for money or whatever but a common scam in this game is gifting this game does let you gift cash shop items from other players sweet and all right? Wrong, as people normally know you need to spend money to be able to even gift (I don't know much about it as I never gifted or brought items from the cash shop) Scammers know this and would say something like give me the money first and ill gift you first or if they want to get something for free from a gifter they'll asked to be gifted first. There are other scams out there, however, that's the most common one other scams aren't done as much however that's the most common one out there.
-THE GRIND
OH GOD, Can I say this game becomes just to grindy to the point you have to do it for hours to just see 5% for level 105 at black bear repeat quest with a party of level 100-105 this game starts to get grindy at levels 61+ and slows and slows down a lot to the point it's not fun to play even with a group of high level players the grind becomes old pretty quick.
The good of this game FINALLY!
So here we are at the good things about fiesta good on you if you read this far into it.
-The community
While this is in the bad part it also has it's good bits it really does if your able to find a guild or a group of players to play with regularly this game becomes VERYYY addictive because of how fun it can be to run a high level kingdom quest or do group repeat quests to level up.
-It's about as classic of a MMORPG as you can get
Title says it all fiesta is for the most part the most classic of a MMORPG as you can get to at least as far as I know.
-The end-
I know this review isn't a perfect one at all but I do hope it help you out a fair bit in not picking this game up.  my personal rating of this game it would have to be 3.3 out of 10.

I would give a neutral rating for this if I could, I thought certain aspects of this game were amazing, the visuals and animations, music, the entire rafting portion of the game was pretty fun. The pacing is not at all like a typical survival game like Don't Starve, in fact I got more of an Oregon Trail vibe from it, until the end of the campaign at least, when it got way too easy and I had too much food and water and everything. I imagine playing it in hard mode would fix that so I'll likely give that a try next. I really liked the mob AI too, boars will shoot around strategically to cut you off at the exit of the path you're running down instead of just chasing you from behind, wolves mainly only attack when you're running away from them, etc.
So, the main disappointment though is that there's just so little to the game. Boars and wolves are literally half of the mobs you'll encounter, the other half being snakes and bears (unless you count the ants, but they're essentially just a ground aoe like poison ivy). The trailer that shows strategies for dealing with different mobs basicallly explains everything from beginning to end in regards to combat in this game. If I had found any mobs at all that I wasn't expecting going in, or combat mechanics I wasn't expecting, I would honestly probably be giving a positive review right now, but the lack of variety/surprise/mystery was just too disappointing. I would also definitely have given it a positive review if it looked like there would maybe be new content added to it someday, but there apparently won't be, according to one of the devs, because they've switched their efforts to their next game and don't think it'd be worth it to put more time into this one, which is understandable really and I do wish them a lot of luck with the next one, but flame in the flood is a bit light on content for $14.99. Just a little bit more...a couple more mobs and combat mechanics, it would have really gone a long way imo.
By the end of the campaign, everything altogether felt quite repetitive and it really didn't feel like there was anything left to experience except for the story bits, which were cool but a bit lacking as well and definitely not enough to really carry the rest of the game or make up for the simplicity of the rest of it. Mind you I beat the game in easy mode in about 4 hours I guess, so it's not really like the repetitivity was because it was dragging on too long, it's really just that there wasn't enough variety. There's 2 ways to kill the mobs, spear traps and poisoned meat (there's a bow too, but I'll mention why I think that's unusable later), and I was very very bored with those things and the combat in general towards the end.
And also, the UI is very bad, the devs will really need to work on that on their next game, because using items in dangerous encounters is basically impossible and there's no way to do it efficiently if a mob is aggroed on you, because you're rooted when you bring up items and having to manually click them on the screen (no hotkeys for them), and then you have to aim and "cast" them more or less. Even using the bow is like that. I used it twice - one was on a sleeping bear to wake it up and one ended with me being eaten by a wolf.

This game is a really hardcore yet casual version of Minesweeper. It sticks to the well-known basics of the game, but brings it to a far grander scale, the only item drops that the description mentions being extra lives (and some canisters to hold your extra lives early on), which is just as it should be.
And you'll need them all, you really will, the global 'record' seems to be level 67 right now which only two people have gotten, and I'm currently working on level 59, and I'm facing a 36x22 board with 219 bombs to flag and 7 lives (plus any others you find on the map) to do it with.
You'll learn so many new tricks and logical leaps out of necessity as to how to figure out the status of squares and try to narrow down the number of 50-50 guesses you have to make, which is why you have that many lives. It's a really engaging non-time-constrained puzzle game, exactly the kind of game that I love running in the background while I do or watch other stuff. Who knew Minesweeper could be so fun?
I didn't run into any bugs or glitches or have any complaint about the UI of the game. Yet. (Edit: I now have run headlong into a fairly major bug but the devs seem responsive and are working on it. (Edit: They fixed it!)) The one background tune it has is also a nice, non-intrusive, non-obnoxious track so I've left it on even after nearly 24h of off-and-on play.

is an atmospheric puzzle platformer with four elements (ice, air, rock and fire).
You will get an introduction into the game which is really needed. First of all you have the element air, as second element you will get ice, next one is rock and at last fire. You will switch through the elements with the arrow keys. Every change will lower your endurance except the change to ice, which doesn't cost any endurance. The endurance will reload automatically over a short periode of time. If your endurance is too low you can't change into another element. You have always to use the environment around you to finish the level.
For example: You have to get through two half-pipes in front of you. Therefore you will change to rock to raise your fall speed and just before you hit the entrance of the first half-pipe you will change to ice to slide through it. After you exit the half-pipe you will change to air to fly above the second half-pipe to repeat the actions again. This means that you have to react often very very fast to get the right speed/timing to fly/roll/slide to the next objective.
There are calm passages like slowly floating as air over lava or wet passages like sliding as ice through water or rolling down a track in a minecart as rock or bouncing as fire from one lava pit to another.
Yeah, that's it.
+ great game concept (like rock-paper-scissors)
+ well designed physic engine
+ tutorial available
+ lovely designed levels (with usage of the rock-paper-scissors principle)
+ non-frustrating autosave system
+ atmospheric style
+ good artwork and nice particle effects
+ awesome sound scenery with calm appropriate music
+ help system (never used)
+ funny text messages with referrals to other games/movies (like 'The Goonies', 'Harry Potter', 'Indiana Jones' or RPGs)
+ good chosen quotes (displayed at the beginning of each level)
(+ steam achievements)
- some parts of some levels are hard as hell (in one level I needed over 100 respawns -.-)
- no story, not even an abstract story
(- no demo)

I do recommend this game, but do note it is not as polished as the previous games in terms of mechanics.

I'm less than 2 hours into the game but so far this game is FANTASTIC!
Gameplay itself is fairly basic. You drive and smack your enemies. But there's enough complexity here to keep your eyes from glazing over as if you're playing Destiny 2. You can block/dodge attacks, grab enemies for interesting setups, throw grenades, shoot powerful guns with which you risk crashing off the road as you aim, kick people into objects/off cliffs... Like I said, there's enough complexity here to pile onto the already snappy controls.
This game is centered around replayability. As you make your way through the campaign you will gain money and EXP to buy bonuses which help you deal with the increasing difficulty. You also unlock new bikes and characters who have their own weapons/stats. There are multiple objectives throughout (Race, Elimination, Time Trials, etc).
You may die and you may die a lot during your time in the campaign.. and guess what? You have to start the entire multiple-level chapter over again. Not fun, right? But hey! The objectives, level design and weapons are randomized so it never really feels like your starting from scratch. It definitely helps to keep me from feeling frustrating upon multiple deaths.
All in all, the game seems worth $20 and you will have a lot of fun depending on your tastes. I love these kinds of racing games with an emphasis on combat. SSX, Furious Karting, NFS Rivals, Burnout... You just gotta love 'em.

text: Lack of diversity in gameplay, and a flash game feel makes this game a hard MEH.

The short:
It's fun, but it shouldn't be.
The long (good):
Basically "training montage simulator". The normal agony of grind (made notoriously bad with MMO, FTO, and mobile games) is a lot of fun (despite all common sense). Very few games pull this off. Kind of has the progression/grind feel of a quarter sized version of Stardew Valley. The act of progression is the satisfying meat of the game (in a relaxing way). The story is pretty basic at first, then goes all over the place with fantasy fighting references and content. It's enjoyable, once. With the fighting, you are playing more a fighting stat manager where you only have some influence between rounds. It's alright. The good part is, with the speed multipliers, this doesn't take long, and you can get back to the fun "training montage" part. It's OK for what it is, and actually good that it's so minor, given how the rest of the game works.
The long (bad):
I'll talk more about the bad than the good, as critisism is easier to notice/remember. Just know the good outweighs the bad. I certainly do recommend the game despite these things.
Very buggy. UI freezes up a lot, or UI elements dissapear. Usually you can "save & exit", reload, and it's fine. And being turn based, you don't loose anything.
Can't ALT+F4 (at least you can still CTRL+ALT+DEL). I've had the game freeze up and had to do this a very few number of times. Story dissables the save/exit option too often. Story will hang up sometimes and save/exit is dissables, thus the ALT+F4 need. Sometimes the story isn't actually hung up, but just looks that way, as it dissables the menu and many options you would normally have. You'd think this would make it more obvious what you need to do, but not always. Would be nice it the game were more sandbox and left all the options so you could continue or do the storyline. The storyline brakes up what you are trying to do at the most inconvenient times, but I suppose, on second thought, that's how story would unfold, not when you want it to. However, it does unfold when you want it to, you just get the interuption notification (which requires travel resources) at inconvenient times.
It's nice that they added end game content. This is a fight ladder. So endless content. The problem is, it's not at all the content I'm interested in. I wish it was. It theoretically sounds good, but removes the "montage simulator" aspect of the game, which is what I like best. Proving that my idea of what the game is all about may not be everyones. I really wish the endgame content let you continue going with your character in sort of an endless mode where you could still have the normall progression feel and even change things up as you continued various types of fights (ladder, endurance, and single fights). The last fighting menu does hold an optional endurance series, but if you progress through the storyline, you can't even come back to the parts of this you missed (I'll see soon if I missed much or not). The game does let you load up your last character again, but there's nothing you can do except sparing at the gym, working out, and doing the first 2 jobs. There's no more actual fights. I don't know why that last menu is gone, it looks like it should still be in the game. So the end game content is a dissapointment for me. I think it's a great thing to have in the game, and wouldn't remove it. It just doesn't highlight what I like about Punch Club.
The future:
So I hear they are removing stat decay in the sequel. This looks bad to me, but I'll try to withold judgement. Here's why though. As describes, I like the training montage aspect of the game most. I don't like the end game ladder. I imagine the sequel will emphasize the ladder and downplay the training. The training was basically an economic balance game. I don't mean $ economics, but the original definition of the word which is more about the resource of time. In punch club, you have only so much time. There's not enough of it to do everything. They manage this by having 4 "bodily" resources that are consumed by working on your stats, income, or the progression of time. The stat decay is done well because it decays a % of your stat level every day, but when you work on a stat, you increase it by points, not %. Couple that with how eacy level costs more points, and you get a balance of it being more work to maintain godly stats. Balancing all those things is the fun part of the game. It's fun to me that you can spend as many days as you want growing. Sometimes I want to spend lots of time doing this, and sometimes i want to spend as little time as possible. I love that I have that choice. Without stat decay, I imagine it will lock you into a certain amount of stat progression in between fights to balance against progressing to maximums. That or it brakes the game like easy more does for the original Punch Club, but I'd be surprised if they let this happen. Or it makes number of days to complete the game the real challenge, which is meaningless to me. Kind of like points in an Atari game, I never cared about that, I only cared about progress and how far I got. But the original was good enough that I'll have my eye on on the sequel and just hope.
Anyways, game recommended, glad I got it. Glad I played it. Still playing it.

50 hours in and I think it's time to write a review. Been playing it on and off rather addictively for the last month or so, most of that due to my unrelenting addiction for minesweeper (and achievements) as well as just wanting to top those leaderboards to make my life seem less worthless...
This is the best minesweeper remake I've ever played, it is a hell of a lot better then the windows remake that was on the windows store (not sure if they actually made it) which was a tragedy.
Like that one this too had pickups, which is an obviously new addition to the classic minesweeper formula and whilst I was pretty skeptical at first it's a very well incorporated addition unlike the other version. There is also classic mode where you only have 1 life and therefore you hit a bomb you die (just like in real life!).
This game has unlimited levelling (until I assume the board is literally just mines) but post level 60, odds are you're going to find it very hard to complete it. This put me off a little at first, since the game then revolved too heavily on luck and not skill but then if it'd be far too easy if everything was solvable by skill, there's not much to really make harder regarding skill in minesweeper.
The sheer difficulty of the higher levels have made me a much better player as I was forced to find new ways and rules to find bombs, which is something games won't normally do!
The graphics are nice but not too distracting and veer too far from the original minecraft, in other words there is nothing over the top and 'included because it's eye candy and omg luk at dem 4k textures'... Sounds are fine, bombs give a nice explosion (and leave a crater in the board) which can be quite unnerving when you're really focusing which brings a lot of tension to the game.
The devs seem to very active, I've seen a lot of activity in the forums from them and they seem to answer and adress the majority of problems that appear which is great. They seem to really care about the game and are not looking for quick monies, especially considering the price!
For £1.99 this is a steal, I think I got this in a greenlight bundle so I paid a lot less and feel like I robbed the devs and also took there clothes but I'd pay at least full price considering I've got 50 hours out of it and I don't feel like I'm going to be uninstalling anytime soon (#1 spot on the leader board here I come!). Even if you are not human and didn't enjoy the original minesweeper, you should still pick this up if you even have the very least bit of passing interest in minesweeper. Recent update made the earlier levels a lot easier so it starts off as a very casual game, perfect for wasting time!
A nice spin for a classic timekiller. Made me kinda happy. :D

So what has this game going for it? There has to be something as it´s based on a free game that is furthermore already installed on every windows pc out there.
Well, there is a mode with more lives so you don´t die instantly, tho as a hardcore Minesweeper lover, that´s nothing for me.
One thing they did well is the first click: it is guaranteed to give you a start, and yes while this is not really innovative as other games did it as well by already revealing an area at the start, it´s definetly a feature that´s missing in Minesweeper...
Tho they forgot to change the biggest flaw of Minesweeper. If they had done that, i´d blindly recommend the game to anyone who likes Minesweeper... but they didnt: You still have to guess.
The more mines you add, the higher the probability of you having to guess meaning that the later stages will have a near to 100% chance that you will need to guess AT LEAST once, if not more times.
And as in any game: the word random should not be able to describe the game. Be it Hearthstone (a Hearthstone referene from a Minesweeper review, yes i did it) or any other game, it will decrease the value by an extreme amount.
So no, i can´t recommend you to buy this game, as it´s essentially the same game as the free version you probably already have installed...
Note: You can´t tell me there is no algorithm for placing the bombs in a way that you don´t have to guess. "Hexcells: Infinite" did it and they had a far more complex ruleset to work with. So yeah, i will just keep waiting until someone may eventually release this game without having to guess, until then, play something else...

It's a good Minesweeper remake! There are dozens of levels now instead of just three, Steam leaderboards to show off with, and the options and controls are just like how you remember them. (Plus, it's got a nice background track that sounds roughly like a cat playing Team Fortress 2.)
That being said, Minesweeper is much more boring than I remember it. It's mostly just a game of matching: spotting which numbers on the board are equal to the amount of adjacent tiles or flagged mines. The only real puzzle aspect to Minesweeper comes when you've spotted all the possible matches, and the only way to progress is to use some deductive reasoning on the remaining numbers. But no matter how hard you try, if there are too many mines clustered together in the wrong way, you're eventually going to have to start guessing, and that's ultimately Minesweeper's biggest downfall.
Luckily, Fine Sweeper gives you lives, so you can step on multiple mines on a level and still keep going. This introduces a completely new skill to the game: when stuck in a guessing situation, instead of just clicking and hoping you don't die, you have to pick the option that would give you the most useful information in a single click. It's a pretty nice touch and it feels like a good evolution of the game of Minesweeper.
But eventually the game starts cranking up the number of mines, enough to remind you of that one time you thought it would be hilarious to make a custom Minesweeper game with the maximum amount of mines, and then soon realized it was completely pointless and impossible. Despite the designer's attempts to balance the difficulty, it's inevitable in Minesweeper that you're going to have to guess a whole lot. But that's a problem with Minesweeper itself, and so this remake shouldn't really be held accountable for it.
Although, it makes me wonder if the level generator could have included a bot that plays through the stage before it is presented, to make sure there are no necessary guesses. Or if there could be seeded boards with an automatic first click that are verified possible without guessing. But even though Fine Sweeper doesn't go all-out in bringing Minesweeper into the HD age, it's still good enough to be worth your time if you were, or still are, a huge fan of the old Windows games; it is a notable improvement on them.

Fine Sweeper is, well, Minesweeper, but with some changes which I found to enhance the basic experience. The game is immediately familiar to anyone who’s played Minesweeper, and it also has a tutorial for anyone who hasn’t.
The main mode of the game is a “campaign” style mode – you basically start with a tiny board to clear, and each time you win you progress to a slightly more difficult board (the backgrounds and colors vary as well). Pretty soon (and I do mean soon, it doesn’t take long to progress through the early levels) you’ll be playing on boards even more difficult than the “Expert” boards from Minesweeper. As you play through the campaign, you earn points for each mine you flag and each board you clear – and you can compare your scores to other players’ on the leaderboards.
This leads me to my only complaint – there’s no way to save your campaign progress. When you quit the campaign, your score is reset. You can still start at the highest level you’ve unlocked, but your score starts at zero. A single save slot would allow you to continue the game through more than one session.
As you play, you randomly unlock and find lives, which are used up whenever you detonate a mine. This single-handedly fixes the main frustration I have with Minesweeper – there’s no second chance if you guess wrong. Of course, once you run out of lives your game is over, but at least some of the frustration has been alleviated.
Custom game boards are included, so you’re able to create your own challenges. And if you’re not a fan of the new lives mechanic, you can play in “Classic” mode to disable it. The developer has proven to be very responsive as well, pushing out updates quickly and regularly based directly on community feedback.
Fine Sweeper provides a comprehensive Minesweeper package and improves on the classic. It’s more than worth the low price point.

For a while I was looking for a game that tested creativity without stumping the player.
In this game you go around each floor completing objectives or quests. There are many ways to approach each objective or quest and that's where the fun comes in. For a game in Alpha I can do nothing but reccomend it. The developer is active on his discord channel. Things this game has coming.
Seeding - This is a Rogue Like game which means perma death. However with seeds you will be able to play the same world more than once. This also opens up oppurtunities for racing your friends.
Custom Characters - Streets of Rogue has many unlockable and playable characters to choose from. But in the future you will be able to create your own.
Custom Mutators - Currently in order to spice the game up you can play with mutators, an extra set of rules that the game applies beforehand to each level. For example one of them makes it so the game runs at 1.3 speed making everything faster. Another makes it so everybody has rocket launchers! Custom mutators are on their way and then it's up to you to decide what happens.
More items - This game has a variety of items and gadgets. With more to come!
New levels - As of right now the game only has a small amount of levels and worlds. But the new ones will be added later and in the mean time there is a mutator that works as sort of a new game plus type deal.
This game is totaly worth the money it costs and it's not even close to being finished yet.
Also if you ever get bored playing alone...There is Local and Online Co-op!

I found Element4l to be very frustrating and contrary to the expectations created by the description of the game and the screenshots/videos. The calm, relaxed aesthetic of the graphics, sound, music, and writing was ruined by the unforgiving twitch gameplay. If you're looking for a relaxing zen game, you won't find it here. And if you're looking for a fast-paced twitch racer to test your reflexes, there are many more polished games available in that genre.
It's a rock, it's a bubble, it's a water droplet, it's a... flame! No, seriously. It's all those things. Solid enough, takes mad keyboard touching skills. 6/10, is pretty cool.

If you like fast paced platformers you will like this.
You play as an "element" trying to find other elements to breathe life into, and its very interesting how the dynamics work together. You have four forms. Air(a bubble which pops if it touches anything but water) Ice (which melts into water sometimes) Fire (which bounces off lava but explodes if it touches anything else) and earth (the sturdiest but also heaviest). Using these different forms you need to float, bounce, slide, and smash your way through the obstacle course of good old mother nature to reach the lost element and save it. There isn't much of a storyline, but that really doesn't matter. This game doesn't need a storyline. Its simple and brilliant with the vague story it has that lets us, the player, compound it with our struggles as we push through level after level.
Pros?
It has amazing art that runs very smoothly. Its actually kind of relaxing. A far different experience than ESJ for sure with soothing colors and almost water color-esque landscapes. You won't find any dizzying sickness or seizure warnings here. The graphics are beautifully crafted and friendly and inviting. Perfect for winding down from a long day with.
The soundtrack is completely unique and ten kinds of amazing, AND it comes FREE with the game, no extra purchases. The music tracks are all long fully fleshed out pieces and are also very soothing without being sleep inducing. They keep a fast pace while using soothing xylo sounds and fit in with the game completely, pulling you in and making you forget about the world outside for a bit.
The gameplay? Fabulous. Its easy enough to get through a level, the question is, can you get through a level without dying, catch all the "sparks" and hit the finish line in a short enough time to get a gold medal? Thats the hard part. Even getting just one of those is the hard part to be honest. The game may have soothing graphics but don't take it lightly- it can still definitely be rage inducing at times. It IS a challenge.
The game has a ton of replay value while you race through levels trying to beat your best time and find that one spark you missed, as well as a racing mode that is incredibly fun if you ever get bored of the solo levels.
Cons?
It tends to get a bit demeaning at times. After you die a few times in one place, I think the number may be as little as three, no matter what level you are on it will start prompting you to ask it for help so it can teach you how to do what it wants you to with a little ghost element for you to follow. This can feel particularly like its just mocking you if you are already doing what it suggests and just havn't quite got the right angle yet and are over shooting or under shooting or not gathering enough momentum.
The levels are quite long for a platformer of this speed, and the save system unhelpful as if you leave and come back you will have entirely forgotten where you are going or how to get there. This is not something to play for a few minutes at a time.
Going to be honest, the level design art is lovely. The cutscene art creeps me out a little bit. It might creep others out as well. Giving cells cute baby faces might not have been the best idea.
Simple, Hard, Fun, Hard, Beautiful, Hard, oh and did I mention it's god damn HARD?

It's pretty much a pretty version of Minesweeper, but you have extra lives, up to 7 maximum, so you can hit up to 7 bombs before losing, and you can also find health pickups when uncovering tiles so you can refill your lives 1 at a time. Of course, there's also Classic mode, which is without the lives like the original Minesweeper.
There's some convenience features, like if there's already a marked bomb next to a "1" for example, you can right click the "1" to auto reveal all tiles around it. Of course, if you marked the wrong tile you'll hit a bomb, but it makes things quite more fluid. Also, they altered it a bit so that the first click on a level
hits a bomb.
You start at level 1, and as you beat levels it gets increasingly harder and harder. Once you've beaten a level, you can choose to start at that level so you don't need to start at the beginning every time.
My only complaint is that you cant save games in progress, so if you want to start at level 1 and see how far you can get, you have to finish that challenge in one sitting, else you'll either have to start over, or start at the last level you remember, which resets the score.
If you like Minesweeper, then this game is definitely worth the cheap price.

I liked this game so much, I felt compelled to write a positive review about it to counteract the people saying it's not worth it.
After playing through the campaign and experiencing a lot of what this game has to offer, I cannot explain where all of these negative reviews are coming from.
I've read through a number of reviews about this game being buggy, or too difficult, but it seems like the developers are very responsive and update the game about every week.
The Pros:
- It has a well developed style and impressive pacing. The music fits well with the theme, a lone traveler and his trusty dog companion. It captures the difficulty of survival in the wild.
- Fun gameplay! It's so rewarding to learn as you drift down the river, stopping at various docks looking for specific supplies. You learn quickly which areas have the best stuff.
- It's long and engaging. The campaign takes you about 40 miles and there are several other games modes and difficulties.
- It's difficult... but I appreciate that about a game. It makes it more fun, gives failing more weight and adds a feeling of reward when you succeed.
- Floating down the river often feels difficult... but I also think that adds realism to the game. White water rafting isn't easy, and controlling a raft by yourself has to be hard.
Cons:
- There are some bugs. I once got stuck in a menu at a cut scene, and when I popped out, I was stuck in the menu, floating down the river with no control.
- If you're someone who absolutely NEEDS a tutorial, you may not like this game. The lead you to some crucial survival ingredients in the beginning, but besides that, it's up to you to figure it out.
- It's difficult and doesn't hold your hand. Don't expect this game to explain every aspect to you along the way. They want you to learn, be innovative.
The Flame in The Flood is a beautiful game. It's very emotional and areas along the river change quite a bit, forcing you to adapt in many ways. Scavenging is something that has to be done weighing risk and reward, you can't risk getting a broken leg or getting mauled by wolves for a couple items.
tl;dr -  It's a difficult game, but its emotional theme and depth make it worth the money.

Quite a fun survival game, one of the better ones out there. It has a really unique art style where everything is a sort of blocky, almost picasso-looking shape.  This game also has a fantastic (and fitting) soundtrack, being a sort of Anericana/folk thing by a guy named Chuck Ragan.
I love how there's an actual campaign in the game with a real story to go along with the infinite mode, it makes the game feel more complete, rather than just plopping you onto a randomly generated river and saying "off you go!"  The story itself is quite good, as it really feels like a long journey, so each major milestone feels important and rewarding, and when you finally reach the end you get an incredible feeling of ease and can finally relax, as the difficulty ramps up quite a bit.
The crafting makes good sense, all items require what you'd assume they would require, and you'll not be running around with all the best stuff within 30 minutes of starting like in other games like this.
I love how you can upgrade your raft to add shelter and a stove and stuff like that, which lowers your need to venture into hostile areas as much to simply find a house.  This is balanced well by making the parts to craft these upgrades exceedingly rare.  For instance in my campaign run I finished the story without ever being able to fully upgrade, simply because I didn't find enough upgrade parts
In general the various health things are balanced and make sense, stuff like hunger and thirst goes down just enough that you have to keep moving to find food and water, but not too fast that you're constantly downing food and water every few minutes.  Something I really love is how sleeping doesn't destroy your thirst/hunger meters like in other games, it is much more reasonable.
I did find however that in the infinite mode the bars deplete much more rapidly, almost reaching the annoying level.
One gripe I do have is with the camera. You have no control over it and that can really be a problem. I've had instances where I've been physically unable to see something important because it was blocked from view by the position of the camera. This can include vital items or dangerous creatures, which can be game ending depending on where you are.
Another gripe I have (pretty small one) is that every little action requires time to do, and that can get really tedious.  Getting on and off the raft takes about 5 seconds each, and you'll probably do that hundreds of times in a game. Crafting every little thing takes several seconds, and again, this will be done countless times. I don't mind some things taking time to do (like cooking or searching containers), but when every little thing requires you to watch a bar fill up it can get annoying. However it gives you a good moment to take a gulp of a drink or grab a bite of a snack
Overall though, well worth the money I spent (I got it for 50% off), great atmosphere will definitely stick with me for a while

The Flame in the Flood is a survival game set in a post apocalyptic world. Not much is told to us, other than what we can infer. A flood destroyed the world, and we're just trying to get by. It uses some RPG elements as well as some rougelike elements. You can upgrade your raft, your clothing and your backpack. You also have a companion, a dog named Aesop, that has its own inventory that will persist between runs.
The gameplay mechanics are somewhat unique. It plays similiarly to Faster than Light where you have several encounters seperated by travel. In the case of The Flame in the Flood, you travel downriver on a raft, evading floating cars and shacks, collecting the occasional loot, and heading ashore to restock on supplies, collect materials to upgrade your raft, and hunt (or be hunted by) wildlife.
The rafting portion of the game is fun. There's a real sense of progression going from a raft which is near impossible to control to getting a rudder and a motor and cruising down the river. Due to the procedural nature of the game, it can be difficult to collect the materials required for the upgrades. However as you progress, new zones will have more of the upgrade materials, making it easy to stockpile them.
The other portion of the game takes place on land, in which you craft traps, weapons, loot abandoned buildings and cars for parts. The game introduces you to wildlife with rabbits. They are easily caught with snares and you can use their pelts to craft your first real gear upgrade. From then on, you can craft the Spear trap which is the most efficient trap in the game. A bow and arrow can be craft, but there's really no point to as arrows are MUCH too expensive and much too weak compared to the Spear trap. Wolves begin to show up in mass quantities late game. If you have an abundance of meat (which you will) you can combine them with certain plants to create poison meat, which will only work on wolves but kills them instantly. Bears also exist and can take up to four spear traps to take down, however the provide Bear Hide which can be used to create some of the best gear in the game.
The game is very stylized, reminding me almost of Borderlands. It works very well for it, however the only complaint I have is that the game is a little misleading. It seems like it would be a relatively easy game to run, however, on max settings my GTX 970 and FX-6350 were pushing it just barely over 60fps @ 1080p. My laptop, i7-7700HQ and GTX 1050, couldn't maintain 60fps @ 1080p on the lowest settings. The animations do get stuck occasionally, or models will disappear sometimes but ultimately
Wonderful OST. Really gives that sort of travelling feel. The sound design is very good as well. The storytelling is fantastic, each character has charm and that's really how I would describe the whole game. It's charming. They tell you so little about the story that you have to fill in the holes yourself. It really makes it feel like you're exploring a world instead of reading out of a history book.
The saving system is frustrating. It seemed a little unclear where and when it saved and what triggered a save. Not being able to save your game when you're going to leave is a little frustrating as well. This is more a gripe than a legitimate point against the game however.
This game is wonderful. It's 100% worth the price (14.99 at time of writing). If you enjoyed FTL or similiar games, you'll enjoy this. It has a few quirks. I ran into some issues with animations and control issues (for example, all movement input just stopped and I had to reload from a check point). They seemed to compound as I got further into my run so it may be related to save sized and or memory limits? Not entirely sure, just speculating.
If you enjoyed FTL, you'll probably like this.

I personally prefer this approach because it gives me a set of discrete goals to accomplish in a reasonable amount of time. I can play for twenty minutes, hit two or three islands and feel like I moved the needle.
I love the stylized graphics and the soundtrack is worth the cost of admission by itself.
Check it out if you find most survival games a bit too complicated and time consuming, but maybe give it a pass if you are a genre veteran craving ever more depth.

EDIT: I also wrote up a guide for the game, you can find it here:
-A wolf wrapped in sheep's clothing, all is not as it appears with this entry to the series, with as much playability and polish as a main series title is (even the game's files refer to it as "FNAF6".)
-Replayability is very high this time around with lots of different approaches to managing your buisness, all leading to different endings and awards you can receive (try to get as little money as possible and settle a lawsuit, for instance). You can even opt for playing through the whole game without seeing a single jumpscare.
-If you're invested in the lore and story for these games, FFPS manages to tie up many loose ends and answer nearly every question that's been left unresolved, tying a nice bow into the "gift" that is the FNaF series.
-Nights have clear objectives, easy to understand mechanics, and won't leave you scratching your head as to how everything works. The game does a stellar job in having you learn its mechanics as you play, even further encouraging replays.
-All of the above is completely free.
-Some mechanics are not as straightforward as others. The "audio response" segments never clearly describe what to look out for when completing them. However, as you play through the game again, you'll pick up on the movements of each animatronic, which makes them easier. These sections also have a strange bug where it won't acknowledge when you've checked the paper and can mess up your run.
-Not as graphically or auditorily pleasing as Sister Location, but as it's done intentionally, it's a very minor negative point.
-The main stage room is a bit of a cluttered mess when you have a few large objects lying around, making everything look sloppy (There IS an in game reason for this, though).
-Requires you to have played nearly EVERY game and have read EVERY book to understand what exactly happens here and when it takes place.
Easily one of the best entries in the Five Nights at Freddy series to date. You'll find yourself distracted playing minigames, buying up new items for your Pizzeria, and wanting to complete each day just to see what the next brings.
Some are stating this might be the last entry in the series, but something tells me this won't be the last time we hear from Scott and FNaF.
If you've never played a single game in the series before and want to see what the fuss is about, this isn't a bad game to start with, and the free price tag makes it all the more inviting. Just don't expect the game to catch you up on any details if you missed out on prior games.

What a great game!
For a while I was looking for a game that tested creativity without stumping the player.
In this game you go around each floor completing objectives or quests. There are many ways to approach each objective or quest and that's where the fun comes in. Will you run and gun your way through while taking mutiple enemies at once? Will you set up distractions and pick off the enemies one by one? Will you set your enemies against eachother and then go in at the end as a clean-up crew? Or will you just stealth your way through?
For a game in Alpha I can do nothing but reccomend it. The developer is active on his discord channel. Things this game has coming.
Seeding - This is a Rogue Like game which means perma death. However with seeds you will be able to play the same world more than once. This also opens up oppurtunities for racing your friends.
Custom Characters - Streets of Rogue has many unlockable and playable characters to choose from. But in the future you will be able to create your own.
Custom Mutators - Currently in order to spice the game up you can play with mutators, an extra set of rules that the game applies beforehand to each level. For example one of them makes it so the game runs at 1.3 speed making everything faster. Another makes it so everybody has rocket launchers! Custom mutators are on their way and then it's up to you to decide what happens.
More items - This game has a variety of items and gadgets. With more to come!
New levels - As of right now the game only has a small amount of levels and worlds. But the new ones will be added later and in the mean time there is a mutator that works as sort of a new game plus type deal.
This game is totaly worth the money it costs and it's not even close to being finished yet.
Also if you ever get bored playing alone...There is Local and Online Co-op!

This charming, feel-good game is based on Scandinavian folklore, which was compelling enough reason for me to try it out, as I find gaming to be a great way to learn about various mythologies of interest when incorporated into this medium of story-telling.
It's of the Point and Click genre, with rather delightful art (
) and adequate voiceovers.
The game is short, but there are 3 different possible endings, each of which give a different Achievement/Achievements, depending on the choices you make throughout the game. Your mission, as the helpful Gnome, is to commit acts of goodness for the local spirits and/or the humans who dwell above your home, ultimately gaining power with which to fight a horrible troll that has evil designs.
I am impressed that this is a mainly One-Person development, with the soundtrack being composed by a second individual, and I experienced no glitches or bugs. The common complaint that the Gnome moves too slowly is easily catered for by double-clicking, or changing settings ingame, so that was no problemmo for me.
I bought this game with a 50% Off coupon, so the price was awesome, but I would pay full price for this if I bought it again - ofc that's personal preference, being due to the little insight I got into this part of the folklore was worth the dollars to me, on top of the other aspects I've written on here. The interest I gained through this inspires further reading and that is a bonus benefit that again, is subjective.
So I would recommend, yes, but I would definitely suggest doing a little research first to see if the price-for-content fits for yourself.

I thoroughly enjoyed this little game. I've read reviews complaining that it's too simple, that the movement is too slow, that it's not "action-oriented" enough. But that's not the point of the game. It's an attempt by someone from one culture to teach at least part of the myths and legends from that culture to the rest of the world, in a form that is accessible to many people.
Also, take into account when you play this that the game, while put out by a company, was actually designed, drawn, and brought to life by one person over just six months. And for those of you who just have to move our little gnome faster, there's a way to speed him up in the options menu.
If you're achievement oriented, then you will have to play the game through at the very least three times in order to reach the different outcomes required by those particular achievements. So, while it can be played through in a short period of time, it cannot be COMPLETED in that single playthrough. Also, the final locked achievement isn't explained anywhere, there is no walkthrough, and looking at the global stats, it's not one that many players either can or bother to figure out.
This is another game that, when I want to step back from destroying the world or making life-altering decisions for characters or watching blood spatter, I come to Midvinter and enjoy the gnome, his friends and helpers, and even the Troll. Maybe I keep hoping that one day I'll actually be able to talk him into going into the bedroom so that I can finally see these mysterious humans who he takes such excellent care of?
At any rate, I recommend this game to anyone who is interested in learning, who isn't so adrenaline addicted that they can't stop killing for even 20 minutes, or even if you simply want an inexpensive game that offers you the ability of gaining both achievements and trading cards.
You could do far worse than spend a little time in...Midvinter.

is a short point & click adventure based on Scandinavian folk lore. It has a fun and original storyline as far as games go and about an hour of content.
is a curious one. Folk lore of Scandinavian people with gnomes, trolls and other fay folk is a rarity not often explored in games. As a Finnish gamer (and our folk lore shares a lot with the Swedish one) I found the theme refreshing.
Taking the role of a house gnome, you are (as per the folk lore goes) a benevolent house spirit that helps out the people living there. New people have moved in, so once again you have a purpose. Unfortunately a troll has also arrived to cause trouble.
plays out like a traditional point & click game, with the difference that you have a time limit (time moves on when you switch scenes). Your actions during this time affect the events and the ending of the story. While a short game, there are four endings (three of which grant an achievement) depending on how you play it out.
Story and its motivation is simple but good. There are relatively lot of things to do on the farm considering the length of the game, and I enjoyed finding the different endings a lot. The game and its puzzles are also rather easy for anyone who's played point & click games before. It would work well for children.
Graphical style is good and does great service to the mythology the game is based on. Soundtrack also fits the theme quite nicely, nothing to complain there.
The English voice acting is the only place that could see some improving. I thought the human dialogue was quite okay but everyone else talked rather awkwardly: the conversations simply didn't sound natural. One could perhaps blame the supernatural origin of the speakers but I found the voice acting on those parts mediocre nevertheless.
This might only concern English: there's Swedish voice acting as well, but I didn't try that. Perhaps it's better, being the native language of the speakers. It's nice that options include setting subtitles and voice acting separately if you'd prefer.
Gameplay has a quirk that you can never simply move. Gnome moves only when interacting with stuff. And boy, does he move slowly! Fortunately you can skip both the movement and dialogues (after enabling this in the settings).
Technically
is pretty good, and I encountered only a couple minor bugs along the way, seeing a duplicate shovel and experiencing one animation freeze that was amended by a reload. By the way, the game saves automatically in each scene. However, the lack of manual saves matters little since the game is so short.
Nevertheless, the problems are rather small. Overall
is a very nice game, albeit also really short one. It could be played thoroughly in a mere hour, even though I spent a leisure 2 hours on it.
Its main issue is ultimately its short length: I don't think it's totally worth 5 € for a one hour experience. Half the price and I think you have a nice purchase.
I'm lovin' it. Would love to get more games like this to play and review.

I'm actually quite surprised with how Assassin's Creed Origins turned out. After Unity I decided to skip Syindicate because it just seemed to be Unity with the same old boring Assassin's Creed formula. What changed for me this time? Well, they took their time with this one and gave the community a setting that was highly demanded. But that is just two things out of the biggest reason of all, they turned it into an RPG. For me, action RPGs have always been a replayed genre. I'd replay Fallout: New Vegas or The Elder Scrolls, to even Dead Island. However, this game may not be much in terms of "replayable" and what I mean is that some tasks can get really boring, specificly the crafting. I've went through two too many Far Cry games in which I have to find, hunt, and kill some poor animals just to craft a quiver that can hold an extra 10 arrows.
I can really appreciate the mix of RPG elements with a stealth adventure game. They have done pretty well with this, even though there are a couple of things that I have to complain about. 1st is that they removed the parkour down system which I thought was a great feature that was added into Unity. I'd tend to find myself struggling to get down something because I have been so used to it. 2nd I can't throw smokes and when you dodge and attempt to assassinate someone you may end up using one smoke bomb. 3rd I have to go through the menu just to equip the tools I want. 4th I liked the cover system from Unity, it helped make assassinating targets easier. 5th the crafting is tedious.
Those are some complaints I have about the game but it still doesn't take away the enjoyment I get out of it. I really enjoy Bayek as a character and his eagle Senu make a great team in a lot of situations. The stealth feels challenging, as it should be. I never really had instances where after alerting someone and taking them down, the entire place know where I am. It's just take that guy down and it's back to stealth. I love the abilities, although it would interesting to see it exapanded upon in someway. Stealth has perhaps been better than most modern stealth genres besides Dishonored or something. It especially has been better for an Assassin's Creed title which I'm thankful for. You can choose to go in and hide bodies, picking people off one by one. Or go for a more aggresive stealth approach. There is also no penalty to XP if guards are alerted and they call for reinforcements like they had in Far Cry. This truly feels like a proper RPG experience that I am glad to play.
The combat is perhaps the best combat I have felt in a video game. This also goes along with the challenging feeling it creates. It's no longer icons on heads indicating an on coming attack. Instead, they offered vareity for once. Which made it even better because you unlocked new combat abilities to add more variety to combat. I think that is one of the things that made it spark, you were able to freely control the situation and the amount of combat varieties you could do made it feel like every fight would be something new.
Of course, there are some things that really♥♥♥♥♥♥me off about the game, but the Assassin's Creed series has always done this. The voices of the random NPC's are so annoying! Especially the kids. But the music does make it better and more bareable.

Let's not beat around the bush - it's just Minesweeper with a facelift.
It has a couple of flaws: it does have an element of chance in it rather than logic as there are some cases where there is no telling which of two cells has the mine underneath, and due to the progression you kind of just have to keep playing until you tire (which for me happened about 20 levels in, way before I felt in any real danger of losing). It also starts out very easy and takes a long time to build up to any real difficulty, although that is a matter entirely of personal preference.
On the other hand, if the idea of a game of minesweeper with a few app-like elements (added lives, some sort of social score thing popping up telling you how far ahead of other players you are etc.) appeals to you then this is a good implementation of this.
Overall, I'd say go for the Hexcells series if you want carefully crafted, more cerebral levels with absolutely no guessing and a higher difficulty threshold, but if you just want to sit and click in a faster-paced way then this may be the game for you. It's kind of the Bejeweled Blitz of Minesweeper clones.

An interesting addition to the tower defense genre with a bunch of serious shortcomings.
A tower defense game that has just one giant map and your goal is to "conquer" all of it while fulfilling a number of tasks that will make your life harder?
Haven't heard that one yet.
But surprisingly, it works. Mostly.
You expand via your buildings and towers (all of which you can move around as they can lift off and fly), mine resources to build them and research new towers and improvements (for example, more electricity to be able to have MORE TOWERS!!).
Meanwhile, you will be attacked from various lairs in the map and have to place your towers so that you can defend your vital buildings: mines, purifiers which make areas buildable and relays that transport electricity to your towers.
In the beginning, only one lair will pester you, but as you grow, more will join the fray as well as other things happening to make your life worse (won't spoil them).
The tasks I wrote about above are to increase your population, gather special resources, use those to build an escape portal (hence the title) and an additional one that is unlocked later on.
The art is very consistent, competently done and just cute.
As is the music and sound. The voices are also well done, but I imagine the "false rastafari style" speech might annoy a few people.
It would be a great little game, really, if it were not for the
:
The biggest problem, as others have pointed out, too, is the grind and pacing.
Instead of steadily increasing what you have to do, the gameplay almost automatically comes to a halt every now and then as you are waiting for research to happen, resources to be gathered or buildings to be built.
It isn't really a fluent experience. Instead you have those phases with nothing happening at all interrupting the rest.
Especially in the first 3-4 hours it is hard to keep yourself motivated.
If you do manage to keep playing, things improve a lot as more and more lairs will be bothering you, as well as other things going on requiring your attention.
But I can understand those that have stopped before that point very well.
Another problem is the balancing of the creatures. The first 5-6 creature types are total pushovers.
But suddenly, one creature type is unlocked that will just waltz right through your towers, destroying them by the dozens before it is dealt with - and there is no way to focus fire as far as I can tell. This can very much ruin your game after 3 hours or so of playing.
Especially since the game might just decide to autosave right in that moment (and there is only one autosave slot instead of rotating ones).
Manual saving is very much recommended.
The controls might also get in your way. While you can use control groups, you can only effectively group defense towers together. If you are like me and used to also grouping same-style producer buildings together to produce quicker, you are out of luck.
Now, you CAN theoretically group together producer buildings, but it is pointless as that doesn't let you build anything while having multiple ones selected.
What really happens is that you'll have to assign each armory (which builds defensive towers) an extra group, same with the mothership and the other building producing non-defense buildings.
To make matters worse, the game has a selection limit for some unfathomable reason. You can have only 20 towers in one group, and trust me, that is not enough by far for anything but the early game. Especially considering that you will lose and have to replace lots of towers, which then means more fiddling around with control groups and the selection limit.
Very annoying and this should have been done much better.
, this is a recommendable game, but you should not expect it to be flawless or entertain you endlessly.
If you like Mine Sweeper games, this is it with a little more features in it, not bad for a buck.

I really enjoyed Hypernova Escape from hadea.
It has RTS and Tower defense mechanics, City building, Tech to research and unlock, and a wonky difficulty curve that starts off insanely easy and then slams you to the ground and mericlessly beats you to death.
I've got 14.4 hours in the game and managed to beat it on normal difficulty in about 12 hours.
With not giving anything away my massive foothold on the planet was litterally crumbling as the last colonist escaped. Had they walked a little slower it would have been all over.
So cons for the game.
It starts off rather slow. The building is slow, the attacks are slow, and it seems extremely easy.
Best bet is to build 2 builders or 3 for the early stage of the game so you can spam buildings quicker.
There is no pause screen which is desperately needed.
The map and ability to identify things needs a bit more work.
Now lets talk about that slow start. Part of the reason its slow is really one of the games  mechanics. You can only move so many buildings at once, can only build so many at once, and then you have the movement time of those buildings to their destinations. All of that takes time Which you dont really have when the aliens are eating your people.
While in the beginning its a bit frustrating cause you cant expand quite as quick as you want, later on it becomes white knuckle panic as your hoping that wave of buildings gets to the front line before it collapses.
All in all Hypernova is a fun game mid to late game that has some flaws that are being worked on. Pause is coming in a new update and I think the folks at Actalogic will fix most of the other QOL changes that are needed.
The game is definitely worth its price point to me as I had a blast with it.

I've played for around 7 years now, and I'm bored, so heres a review of my favorite mmorpg of all time.
PROS
-Best action combat game, theres no other game that quite matches up with it
-PvP is EXTREMELY fun with this combat system. In tab targetting games it just feels like a matter of who presses thier buttons in the right order and manages thier cooldowns best, while with action combat PvP, you have to do that, but you also have to time your dodges, aim your skills, read your opponents moves and learn the animation tells for each classes skills. It adds a ton of fun and skill cap to the PvP I havnt experienced in other games
-PvE is also extremely fun. again theres a higher skill needed than with tab targetting games as you need to learn animation tells and time your dodges and invincibilty frames well. You can also farm boss monsters out in the world to level if questing bores you, dungeons are fun. You can play the entire game solo if you wanted. It will take a bit longer to reach max level but it's possible, and I'm happy it caters to solo players and doesn't force them to do stuff they don't want to.
-It's a visually stunning game. Even all these years later I'm still entranced by the beauty of some of the games areas. Theres also little side areas not shown on the map all the time. You can get entirely off the map and reach some of the scenery in the distance, like the mountain range behind highwatch. Its fun to get to the highest point you can reach on a mountain and just see all of the different zones below you. Exploration is extremely fun and some of the places and views you'll find are simply breathtaking.
Now for the cons, which there are a LOT more of unfortunately
-The game is dying. With the release of B&S and BDO came the loss of a fair amount of TERAs players. I think they'll come back eventually, due to the fact that B&S just isn't a good alternative to TERA, and BDO is too grindy for alot of the people who played TERA with the lack of dungeons and questing experience. So I think TERA will get some players back, but not a lot. Eventually as more alternatives come out over the next few years TERA will be forgotten I feel.
-PvP is basically dead at this point. Unless you're on Mount Tyranas, you won't be able to find much PvP. Currently my characters are on highwatch and I rarely see people at the dueling square outside Velika, alliance territories are deserted, and queue times for any battleground are insanely long, even Corsair's Stronghold.
-The endgame can get very boring, very fast. Used to be there was wonderholme and nexus and alliance territories and a bunch of fun stuff to go do at max level. Wonderholme would take HOURS to finish, there were traps and fun mechanics for the fights, it felt like a real endgame dungeon. Then they took it away. Nexus was a fun gathering of a bunch of max level players where the goal was to get as much damage on the mobs as possible, and you had to run from point to point and then go kill the boss. Then they took it away. The alliance territories were fun PvP zones you could access even on PvE servers and kill harder BAMs and form hunting parties to kill either enemy alliances players or BAMs. You had to sneak around and gather your noctenium and hope nobody hunted you down and found you. When you were running from people you hoped and prayed you didnt run into an invisiBAM. It was a ton of fun and a nice change from only having battlegrounds and GvG in PvE servers. Then nothing was ever updated or done with it, and now it's pretty much dead except on a couple servers. Now your options for endgame are talk to friends, run dailies, wait for the hour+ it takes to get into a battleground and get to play that for about 30 minutes at most, or run the dungeons you're sick of after running them over and over again week after week. The dungeons are fun, but there's not any hugely fun mechanics, and none of them feel any harder than the dungeons your ran while leveling up. None of the endgame dungeons feel like an endgame dungeon really. Also due to it being the only thing left to do, running a dungeon becomes boring after the first few times cause you've learned the bosses and it gets to the point where you feel like you're just going through the motions.
-The loot system. To force you to run the repetitive dungeons again and again and make you feel like theres a point, the loot system is ♥♥♥♥ed. You even get your PvP gear from dungeons now instead of having to play PvP to get the materials to craft it. Getting your endgame gear is painstaking, annoying, and downright infuriating at times. The drop rates are stupid, forcing you to run a dungeon for sometimes an entire week before the piece of gear you need drops. Then you have to hope nobody else in your party uses that weapon/armor and needs it. Then you have to hope that somebody doesnt take it for fodder. See unless the party changes the loot rules, anyone can roll on anything. A gunner can roll on those swords you've been trying to get for the past week, and if they roll higher theres nothing you can do about it, you're just♥♥♥♥♥♥outa luck and have to farm for another week. Also you can only run each dungeon at endgame once a day which means you're gonna be farming your gear for a LONG time unless you're very lucky, and also after you run them there won't be anything fun left to do but sit in hour long battleground queues and talk to people. BUT REJOICE, because you can buy instance reset scrolls!! These replenish all of your dungeon runs, but you better have some gold or real life cash to get them. BUT WAIT, THERE'S MORE. For the low price of $15/month, you get DOUBLE the dungeon runs, AND a free instance reset scroll every day!! YIPPEEEEE!!! Now I'm not gonna lie, elite status is worth it. If you love to explore the off the map places, the travel journal is simply amazing as you can save your favorite spots and return to them easily. The town atlas is great, you no longer have to sit through unneccesarily long pegasus rides and can meet your friends easier. The reputation, experience, and gold boosts are also EXTREMELY nice, as you no longer have to buy the scrolls for them. You can also get some pretty nice stuff out of your daily gift box, plus a 280 speed mount is given to you. After you've had elite status, playing the game without it will be hard.
-You're probably gonna spend some money. Between the extra dungeon runs from elite, the need for a 280 mount, the costumes, etc, you'll probably end up spending some money. It's possible to get these things without spending money though, as you can buy them off the broker with gold, but theyre generally extremely expensive and you have to do a ton of farming and crafting and dungeon running to get them.
-The biggest complaint, and the other major reason people are leaving, is the consistent female locking of new classes. Male brawler would make a lot of sense right? Well not according to EnMasse and BHS, human females are the only people who could ever do that. On top of this, the older classes cant even compete with the new ones. Brawlers are consistently the top damage dealt in dungeons, and they're the TANK. PvP against even a half decent brawler is hard.
-You have to read every wall of text on the main questline to have any idea whats happening and why. It gets pretty tedious.
Theres a LOT wrong with TERA, and it's dying out after all these years due to EnMasse and BHS being more interested in cashing in on the female character sex appeal and costumes than keeping the players happy. Despite all of this, I still love playing TERA. No other MMO right now has the same feel with its combat, no other mmo allows me to climb the scenery and find incredible and breathtaking views like TERA does. TERA is the only MMO where I felt like I was on an adventure. Despite all the bad, I would still recommend this game to anyone wanting to find something refreshing and exciting.

Not often do I write reviews however, I think credit is due here. An amazing game and I'm only about 5hours into it!
The basic premise of this game is that there's been a great, society collapsing flood that has destroyed the (country). You control the protagonist, Scout as she tries to find a way out of the flood with the help of her dog. You pilot a small raft down a river, stopping at various islands to trap animals, gather plants, collect drinkable water and scavenge scrap that you use to build things, all while avoiding the perils of sickness, starvation, disease, hypothermia, the raft's destruction, poisonous plants and hostile animals. Ocassionally you'll run into a person that needs help or a helpful stranger - the riverfolk.
I honestly enjoyed this game, it felt like a mix of Dont Starve and the Oregon trail. The soundtrack is amazing and fits the tone of the game and the artstyle is one to be envied. The game features an RNG factor. Sometimes you'll get really lucky and you'll start a game overladen with riches and other times you'll be starving for something you need for a very very long time. Though this can get frustrating, it adds to the replay value. The "biomes" and "islands" are never in the same order making the game a hell of a lot fun.
My main point, inventory management. If you're going to play this expect to do a lot of inventory management. A lot. This is one of the games where everything, and I mean EVERYTHING is done in your inventory. From crafting, to reading up on wounds. Quests, consuming items, equpping armour and weapons. My biggest problem with the game however, is not the time you spend in the inventory but the fact that the game doesnt pause whilst in the inventory, forcing you to hurry and forget to do things because you got jumped apon by a wolf. Speaking of wolves, theres alot of them and theyre hard to get away from. I mean really hard. There is also a constant demand for materials - materials that can be scarce but again, this is all just based on the RNG factor. As I said, youll either love or hate the RNG.
All in all, despite my complaints, there's still a good game under there and I think it's really going to people who like survival games, including myself. The art style's amazing, there's some thought put into the crafting and after playing this I really can't count the number of games I wished would just let me put an herb in water to make tea. The soundtrack has got to be one of the best parts about the game and the easy to learn, hard to master feel makes the game fun and enjoyable. All in all, definantly one of the better games I've played for 7$.

Had me at Deus Ex.
There is immense depth to the gameplay, this is an excellent example of the "emergent" gameplay design principle. There is an open world, that responds in a variety of logical ways to actions that happen within it, both the player and NPCs can act upon the world, there are many tools players and NPCs have access to and many actions they can choose take. On top of all that there are varied and interesting goals for the player to accomplish. It all adds up for unpredictable gameplay where the player is encouraged to experiment. Examples:
I had to kill a drug dealer, who was surrounded by powerful guards. So I bought a drug from the dealer that made me HUGE, took the drug, got HUGE and smashed my way through him and his guards. Not only did the guards and dealer get smashed, but I destroyed the entire building in the process. When that was done the drug hadn't worn off yet, so I smashed through the walls of another building to complete a different mission.
I had to assassinate a prisoner in a guarded complex. There was a window near his cell with an explosive trip wire. I threw a rock through the window, setting off the bomb, hurting my target and destroying the wall of his cell. While the wounded prisoner tried to escape a guard gunned him down, mission accomplished!
There are a great variety of characters you can choose to be which mixes up gameplay. You can be a gorilla who has massive strength but can't speak to NPCs. A hacker who is super weak but can hack any computer he wants. There's perks you can unlock and weapons and all sorts of things to mix up how you play.
The one downside is that there are only 6 levels. Randomly generated levels yes, but still only 6. The dev seems like a good guy and I expect the game has a very bright future. Oh and the game is pretty funny too!
It is great. Gives me the sense of flow I would get from a good Deus Ex session.

I have sunk a few years into this game. I originally had it before it came out on Steam, and the only reason I got it through steam was because I stopped playing and uninstalled it at one point. It was originally owned by a company called Outspark, and it hasn't changed all that much since it switched over to Gamigo. Mostly skin changes for monsters and the starter town.. oh and maybe some NPCs.
In terms of classes, it doesnt really matter what you pick since all the quests are the same. There is no story line whatsoever. There are seasonal events, and the premium item store holds some goodies if you are willing to spend real cash in order to get store currency. It has been said that FO has become a pay to win game, but as long as you're willing to put in the hours, it is possible to reach cap without premium items. I dont suggest battlefields, pvp dungeons or PVP kingdom quests without premium items... which I guess proves the pay to win section.
The enhancement system is also a lot harder if you dont use premium items, and even though enhancement offers some perks, and makes your gear prettier... it is still possible to play without, or you can always farm/sell for in game currency and hope to buy off another player. Players stores can be ridiculously priced though.. unfortunately people dont really offer an item for what it's really worth and tend to overprice useless gear. Be mindful of your class and stats before buying from other players, and really consider whether it is actually worth the price.
It has its pros and cons like any game, but if you're into things like this then by all means give it a go. It's not so bad, as long as you're willing to sink hours into it.
