I didn't cry when my nan died. I didn't cry when my pets died. I didn't cry when any of my girlfriends left me (most of them left because I never show emotions).
This game had me bawling my eyes out for two hours solid, and ten years after playing it for the first time, I still choke up every time I think about it. Not just the sad parts -- I wept with joy at the happy parts. I laughed till I cried at the funny parts. I overflowed with awe at the beautiful parts.
If you are a cold hearted emotionless robot of a person, and you wonder what it must be like to be a normal person who feels things, I recommend reading this story to find out. If you are a normal person, I recommend it too, and I also recommend a large stack of tissues to help you see the screen once the story gets going.
I am fairly sure that nobody will ever create a kinetic novel which is similar to this and better than it, so even if it doesn't sound interesting to you, I'd say play it anyway just to see what a tiny shard of perfection looks like.

This visual novel is a true display of how amazing visual novels can be.
The visuals and artwork are beautifully crafted down to every last detail, from the character art to the backgrounds, everything is perfectly defined, a masterpiece of modern Japanese anime art.
Sound is equally brilliant, from the voice acting down to the music, every word, every tone, every little tune is perfectly placed and fits equisitely with the mood throughout.
And of course, the main part of a visual novel, the story.  What can I say about the story?  Well...
Planterian, in short, is one of the most emotionally powerful things I've ever experienced in my life.  I'm accustomed to visual novels and their abilities to create an emotional response, whether it's happiness, sadness, anger or any other range of emotions, but what I didn't expect from this was that it would have me crying so much that I felt like my eyeballs were going to explode because my tear ducts couldn't excrete tears fast enough to keep up with what was going on.  It's a real heart-breaker of a story, and at the end you won't feel like you're just losing another character in another game, you'll feel like you're losing a much loved friend, it'll shatter your heart into a million pieces and scatter them across the night sky like the twinkling stars of Yumemi's planetarium.  It's worth more than the price it's selling for on Steam, and I recommend that anyone, whether you like visual novels or not, should sit down with this, switch it on auto, get a box of tissues, and prepare to witness something that will stay in your heart and your memories forever. x

Where to start, this is a KEY visual novel so expect tears and emotional scenes. The heroine Hoshino yomemi is a special robot girl waiting for customers; wanting your happiness, and just seeing you smile. That is where it starts, the emotional scenes are full of happiness and just filled with this striving feeling of protecting her. The star scene itself will get you in tears but this visual novel will make you sad, happy and just a overall sense of catharsism. I recommend this game.
This was an amazing experience. Though it's a shame that epilogue was not included.

A stunningly beautiful tale of a broken world full of broken people and broken machines. Each minute spent with Yumemi is one to treasure and hold close to your heart as her childlike innocence is the only beacon of hope left in a dead city. Hats off to KEY for being able to make the audience grow so attached to a robot in such a short time. Absolutely worth the time and money.

For being the first game of Talecore studios, it's a very nice and warm experience, still fantastic to think that it has been made by one person alone in such a short time. It seems like there are very few games today inspired by nordic mythology, especially the very small and mundane, that was very common in countries like Sweden, when people were still very superstitious and afraid of the dark. Images like Näcken, the fierce but beautiful portrayal of a man, said to drown those who come close enough to hear his tunes on his violin, and the Skogsrå, lone protector of the forest, are just two common creatures of nordic mythology that appears in the game. Midvinter brings back that fairytale feeling I used to grow up with as a child. It makes you want to sit in front of a warm hearth, and just admire the snow outside your window, while in reality as I sit playing the game, it's just the start of a hot summer.
It's a short and cosy experience, leaving me longing for more. I could go back to play Skyrim, but the nordic feeling doesn't carry the same kind of mood, with it's combat-oriented gameplay. In truth, I'd love to see more titles striving for this kind of depiction of old folklore. Quiet, somber, cozy, and chilly, just like the arts of John Bauer.
Definitely looking forward to any kind of similar follow-up, revolving around the same setting.

This game is disappointing because I might've enjoyed a slightly different game.  It was definitely a little fun at first: figuring out the game mechanics, managing the police department, and making decisions about where to spend resources.  The game also had a storyline that started out interesting but didn't really develop into anything interesting or well-explained.
The gameplay mechanics are decent but quite slow at times and there's no way to accelerate game time.  As a result, I spent quite a bit of the game just sitting and waiting for police cars to get from point A to point B (but not enough that I wanted to put the game down for that reason alone).  This was especially true towards the very end of the game, which felt artifically slow since no new plot lines were developing.  As I approached the end of the game, I had some guesses about what sort of ending might appear based upon my slightly-corrupt-yet-not-murderous time as a police chief.
The tutorial-style hints give you some sense that you have a choice in the flow of the story and that how you play could affect the outcome, but this isn't true at all.  There are two victorious endings and the ending you receive is entirely determined by which of two buttons you press close to the end of the game; none of your other decisions matter.  These endings are unsatisfying in that many aspects of the story are left unexplained.  To be clear: I'm not complaining about the content of the ending but rather the *lack* of it.
From a social perspective, the game content is concerning at best.  I understand that this is supposed to be a gritty, noir police drama.  The game's antagonistic characters are bigoted and corrupt and the storyline condemns this in a sort of fatalistic way.  But the game content in between -- the investigations and police calls to which your staff responds -- tell a different story.  The content of the cutscenes suggest that the story takes place in the mid 1980s, which *might* explain the plethora of racism and homophobia exhibited by gangs and regular citizens alike.  But a few things caught my attention as I played.
In a decision I will ascribe to the
, I powered through to the ending.  I had expected to replay the game for the ending I'd receive as a completely clean police chief, but (1) no such ending exists, (2) I'd have to play through a game that got pretty slow and dull by the end the first time, and (3) I'd have to play through all of those uncomfortable social issues again (which is much easier for me, a white male, than for most people).
In summary, the game could've been interesting but sells itself as something it's not.  The description on the store page seems to suggest a dynamic game with a deep and varied story that responds to the decisions you make.  In reality, the game is perfectly linear, the story is tropey and disappointing, and nothing you do has an impact at the end.

However, there are some issues. Early on city hall demands constant changes to your police force. It is extremely annoying. Every now and then you have to replace or fire a certain amount of officers and there is no way to do this without serious repercussions. If you don't do it, city hall is going to reduce funding and you have fewer and fewer officers. There is no way to keep good officers because sooner or later you have to illegaly fire or kill them. That way the whole skill system is basically useless because nobody stays long enough to seriously improve their skills.
I'm not sure about the investigations either. In the beginning it made sense and was solveable, but now I have several of them and no matter what I do, no matter how thorough I am with everything (reading the testimonies over again, looking at every image the 10th time), there seems to be no solution and I'm almost out of detectives. There is no feedback at all. When the game says they have no new frames, does that mean I need better detectives? Or does it mean I should be able to solve it? Who knows.
All in all it is a good game and it has everything in it that makes it very likeable for me, but especially the (very) ridiculous demands from city hall make everything very tedious. I fully expect them to demand sooner or later that I simply fire all of my officers because the mayor needs some more room to store his money.

Road Redemption prides itself on being the spiritual successor to Road Rash, a Sega Genesis game series from the 90s. Maybe it's just me, but Road Rash is THE pinnacle of 90s childhood gaming. I grew up on Road Rash, I can still remember the feel of getting the highest tier motorcycle and going so fast you can't control it, I remember the smell of the road meeting the tires, I remember the grungy style and poor taste in artwork that made the game a great childhood memory. So I pride myself in being apt to answer the question that’s on everyone’s mind.
Yes, Road Redemption is a solid spiritual successor to Road Rash and is so close to what I wanted from a 2017 Road Rash.
What this game does right it really gets right.  RR gives you that feel of chaotic nonsense on the road and the feeling of smashing people’s faces in while running from cops and shooting guns.  It’s an adrenaline fueled rush that keeps the driving fun and exhilarating.  There are multiple racing types to keep the game from getting stale too quickly.  In some levels you have to just get first place, in other levels you’ll have cars raining from the sky to dodge. It’s combat centric over racing centric, which means you’ll spend more time beating heads in then hardcore gran turismo driving. What this game gets done right outshines its shortcomings, but unfortunately its shortcomings are pretty severe.
The biggest problem RR has is how they decided to present their gameplay in terms of progression, pacing, and choice.  This game is a “rogue-lite” in the sense that when you die you restart at the very beginning of the “randomly” generated levels.  This is an awful idea.  The complete fun and enjoyment of the game is put behind an annoying wall of dying over and over to make minimal skill tree progression.  When I do finally make headway in the campaign I encounter new levels and new aesthetics that keep me interested, but when I die I have to go back to restarting  from the desert zone for the 30th time.  I’m not entirely sure why this style of gameplay was even put into the game.  In the original Road Rash, you pick a bike, then you pick a level, depending on your performance you get cash which is deducted by how badly you screw up your vehicle in the process.  It’s a grind but it’s a grind with a point, you can see the better vehicles, you can walk inside the fancy shop and look at bikes and go “I want that!” but the vehicle you’re stuck with is a dingy piece of trash.  You begin to grow a connection to not only your bike as it carries you through easy races and becomes your “valiant steed” but to the levels as well.  You start to enjoy certain levels because of their cash output or their aesthetics.  You can choose to play it safe and go to the hills area, or risk it all in a dangerous city run with a higher output of cash.  The pacing is entirely the player’s choice, and this is what made Road Rash so damn good.  Fast forward to Road Redemption and they entirely missed that point.  In a game about driving in the open road bashing people’s faces in with a crowbar, they completely took away all freedom from the player when it comes to choice and replaced it with a very inauthentic rpg style “gain x% more damage” buffs.  Does this choice ruin the game? Not entirely.  But the game is missing its whip cream topping, it’s thing that makes it pop; it’s missing the thrill of being free to make your own choices.
Another criticism I have is the lack of character the game has.  I talked previously about how Road Rash worked and how all these choices made the player attached to the world, the art, the characters.  Road Redemption doesn’t have anything that connects me to the game.  There’s no quirky artwork, there’s no interesting characters, there’s not even anything that keeps me attached to the one thing that matters, the bike I ride.  I talked briefly to the developer about his thoughts on the game and he talked about his focus being on gameplay rather than plot, and whereas I like the idea, an indie company cutting the unnecessary fat to make a better polished gameplay experience, I don’t like how they did it (or rather didn’t) in Road Redemption (this was a very informal call where I called up the developer upon seeing his phone number in the game).  Road Rash didn’t have a plot (or if it did I didn’t notice) but instead characterized the game with short dialog and pictures, and that alone made the game feel alive.  Road Redemption didn’t even try to give its game personality outside of a few lines the enemies drop during the race.  There’s no uniqueness in any of the bikes or characters other than a lump of stats which all in all mean nothing, add in the fact that it took me 4 hours to unlock my third person, and you’ve got a very slow, grindy, non personal playstyle that just feels like the all too modern idea of games that go “fill up this xp bar, now you unlock thing!” which gives the illusion of choice (how you fill up the xp bar) but none of the freedom.
So that’s a lot of bad, I know, I tend to focus on the bad.  But just because there’s a lot wrong with this game doesn’t mean it’s not a great game.  I like to think of it like going out to dinner, sure my server was lazy and the restaurant smelled like a sock, but my meal was freaking delicious.  I’m not excusing game developers from having a badly fleshed out game.  In fact, not having solid characters or a good progression system is, quite frankly, moronic.  But sometimes really smart, well intentioned people do moronic things, and I feel strongly this way towards Road Redemption.  In a game with such fun gameplay and a good homage to Road Rash I have a hard time believing they were lazy when it came to world design or player choice.  My theory is they just didn’t think it was that big of a deal, and maybe it’s not.  I am willing to admit that my nostalgia goggles are very foggy on this one when I look back and try to compare a game to the (quite literally) most influential game of my childhood.
Overall the problems with this game don’t ruin it, they just turn this game that I  could have spent 40+ hours on into a 6 hour experience.  More than anything I would love to see the developers release different game modes, but unfortunately it might be too late for the game because the initial release was lackluster at best.  Either way, I highly recommend this game, I seriously haven’t had that much fun playing a game for a long time.  Road Redemption is honestly just so damn fun, and that’s what makes me hate its issues so much, not because the game is bad, but because the game is a few hairs short of amazing.
TL;DR Amazing, adrenaline fueled, gameplay that is put behind an unnecessary rogue lite system where progression is reset every time you die.  Could benefit significantly from characterization, making the bikes different or unique, and just overhauling the way the game is presented outside of gameplay (ie implementing a shop system).  It missed the nuances of being a Road Rash successor but nailed the gameplay 100%, with some work this game could absolutely live up to the Road Rash name.

Welcome to Road Rampage, a game about tracking down the assassin of the Iron Sights Cartel and bringing him to justice.
And by justice, I mean collecting the $15,000,000 bounty that is on his head.
You play as selectable characters that are unlocked by completeing certain milestones, such as beating the campaign or getting to a certain part of the campaign. These characters each have their own weapons that they carry, and also have certain stat bonuses (and hinderances) that are applied for the campaign. Each character is therefore unique, especially the guy with one arm. He's pretty cool.
You also get to select a bike on each run, and these all have their own custom handling stats and acceleration, etc., etc. You unlock them like you do the characters, and so you can get a really nice assortment of mixing and matching that you don't really expect to get in a game like this. That being said, that's where the line of customization gets drawn in the sand.
After each level, of which there are many different types of objectives, you get to spend money (earned via murder and completion of objectives) on upgrades. Most of these upgrades are going to be for boosting your health or money gain from killing people, and so it really helps give a little randomness to each run. However, it isn't really as random as I, personally would prefer. I would love it if instead of upgrading my sword, I could replace it with a sickle or some other weapon, allowing for different attack ranges and some more freedom with gameplay. There also need to be some more upgrades, like one that increases your kicking strength so you can clear more people out of the way.
The campaign of this game revolves around the concept of going through gang territory and fighting over the bounty, leaving a very long trail of corpses behind as you try, and inevitably succeed, in catching up with the assassin. Each gang territory is about 6 levels, ending with you killing the gang leader and continuing along the road on your hunt for glory and money. Each level will either be a race, a survival, a time trial, or a extermination style mission. Races are like any other race in a video game, except for the fact that you can kill your opponents and ensure victory. Survivals are missions that task you with making it to the end of the level without losing all your health, usually having to deal with cops that drive both motorcycles and squad cars. Time Trials are like survival but with a timer, and Exterminations are like races but without positions.
Look, it's not the most original when it comes to objectives, but the levels can get pretty hairy. You will sometimes encounter hallucinogenic areas that will leave you dodgin falling cars as you try to complete your objective. The main goal of this game is a rampage, as stated in the name, so you should expect it pushing you towards killing as many people as you can as you rip your way through each gang territory.
All in all, the game is super entertaining. It's pretty well optimized, so much so that I really don't experience much of a slow down during the most chaotic of times, and the gameplay is entertaining. I personally would recommend this game, and say thatbuying it at full price is a reasonable expense. Buying it during a sale would be an absolute steal!
So, hop on your cycles and get ready to raise some hell!

How good are you at coin flipping?
That's what the more advanced stages of this game hinge on.
In campaign mode, starting around level 20, you're not going to be able to sweep an entire board without guess work.  Granted, you're going to have better than 50/50 odds on lots of guesses, but many guesses are no more than straight coin flips.  At level 20, the game stops being about skill, and transforms into a game of luck, whether it's if you can run hot at coin flipping, or whether you're fortunate enough to encounter lots of arbitrary heart health drops when you get in trouble.  Reaching level 20 in campaign mode is elementary for a skilled player, and since your health is fully replenished every ten levels (you receive full health at the start of level 20), plowing through levels 1 through 19 becomes tiring and is a pointless chore (but a necessary chore since if you're aiming for a high score, starting at level 1 will earn you the most cumulative points).  In levels 1 through 19, there is no reason to be careful with your clicks, not only because of too frequent health drops, but because at level 20 you're going to get all your health back anyway.
The one quantifier which made the original Minesweeper competitive, speed, seems to be completely neglected in this game.  I can't see any correlation between how fast you can sweep a board and scoring a higher number of points.
I've played more Minesweeper in my life than I care to admit; my fastest time on "Expert" in the Windows game is somewhere barely over 60 seconds.  As of the June 3rd writing of this review, I have the fourth highest campaign score on the leaderboard at 379,984.  That score would be a lot lower if on that particular run for a time being a divine entity had not told me which tiles to guess, and would be higher if I didn't lose three straight 50/50 coin flips at the very end of a level, which prevented me from clearing that particular stage and getting a large bonus.  At its low price I think that most people will get good value out of this game, however not even the most enthusiastic of Minesweeper fans will be piling up a ton of hours on this game.
Recommendations I would make to the developers:
- Make heart drops less frequent in low levels (1-19), and a little more frequent in difficult levels (20+)
- Make the penalty for triggering a bomb greater, losing points for stepping on a bomb is meaningless if you can reclaim those same points by clicking on a heart
- Eliminate health being fully replenished on levels divisible by ten
- Have the time you take to clear the board reflected in a multiplier for your score, the faster your time the higher your multiple
- In campaign mode, sometimes after clearing a board, it will have me immediately repeat the same level, sometimes more than once.  I'm not sure why this is, but I don't see the point of it, and it becomes tedious, so I would recommend eliminating that feature.

Director's commentary: "We added more wolves to each island that you land on, because who doesn't love more man-eating wolves?"
"One of our interns asked us how all these wolves were able to survive on such tiny little islands. You know how we answered him: More wolves!"
If you find yourself rooting for the predator when you watch nature documentaries then this game is probably for you. It's the best wolf-to-dollar entertainment investment that you can make.
Did I mention there's wolves?
The basic premise of this game is that there's been a great, society collapsing flood and you try to help this teenage girl named Scout survive as she's trying to reach this better area. You pilot a little raft down a river, stopping at islands to trap game, gather plants, collect drinkable water and scavenge scrap that you use to build things. While avoiding the perils of sickness, starvation, disease, hypothermia, the raft's destruction, poisonous plants and hostile animals. Ocassionally you'll run into a person that needs help or a helpful stranger.
I honestly enjoyed this game but I had to stop playing it because the sheer volume of wolves they throw at you is ridiculous. It's not that you can't overcome them with torches or the like, it's just a nuisance. The game starts out alright but then the things become as ubiquitous as cliffracers in Morrownd. At first you might encounter one on every tenth island, but eventually they're on every island and there'll be like 2-5 of them. You can't go ten feet without hearing another howl. I feel bad just quitting because I came to care about this girl and her little dog's journey down the river but I do not find the game fun at the point when the wolves are basically in charge of every island and I am having to run in and out as fast as I can like I was on supermarket spree.
Also, if you're going to play this expect to do a lot of inventory management. A lot. There's also an RNG factor. Sometimes you'll get really lucky and you'll start a game overladen with riches and other times you'll be starving for something you need for a very very long time and it's not your fault.
I'm still recommending it because despite my complaints, there's still a good game under there and I think it's really going to appeal to some people. Had me at Deus Ex.
There is immense depth to the gameplay, this is an excellent example of the "emergent" gameplay design principle. There is an open world, that responds in a variety of logical ways to actions that happen within it, both the player and NPCs can act upon the world, there are many tools players and NPCs have access to and many actions they can choose take. On top of all that there are varied and interesting goals for the player to accomplish. It all adds up for unpredictable gameplay where the player is encouraged to experiment. Examples:
I had to kill a drug dealer, who was surrounded by powerful guards. So I bought a drug from the dealer that made me HUGE, took the drug, got HUGE and smashed my way through him and his guards. Not only did the guards and dealer get smashed, but I destroyed the entire building in the process. When that was done the drug hadn't worn off yet, so I smashed through the walls of another building to complete a different mission.
I had to assassinate a prisoner in a guarded complex. There was a window near his cell with an explosive trip wire. I threw a rock through the window, setting off the bomb, hurting my target and destroying the wall of his cell. While the wounded prisoner tried to escape a guard gunned him down, mission accomplished!
There are a great variety of characters you can choose to be which mixes up gameplay. You can be a gorilla who has massive strength but can't speak to NPCs. A hacker who is super weak but can hack any computer he wants. There's perks you can unlock and weapons and all sorts of things to mix up how you play.
The one downside is that there are only 6 levels. Randomly generated levels yes, but still only 6. The dev seems like a good guy and I expect the game has a very bright future. Oh and the game is pretty funny too!
It is great. Gives me the sense of flow I would get from a good Deus Ex session.

This was my first visual novel and my overall experience, enjoyment, impression was very positive though there were some minor things that kept it from being perfect.  All in all, I highly recommend.
Like many good stories, when this one was over I wished there was much more to it.  (I have kept my description of the story separate below).  The beginning was a bit slow and there were times during the story that it seemed to meander.  And there were some jumps in the story from current time to memory that could have been smoother.  However, if you watch/read this VN push through the parts that seem slow because they give perspective and provide background to frame later parts of the story.  All in all a complete story was built and came together wonderfully right through to its completion.
More about the story if you want to know (no spoilers)...
This is a tale told through a protagonist that you never see and his interaction with a robot.  The protagonist is a junker that scavenges cities et al to survive.  As the interaction between the junker and the robot progressess you learn why the world is in a dismal, post-apocalyptic state and how the protagonist has experienced it.  His view on the world, built from his experiences, is grim and hopeless.  Yumemi, the robot, has a childlike, hopeful view of things as she has been mostly shielded from the events of the last thirty years.  As the host at a planetarium she waits to show visitors the wonders of the stars - a wonder that has long been forgotten in a world of constant rain and gray skies.  The junker sees Yumemi as a mild annoyance and he expresses his annoyance at times.  Yumemi, however, remains positive and optimistic in her interacton with the junker.  How this chance encounter progresses and what we learn about the world, the people, and the robots, is, to me, the core and beauty of the story.  Oh yeah, and there are some emotional moments if you hadn't already guessed.  I highly recommend.

Deep inside the old sarcophagus city, while searching for food, weapons, or resellable scraps, you make an unlikely discovery: What you'd assumed to be an abandoned military facility is actually a pre-war planetarium. And as it turns out,
.
Let's talk about
.
It's a
(a visual novel without any choices or other interactive game elements), so the only thing that the player/reader controls is the pace of the story. Do what you will with that information.
Originally developed by
in 2004 and recently published on Steam by
, this is widely considered a classic in the VN community, and a very worthwhile addition to the still meager selection of good visual novels on Steam. It's a short story about a world full of desolation, hopelessness, cynicism and resignation, and about a little robot girl who's immune to all of it. It's also about going stargazing in a world without stars.
The backgrounds and character sprites in
are somewhat sparse in direct comparison to some of the more visually bombastic VNs out there. It is however very evocative, and with that it falls in line with the writing. The whole novel follows a slow pace -- never dragged out, but certainly deliberate. It leaves plenty of time for you and your own thoughts, and I urge you to take advantage of this invitation. I ended up with just over three hours of total playtime, which included some breathing room for the fantastic voice acting.
Any good visual novel swings in tune with its soundtrack, and
is no exception. Opening with the music box lullaby "
" it immediately offers you a glimpse of its gentle mood. Tracks like "
" accentuate the day-to-day interactions of the main characters with a lax and childish air, while the perhaps most iconic song of the roster, "
", cushions some of the more tender scenes in an aura of warmth and belonging (and I would encourage you to keep that last one playing in the background while you read the rest of this review).
Visual novels as a medium don't lend themselves especially well to twitchy action stories, and despite the occasional surprise in that regard, the bulk of
is about its characters and their interactions. Of the two main characters, only one actually appears on screen, and it would be a fair assessment to say that the story is about her, in several ways.
Yumemi (translated as "Reverie" in some localizations) is not the kind of quasi-human A.I. that we're used to from the likes of Cortana or EDI. She is a robot programmed for a very straightforward purpose. She oscillates between toddler-like naiveté at best, and robotic-algorithmic behavior at worst. So why do you entertain her thoughts of repairing the old projector? Why do you, a looter perpetually on the verge of starvation, end up tacking another night onto your stay at the old planetarium?
This story isn't about what Yumemi
, but about what she
.
Spending valuable time and energy on a planetarium of all things should feel frivolous, yes, downright sacrilegious. But there is something peculiar inside you, easy to explain away as idle curiosity about the starry night sky that you only know from old people's stories. Something you probably didn't think you still had. They say there was a time before the war, before the planet was shrouded by a thick layer of acid clouds, when people were able to look at the stars whenever they wanted. When there was still a notion of mankind eventually travelling to, and settling on, foreign worlds.
Back when people still had hope for the future.
Yumemi was left behind at the beginning of the war, and despite not having had any sort of human contact in years, she diligently awaits the day's customers. There's only one thing she wants out of this existence, one thing she wants to do more than anything else in the world: to show you the stars.
The little robot girl, once built for the simple goal of caring for the planetarium's customers, ends up fulfilling a much grander purpose. Tucked away in her own little corner of a gray world inhabited by people who have forgotten what it means to be human, Yumemi is a shining beacon, a time capsule, a reminder that there is a star-filled sky right behind the acid clouds. Yumemi is the child, the lamb. She embodies innocence, childlike wonder, relentless optimism. Looking into her eyes, you cannot help but feel deeply ashamed for what the world has become.
What was it, then, that made you stay at the planetarium? Was it really just idle curiosity? Or is there more to this little thought in the back of your head after all? Do you feel in your stomach what the place emanates? Does Yumemi give you the strength to dare to form the words, that maybe, just maybe... there is some hope left in this world? That there is such a thing as "the future"?
You should read
if you have any interest in visual novels, if you haven't experienced a good story in a while, if you like looking up at the stars and wondering what the future holds, or if that little spark deep inside you that is almost drowned by cynicism needs a little bit of nourishment. Wholeheartedly recommended.

So, I have to take the time out to give this game a review. Despite the number of hours logged through Steam, I have played this game for a very long time. It deserves some love. Let me tell you a little about Fiesta Online.
If you're looking for the next-big-thing, this isn't it. No, it's not like WoW or TERA. It's not Black Desert, either. It's an older game that's changed companies a few times, had it's share of population dips, and (shock) still has some bugs. It IS, however, still a very good game and will provide you with a lot of old-fashioned entertainment.
I'm not going to do a formal Pros/Cons, but I am going to casually tell you about the game should you be in the midst of a decision on whether or not you want to try it out.
This game is very generic in a lot of good ways. Yep, you read that right. It has all of the traditional things you would want in a MMO. Yes, you can buy and level up skills. Yeah, you can quest to your heart's content. It's got the trinity system you'd want from a standard game like this. The game still gets new content. It still gets patches that work on improving existing problems. The graphics have even been updated recently. It has six classes with each having a branch-choice at level 100 for a total of 12 end-game roles. The game has just the right amount of tradtion to relax ya. Grab a cold drink, sit  back, and enjoy some good old-fashioned game play.
Aesthetically speaking, the maps are bright, colorful, and easy on the eyes. There's not a huge deal of customization, but you do have the option of furthering your character's design through the cash shop. Speaking of, I've always leveled just fine without using the Cash Shop. (That pay-to-win crap is, well, crap). If you're looking for a good ole anime game, then this is it! (However, I would like to throw out there that I've always found it odd that your characters can only be light-skinned. Then again, they don't have natural hair colors much either).
Perhaps the most enjoyable, and unique, aspect of the game is the "Kingdom Quest" system. It's an instance-based raid, but it doesn't depend on your class. So, no, dear DPS players, you're not going to wait an hour in que. It's not a perfect system, but it's different, fun, and is currently working very well. When the game changed companies awhile back, the population dropped a bit. This made the Kingdom Quest system kind of broken. I mean, it's hard to run an instance with no people in it. They cared enough to finally merge the servers, and they're working great now. If all else fails, you do have the traditional instances where you find your own party members.
The game isn't easy to level. It plays like a casual game, but it actually has some pretty thought-provoking challenges in it. While it's not as hard as it used to be, you're not going to cap in a month. It takes time, effort, and by the time you're there, it feels fantastic! Not to mention, the game has new bosses and raids for end-game. I'm looking forward to them!
So, no, Fiesta isn't the best game in the world, but it WILL be fun for you to play should you decide to stick with it. I hope you decide to give the game a go and make tons of new friends in the end!
Best of luck,

I have mixed feelings about this game, which is good but has some annoying features.
I really like the art style of the game and the gameplay. The cut scenes are well made. The voice acting is just perfect. Lack of choices might be true, but then again there are only very few games which offer you more than just the illusion of choice.
However, there are some issues. Early on city hall demands constant changes to your police force. It is extremely annoying. Every now and then you have to replace or fire a certain amount of officers and there is no way to do this without serious repercussions. If you don't do it, city hall is going to reduce funding and you have fewer and fewer officers. There is no way to keep good officers because sooner or later you have to illegaly fire or kill them. That way the whole skill system is basically useless because nobody stays long enough to seriously improve their skills.
I'm not sure about the investigations either. In the beginning it made sense and was solveable, but now I have several of them and no matter what I do, no matter how thorough I am with everything (reading the testimonies over again, looking at every image the 10th time), there seems to be no solution and I'm almost out of detectives. There is no feedback at all. When the game says they have no new frames, does that mean I need better detectives? Or does it mean I should be able to solve it? Who knows.
All in all it is a good game and it has everything in it that makes it very likeable for me, but especially the (very) ridiculous demands from city hall make everything very tedious. I fully expect them to demand sooner or later that I simply fire all of my officers because the mayor needs some more room to store his money.
I'm not sure I'll ever play the whole 180 days. For now I'll let it be but I really hope to continue at some other time.

Gorgeous art, terrible gameplay.
The concept of This Is The Police caught me instantly. You play as a police chief 6 months from retirement, who can choose between being morally upstanding, a mafia stooge, or anything in between, essentially having to decide whether building up a retirement fund(legally or not) or staying true to his position. It seemed like it could be a fun ride.
The art? Interesting, unique, haven't seen a game with quite the same art before.
The gameplay? Conceptually good, but the issue is an absolute absence of what I'd call "feedback."
Say that I can send between 1 and 4 officers on a particular case. Let's assume I decide to send one guy with great skills, because everyone else is occupied and the case will time out shortly. And then assume that I fail: is it because that was too few officers? Because that officer had too poor skills? Did I actually have a 90% success chance and just flubbed the RNG roll? Was there even an RNG roll, or was it just a deterministic adding-up of office numbers and skills?
The game never lets you in on what's happening behind the scenes. Similarly, some cases offer short multiple-choice narratives. I pick a given option and end up with two dead officers, an escaped offender and a dead civilian. Was that the only potential result of that option? Was it the result because my officers sucked? Or was it just random chance? Again, you never know.
If I have to read a wiki or decrypt the game's code to figure out how it fundamentally works, the game has failed. I'd recommend against getting this.

•You can pull arrows out of your shield to use for yourself.
•You can put dead bodies laden with poison on the backs of horses and camels and send them into enemy encampments to poison crowds of enemies.
•There is now a loot system based on the rarity and attributes of equipment.
•Items can be broken down into crafting materials.
•Scoping out enemy encampments is now easier than ever with Senu.
•You can seemlessly explore underwater now for new gear or just for the fun of exploring.
•Viewpoints are no longer an actual necessity for opening up the world map.
•Animals can be tamed and become allies.
•Side quests tell their own stories similar to the way The Witcher 3 handled them.
•Everyone in the game lives their own lives which opens up numerous options for assassinations.
•The hood can be taken off and put back on.
•You can pass time with the press of a button.
•You can climb anything now so pesky mountains won't get in the way.
•We get to see the beginnings of the brotherhood as we know it.
•Stealth is still incorporating the awesome crouch and behind cover features from Unity and Syndicate but also adding a free aim bow for the first time.
•Senu can be called in to attack or distract which adds another useful and tactical element to scenarios.
•Combat has taken from the much loved styles of the Souls series and The Witcher 3. You are much more involved this time around and it isn't about button mashing counters and finishers anymore. This involves parrying, blocking, and dodging.
•We see the return of tomb raiding and it will be very beneficial for those who seek money, equipment, and earning skill points.
•Regular enemies will stand back and watch and cheer as you fight their captain single combat.
•You can light arrows on fire by standing next to any fire including your own torch.
•Enemy AI responds to just a glimpse if you by investigating the area they thought they saw something which is a big step up from the previous AI who would stand in place and look for a few seconds before deciding their minds were playing tricks. They will also hear an air assassination or headshot if close enough.
•Bayek is a well rounded character who is out for blood with an angry vengeance but often shows a lighthearted side as well.
•The story is well paced and you can walk away from quests now at any time without worrying about failing.
•Tailing missions are gone and replaced with finding out information through other more interesting and fun means such as investigation and interrogation.
•The formula has been changed dramatically from the previous entries in the series and has moved towards the more popular RPG style of game yet it still keeps important staples of the series.

Ubisoft made a wise decision when they gave Assassins Creed a break from its annual release schedule and Assassins Creed Origins has benefited greatly from it. If you're hoping for a complete fresh experience though you might be in for disappointment.
Assassins Creed Origins doesn't reinvent the wheel but it's a much more refined experience than some of the earlier games with various game mechanics receiving a bit of a tweak more thoughtful use of the open world and simply beautiful visuals. I opted to buy the PC version of the game and am running it at native 4k with the settings pretty much maxed out.
Aside from a few audio glitches and the odd stutter I haven't suffered any major performance issues. Assassins Creed Origins takes place during Ancient Egypt and the game world has been beautifully crafted to give a genuinely authentic feel. The ambient sounds and the sound track further add to this immersion.
The story feels a bit slow to get going and with so much o do in the game world it is easy to forget what's going on which in turn has led to me not really connecting with the main character like I would hope. Once you get going though things seem to flow much more freely and becomes easier to follow.
The games controls feel tight, with combat getting a rework which for the most part works well. The loot system has also recieved attention and feels meanigful and worthy of your time. Theres awide variety of weapons for you to master and if you find something you like you can upgrade them so you can continue to use them on your travels.
The AI can be challenging when playing on hard mode but I've not found them to be too frustrating. If anything I think they could do with being a bit harder to offer more of a challenge but all in all Ubisoft have done a decent job. There's plenty to do in this open world game and whilst you will find similar tasks repeat where ever you go it's not as bad as it's been in other Ubisoft open world games. Completing the tasks on offer are for the most part fun and rewarding which in turn encourages you to complete other that you come across.
Assassins Creed Origins comes complete with a photo mode which you'll find yourself using as the game world is Stunning to look At, especially in 4k. What's good is that your pictures can be seen by other players.
The RPG elements of the game have been implemented thoughtfully and give a nice feel of progression as you make your way through the game. Theres a lot of upgrading to be done and various routes you can take with each having their own unique feel. Theres a nice sense of variety in how you can approach various tasks and the thoughtfulness put into the games design is easy to pick up on.
Assassins Creed is a series that desperately needed some attention and it's paid off with Origins. The game feels fresh, plays great, looks and sounds awesome and is a he'll of a lot of fun to play. It's great to see the series return to form.

Some of the reaction times needed are a bit unfair to the player, and the levels are always designed to be harder rather than more fun. There's this odd little feature, where it shows you a ghost of the developer beating the portion of the level you're at if you're stuck and need to see what's needed to beat the game. This feature is fine, but I swear, for a good chunk of the game I feel that if you don't act out the exact same steps the ghost performed, then you will not beat the game. In that sense, the game becomes more about emulating the ghost's actions rather than doing it yourself. I feel that's just bad game design.
If you're looking for a good, unique, and frustraing platformer, Element4l is the one for you. 5/10

1 – GENERAL
Punch Club is a Indie RPG, retro style fighting simulator. Seems a bit of a mesh of concepts but the final product is interesting.
Sounds and music are very good. That traditional 80s environment very well made in this game, combined with sublime 16 bit graphics and a lot of pop culture elements added into the game.
A huge rule in a RPG is a proper story, and in this case I cannot go that far. The story is good enough, but nothing fancy. It gets the job done, and that is more than enough.
2 – GAMEPLAY
When you start playing you will be very excited with every new action or achievement that you got. You have to manage when to train, sleep, eat, work, and that seems simple and balanced enough. At this point you do not have many strategical choices when fighting, but you don't care, you are having fun. But then you start progressing, and you get into underground fights, being a hero, having friends and a girlfriend, you have to save to built a gym, and you are always being mugged when you have money in your pocket.
Then you start to get bored with so much grind. When you start to get annoyed you realize that probably you have made some bad choices when building your skilltree. And at this point I can talk a bit about the replay value. On paper it has a lot. New skills, new fighting styles, new training options... but will you play the game again knowing that you have to grind all the way through all over again?
3 – CONCLUSION
So, are you a grinder? Are you ready to work hard to progress very slowly? If yes, I have to say that all that grind makes the game very realistic, but I want to have fun in a game, and at some point Punch Club becomes a full time job, and that's too much for me.

Fine Sweeper is a superb Minesweeper variant, with great Steam integration: leaderboards, achievements, and trading cards. The game mechanics are similar to what you remember from the old Windows Minesweeper games, but with updated twists. A campaign mode has levels that get progressively harder, with cumulative scoring and timing. There are item drops, and you have the option to play in classic mode (in which hitting a mine will end the game and restart from the first level) or a mode in which you have multiple "lives" in which to carry on playing even if you hit an occasional mine. All of this is packaged in a slick interface, at least comparatively. Not everything is brand new though, it's every bit as addictive as the original.

As much as I love minesweeper I just can't recommend this game. There isn't enough new and the new stuff isn't up to a good enough standard.
As soon as I saw this game on steam I had to buy it. I am a huge minesweeper fan and I just couldn't pass up a new version of it being released. However this game isn't much better than the original.
The main mode that this version features is a continuous mode. This mode continues going with levels of increasing difficulty. They basically increase the difficulty by growing the board size and adding more bombs. The score increases as a sum of all the levels you do and it measures the time you take on each level. This is incorperated into a high score system that lets you compare your score with friends and other people. This is a nice addition that gives a new reason to play minesweeper.
However the problem with this mode is that there is no way to save it. I found myself going on a continuous run for over an hour earlier today. At that point I was getting pretty tired of it. I would have liked to quit the game and continue it later. But this wasn't possible since the game offers no way of saving it.
But this isn't the biggest problem the game has. It is horrible to play as you get further into the game with bigger boards. It is basically a guessing game at this point. Very little skill is involved. This is because the game puts you in situations where no amount of skill will let you figure out where there is a bomb and where there isn't so instead you just have to guess and hope for the best. I know this was a problem in the original minesweeper, but it definitely wasn't as big as a problem as it is in this game. When you get later into the game, i'd say around level 30ish, you start having to guess so often! This wasn't a fun experience and it isn't in the true light of minesweeper to have to guess instead of use skill.
The game does attempt to counteract this problem in a way. They use a life system. You find lives under blocks that you clear on the level which you can add to your collection. Everytime you hit a bomb you loose a life. Some people that are perhaps less skilled at minesweeper may like this addition. But to a hardcore player who has been playing for a long time this isn't of much use to me. I would much prefer to have only one life. I would prefer it if they would fix the guessing issue instead of using this lazy alternative to fix it. They don't even have an option to disable the life system which I would have done.
What I used to love about the original minesweeper is the ginourmous size boards you could make and play on. Whenever I played it I used to make one of the biggest boards possible and then I would end up playing for about half an hour or so just on the one board. Fine sweeper features a similar mode to setup a custom sized board. But is no where near the scale that you can do on traditional minesweeper. In fact the boards are puny in size compared to the original. It's quite laughable to see it actually. Even when you go to the biggest scale possible. I have no idea why the developer limited it so much!
The options menu of the game is also extremely lacking. The only option of note is the audio sliders of which there is a seperate one for music and for other sounds. It's also probably worth noting that the music and sounds aren't particularly good in my opinion. I had them off for my entire time playing it. And the only other option there really is the nostalgic colours  option. That is it. They could at very least have some resolution options or something else!
There was only one thing in this game that I could find that may lead you to play this instead of the original minesweeper. The graphics. They are such an improvement over the classic original minesweeper. Although i'm sure you really need it to play a simple game like this. If only the developer could have put as much effort into making the game unique and work properly as they put in on the graphics!
Overall I cannot recommend this game. There are so many issues that it isn't actually fun to play. Theres not enough different for anyone to even consider playing it over the original. I am gonna go back to playing the original as well and I think you should to. I would also like to take the time here to recommend a great alternative to minesweeper that improves drastically on the original formula and of which I greatly enjoyed called "hexcells". If your a minesweeper fan and your wanting something new go and try that instead of this game.

Forget what you know about ActaLogic games of the past. The developer is now free from crummy German simulatior publishers that have provided only limited funding, pre-launch development time, creativity and post launch support. This is ActaLogic going indie, and as a result, HyperNova: Escape from Hadea is an original Strategy sub genre bending game that shows what a developer can do when they're free of Publisher / Investor influences!
Hypernova is part Planetary Colony Sim, part RTS, part Tower defence/offense. I would go as far as to say that the game also has strongly inspired 4X elements in it too (I'll justify my reasoning below). A combination that works surprisingly well.
So what do you do? Well you arrive just above the Hayan Moon's surface with a single Mothership, which is a giant 3D printing Mobile Construction yard. From there, you can explore the large map in your own time and choose absolutely anywhere in which to land and settle your colony with varying degrees of difficulty. From there you must eXpand your colony and eXploit the resources available to you. You must continue to then explore, expand and exploit the map further in order to increase your colony's population to a high set limit, research technologies from a reasonable sized tech tree and discover 4 extremely rare resources that will allow you to build the final Stellar Bridge technology so you can escape the threat of the sun going Hypernova.
So what about the eXterminate element? Well the landscape is littered with local wildlife that are none too happy to see you arrive. In-fact the more you expand and take a foothold, the more they'll get ever increasingly hacked off! So in true Tower defence style, you research and build a number of towers to protect your colony from harm. You cannot sit back and take it though. The wildlife spawn from Hives in ever increasing waves. The level of threat to a hive you pose determines how often those waves come, and not all Hives are equal. Some are docile, others are (especially in the later game) willing to give Starcraft's persistent Zerg Rushes a run for their money!
Luckily towers are effectively your units, and like many of the other structures in the game, can be moved anywhere where you have cleared the harmful atmosphere and are able to supply power. This means you will take the fight to their hives, and quite literally set off the hornet's nest as the wildlife makes their last stand to survive.
The game will start off particularly easy, and you'll find yourself becoming a little complacent. But as time goes on, the difficulty will ramp gradually until you are attacking and defending on multiple fronts, strategically trying to manage the resources available so they don't expire too fast (they do regenerate), whilst trying to manage your colony effectively to reach the next population milestone, so you can research more technologies to gain the edge.
- An original and innovative strategy sub-genre blend that's incredibly fun to play & draws you in!
- Plenty of depth, management, and strategy!
- A great game for those who enjoy slow-burn strategy games from RTS/TD/4X & Management sims.
- Fantastic colourful world, lore and characters.
- Even after many hours of game time, no crashes or noticable bugs!
- Plenty of potential replayability with 3 difficulty levels, and different challenges and outcomes based on where you land!
- The music, whilst not annoying, can get a little repetitive.
- The game is slow-burn (Not really a con in my eyes). So not advised for anyone wishing to start and finish within 30-60 minutes
- The game can become rather micro intensive and fiddly in later stages when multiple battles are taking place across many fronts.
- Single Player Only
- Only 1 Map, 1 Campaign Game Mode. No Skirmish.
All in all, this is ActaLogic's greatest game to date! Not just by a country mile, but a Marathon and then some. As a result, we have one of the most innovative, original and fun Strategy games to be released in quite a long time!
I highly recommend it!

If you're an old player returning to fiesta out of nostalgia, keep in mind that its not the same game anymore. Leveling isnt as hard as it used to be, and quests feel rushed. It feels like rather than increasing the exp rate of the game, Gamigo decided to add more, seemingly meaningless quests which give ridiculous amounts of exp. You can accept and turn in quests without even being near the NPC you got it from. This does mean that the "pay to level" system of the older outspark game is gone, but it doesnt feel as satisfying to level (I hit level 60 in 3 days, whereas it used to be a huge achievement). The Trickster felt like Outsparks final attempt to reinvigorate the game before they turned it over to gamigo. And gamigo responded by adding the Crusader, a class which seems so rushed that it doesnt even exist below level 60, and it even has some skills copy pasted from other classes.
I can see that Gamigo are really trying to update and reinvent the game, with graphics updates, new quests, and a quicker leveling system, which allows you to get into the action faster. It even merged all the servers into a couple of servers to make the servers full of people again. As a result, this isnt the same game as it used to be, but its an evolving, fun game nonetheless.
Ultimately, this isnt the golden '105 cap' fiesta that I remember, but I'm not gonna say it isn't worth playing. While its not the game I poured endless hours of my childhood into, its still a good game. Fiesta used to be hailed as a "pay to win" game, but now more than ever I feel that this isnt true. You can do really well without paying a cent. Im going to miss the days of stacking, endless grinding and massive guild raids on Karen, but the game is still fun. If you're coming to revive an old interest, you may be better off on a private server. But if you're willing to try a new game, this will be good.

I've not played lots of this. But what I have played, has impressed me. I'm not big on puzzle-platformer types, but I adore this game regardless.
The Soundtrack is absolutely wonderful. It's so ambient and it REALLY fits the game. It genuinely makes you feel like you're solving a puzzle. There's some interesting, occasionally creepy sound-effects [childrens laughter] that definitely adds to the  very odd atmosphere. There's no real way to decribe the kind of atmosphere it generates. It's simply unique.
The Artwork/Aesthetic. It's gorgeous. Vibrant colour themes and pleasant contrasts. It's quite simply an interesting game to look at.
The gameplay is, not really for me. The game can get difficult very quickly, which is always an issue with puzzle-platformers. Certainly some levels are more intuitive than others. But it consistently provides a challenge. I imagine, at higher levels, it must feel fantastic to glide through the levels executing each move required perfectly. Sadly, I very rarely - often accidentally - replicate this feeling. It's usually the moment I realize how fluid the game feels that I die! The main issue for me is that when you do die, it really slows the gameplay. What is fluid when executed perfectly feels sluggish when you die, as you often re-spawn stationary, or with little momentum.
But I can't stress enough how polished it is, especially for an indie title. There's some lovely written commentary provided in-game as you pass certain obstacles. If you love puzzle-platformers and unique games, you'll like this game. Even if you don't, I'd argue it's worth buying for the soundtrack and aesthetic in-game. It's simply beautiful. Fully recommended.

Overall, definite 8.5/10.

Ice can slide, fire is invincible (to other fire), air is free and stone is heavy. How well the player can change amongst these forms is based on patience and the sleight of hand.

It is with a heavy heart that I review this game with a Not Recommended rating.  The gameplay is pretty fun, it has a surprising amount of depth to the story, and the number of options available to create your fighter is rather large.
However, as many people seem to agree, the game has one major flaw that makes it plateau pretty hard -- the stat decay.  I know the developer just released a game mode that does away with stat decay, but the Normal difficulty shouldn't feel as if you get stuck anywhere so hard for so long.
What starts as a great introduction to a fighting sim slowly but exponentially turns into you desperately trying to maintain your fighter into someone that can at least stand up to a bit of damage.  Three hours in and I feel like all of my actions on a daily basis are just to maintain my abysmal stats that don't even win me fights anymore.  There's some ways to min-max you character to help: Work a job from the day the Home Equipment store opens until you have enough money to buy the home gym complete set, then rotate between working a job and training with Silver for the skill points.  I would guess several hours in you might have someone that can beat the game.
I'll keep playing and edit the review if my feelings change, but the bottom line is that I'm struggling to maintain a 5 in stats and I'm 70 days in.  The people I am fighting now have 7s, 8s, and 9s.  I lose every fight and receive broken bones from the underground arena so my training efforts are for naught.  This has been going on since day 30.  Each day I lose 50 points towards my stats, but it takes three days to get enough money and food and rest and happiness to get the stats just a little higher.  I can't even say it feels like two steps forward and one step back, it's closer to sidestepping out of the way.

The Flame in the Flood is another Roguelite. It borrows the general structure of FTL (moving forward but branching) and its main gameplay from Don't Starve (craft stuff to not let you vital meters reach zero).
So you're navigating a river and visit different islands/shores, with an arcade touch because you have to avoid crashing into rocks. Once ashore, you must gather resources and craft stuff to eat/drink/keep you warm/defend against wild animals. But it's all extremely basic and repetitive. We're nowhere near the complexity of Don't Starve. Also, the process of managing one's inventory is needlessly frustrating, purely because of a badly thought of user interface.
It's not a broken game, and the audiovisuals are more than decent. It's clearly not one of those games where you feel the developers just try to rip you off. But there just wasn't enough variety to carry me to the end, so I cannot recommend it.

Come on Valve, Yes/No recommendations are not sufficient so if you insist on limiting to a simple Yes/No I will always err on the side of caution and go with Not Recommended. If games are "just good enough" to get a positive recommendation then I feel it undermines the whole point of a recommendation, so I will save mine for the truly solid gems...this game, unfortunately, is not one of them.
This game could have been a solid gem but I feel that the developers did a poor job making the game accessible. There doesn't seem to be much of a point to it either. You travel on your raft from stop to stop gathering supplies as you go and that's it. Occasionally you have to run from wild animals, some that won't ever give you a break, even at the very beginning of the game, so that area is cut off from you. There's no backtracking to pick up forgotten/dropped supplies which makes trying to prepare for what's upcoming overly difficult but usually impossible. The crafting systems seems very shallow and you're afforded very little time to "learn" the game they don't want to teach you. Micro-managing your inventory is tedious as are most of the things you do.

A linear take on "cartoony" survival games. The Flame in the Flood is more about immersion, story telling and adventure than mastering a crafting tree and surviving in a post apocalytpic world. A short but very intense "die and repeat" experience, with amazing music and beautiful art style.
If you enjoyed games like Don't Starve or Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons, give this a go.

I feel that because of that you miss out on the interesting features this game has to offer, as there is never time to wander around or plan your next move. You'll also spend a lot of time in the menus (managing inventory, crafting etc.). I usually like that sort of gameplay, but as the ingame time doesn't stop while browsing the menu/inventory you'll spend your time rushing through things and eventually making a mistake caused by lack of time which leads to your characters death. Like I said before, I wish the game wouldn't be so hectic (and still be challenging), but the way it is designed just wasn't for me and because of that I can't recommend it.

At it's base it's a polished version of Minesweeper with progression to feed gratification and lives to continue playing if you make a small hiccup.
Unfortunately, there are some negatives which I hope will be patched in at a later date, these would include:
First click not being an island--This is a fairly basic mechanic featured on some of the more simpler versions of Minesweeper found on the web. Not sure why this wasn't included from the start, since otherwise you are taking random guesses and unfairly losing lives (albeit there are some situations you have to guess no matter what, but the first click shouldn't be it).
When you set off a bomb it changes the numbers around the explosion--When this first happened and a 2 changed to a 1, I didn't realise and thought "Oh, so the bomb went off on the one so I'll free these other spaces around the 1" and then set off another bomb. Maybe some people prefer this but I feel like it's misleading and completely interrupts my flow and I have to re-read the board to make sure the numbers that may have changed don't have the appropriate amount of flags already.
Along with this, when a bomb explodes, the numbers underneath are barely readable. As well as numbers underneath heart pickups, and the very font to be honest is a bit poor. I would much prefer a clear-cut font like the font used to display the amount of bombs left on the map to be used, perhaps it can be a customisable option or something.
The Game Over screen completely covers the board when you die, which is frustrating because you can't see your mistake and learn from it.
And finally, I looked at the 'things to come' screenshot quickly from the Dev (couldn't find a list of things he's patching otherwise I might have left some things off this list if he's patching them) but the colour contrast on the new colours for numbers looks quite poor and hard to read on darker levels--while not officially a thing that can be reviewed right now since it's not even in the game, I thought on the off-chance the dev reads this he can brighten up the colours for the numbers a bit.
Criticism aside, it's a nice looking iteration of Minesweeper and £1.59 isn't much to pay for a game which you can easily lose 30 mins or so of your day every time you load it, which adds up if you pace yourself. I would recommend, and I hope the dev updates it to become even more polished.

Pixel Prophecy have updated the game and have with that fixed one of the major problems in the game (and a few others too!). I would like to say to anyone considering buying this game that this game is not a big Minesweeper overhaul or improvement: it just adds a neat little feature to it.
While my biggest complaint has been fixed, a few other do remain. This would include the lack of statistics (e.g. games played/won/lost; I do not mean a leaderboard), the ability to replay the same level (without the level regenerating), the ability to look at the board after having lost a game (to see what went wrong; currently a message box saying 'Game Over' is in the way) and lastly a fix for unsolvable levels.
These first three functions have been included in earlier versions of Microsoft Minesweeper, but the fourth one would definitely be a big improvement over Microsoft's game.
Of course, the game also has functions that Microsoft did not put in their game, namely multiple lives (clicking a mine does not end the current game) , online leaderboards, achievements and a variety of levels.
Perhaps that these things will be fixed/added with the next patch. But until then, I can say that I would recommend Fine Sweeper, keeping in mind that Microsoft Minesweeper is still a strong rival.

I'll get straight to the point immediately: in my opinion, this game is great. It's a management game of sorts, in that you have to decide which and how many officers to send on calls, whether or not officers have legitimate reasons for wanting to take the day off, hiring, firing, and replacing slain officers as necessary, and things like that. That's basically all you do, but the game still finds a way to make it fun rather than tedious or boring. The game also has a moral choice system; you can choose to be "good cop" or "bad cop", but in as far as I've played, once you make the choice to be one or the other, you're given few, if any, opportunities to change your mind. With all that in mind, let's get to my favorite aspect of the game: its sense of humor. Sure, sometimes it can be rather dark, even gallows humor, but I'm into that sort of thing, so this game has gotten a fair few laughs out of me during the mere 97 minutes I've played it. All in all, if that sounds appealing to you, this game just might be right up your alley.

Never I would think that a game with story about a police chief, with a pretty simple gameplay. Would be intresting. Narrative was told pretty smooth, showing nice art style along with nice music, making you care at least what is happening around our Jack.
It's sometimes stressful managing your officers, since you are afraid of losing your best ones or losing a lot them. Making you sometimes or often scared to send your best officers and have a chance to lose them, if something goes wrong.(Especially when Main Hall, loves to give you tasks which are hard to do. Not because they are hard, but because if you accept it. You can get screwed over. But even if you do help them, they will still try to do it anyway. In which they will cut part of your roster.) Making it more tragic or hard experience to see your favorite officer vanish, if that happens.
One of the cons I have, that the game really forces you to follow a specific path. If you are 100% nice cop, prepare to say Game Over quickly. Which can be understandible in some sense for the narrative, that you must play along with whatever is happening. But it's not really giving you a lot of options if you want to keep going without being killed, if you want to be a good cop. The other con is there is not a lot of choices. Most of the time Jack decides himself what he wants to do, whatever if you want him to do that or not. Sometimes making him look like a good caring person or a♥♥♥♥♥♥(But I guess that was the aim.)
There is not much variety when it comes to gameplay. You are 85% of the game ordering your officers go there and deal with it. Only giving variety with detective investigations or small mini game here and there. After every task you get one of the results, which does not get in detail on what exactly happen. When it's a false alarm, it does give some information. But does not do the same for real crime events. If there is for example a psychopath in the bathroom with a knife. And you decided to speak with him and if you succeed. You don't know if he was distracted and officer took his chances or he was reasoned with. The last thing that was annoying me, proper saves are every Monday of in game week time. Sure you have checkpoints for each day. But if you want to re-play a certain day, you must play the entire week where that day is.
Overall, I enjoyed the game. Even with it's small repetitive gameplay. I still want to continue, improving my officers so they could get better or maybe deal with the investigation which is so close to be solved.

Aahh... what a glorious trainwreck. And by glorious I mean insufferable.
So this is what you get when a game takes away direct control, replaces it with physics puzzles, and then still asks you to be precise. It's fortunate that there's a helpful "you failed too much" guide since some of the puzzles are practically impossible to figure out otherwise. The physics don't feel like thye behave too consistently and they're very touchy to begin with. The end result is a frustrating mess without any sense of accomplishment as a victory feels like "oh, the game's physics worked right this time" more than "I did it, I am the best". The game looks nice and sounds nice, at least, but it's so inherently unfun that I can't recommend it to anyone.

I've been playing Streets of Rogue since it was in Alpha, and it's quickly become one of my favourite indie games of all time. Dabrowski isn't exaggerating when he compares his game to Deus Ex - every task or mission in the game can be tackled in at least a dozen different ways.
Let me give you a hypothetical scenario: you have to retrieve a briefcase from a bank vault. If you're a thief, you might cut through the break room window to enter the building without being detected, lockpick your way into the vault room, and then use a safecracking tool to retrieve your prize. Alternatively, a shapeshifter might sneak inside disguised as a townsperson, leap into the bank teller's body, and walk into the vault room without anyone batting an eye. Or maybe you're a merchant; in that case, you can simply bribe the teller and convince him to sell you the keys and safe combination.
Did I mention that those are just three of the 20-odd character classes available? Your choices range from police officer to gorilla, and each come with wildly different abilities and restrictions. These abilities are supplemented with a huge range of weapons and items, which can be obtained in many different ways: robbing houses, completing quests, and even rooting through trash cans, to name a few.
The gameplay is something of a cross between a roguelike, an open-world RPG, and a twin-stick shooter. You make your way through a modern city, completing quests to move between stages, and often leaving entire districts in ruins as a result of your "heroics". This is a game that doesn't take itself too seriously - the sense of humor and general atmosphere are reminiscent of the Saints Row games.
There's so much more I could rave about, but I don't want to be here all day. Just trust me on this: Streets of Rogue is one of the best games you've never played. Pick up a copy - it's well-worth the asking price.

Watch Dogs 1 was a great game but a let down on certain points. Watch Dogs 2 improves on almost all of those points and is a really fun game overall.

Let's begin with the main mechanic of Watch Dogs which is of course: hacking! Hacking has been improved upon. It works better, there is more to hack and the newly added Drone & RC car make exploring the area and hacking a lot more interesting!
Instead of giving you everything from the start, you now get introduced to new things to hack and get new gadgets throughout the game. Upgrades can be bought with follower points you earn by playing missions etc. From upgrading your hacking and combat abilities, to unlocking new mechanics, there are loads of things to choose from! Next to this you unlock new weapons and gadgets by printing them out of your 3D printer! It doesn't change much from the traditional way of purchasing them in a shop but it's the small things like this that make Watch Dogs 2 so awesome and give it character.

Now the story of Watch Dogs 1 was a big let down. It was poorly written and the main character wasn't all to interesting either. This time however, although a bit hipster and mainstream, the main characters have some actual character to them and although the story itself isn't the best and could be better for sure, it does stay interesting with some twists, original things and a good amount of humor here and there.

The most impressive part in both Watch dogs 1 and 2 is the world itself. The world feels alive, NPC's aren't just there to walk or be killed. They're living their own lives. From phone calls, to drone flying to playing sports. They just live their own lives. The ability to hack their phone and read their personal info/listen to their phone calls or read their chat messages to friends & family makes it even more realistic. This together with a fun, interesting and beautiful looking world makes for some great immersion.

Something note-worthy is how Watch Dogs 2 handles the phone. Instead of just giving you a phone with a camera and some contacts to call, you also get a Appstore to download various apps like: Car On Demand, Media Player, Nudle Maps and much more!

A few downsides of the game however are, missions can get a bit repetitive. You need to infiltrate an area and hack component X most of the time. However, the fact you have a lot of different play styles to choose from and can complete the mission on a lot of different ways does make up for that part a bit. Vehicle mechanics aren't the best and enemy AI isn't always the best either. Which is weird considering the AI of normal citizens is pretty good and as mentioned earlier, is really interesting.

Overall, I would recommend Watch Dogs 2 to anyone who enjoys open world games and enjoys walking around in a big living city. The game has it cons and can be a bit repetitive, but the game is great nonetheless.
