If you want to receive a firm reminder that you have a heart, this is the visual novel for you.
I will admit, I dived straight in to purchase this one because I'm familiar with Key, and their popularity. Needless to say, while this is a rather short experience... it'll be one that I'll cherish for many years to come.
The story, ranging from about 2-5 hours in length (depending on how fast you read), is set on a post-apocalyptic Earth far into the future. Resources, such as food, alcohol, and cigarettes are a rare and fought over commodity, resulting in life being drawn down to one fight after another, with the reward being to live another day on a barren, devoid of life Earth.
This is what sets the surprising tone for the male protagonist, who finds himself suddenly stumble upon a rather peaceful planetarium inhabited by but a sole female robot named Yumemi - modeled to be about 15/16 years old. Exhausted from fatigue, the nameless protagonist finds himself spending the evening inside the surprisingly well kept planetarium, which subsequently leads to him building an interestingly adorable relationship with Yumemi.
Throughout, there are many laughable, sad, and also down right depressing moments, each of them fitting very cleanly into their scenes. The translation was also very good I feel, and I have no complaints beside a singular word that was not word wrapped, spreading over two lines - and this is me literally trying to squeeze out any issues, of which I feel there are none at all.
Upon completion, there is also a Music and CG gallery unlocked.
For the price, it can be argued that $10 might be pushing it for some, but I don't like to aptly slap a value on an experience. Everyone will value this visual novel differently, and I would rather leave it for you to decide if it's priced right for you to experience a short, yet amazing story.
I highly recommend this, both to visual novels veterans, and people new to the genre that would like to start somewhere easygoing.

Game seems to be in deep beta, so I'm gonna give it the benefit of the doubt a recommend it.
First of all, it is not a game for adults - it is something you might wanna buy your kid in elementary school to help him undestand physics in a fun and accessible way. I'm having trouble thinking about this as a game - more like an interactive activitity you might do under your teacher's supervision, to demonstrate how science behind those simple experiments. So I don't recommend it for someone who is looking for a puzzle game to play - you can pass all of them by moving objects randomly and if you went to semi-decent school you did some of the experiments yourself or know them from discovery channel or something. So, just to reiterate, this ain't for adults.
The good:
- Graphics look ok for this type of game.
- Good educational value, if you are in elementary school and are about to learn about physics.
- Controls needs getting used to, but are otherwise intuitive. Got confused early because "Click" in this game means "Right-button click".
- Backstory seems solid enough, characters might not be the most cleverly written, but are engaging enough for children.
The bad:
- Some experiments are bugged and only register as done if objects are moved in a specific order. I did the one with grapes correctly from the start, but then I had to throw them to still water as well to complete the level.
- The price right now is rudiculous. 8 EUR for 30 min of content is borderline robbery. I understand that the funds from Early Access will be used to finish the game, but people pointed out that this is not a sustainable strategy, and so far I see only another 10 levels in the making. So what, 8 EUR for 1h of "gameplay"? Price should be lower or MUCH more content should be added soon to make the price more sensible.
- Objects clip and behave weird when touching. In the pinball level I hade that "ball" clip through the flipper (clipper?) every time I hit it.
- Voice of the GlaDOS wannabe makes me cringe - there is something off with her accent. I dunno, maybe it's just me.
Minor issues, that can be improved + ideas:
- More interactive options, even incorrect ones, should be available, just to add some fun value. Every item should interact with every other item available, just to add some difficulty and give the robots premise for heckling you :)
- With that in mind, hints should be available for when people are stuck with. Not needed now, but might be helpful if the devs tackle some more complex experiments.
- Science behind the experiments should be explained more thoroughly, with more paragraphs of text, just to have the more curious of children something to refer to if they wanted science behind the experiment explained. The game has a potential to be a valuable learning tool, so it shouldn't dumb the science down. You could add animations explaining the termodynamics behind the egg in the bottle trick, maybe a video clip - some strictly educational stuff to back the gameplay up. Not right there in the game, but some more materials could be available after finishing level ("Learn more" button, besides the "Next Level")
- The AR was selling point for the first Professor Why game, I think implementing it here might add some value. People, kids especially, love gimmicks so AR cards could make the game more immersive and enjoyable.
- VR support could take this to a who new level!

TERA did not start out as a FTP game... Originally, it was a full retail plus subscription cost.  While F2P has the image of being amateurish or unpolished, this game is neither.  The landscapes are art are absolutely breathtaking.
The most drawing aspect of TERA is the real time combat system.  Think more like Monster Hunter, and less like World of Warcraft.  If you want to dodge... you need to dodge... There's no accuracy stat, your accuracy is based on how good you are controlling your character.
However, with every pro, there are cons.  The endgame in TERA is incredibly elitist, grindy, and very Random-Number heavy, and not really as much fun as you might expect, or may have experienced in a FFXI, or WOW.  Now, I know you may think random number heavy is like any loot drop mechanics, but this goes one step further in the enchanting system as well.  I had more fun grinding to cap than playing at cap.
There's also a slight memory leak in the gake if you play too long... but that's kind of the norm nowadays.
The other major pro/con, is because this is F2P, their business model is based on aethetic aspects to character customization.  You will not get 100% immersion, because the first thing you'll see is a tiny Elin dressed up like a cop in a little police vehicle with a siren.  Or an elf or human in nothing but a bakini that looks like it was lifted from Dead or Live.
Overall, this scratches the MMO itch, it's a great combat system, very fun to play.  While the endgame isn't amazing, it's definitely worth picking up and trying.

TERA is extremely boring alone. If you want to play this game make sure you play it with friends. Not only will it make the game less difficult if you are playing a class that isn't good solo, but it will help kill the monotony of the questing/dungeons pre-end game. If you don't have friends, simply join a guild and quest with guildees. If you are tackling the game solo however here are some tips and warnings:
1. Make sure you are completeing quests in the right order, or else you will have to backtrack to the beginning of the zone to complete main quests you didn't realize you weren't completeing (it is easier to mess up than it sounds).
2. If you are playing solo make sure you pick a class that is good solo. A lot of classes in this game are balanced very strongly in a tank/dps/healing set-up and a lot of the big mobs in level 30+ zones get incredibly stronger than they were in previous zones. I recommend the brawler class as a great starting class. I played brawler and didn't have any issues with questing (or running dungeons) solo until around level 50+ when the level of the content was catching up with how far ahead my character was.
Every single zone in the game has the exact same leveling experience. 3 differen't locations per zone where you get quest type A. (kill 10 mobs quest), quest type B. (collect 10 items quest), and quest type C. (kill 5 big strong mob quest) once you complete those quests you move on to the next hub. After all 3 hubs in each sub-zone of a region you will get a quest chain to go through a solo-dungeon and repeat the whole thing and then eventually you will finally move on to the next leveled region and start all over again. I was hoping at least the expansion from 60-65 would have changed the questing experience a little, but honestly it was exactly the same. This game has by far the most undesireable questing experience I have ever participated in. I have played WoW, FFXIV, EverQuest, ArcheAge, Black Desert Online, Blade and Soul, Aion, Rift and many other MMOs, but this one takes the cake for the most boring grindy questing of them all. Luckily there are other options to choose from while questing.
This game really has none of it.
Duneons in TERA are fun at first (literally the first dungeon), but you will soon realize like the questing that they are all exactly the same. A lot of them use the same assets so enemies and layout look exactly the same as the dungeon you just did, but with a differen't coat of paint. Essentially kill 3 rooms of mobs, fight a boss, next three rooms, another boss, ect. If you are using dungeons to get to 65 (that is what I would recommend) then prepare to take a lot of breaks, or put on some music while you do them. I didn't give dungeons a 1/10 simply because some of the bosses actually look pretty damn badass, and the gear you can get in dungeons is pretty awesome. However, dungeon bosses still all lack creative mechanics most you can just tank and spank, as well as any real exciting reason as to why you should want to kill them (until the expansion). Once you hit upper 50 dungeons and the expansion dungeons nothing really changes, but they get more exciting lore wise and you will actually feel like you have a purpose for running them to get geared for raids.
Not a long section. I didn't play much of the raids, but they meet your typical mmorpg "get geared in dungeons then increase in raid tier" format. From what I played of them they are pretty fun and challenging, but I had a hard time keeping aggro so I didn't play much of them after getting the first raid tier gear.
I don't really have anything to say about the lore for pre-Arun expac, other than it is pretty boring and lacking (imo), but Fate of Arun's story can get pretty exciting esspecially anything centered around the character Zolyn and her friends since they are the only redeeming lore characters in the whole game. As for classes warrior is a pain in the butt I don't recommend playing it if you are new to the game, but most of the classes that I tried seemed fun you purchase skills with money from trainers. Brawler was a blast for me to play and probably in my top 5 favorite classes of mmorpg history. The combat in TERA started the action style combat breaking away from games like WoW so in that regard the combat is fluid and great for the most part. Keeping aggro as a tank seemed to be difficult for me as the only thing, dps pull insanely high in this game, but that could be just because I suck at tanking (most likely). All in all this game is literally known for it's combat and is why it has so many players.
I didn't participate in end-game world pvp so I cannot say how fun it is although it seemed pretty fun like most game with world pvp. Prepare to get ganked A LOT when you are leveling though. And yes, this game has pvp AND pve servers so if you have a preference between the two you will be covered either way. Battlegrounds are fun and unique.... for what there is. I gave the battlegrounds a good score in this game, but honestly there are a very low amount of them which can cause boredom to some players very quickly. If you want a more elaborate discussion on TERA's pvp feel free to message me. Also if you want to know about class balance I am the wrong person to ask as I only leveled to 65 with brawler and it was pretty OP at the time (they may have nerfed it by now).
First off this game has a very friendly community you will mostly only encounter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s in pvp related activities (like when you get that one guy in battlegrounds who thinks he is better than everybody else and he is carrying the team). Secondly, my opinion is a little biased because this game has a huge anime crowd which I do not mind (warning to those of you who do not like anime you are going to be seeing fans of it pretty much around every corner). It only gets a little cringy around people who are huge Elin fanboys I recommend staying away from them anyway (no offense, but look at what you are playing a little more closely and realize why others might want to stay away from you).
It is your standard MMO crafting much like WoW's so I can't really throw an opinion on this one as it is a hit or miss for most. A lot of players don't care about the crafting at all.
Game looks great and the artsyle is very pretty. Some zones have amazing screenshot-picture-perfect areas. Some of the best looking zones I have seen in an MMO (too bad the questing ruins it).
Q. Is the game P2W? ("Pay to win" meaning, do you have to pay for in-game shop items with real money to not fall behind other players)
A. No, this game has the best F2P model I have ever seen. All of the in-game shop items are cosmetics to make your characters look cool. The game has a subscription you can pay, but honestly I found it pretty much worhtless. It doesn't give you anything you cannot get for free except a teleport book so you don't have to take flight paths.
TERA has a lot going for it in the free to play market and can provide many hours of fullfilling mmo experience. The questing is beyond dull and more than half of the dungeons in the game have been cut out. Dungeons in general are uninteresting and bland until level 55+. Story isn't that great until Fate of Arun at 60, but the combat and visuals of the game are top notch and fun. PvP is lacking in content, but still fun nonetheless. Great game to try for free, but you might get bored fast. I recommend Black Desert Online Instead.

Fiesta Online is a free-to-play MMORPG. Fairly standard stuff. The cartoonish graphics are easy on the eyes and the Lore is fairly rich. Most importantly, however, the community is fairly nice and it's easy to make friends here. While there are items that require cash to buy, there's no real pressure in the game to get them. If I were to recommend any MMORPG to someone, it would
be this one.
However, Fiesta Online has one critical flaw: it is a time-draining, virtually-endless game. Do not play this game unless you are willing to sacrifice at least 4 hours a day, every day, for the rest of your life. The game is definitely easy to work with for the first ten levels, but the next ten are truly horrifying. Getting to level 20 in this game is incredibly difficult. It's not that the game is challenging; the hard part comes from forcing yourself to sit there and grind for the countless hours necessary to get out of the gloom that is the lv. 17-19 range. The game picks up after that, but only for so long. The cruel cycle continues to repeat itself.
If you like the typical WoW-style MMORPG setup, then, sure, this game is great. However, ultimately, I cannot in good conscience recommend this game to anyone.

I got a key for Road Redemption a long, long time ago, from one of the people working on the game. I was pretty happy about that since I was very much interested in the game from the moment I first heard about it. Whacking people off bikes at high speed will never not be a fun way to spend an afternoon, so I immediatelly tried the game. And I was pretty let down. NOT because the game was bad, as even in it's early stages of development it was quite fun and delivered exactly what it set out to, but because performance would decrease drastically as I played to the point that once i got to the second stage, it was impossible to play. Of course this made it so I couldn't actually experience the game and leave a review earlier, like I had planned, but I also didn't hold it against the game or devs because not only did ♥♥♥♥ing Unity always have it out for my toaster for whatever reason, but it was an early access game that was actively getting worked on. So I cut it some slack and just came back to it every few months, see the state it was in. And it was constantly getting better.
And now it's finally released. And it's a really much bigger game than it was at early access release.
It's got much more content and a plethora of improvments. And the performance  was fixed. Hurray.
You get the whole idea of the game from the screenshots in the store page: you ride a bike, you smack people with different kinds of weapons. Sometimes you also kick them. Very rarely you shoot them, because it's incredibly hard to aim with the guns at those speeds. So you blundgeon your way through each stage of a roguelike styled campaign: each level/track is generated randomly, with a bunch of possible objectives to complete (from simply racing, to getting a determined number of kills, to reaching the end of the track in a set time while cars and trucks fall from the sky) get some upgrades between each of them and items and health carry over between them too. You die, it's over. You get a chance to purchase a permanent upgrade and start over again. And it works pretty good, making the game really easy to pick up and play for short bursts.
However, it doesn't really have too much staying power. Fun as it is, and despite all the unlockable content (bikes and riders with different stats), I really have to emphasize the "short bursts) aspect.
It's terrific to kill 20/30 minutes, or to spends a couple of hours playing with friends (up to 4 players, online or local), or if you have nostalgia for Road Rash, but not to invest a huge amount of hours. It doesn't really have much in the way of depth, which in itself isn't a bad thing.
Bottom line is, it's a good game. It's a very fun game. It's a relatively casual game. If you're looking for something you can play for a little bit every now and again to let off some steam without having to invest too much into it, then Road Redemption is perfect and you should jump into it without fear. For the asking price it has a lot of quality and content.

This game is truly the best city-building-managment-simulation game out there. Though I have to agree the DLC is ridiclous, the overall gameplay is great. It really gets you into the city managing position more then SimCity 2013 ever could. The graphics are also marvellous, so marvellous something as simple as the water next to your city is now more then just water, it's like an aspect of the game thats supposed to be there.
The ability to freely rename citizens, buildings, vehicles, districts, roads, etc. is a nice added bonus. Though it doesn't effect gameplay, its funny to gock at your inside joke being displayed on a building, or a citizen named you or something... different. District policies are also really nice to have, because it lets you really customize your city. For example, if you wanted to have an industrial district of your city have high tech housing like a futristic neighborhood, and the other to show how far humanity has come, you can do that for whatever reason.
And I find it amazing someone recreated Downtown Chicago in this game, and I also find the workshop vast and growing everyday, with an amazing community. Other communities on steam are filled with kids yelling and swearing at people when they call their favorite character stupid or anything rather then the character's name. But this community? Supportive community and superb modmakers, plus asset editors who publish their assets on the workshop.
Overall, I HIGHLY RECOMMEND this game to anyone who likes city building, and to hasn't even played a video game before. This is one of those games that we'll remember as spectacular and mind-bending. The only thing I could ask for is more in the base game instead of paid DLC.

I bought this game purely out of boredom after a friend had recommended it. The game starts off as you would expect from a city builder. Build a little town with houses, roads and commercial zones while carefully spending your budget. As the city grows you unlock more content. The further you progress with the game the more details you notice. Every cim has a routine, a name, a work place and some destination he/she is heading to. Soon your city expands and you have so much to plan and manage that the game totally grips you. Before you know it your starter roads can no longer contain the traffic and you realize you should have planned further ahead. The traffic engine is amazing and the option for road building could be a game in itself. You have all the public services like healthcare, policing, fire departments, various forms of public transport and much more. Raise/lower taxes, take out loans, create districts with various different policies. The list goes on. Just as you think you have everything under control you notice that your entire city has flooded because you didn't know there is actual water physics after building a hydro electric dam wall in a river. Devs please.

This game has came a long way. When it first launched, it was a typical bug-riddled Ubisoft release, but fast-forward a couple of years later and it's one of the top played games on Steam. You can tell the devs really saw the potential in this game and invested the proper resources to make it into one of the best tactical shooters out there. While it's not perfect it does some things phenomenally and some things not as much.
Pros:
- Snappy and responsive gunplay
- Something for all levels of play
- Destructive environments
- Operator diversity keeps the game fresh
- Great community
- Free map expansions
- Weapon and Operator personalization
- Fast matchmaking
- Great with friends
- Frequent free weekends (great to try the game/get friends to try it)
Neutral:
- Cosmetic loot boxes
- Fast time to kill (all head shots are one hit kills)
- Reliant on teamwork
- Search & Destroy type game modes
- Objective based
Cons:
- Uplay
- Too many different editions of the game make it confusing for consumers
- Starter edition is cheaper but turns the game into a grind (You can’t upgrade either if you change your mind and want the normal version of the game later on.)
- DLC Operators cost a way too much renown, pretty much forcing you to buy the Season Pass to get them unless you want to grind
- Occasional server issues
- No straightforward methods for reporting toxic players when encountered
- Way too many load screens
- Did I mention Uplay?
TL;DR
Great tactical shooter reliant on teamwork and using strategy to win. Great if you can tolerate the heavy Uplay integration. Whatever you do, don’t get the starter edition if you’re interested in the game.

Element4l - it is charming, adorable, beautiful... If you just look at the trailers or pieces of gameplay, you'll probably come to a conslusion that this is a very relaxing and soothing game. I'll clear that up in just a second.
But first. What exactly is the game? The mechanics are simple, technically it's even called a platformer... You travel different environments: rocky and green, fire with lava, icy and snowy, or watery. And you are an element. First you are a bubble of air, then you gain the ability to turn into a cube of ice, then a little rock, and finally a fire spark. Each form has other abilities and weaknesses. The only control you have, is the form you take. You don't really control the movement, you just turn into the right element in the right area to fly, swim, slide, or bounce around.
The mechanics are brilliant in their simplicity. You press up for air, down for rock, left for ice, and right for fire. That's all you have control of. So it should be pretty easy, right? A simple, pleasant game.
WRONG! Honestly, I don't remember the last time I screamed, grunted, moaned, and cried this much during a game. Since the control is so minimal, you have to hit everything just right, at the right moment, with the right speed and angle. If you don't, you're screwed. Do over.
I'm a rage game masochist. So I just completely adore this game, and can't pull myself away from it. But if you don't enjoy getting absolutely infuriated during a game, maybe you shouldn't try it.
Now, apart from the brilliant mechanics, this game is just gorgeus. The environments are made in a beautiful, soft style. The elements are tiny, with an adorable little smiley kawaii face. The music is gentle and soothing, almost like a lullaby. And, every here and there, you get small remarks from the element that you are controlling, written somewhere on the screen. Like, when you are going underground the element mentions Gollum and the One Ring.
So the whole thing, looking objectively is really just cute, pretty, sweet and adorable.
And then if you play it, and you aren't very adept at it yet, it's hell on Earth.
I love it. If I haven't scared you off yet, try it. It's different, it's clever, it's difficult, and it's cute.

As someone who has been gaming for 30 years I may have different perspective than others on what I want out of game.
The main things I look for in a game are: challenge, uniqueness(doesn't seem like just a prettier version of a hundred other games i've played), pacing(I don't like watching cinematics and doing lame quests that just feel like work), and lastly I like games that make me feel something.
Flame in Flood hits all of these for me.  I've seen others say the game is too hard, I think it was just right, maybe a little too easy if anything.  I only died twice before beating the game, and came really close a few more times.
This is where the feels come in.  The feeling of desperation as I'm hurling my raft down the river at max speed with reckless abandon smashing in to rocks and debris, trying to find medicine to cure my snake bite was one the most intense  gaming moments I've had in a long time.  In other moments this game also invoked feelings of fear, joy, peacfulness, loss, lonliness, triumph and humor.
I paid full price for this game and feel like I got a bargain.  While it may not provide hundreds of hours of replayabilty.  The amazing and unique experience of the first couple of play throughs are well worth the price.

Very beautiful but poorly designed.
This game shines in terms of art and music. It does a great job of conjuring an environment not commonly explored by videogames. The result is beautifully atmospheric.
It is a shame therefore that the gameplay is so uninspiring. It's all about inventory management and crafting following set out rules. There is little to no room for creatively organic play. It is entirely a mechanical process of "to solve problem A get items B and C from location D and craft them to make item E ..." This could be OK in a more forgiving game, but it wants to be a roguelike, survival game. So you end up restarting a lot and working through the same sequence of early crafting processes -- get flint to build a knife and a hammer, build a trap, catch a rabbit, skin the rabbit, etc ...
Most good roguelikes (e.g. Nethack, Spelunky) are built around fine-grained mechanics which interact with one another in interesting ways, so the random level generation creates a wide variety of novel situations. TFITF doesn't have that kind of granularity or organic interaction. Each location is basically a big random loot-drop, perhaps with an enemy guarding it.
On the top of all this, there are a bunch of bad UI design decisions. For a game that is mostly about inventory management, the inventory UI is cumbersome. E.g. you can't access your inventory while looting a container. So if your inventory is nearly full, you'll find yourself clicking back and forth between the inventory screen and the looting screen. Likewise when you are crafting.
I really wanted to like this game. I keep coming back to it to give it another go, and each time I am disappointed.

RACE.A.BIT:
~~~~~~~~~
Ladies and Gentleman, it’s time to rev up your engine! Are you ready to show your driving expertise and rise to the top of the world RACE.A.BIT leader board? Well, what are you waiting for? Jump in your car and go for the gold and the number “ONE” spot!
RACE.A.BIT is a fabulous retro racing game with an excellent and easy level editor. RACE.A.BIT has 20 official tracks to race and the aim is to race around the track (usually 3 laps) as fast as you can to score the prestigious RACE.A.BIT Gold Medal. The first couple of tracks are quite easy but as you progress and unlock the other ones, you will have obstacles to avoid. In addition you will have to deal with different terrains and objects that assist you to go faster or help you to surmount obstacles. If you are extremely competitive (most gamers are), why don’t you try to knock the number one spot-holder on the leader board for each track. That would be a great challenge! Also, you can challenge a friend on a specific track, which is really fun too.
The level editor is actually very easy to use and fun. First you choose how big the map is. Then you design your own track (s). You decide where to put the obstacles (bombs, icy road, etc) and place assisting objects. Then, when you finish your “Grand Prix” track, you can test it and change it if needs be. I must admit that my creations were all over the joint, but I had a lot of fun. This aspect gives the game a huge amount of re-playability for yourself and for the community.
The controls are very responsive, the graphics represent well the 80’s era. Just great!!
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great retro racing game
-	Fabulous and easy level editor
-	Online Leaderboard
-	Great game for all ages, fun and addictive
-	Achievements & trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Soundtracks can be a bit annoying

Ubisoft took a year off to deliver an experience that woul bring back the series to greatness. In my humble opinion they have succeeded. This release does have some issues but they are minimal compared to what we are used from the past few releases.
They bring back the old formula with a few changes for innovation's sake. The battle system received a complete overhaul, resulting in a more challenging battle experience albeit somewhat unrefined. I'm willing to cut them some slack here since this is the first time they are implementing this new battle system.
The visuals and the game world are - as expected - absolutely gorgeous. This game's world just may be the biggest one so far. You can spend exploring for hours and hours and still find new places. You got it all, desert, riverlands, temples, tombs, mountains and cliffs, there's naval combat too. The story picks up the pace again as well. Ends that seemed somewhat loose and neglected for the past few titles are picked up and developed further again.
There is a system of microtransactions, true. I'm not a fan of it either, however it's minimally invasive and apart from timesavers and some cosmetic stuff you can just as well get those items with ingame currency.
Should you dare to buy this, even at full price? Yes, you should, especially if you're a fan of the series, you will most surely enjoy this very much.

Set in a dystopian future ravaged by biological- and nuclear warfare, a middle-aged junker finds his way to a seemingly undamanged and abandoned planetarium. Upon entering he is unexpectedly greeted by the ever talkative gynoid attendant (the last staff member left), Yumeni. Having been unable to connect to her databases she is unaware of the happenings the past 30 years and thus welcomes the junker as any other guest. Her undying loyalty, attentive and happiness ulitmately makes the protagonist grow fond of her. He discovers through Yumeni's memories how the planet used to be and what's behind the constant poisonous and corrisve rain.
As the story progresses, it is evident that writer Yūichi Suzumoto understands how to play with the reader's emotions and how to create a unique setting for his story. Mixed with very appealing illustrations, music and dialogues the character development furthermore remains intriguing and charming.
When that's said, then planetarian ~the reverie of a little planet~  is not a game (or story) for everyone. A passion for anime is an absolutely minimum requirement, and an acceptance of the fact that there are no choices or interaction to be made beyond the dialogue speed. However, if you like anime and don't mind a kinetic novel, then planetarian ~the reverie of a little planet~ is a great choice for an emotional and solid story.

A masterfully written story full of sad moments, uplifting moments and some downright depressing ones too. Even though it is just back and forth dialogue between a robot programmed to take care of guests at a planetarium and one man in a post-apocalyptic setting, you'd have a difficult time finding other visual novels that offer a more engrossing story. Key are kings of the genre and hopefully more of their titles will end up getting localised on Steam. What a great VN.

Summary: Fiesta is an anime-themed massively multiplayer online (MMO) game that emphasizes group play. It is simple enough for ten-year-olds, but a few annoying bugs and a very grindy lategame may discourage you after many hours of play. It is free, and buying in-game items can help speed you along without breaking the game.
Positives:
1. Fiesta is simple as MMOs go: you don't so much *win* the game, but you gain levels by earning EXP from completing quests. Quests mostly require killing monsters, collecting drops from monsters, or gathering items in the wilderness. The quests and overarching storyline are text-based and perhaps tangential to the game itself; there is virtually no real "roleplaying" of your character. Don't let the anime feel fool you: you spend the bulk of your active gaming time looking for monster spawn points and exterminating them.
2. If dressing up your character in funny and cute cosmetic items is a draw for you, you will be pleasantly surprised at the wide variety of available costumes, hats, ears, pets, and mounts you can (rarely) earn or buy in the real-money store. Most cosmetics give a mild buff, such as increased critical hits or more EXP, and some can be earned by leveling, playing games of chance in the Lucky House, or completing timed rewards during in-game events.  You can run around in a t-shirt, butterfly wings and rainbow tube socks while fighting the bad guys, and still have all your gear equipped and active. Even a free-to-player can earn about 15 specific cosmetics by the time a character reaches level 66.
3. A handful of typical classes provides some variety, but you only acquire perhaps 10-20 skills unique to each class, so there isn't the deep customization you would find in action RPGs like Diablo or World of Warcraft. That said, you can spend skill points on your favorite skills to make them more powerful, cheaper to cast, or to refresh their cooldowns faster. You also get stat points to increase the raw abilities of your character also.
4. Fiesta boasts one one of the few truly female-friendly gaming communities. Also, the gender of your character can be chosen on creation regardless of class and without effect on your character's stats. Also, if you're a parent of a potential user, Fiesta has virtually no content that is inappropriate for preteens; only the chatter of the other players need be monitored. There is also no way in-game to purchase real-money content; the store is on a separate, secure website.
Negatives:
1. Fiesta needs to address a few bugs that cause the game to crash repeatedly, usually caused by switching areas or standing around in populated areas. This is causing the existing community to slowly leave, however the most popular server (Bijou as of this writing) still enjoys a large population. If you want to play alone or just with some close friends, you can choose one of the other servers and not be bothered much by chat spammers or other annoyances.
2. No Steam overlay for a Steam game.  No Steam Guard for a Steam game; it still utilizes a third-party anti-malware software (X-Trap). You can't use Steam Wallet Funds to buy Slime Coins, the currency used by the parent company, Gamigo (at least that I can find). Steam does little more than hold the shortcut for you, much like a non-Steam game you've added to your library. So what's the advantage of being a Steam game...?
3. Some of the crafting skills (i.e. making potions and scrolls) require you to spend hours of real time crafting many more items than you will ever need or sell. It's something you can have the game running in the background while you do other tasks, but it is kind of a pain.
4. On one hand, the game is growing: some low-level maps have had graphical updates, and the level cap has increased to 125 replete with new areas, quests, and items to find.  On the other hand, the North American servers are slowly depopulating, just because there are so many other games out there to play, and that the patches (and bugfixes!) of new content are coming too slowly. If you can find friendly players and join a Guild Academy, you are more likely to stick with playing longer. But playing solo is a real grind (even for me, and I'm used to grinding solo).
Free Advice:
1. You will level MUCH slower if you ignore the quests and just find a place to grind.  Until level 30 you can play as you wish, but in later levels, most of your EXP will come from completing repeated quests, not from defeating the monsters required by the quests.  That said, I hope you like grinding, because in the mid-game (say your level is in the 60s) a typical quest may require you to kill 40 of a monster for 4% of your required EXP to gain a level, and a repeatable quest will require 120 of a monster to earn 7% of the required EXP.
2. Save your skill points until you have played the character for a few hours and have become comfortable with your hot-keyed skills. You cannot unspend the skill points unless you spend real money to do so. Maxing out the power and maxing out reduced cooldown time of your main attack skills is common.
3. As far as your stat points, most players maximize their character's Strength in order to increase damage, unless you are a Wizard (max INT instead). Depending how you play your character, however, you may put a few points in SPR (to have some more SP and to crit more often), and perhaps a bunch in END (for extra health when you intend to get hit a lot).
4. You can earn a lot of random cosmetic items by participating in month-long Attendance Events. By logging on for one hour a day per character, that character can earn a reward of 1-3 cosmetic items per week, as well as another reward for earning attendance for at least 21 of the 28-day event. Stash these items, then use them when you're bored or when you plan to do a lot of leveling!

This also involves deciding whether officers can take a day off; at the beginning of each day, pop-up messages will show their excuse. For example, someone's dog could've died the previous day or they could've come to work drunk. The player chooses which excuses are acceptable.
One can choose to fraternize with the mafia, do the mayor's dirty work, do business with the Atticus Group, do favors for The Church, or help the Labor Union with their dirty work. Doing any of those things has pros and cons, but the worst con of all is becoming corrupt in the process.

Pretty fun game. The controls take some getting used to and can be a little unintuitive (especially shooting), but overall the combat is very satisfying and quick-paced. You get plenty of weapons to switch things up with, and you unlock more characters, vehicles, and skills as you play. You feel like your hits pack a punch, and as long as you're not trying to shoot someone or drop a bomb while you're surrounded, you won't feel too overwhelmed. Stun gun guys though. F**k those guys.
The racing, however, is trash. The severe rubberbanding in place in order to help yourself and enemies stay locked together for combat doesn't mesh well with trying to get to the finish line first. The driving controls are also pretty finicky, especially combined with some of the tracks which will have steep hills immediately followed by sharp turns or a sideways-parked vehicle right in front of you, causing you to go flying off the road. Boost helps, but not all tracks have pickups for it, so sometimes you're just SOL if you've used it all and then an enemy truck blindsides you into a pole and makes you instantly loose all momentum.
And almost all of the missions are racing missions. There are these missions where you have to eliminate a certain number of certain enemies before they "escape" by crossing a line on the road. So it's a race, basically. It could have been like a traditional Burnout-style road rage with enemies always coming in from behind as well as you catching ones in front, but instead there is a limited supply of the enemies and they all start out a quarter mile down the road from you. This mission type can get kind of frustrating when you get bumped off the road and you lose because one guy crosses the line before you could get him. And sometimes these missions come one after the other, over and over again, with your lost health and boost carrying over every time you lose, until someone kills you with a club because you aren't able to parry while putting C4 on a vehicle. Then you basically get to start the whole game over.
But I'm still recommending it because when you've got the controls down and you're focused, the combat is a lot of fun. Even dodging oncoming cars and other vehicles flying around is pretty cool when they aren't driving straight into you out of a blind turn. Some tweaking to the controls and racing balance would be nice, but it's still very enjoyable as is if you don't mind the occasional rage.
If it's on sale for $15 or even $10, get it for sure, it's definitely worth it. At $20, make sure it's your cup of tea first.

In summary, one of the critic's reviews states it perfectly.
"I’ll remember this platformer mainly as a torture. It’s really ruthless when it comes to making you feel helpless. [CD-Action 08/2013, p.81]"
I will start off by saying I did enjoy it... for the first 20 minutes. But the learning curve is rediculous. Shortly after you learn all the elements the difficulty just goes through the roof past the moon and all the way to pluto. After a few deaths it gives you the option to press "h" which places a ghost you on the screen doing it the correct way. That's all nice and dandy, but at parts the tutorial ghost you will go off screen and you won't be able to see what to do next. On top of that, there is literally only one way to do it. If you do not copy exactly what the ghost does, you -will- die.
The physics... are off. Your momentum is something you will be constantly fighting with. As "air" you can only move about two seconds before all your forward momentum (typically right on the screen) completely disappears. You can use "fire" to get some momentum, but here is where (in my opinion) the worst mechanic lies. There is simply not enough energy. All your elemental forms cost energy except for ice. You can only use about three elements in quick succession before you are out of energy. So you have to perfectly time each use of your energy. If you're sliding as ice and need to use air to get up and to the right, you must switch to air exactly when the game wants you to. If you switch a half second too late you won't have enough momentum and you can't use air enough times to get high enough, or if you get high enough you won't have enough energy to use fire to get to the right. If you press it a half second too early then you will have too much momentum and you will crash into the wall and die.
This becomes quickly frustrating as more or less it is about just being lucky enough to hit the button at the right time. For the most part there was no guessing as to what to do next. With only four elements there was no confusion factor.
The other big flaw of the game is respawning. When you die, as you will most definitly die a lot, you respawn sometimes in seemingly random locations. You respawn as rock, which will almost immediatly slow your momentum, the most important factor in the game. If you spawned as ice, it wouldn't be quite so bad. Some places you spawn will be in a dead stop as well. This forces you to use air to get off the ground and then fire to get some momentum, which right off the bat uses up 2/3 of your energy.
I really did want to like the game. It is aboslutely beautiful and the sountrack is amazing. But the actual gameplay is just torture. I finally quit when you start in a hole and have to go back and forth trying to build up your -you guessed it- momentum! in order to get out of it. The 'help' button was basically worthless.
All in all, I do not reccomend this game. If you're a masochist and love constantly dying while trying to figure out the exact timing the game wants, then this is for you. Otherwise I wouldn't pay any more than $0.25 for this game.

This is one of the most unique survival games in look and feel that I have played since the genre started taking off. With a fun art style and amazing folksy music, The Flame in the Flood achieves levels of immersion reminiscent of games such as Bioshock and The Long Dark. With your trusty dog companion by your side, you will pilot your raft down a winding, at times turbulent river peppered with a variety of scavenging locales. Semi-procedurally generated rivers create a new journey each time.
Graphics- The art style reminds me of some of the best recent Image comics, dark and gritty and yet whimsical. The only minor quibble I'd have is that I find the protagonist a bit creepy-looking, and harder to relate to.
Audio- As mentioned before, the music is FANTASTIC. It sets the mood for the game perfectly and is a treat to listen to while playing. Sound effects are well done and give crucial clues to survival, i.e. you learn to pay attention to your dog's barks and growls, as they have different meanings, etc.
Controls- Decent. However, right clicking to do everything can lead to frustrating misclicks that may cost you your life. Nothing like finally having everything needed for that raft upgrade and then jumping back on board and downriver instead of using the winch! Raft steering is difficult at first, but improves greatly with the addition of a rudder.
Story- Pretty light so far as I've played. There are a few NPCs to meet along the way, and I've read several pieces of a tale writted on quilts scattered along the river, but maybe there is more to be found if I can quit getting eaten by wolves, which brings me to:
Gameplay. Fairly standard survival play, however the difficulty ramps up big time once you pass the first leg of the river. Easily one of the more challenging games of the genre. Crafting is simple, fun and rewarding, but inventory management can be a bit of a slowdown to play.
I'm really enjoying this title, even though I keep dying and having to start over! If you're a fan of survival games, definitely worth checking out.

The roar of the engine, the smell of petrol in your nostrils, the blinding sun penetrating the windshield.  You sit behind the wheel of your five hundred thousand dollar race car, a pair of worn black sunglasses (The Rowdy ones) rest half-cocked off your nose.  You rev the engine, hearing it purr like a kitten, the heat raises inside the beast..  You feel trickles of sweat running down your face... No time to relax, it's only time to win, everyone knows "if you ain't first, you're last" (Ricky Bobby for the win)
Well unfortunately the situation I described above won't be something you'll find in Race.a.bit, what you will find is a pleasant throwback to 80's gaming.  Devoid of all the modern trappings graphically overproduced piles of dung 3d racing games that exist to simply look good but have zero substance.  The simplistic nature of Race.a.bit will be a nice refreshing change of pace.  Kick back, and hit up some crazy tracks with your square or diamond shaped block.  Anyone born prior to 1990 will appreciate the game, people who grew up playing games like Super Sprint.

The music...

I'll start off by saying if you were born after 1990, you won't like the game and should probably avoid it. (unless you are a fan of retro gaming) Anyone born in the 80's, when A.l.F from Melmac was attempted to eat the Tanner's cat lucky, or you were fighting for your right to Party, or you still think Cyndi Lauper is a chart topper with perfect pitch, you'll most likely love this game.  Playing it really took me back in time, I remembered all those amazing times in the 80's, it was prior to me donning my Hammer Pants and thinking Ice Ice Baby was cool, back when my life was atari and then nintendo, playing old school racing games, trying to beat the high score, trying to show (heck no multiplayer back then, so it was all about topping my brother) my friends who the king of the neighborhood was.
So I totally recommend you get this game, it'll bring you back to a better time, a time when video games weren't all about trying to pack cutting edge graphics and sound into the games with the worst possible gameplay.  A time when games weren't released broken and fixed later with patches, and certainly a time when games were released complete and not cut apart and sold back to us in mini pieces..

PLanetarian is a Japanese visual novel by the company Key. Compared to other Key works (which run around 50+ hours at least) Planetarian is a short story and can be completed between 4 and 6 hours. There are no choices to be made here, so just grab a tissue box and enjoy the emotional ride.
hands down the best post-apocalyptic game on steam.

Played it again when the voice acting was added a couple years later...
Cried so hard I died of dehydration.
Been dead ever since.
10/10

It's a little short for my taste. I expected a more elaborate story, not located in a single location. For this reason i think the price is a little high for the content included. I've played other visual novels which were the same price and which had 3 to 4 times more content and just as if not more enjoyable. So a little overpriced.
However it is a nice story and i enjoyed it very much. Just would have loved to see more of the world and a little more adventure. Would I recommend this:
Yes, if you like a touching short story which revolves around a Robots "dreams".
No, if you prefer the adventure type of visual novel. There is pretty much no adventure in this novel.

I remember playing this around 10 years ago, so it's really great now that Key and Sekai Project are able to release this internationally.
Key somehow always has a way of making you really feel for the characters; planetarian, even with its short and simple story, is no different.
I would highly recommend it to anyone. It won't take too much of your time, but I believe you're going to enjoy it.
Also, if you enjoyed the setting of planetarian, Key has released a drama CD containing sides stories, which include a prologue and an epilogue for planetarian as well. I also recommend looking out for those, Hopefully Sekai Project finds a way to release those on Steam too.

The combat and controls are kinda funky but you honestly get used to it after an hour or two, and once you do you have a really great open world exploration RPG with a fantastic story, great voice acting and characters, and genuinely interesting and fun combat.
Sure, there are a few issues with it (like enemies tracking the player even after they're out of view or the occasional minor bug) but it's nothing game breaking or that weren't in games like the Witcher 3.
I can't stress enough that you need to give it an hour or so to adjust to the new controls. I thought about getting a refund but once the tutorial was over I realized I had adapted completely and the game became incredibly fun. Im really enjoying this game, having played most of the other AC games, this one stands out with its new combat system and more of a focus on exploring in an open world. I've encountered some very minor bugs but nothing to make me feel like the game is unplayable. The combat system also tends to feel a bit unpolished, and would be best to describe it as a "light" version of what you got in For Honor. You lock on, and you swing at the guy. Theres not much variety or tactics outside of that in a fight. The lock on can be a hinderence at times, but I've found manually aiming works well enough with a mouse and keyboard. I did have to rebind the buttons a bit to have it feel a little more intuitive.
Might be opinion but Bayek is also a pretty interesting protagonist so far compared to some of the other protagonists you might play as in prior AC games. Again, mileage may vary as this is a personal opinion. I find ancient egypt more interesting than some of the settings in the other games.

This is a great game and a great addition to assassins creed.  It is different than all the other assassins creed goes as far as weapons, combat, and RPG elements with loot go.  For instance; the combat is much more like Dark Souls or the Witcher 3's combat with rolling and counter attacking.  The combat is NOT Hard at all in my opinion.  I saw somone complaining saying it was waaaay too hard but it's not.  It is incredibly easy if you arent stupid.  Don't attack things 5+ levels above you and don't run into 20 enemies at once.  Ive played for 9.3 hours on hard difficulty and have had no difficulty problems unless running into enemies 5+ levels higher than me.  The Parkour is another thing i saw somone complain about; I have had only 1 "bad" parkour event where i was trying to go straight but ended up jumping off a platform.  It was once out of 9.3 hours of parkouring.
PROS:
So far, great story
great characters IMO
Fun Combat; provides a challenge and encourages headshots + well timed attacks
Good side quests; ive had lots of interesting and non-cliche side quests that have been great.
Great exporation; however it is limited by leveled zones.
Cons:
To me their is only one big Con and that is the performance issues.  I run a GTX 1070 with good CPU and motherboard etc etc but i get choppy 30-60 fps on high settings.  Normally sit around 36 and itll shoot up if the area becomes less dense.  I would love more optimization and smoother fps.
Great game. Buy it if you have a decent PC; else, get it on PS4 or XBOX

I read another review here that said that this game is recommended to those who are just starting to play mmorpgs. I completely agree. Fiesta was one of the first mmorpgs I've ever played and somehow, I still love it (even with all the repetiveness and grinding). Why? The community is nice (which I find very assuring when you're just a starter, so this is the big concept I want to point out to beginners). People will always help you when you're least expecting it; whether it be a random buff from a cleric or people asking if you need help in your guild -you can always rely on the community.
I might be naive saying this, but I've played other mmorpgs to some extent as well, and at some point they all have their repetiveness, so as far as the gameplay goes... what's so bad? The skills have increasing levels that you unlock as you level up, and skills that you eventually come to gain. You don't come equipped with all your skills and for me, I found that such an exciting experience when I first started playing. [If anyone else has played Vindictus then I would like to compare: you do get skills along the way, and can level them up to some degree, but unless you're not into the whole paladin/dark knight thing then there's no other skills] I always looked forward to getting new skills in Fiesta and still do (because I haven't reached the level cap yet since I've taken such a long time off this game, but I still come back to it).
Now if you don't like grinding or P2W then sorry; this is definitely NOT the game for you if you plan on playing it for a while. This is the reason I've taken long breaks and the only reason.
Overall, I definitely recommend this games to starters of the mmorpg worlds.
Even so, I still recommend this game to experienced mmorpg players as well. This game goes back to the classics. Classes of Fighter, Mage, Cleric, and Archer can never let you down. To add, the developers have even added Trickster, and Crusader to those who want a little variety. note* Crusader becomes availible at level 60. I always seem to come back to this game even if it is repetitive because I miss it, and I think others who have reviewed have the same feelings. It's a relaxing game that has cute sprites and reliable gameplay. I think that's all from me ^^

Downside of the game is that again it is a Ubisoft game and as with all Ubisoft games they have s*** servers so expect the game to bug out a lot. Besides the server issues there are in game bugs with the game physics as well but that’s standard for all MMO games.
All in all, the game is good and personally I think because of the different price tier to join the game this allows more people to buy in and decide whether the game is worth their time if not they wouldn’t have spent a lot of money buying a full price game just to see if they like the game.

Well I enjoyed my time enough to bother writing out my opinions. That says something. Anyway, here's the pros/cons.
Pros-
Wonderful sound track, although the guy who sings isn't amazing. The overall feel and style of the game is unique and fun to look at.
The first few times where you die before you reach the end are very interesting whilest you figure out the game.
Interesting world design with every first time being very exciting (such as the first time you see a bear or get to the wasteland).
Neat little ending that left me with a smile and satisfied with the run through the game.
Cons-
Low replay value. Unless you really enjoyed your first run through the isn't much reason to keep playing after beating it.
Suprisingly small amount of content. Only four kinds of animal, all of which do the same thing for you (upgrade cloths and give you food). Crafing possibilites are also limited with very few interesting and unique items to make and find.
It gets pretty darn repetative. Due to the lack of content most areas end up feeling like re-skins of previous areas just  with fewer suppiles.
Few bugs about the place.
Conclusion-
It reminds me a bit of MASSIVE CHALICE. Great core gameplay with an interesting are style and theme, but desperatly lacking in depth (bit like my spelling). One of those games where if time and money wasn't an issue and it had another 6-12 months to just keep updating it could have been one of the all time great survival games.
It's memorable and fun; unfortunately nothing more.

Tried hard to give this game a chance but failed. Bad game is bad.
Flame in the Flood should be called Turd in the Flood and have the "Floating Turd Simulator" tag, its that bad.
So whats this game about?
Raft down a river, if you pay attention you will notice there are certain "rails" that you can follow (white trails visible on the water) and if you pay attention to the rather intuitive controls, you will manage to control your raft quite well, and thats before even upgrading it, so i dont understand the rafting control complaints, the controls are fine and dandy, one of the very few things in the game that are actually well done, because everything else is a mess.
Soooo....you raft down a river..cool so far. With a little attention and effort you will avoid bumping into obstacles that can send you to a watery grave....fantastic.
Then you get to certain spots that you can dock...and you dock...that leads to you roaming a minimap that is like 2-3 screens big, and harvesting whatever there is to harvest there. There is no exploration, no nothing, you just walk around a small arena and collect stuff.
Collecting enough stuff opens up recipes to craft.
Everything is totally random: harvestables, recipes, docking places, hazards, you name it, all random, so you cant plan anything really, you are a floating turd at the mercy of the RNG GOD....and that wouldnt be THAT bad, if the developer didnt feel the need to pull special game mechanics right out of his behind...
Small example: you dock on an island and you encounter some wolves....at this moment you lose control over your characters movement, so you cant run, you cant do anything much other than accumulate status conditions with each and every hit that the wolves inflict on you.
Its likely there is some item or mechanic to deal with this situation, but i still dont understand why should i bother torturing myself trying to find out, when the game as a whole is so underwhelming.
I dont mind some pain when its worth it, but this game is really not worth my while, and thats the main problem here.
Its a minor insignificant game, and whatever "depth" the developer intended, is not worth looking for because its simply not fun....well...at least not for me, because everything is subjective.
My subjective opinion is that this game is a turd and the developer has good connections in the industry to grant him the praise he got, which i consider to be undeserved....personal opinion of course, dont take it any other way.

Honestly, this is one of the best installments in the series in my opinion. The parkour in this is awesome, but there isn't much to climb on besides trees and two-story buildings, which is okay with me. Finally, the story in this is pretty good, if you pay attention and watch the cutscenes.
Overall, this game got a lot of hate and is still considered one of the worst games in the franchise, but that is completely opinion-based. If you're looking for a bit of history, war, parkour, and a badass assassin-indian, look no further! Visual Novels are a strange medium to break into. On one hand, there's the base concept that you're essentially reading a book, just with more visual elements. On the other hand, you've got a great deal of depth provided by branching choices and character investment as a result. Planetarian is a kinetic novel - that is, a visual novel without choices - and it's
best introduction one can get to the medium, bar none. The experience is short - maybe four to five hours, depending on your reading speed - but substantial, and the primary drive of the experience, the story, is yet another masterpiece from Key Visual Arts.
You play "The Junker" and you meet "The Reverie," a girl in a planetarium in the dark, dystopian future. That's the game, that's the story - and yet, for all its simplicity, the beauty the narrative manages to portray and the attachment it builds for the characters in such a short time span is astounding, especially in a gaming scene where it's common for the story to be so shallow that remembering any element of it is a monumental task (remind me, exactly
did I do in the last five Call of Duty installments?).
Planetarian is a quick, satisfying story that is an excellent introduction to the Visual Novel medium. Well worth the cost, well worth the time spent.

This visual novel is a fairly quick read, especially considering the games before and after planetarian's position in the Key timeline. It took me about 4.6 hours. This game does Key justice, once again. I would highly recommend this visual novel/game to others because it's an easy read, considerably quick, and it makes you feel something. Regardless of what the feelings may be, it accomplishes what it sets out to do. This visual novel evokes emotions and it's even a little educational, in the aspect of astronomy. Like many other Key productions, the story sticks with you. The story takes you somewhere else during certain parts and the soundtrack is wonderful. I, honestly, have no regrets from buying it and have no negative comments.

I have already played this game before it was licensed and I even bought it when I found an iPhone version. The fact I'm playing it for a second time means that it's doing something right.
Developed by Key, 'Planetarian: ~The Reverie of a Little Planet~' takes place in a post-apocalyptic Japan. The Junker (the character you follow) hears rumours of a city that hasn't been exploited by other scavengers. In hopes to claim any goods, the Junker stumbles upon nothing but ruins and a robot girl named Yumemi Hoshino.
The story itself isn't very long, which is good considering it doesn't have a thousand story arcs like Clannad or Rewrite (some of Key's other works). It's just the right length to develop your characters and see them interact with each other as they try to overcome the problem at hand.
The Junker starts off as a jerk (although that's understandable) and he I didn't find him ver likeable in the beginning. What I don't like the most is that we are given bits of his past but they act more like references than tools to develop his character.
Yumemi, however, is the true star. She's a very thoughful and respective robot that takes care of the planetarian in the absence of civilization. Her attitude and general presence is almost heartlifting, and if you engrose yourself in the game you might even grow a smile on your face. You almost forget she's a robot by the end of the game.
The music is pretty nice. It's calming when it needs to be, but there are moments when the music stops and the only audio playing is the rain, which is really calming.
Speaking of which, the atmosphere is mostly pretty cheerful. Most of the time it's just the Junker and Yumemi talking, and the music in the background works very well in this respect. There are times when the rain just goes and it lets you take in everything you are experiencing. You can also tell by the end of the story just how heavy things are getting.
If you are considering this game I highly recommend you buy it. If you aren't interested in a story with no gameplay stay clear of this one there is no gameplay other than clicking to prceed to the next text. There aren't English voice actors either, so if you aren't fond of listening to two Japanese actors talking to each other I also recommend you stay clear of this game.

I wanted to like Punch Club, I really did. Initially, the really bright and detailed location screens and the rather unique game concept of training a boxer up Rocky Balboa style drew me in and had me excited for more. However, after spending some time in the game, the shine started to wear off. The gameplay (fights, training, and social interaction) is simple and became repetitive very early on, offering hardly any progression in terms of mechanics after your initial introduction to the basics at the beginning of the game. Additionally, you have to go through a lot of dialogue in the game, often times having the same EXACT conversation with characters every day to get basic stuff like training done. This combined with the fact that the writing itself was not too inspired and had many grammatical errors had me wishing for an option to turn off unnecessary dialogue in the game altogether! To top it all off, the story felt extremely contrived and at times had me scratching my head trying to piece together what had just happened.
I came into this game excited about trying something new and original, something with excellent art and a compelling gameplay / story narrative. What I got didn't quite live up to my expectations. I would recommend picking this up if it's on sale though if you don't mind a very grindy game and if that concept seems interesting to you!
Side note: At the time of my playing (long after release) the game still had plenty of little bugs that popped up regularly. While none of them were game breaking, it was a bit of a pain to have to constantly work around them. Cheers!

This game is pretty much dead in the water. I played this game in it's first few years, 2007-2010, and it was great.. I made lots of online friends (many of which i still keep in touch and/or play other games with) and generally had a really good time. The game itself is a generic mmo with rather simple mechanics, it's essentially a beginner's MMO... but of course that's not what made Fiesta fun, what made it fun was the social aspect.. unless you make friends and join a guild you ARE NOT GOING TO HAVE FUN, this game isn't for "lone wolfs" that are just looking to play a game and level up because it gets extremely tedious.
I downloaded this game again after seeing it on Steam while mindlessly browsing in order to see how much it has changed and damn, has it changed. This game is now just a shadow of the shell of what it used to be..that's right, it's not even just a shell of it's former self, it's the shadow of it's shell... the reason being, there's very few people playing and even fewer new players getting into the game, it's currently Friday night and the server populations are all on Low.... It's mostly just populated by a handful of true newbies that in all likelyhood won't make it past level 50 and the rest are veteran gamers that have sunk way too much time and/or money to quit, which is made evident by the high number of not only high level characters but also mid to low level characters with +9 - +11 gear whom are most likely just alts belonging to veterans. I looked around the low level maps and saw only a few people doing quests, all of them by themselves of course.. Roumen to Uruga ( they're the maps for levels 1 to 60 ), checked all the maps in between and didn't see more than 10 people, none of them were in parties/groups.. just solo'ing. If you look at the screenshot of a group of players above, that's pretty all the people you'll see in Elderine which is the main vendor map...half of those people will most likely be AFK though, so you'll only see around 20 active players in that main city map.
So in short, don't bother playing this game.. I imagine it won't be around for another year or two.
*sigh* it really was nostalgic running through the maps though, almost brought a tear to my eye remembering all the good times I had with my old guildmates.. all the fun, drama, and plain old silliness.

I've been playing through this game with a friend for every version since Sean released it for Kickstarter backers at the very beginning, and I have to say though it looks very similar to Magicite, it really continues to build off that excellent game. Sean has been super great as far as regular updates to the game and responding to feedback from the community. So buying it in early access, here's what I like about the game so far.
What I love:
►Challenging gameplay. You need to play smart and careful if you want to survive.
►Cafting system. No recipes to memorize, rewards experimentation rather than memorization.
►Better multiplayer. Magicite was a lot of fun in multiplayer, but had many bugs with syncing, enemies disappearing, warp glitches. Things have been much more stable in Roguelands.
►Roguelike but also persistent. The way the game works is that each character you create only has one life, however you can bank items on your ship to be used in future playthroughs. The plan is also that you'll unlock new classes, races, and abilities as you play as well (not implemented as of v 0.4.6 though so can't really say much on that).
That's all for now, can't wait to see where development goes for this, but I have been very impressed with the quality and responsiveness in each update so far.

Element4l is an absolutley amazing game. The controls are great, albiet a bit strange. The concept is that instead of moving left, right, and jumping like in normal platformers you switch between four elements to navigate through levels, whether you need to go forward, fly a bit, or gain a little bit of weight.
Not only does it have a nice concept, but the levels and music are butifully designed. The surrounding area adds a nice bit to the game, not very clearly marking where you go next (a good thing, by the way). There is only one soundtrack as far as I've played, but it's so long that I couldn't even tell that it was repeating constantly.
Finally, the levels are ordered nicely. It never gives you anything you wouldn't be able to figure out due to previous shenanigans.  It gets harder and harder the farther you go, never dropping in difficulty. If you ever get stuck, you can always consult the 'help' button, and if you DO get stuck there are nice bits of text to lighten your rage levels.
Anyone who has played the game can tell you it is a bit linear. There isn't much exploration (although there is still quite a bit if you want to get the lost soul thingies). This is only due to the control scheme, the makers couldn't have it many other ways.
All in all, this is a game worth getting. I will admit, I'm not yet sure if it's worth ten dollars, but five bucks is definitley underpriced for this gem.

Ubisoft took a year off to deliver an experience that woul bring back the series to greatness. In my humble opinion they have succeeded. This release does have some issues but they are minimal compared to what we are used from the past few releases.
They bring back the old formula with a few changes for innovation's sake. The battle system received a complete overhaul, resulting in a more challenging battle experience albeit somewhat unrefined. I'm willing to cut them some slack here since this is the first time they are implementing this new battle system.
The visuals and the game world are - as expected - absolutely gorgeous. This game's world just may be the biggest one so far. You can spend exploring for hours and hours and still find new places. You got it all, desert, riverlands, temples, tombs, mountains and cliffs, there's naval combat too. The story picks up the pace again as well. Ends that seemed somewhat loose and neglected for the past few titles are picked up and developed further again.
There is a system of microtransactions, true. I'm not a fan of it either, however it's minimally invasive and apart from timesavers and some cosmetic stuff you can just as well get those items with ingame currency.
Should you dare to buy this, even at full price? Yes, you should, especially if you're a fan of the series, you will most surely enjoy this very much.
If you like tactical-shooters then this game is for you, but beware the wrath of the semi toxic community.

tl;dr - Great game aside from a couple of control issues.
I backed this game on Kickstarter. I played a couple hours of it during the early access period and a few more hours today after it was released.
I'm not a veteran of any of the Road Rash games. I think I played a little bit of one of the PlayStation 1 version but I barely remember any of it. That said, I'm really enjoying Road Redemption. There's nothing else like it on PC; I think the closest relative would be something like Carmageddon (which I also love). So if you have played and enjoyed Carma I'd say there's a good chance you'll like RR.
The best part about the game is the combat variety. There are 4 weapon categories (blunt melee, swords, guns, explosives) and each category has two or more different variants. I pretty much always used all 4 types of weapons at some point in every race. Different enemies called for different weapons depending on their strength or weakness and also whether they are next to you or at some distance, so plan on doing a lot of switching around while you're riding.
On that note, the game can be played with either mouse/keyboard or with a gamepad. I tried both, and both options have downsides. The controls are the game's biggest shortcoming right now.
The mouse has a major advantage in being able to use much more precise aiming when using guns, but I prefer the gamepad since it's more comfortable to switch weapons using the d-pad rather than the mouse wheel or keyboard keys (for me at least). If you do use mouse/keyboard it would help to have a mouse with at least 5 buttons, because there are a lot of controls you'll need to access quickly.
Unfortunately, although the mouse/keyboard buttons can be rebound, the gamepad controls cannot. That leads to the biggest problem with the gamepad which is that Nitro is bound to double-tapping the right trigger. Nitro is a critical component of the game that you'll be using constantly, both to catch up to the other riders or to boost past them. But double-tapping RT doesn't work very well - it seems to randomly require a triple-press sometimes, while other times it will engage on only one press. So that's annoying.
Hopefully the controls will be improved with a patch or two. Even if they aren't though, I would still absolutely recommend Road Redemption. The single-player campaign is worth $20 by itself, but there is also both split-screen and online multiplayer. I tested a few matches online and everything seemed to work smoothly - no lag or anything like that. Online opponents are a lot tougher than the A.I. though, so be ready for a challenge.
The graphics are a little basic but it looks well enough to me. Nice physics though which is surprising for a Unity game. The music is not very memorable but fits the mood of the game, and I also liked the voice-over dialogue. It's cheesy but funny and suitably vulgar, and everyone has an Australian accent which feels like a bonus for Mad Max fans.

The only drawback is the game doesn't include the soundtrack or there's no option to buy it separately on the Steam page, though I'm sure with a quick Google search I can find a place to purchase it.  The game is definitely a "learn as you play it" experience where you learn quick and hard the things to do and not to do to try and guarantee your survival just a little bit further each time.  The trick seems to typically be picking the most optimal place to make landfall when you arrive at places you can dock at and scavenge for resources.  Once you realize what each type of place offers you can plan accordingly as you see the types of places to dock approaching, since making landfalll at each and every one of them is near impossible since some are VERY out of the way from one another, and when battling the strong river rapids it's not easy to move about.
These are all very early impressions of the game and have barely scraped the surface of the game, but I can already tell this is a game I'm going to constantly fall more and more in love with the deeper I dig into it.
